FOREWORD 1. Purpose. The Procurement Legal Service is intended to provide prompt information on current developments in Government contract law to legal personnel of the Army engaged in procurement activities. Editorial comment is always inclosed in brackets. It is distributed for information purposes only and may not be cited as legal authority. The interpretation of the matters digested represents the opinion of an individual specialist in procurement law and does not necessarily represent the opinion or view of any authority. 

2. Comments and Recommendations. Comments on matters published, recommendations with respect to material for future publications, and any other suggestions for improving the Procurement Legal Service are solicited and should be sent direct to the Commandant of the Judge 

Advocate General's School, Charlottesville, Virginia.

1. Prohibition of Unauthorized Payments Not Violated by Payment Under Total Costs Clause Even Though Unliquidated Progress Payments Already Exceed Fair Value of Work Accomplished on Undelivered Portion of Contract. A fixed-price Army contract with a small business concern contained a Total 

Costs Clause (identical to that in ASPR

E-510.1) authorizing progress payments up to 

100% of the incurred costs, provided that the contract price was not exceeded. It was proposed to make a payment to the contractor under the following circumstances: More than 

80% of the contract was completed. The unliquidated progress payments exceeded the fair value of the work accomplished on the undelivered portion of the contract. Even if the proposed payment were made, the total payments to the contractor would not exceed either the contract price or the amount the contractor actually expended. The contractor was in grave financial difficulties. It was estimated that if the proposed payment were made, the Government would receive delivery of $175,000 worth of completed items that might not otherwise be available. The USASSA and Signal Corps took the position that the proposed payment would not be a progress payment but an advance payment governed by the following statute:

No advance of public money shall be made in any case unless authorized by the appropriation concerned or other law. And in all cases of contracts for the performance of any service, or the delivery of articles of any description, for the use of the United States, payment shall not exceed the value of the service rendered, or of the articles delivered previously to such payment. 31 U.S.C. § 529. 

Opinion: The proposed payment would not come within 31 U.S.C. § 529. The Comptroller General has ruled that 31 U.S.C. § 529 does not prohibit progress payments if the amount of the payment has been earned by the contractor and the United States has received an equivalent in exchange. 1 Comp. Gen. 143 

(1921). Where progress payments are based on costs, as in this case, rather than on percentage or stage of completion, the value of the work and services rendered is measured in terms of incurred costs. That this is true is apparent from the contract clause. The drafters of that clause not only contemplated the possibility that unliquidated progress payments might exceed the fair value of the work performed on the undelivered portion of the contract, but also provided that in such instances the contracting officer may reduce or suspend progress payments. (ASPR E-510.1 (c)). Such action is discretionary. (ASPR E-524 through E-524.5).

If the conclusion of the Signal Corps and 

USASSA were correct, the contract provision like that in ASPR E-510.1 (c) (v) would be meaningless and misleading, ASPR E-524 and 

E-524.5 could mislead a contracting officer into an inadvertent statutory violation, and 31 U.S.C. § 529 would be violated whenever progress payments were made that resulted in unliquidated progress payments exceeding the fair value of the work accomplished on the un- AGO 9111A

ALLOWABLE COSTS 

delivered portion of the contract. In the instant case, if the proposed payment is made, neither the contract price nor the amount expended by the contractor will be exceeded. Accordingly, the amount actually earned by the contractor will not be exceeded. Moreover, since the contract provides that title to all property on which a progress payment is made shall vest in the Government when the payment is made, the Government will receive a benefit to justify making the proposed payment.

JAGT 1961/5934, 16 February 1961.

3. Under Cost-Reimbursement Contract a Contractor May Recover Unnecessary Costs Incurred As Result of Isolated Acts of Clerical 

Employees Involving Omission, Commission, or Both. The contractor seeks reimbursement for costs incurred through errors of its employees committed during the performance of two separate contracts. The contract involved in the first appeal was for production and delivery of 

F-102B aircraft having an estimated cost of $78,800,000 and a fixed fee of $4,728,000. During performance of the contract, a key number was left off of an advance bill of materials for aluminum sheets. The key number is a part of the processing system of the contractor and permits use of data processing machines. As the "key" was left off, the advance bill of materials had to be processed manually, wholly independent of the data processing machines. It was during manual processing that the contractor's computer clerk made an error in arithmetic; multiplying fifteen by four she reached a result of 600. Her mistake was perpetuated in a purchase order to a subcontractor in June. The need for the materials ceased to exist shortly thereafter. However, either the notice signalling the end of the need for the aluminum or else the request to terminate the subcontract was misplaced; in any event the termination was not initiated until September, after the subcontractor had completed performance. The error of arithmetic also was not discovered until after the subcontractor had completed performance. The contracting officer denied recovery on the ground that the costs claimed were unreasonable and therefore un allowable under Part 2, Section XV of ASPR. 

The record shows both that the Government is impressed by the contractor's system, which is concededly overall a good procedure, and that the mistake and termination delay attending the subcontractor in question were exceptional occurrences under the system. Further, the contractor was not negligent in hiring or retaining negligent employees. Once employees were hired the contractor took reasonable measures to insure that they were fully trained to discharge duties within the ambit of their responsibilities.

The contract involved in the second appeal was a "call" type CPFF contract for items of kits and spare parts for B-36 aircraft. The contract included a provision for termination for the convenience of the Government which required the contractor, upon receiving notice of such a termination, to "terminate all orders and subcontracts to the extent that they relate to the performance of work terminated . . . ." 

Pursuant to a "call" issued in September 1954, the contractor undertook to fulfill the Government's requirements and in so doing entered into a subcontract with Bendix Corporation for actuator assemblies. Subsequently the Government partially terminated the subject matter of the "call." Notice of partial termination was received by the contractor on 27 June 1955, at which time it immediately instituted action to process, in accordance with its established procedure, a partial termination of the subcontract with Bendix. Its procedure involved two groups, the Material Release Group and the Termination Group, as a precaution against error. In this case the Material Release Group lost or misplaced its copy of the termination AGO 9111A

ALLOWABLE COSTS—Continued sales order and therefore never issued a termi nation authorization to the Termination Group or to the buyer. At the same time the Termination Group employee, presumably because of an extraordinary workload, was dilatory in making inquiry, with the result that the discrepancy was not uncovered until 9 September 1955. By reason of the large number of units involved, routine processing consumed an additional forty days' time and the subcontract was not terminated until 20 October 1955. The contracting officer denied recovery of all costs incurred after the time the subcontract would ordinarily have been terminated. He determined that reimbursement of such costs would be improper under the cost principles of Part 2, Section XV of ASPR and in the alternative that the contractor failed to comply with contractual provisions regarding subcontract termination.

Concededly all of the employees involved in the events of this appeal, including the Termination Group employee, had been given reasonably sufficient prior training. Further, of 18,284 subcontracts involving termination action by the contractor during the years 1954-1958 inclusive and generating settlements aggregating $3,900,000, only the costs here in question have been subjected to disallowance.

Held, the appeals are sustained and the contractor is to be reimbursed for its costs. The contractor's contractual duties included (1) employment and utilization of competent personnel; (2) nonretention of careless personnel; and (3) design and utilization of purchasing and termination procedures reasonably calculated to procure materials and to cancel subcontracts without incurrence of disproportionate administrative expense. With respect to the first two contractual duties, it is unnecessary to reach the questions of negligent hiring and negligent retention because both of these concepts presuppose negligent employees, and a single error of omission or commission of an employee, whose performance over a relatively long period is without blemish, does not make for a negligent employee. The record likewise does not support a finding that the contractor disregarded contractual duty insofar as its purchasing and termination systems were concerned. The standard for application is the contractual criterion of reasonableness. This criterion required the contractor to exercise no higher standard of care than that expected to be exercised by a reasonably prudent businessman under like circumstances. The contractor's systems were not required to be so full of checks and balances in anticipation of every conceivable human error and omission that perfection was attained but costs of operation were ignored. Nor is hindsight the test to establish that the contractor was previously derelict in its contractual obligation.

As to the contractor's obligation under its Termination clause "to proceed immediately" with the termination of the subcontract, its management was required to feed the Bendix subcontract into its termination system without delay. It is not contended that the contractor's management was remiss in doing so. 

Since no delay intervened between receipt of the Government's termination notice and the contractor's commencement of termination processing, the partial bar to recovery implicit in the clause has no application here. 

General Dynamics Corp., ASBCA Nos. 5166, 

5271, 29 February 1960, 60–1 BCA 2556.

8. Price Escalation for Steel Price Increase

Allowed on Units on Which Contractor Was Delinquent When Steel Price Increase Became 

Effective. The appellant had an Army fixedprice supply contract that contained, besides the standard Default and Changes Clauses, an escalation clause providing in part: 

a. The contractor represents and warrants that the prices set forth in this contract do not include any contingency allowance to cover possible increase[s] in the cost the contractor is required to pay for steel. 

b. In the event that, at any time during the performance of this contract, the contractor is required to pay prices for steel in excess of, or less than those upon which the unit price for supplies to be delivered under this contract are based, the unit price set forth in this contract may be revised upward or downward . . . with respect to the unit completed subsequent to the effective date of any such increase by an amount equivalent to the increase or decrease in cost per uncompleted unit occasioned by the increase or decrease in [the] price of steel.

For various reasons, including a strike and the issuance of change orders, the appellant was unable to meet the contract delivery schedule. 

He was granted an extension, with 11 June 

1954 as the date for final delivery. However, he made, and the Government accepted, deliveries until 21 April 1955, by which time the contract quantity had been delivered. The contractor claimed entitlement to an escalation of the price for a steel price increase that had be come effective in JULY 1954. The contracting officer denied the claim. When an appeal was taken to the ASBCA, the Board held that the contractor was entitled to an additional extension of the delivery schedule, so that the appellant had been delinquent as to only some of the units delivered after the July 1954 steel price increase. The Board then dealt with the question whether the appellant was entitled to price escalation on those units.

Held, the appellant may recover. The contract should not be interpreted as limiting escalation to units on which the appellant was not delinquent at the time of a steel price increase.

The escalation clause provides for escalation for any increase in the price of steel the appellant was required to pay "at any time during performance." The purpose of that clause, as is apparent from paragraph a, was to secure for the Government a price not padded with an allowance for the risk of a steel price increase.

See G. A. Gray Co., ASBCA No. 3122 (3 Dec 

1956), 56-2 BCA 1087. It is doubtful whether that purpose would be achieved if the clause were interpreted as barring escalation for delinquent deliveries, particularly those delinquent, as was true here, because of unexpected production difficulties occurring without any fault or negligence on the contractor's part.

There is no general rule disallowing all performance costs that would not have been incurred but for the contractor's fault or negligence. No instance has been found where an equitable adjustment under a changes clause or a cost under a price redetermination clause was denied because the claim would not have resulted but for the contractor's unexcused delay in performing. Moreover, under a cost-plusfixed-fee contract, a cost of performance will not be disallowed on the ground that it was incurred as a result of the negligence of the contractor's employees, unless the cost was produced by "the contractor's own fault or folly" or "careless conduct of the work or other disregard of his contractual duties." 21 Comp. 

Gen. 149, 151 (1941). There is no allegation AGO 9111A

APPROPRIATIONS 

that the appellant's delinquency was due to the causes thus described. 

The Comptroller General has repeatedly held that delinquent deliveries may not be the basis for a price increase under an escalation clause. 

See, e.g., Ms. Comp. Gen B-144907 (17 Mar 

1961); 38 Comp. Gen. 826 (1959). The Comptroller General stated in 34 Comp. Gen. 565, 

The General Accounting Office has consistently refused to allow price increases in cases such as this except where the delay was caused by the Government or otherwise was excusable under the terms of the contract. The basis for our position in this regard is that we perceive no valid reason, in law or equity, for requiring the Government to assume the burden of price increases occurring after the final date delivery would have been made but for the contractor's own fault or negligence.

To require the Government to pay such price increases would permit the contractor to benefit from his own delinquency and would penalize the Government for minimizing the contractor's loss which would have resulted had the contract been terminated because of the contractor's default. 

Furthermore, it is well settled that a waiver of the right to rescind or terminate a contract by accept-. ance of late delivery does not include a waiver of the right to damages resulting from the delay. . . .

In our view, it would be entirely inconsistent to charge the Government with additional costs arising as a result of the same delay which would have given the Government the right to recover damages.

It may be argued that the instant case is distinguishable from the Comptroller General's holdings because of the language of the appellant's escalation clause. First, that clause provides for downward as well as upward escalation. To interpret the clause as inapplicable to late deliveries would deprive the Government of the right to claim a downward adjustment for a decrease in the steel price. Second, the escalation clause in the appellant's contract, unlike the clause discussed in the quotation from the Comptroller General, would not permit the contractor to benefit by his own delinquency. The clause would only permit the appellant to achieve the position he would have held had he completed the contract before the steel price increase. However, a review of the

Comptroller General's decisions indicates that the result he reached was not based on the wording of the escalation clauses involved. It is unlikely that the Comptroller General would reach any different result in interpreting the form of escalation clause used in the appellant's contract. Nevertheless, in no case has the Comptroller General denied escalation where the contractor performed with skill and diligence and the delay in delivery was not caused wholly or partly by any fault or negligence of the contractor. Since those criteria are met here, the appellant may recover.

National U.S. Radiator Corp., ASBCA No. 

3506, 31 October 1961, 61-2 BCA 3192. [Note: Although finding that the appellant performed with skill and diligence and that his delinquency was not due to his fault or negligence, the Board warned that nothing in the opinion should be interpreted as a holding whether the production difficulties were excusable causes of delay under the default clause.] 9. APPROPRIATIONS 1. Congress Must Specifically Authorize Use of Appropriated Funds To Improve State- Owned Access Road to Federal Project. The 

Assistant Secretary of the Army for Manpower, Personnel and Reserve Forces requested an opinion as to whether Federal funds could be used to improve a West Virginia secondary route leading to a Federal lock and dam on the Monongahela River. Under the proposed contract, West Virginia, using Federal funds, would improve the road to provide all weather access for Federal employees at one-half the estimated cost to the Government of building a new road.

Opinion: The federal funds are not available. 

The appropriation sought to be charged is con tained in the Public Works Appropriation Act 

AGO 9111A

APPROPRIATIONS-Continued of 1960, 73 Stat. 491, which appropriates funds "For the prosecution of river and harbor, flood control, shore protection, and related projects authorized by law. . ." Construction of the lock and dam involved in this case was authorized by Section 101 of the River and Harbor Act of 1950, 64 Stat. 163. This act and Senate Docu ment No. 100, 81st Congress, however, do not authorize the construction or improvement of access roads outside of the project. Thus, the proposed improvement is not authorized by either the appropriation concerned or substantive law and cannot be approved. See 2 Comp.

Gen. 308 (1922); 6 Comp. Gen. 97 and 353 

(1926). Specific congressional authority is required before federal funds can be used for public improvements on either federal or state property. See 41 U.S.C. 12; 32 Comp. Gen. 296 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-141144, 18 November 1959, 39 Comp. Gen. 388. 

2. Prohibition Against Use of Appropriated Funds To Expedite Construction Is Inapplicable Where Contractor Is Not Required To Perform in Less Time Than Originally Stipulated in Con tract. In October 1956, the contractor entered into a $19,400,000 contract for the construction of the Air Force Academy academic complex. 

The contract contained SF 23A (March 1953) 

and was to be completed by 29 July 1958. Contract performance was delayed at various stages by strikes, Government change orders. and the nonavailability of essential materials. 

The Air Force, however, refused to extend the work schedule and insisted that the original completion date be met. The contractor was ordered to work overtime and employ more personnel and threatened with a termination for default. When the contract was finally completed, the contractor requested an equitable adjustment in contract price as compensation for extra costs caused by a 243 day delay. This was denied by the contracting officer. On appeal, the Government denied that the delay was excusable but, in the alternative, argued that the claim was barred by the prohibition against using appropriated funds to expedite contract performance. 

Held, the appeal is sustained. The causes of the 243 day delay were unforeseeable and not within the control or due to the fault or negli gence of the contractor. SF 23A, clause 5(c). 

Consequently, the Government improperly refused to grant a time extension and forced the contractor to accelerate completion and to incur excess costs. These costs may be reimbursed under the Changes Clause by an equitable adjustment in contract price. See Standard Store

Equipment Co., Inc., ASBCA No. 4348 (28 Aug. 1958), 58-2 BCA 1902. The Government argues, however, that the change expedited performance and that the additional costs incurred may not be reimbursed out of appropriated funds. Section 303, Appropriation Act of 1956 

"None of the funds appropriated in this chapter shall be expended for additional costs involved in expediting construction unless the Secretary of Defense certifies such costs to be necessary to protect the national interest and establishes a reasonable completion date for each project . 

70 Stat. 

678,681. 

This prohibition, however, applies only where a contractor is required to perform a contract in less time than originally required, Spera Con struction Co., ASBCA No. 3063 (4 Oct 1956), not where a contractor is required to perform within an original time schedule which has not been properly extended to provide for excusable delay. The case is remanded to the parties for negotiation of the equitable adjustment amount. 

Farnsworth & Chambers Company, ASBCA 

Nos. 4945, 4978 & 5129, 24 November 1959, 59

BCA 2443.

4. Litigation by Department of Justice for Other Agencies-Administrative Agency Whose Activities Result in a Suit Against the United States and Which Alone Is in a Position To Review Reports and Furnish Material Required by the Department of Justice To Defend the Suit, Has a Duty To Review or Furnish Such Material Without Reimbursement by the De partment of Justice.

As a result of flood dam- 10 AGO 9111A

APPROPRIATIONS-Continued age caused by breaks in levees constructed by the Corps of Engineers, 20 actions were filed against the United States involving 310 plaintiffs and approximately $13,169,000 in claimed damages. The complaints filed allege that the 

United States is liable because the Corps of Engineers negligently planned, designed, constructed and maintained the levees which failed. 

The Department of Justice is conducting the defense of the suits. In order to facilitate the defense, the Corps of Engineers prepared digests and engineering studies and reviewed State-prepared data for the Department of Justice. The Corps of Engineers seeks reimbursement from the Department of Justice for the costs of rendering the services. 

Held, the Corps of Engineers is not entitled to reimbursement by the Department of Justice for the expense of preparing the digests and engineering studies and reviewing the data. 

The Attorney General has the duty, as chief law officer of the Government, to institute, prosecute and defend actions on behalf of the United States in matters involving court proceedings, and to defray the necessary expenses incident thereto from the appropriations of the Department of Justice rather than from appropriations of the administrative office which may be involved in the proceedings. See Ms. Comp. 

Gen. B-45799, 5 December 1944; Ms. Comp. 

Gen. B-122671, 28 March 1955; 15 Comp. Gen. 

81 (1935); 18 id. 592 (1939); 19 id. 551 (1939); 

32 id. 118 (1952); and 38 id. 343 (1958). However, none of the cited opinions involved services performed by an administrative agency based on knowledge, information, data and experience possessed by it and its personnel. In the instant opinion, outside engineers could not perform the services in question independently of the Corps of Engineers and only the Corps possesses (in its files or through its personnel) the data and information necessary to make the special studies and review the State-prepared data.

The Corps of Engineers has a duty to review the reports and furnish the required material to the Department of Justice without reimbursement. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-140600, 17 March 1960, 39 Comp. Gen. 643. 

[Note: The opinion rests on the fact that the 

Department of Justice could not have purchased the services from a private contractor because the required information was only available to engineer personnel. If the services required were merely surveys of the damaged levees to ascertain the locations and nature of the breaches causing the floods, presumably a private engineering firm could have done the job and the Department of Justice, as the Department of the chief law officer of the Government, would have been responsible for obtaining and paying for such services. See 38 Comp. Gen. 

343 (1958). If the Department of Justice were then to obtain such services from the Corps of Engineers instead of from a private firm, the reasoning of the instant opinion together with that of 38 Comp. Gen. 343, supra, and 32 Comp.

Gen. 118 (1952) indicate that the Corps of 

Engineers would then be entitled to reimbursement.] 

5. Fiscal Year 1960 Funds Not Obligated

Where Attempted Acceptance Of Low Bid in Fiscal Year 1960 Was Ineffective and Binding Contract Did Not Result Until Fiscal Year 1961. 

On 29 June 1960, a letter notice of award to bidder A was signed by the contracting officer. 

On 30 June 1960, the notice of award was placed in the mail, but the envelope was inadvertently addressed to bidder B. On the following day, 1

July 1960, bidder A was notified by telephone that notice of award had been mailed. On the same day, bidder B returned the notice of award to the contracting officer, thereby bringing the mailing error to his attention. Bidder A was then advised that the notice of award had not in fact been sent him. The Comptroller General was asked to decide whether Fiscal Year 1960 funds were obligated by the intended award or could be so obligated if a contract with bidder A is now entered into. 

Held, Fiscal Year 1960 funds were not obligated by the intended award nor can they be obligated if a contract is now entered into with Bidder A. In order to obligate fiscal year funds, a binding agreement in writing between the parties is required to be entered into in the same fiscal year. 31 U.S.C. § 200. A binding agreement requires an offer and acceptance. 

In order for the Government's acceptance to be AGO 9111A 11

APPROPRIATIONS—Continued effective by mailing, it must be contained in an envelope properly stamped, addressed and posted for transmission. 17 C.J.S. Contracts 

§ 52. Since the notice of award to bidder A was not properly addressed, it did not constitute an effective acceptance. Thus, there was no binding agreement in Fiscal Year 1960 which obligated Fiscal Year 1960 funds. If a contract is now awarded to bidder A, Fiscal Year 1961 funds will be obligated. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143514, 1 September 1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 147. 

6. Price of Necessary Air-Conditioners Is Chargeable Against Statutory Limitation on Vehicle Purchase Cost. The Secretary of Health, 

Education, and Welfare asked whether airconditioners, could be purchased for two station wagons if the cost of the conditioners, together with the original cost of the vehicles would exceed $1,950. That sum is the maximum prescribed for station wagons purchased by all Government departments. 5 U.S.C. 78 (c) 

(1) and § 201 of the General Government Matters Appropriation Act, 1960, 73 Stat. 165. The vehicles had been bought without air-conditioners because station wagons with such units would have cost more than $1,950. The vehicles were used primarily to carry perishable laboratory samples and sensitive scientific instruments which needed in transit protection against high temperatures and humidity characteristic of the area. Cooling by ice had been rejected because it failed to lower the humidity. 

The Secretary said he sought the ruling because of doubt as to the application of the statute as interpreted in earlier Comptroller General decisions, particularly the one at 36 Comp. Gen. 

725. That opinion ruled that items such as heavy-duty batteries were chargeable against the statutory limitation because they were essential to the efficient operation of the vehicle even though they only incidentally affected the passengers' convenience. 

Held, the air-conditioners may not be purchased. The statute's limit is on the cost of a vehicle completely equipped for operation, without regard to whether passengers or materials will be transported. Only with air-conditioners would the station wagons be fully equipped for operation. Furthermore, the air-conditioners would be permanent fixtures, would permanently enhance the vehicles' value, and would affect the passengers' convenience. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143891, 7 October 1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 205. 

7. In Single Court Case Where Total of Judg ments Exceeds $100,000, Individual Judgments 

Not Exceeding $100,000 Each Are Payable

From Appropriation for Payment of Judgments 

"Not in Excess of $100,000 in Any One Case." 

In a tort action against the United States, a widow and several other parties were awarded judgments by the United States district court. 

The widow's judgment was for $122,150; each judgment awarded the other parties was for less than $100,000. Section 1302 of the Sup plemental Appropriation Act of 1957, 70 Stat. 

694, 31 U.S.C. § 724a (1958), appropriated funds for paying final judgments, "not in excess of $100,000 in any one case," rendered against the United States by the Court of Claims or a federal district court. The Treasury 

Department requested the Comptroller General to decide whether the permanent appropriation of 31 U.S.C. § 724a could be used to pay the individual judgments under $100,000.

Held, all the judgments except that awarded the widow may be paid from the appropriation in section 1302. Decision of the question involves the meaning that Congress intended should be given to the limitation, "not in excess of $100,000 in any one case." In the instant case each plaintiff had a cause of action against the United States and could have sued separately. Judgments for $100,000 or less obtained in separate suits clearly would be payable from the appropriation of section 1302. Since the joining of all the parties in one suit is merely for the convenience of the court and the litigants, the availability of the appropriation should not be affected. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144395, 17 November 

1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 307. 

8. Recovery of Silver From Chemical Solution Is Not a Purpose for Which the Supply Fund for the Veterans Administration May Be Used-Absent Express Statutory Authority for Crediting a Fund or Appropriation With Proceeds From the Sale of Scrap or Surplus Property, Such Proceeds Should Be Deposited 

12 AGO 9111A

APPROPRIATIONS-Continued 

in the Treasury as Miscellaneous Receipts. 

X-ray film contains a small quantity of pure silver. When this film is exposed and developed at least 50 percent of the silver is washed from the film into the chemical fixing solution. Many 

Veterans Administration field stations have no provision for silver recovery and many that do are inefficient.

The Administrator, Veterans Administration, requested the Comptroller General's approval of a plan to use the "Supply Fund, Veterans 

Administration" (established by the Second Independent Offices Appropriation Act, 1954, 67 Stat.

193, and reenacted as section 1711 of the Veterans Benefits Act of 1957, 71 Stat. 

142) to finance and operate an efficient centralized silver reclamation program, and to reimburse the fund from the proceeds derived from the sale of the silver.

Held, the supply fund may not be used to finance the silver recovery program, nor may the proceeds of that program be credited to the fund. The proposal appears predicated on the assumption that the authority for the establishment and capitalization of the supply fund, and operation and maintenance of a supply system is sufficiently broad to authorize activities in the nature of silver reclamation and that personal property purchased with funds appropriated for payment of salaries and expenses, and determined to be no longer required for the purposes for which it was purchased or the use to which it was applied may be reverted as supply fund property simply because it was initially purchased or acquired by the fund. 

Congress in providing a revolving fund type of financing for the operation and maintenance of a supply system for the Veterans Administration qualified the use thereof on the basis of adjustment between the supply fund and the consuming appropriations for the cost of services, equipment and supplies furnished the appropriations otherwise available for payment of such expenses. It is apparent, therefore, that application of the supply fund must be limited to the extent that expenditures therefrom are reasonably connected with and incident to the accomplishment of the purposes for which specific appropriations are made to the Veterans Administration. 

The appropriations made to the Veterans Administration for the purchase of X-ray film and the chemical developing solution are provided for under the titles "Inpatient Care" and "Outpatient Care" which are for certain specific purposes not in any way connected with the recovery of silver. Since the Congress has seen fit to limit application of the supply fund, no legal basis exists for extending its use to an industrial activity unrelated to the supply and service activities which the supply fund was designed to serve.

Moreover, while under the law property no longer required for the purposes of the appropriation from which it was purchased may be reassigned within the agency for purposes of effective utilization, it does not follow that property so acquired by an appropriation through the supply fund and subsequently converted into cash may be retained and used by the fund. The effect of such action is to supplement the working capital of the fund in a manner not authorized by Congress. Proceeds from the sale of such property determined to be excess or surplus are for deposit into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts less, of course, the items of expense which pertain directly to the sale of the property. 40 U.S.C. 

§ 485. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-116651, 13 December 

1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 356. (1960) [Note: In support of its proposal to use the supply fund to finance the silver recovery program, the Veterans Administration pointed out that it had followed the practice of gathering and disposing of surplus gold from its dental activities. Proceeds from the sale of the gold were credited to the supply fund. No extensive operation was involved in the gathering of gold scrap. The Comptroller General in the instant opinion noted that he had never passed on the propriety of the financing of the gold recovery program and the crediting of the supply fund with the proceeds of that program. He then stated that even if the service function of accumulating the scrap gold and the disposition thereof is a proper supply fund activity, the performance of the service does not operate to convert the scrap gold or the proceeds therefrom into supply fund property. 9. Excess Costs Recovered From Defaulted Contractor or His Surety Need Not Be Con sidered in Computing the Costs of Capehart 

Housing Work To Determine Whether the Statutory Ceiling Is Exceeded. Section 1748i of Title 12, U.S.C., authorizes appropriation of funds for acquiring land, installing outside utilities and preparing the site for Capehart housing projects, but imposes a maximum expenditure per housing unit. The Air Force awarded a contract that, after it was modified, was $10,577.42 less than the $265,500 statutory maximum. When the contract was later terminated for the contractor's default, the contractor had been paid $175,561.36, so only $89,938.64 remained available for reprocurement before the statutory maximum was reached. After the surety of the defaulted contractor declined to complete the work, the 

Air Force approved a reprocurement contract for $122,120. Since that amount, together with the amount paid the original contractor, would exceed the statutory maximum, the reprocurement was divided between the on-site and the off-site work. The reprocurement contract was to perform the on-site work for $81,220 and gave the Air Force an option for having the off-site work completed for $40,900. The Air 

Force hoped to finance the off-site work from money from the surety. However, the surety insisted that all balances remaining under the defaulted contract be used before a demand for any deficiency was made. The Air Force, concerned because none of the housing project could be occupied until the off-site work was completed, asked the Comptroller General whether appropriated funds could be used for that work.

Held, there is no objection to exercising the option if there is no doubt the surety is liable for at least all costs in excess of the statutory maximum. The GAO generally has viewed a repurchase contract as constituting, in effect, a purchase against the defaulting contractor and as being properly chargeable to the appropriation obligated by the defaulted contract. On the basis of the present record there is no authority whereby any excess costs recovered from the defaulted contractor or its surety may be used to reimburse the appropriation originally obligated. See, in this connection, 27 

Comp. Gen. 117 (1947) for a discussion of the general rule that amounts recovered from defaulted contractors are to be deposited in the 

Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. However, excess costs recovered from the defaulted contractor or his surety need not be considered in computing the maximum costs that may be in curred under 12 U.S.C. § 1748i. An Air Force 

Judge Advocate has determined that the surety is liable for approximately $127,000, an amount greater than the sum by which the repurchase contract would exceed the statutory maximum if the option is exercised. The record indicates that the defaulting contractor has appealed the default termination to the ASBCA. While the record provided shows that the contractor was clearly in default, the appeal papers were not enclosed. However, if it is the best judgment of the Air Force that the surety is liable for at least all costs above the statutory maximum, there will be no objection to an exercise of the option. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145566, 20 April, 1961, 40 Comp. Gen. 590. 

10. Appropriated Funds. May Be Used To Obtain Burglar Alarm Services for Post Ex changes Only in Exceptional Circumstances.

According to 10 U.S.C. § 4779 (c) (1948): 

No money appropriated for the support of the Army may be spent for . . Army Exchanges. 

However, this does not prevent Army Exchanges from using public buildings... that, in the opinion of the office or officer designated by the Secretary, are not needed for other purposes. 

The Judge Advocate General was asked about the propriety of using appropriated funds for the "service" of having a contractor install and maintain his own burglar alarms in a post exchange. The burglar alarms apparently could be installed by small hand tools, such as a hammer and screwdriver. That appropriated funds may be so used is indicated in "Instruc tions for the Administration of A&AFES Capital Expenditure Program," January 1962, transmitted to all major commands by TAG 

letter AGAM-P (M) 123 (30 Jan 1962) 

14 AGO 9111A

APPROPRIATIONS-Continued AAFBD, Subj: A&AFES Capital Expenditure Program (Reports Control Symbol AAFES-30), 

14 February 1962. Paragraph 10 of the "Instructions" state:

In accordance with paragraph 12b (3), AR 60-10/ AFR 147-7A, burglar alarm systems required to protect exchange facilities are an appropriated fund responsibility. The use of exchange funds for burglar alarm systems is not authorized. 

AR 60-10, paragraph 126 says:

When so directed, the installation commander is charged with the following functions: (3) Providing necessary buildings and facilities and adequate security, fire protection, and sanitation facilities. 

Held, only in exceptional circumstances may appropriated funds be used for post exchange burglar alarm systems. Traditionally the security, fire protection, and sanitation facilities furnished to exchanges are those available within the normal capabilities of the installation and furnished to comparable activities at the installation. If activities such as the commissary, finance office, or post laundry are furnished security by a typical military guard system, the security furnished a post exchange should be commensurate; appropriated funds should not be used to furnish security greater than that standard.

In directing an installation commander to provide security for a post exchange, a major commander should qualify his directive so as to preclude the use of appropriated funds for a burglar alarm system or device if it is of a type proscribed by 5 U.S.C. § 53 (1958) [prohibiting contracts with a detective agency] and unless (i) the device or system is part of an authorized security plan for the installation and extends to other buildings and activities, or (ii) the use of the device or system results in a demonstrable saving in appropriated funds and use of a less expensive security measure is not feasible.

It is understood that DCSLOG is planning to provide guidance on this matter in an Army 

Procurement Circular, DA Cir 715-2-series. 

JAGT 1962/6139, 8 May 1962. 

11. Comptroller General Disapproves Use of 

Operational and Maintenance Funds for $318,- 

397 Conversion of Heating Plant From Coal to 

Gas. The Army was considering converting part of a fort's heating plant from coal to gas. 

One plan was to have the gas company install, retain title to, and maintain the pipeline and metering station. The company would impose a minimum charge that would be far below the Government's consumption requirements. As consideration for the furnishing of the pipeline and metering facilities, the Government would promise to pay a termination charge for terminating service within ten years. The termination charge would be based on the initial cost of the facilities, $595,000, subject to annual deductions for depreciation and salvage value, and at the end of the ninth year the termination charge would be about 65% of cost. The company would agree to write off the entire cost at the end of the tenth year. The Government would convert the heating plant from coal to gas, and the estimated cost of $318,397 would be paid from funds appropriated for operation and maintenance. The second plan differed from the first only in that the gas company would pay for the conversion to gas, with the cost added to the termination charge and reduced at 5% yearly. Like the cost of the pipeline and metering facilities, the cost would presumably also be reflected in the rate charged for gas. The converted facilities would be 

Government property. 

The Army asked the Comptroller General two questions. The first was whether about $318,- 

397 of Army operation and maintenance funds under the 1962 DOD Appropriation Act could legally be spent for the conversion in view of the following restriction in that act: 

637. Funds appropriated in this Act for maintenance and repair of facilities and installations shall not be available for acquisition of new facilities, or alteration, expansion, extension or addition of existing facilities, as defined in Department of 

Defense Directive 7040.2, dated January 18, 1961, in excess of $25,000: Provided, That the Secretary of Defense may amend or change the said directive during the current fiscal year, consistent with the purpose of this section. 

The directive referred to in Section 637 defined alterations as: 

The work required to adjust interior arrangements, on-base location, or other physical characteristics AGO 9111A 15

APPROPRIATIONS-Continued of an existing facility so that it may be more effectively adapted to or utilized for its designated purpose. Additions, expansions and extensions are not included in alterations. 

The second question was whether there was any legal objection to a contract founded on annual operation and maintenance appropriations with provisions binding the gas company to convert the heating plant at no cost (except as reflected in the service rates) subject to payment of the termination charge as described above. 

Held, the first question is answered in the negative and the second in the affirmative. As to the first, in fiscal year 1957 and for several years before the Department of Defense appropriation acts made Army operation and maintenance funds available for "alteration, extension and repair of structures and property." However, one of the general provisions of the acts provided that not more than $200,000 of either operation and maintenance or construction funds could be used for each project of converting or extending existing structures. No specific mention was made of alterations. When that general provision was enacted into permanent law in 70 Stat. 1016 (1958), 10 U.S.C. § 2674 (1958), the use of operation and maintenance funds for the specified purposes was limited to projects not costing more than $25,- 000. Legislative history indicates the change was made to check the use of operation and maintenance funds for projects that should be classified as construction. A similar purpose lay behind the subsequent deletion from the appropriation acts of the specific provision for using operation and maintenance funds for "alteration, extension and repair of structures and property." The phrase "repair of facilities" was substituted. Thus, while 10 U.S.C. § 2674 makes no specific reference to "alterations," Congress apparently considered that term as included in the other terms used there.

In January 1961 the General Accounting 

Office submitted to Congress a report on a review of the programming and financing of selected construction activities at several military installations. The report concluded that, notwithstanding the existing laws, operation and maintenance funds exceeding $25,000 were being used to finance various types of construction work. As a result of the report the House 

Committee on Appropriations inserted in the 

Department of Defense Appropriation bill for fiscal year 1962 the following: 

Funds appropriated in this Act for maintenance and repair of facilities and installations shall not be available for repair and alteration projects, as defined in Department of Defense Directive 7040.2, dated January 18, 1961, in excess of $25,000: 

Provided, That the Secretary of Defense may amend or change the said directive during the current fiscal year, consistent with the purpose of this section.

The House approved that section, but the Senate Committee on Appropriations agreed with the view of Defense Department officials that the section would prohibit accomplishment of many necessary repairs and alterations. The 

Committee deleted "repair and alteration projects" and substituted "acquisition of new facilities or expansion, extension or addition of existing facilities." Conference action on the bill resulted in restoration of the word "alterations."

In view of this legislative history, and of the intent of the appropriations committees of both houses of Congress that DOD Directive 7040.2 be strictly enforced, there can be no question but that Congress intended that work like the conversion of the heating plant should be handled as construction for purposes of authorization and appropriations. appropriations. Moreover, the construction work is of such scope as to be an "alteration of structures and property" as that phrase was used in earlier annual appropriation acts. The use of operation and maintenance funds for such purposes is presently limited to projects costing not more than $25,000. Thus, even if the conversion work were not covered by the term "alterations" as defined in DOD 

Directive 7040.2, or even if Section 637 had not been enacted, operation and maintenance funds could not be used.

With respect to the second question asked, the Army has stated that the work is suitable for competitive bidding and goes beyond the requirements of the usual utility procurement and connection line procedures. If the proposed procedure were approved, there would be almost no limit to which it could be carried. It violates the formal advertising requirements as well as Section 637. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-147843, 5 February 1962.

12. The Judge Advocate General Analyzes Authority To Use O&M Funds To Construct Clothesline Poles in Capehart Housing Areas 

After Option To Add Those Posts to Original 

Project Was Not Exercised and the Project Was Completed. The specifications for Cape hart housing in five mortgage areas included as an optional additive alternate a portion on clothesline posts. The contracting officer exercised the option as to only one area. At the closing of the mortgages, the project cost was $148,919 below the statutory limitation. The 

Office of the Judge Advocate General was asked about a proposal to use $16,736 of O&M funds for the installation of clothesline posts for the areas on which the additive alternate option had not been exercised.

Held, the proposal is concurred in, subject to the following: The rationale offered to support the proposed expenditure and used in precedents in the file is that because the proposed work was intended but not accomplished as part of the original project, the work is not a new project designed to evade statutory limitations but may be financed with O&M funds if a finding of urgency is made. This rationale is dangerous because its literal application to many situations would violate 10 U.S.C. § 2674 (imposing restrictions on minor construction), P.L. 87-577, § 536 (restricting use of O&M funds for acquisition of new facilities or alteration, expansion, extension or addition of existing facilities), statutes imposing space and other limits, and numerous regulations, particularly those dealing with incremental construction (AR 415-35, par. 6), improvements to newly constructed facilities (AR 415-35, par. 

6d), limits on the funded costs of projects (AR 

420-10, par. 7), and funding of Capehart

Housing (DOD Instruction 4270.21, § VI.21). 

Because installing the posts is neither maintenance nor repair as defined in DOD Directive 

7040.2, there is no authority inherent in the

O&M appropriation to use O&M funds, and such authority must be sought elsewhere. The work consists of installing appurtenances or adding an improvement to family housing. Accordingly, sufficient statutory authority may be provided by 10 U.S.C. § 2674: 

(a) . . . [T]he Secretary of a military department may acquire, construct, convert, extend, and install, at military installations and facilities, urgently needed public works not otherwise authorized by law, including the preparation of sites and the furnishing of appurtenances, utilities and equipment, but excluding the construction of family quarters. (c) Not more than one allotment may be made for any project authorized under this section. (e) Appropriation available for military construction may be used for the purposes of this section. 

In addition the Secretary concerned may spend, from appropriations available for maintenance and operations, amounts necessary for any project costing not more than $25,000 that is authorized under this section. 

Of course, this statute may be used only if the work is urgently needed and only one allotment will be used. The prohibition in paragraph (a) against "construction of family quarters" prohibits adding to the inventory of family quarters by new construction of one or more sets of quarters but does not prohibit the conversion of, extension of, or installation of appurtenances in family housing. 

However, subparagraphs a and b of Section 

VI.21 of DOD Instruction 4270.21 require that a fully adequate housing project be provided from the construction funds specifically designated for the project. In this case, those funds would be from the mortgages. Those subparagraphs also preclude the unreimbursed use of other than the original project funds. Moreover, subparagraph prohibits additional improvements within three years of total beneficial occupancy. Accordingly, approval of the proposed work involves a deviation from the 

DOD Instruction. Department of the Army ap proval should be granted only after coordination with DOD. If Department of the Army approval is granted, notification of it should: (a) be subject both to proper classification of the work as a single project and to compliance with AR 415-35, para. 5d; (b) omit any reference to the rationale offered to support the expenditure and discussed above; (c) omit any reference to the proposed work as the correction of a deficiency. The proposed work is not to correct a deficiency, since the posts were an optional additive item for which the option was not exercised.

JAGT 1962/6701, 13 September 1962.

ARBITRATION 1. Dispute Arising Under Government Con tract May Not Be Submitted to Arbitration. 

The Corps of Engineers requested an opinion as to the legality of submitting a contract dispute to arbitration.

Opinion: In the absence of specific statutory authority, the Department of the Army is without authority to settle a claim for unliquidated damages arising out of a breach of contract by submitting or agreeing to submit such claim to arbitration. 32 Comp. Gen. 333 (1953). Since the head of an executive department has no authority to settle claims for unliquidated damages, such authority cannot be conferred by the contract upon arbitrators. 33 Op. Atty. 

Gen. 354 (1922). Arbitration is further objectionable since it would violate the statutory provision that no Government contract shall contain a provision making the decision of an administrative official final on a question of law. 41 U.S.C. § 322 (1958). See JAGR 

1956/7292.

Board's Rules Contemplate Only One Re consideration, but a Reconsideration Will Be

Considered To Be the Original Decision on a 

Claim on Which Proof Was First Presented at the Reconsideration. The contractor's appeal to the ASBCA involved two claims. Both parties presented proof on the first claim. A mere offer of proof by the Government on the second claim was considered sufficient by the Board so the Government presented no proof. The appeal was sustained as to the first claim and denied as to the second. The decision was reconsidered and proof was presented on both claims. The appeal was then sustained as to both claims. 

The Government moved for reconsideration. 

The contractor declined to be heard, asserting that multiple motions for reconsideration are not permitted by the Board's rules. 

Held, as to the first claim, the motion for reconsideration is dismissed; as to the second claim, the motion for reconsideration is granted and the decision affirmed. Only one motion for reconsideration is contemplated by the Board's rules. The first reconsideration administratively completed the first claim, but not the second claim. The original decision on the latter had been adverse to the contractor and had been based on the Government's offer of proof without actual presentation of proof. The decision on reconsideration was the first decision on the second claim rendered after proof and was, therefore, the first valid decision on that claim. On the merits, the decision for the contractor on the second claim is affirmed.

11. Interest May Be Charged Contractor From Date of Contracting Officer's Unilateral Determination of Amount of Overpayment Made to Contractor, Even Though ASBCA Later Held Lesser Amount Had Been Overpaid. 

(6th Cir.) See INTEREST (par. 1) 12. Contractor's Letter Listing Acts and 

Omissions of Government for Which Contrac tual Relief Was Available and Advising Government of Contractor's Intent To Request 

Price Relief on the Contract, Coupled With the 

Facts and Comments Set Forth in Its Requests for Title II Relief, All of which Were Submitted Before Alleged Final Payment, Held To Con stitute a Timely Claim for Relief Under the

Changes Clause Even Though No Specific Re quest Therefor Was Made Until Long After 

Alleged Final Payment. On 10 April 1951 the 

Government entered into a classified contract with the contractor for the manufacture and delivery of electronic tubes. The contract con tained SF 32 (Nov. 1949 ed.), set forth fixed unit prices that were subject to price redetermination (ultimately pursuant to the Form IV PRD article), and established target and ceiling prices of approximately $900,000 and $1,000,000 respectively. In August 1951 the 

Government, being "unable to furnish certain drawings and/or test equipment called for in the specifications," agreed to furnish the contractor samples (the product of another contractor) of each of the three types of tubes called for under the contract and also incorpo rated a Government-furnished Property Clause into the contract. In May 1952 the contractor notified the Government of reasons why its incurred costs exceeded estimated costs and, further, of its intent to request price relief on AGO 9111A 19

ARMED SERVICES BOARD OF CONTRACT APPEALS-Continued the contract. These reasons included: (1) the 

Government's failure to furnish some drawings when needed and its total failure to furnish other drawings; (2) confusion and delay resulting from misunderstanding as to applicable test methods and standards; (3) substitution by Government of more complex test methods. 

Evidence was introduced before the Board of Contract Appeals to show that during the first half of 1952, the contractor held conversations with personnel of the Ordnance District legal department in which it expressed its desires to obtain price relief either within or without the terms of the contract for the additional costs incurred over and above the ceiling price; and that the Government representative suggested that contractor apply for relief under

Title II of the First War Powers Act, 1941. 

The contractor did so apply in a request dated 

26 January 1953, forwarded by a letter dated 

16 February 1953. The request was for relief in an amount in excess of $500,000 and was based on a theory of mutual mistake. The request "had many references to situations which might justify equitable adjustments under the 

Changes and/or Government-furnished Prop erty articles, e.g., the imposition of improper or extra-contractual test procedures, changes in design and unsuitability of the Governmentfurnished sample tubes." The contractor pointed out that many of the principal difficulties were such as would have justified requests for engineering changes but that the contractor had been unwilling to interrupt progress under the contract to negotiate changes. The net result of the Government's actions in administering the contract was, in the contractor's word's, that "what was thought to be an educational contract turned out, instead, to be a production development contract." On 28 

January 1954, the contractor submitted 26 pages of consolidated data in support of its request for Title II relief. This relief was de nied on 20 January 1955.

Between January 1953 and January 1955 

other matters in the nature of contract administration occurred. The contractor apparently completed performance prior to 13 March 1953; cost data were submitted; action under the PRD article was concluded by a supplemental agreement in September 1953 that established the final contract price within the limits of the existing ceiling price, but without prejudice to the pending claim for Title II relief; and in February 1954 the contractor received the Government's last payment under the contract.

Between January 1955 and July 1959 other events occurred which may be briefly recounted as: (1) the execution of a supplemental agree ment transferring certain Government tooling to the contractor; (2) the contractor's submis sion of another request for Title II relief and its denial in May 1958; and (3) the contractor's submission and the Government's denial of a request for the issuance of change orders to cover the additional work caused by the Government's administration of the contract. 

Finally, on 2 July 1959, in response to a specific request of the contractor, the contracting officer issued his decision that the contract had been administratively finalized; that he had no further authority in the matter; and that the contractor's request for the issuance of change orders and/or findings and determinations under the Disputes Clause was denied. The present appeal was taken from this decision on 20 

July 1959. The contractor is demanding an equitable adjustment in excess of $330,000 for alleged changes. The Government, by a motion to dismiss or to deny, raised several matters in the nature of affirmative defenses, At the time of the decision these had been resolved except for that relating to the timeliness of contractor's claim for equitable adjustment. 

Held, the contractor's claim was timely; the 

Government's affirmative defenses are denied. 

The vital issue is whether a valid request or claim for equitable adjustment under the 

Changes Clause was made prior to 4-9 February 1954, which the Government insists is the date of "final payment." "[T]he facts and comments set forth in the Title II requests here and the letter of 23 May 1952 clearly apprised the Government of the applicable alternative forms of relief under Title II and under the contract and of the fact that appellant was claiming for additional costs incurred, at least in large part, as a result of de facto changes but that for reasons of cooperation and expedition appellant 20 AGO 9111A

ARMED SERVICES BOARD OF CONTRACT APPEALS-Continued had not requested the issuance of Change Orders and was accordingly proceeding to obtain relief by way of the Title II route." Here the contractor clearly recognized and so advised the Government that it had a claim of right under the contract, but chose to seek extra-contractual relief. In this respect the case is distinguishable from that of Specialty Assembling and Packing 

Co., ASBCA Nos. 4523-32 (29 Sep 1959), 59-2 

BCA 2370, digested under CHANGES, par. 1, in which the contractor failed to submit its specific request for equitable adjustments under the contract until after final payment and more than six months after the denial of its requests for Title II relief. Specialty sought to excuse such failure for the reasons that (1) it had requested the contracting officer to increase the contract price because of the increased costs it was experiencing and (2) it had applied for 

Title II relief. However, the Board stated that these were requests for relief as a matter of grace; they were not assertions or recognitions of a legal right under the contract. Recognition of the possibility that relief for the actions of the Government might be obtained pursuant to the Changes Clause came long after the Govern ment's action on Specialty's request for Title II 

relief. 

Lansdale Tube Co., ASBCA No. 5837, 14 July 

1961, 61-2 BCA 3105.

13. ASBCA Lacks Jurisdiction To Consider Claim Under Termination for Convenience Clause for Costs Incurred Before and As a Result of Contract Cancellation Ordered by Comptroller General. (ASBCA) See INVALID CONTRACTS (par. 10) 14. Board Lacks Jurisdiction Over Claim for Breach of Duty That Arises From Contract but Is Basically One Defined by Law as Duty Not 

To Perform Negligently. As part of his architect-engineer contract the appellant designed a divided boulevard with a center space filled with the trees already there. When the construction contractor used the appellant's design to lay out the work on the road, the Government decided the clearance between one edge of the road and the nearest row of trees was inadequate. The Government attributed the difficulty to a design error by the appellant. 

As ordered by the Government, the construction contractor removed one row of trees and was compensated for the extra work. The 

Government attempted to set off from amounts due the appellant under his contract the value of the trees and the sum paid for tree removal. 

A timely appeal was taken to the ASBCA.

Held, appeal dismissed for want of jurisdiction. The cause of action sounds essentially in tort. Though arising from a contractual relationship, the appellant's duty is defined by a general rule of law. It is, in short, a duty not to perform negligently. See, e.g., Simpson Bros. 

Corp. v. Merriman Chemical Co., 248 Mass. 

346, 142 N.E. 922 (1924). The Board has no jurisdiction over tort claims or over a claim for damages extraneous to the contract.

Benedict, Beckler & Associates, ASBCA No. 

7172, 31 August 1962, 1962 BCA 7172.

Assignment of Contract Receivables to Trustee for Benefit of Party Financing Government Contractor-Effect of Contractor Fraud on Assignee's Claim to Contract Proceeds. 

Between November 1951 and February 1952, the plaintiff, a factor, loaned $25,132.10 to the contractor to purchase frozen food for resale to the Government. As collateral the contractor delivered warehouse receipts to the plaintiff who in turn pledged them to a bank as security for a $20,200 loan. The contractor was then awarded two Quartermaster contracts for the frozen food at a fixed price of $36,631. The plaintiff and the bank agreed to release the food for delivery if the contractor substituted an assignment of contract receivables for the warehouse receipts. Pursuant to the Assignment of 

Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 203, which was incorporated into the Government contracts, the plaintiff prepared two assignments on standard forms which named the bank as assignee of the contract proceeds. Under an independent written agreement, the plaintiff was entitled to all proceeds received by the bank in excess of the amount necessary to liquidate its indebtedness to the bank. The bank, as required by the 

Act, sent a written notice and copies of the assignments to both the contracting officer and the disbursing officer.

The contractor's first delivery was rejected by the Government for improper packaging and excess costs of $825 were incurred in a later repurchase. The second delivery was accepted and a check for $15,936.27 sent to the assignee bank. Subsequently, the Government discovered a shortage in the food delivered and determined that the bank had been overpaid in the amount of $1,138.31. The Government also accepted the final delivery but withheld payment of the contract price ($13,369.65) when further shortages were discovered. Upon inquiry from the plaintiff, the contractor admitted shortages in deliveries and stated that the Government was investigating the possibility of fraud. The plaintiff then wrote a letter to the bank which represented that it had no explanation for the delay in payment and requested the bank to make efforts to obtain payment. Shortly thereafter the contractor was adjudged bankrupt and its principal officers were convicted of fraud under 18 U.S.C. § 1001, thus forfeiting all claims against the 

United States. 28 U.S.C. § 2514. The bank then applied the $15,936 received from the Government in partial satisfaction of the plaintiff's independent $20,200 indebtedness and canceled the obligation when the plaintiff paid the remainder. Its financial interest satisfied, the bank refused to assert a claim on behalf of the plaintiff to the contract proceeds withheld by the Government. The plaintiff, however, obtained a reassignment of the bank's claim and brought this action in its own name to recover the funds. 

Held, the plaintiff is entitled to the $13,369.65 withheld less $1,963.31 for the excess costs incurred and overpayments made. The Government raises several objections to the plaintiff's right to recover. The first is that the assignment was made to the bank rather than the plaintiff and since the plaintiff's loan to the contractor was not secured by the assignment no right to the withheld proceeds exists. The 

Act, however, authorizes an assignment "to one party as agent or trustee for two or more parties participating in such financing." Under the facts of the instant case, the bank was a trustee since it agreed to hold contract proceeds in excess of the independent debt owed by the plaintiff for the plaintiff's benefit. While the bank had legal title to all contract proceeds the bank had an equitable interest in the excess. 

The Act does not require that all persons with an equitable interest in the proceeds shall notify the Government. The requirement of notice is satisfied if the trustee informs the Government to whom the proceeds should be paid. If the 

Government were notified of all equities, would it be proper to pay the proceeds to just one of the potential claimants? The Act was intended 22 AGO 9111A

ASSIGNMENT OF CLAIMS-Continued to facilitate the financing of Government contracts through private capital, not to encourage the multiplication of court actions. It is concluded, therefore, that the plaintiff is a secured assignee within the meaning of the Act and that its rights were perfected when the bank, as trustee, gave written notice to the Government.

While the contractor forfeited its claim against the Government because of fraud, this fraud or its consequences are not imputable to an assignee who was not involved. Arlington 

Trust Company v. United States, 121 Ct. Cl. 32 (1952). The Government argues, however, that the plaintiff committed fraud by its letter requesting the bank to collect the withheld payments. This letter was misleading since the plaintiff did not disclose the known shortages and the Government fraud investigation. While the letter did not reveal all, the plaintiff knew that the Government was aware of the shortages. How, then, could the Government be induced to pay for goods it had not received? 

The purpose of 28 U.S.C. § 2514 is to penalize for fraud not for lack of frankness, especially where the failure to disclose could mislead no one. Finally, the Government argues that since the reassignment of the bank's claim to the plaintiff occurred after the fraud was disclosed. the plaintiff took legal title subject to the defense of fraud. Yet at the time of the assignment the bank took legal title and the plaintiff received an equitable interest as purchasers in good faith. This status was not altered when the legal and equitable rights were merged by the reassignment after the fraud was revealed. 

Since the contracts, pursuant to the Act, expressly authorized the reassignment there is no occasion to consider the plaintiff's standing to sue if the reassignment were not permitted. 

Chelsea Factors, Inc. v. United States, 181 F. 

Supp. 685, (Ct. Cl. 1960).
