3. Amounts Paid Contractor's Assignee After Government Received Notice That Surety Had Paid Materialmen Are Recoverable by Cross Claim. The United States entered into several contracts with the Gray Construction Company. Plaintiff was surety on Gray's labor and materialmen's bonds. Gray assigned the proceeds of the two contracts involved in this suit to Pioneer Bank and Trust Company.

Pioneer gave to the United States and to plaintiff the notice of assignment required by the 

Assignment of Claims Act of 1940 (31 U.S.C. 

203).

Although it completed the work, Gray did not pay all the laborers and materialmen. 

The obligation to do so devolved upon plaintiff. 

The United States, on notice of plaintiff's claim to the outstanding payments due Gray for completing the contracts, nevertheless paid such sums to Pioneer as assignee of Gray.

Plaintiff now seeks judgment for the amount of the payments made to Pioneer after the United States was notified of plaintiff's claim. 

In a cross-claim against Pioneer the United States contends that in the event it is held liable to plaintiff, it should have judgment against Pioneer for the same amount on the theory that payments made to Pioneer were the result of mistakes of law and fact. Pioneer filed a motion to dismiss in reliance on that portion of the fourth paragraph of the Assignment of Claims Act as amended in 1951 (41 

U.S.C. 15) which provides: In any case in which moneys due or to become due under any contract are assigned pursuant to this section, no liability of any nature of the assignor to the United States. . ., whether arising from or independently of such contract, shall create or impose any liability on the part of the assignee to make restitution, refund or repayment to the 

United States of any amount . . . received under the assignment.

The Government argues that this portion of the statute is inapplicable.

Held, motion to dismiss is overruled. No 

Government agent has the power irrevocably to dispose of Government money by payments made under mistakes of fact or law. This doctrine may be waived only by a clear manifestation of congressional intent. 

The purpose of the Assignment of Claims Act was to protect an assignee's interest in "moneys due or to become due under any con- AGO 9111A 23

ASSIGNMENT OF CLAIMS—Continued tract." However, money does not become due under a contract for the purposes of the act until the terms of the contract including those requiring payment by the contractor of his obligations have been complied with. The surety has first call on all funds necessary for the purpose of assuring that all terms of the contract are complied with. The assignee has first call on all funds earned under the contract which are in excess of amount needed to fulfill the contractor's obligation to pay for labor and materials. 

Here Pioneer mistakenly received funds committed to the payment of labor and materials; funds which were in excess of amounts due or which became due under the contract. To this extent it received a windfall; it received funds which were beyond the scope of the protective statute. This being so, Pioneer is a proper third party defendant. 

Newark Ins. Co. v. United States, 181 F. 

Supp. 246 (Ct. Cl. 1960). 

4. Pension Trust Together With Trustees Held To Be a Financing Institution Within the. 

Assignment of Claims Act of 1940. The Assignment of Claims Act of 1940, 31 U.S.C. § 

203, provides that moneys due or to become due from the United States under a contract providing payments of $1,000 or more may be assigned to a "bank, trust company, or other financing institution." The Comptroller General was asked whether that act permits an assignment to a pension trust.

Held, the proposed assignment is proper. 

No reason against making assignments to a pension trust can be found in the interests of any party to the transaction or in the congressional history and purpose of the Assignment of Claims Act. The trustees of the pension trust involved here have a duty to invest and reinvest principal and interest in loans, securities, and property. It was held in 36 Comp. 

Gen. 290 (1956) that pension trust funds may be used for loans secured by an assignment to a bank acting as trustee. Therefore, the assignment to a pension trust is. proper if the assignee qualifies as a "financing institution" under that act. 

A "financing institution" is one that deals in money rather than other commoditiesas the primary function of its business activity. 

22 Comp. Gen. 44 (1942). The institution may be an individual, a partnership, or a corporate organization. 20 Comp. Gen. 415 (1941). The trustees, seven individuals, hold the trust corpus as joint tenants. 1 Restatement, Trusts 

2d § 103. They must act in unison on discretionary actions such as the lending of large sums of money. They form one collective trustee Vandever's Appeal, 8 W. & S. 405 (Pa. 

1845), 42 Am. Dec. 305. While the trustees in this case cannot be said to be formed into the kind of entity normally regarded as an institution, their relationship to each other and to the trust is such as to permit equating them to an individual for purposes of determining whether they qualify as a financial institution. 

A trust itself is not an institution. 36 Comp. 

Gen. 290 (1956). However, the trust corpus, together with the trustees, whether individual, corporate or otherwise, having as a primary function the investing of assets of the trust, may be regarded as a financing institution within the meaning of the Assignment of 

Claims Act. See Tax Commission v. Paxson, 

118 Ohio St. 36, 160 N.E. 468, 469 (1928), and

Central National Bank v. Department of Taxa tion, 126 Ohio St. 1, 120 N.E. 2d 437 (1954). 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143922, 16 September 

1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 174. 

[Note: In 36 Comp. Gen. 290 (1956), a pen sion trust was declared not to be a “financing institution," although an assignment to a bank acting as trustee for a pension trust was upheld. By allowing the trustees to be considered together with the trust, the instant opinion may represent a more liberal attitude toward what constitutes a "financing institution." In this connection, compare Chelsea Factors, Inc. 

v. United States, 181 F. Supp. 685 (Ct. Cl. 

1960), where a factor was permitted to be the assignee of a claim.] 

5. Assignment of Contract Proceeds Is not

Rendered Invalid by Fact That Loans for 

Which Assignment Was Made Were Paid to

Someone Other Than Assignor-Assignment of 

Contract Proceeds Is Invalid to Extent Loans for Which Assignment Was Made Were Paid to Third Party and Used in Manner Not Fur thering Completion of Contract. The F Co. as- 

24 AGO 9111A

ASSIGNMENT OF CONTRACTS 

signed to a bank the proceeds of a Government contract. The Government was duly notified of the assignment. No loans or advances were made by the bank directly to the F Co. Instead, the money was paid to a controlled account maintained in the name of Mr. L, who-with his wife and the president of the F Co.-had signed a note given to the bank. Mr. L was to insure that the money paid to the controlled account would be used for the F Co.'s performance of two Government contracts, one of them the contract involved in the assignment. After full performance by the F Co., the Government withheld some of the proceeds claimed by the assignee bank. The withholding was based on a contention that the F Co. owed the Government under other contracts amounts that exceeded the sum withheld. Although conceding that the F Co.'s claim had been assignable under the Assignment of Claims Act of 1940, 54 Stat. 1029 (1940), as amended, 31 U.S.C. § 203 (1958), the Government argued that the assignment was invalid, so that the "no set-off" provisions of that statute were inapplicable.

The argument was based on the grounds that (1) no money had been paid or loaned by the bank directly to the F Co. and (2) the assignment was valid only to the extent that the F Co. actually received the loan proceeds. These grounds were advanced as the basis of a motion for summary judgment when the F Co.'s receiver in bankruptcy and the bank sued in the 

Court of Claims. 

Held, motion denied. The arrangement between the F Co., Mr. L, and the bank does not appear to have been illegal. See 35 Comp. Gen. 

104, 106 (1955). The Government has argued that the Assignment of Claims Act was not designed to protect an institution that does not assist an assignor-contractor by way of loans attendant to the performance of a Government contract. However, the Government has cited no authority or statutory language to support that argument. The act does require an assignment to one party alone but specifically permits that party to act as agent or trustee for two or more parties participating in the financing. Thus the act clearly has no policy against indirect financing. Moreover, the act should be construed to encourage the financing of Government contracts by private capital. Chelsea Factors, Inc. v. United States, 

under ASSIGNMENT OF CLAIMS, par. 1]. 

Absent specific statutory language to the contrary, an assignment should not be declared invalid merely on the ground that loans are not made directly to the assignor. 

The Government has contended that the assignment is valid only to the extent the F Co. received the loan proceeds. It is true that, if the loan was used for a purpose other than completion of the contract, the act's purposeto stimulate financing of Government contracts -would not have been fulfilled. However, if lending institutions know that the validity of an assignment is conditioned upon the use to which the funds are put, they would be reluctant to take assignments. Therefore, if loans are made directly to a contractor, the use made of the funds will not impair an assignment's validity.

Nevertheless, here the loan was made through Mr. L. It is not unreasonable to charge the bank with the information in Mr. L's possession if he spent the funds for the F Co. in a manner that did not promote completion of the contract. To the extent that Mr. L so expended the funds, the assignment should be defeated. Thus the assignment is valid only to the extent that the moneys were actually paid to the F Co. by either Mr. L. or the bank, or to the extent that they were spent by Mr. L to aid the F Co. in completing the contract.

Since the record is not clear about the disposition of the funds, the motion for summary judgment must be denied and a hearing on the facts conducted.

Coleman v. United States, Ct. Cl. No. 3-60, 18 July 1962. 

ASSIGNMENT OF CONTRACTS 1. Contract Annulled Where Contractor Authorizes Third Party To Perform in Her Place and Divests Self of Power To Compel Performance. The Department of Labor requested bids for the furnishing of meals to Mexican Laborers who were brought into this country by the Farm Placement Services. The plaintiff's bid, while apparently low, contained certain AGO 9111A 25

BANKRUPTCY 

ambiguities which prompted a Department official to request a telegraphic clarification. 

This was done after the bids were opened and the plaintiff ultimately received the award.

Shortly thereafter, the validity of this acceptance was questioned by the Department and the matter was submitted to the Comptroller General. Although the plaintiff was informed of this action, she executed the required performance bond and made arrangements for financial assistance with a Mr. Toledo. Under a so called "Management Agreement," Toledo was given general authority to operate and manage the feedings, to purchase and sell supplies, to financially obligate the plaintiff and to do all things that he considered to be necessary and useful. In addition, Toledo was given a power of attorney to act in plantiff's "place and stead." While the agreement contemplated an equal division of profits, the plaintiff was entitled to no contract proceeds until Toledo saw fit. 

After the Management Agreement was executed, the Comptroller General advised that the telegraphic clarification of the plaintiff's ambiguous bid after all bids were opened conferred an unfair advantage. Although the opinion did not find that the acceptance was invalid, the Department of Labor advised the plaintiff that no contract existed and refused to permit performance to continue. The plaintiff then brought suit for damages, including out of pocket expenses and loss of profits. 

Held, the suit is dismissed. The Government argues that the plaintiff's telegraphic clarification was in fact a new proposal presented without advertising. Consequently, its acceptance was contrary to the provisions of 41 U.S.C. § 5 

which requires that Government contracts be made "only after advertising a sufficient time previously for proposals." It is not necessary to decide this question, however, for assuming that a contract was created it was annulled by the plaintiff's Management Agreement with Toledo. 

41 U.S.C. § 15 provides in part: "No contract or order, or any interest therein, shall be transferred by the party to whom such contract or order is given to any other party, and any such transfer shall cause the annulment of the contract or order transferred, so far as the United States are concerned." The purpose of this provision is to protect the Government from harassment "by multiplying the number of persons with whom it had to deal" and enabling the Government to know "with whom it was dealing until the contract was completed and the settlement made." Hobbs v. McLean, 117 

U.S. 567, 576 (1885). The statute does not apply to agreements with third parties to share profits or losses, Field v. United States, 16 Ct. 

Cl. 434 (1885), or to subcontracts, Chemicals

Recovery Co. v. United States, 122 Ct. Cl. 166 

(1952), because the contractor remains primarily liable to the Government and retains the power to perform or require performance of the contract. In the instant case, however, the 

Government is forced to deal with a stranger since the plaintiff vested complete control of performance in Toledo. Toledo was given all power necessary to control performance and the authority to act as attorney for the plaintiff in her place and stead. Consequently, the Government, to obtain effective contract performance, would be forced to deal with Toledo since the plaintiff has rendered herself powerless to compel performance.

McPhail v. United States, 181 F. Supp. 251

Opinion: In a previous opinion, JAGT 

1956/4018, 4 May 1956, an invitation for bids. which did not require test samples where the equality of the sample was known to the Government but did require a sample where the quality was not known was found legally objectionable. In view of two recent opinions by the Comptroller General, this opinion should no longer be followed. In Ms. Comp. Gen. 

B-140361, 10 November 1959, a similar procedure was approved where the bidder had previously furnished or received approval of the same sample. The relinquishment of a theoretical right to require a useless gesture cannot be considered a waiver of a material provision, unless further testing would add to the Government's knowledge of acceptability. 

Before the sample requirement can be waived, therefore, the contracting officer should verify that the product previously tested is adequate to meet the requirements of the invitation for bids. 37 Comp. Gen. 814 (1958).

2. Rejected Low Bidder Fails To Prove That 

Government Breached Promises Which Were

Implied by Solicitation of Bids. The plaintiff was low bidder on an invitation, issued by the 

Ordnance Tank Automotive Center (OTAC), for 5,500 low voltage circuit testers. The contract, however, was awarded to a bidder whose price exceeded by $190,043 that of the plaintiff. 

In an action against the United States, the plaintiff alleged that the award was a "deliberate artifice to retaliate against plaintiff for testifying against OTAC at a Senate hearing in 1952," and that the Government wished to favor the higher bidder and did so by conduct which was arbitrary, capricious and in bad faith. The petition sought $7,000 for the cost of submitting the bid and $38,000 for lost profits. The Government's motion to dismiss was denied for the reason that the allegations, if taken to be true, showed discrimination against the plaintiff and favoritism toward the awardee which made it impossible to conclude that the award was advantageous to the Government. Heyer

Products Company v. U.S., 140 F. Supp. 409 

(Ct. Cl. 1956), DA Pam 715-50-1, p. 78, par. 

12. The case was then heard on the merits.

Held, the evidence does not support the plaintiff's claim and the case is dismissed. The plaintiff's right of action is based upon implied promises by the Government to give honest and fair consideration to all bids submitted, to not arbitrarily or capriciously reject them and to award a contract only upon an honest belief that it is advantageous to the Government. If these promises have been breached, the plaintiff may recover costs incurred in submitting the bid. Loss of profits, however, is not compensable.

The Government argues that the bid was properly rejected for failing to meet the specifications. Tests made on submitted samples indicate that the voltmeter did not measure voltage with the degree of accuracy required.

This major defect coupled with several others of a less serious nature support the conclusion that the sample did not, as required, conform "in every respect" to the specifications. As such, OTAC was fully justified in rejecting the bid and its conduct was not arbitrary or capricious. While this is sufficient to deny the claim, the vigor with which this case has been argued prompts an examination of the award to the higher bidder. It is concluded that, despite the higher price, the award was in good faith and based upon an honest judgment that it was advantageous to the Government. 

Heyer Products Co. v. U.S., 177 F. Supp. 

251 (Ct. Cl. 1959). 

3. Bid Bond in Smaller Amount Than Re quired by Invitation for Bids Renders Accom panying Bid Nonresponsive. The Federal 

Maritime Board issued an invitation for bids for the conversion of two combination passenger cargo vessels which were owned by the American President Lines, Ltd. The invitation provided that no bid would be considered unless accompanied by a $200,000 bid bond which contained the following conditions:

NOW, THEREFORE, if the principal . . . shall 

AGO 9111A 27

keep its bid open as required by the Invitation for 

Bids, execute the conversion contract within five days after tender by the Owner, and furnish the bonds required thereunder within the time specified in such contract, then the above obligations shall be null and void, otherwise to be and to remain in full force and effect and the principal amount of this bond... to be forfeited as liquidated damages for failure of the principal to keep its bid open, to execute the contract, or to furnish the bonds. 

The low bidder submited a bond which conformed in every respect except that the amount of recovery in the event of forfeiture was limited to the difference between the amount bid and the cost of obtaining a substitute performance. This variance was justified on the ground that the invitation implied that recovery on the bond would be limited to actual damages for breach of condition, i.e., some $34,000, the difference between the low bid and the second low bid, and that in any event, the $200,000 liquidated damages penalty was not a reasonable forecast of just compensation for a breach of condition. The Maritime Board rejected the bid as nonresponsive and asked whether the Comptroller General concurred.

Held, the bid is nonresponsive and was properly rejected. A determination that a bid bond is required in a given procurement establishes a material condition which must be met before bids may be considered. 38 Comp. Gen. 

532 (1959), DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 84, par. 98.

A bond which is in a smaller amount than specified in the invitation does not satisfy this condition and the accompanying bid must be rejected as nonresponsive. 38 Comp. Gen. 

851 (1959). Here, the Maritime Board and the owners of the vessel determined that a reasonable estimate of damages for breach of the bid bond conditions was $200,000. This figure included far more than the easily ascertainable difference between the low bid and the second low bid. Other elements of damage were the estimated losses of ship revenue resulting from the breach and other intangible losses, such as loss of passenger fees, which are extremely difficult to calculate. It is concluded, therefore, that the liquidated damages of $200,000 were a reasonable forecast of just compensation for a breach of condition and that the damage involved could not be accurately estimated. See Restatement, Contracts, sec. 

339; Taylor v. United States, 150 F. Supp. 567 (Ct. Cl. 1957). Accordingly, the bid bond was in an amount smaller than required by the invitation and the accompanying bid should be rejected.

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-141215, 3 December 1959, 39 Comp. Gen. 418. 

[Note: See also, 39 Comp. Gen. 83 (1959), DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 79, par. 91. In Ms.

Comp. Gen. B-141637, 3 March 1960, the Air 

Force required a bid bond in the amount of 20% of the total bid for several items of surplus property. One bid bond was defective when considered with regard to the bid for all items offered for sale but exceeded 20% of the separate items for which the bidder was successful. This bid was accepted since the 

Government's interest was adequately protected on the items for which the bidder successfully bid.] 

4. Where Contracting Officer Erroneously Rejects All Bids and Readvertises, Comptroller General Cancels Award to Low Bidder on Second Invitation and Awards Contract to Low Bidder on the First Invitation. The Air Force issued an invitation for bids to move, handle and store household goods for personnel stationed in Hawaii during fiscal year 1960. The invitation listed each service as a separate item and estimated the Government's requirements for each. While the invitation did not specify the type of award contemplated, all bidders submitted an aggregate bid on the assumption that the Air Force would award all requirements to one bidder. After the bids were opened and the low bidder determined, however, the contracting officer rejected all bids and readvertised because of "omissions in the specifications and the Government's inability to make multiple awards." Apparently, the contracting officer believed that since an aggregate award was not specifically authorized a multiple award was required and that this was impractical under the circumstances. The second invitation specified that a single award would be made. 

When the contract was awarded to a new low bidder, however, the low bidder on the first advertisement protested.

Held, the protest is allowed. There must be cogent reasons to justify a rejection of all bids 28 AGO 9111A

after opening since it permits each bidder to learn his competitor's price. Massman Construction Co. v. United States, 102 Ct. Cl. 669 (1945). While the contracting officer's discretion in this area is broad, the decision cannot be arbitrary. See 36 Comp. Gen. 62, 66 (1956).

Here, an aggregate bid was required by the nature of the procurement and expected by the bidders. Further, a multiple award was not proper unless authorized by the invitation. 

AFPI 2-406.3 (d). Thus, the contracting officer, because of the position he occupied, either knew or should have known that an aggregate award under the first invitation was both authorized and normal procedure. Accordingly, there was no cogent reason based upon law or regulation to reject all bids. The contract should be canceled and awarded to the low bidder under the first invitation for the remainder of fiscal year 1960. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-140175, 25 November 

1959, 39 Comp. Gen. 396. 

[Note: If all bids are properly rejected, the parties are restored to their previous position and the Government's power of acceptance is destroyed. See 35 Comp. Gen. 255 (1955).

Necessarily, the low bidder must consent if the Government subsequently decides to reinstate his bid. See 34 Comp. Gen. 535 (1955). If consent is given, the important question is whether the Government may award the contract without complying with the requirements of formal advertising. The instant case holds yes, and awarded the contract five months after the rejection without considering whether a better competitive price could be obtained. In the light of previous decisions this approach may be questionable. See 35 Comp. Gen. 255 (1955) and cases cited. An even more interesting possibility is presented. Suppose the low bidder did not consent to the reinstatement of his bid and the second advertisement resulted in a higher low bid than the first. Could the 

Government accept the first low bid which had been erroneously rejected without the low bidder's consent?]

8. Use of DD Form 747 by Prospective Con tractor Does Not Constitute an Offer Suscepti ble of Acceptance by Government. An Army agency received a quotation on a DD Form 747 which contained the language "This is a request for information only. The quotation contained herein shall not constitute an offer to the Government." Contracting officer issued two purchase orders on DD Form 1155. The supplier neither accepted the orders nor did he undertake performance. The contracting officer, two weeks after issuing a ten day warning, issued a notice of termination for default. The Government's requirements were reprocured and excess costs of over $200 assessed against the supplier. The opinion of the Judge Advocate

General was requested as to whether or not a binding contract existed between supplier and the Government and as to the propriety of the assessment of excess costs.

Opinion: The 1 May 1958 edition of DD Form 

747 which was used in this case was intended to eliminate the confusion which existed as to whether use by a supplier of the previous edition (which did not contain the above quoted language) constituted an offer susceptible of acceptance by the Government, or a mere price quotation. See 37 Comp. Gen. 358 (1957). 

ASPR 16-201.2 (9 Jan 1959) which governed the use of the Form 747 during the time concerned in this case provided that a quotation submitted on the form would not be construed as an offer; that the Government's issuance of a purchase order after receipt of a Form 747 did not create a contract, but merely constituted an offer by the Government. In view of the specific provision in DD Form 747 that the quotation shall not constitute an offer, the provisions of ASPR and the absence of express AGO 9111A 29

consent or performance by the supplier, no binding contract came into existence and there is no basis for an assessment of excess costs. 

JAGT 1960/5827, 10 February 1960. 

[Note: The use of DD Form 747 was discon tinued 1 April 1960 in favor of the use of

Standard Form 18 (Request for Quotation) dated May 1959. The latter provides: "This is a request for information and quotations furnished are not offers." ASPR 16-201 (4 Jan 

1960) provides instructions concerning the use of the new form similar to those discussed above relative to the discontinued form. The legal principles expressed in the digested opinion are applicable to either form. See also, JAGT 1960/6146, 14 April 1960, digested under

TYPES OF CONTRACTS (PURCHASE ORDER), par. 2.] 9. Award May Be Cancelled and Purchase

See MISTAKES IN BIDS (par. 3) 10. Establishment of an Irrevocable Credit by a Domestic Bank in Favor of the Govern ment Constitutes Adequate Bid Security. The 

Bureau of Reclamation issued invitations for bids, on Standard Form 33 (Oct 1957 Edition), for furnishing a hoist for a wheel gate. The in vitation contained the following Special Condi tion:

A-1. Bonds. (a) Bid security-Guaranty will be required with each bid in an amount not less than 10 percent of the total price bid. This requirement for bid guaranty will not be waived. Bid bonds or other bid securities which are not received prior to the time specified for receipt of bids will not be acceptable unless the lateness was due solely to delay in the mails for which the bidder was not responsible.

The bidder, at his option, may furnish a guaranty bond on Standard Form 24 or certified check drawn on a United States Bank, or may deposit . . negotiable bonds or notes of the United States.. as security.. 

Bid opening was scheduled for and held on 

January 5, 1960. On January 4, 1960, the bid opening office received telephonic advice from the Denver United States National Bank that the bank had received a telegram from the 

Chase Manhattan Bank of New York advising that the latter confirmed an irrevocable credit in the amount of $7,000 issued by the Creditanstalt-Bankverein of Vienna, Austria, in favor of the Bureau for the account of 

Vereinigte Osterreichische Eisen-Und Stahl werke Aktiengesellschaft (hereinafter referred to as VOEST) as guaranty of its bid obligations under the involved invitation. At bid opening on January 5, 1960, VOEST was deter mined to be the low bidder (with a bid of $72,- 

747.80), taking into consideration the differential on products from foreign sources and 

Government freight costs. On January 6, 1960, the bid opening office received in the mail a photostat of the telegram sent by the Chase 

Manhattan Bank to the Denver United States 

National Bank. It was determined that the failure of the photostat to be received by the bid opening time was due solely to delay in the mails for which the bidder may be excused, pursuant to the provisions of paragraph 4 of the Terms and Conditions of the Invitation for 

Bids. The question presented to the Comptrol ler General is whether the bid of VOEST was accompanied by an acceptable bid guaranty. 

The telegram from the Chase Manhattan Bank not only advised the Denver National Bank that the Austrian Bank had established the irrevocable credit in favor of the United States for

VOEST, but the telegram also stated that "WE 

ADD OUR CONFIRMATIO [sic] OUR REF- ERENCE E826772 NOTIFY BENEFICIARY BY TELEPHONE." Thus, the Chase Man hattan Bank confirmed the credit.

Held, the credit would appear to represent substantial compliance with the bid security requirements and the VOEST bid may be considered if otherwise acceptable.

The effect of the confirmation of the credit is set forth in the Uniform Customs and Prac tice for Commercial Documentary Credits (1951 Revision) fixed by the XIIIth Congress of the International Chamber of Commerce 

(Lisbon, June 11-16, 1951); Brochure I.C.C. 

151 E.F. 1951: 

When the issuing Bank instructs another Bank to confirm its irrevocable credit and when the latter does so, the confirmation implies a definite under- 30 AGO 9111A

taking of the confirming Bank as from the date on which it gives confirmation. Such undertakings can neither be modified nor cancelled without the agreement of all concerned. 

Since the Chase Manhattan Bank, by confirming the irrevocable letter of credit of the Austrian Bank, became primarily liable to the Government for the amount of the credit involved, and since Chase's assumption of primary responsibility in the matter was communicated in writing to the bid opening office within the time allowed for submission of bids delayed in the mails, the credit thus established represents substantial compliance with the bid security requirements. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-141872, 7 March 1960, 39
