11. Bid Bond Deficiency May Be Waived Where Only One Acceptable Bid if Award in Best Interest of Government. The Bureau of 

Land Management, pursuant to section 8 of the 

Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, 67 Stat. 

462, issued invitations to bid on oil and gas leases for several tracts of land. The only acceptable bid on two tracts was not, as required by the invitation, accompanied by a deposit of one-fifth of the bid amount. This bid and the bidder's subsequent attempt to correct the deficiency were rejected, apparently on the theory that the bid deposit requirements in the invitation should be strictly enforced. See 38 Comp.

Gen. 532 (1959). The Secretary of the Interior requested an opinion as to whether the bid was properly rejected. 

Held, the rejection was improper in this case.

The primary purpose of a bid bond is to protect the Government against irresponsible or improvident bidders. Bid bond requirements are strictly enforced to avoid possible discrimination between bidders, to prevent bidders from exercising an option to correct bid deficiencies after opening and to eliminate the administrative burden of evaluating excuses offered for bid deposit deficiencies. But if only one acceptable bid is submitted, there is no question of discrimination and an acceptance creates a contract even though no offer to correct the deflciency is made. Consequently, the only factor for consideration in this case is the interest of the Government. If acceptance of this bid will serve the Government's interest, the deposit defect may be waived. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-142869, 27 May 1960, 39

Comp. Gen. 796. 

12. Restrictive Specification Waived Where Detriment to Low Bidder in Readvertising Out weighed Prejudice to Competition and Other 

Bidders. In an invitation for bids Naval Ordnance specified that all gas heaters to be supplied bear the seal of the American Gas 

Association. Deliveries were required within 

30 days of award. Of the six bidders responding, four, including the low bidder, did not obtain the required AGA seal. The low bidder's unit, however, met AGA standards and, relying upon the prospect of award, it made commitments with suppliers. The third low bidder, who had obtained an AGA seal, protested any consideration of the low bid because of the seal defect. On the assumption that the seal requirement was restrictive, the contracting officer cancelled the invitation and readvertised. The low bidder then protested that since its unit actually met AGA standards the seal omission was a minor discrepancy and that it would be penalized by a readvertisement since its low bid was disclosed and supplier. commitments had been made.

Held, the protest is allowed. Normally, a requirement that supplies bear the seal of a private testing organization is regarded as restrictive of competition and in violation of the formal advertising statutes. 33 Comp. Gen. 

573 (1954). On the other hand, the rejection of all bids after opening is also detrimental to the advertising system. Consequently, a readvertisement should be required only where the prejudice to other bidders and the theoretical elimination of competition by the seal requirement outweighs the detriment to the low bidder in having to rebid. 

In view of the short 30 day delivery period and the delay encountered in obtaining AGA approvals, it is apparent that no bidder who did not have a seal when receiving the invitation could have expected to obtain one in time to perform the contract. Even so, four bidders submitted bids without seals and it cannot be said that the seal requirement unduly restricted AGO 9111A 31

competition. Further, since the two bidders with seals had obtained and paid for AGA approval prior to receiving the invitation and were not required to incur additional expense for this contract, they would not be prejudiced if the seal requirement were waived. Accordingly, it is concluded that the detriment to the low bidder in a readvertisement outweighs the prejudice to other bidders if the seal requirement is waived. The integrity of the competitive bidding system, therefore, will best be served by awarding the contract to the lowest responsible bidder under the original invitation. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-141670, 8 February 1960, 39 Comp. Gen. 563. 

13. Prior Unsatisfactory Performance Unre lated to Capacity or Credit Which Has Not Been

Explained Supports Contracting Officer's Determination That Small Business Concern Is 

Not Responsible. The contractor, a small business concern, received a partial award of both the formal and the set aside portion of a quartermaster coverall procurement. In order to obtain the set aside award, the contractor agreed to perform the contract in a specified facility which had adequate capacity to assure timely deliveries. Final deliveries under the set aside contract, however, were 109 days late because the contractor refused to perform at the agreed facility. Rather, the contractor waited until sufficient capacity developed at another facility where the formal portion of the coverall contract was being performed. No reason was offered for the refusal to perform at the agreed facility.

A short time later, the contractor was low bidder on another procurement. The contracting officer, however, determined that the contractor was not responsible due to the prior unsatisfactory contract performance. The reason for this determination was unrelated to the contractor's capacity or credit. The contractor protested the determination and subsequent award to another bidder.

Held, the protest is denied. On the basis of the record there is ample support for the contracting officer's determination that contractor's prior performance was unsatisfactory for reasons unrelated to either capacity or credit.

The contractor steadfastly refused to perform at the agreed facility and offered no excuse for this conduct or the 109 day delay. Consequently, the contracting officer, as required by 

ASPR 1-904 (1 Jul 1960), could not make an affirmative determination that the contractor was responsible within the meaning of ASPR 1-903 (1 Jul 1960). See 38 Comp. Gen. 289 (1959). 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-142208, 20 May 1960. 

[Note: If the contractor's unexplained re fusal to perform at the agreed facility goes to the matter of "business integrity" and is not related to capacity or credit, the issuance of a 

Small Business Administration certificate of competency would not change the result in this case. 38 Comp. Gen. 864 (1959).] 14. Bidders Evidence of Exact Time That Late Bid Was Mailed Must Be Substantiated By Post Office-Reliability of Metered Mail in Establishing Date of Mailing Questioned. The low bid on an Army invitation arrived, after the opening of bids, inclosed in an envelope bearing a metered stamp but not a post office cancellation stamp. The metered stamp estab lished only that the bid was mailed on the day before the time set for opening. The contracting officer determined that the bid was late within the meaning of ASPR 2-303.2 (i) and advised the low bidder that the bid would be rejected "unless clear and convincing evidence is submitted promptly, showing that your bid was actually deposited in the mails in sufficient time to reach this office by ordinary course of mails before the scheduled time for opening and that late receipt was due solely to delay in the mails, for which you were not responsible."

The low bidder submitted employee affidavits which established the precise time of mailing and the statement of a post office clerk that if the bid were mailed at that time it would arrive in due course of mails before the opening. 

DCSLOG requested an opinion as to whether the bid should be considered for award.

Held, the bid must be rejected as nonresponsive. A mailed bid which is received after the time set for opening may be considered only where it arrives before award and was mailed in time to arrive before the opening except for a delay due solely to the mails for which the bidder was not responsible. ASPR 2-303.2 (i). 32 AGO 9111A

The problem here is to determine the exact time of mailing since the metered stamp revealed only the date. Unless the low bidder has sustained the burden of demonstrating the exact hour of mailing, it is presumed that the time of mailing shall be the last minute of the date shown by the metered stamp, i.e., 11:59 P.M. 

See ASPR 2-303.3 (iii). In the instant case, this would be too late to arrive in time for the opening of bids. The low bidder's evidence reveals that the bid was actually mailed at an earlier hour and in time to arrive before the opening. This evidence, however, is self-serving and the actual hour of mailing has not been substantiated by the post office of mailing. 

ASPR 2-303 (a) (vi). See 38 Comp. Gen. 21 (1958). A postal officer must affirm from personal knowledge that the bid envelope was actually received for mailing in sufficient time to arrive before the opening of bids. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143661, 12 August 1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 91. 

[Note: In the instant case, the reliability of the metered stamp in establishing the date of mailing was not in issue. The question was the validity of the low bidder's evidence establishing the exact hour of mailing on that date.

In Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143772, 1 September 

1960, the date of mailing was in issue. The envelope inclosing a late low bid bore a meter stamp with a date of 10 June, however, the bidder admitted that the bid was actually mailed on 11 June, which was still early enough to arrive in time for the bid opening. It appeared that postal employees had failed to discover the error under procedures which require a postmark if the meter date is not correct. 

Section 2-303.3 (a) (i) of ASPR provides that, in the case of metered mail, the date of mailing is established by the meter date. However, this provision could not be invoked in this case since the bidder made a statement against interest that the metered date was incorrect. Nor was the evidence of the actual date of mailing acceptable as it was self-serving and unsubstantiated by the post office. The Comptroller 

General questioned the reliability of the metered stamp as establishing the date of mailing and recommended a change in ASPR 2-303.3 (a) (i). 

Since the time of mailing is a vital issue in these late bid cases, we think that to avoid any future uncertainty as to the time of mailing, the date and hour should be established by the most accurate, reliable and impartial method available. Therefore, we are recommending to the Secretary of Defense that appropriate steps be taken to amend the ASPR so that in future procurements the invitation for bids will include in the late bid clause an additional statement that no bid or modification sent through the mail and bearing a stamp affixed by a metering device which is received after the bid opening time will be considered for award unless it also bears a post office cancellation stamp showing the hour and date of posting.] 

15. Invitation For Bids Canceled And Procure ment Readvertised Where Amendment Deprived

Low Bidder Of Sufficient Time Within Which Properly To Submit Required Bid Bond. Bids for the rehabilitation of railroad trackage at 

Ft. Bliss were to be opened at 3:00 PM, 29

June 1960. The invitation authorized telegraphic bids but contained the following bid bond requirement:

If the bid bond is not received at the designated office prior to the specified time for bid opening, the bid will be rejected as nonresponsive EXCEPT that bid bonds received after the specified time for bid opening and prior to award may be considered if the failure of the bid bond to arrive on time was due solely to delay in the mails for which the bidder was not responsible.

Two days before the time set for opening, notice of an amendment to the invitation which required a price recomputation was dispatched by priority message to all prospective bidders. 

On the morning of 29 June, the contracting officer, upon the request of Bidder A, advised that under the circumstances and because a bid bond could not accompany a telegraphic bid it would be proper to submit the bid by telegraph and the bid bond by airmail. Bidder A's telegraphic bid, while low, was late. It was determined, however, that the delay was caused by the Western Union Company, not by the bidder. The bid bond arrived by air mail letter, postmarked four hours after the time set for opening and after the time that Bidder A knew its bid was low. The contracting officer decided to award the contract to Bidder A. Head quarters, Fourth U.S. Army, however, recommended that the invitation be canceled and the procurement be readvertised to permit the AGO 9111A 33

proper and orderly submission of bids and bid bonds. 

Held, the invitation should be canceled and the procurement readvertised. Despite the time problem created by the amendment and the fact that telegraphic bids were authorized, the invitation required bid bonds to be submitted "prior to the specified time for bid opening" unless the failure is "due solely to delay in the mails for which the bidder was not responsible." Since the delay was not excusable here, the bid of Bidder A was not responsive and should be rejected. 39 Comp. Gen. 430 (1959). In cases where the bid price may be uncertain until the last minute, bidders often first submit a formal bid and bid bond and thereafter submit by a timely telegram their firm-fixed price, either as an original quotation or as an amendment to their prior bid. But in the instant case, the time problem canised by the amendment dictates that the invitation be canceled and the procurement readvertised. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143470, 2 September 1960. 

16. Two-Step Formal Advertising Is Not Unreasonably Restrictive of Competition. The Air 

Force, in the first phase of a two-step formal advertisement, requested technical proposals without prices to meet the performance specifications of a 70-mm camera and reserved the right "to negotiate with firms having marginal technical proposals that may become acceptable to meet the requirements of the Air Force." 

Firms submitting acceptable technical proposals were to be invited to bid in phase two under normal formal advertising procedures, but required to price on the basis of the approved proposal. See AFPI 2-2100 et seq. 

The protesting bidder's proposal was rejected without negotiation in phase one because it was materially defective and, therefore, did not fall into the "marginal" category. This determination was made by five engineers who evaluated all of the proposals submitted. As a result it is argued that the two-step procedure is unreasonably restrictive of competition or, in the alternative, that the Air Force should have given the protesting bidder an opportunity to qualify the deficient proposal.

Held, the protest is denied. The Air Force two-step procedure was adopted at the suggestion of the Subcommittee for Special Investiga tions of the House Armed Services Committee. 

It is designed for use when existing specifications in technical procurements are not sufficiently definite to permit full and free competition without further negotiation between prospective offerors and the Government. The responsibility of evaluating proposals in phase one is solely that of the procuring activity. The purpose of two-step formal advertising is to achieve a broader use of formal advertising in situations where negotiation had previously been employed.

The Special Subcommittee anticipated the type of protest presented here and concluded that the expected benefits of two-step formal advertising outweighed its shortcomings. In addition, procurement agencies must have discretion to reasonably restrict competition where necessary to complete evaluations within existing time limitations. This discretion is illustrated by qualified products procurement where an award is not illegal simply because some of the bidders were unable to qualify their products in time. See 36 Comp. Gen. 809 (1957).

This reasoning supports, as a legitimate restriction on competition, the discretionary right of qualified procurement officials to summarily reject materially defective proposals in phase one. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143277, 20 July 1960, 40

Comp. Gen. 40. 

[Note: Two-step formal advertising is now provided for in ASPR § 2, Part 5.] 

17. Low Bid Which Was Signed by an Un authorized Agent of Bidder May Not Be Con sidered for Award Even Though Act Ratified by Bidder After Opening. The low bid on a construction project was defective because the agent who signed the bid on behalf of the bidder had no actual authority to act. While this act was ratified by the bidder after the opening of bids, the contracting officer determined that the low bid could not be considered for award. The low bidder protested the rejection and subsequent award to the second low bidder on the ground that actual authority was conferred on the agent after opening and that, in any event, the agent had apparent authority to act when the bids were submitted. 34 AGO 9111A

Held, the protest is denied. In formal advertising, a bidder may not withdraw a bid after opening until the time reserved by the 

Government to evaluate the bids has expired. 

Refining Associates v. United States, 124 Ct. 

Cl. 115 (1953). If a bidder on whose behalf an unauthorized agent has submitted a bid is permitted to have the option of ratification after opening, the value of competitive bidding would be impaired. Thus, a bid may not be considered for award unless at the time of submission it is a valid, irrevocable offer which will "ripen into a contract" if accepted by the Government within the time specified. 

It is argued that the bid was a valid, irrevocable offer since the agent had apparent authority to act. This argument is sound only if the apparent authority is so clear that the contracting officer would not be placed at a disadvantage by being required to accept the bid which was in fact unauthorized. See 15 

Comp. Gen. 566 (1935). But in this case the contracting officer knew that the agent did not have actual authority. Consequently, the doctrine of apparent authority was not applicable and the bidder could not have been bound at the time the bids were submitted. Cf. American Nat'l Bank v. Barlett, 40 F. 2d 21 (10th 

Cir. 1930).

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143416, 7 September 1960. 

18. Award Defective Where Bids Requested Upon F.O.B. Origin Basis Are Evaluated by Using Shipping Weights Submitted After Bid 

Opening. Basic unit prices in an Ordnance procurement were to be evaluated by adding the

Government's transportation cost from the point of origin to the destination. The invitation for bids, however, neither required bidders to state guaranteed shipping weights nor imposed liability upon the bidders for extra transportation costs caused by variations between the guaranteed and actual shipping weights. 

After bid opening, the two low bidders submitted the approximate weight of their units. 

Later, the second low bidder on the basis of unadjusted unit price advised that its shipping weight should have been 31 pounds less per unit. This correction was used by the contracting officer to evaluate the bids. As a result, the second low bidder became the low bidder, price and other factors considered. The rejected bidder protested.

Held, the protest is allowed. The award is defective because the contracting officer evaluated bids on the basis of shipping weights furnished and adjusted after bid opening. In f.o.b. origin bids, shipping weight is one of the "other factors considered" to fix the exact cost to the Government. See 37 Comp. Gen. 550 (1958). To permit this information to be submitted and changed after opening destroys the competitive character of formal advertising by allowing a bidder to vary his relative price position after bid opening. 17 Comp. Gen. 554 (1938). The result is a negotiation process not authorized by law.

To provide an equitable basis for evaluating transportation costs, the invitation for bids, where appropriate, should require prospective bidders to furnish guaranteed shipping weights prior to bid opening. See ASPR 1-1305.1 (1 

July 1960). 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143153, 9 September 

1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 160. 

[Note: While the contract award was im proper, the Comptroller General deemed it equitable to the contractor and in the interests of the Government to accept units already completed for delivery. The contract for the remaining units was cancelled.] 

19. Bidder Must Be Given Notice of Sus pected Error by Contracting Officer. (C.G.)

See MISTAKES IN BIDS (par. 4) 20. Comptroller General Overrules Decision Permitting Waiver of Prohibition of Tele graphic Bids. When no bid received met the invitation's delivery requirement, the contracting officer followed dicta in 34 Comp. Gen. 364 (1955) and accepted the best substitute offered. 

The mailed bid of the winning contractor had arrived three days late, but the contractor had advised the contracting officer by a telegram the day before bid opening that an offer of a certain price had been mailed. The contracting officer based the award on the telegram, although the invitation had provided that telegraphic bids would not be considered. The contracting officer relied on Ms. Comp. Gen. 

B-116567 (25 Aug 1953), which ruled that a prohibition of telegraphic bids could be waived AGO 9111A 35

if the reason for the rule-prejudice to other bidders did not exist. One of the rejected bidders protested, and the Comptroller General was asked for an opinion.

Held, waiver of the prohibition of telegraphic bids is disapproved, but the award will not be upset. Several decisions after Ms. 

Comp. Gen. B-116567 (25 Aug 1953) con sidered the acceptability of unauthorized telegraphic bids and uniformly decided they should be disregarded. Such a rule will, if uniformly followed, "best serve the interests of the United

States, as well as all potential suppliers to the 

Government." Therefore, Ms. Comp. Gen. B— 

116567 should no longer be followed. Nevertheless, "in the circumstances of this case we do not feel that the legality of the award should be further questioned."

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143376, 15 November 

1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 279. [Note: Telegraphic bids are acceptable only when specifically authorized by the invitation for bids. ASPR 2-202.2 and 2-301 (b); S.F. 33, par. 2(a). If telegraphic bids are authorized, the requirement of timely submission is applicable; the bidder must demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that a late telegraphic bid was filed with the telegraph company in time to have been delivered by "normal transmission procedure" before the time set for opening. ASPR 2-303.4. But see 37 Comp.

Gen. 595 (1958) (special IFB provision pre cluded consideration of late telegraphic bid even though delay excusable). On the other hand, telegraphic modifications of mailed bids are always authorized, subject to the rules governing "late" modifications. See ASPR 

2–305 (a) (1) (B); 35 Comp. Gen. 468 (1956), DA Pam 715-50-1, p. 104, par. 66. Thus, where telegraphic bids are not authorized, prospective suppliers may first submit a formal, mailed bid and thereafter protect themselves against price variations by the submission of timely telegraphic modifications. Cf. Ms. Comp. Gen. 

B-143470 (2 Sep 1960), digested under BIDS 

& AWARDS, par. 15. 

The instant opinion holds that a prohibition of telegraphic bids may never be waived. The justification for this rule is not clear. The mode of a bid's transmission would not seem to be a material element affecting price, quantity, or quality. Telegraphic facilities are probably equally available to all potential suppliers. 

Telegrams can incorporate by reference all promises required by the invitation. However, the rule denying waiver may arguably be based on considerations of prejudice and administrative burdens. The reference in the instant opinion to Ms. Comp. Gen. B-116567 (25 Aug 

1953) indicated obliquely that the Comptroller General believes the vice in telegraphic bids is the prejudice to bidders who obey the prohibition against them. Although it is doubtful that there will be prejudice whenever a bidder disobeys such a prohibition, the subjectivity of the determinations and the time involved in deciding whether prejudice actually exists may justify a blanket prohibition against waiver. 

Cf. 38 Comp. Gen. 532 (1959).

It may be argued, nevertheless, that the best solution is to eliminate the prohibition against telegraphic bids. Taking such action would not only remove the problems that waivers entail, but it would also prevent prejudice. When all bidders may telegraph, none can be prejudiced. Authorizing telegraphic bids in every procurement would not create administrative burdens. If proof of transmission in time for delivery before bid opening is more difficult to obtain for telegrams than for mailed or handdelivered bids, the added burden falls on contractors who choose to telegraph. ASPR 2303.4. It might be contended that the increased use of the telegram would increase the number of late bid determinations as bidders exercise a natural propensity to wait until the last minute. This propensity, though, must operate even when telegraphic bids are not allowed, and there is no reason to believe that there would be more late telegraphic bids than late mailed and hand-delivered bids. If it is argued that telegrams are not suited for submitting descriptive literature and samples, the answer is that such materials may be mailed or hand-delivered early because they involve little investigation and calculation.

Similarly, bid bonds may be mailed early if calculated on a price which is certain not to be lower than the telegraphed price. Cf. Ms. 

Comp. Gen. B-143470 (2 Sep 1960), digested 

36 AGO 9111A

under BIDS & AWARDS, par. 15. Moreover, there seems to be no reason why a bondsman could not telegraph his bond. Cf. Ms. Comp. 

Gen. B-141872 (7 Mar 1960), digested under

BIDS & AWARDS, par. 10. 

Perhaps the strongest argument against authorizing telegraphic bids lies in the availability of telegraphic modifications. Any bidder who needs all the available time to calculate his bid may telegraph at the last minute a modification of a price mailed earlier. Cf. Ms. 

Comp. Gen. B-143470 (2 Sep 1960), digested under BIDS & AWARDS, par. 15. This fact, however, is double-edged. It indicates not only that telegraphic bids are not needed, but also that prohibiting them is not soundly reasoned if their functional equivalent is unobjectionable. Little harm is caused by requiring bidders who wish to quote a price at the last minute to submit two documents when one would suffice. But there is correspondingly little justification. Thus it would seem best to eliminate the prohibition of telegraphic bids.] 

21. Bid Nonresponsive When Bidder Omits Descriptive Literature Required by Invitation as Part of Bid to Facilitate Evaluation. The National Aeronautics and Space Administra tion issued invitations for bids for the construction of a closed circuit television system at 

Wallops Island, Virginia. The invitation con tained the following requirements: 

Note "B":

The following data is required for evaluation of bids: 

3. A complete list of each system unit (amplifier, camera, camera control unit, pan-tilt mechanism, tripod monitor, cable, etc.) by manufacturer and type number. To this list shall be attached manufacturer's descriptive technical literature, and any other technical data necessary to establish that the unit will satisfy the specified unit and/or system performance. 

Note "C":

Bidders are cautioned that the above requirements for the submission of data should be strictly complied with. Failure to submit the data may be cause for rejection of the bid. When it is in the best interest of the Government, informalities in data furnished may be corrected prior to award if such informalities do not affect the price or quality.

The low, responsible bidder inadverently omitted the description of certain equalizing amplifiers which were essential to the proper operation of the unit offered. The bid was accompanied, however, by an over-all offer to comply with the specifications, notwithstanding any omissions or inadequacies in the de scriptive literature. The contracting officer re jected the bid as not responsive and the bidder protested.

Held, the protest is denied. First, the protesting bidder argues that it is impossible to describe every nut and bolt, particularly where the amplifiers represent barely more than 1% of the total bid price and were required to operate the system. However, the omission was material because not all equalizing amplifiers have the same performance capability and detailed information regarding the exact amplifier offered is required to determine if the proposed unit meets the specifications. Cf. Ms.

Comp. Gen. B-135865, 13 October 1958. This is not a case where the descriptive information was required to determine if the bidder could perform assuming that the unit offered met the specifications. See 37 Comp. Gen. 143 (1957). The information was requested as an integral part of the bid to evaluate the bidder's responsiveness rather than his responsibility. Consequently, the integrity of the competitive bidding system would be impaired if the bidder were permitted to submit a new bid after opening but before award. See United 

States v. Brookridge Farm, 111 F. 2d 461 

(10th Cir. 1940). 

Second, it is argued that the omission did not affect "price or quality" since the bidder intended to comply and inadvertently omitted the data and since an over-all offer to comply with the specifications was made with the bid. 

It is suggested, therefore, that the omission was a minor informality which the Government may waive under the invitation for bids. 

Even though the bidder mistakenly omitted the data and this mistake is apparent from the worksheets, the bid may not be corrected after opening because it was not responsive in the form submitted. 38 Comp. Gen. 819 (1959).

Further, an over-all offer to comply with specifications does not overcome an omission of material data required by the invitation for bids. 36 Comp. Gen. 415, 417 (1956). AGO 9111A 37

Exercising proper discretion, the contracting agency determined that descriptive literature concerning equalizing amplifiers was essential to a proper evaluation of bids and required in the invitation that such information be submitted with the bids. Notwithstanding the apparent discretion conferred on the contracting officer to determine whether an omission was an informality, any failure to comply must be regarded as material. 39 Comp. Gen. 595 (1960). In any event, the proper criterion for determining whether an omission is an informality is the difference between what is offered on the face of the bid and what is required by the invitation, not the difference between the invitation's requirement and what the bidder intended to bid. See 30 Comp. Gen. 

179 (1950). Consequently, the bid must be rejected under the circumstances of this case. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143688, 25 August 1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 132. 

[Note: In complex procurements where the specifications cannot be stated with certainty, descriptive literature is often requested as part of the bid to show exactly what the bidder intends to furnish. Cf. 17 Comp. Gen. 940, 944 (1938). The invitation for bids should clearly state: (1) what descriptive literature is re quired, (2) the purpose of its submission, and (3) the consequences if a bidder fails to comply. ASPR 2-202.5. See 36 Comp. Gen. 376 (1956). 

When the purpose of descriptive literature is to facilitate evaluation yet the invitation states or implies that regardless of the literature the specifications shall govern, a bid which is not accompanied by the required literature will be considered if the bidder offers to meet the specifications. See 39 Comp. Gen. 684 (1960); 38 Comp. Gen. 300 (1958). On the other hand, if rejection of bids is prescribed as the penalty for noncompliance, a general offer to meet the specifications will not save the bid.

Here the literature is made a material part of the bid and strict compliance is required. 36 

Comp. Gen. 415 (1956). But see 37 Comp. Gen. 

27 (1957) (offer to comply cures non-responsiveness caused by mistaken inclusion of unauthorized data). 

The contracting officer, however, may waive minor informalities in submission if his decision is based upon factors reasonably suggested by the invitation, 36 Comp. Gen. 380 (1956), and the bidder has substantially complied with the invitation. As was stated in 39 Comp. Gen. 595, 597 (1960): 

It is to be presumed that descriptive material or data required to be furnished by bidders with their bids is needed for some purpose relevant to the proper evaluation of the bids; if the purpose is reasonably clear and appears to be substantially met by the material furnished, we do not believe that the interest of the Government or of competing bidders require that a bid be rejected because of deficiencies merely of form. 

Therefore, if the contracting agency requires descriptive literature as part of the bid and specifies rejection as a penalty for non-compliance, the invitation imposes a material condition with which all bidders must substantially comply. In the instant case, the contracting officer had authority to correct minor deficiencies not affecting price or quality. The omission of equalizing amplifiers, however, made uncertain the quality of the unit offered by the protesting bidder. Notwithstanding the dictum that "where the language of an invitation requires the submission of data with the bid any failure to comply therewith must be regarded as material," 40 Comp. Gen. 132, 135 (1960), it is suggested that the instant case holds that the omission was not substantial compliance, rather than that the contracting officer had no authority to waive any minor deviation from the invitation.

If the stated purpose of descriptive literature is to determine the bidder's performance capability, i.e., responsibility, rather than whether the unit offered meets the specifications, i.e., responsiveness, a different rule is applicable: an omission at the time of bid opening may be waived even though the invitation states that defective submissions will be cause for rejection. The bidder, of course, must offer to meet the specifications and actually supply the requested information in time for a determination of responsibility prior to award. 37 Comp. 

Gen. 143 (1957). In most cases, the nature of the requested information will indicate that its purpose is to evaluate the bidder's capacity and credit. See 39 Comp. Gen. 247 (1959) (list 38 AGO 9111 A

BIDS & AWARDS Continued of subcontractors); 39 Comp. Gen. 881 (1960) (list of business affiliates); 39 Comp. Gen. 62 (1959) (proposed sources of financing). But as the instant case suggests, the crucial factor is whether the descriptive literature is required by the invitation as part of the bid or simply for the benefit of the Government. See 37

Comp. Gen. 143, 146 (1957). This question must be resolved by resort to the language of the invitation for bids.] 

22. Comptroller General Interprets Require ment of Filing Telegraphic Modifications in

Time for Delivery by Normal Transmission Pro cedure-Obviously Tentative Mailed Bid May

Be Disregarded. According to ASPR 2-303.4 

and 2-305: 

A late telegraphic [modification] shall be presumed to have been filed with the telegraph company too late to be received in time, except where the bidder demonstrates by clear and convincing evidence which includes substantiation by an authorized official of the telegraph company that the [modification] as received in the office designated in the invitation for bids, was filed with the telegraph company in sufficient time to have been delivered on time by normal transmission procedure, so as not to have been late.

The Comptroller General applied this rule in two opinions involving telegraphic modifications received after bid opening. (a) In Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144371, 16 November 1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 290, the low bidder mailed a bid of $2,500,000 for a procurement in which the other bids were around $4,000,000. 

Forty minutes before the bid opening in New 

York City the low bidder sent an RX (high priority) telegram from Newtonville, Massachusetts, to increase the bid. The telegram arrived ten minutes after bid opening. To prove the telegram had been timely deposited, the bidder submitted evidence of a test transmission over the same route. He also provided statements by Western Union officials that a telegram sent at the time and under the circumstances when the modification was transmitted should have been delivered before the bid opening. The Comptroller General was asked whether the modification should be considered effective. 

Held, the modification may not be considered for award. A bidder must show that his message was deposited in sufficient time to allow for any "normal, usual, or forseeable delays." 

39 Comp. Gen. 586 (1960). Even though an

RX telegram has preference over regular telegrams, the bidder could not reasonably have believed that delivery of his telegram within forty minutes would be prevented only if there were abnormal, unusual or unforeseeable delays. At most, the evidence presented shows that the telegram could have been delivered within forty minutes under favorable conditions. Yet although the mailed bid may not be modified, it may be disregarded because it is clear from the record that it was only tentative. (b) In Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144206, 6 December 1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 337, a bidder in New 

York City sent the contracting officer in Chicago a day letter telegram as a bid modification.

Although it was deposited for transmission nearly four and one-half hours before bid opening, the telegram arrived an hour after the opening. The bidder furnished a statement from Western Union that unexpected congestion in the traffic department at the New York office had delayed the bidder's telegram four hours, but that the normal time. for transmitting a day letter from New York City to

Chicago was one hour plus delivery time at the destination. The bidder protested to the 

Comptroller General when the telegraphic modification was not considered. 

Held, the modification must be disregarded. 

A day-letter telegram is a deferred service. The only assurance given by Western Union is that such a message will be delivered on the day of transmission. It is reasonable to conclude, therefore, that the tardiness of the modification was a result of the bidder's failure to select a priority service. 

23. Rejecting All Bids and Readvertising a 

Procurement May Be Justified by the Possibility That Readvertising With Changed Specifica tions Will Produce a Substantial Saving. An invitation for bids on garbage removal from 

Ft. McNair required collection from 32-gallon cans at many points and from 5-cubic-yard containers at a few points where extra garbage was deposited. The contractor was to supply the 5-cubic-yard containers. Bids were received from B Co., S Co., and S Bros., quoting monthly AGO 9111A -39

rates of $850, $1,300, and $1,362, respectively.

The bid of B Co. offered a combination of smaller containers in place of each 5-cubic-yard container. The B Co. complained that the specifications were restrictive because equivalent service could be provided more cheaply if a combination of smaller containers were substituted for each 5-cubic-yard container. The procurement agency proposed to reject the bid of B Co. as nonresponsive and to accept the bid of S Co. However, higher authority disapproved the proposed award on the ground that an expenditure of $1,300 monthly was unjustified because collection solely from 32-gallon containers had previously cost only $900 monthly. The procurement agency was directed to reject all bids and to send out a new invitation with a provision permitting offers of containers smaller than 5-cubic yards. On the readvertisement, bids were received from B Co., S Co., and S Bros., for $725, $1,357.50 and $1,442 per month, respectively. The latter two firms bid on providing 5-cubic-yard containers; the first firm bid on providing a combination of smaller containers. The S Co., protested the readvertisement, arguing that bids once disclosed should be rejected only for a reason more cogent than the possibility of a substantial saving. Held, there is no legal basis for questioning the readvertisement. On the basis of the bids received on the first invitation, a 35% saving appeared possible if small containers were permitted. A 45% saving was actually achieved by the readvertisement. The S Co. contends that such a saving was not a sufficient reason for readvertising. However, the primary purpose of formal advertising is to obtain the best price competition affords. A cardinal tenet of formal advertising is that specifications should be only as broad as necessary to meet the Government's needs. We have consistently agreed with the dictum in Massman Constr. Co. v. 

United States, 102 Ct. Cl. 699, 719 (1945) that only for cogent reasons should a procurement be advertised after bids have been opened. Yet not infrequently prospective contractors think of ways to fulfill the Government's needs in a manner not contemplated by and less costly than that specified in an invitation. If the possible saving is first brought to the attention of the procurement personnel by an unresponsive bid, we are aware of no principle requiring them to make an award on the basis of specifications that have been shown to be unnecessarily restrictive and costly. Such a saving may well be a cogent reason for rejecting all bids and readvertising. The decision that there may be a substantial saving may not, of course, be arbitrary and capricious. On this basis, 39 

Comp. Gen. 396 (1959) must be distinguished from this case. There the differences between the specifications for the two invitations were insubstantial and there was no indication when the bids from the first invitation were rejected that any substantial saving might result from readvertising with new specifications. The facts in the instant case demonstrate a reasonable basis for the conclusion that the increased cost involved did not justify the allegedly superior service resulting from the use of 5cubic-yard containers. The decision to accept the use of smaller containers at a substantial saving appears to have been a proper exercise of administrative discretion. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143263, 22 December 1960. 

24. Where the Surety's Liability on an In complete Bid Bond Is Clear From the Bid as a

Whole the Bid Is Valid-Where the Amount of the Bid Bond Is Left Blank but the Obligation of the Surety in the Required Amount Is Clear the Bid Is Valid. The Bureau of Public Roads opened bids for the construction of a public parkway and found that the low bidder had submitted a proper bid but had omitted the penal sum from the accompanying bid bond. 

The bid contained the statement: "Enclosed is bid guarantee, consisting of Bid Bond in the amount of five percent (5%) of amount bid."

Both the low bidder and the surety wrote letters after the bid opening. The surety claimed that it had deliberately left the space for penal sum blank and had authorized the bidder to fill in the required amount, five percent of the bid price. The bidder claimed that the bond had been issued with the understanding that the penal amount would be filled in by the bidder, but that through oversight the amount had been omitted. The Bureau of Public Roads re- 40 AGO 9111A

BIDS & AWARDS Continued quested a decision by the Comptroller General whether award could be made to the low bidder. 

Held, award can be made to the low bidder on the basis of the bid submitted. The question for consideration is whether the bid bond as submitted could be enforced against the surety. 

It appears to be established by the record that the surety authorized the bidder to insert the penal sum in the bid bond. Even without the confirmation of the surety it would appear that such authority could be inferred. See Butler v. 

United States, 88 U.S. (21 Wall.) 272 (1875); 

Stearns, Suretyship, § 2.12. We are therefore of the opinion that the bond, read in connection with the bid to which it is attached, is sufficiently complete to support an action against the surety in case of default. In addition although the decisions are in conflict, there is substantial authority in support of the view that the Government as obligee in the bond has implied authority to fill in the blank. See Annotation at 37 A.L.R. 1395 (1925). In the circumstances here the intention of the parties respecting the obligation of the surety is so clear that a binding contract exists. Therefore, the bid may be considered for award. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144356, 23 November 

1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 314. 

25. Failure To Give Timely Notice of Product Qualification Requirement to Interested Sup plier Invalidates the Invitation for Bids. On 17 

June 1960, an Air Force procurement activity issued an invitation for bids on safety glasses.

The invitation provided: 

[A]wards will be made only for such products as have, prior to the time set for opening of bids, been tested and qualify for inclusion in the Qualified Products List . . ., whether or not such products have actually been included in the list by that date. 

Manufacturers are urged to communicate with the 

Bureau of Ships, Department of the Navy, Washington 25, D.C. and arrange to have the products that they propose to offer tested for qualification. 

When the bids were opened as scheduled on 19 July 1960, it was found that the low bidder had not had his product qualified as required. The low bidder held the contract for supplying the product immediately prior to the period covered by the invitation. No qualification was required under the earlier contract. The low bidder had not been notified when, shortly after 18 February 1960, the procuring installation had learned that an Interim Federal Specification requiring qualification testing for safety glasses had been approved for Air Force use. About 13

May 1960 he had been notified that a new specification requiring qualification of safety glasses had been published and that an invitation for bids incorporating the specification would be issued soon if the specification was applicable to Air Force procurements. About 14 June 

1960, the low bidder had been advised to make efforts to qualify his product for the instant procurement. The contracting officer proposed to reject the low bid for failure to offer glasses on the Qualified Products List. The low bidder protested, claiming he had been given insufficient notice to permit him to qualify his product. The Comptroller General was asked for an opinion.

Held, the low bidder was given inadequate notice. ASPR and AFPI 1-1103.1 require that when the qualified product method of procurement is to be used, all firms known to be interested will be individually contacted in sufficient time to arrange for qualification before the first procurement and advised of the need for qualification and the name and address of the agency from which further information may be obtained. It is conceded that the low bidder, who as the current contractor should have been regarded as an interested person, was not given the required notice when the procuring agency first learned that a qualified products list for safety glasses had been approved for Air Force use. The argument made is that the procurement should not be invalidated by that failure to give notice because the low bidder was advised of the intended procurement and the qualification requirement in sufficient time prior to bid opening to have permitted qualification if normal diligence had been used. However, the notification around May 13 cannot be regarded as adequate because it indicated only the possibility that the specification would be employed and since it was not accompanied by the name and address of the office to which the qualification request should be submitted. With respect to the June 14 communication, even if the low bidder had gone forward at that time with an attempt at qualification, the possibility AGO 9111A 41

of meeting the deadline was remote. The record indicates that the normal time for qualifying glasses is sixty to ninety days, but that the period "might" be shortened to thirty to sixty days by special handling if "all phases of the process were completely satisfactory." Thus the low bidder could have competed only if the qualification process could have been completed within the first few days of a period described as minimal and put forth only reluctantly and conditionally by the testing agency. Moreover, meeting the deadline would have depended not only upon unusual efforts by the testing agency, but also upon "all phases of the process being completely satisfactory." This apparently would impose a much higher standard upon the low bidder than on those prospective suppliers who were notified at the time and in the manner contemplated by the regulations. Under these circumstances, there is no reason not to apply the general rule invalidating invitations when there is a failure to conform to the material requirements of regulations designed to obtain for the United States the benefits of full and free competition. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143792, 9 December 1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 348.

27. Government Invitations and Contracts May Contain a Provision That All Subcontracts Are Subject to the Approval of the Contracting Officer on the Basis of the Proposed Subcontractor's Qualifications To Perform in a Capable and Responsible Manner. (JAGT) See SUBCONTRACTS (par. 6) 28. Contracting Officer Properly Refused To 

Consider Bid That Neither Was Accompanied

By Material Showing Bidder's Intent To Be Bound Nor Bore Any Signature Other Than Typewritten One Not Shown To Be Authorized. 

The low bid in response to an invitation was submitted in triplicate, as required, and each copy of the bid form and an amendment thereto bore in the proper places the typewritten name and address of the bidder as well as the name and title of the bidder's president. However, no signature appeared on any of the copies of the bid in the block entitled "Signature of Person 

Authorized To Sign Bid," nor was there any accompanying letter or any place on the bid or amendment that bore any signature. The bidder protested to the Comptroller General the contracting officer's decision to reject the bid for want of a signature. In support of the protest a letter was filed stating that the bidder's president, a responsible officer of the firm, had personally prepared the bid, typed in the information required on the bid forms, and mailed the bid with the clear intent to bind the bidder.

The 

Held, the bid properly was rejected. contention that the lack of a signature was inadvertent is not questioned. The decisive issue is whether acceptance of the bid as submitted would bind the bidder. Ms. Comp. Gen. B- 

131767 (20 Jun 1957). A bid lacking a signature may be considered only if (1) the bidder has formally adopted or authorized the execution of documents by typewritten, printed, or rubber-stamped signature and submits evidence of such authorization, and the bid carries such a signature, or (2) the bid includes other material indicating clearly that the bidder intended to be bound by the bid. ASPR 2-402; 

34 Comp. Gen. 439 (1955). In the instant case the bid was not accompanied by anything bearing a signature, and the administrative office reports having no information whatever that the bidder has ever adopted or authorized the execution of documents by a typewritten name. 

Therefore, the bidder could have accepted or rejected a tendered award. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144185, 25 January 1961. 

29. Where Prices On Sub-Items Were Separable, Late Bid Modification Could Be Accepted On Sub-Items For Which Sender Was Already The Low Bidder. A Quartermaster Depot issued an invitation for bids on a total of 156,800 undershirts to four destinations and a total of 129,040 shorts to two destinations. The clothing for each destination was listed as a separate subitem. The invitation provided that unless a bidder specified otherwise, the Government could accept any item or group of items and any quantity less than that bid upon. When the bids were opened, the contracting officer found 42 AGO 9111A

that M was low bidder on the 129,040 shorts and on 96,800 undershirts. F was low bidder on the remaining 60,000 undershirts. A telegram received from M after the bid opening lowered his prices on all sub-items. If considered effective, the telegram would have made M low bidder for the entire procurement. The contracting officer determined that the tardiness of the telegram was not due solely to transmission delay. 

He rejected the modifications that would have displaced F, but accepted the modifications for the garments on which M was originally the low bidder. In his bid and modifications the only limitation M had placed on the award he would accept was a specification that 50,000 garments was a minimum. M protested that the 

Government had not reserved the right to accept a late modification of a bid and that the telegram should have been rejected in full. The protest was referred to the Comptroller General. 

Held, the contracting officer acted properly. 

First, the limitation on considering late modifications was designed solely to prevent any bidder from obtaining an unfair advantage.

Leitman v. United States, 104 Ct. Cl. 324 

(1945). There can be no objection to a low bidder voluntarily decreasing the amount of his bid. Second, the prices quoted for the subitems were separable. The bid quoted separate prices for each sub-item. Although afforded an opportunity to specify maximum or minimum quantities for each item, M did not do so. 

Instead, he merely stated that he would accept award exceeding the minimum he specified. combination of shorts and undershirts. He cannot now complain, for he has received an award exceeding the premium he specified. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144430, 20 February 1961, 40 Comp. Gen. 466. 

30. Invitation Should Be Cancelled Because 

It Disclosed Proprietary Data Submitted in Confidence to the Government by One of the 

Bidders-Government Should Not Infringe Proprietary Right by Competitive Procurement. 

The G Co. submitted to the Air Force an unsolicited proposal for improving static dischargers. After examining the proposal, the Air 

Force requested the G Co. to incorporate the suggested improvements into an exhibit to mili tary specifications. The firm furnished the exhibit to the Air Force, subject to the condition that the information would "be handled in accordance with established governmental procedures for safeguarding such . . . information against unauthorized disclosure." The pertinent Air Force regulation provided that: 

Unsolicited proposals, articles, and disclosures will not be reproduced, copied, photographed, or reduced to drawings, except for record or necessary administrative purpose 

If, after evaluation, the subject matter of a particular unsolicited disclosure or other submission is desired for any purpose other than record purposes, action should be taken to obtain that subject matter by normal procurement contracting procedures.

The Air Force asked the G Co. to submit a proposal for 133,500 static discharges to be manufactured in accordance with the military specifications and the firm's exhibit. The D Co. 

was also given an opportunity, under the twostep method of advertising; to submit a technical proposal responsive to the specification and the G Co.'s exhibit. However, the G Co. had given the Air Force no permission to show the exhibit to the D Co. Pursuant to a subsequent invitation, the G and D Companies submitted bids. The D Co. was the low bidder. The G Co. protested to the Comptroller General, claiming that the firm's exhibit had been used in a manner inconsistent with the Government's obligation to treat the exhibit as confidential. 

Held, the integrity of the Government as a contractor requires that the invitation be cancelled. The information included in the exhibit constituted proprietary data and was disclosed contrary to the Air Force's regulation. An award under the invitation would not be "most advantageous to the United States," as required by 10 U.S.C. § 2305 (c). Any contract awarded to the low bidder would embody specifications that were not rightfully the Government's property and would unreasonably compound the injury already suffered by the G Co. Moreover, the Government should not infringe a proprietary right by competitive procurement. It should be noted that the G Co. has no readily available statutory remedy to pursue as would be the case if a patent were infringed under a Govern ment contract. 28 U.S.C. § 1498; 38 Comp. Gen. 

276 (1958).

In this connection, attention should AGO 9111A 43

BIDS & AWARDS—Continued be paid Public Law 85-726, 74 Stat. 855, which extends the provisions of 28 U.S.C. § 1498 to infringements by the Government, or by any contractor acting with its consent, of any work protected under the copyright laws. See also 

Towle v. Ross, 32 F. Supp. 125 (D. Ore. 1940).

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143711, 22 December 1960. 

31. Comptroller General Analyzes Consequences of Failure To Submit Descriptive Literature Required To Show Whether Product Offered by Bidder Is Equal to Specified Brandname Article. The Comptroller General in two opinions analyzed the effect of bidders' failures to comply with special rules for bidding on products advertised on a "brand-name or equal" basis. (a) In Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144912, 8 February 1961, the invitation described 16 articles in terms of "brand-name or equal." The invitation provided that a bid would be rejected unless it either stated that a brand name was offered or described in detail the "or equal" article offered. 

The Comptroller General was asked whether the procuring agency could consider a bid that did not indicate whether brand-name articles or their equal were offered. 

Held, the bid may not be considered. The requirement that information deemed essential to evaluation of bids be submitted cannot be waived. 36 Comp. Gen. 415 (1956). The omis sion of such information goes to the "substance of the bid." 30 Comp. Gen. 179 (1950); Ms.

Comp. Gen. B-139761, 15 June 1959. To con sider the bid involved in the instant case would give the bidder the option after bid opening of either securing or avoiding an award. The established rule is that giving a bidder two chances at a procurement in such a fashion would prejudice other bidders and conflict with the purposes of the competitive bidding statutes. See, e.g., 38 Comp. Gen. 532, 536 (1959). (b) In Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144753, 30 January 1961, 40 Comp. Gen. 435, the AEC had advertised for bids on 560 Radiation Biology

Accessory Kits. The invitation described the 

25 articles in each kit in terms of "brand-name or equal" and provided that:

Bids offering articles other than brand-name articles referenced in this invitation will be considered: 

Provided, that such offered articles are clearly 

identified in the bids and bidders furnish with their bids (1) descriptive material . . . which will clearly show the characteristics of the articles offered, and (2) a statement showing in detail the differences between the articles offered and those referenced in the invitation. Failure to furnish the information required by (1) and (2) above will require rejection of the bids.

The low bidder, ARL, included with the bid a 

"List of Contents Atom-Kit No. 160" listing each of the articles to be supplied, along with the quantity and the ARL model number of each. Under the heading "Brand Name," the list indicated that on 9 of the 25 articles ARL 

was offering the brand-name product specified in the invitation. On 12 articles the list indicated that ARL was offering substitute articles, named the manufacturer of the articles, and advised that the articles were the same brand supplied to the AEC in 1960 by ARL under another contract. The list stated that samples of the 12 articles were available on request. 

On the remaining 4 articles the list named manufacturers other than ARL and showed the ARL model number assigned to the articles, but failed to indicate such articles were provided under the 1960 contract. That contract had involved kits identical to those advertised in the present invitation, and had been fulfilled by ARL's delivery of the identical articlesincluding the four identified only by manufacturers' names and ARL model number-that were tabulated in the "List of Contents" submitted in response to the present invitation. 

All articles furnished under the prior contract were found to be equal to the brand names specified in the present invitation. The AEC asked the Comptroller General whether ARL's bid was responsive. 

Held, the bid is responsive. The general rule is that a descriptive data requirement, accompanied by language compelling rejection of bids that fail to comply with the requirement, must be construed and enforced as written. However, as stated at 39 Comp. Gen. 595, 597 (1960), an automatic rejection of a bid because of a failure to conform to a purely technical or too literal reading of the stated requirements may be as arbitrary as the waiver of non-responsiveness to a material and substantial requirement. That decision stated that the purpose of 44 AGO 9111A

data required with a bid is to permit the procuring agency to determine what the bidder proposes, and will be bound, to furnish if awarded the contract. Therefore, a distinction must be drawn, with respect to failures to comply fully with data requirements, between a failure to comply resulting in doubt as to the precise articles offered or the performance standards to which the bidder will be bound by a contract, and a failure that does not affect the ability of the procuring agency to evaluate the bid and to bind the bidder to strict compliance with the specifications by accepting the bid. While the provisions of the instant invitation, as quoted above, are prescribed by FPR 

1-1.307-6(b), the only legitimate purpose served by requiring bidders to submit descriptive material and a statement of differences if a bid offers articles other than the brand-name products specified by the invitation is to assure the availability of sufficient information to permit the procuring agency to determine (1) the exact nature of the articles offered by a bidder and (2) whether those articles are equal for the Government's purposes, to those specified by brand name in the invitation. In the absence of any disclosure in the brand-name specification of the particular characteristics that are considered essential to the Government's needs or material to the determination of equality of other brands, strict and literal enforcement of the requirement of a "statement showing in detail the differences between the articles offered and those referenced in the invitation" could easily result in rejection of bids offering articles in every material respect suitable for the Government's requirements simply because a bidder failed to point out wholly immaterial differences. The imperative phrasing of the requirement also tends to discourage offering of alternative brands.

Since the kit involved in the present invitation and the kit supplied by ARL in 1960 are identical and all of the substitute articles in the 1960 kit were satisfactory and equal to the brand-name products specified in the present invitation, there is no basis for contending that 

ARL's failure to comply literally with the descriptive material requirement precludes an adequate or accurate evaluation of the bid.

Nor would any doubt exist about the exact articles ARL would be bound to supply if its bid were accepted. The bid should, therefore, be considered responsive.

Attention is invited to the provisions of 

FPR 1-1.307-4 expressing preference for use of purchase descriptions consisting of references to more than one commercial product described by brand name and number. It is suggested that, in future procurements of articles advertised on an "or equal" basis, consideration be given to including specific reference in the invitation of all articles previously purchased and found satisfactory. No useful purpose appears to be served by requiring the submission of detailed descriptive data on articles known to meet the needs of the procuring agency.

May Be Considered Responsive Because Responsible Government Employees Established 

Both That the Omission of the Bond Was In advertent and That the Contractor Had No Opportunity To Choose Whether To Submit the Bond. (C.G.) See BONDS (par. 9) 

33. Bid Was Properly Submitted Even 

Though Given to Bid Opening Officer in Room

Other Than the One Where Invitation Provided 

Bids "Will Be Received"-Bid Opening Officer

Has Discretion To Determine When Bid Open ing Time Occurs. An invitation for bids provided that bids "will be received at Room 300" of a designated building until 1100 hours, 17 

May. A notice posted in the building's lobby stated that bids would be received in Room 

300 and opened in Room 527b. The low bid was submitted to the bid opening officer in 

Room 527b on 17 May at what the clock on the wall and the watch of the bid opening officer's counsel indicated was 1059 hours. The second low bidder protested against a proposed award to the low bidder on the grounds that the low bid had not been submitted at Room 300 "as required" and had been late because it was not delivered to that place before 1100 hours. It was also urged that, because the wall clock in Room 527b and the time stamp in 

Room 300 were not coordinated, the bid open AGO 9111A 45

BIDS & AWARDS Continued ing officer had no way of knowing that the low bid had been submitted before the time for bid submission had passed on the time stamp in Room 300.

Held, protest denied. The invitation's provision that bids "will be received" in Room 300 does not appear to have been written with the intent that a timely submission of a bid to the proper Government official in any other place would be invalid. Rather, it seems more reasonable to interpret the provision as notifying a bidder that he could insure consideration of his bid by submitting it at the designated room within the designated time.

The bid was not late. The purpose of the rule requiring timely submission is to eliminate the opportunity for bidders to commit fraud or to have an undue advantage over other bidders. All that should be required is that a bid be in the hands of the bid opening officer, or other Government representative authorized to receive it, at opening time. As to when the opening time occurred, there could in most cases be a dispute. It is presumably for that reason that under ASPR 2-204.1 the bid opening officer has authority to decide when the opening time arrives. In the instant case he determined that the low bid was timely submitted. While it has been demonstrated that the clock the officer used as the standard may have varied from the correct time, there has been neither an allegation nor proof that the time set for the receipt of bids had expired when the bid opening officer accepted the low bid. At the very least, there is a presumption of the correctness of the time used by the bid opening officer, and that presumption has not been overcome. See Ms. Comp. Gen. B-137686, 24 October 1958. In view of the foregoing, and because there is no showing the low bidder was given an unfair advantage, the low bid could properly be considered for award. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145961, 21 June 1961, 40

Comp. Gen. 709. 

34. Bid Responsive Even Though It Offered Prices Based on Increments Different From 

Those on Which the Invitation Sought Quotations. An invitation for bids on aircraft maintenance stands provided that "Bids shall be submitted in the following increments: "from 189 each to 376 each inclusive "from 377 each to 564 each inclusive "from 565 each to 750 each inclusive "from 751 each to 938 each inclusive."

The low bidder, instead of bidding on the designated increments, submitted the following bid prices:

Quantity 

200 each 

375 each 

550 each 

750 each 

Unit price $503.30 482.65 

456.35 

An award for 751 units was made to the low bidder at a unit price of $456.35. The next low bidder protested to the Comptroller General, arguing that (a) the invitation required submission of bids in the stated increments and failure to do so rendered the low bid nonresponsive; (b) the low bid should be interpreted as offering to furnish only the four listed quantities and thus not only was nonresponsive but also could not properly be compared with bids conforming to the invitation because the latter had to average in the higher unit costs for lower quantities, thus presenting a higher price for the specific quantity offered by the low bid; (c) the low bid offered to furnish a maximum of 750 units, so an award of 751 units was a counter-offer, which the low bidder could accept or reject.

Held, protest denied. First, it is not reasonable to interpret the low bid as offering only the four quantities listed. No reason appears for any bidder to limit his offer in that fashion. 

If a bidder is willing to furnish 375 units he reasonably may be expected to furnish 374 or 376 units. In view of this and of the positioning in the low bid of the unit quantities opposite the stated increments, the unit prices clearly were intended to apply to any quantities between the numbers listed. In this connection, informal advice indicates that the cost of aluminum, the largest constituent of the item procured, changed at the quantities listed in the low bid. This fact also tends to establish that the low bid should properly be interpreted as offering quantities in increments, although using points of division differing from those proposed by the invitation form. Second, even if the use of different division points could have 46 AGO 9111A

given the low bidder an undue advantagesince the higher unit cost of the lower quantities within the quantity groups stated in the invitation would not have been averaged into the lower unit cost of the higher quantities within the same respective groups-there is no indication of any undue advantage in the instant case. The low bid on the lowest category is lower than the second low bid on the second category, the low bid on the second category is lower than the second low bid on the third category, and so forth. Therefore, even if the advantage obtained by the low bidder in reorganizing the increments is taken into account, the low bid on any quantity category is still lower than that of any other bidder. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145813, 1 June 1961, 40

Comp. Gen. 653. 

35. Procuring Agencies Have Discretion in Determining Whether Available Data Is So Inadequate That Use of Two-Step Formal Advertising Is Justified-Two-Step Formal Advertis ing Is Not Improper Even Though Bidders

Cannot Base Bid Prices on Cheaper Components That Might Become Available After Technical Proposals Are Accepted. A bidder on an Air 

Force procurement handled through two-step formal advertising protested against the procedures used. He argued (1) that the procurement should have been handled through singlestep formal advertising, and (2) that if bidders were required to conform to the technical proposal submitted during the first step of the two-step procedure, free and open competition was eliminated because bidders would be precluded from basing their bid prices on cheaper components that might become available after acceptance of the technical proposals. 

Held, protest denied. First, before the procurement was opened to bidders, the available data was reviewed and was determined to be inadequate to meet the requirements of singlestep advertised procurement and to be best suited for the two-step method. The Air Force states that the insufficiency of the procurement data for single-step procurement is demonstrated by the fact that changes in thirty-five discrepant areas in the technical proposals submitted in the first step were required in order to arrive at a satisfactory basis of understanding. The procurement officials are better qualified to evaluate the sufficiency of available technical data to determine whether it is satisfactory to procure equipment with the qualitative requirements established, and the determination of those officials will not be overturned in the instant case.

Second, the contention about lack of freedom to bid on the lowest priced equipment available cannot be accepted as a valid basis for questioning the procedures followed. In submitting technical proposals, bidders were left free by the request for proposals to select any component that would meet the minimum requirements of the specifications. Furthermore, the 

Air Force states that to permit bidders to submit prices on the basis of using different components from those indicated in their technical proposals would require additional technical evaluation that would so delay the procurement as as to nullify the advantages sought to be obtained from the use of the two-step system. The Air Force points out that the time interval between the two proposals was the same for all bidders so that no bidder was prejudiced for this reason. The controlling rule was stated in 40 Comp. Gen. 40 (1960): "[A] procedure that permits procurement officials to reasonably circumscribe the area of consideration of proposals in certain cases is necessary if they are to achieve evaluation and consummate their commitments within their limitations."

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144432, 16 March 1961, 40 Comp. Gen. 514. 

36. Bid May Be Evaluated on Basis of Discount Mentioned on Only One of Three Bid Copies Submitted. The discount would make the bid lowest, displacing another bid.

some ambiguity in the bid as submitted, the contracting officer interpreted the discount noted on one copy as being applicable to all copies. This interpretation was proper under the principle that an ambiguous bid is to be construed against the bidder. 39 Comp. Gen. 

546 (1960).
