38. Where Cancellation Would Cause Unac ceptable Delay in Construction Needed for Na tional Defense, Contract Should Not Be Can celled Even Though It Was Awarded on Basis of Erroneous Determination That Bidder Met 

Requirement of Being a Small Business. The 

Air Force solicited bids on a SAC missile facility construction project that was restricted to small business concerns. The second low bidder asked the SBA to determine whether the low bidder was a small business. The SBA held the low bidder qualified as a small business, and the Air Force awarded a contract to the low bidder. The second low bidder then persuaded the Comptroller General to ask the SBA to reconsider the determination that the low bidder was a small business. The SBA held the earlier determination had been erroneous. The second low bidder asked the Comptroller General to direct cancellation of the award to the low bidder. 

Held, the award should not be cancelled. The

Air Force advised that cancellation would cause serious and unacceptable delay in the construction project. Although 34 Comp. Gen. 115 (1954) held a contract should be cancelled because its recipient was not a small business, the instant case involves a project closely identified with the national defense effort and cancellation would be deterimental to the best interests of the Government. Consequently, the Government is not required to, and should not, cancel the contract. See Ms. Comp. Gen. B-137689 (14 Jun 1960 and 21 Jan 1959); 37 Comp. Gen. 

679 (1958). 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145948, 2 August 1961. 

39. Oral Notice of Award of Formally Advertised Contract Is Not a Binding Acceptance. 

The P Co. submitted a bid on Standard Form 

21, which provided in part: 

[The bidder agrees] . . . that, upon written acceptance of this bid, mailed, or otherwise furnished, within 30 calendar days . . . after the date of opening of bids, he will within 10 calendar days. after receipt of the prescribed forms, execute 

Standard Form 23, Construction Contract, and give performance bond and payment bond . . . . 

The contracting officer by telephone notified the P Co. that it was awarded a contract for the two items on which it was low bidder. A written Notice to Proceed was sent to the P Co. 

However, no Notice of Award was ever furnished the P Co. in written form. The P Co. contended no contract had been made, and the contracting officer reprocured the work at a cost greater than the price the P Co. had bid.

A dispute arose over whether the surety on the P Co.'s bid bond was liable for the excess costs. 

The Judge Advocate General was asked for an opinion. 

Held, the surety may not be assessed excess costs. No binding contract was formed. The 

Comptroller General has ruled that the requirement in 10 U.S.C. § 2305 (c) of a written notice of award clearly forbids the oral formation of a formally advertised contract, even though the invitation provides that the award may be mailed or "otherwise furnished" the bidder. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-122888, 18 Apr 1955; Ms.

Comp. Gen. B-109054, 30 Jun 1952. The Notice to Proceed stated "In accordance with your accepted bid, you are hereby notified to proceed with the specified work under the above contract

It is obvious that the Government did not intend to consider that Notice as a written acceptance meeting the statutory requirement. 

JAGT 1961/6588, 6 June 1961. 

[Note: A portion of the material forwarded to the Judge Advocate General indicated that the procuring activity had been directed by its headquarters not to issue a Notice of Award so that the Government would not be bound before a formal contract was signed. The Judge Advocate General recommended that this practice be brought to the attention of DCSLOG for any remedial action necessary in light of ASPR 

2-407.1, which provides in part: 48 AGO 9111A

Awards shall be made by mailing or otherwise furnishing to the bidder a properly executed award document. . . or notice of award on such form as may be prescribed by the procuring activity.] 

40. Readvertising Must Be Undertaken When Substantial Changes Are Made in Specifications After Bid Opening and Before Award. The Air 

Force advertised for bids on an air base communications system. The low bidder alleged he had intended to bid $6,656,731.61, rather than $4,947,707, the bid price. He was able to prove an error was made but not what his intended price was, so the Comptroller General ordered the bid disregarded. Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145109, 10 Mar 1961. The Comptroller General com mented that because of a large gap between the price the low bidder claimed he intended to bid and the low acceptable bid, readvertisement might be considered. The procurement was readvertised under the same specifications, with some differences in the applicable prevailing wage rates. The bids of the firms bidding on each advertisement were:

Bidder 

First advertisment 

$4,947,707.00

$8,508,300.00

$9,911,000.00

$12,740,000.00

$13,573,175.77

$13,790,000.00

Readvertisment 

$8,420,000.00 $8,658,000.00 $10,488,000.00 $8,947,000.00 $11,461,377.23 $11,500,000.00

After the bids on the readvertisement were opened, the procuring activity learned of proposed changes in the specifications. The first change was an increase in the permissible grade of trenching from 15% to 35%. The change probably would decrease the cost, although no definite prediction could be made. The second change was the laying of cable 6 inches deeper in arable land than originally required. The cost of the change was approximately $212,000. 

The third change involved splicing cases. Since neither the configuration nor the quantity of the cases could be determined, the readvertisement had not asked for bids on the cases. Instead, negotiation was to be used. Under the change, bidders would be requested to submit a unit price on each of three types of cases. 

The total cost to the Government of the change was estimated as $250,000. Noting that the cost of the first change was not determinable, that the estimated cost of the second change was less than the difference between the two lowest bids, and that the third change dealt with a requirement subject to negotiation under the readvertisement, the Air Force concluded that a new advertisement might be influenced less by changes in specifications than by exposure of the bids. The Air Force asked the 

Comptroller General whether the procurement had to be readvertised again or whether an award could be made without readvertisement and the changes made by negotiation after award. 

Held, the procurement must be readvertised with specifications incorporating the changes.

Two principles require this result. First, the requirement of formal advertising neither contemplates nor sanctions selecting a contractor on the basis of a government estimate about what might have been bid for work not advertised. Second, a formally advertised contract may not be expanded to include additional work of any considerable magnitude, without compliance with the advertising statutes, unless the additional work (1) was not in contemplation when the contract was made and (2) is such an inseparable part of the work that performance by anyone other than the original contractor is reasonably impossible. This principle has been applied to a decrease in work that would have reduced the contract price by only a small percentage of the difference between the two low bids. 40 Comp. Gen. 55 (1960).

In the instant case the tabulation of bids, as shown above, tends to indicate that at least some bidders have been influenced more by the exposed bids of competitors than by changes in specifications. It may also be true that ultimately the net cost of the changes may be so small as not to alter the relative standing of the bidders. On the other hand, there is at least a possibility that the changes will have a greater effect on the bids than anticipated and that readvertising will be in the best interest of the Government. The net effect of the three changes with regard to the standings of two bidders might well be cumulative. In any case, the changes are of considerable size. The probable effect of the changes on bids can only be estimated. It cannot be said with certainty that the relative standing of bidders would have AGO 9111A 49

been the same had the changes been included in the advertised specifications.

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145109, 1 May 1961. 

41. Equitable Adjustment of Difference Between Cost of Domestic and Foreign Copper May Be Made Where Contract Inadvertently Added Copper to the Invitation for Bid's List of Items Exempt From Buy American Act Provisions and a Change Order Deleted Copper From the List After the Contractor Had Pur chased Foreign Copper. (C.G.)

See CHANGES (par. 19) 42. Changing Place of Inspection and Acceptance From Destination to Source Did Not Ren der Bid Non-responsive. A Signal Corps invitation for bids incorporating Standard Form 32 (Oct. 1957 ed.), provided that final inspection and acceptance would be at destination. The low bid altered that provision to state that final inspection and acceptance would be at the source. The low bidder protested to the 

Comptroller General against the proposed rejection of its bid. In the administrative report from the Signal Corps to the Comptroller General was a notation that because of other Signal Corps contracts held by the low bidder, Signal Corps inspectors would be in residence at the low bidder's plant at the time of performance of the contract in question, so inspection could be made at that plant without additional cost or inconvenience to the Government. 

Held, protest upheld. Qualifying the low bid by providing for inspection and acceptance at source did not affect price, quantity, or quality. 

First, the qualification does not increase the government's cost, since government inspectors will be in residence at the low bidder's plant. 

Indeed, since the bidder's plant and facilities will be used for inspection and final acceptance, the qualification may be regarded as providing the Government an additional advantage. Second, the qualification does not change the responsibility for the supplies between the time of acceptance under the low bid and under the invitation. Paragraph 6 of SF 32 makes the contractor responsible for supplies until delivered to the designated receiving point, regardless where inspection is made. Since delivery is on an f.o.b. destination basis, the low bid makes the contractor responsible until delivery. This period of responsibility is the same as that required by the invitation. Third, the qualification does not change the time of payment. Paragraph 7 of SF 32 provides for payment to the contractor upon the submission of proper invoices or vouchers for supplies "delivered and accepted." As indicated above, the time and point of delivery are not changed by the low bid. Therefore, the time of payment would remain the same. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145645, 28 June 1961. 

43. Late Hand Carried Bid Delivered After Other Bids Opened May Not Be Considered Even Though Lateness Was Allegedly Caused by Action of Government Personnel. A bid der's employee hand carrying a bid arrived at the bid opening office 6 minutes after the deadline for submission of bids. Several bids had already been opened and read. There, as here, at least one bid had been opened and read when the hand carried bid arrived. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145690, 20 June 1961.

44. Bidder Permitted To Displace Lower Bidder By Correcting Error Telegraphic Agency Made When Transmitting Modification. At the time of opening of bids on a construction con tract advertised by a Federal Aviation Agency office in Fort Worth, Texas, the low bid was from the M Co., for $1,700,000. The I Co's bid read $2,000,000, and seven other bids received ranged from $1,949,000 to $3,000,000. A telegram received before the bid opening from the I Co. had been garbled in transmission, but was said by Western Union a half hour after the bid opening to request a deduction of $47,- 000 in the total bid. Thirty-seven minutes after the bid opening, the FAA message center received from the M Co. a telegram which had been sent by the M Co. at Miami, Florida, 40 minutes before the bid opening. The telegram attempted to add $160,000 to the M Co.'s bid. 

The I Co. claimed that its telegram, which had originally been garbled when received should have stated a reduction of $147,000, instead of the $47,000 figure given by Western Union. 

The FAA contacted Western Union, which stated that (1) the I Co.'s telegram when filed had reduced the price $147,000, a figure which was erroneously altered in transmission; (2) the M Co.'s modification would, in the ordinary course of transmission, have been delivered before the bid opening but had been abnormally delayed. Protests arising out of these facts were filed with the Comptroller General. That official declined to question the administrative determination that the M Co.'s modification should be considered. The major question then 

Iwas whether the I Co.'s bid decrease should be taken as $147,000 or only $47,000.

Held, the modification may be considered as $147,000. The general rule is the bid correction should not be permitted, if the result is displacement of another bid, unless the correct bid is substantially ascertainable from the bid and accompanying papers. 37 Comp. Gen. 

210, 212 (1957). However, in that and similar decisions, the bidder had himself made the error. Here the error was that of Western

Union. The weight of authority is that Western Union is an independent contractor, or at most an agent whose authority to bind the sender is limited to transmission of the message actually given it. Western Union Telegraph Co. v. Cowin & Co., 20 F. 2d 103 (1927);

Annot., 42 A.L.R. 293 (1926). One of the underlying reasons for the rule against corrections that displace lower bids is the necessity of resorting to extraneous evidence that has been prepared by the bidder or his estimators and was subject to the bidder's supervision. 

Correction in such cases results in overlooking or forgiving the bidder's own carelessness to the prejudice of more careful bidders. In this case the error was made by an independent agency over which the bidder exercised no supervisory control. In such circumstances the rule against making a correction that displaces a lower bidder should not apply. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-146295, 28 August 1961, 41 Comp. Gen. 165. 

[Note: In the instant case the Comptroller 

General was asked to treat the I Co.'s telegram as a late telegraphic bid modification. That treatment would permit consideration of the modification if it had been late due solely to delay by the telegraphic company for which the bidder was not responsible. The Comptroller 

General declined to treat the telegram as a late modification because there was no delay of a modification that would eventually arrive, but simply a failure to deliver the correct message.

In discussing this distinction the Comptroller 

General said: 

In the case of error in a telegram, delivery of the supposed message has been made and unless inquiry is made by someone no further communication will be delivered. For example, in the instant case, assuming the . . . [I Co.'s] telegram first delivered had clearly stated a deduction of $47,000, and assuming further that the . . . [I Co.'s] bid was low by reason of that deduction, the contracting office never would have received the 'late' correct modification unless [the I Co.] had requested it from Western Union. 

The Comptroller General's hypothetical indi cates that the result of the instant case permits a bidder a "second bite at the apple." The bidder is given a choice whether to allege the existence of an error. Of course, the bidder

AGO 9111A 51

who relies on material submitted with the bid as a basis for correcting an error is given the same choice when the Government does not spot the error.] 

45. Contract Must Be Readvertised if Davis- Bacon Wage Determination Incorporated in Specifications Expires Before Award Is Made. 

(C.G.) 

See DAVIS-BACON ACT (par. 2) 46. Contractng Agency May Waive Failure To Acknowledge Addendum That Reduced Cost of Work by Amount That Was Trivial Compared With Total of Bid and With Differences Between Bid and Next Higher Bid. The bidder that was low by $1,115 on a formally advertised procurement (with a total bid of $5,535) failed to acknowledge receipt of an addendum. 

The cost of the work eliminated by the addendum was administratively estimated as $15. 

The procuring activity asked the Comptroller General whether the low bid could be considered. 

Held, the bid may be considered. Waiver of a failure to acknowledge an addendum has been permitted where the addendum could have affected the cost of the work only negligibly or where the additional cost was too trivial as a practical matter when compared with the work's total cost. 34 Comp. Gen. 581 (1955); 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-141383 (14 Jan 1960). Here the addendum reduced the work's cost by only $15, and the second low bid was $1,115 higher than the low bid. Furthermore, the $15 reduction cannot be said to be more than negligible in relation to the total cost of the procurement. 

Thus other bidders would not be prejudiced by the low bidder's failure to acknowledge the addendum. Indeed, if that failure was caused by ignorance of the addendum's existence, the low bid would not reflect the lessened requirements. 

Consequently, the failure would prejudice the low bidder and possibly be beneficial to the other bidders. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-148162, 20 February 1962. 

47. Bids Held Responsive Despite a Failure To Include Information Required by Invitation About the Nature and Extent of Work the Bidders Would Themselves Perform. An invitation for bids issued by the Corps of Engineers provided that the contractor would be required to perform on the site, and with his own organization, work equal to at least twenty per cent of the total amount of work to be performed under the contract. The invitation also stated that Each bidder shall submit with his bid a statement of the work which he will perform with his own organization . . ., the percentage of the total work this represents, and the estimated cost thereof. 

That percentage shall be equal to or greater than [twenty per cent]; otherwise the bid will be considered non-responsive. 

The two low bidders did not furnish the required statement until after the bid opening. 

The third low bidder, who had furnished the statement with his bid, protested to the Comptroller General that the omission of the statement had made the two low bids unresponsive. 

Held, protest rejected. Information about the percentage of work to be performed is required for the purpose of determining bidders' 

responsibility. See 41 Comp. Gen. 106 (1961). 

That purpose is not altered by language making mandatory the submission of the information. 

The argument has been made that permitting performance information to be submitted after opening has a prejudicial effect parallel to that involved in the post-opening receipt of bid bonds. Compare 38 Comp. Gen. 532 (1959) 

[digested in DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 84, par. 8].

The prejudice is allegedly in the ability of the low bidder to obtain better prices from subcontractors after the bid opening and thus to alter his arrangements so as to conform to the twenty per cent limitation. However, whether or not a bidder furnishes the performance information, he is bound by the twenty per cent minimum. 41 Comp. Gen. 106, 109 (1961). 

Therefore, he bears the risk involved in waiting until after the bid opening to determine whether the twenty per cent limitation can be observed. Moreover, nothing prevents a bidder who furnishes the performance information from changing his subcontracting arrangements after bid opening so long as he stays within the twenty per cent limitation. Therefore, the bidder who does not provide the information is no better off than the bidder who does. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-147902, 23 February 1962. 52 AGO 9111A

48. Propriety of Options for Additional Quantities in Set-Aside Procurements Discussed. (JAGT) See SET-ASIDES (par. 5) 49. Intention That Bid Lacking Manual Signature Be Binding May Not Be Inferred From Fact That President of Bidding Firm, Who Was Unknown to Officials Presiding at Opening, Per sonally Submitted the Bid and Attended the 

Opening. Mr. D, the president of the B Co., personally delivered the firm's bid to the designated Navy procurement office. The bid was then time-stamped in the presence of the contract specialist. Mr. D then attended the bid opening, at which time his identity was unknown to the contract specialist and the bid officer who were presiding over the opening. 

The register of persons attending the opening included, among others, Mr. D's name, followed by "the B Co." The firm's bid proved to be without a manual signature and had only the typewritten name of Mr. D. The Comptroller 

General was asked whether the bid could be considered.

Held, the bid should be disregarded. The generally followed rule is that manually unsigned bids bearing a typewritten name may be considered for award only if they are accompanied by documentary evidence showing a clear intent to submit a bid. 36 Comp. Gen. 

523 (1957). However, in one case intent to submit the bid was established by the fact that the bid was accompanied by samples required to be submitted. Ms. Comp. Gen. B- 

124029, 1 June 1955. In Ms. Comp. Gen.

B-144470, 14 March 1961, there was an implication that there may be circumstances where the act of the individual submitting the bid unaccompanied by documentary evidence of intent to bid may be construed as an intent to submit a binding offer. ASPR 2-405 (iii) is in general accord with the cases. 

The question is whether the documents or circumstances accompanying the submission of the unsigned bid would clearly and convincingly overcome any attempt by the bidder to disavow the bid on the ground that there was no authorized signature. See, e.g., Ms. Comp. 

Gen. B-144185, 25 January 1961. In the instant case the procurement officials did not know until after the bids were opened that the individual delivering the B Co.'s bid was the president of the firm. Therefore, if he chose to remain silent at the bid opening, the company could successfully avoid award by disavowing the bid because of the absence of an authorized signature. Since the Government would not have known that the president had submitted the bid in person, that fact could not have been relied upon as evidence of intent. That the president attended the bid opening is not significant because bid openings are public and may be attended by anyone, even persons who are not bidders. In any event, the president remained unknown to the officers presiding over the bid opening until he revealed his relationship. Since there was no manual signature and no clear intention to submit a binding offer, the bid should not be considered.

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-148235, 23 March 1962. 

50. Bid May Not Be Rejected on Ground That

Proposed Supplier Is on Debarred Bidders' List Unless Invitation Specifies That Fitness of Subcontractors Is Subject to Contracting Officer's Determination. The proposed supplier of the low bidder on a procurement formally advertised by the Army was listed as a debarred bidder under the authority of Section 1 (a) of the Walsh-Healey Act, 49 Stat. 2036 (1936), as amended, 41 U.S.C. § 35 (a) [requiring that a contractor be a manufacturer or regular dealer]. The procuring activity rejected the bid pursuant to ASPR 1-603 (c), which provides that where a concern listed on a debarred bidders' list is proposed as a subcontractor, the contracting officer should, where appropriate, decline to subcontract with the concern. The low bidder protested to the Comptroller General. 

Held, the rejection was improper. Nothing in the Walsh-Healey Act prohibits award of a contract to a firm contemplating subcontracting. 34 Comp. Gen. 595 (1955). Moreover, a bidder's responsibility generally may not be evaluted on the basis of the qualifications of his intended subcontractor unless the applicable invitation so provides. 38 Comp. Gen. 778, 780 (1959) and cases cited there. The invitation and contract in this procurement contained no provision that the qualifications of

AGO 9111A 53

BONDS 

subcontractors and suppliers would be subject to determination and approval by the contracting officer. If such a provision had been included, the same standards then could have been applied in ascertaining the fitness of a subcontractor or supplier that were observed in testing the fitness of the prime contractor. 

37 Comp. Gen. 544, 546 (1958). Without such a provision, the agency had neither contractual nor statutory authority to question a supplier's qualifications.

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-149781, 29 October 1962.

5. Surety Who Completes Work Under Terms Of Terminated Construction Contract Liable In Liquidated Damages For Delay Caused By Acts Of Contractor Prior To Default. Upon the termi nation of a construction contract for default, the performance bond surety entered into a "take over" contract with the Government wherein it agreed to complete construction in accordance with the terms and conditions of the terminated contract, including SF 23A.

When work was completed the Government assessed liquidated damages in the amount of $29,700 against the surety for delay. The surety appealed to the Engineers Board of Contract Appeals and argued that the delay was excusable since it was caused by the Government's failure to promptly terminate the contractor and acts of the contractor beyond the surety's control and without its fault or negligence. 

Held, the appeal is denied. Article 5 of the terminated contract provided:

If the Government does not terminate the right of the Contractor to proceed . . . the Contractor shall continue the work, in which event he and his sureties shall be liable to the Government, in the amount set forth in the specifications or accompanying papers, for fixed, agreed, and liquidated damages for each calendar day or delay until the work is completed or accepted... 

Thus, one of the risks for which the surety was being compensated was that liquidated damages might be assessed if the Government exercised its undoubted right to permit the contractor to continue performance. Even so, there is no evidence that the contracting officer's timing of the termination was unreasonable. 

The surety next argues that the "take over" contract was a new contract rather than a supplemental agreement. Consequently, under 

Article 5 of SF 23A the surety was not to be "charged with liquidated or actual damages because of any delays in the completion of the work due to . . . causes beyond the control and without the fault or negligence of the 

Contractor, including, but not restricted to... acts of another contractor in the performance of a contract with the Government. . . ." While it might be argued that the terminated contractor was "another contractor" whose acts caused the delay in question, the assertion is not supported if the entire "take over" contract is considered in the light of circumstances existing at the time of execution. The Government was entitled to receive complete performance of the work within the time specified in the terminated contract. Further, the "take over" agreement specified that the respective rights of the parties regarding liquidated damages would not be prejudiced. Thus, the surety assumed the responsibility of completing work within the time specified regardless of the difficulties posed by the terminated contractor's acts. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the surety and the Government did not extend the contract completion date even though it would have been an easy matter for them to have done so. 54 AGO 9111A

BONDS-Continued

The Buckeye Union Casualty Co., Eng. BCA No. 1830, 3 August 1960.

9. Even Though a Bid Was Not Accompanied

By Bond Required By Invitation, the Bid May Be Considered Responsive Because Responsible Government Employees Established Both That the Omission of the Bond Was Inadvertent and

That the Contractor Had No Opportunity To 

Choose Whether To Submit the Bond. In an invitation for bids the Office of the Area 

Engineer of the Corps of Engineers required submission of bid bonds. Shortly before the bids were opened, a representative of the low bidder was permitted to use the telephone on the Area Engineer's desk near the bid opening room. After finishing his call, the representative inserted his bid documents into an en velope. The Area Engineer and his secretary saw the representative look over the Area

Engineer's desk, which was covered with papers, and on the floor, as if something were missing. The representative then submitted the bid, which was found at the bid opening to lack the required bond. However, the bid stated that a bond was enclosed. Remembering the representative's apparent search for something missing, the Area Engineer searched the desk where the representative had used the telephone. A bid bond meeting the invitation's requirements, with the low bidder as the principal, was discovered mixed with the papers on the desk. Neither the low bidder's representative nor anyone other than the Area Engineer had been near the desk between the bid opening and the discovery of the bid bond. 

The bondsman stated that the bond had been 

Idelivered to the low bidder at least five hours before the bid opening. The Office of the Chief of Engineers decided the low bid was responsive, and the second low bidder protested to the Comptroller General. 

Held, protest denied. Although it was once the rule that failure to comply with an invitation's requirement of a bid bond could be waived if the failure was the result of an excusable cause unrelated to the bidder's ability to secure a bond, the decision in 38 Comp. Gen. 

532 (1959) held that such a failure would require the bid to be rejected as nonresponsive. 

However, the reasons for altering the earlier rule should be noted. One objection to that rule was the difficulty of determining objectively whether the failure to furnish a bond with the bid was the result of inadvertence or other excusable cause. Usually inadvertence could not AGO 9111A 55

BREACH OF CONTRACT 

be established by evidence independent of that offered by the bidder. Moreover, the bidder's ability to obtain a bond was sometimes improved by the result of the bidding, so there was a difficulty in determining whether a bond could have been obtained before bid opening. 

In the instant case, the statements of responsible Government personnel establish conclusively that a proper bid bond was obtained in time for submission with the bid and that the bond's omission was inadvertent.

The second basic objection to the rule followed before 38 Comp. Gen. 532 was that the rule gave bidders an opportunity to obtain "two bites at the apple" because they could choose after learning the bid results whether to make bids responsive by submitting the required bonds. In the instant case the low bidder had no such choice. Government personnel have stated that the bond was left accidentally on the Area Engineer's desk prior to the bid opening and remained on the desk until after the opening. No one other than Government personnel had access to the desk in the interim. 

Therefore, the objections that led to the rule adopted in 38 Comp. Gen. 532 do not apply in the instant case. Consequently, it may be concluded that for all practical purposes the low bid was accompanied by a bond as required. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144597, 20 February 1961, 40 Comp. Gen. 469.

6. Government Breached Contract by Withholding From Contractor Information Government Obtained From Another Contract and Relevant to Contractor's Calculation of His 

Price. The plaintiff's Army contract for rebuilding tank engines provided a fixed price (with Type D redetermination) for the costs of rebuilding and a cost-reimbursement arrangement for the cost of parts required. In calculating the amount to be included in the fixed price for the cost of ordering and handling parts, the plaintiff had almost no information about the number of parts that would be required. He relied on an estimate of the parts requirements that was proposed by the government negotiator. That estimate was far too low, a fact the government negotiator should have known from experience with a similar contract with another firm. The plaintiff later claimed he was entitled to recover the cost of the extra work involved in handling the parts in excess of the estimated amount. The contracting officer and the ASBCA successively denied the claim. Snyder-Lynch Motors, Inc.,

ASBCA No. 2837 (24 Feb. 1956). The plaintiff then filed suit in the Court of Claims, alleging misrepresentation by the Government of the amount of parts required.

Held, claim allowed. The Government was remiss in not making available to the plaintiff the information gained from the similar contract with the other firm. The withholding of the information constituted a breach of contract, and the plaintiff is entitled to recover damages. See e.g., Ragonese v. United States, 128 Ct. Cl. 156 (1954). The damages are the costs of procuring the parts in excess of the estimated requirements. 56 AGO 9111A

Snyder-Lynch Motors, Inc. v. United States, 292 F.2d 907 (Ct. Cl. 1961).

1. Administrative Test for Determining Reasonableness of Domestic Bids Is Consistent With Buy American Act Legislative History. 

A domestic concern in a labor surplus area submitted a bid of $2,789,502 to Army Engineers for the installation of hydraulic turbines.

This bid exceeded by 42.8% the low bid of a foreign corporation which intended to import the electrical generating equipment. After adding 12% to the foreign bid, the contracting officer determined that the domestic bid was unreasonable, see ASPR 6-104.4 (1 Oct 1959), and that the Buy American Act, 41 U.S.C. 10a, did not apply. Accordingly, the foreign bidder received the award. The domestic bidder protested. 

Held, the protest is denied. The protesting bidder argues that the method authorized by 

ASPR and Executive Order No. 10582, 17 De cember 1954, for determining the reasonableness of domestic costs was not intended by the Buy American Act, and that, rather than measuring the excess of domestic over foreign costs to determine whether the Act applies, the contracting officer should have compared domestic costs and profits with differing foreign wage rates and the benefits conferred upon foreign producers by devalued currency. While the Act does not prescribe the method by which reasonableness is determined, the legislative history indicates that the test was to be an evaluation of the excess of domestic over foreign bid prices. Since the Executive Order and ASPR are consistent with this intention, there is no legal basis for a determination of reasonableness on any other ground. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-139912, 26 October 1959, 39 Comp. Gen. 309. 

2. Small Business Concern Who Assembles End Products Is Manufacturer Rather Than Regular Dealer and, Even Though Work Is Minor in Nature, Is Not Subject to Buy American Domestic Source Requirements. In a nego tiated small business total set-aside, the Navy requested proposals for wire rope assemblies on a nonreturnable reel. The low offeror planned to secure the wire from a foreign source, perform a twisting operation, add a small domestic component, and wind the completed product on nonreturnable reels for delivery. The contracting officer determined that the low offeror was a small business manufacturer rather than a dealer even though most of the material used was of a foreign source. 

See ASPR 1-701.1 (4 Jan 1960), and ASPR 

1-201.9 (27 Feb 1959). The second low bidder protested. 

Held, the protest is denied. The low offeror is concededly a small business concern using a foreign end product. The domestic source re quirements of the Buy American Act, 41 U.S.C. 

§ 10a-d, however, do not apply if the cost of domestic products is unreasonable, i.e., exceeds by 12% the cost of foreign end products. 

ASPR 6-104.4 (4 Jun 1960). Here the excess of domestic over foreign cost is 36%.

The protestor argues that the low offeror is a small business dealer rather than a manufacturer because the work to be performed on the end item is minor in nature. See ASPR 

1-701.4 (1 April 1960). While there are no regulations defining "manufacture" for this purpose, the concept is not limited to production from raw materials. Manufacturing may include the assembly of parts previously produced from raw materials. The operations performed by the low offeror on the foreign wire qualify as manufacturing here, even though the labor and material cost was small in comparison to the finished product. The domestic source requirement for small business dealers, therefore, is not applicable.

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-140904, 11 December 

1959, 39 Comp. Gen. 435.

Clause, Claim for Equitable Adjustment or 

Other Claim for Price Adjustment Arising

Under Contract Must Be Asserted Before Final Payment. Between March 1949 and June 1950, the contractor entered into ten contracts with the Signal Corps for the final assembly of Government furnished components into electronic equipment. Three of these contracts contained a Changes Clause (SF 32, Nov 1949) which provided that a claim for an equitable price adjustment: must be asserted within 30 days from the date of receipt by the Contractor of the notification of change: Provided, however, That the Contracting Officer, if he decides that the facts justify such action, may receive and act upon any such claim asserted at any time prior to final payment under this contract.

The remaining contracts contained an older version of the Changes clause which conditioned the claim only upon assertion "at any time prior to the date of final settlement of the contract." Due to the Korean war, the Government was unable to furnish certain specifications or drawings at the agreed time. For this and other reasons the contractor was delayed during a period of rising costs. The contractor asked for an increase in price, the insertion of price redetermination clauses in his contracts, and finally that some of his contracts be cancelled at no cost to the Government. In none of these requests, which were denied, did the contractor indicate that he was entitled to relief under the Changes Clauses of his contracts. 

Each of the ten contracts was completed at a loss, the total of which was $548,471.38. The contractor completed deliveries under one of the two contracts here under consideration in May, 1952, and received payment at the contract price shortly thereafter. This contract had been modified to provide for the furnishing of parts and spares at a specified price subject to price redetermination. The price was eventually increased. The contractor did not claim that all the increase was not paid, but the record did not reveal the fact of payment. No contractual activity took place between 20 July 58 AGO 9111A

CHANGES-Continued 

1955 and 17 December 1956, when the contractor first applied for relief under the Changes 

Clause. In the other contract, deliveries were completed on 11 December 1952. The parties stipulated that the "last" payment was made in September, 1953, after which there was no contractual activity until 27 February 1957, when the contractor applied for relief under the 

Changes article. In June 1953, the contractor sought relief under Title II of the First War Powers Act, 50 U.S.C. App. 611. This was denied, and in May and June 1955 the contractor filed ten separate appeals to the Secretary of the Army from the contracting officer's notice of denial. The ASBCA, however, refused to docket the appeals when the Army Contract Adjustment Board reaffirmed the denial of 

Title II relief. In August 1955, pursuant to the contractor's request, the contracting officer submitted a finding of fact which stated that Title II relief had been denied on six contracts because the claim was untimely and on the remainder because the Act provided no basis for relief. The claim was untimely because it was submitted after contract performance was completed and final payment made. The contractor did not appeal from this finding of fact. 

Between December 1956 and February 1957, the contractor filed requests for ten supplemental agreements granting equitable adjustments under the Changes Clause. In each case, the amount requested equaled the contract loss. 

On 12 July 1957, the contracting officer denied each request on the ground that the claim was not asserted within 30 days of notification by the Government of the change or prior to final payment under the contract. The contractor appealed and the Government filed a motion to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction.

Held, the motion is granted and the appeal dismissed. Only two of the ten appeals will be considered. The parties have stipulated and the 

Board agrees that if these are dismissed on jurisdictional grounds the other shall also be dismissed. The Government first contends that the appeals are untimely since the contractor neglected to appeal from the August 1955 finding of fact. This determination, however, did not relate to the matter in dispute here. It was merely an explanation of why Title II relief was not granted.

Since the Board has no juris diction to review denials of Title II relief, Action Manufacturing Co., ASBCA No. 4000 

(7 Jan 1957), an appeal would have been dismissed. Further, the determination did not put the contractor on notice that an appeal was required. Standard Coil Products Co., ASBCA 

No. 5274 (18 May 1959). Since there was no decision under the Changes Clause prior to July 1957, it is therefore apparent that the contractor is not attempting to revive an expired appeal. 

The Government next contends that because the Changes claim was not asserted before "final payment" or "final settlement" of the contract the Board has no authority to grant relief. 

This contention is well taken. Assuming that the Government's action constituted a change, there is no question that the dispute arose under the terms of the contract. The equitable adjustment requested by the contractor is specifically authorized by the Changes Clause. 

See Sheldon Manufacturing Co., ASBCA No. 

402 (29 Jan 1951); Newark Steel Drum Co.,

ASBCA No. 1910 (24 Jun 1954); American Air Export & Import Co., ASBCA No. 3857 (27 May 1958), 58-1 BCA 1770. The real issue is whether the contractor has met the conditions which entitle him to relief. Whether the 

Changes Clause required assertion of the claim before final payment or final settlement, the apparent purpose of the contract was to limit the right of equitable adjustment to claims submitted within the period of normal contract administration. Cf. Restatement, Contracts sec. 236 (b). The failure to meet this condition in the instant case discharged the contract right, Restatement, Contracts sec. 395, and deprived the Board of authority to consider the claim. The contractor argues that the failure to submit a claim under the Changes Clause should be excused since an increase in contract price and Title II relief was requested. These requests, however, were a matter of grace and did not find a contractual basis. While it may not be necessary to file a claim specifically referring to the Changes Clause, there must be a claim based upon a contract right asserted before final payment or settlement. Since this condition was not met here, these two appeals and AGO 9111A 59

CHANGES—Continued the others covered by the stipulation are dismissed. 

Specialty Assembling & Packing Company, ASBCA Nos. 4523 through 4532, 29 September 1959, 59-2 BCA 2370. 

2. Government Failure To Provide Promised Timber Is Not Breach of Contract Which Deprives Board of Jurisdiction and Contractor Is 

Entitled to Equitable Adjustment Under 

Changes Article. The contractor was awarded a contract to clear and snag land for the Government with the understanding that it would be entitled to all merchantable timber within the work area. The contract contained a Changes 

Clause, ASPR 7-103.2 (17 Mar 1958), and provided that "Rights-of-way for the work to be performed under this contract will be provided by the Government without cost to the contractor." The Government, however, failed to obtain these rights-of-way. As a consequence, the contractor was delayed and was finally permitted to enter the land upon the condition that the landowner remove and dispose of merchantable timber. Upon the contractor's request, the contracting officer granted additional costs of $460.54 for the delay. A claim for the loss of merchantable timber, however, was denied on the ground that it was an unliquidated claim for damages arising out of a breach of contract and not within the disputes procedure. 

The contractor appealed. 

Held, the appeal is sustained. The amount claimed is not unliquidated since the parties have agreed that the value of the merchantable timber is $5,975. Further, the contract contained the promise which the Government allegedly breached. It is, therefore, difficult to argue that the contractor lacks a contract remedy since if the Government promised to give the contractor merchantable timber it can delete the promise and make an equitable adjustment under the Changes Clause. Finally, since the contract provides a remedy, an administrative board had authority to grant relief under the disputes clause. A breach of contract occurs only where the board has erroneously rejected administrative relief. Cf. Delta Equipment & Construction Company v. United States, 122 Ct. Cl. 340 (1952).

Allison & Holland Company, Eng. BCA No. 

1559, 20 August 1959.

See DISPUTES (par. 12) 5. Conditions Which Arose Long After Contract Execution Are Not Contemplated by the Changed Conditions Clause. Appellant was gen eral contractor on the Cadet Quarter's Complex at the Air Force Academy. Close to appellant's work was the construction of the Academic 

Complex under the direction of another prime contractor. The contracting officer, concerned with the lagging progress of the mechanical subcontractor on the Academic Complex, issued a directive that the latter increase his forces and hours of work and that he go on a seven day work week. Compliance with the directive resulted in workmen on the Academic Complex reaping overtime wages because of the 10 hour day, seven-day week. Appellant's insulation sub-subcontractor had about twenty per cent of his work remaining when the accelerated schedule went into effect. He claims that the accelerated schedule resulted in discontent among his workmen, difficulty in his hiring of new workers and retaining old ones, and generally in a drastic reduction (estimated as 62%) of production efficiency and a concomitant increase in labor costs.

Appellant asserted a claim in excess of $61,- 000 to cover these increased costs. The claim was denied and this timely appeal filed. Appellant urges entitlement to an equitable adjustment under the changed conditions clause or in the alternative that the Government is obligated to it for breach of the implied obligation not to hinder performance of the contract. 

The Government moved for dismissal on the grounds, inter alia, that the "contract contains 60 AGO 9111A

CHANGESContinued no provision allowing for the relief contended for." 

Held, Government's motion to dismiss is granted. Any relief granted must be based on authority contained in the contract. The changed conditions clause is the only contract provision relied on by the appellant to support its position. 

However, the "Changed Conditions" contemplated by the clause, particularly the second part thereof, are physical conditions of an unusual nature and unknown to the parties at the time the contract was executed; they are not represented by the conditions involved hereconditions which arose long after contract execution and which concern a different contract on a different building. 

Robert E. McKee, ASBCA No. 5621, 28 January 1960, 60-1 BCA 2504. 

6. Computation of Equitable Adjustment Can Be Based on Difference Between Actual 

Costs, if Reasonably Incurred in Diligent Per formance, and Estimate of Actual Costs Made by Contractor and Supported by Substantial Evidence-Profit Allowance Appropriate in Equitable Adjustment Even on Loss Contract. 

The contractor entered into a contract for the manufacture of trousers from Governmentfurnished cloth. The cloth concededly did not comply with the specifications and was unsuitable, requiring the contractor, in order to perform, to slow down its machines. The contractor submitted its claim for equitable adjustment computed as follows: 

1. Estimated direct labor costs to perform with suitable cloth 

2. Actual direct labor costs incurred in performance of contract $26,233.84 44,680.68 

3. Excess direct labor costs (2 minus 1) $18,446.84 

4. Overhead on excess direct labor (at 85.5%) 

5. Total excess costs 

6. Profit (6%) 

7. Total price increase requested 15,772.05 $34,218.89 2,053.13 $36,272.02

The contract price (based on the contractor's bid) was concededly too low and the contractor would have lost money in performance even if the cloth had been suitable. However, the contractor's estimated direct labor costs to perform with suitable cloth (Item 1 of the computation) are not based on the contract price but are based on the estimates made by the contractor's superintendent in establishing piece-work rates. These rates were actually used prior to the discovery of defects in the Government-furnished cloth. The superintendent was a man of much experience in garment making, as a plant manager and in estimating labor costs and computing piece rates. The actual direct labor costs incurred in performance (Item 2 of the computation) were affected by an increase in minimum wage caused by a statutory amendment to the Walsh-Healey Act raising the minimum wage from 75 cents to $1.00 per hour. The contract would have been completed prior to the effective date of the amendment if the cloth had been suitable. 

Held, the contractor's computations are accepted as the amount of equitable adjustment to which it is entitled. In order for the contractor's figures to constitute a valid basis for computing the increased labor costs, it must be established (1) that the actual labor costs incurred were reasonable under the circumstances, (2) that the estimated labor costs were reasonable and realistic for making the trousers with suitable material and (3) that the difference between the actual and estimated labor costs was due entirely to the unsuitability of the Government-furnished cloth. The Board finds all three requirements to be established by the facts. The inclusion of the increase in hourly wage due to the statutory amendment of the Walsh-Healey Act in the actual direct labor costs is determined to be proper. The wage increase would be appropriate for inclusion in an equitable adjustment under the changes clause (see Lonergan Mfg. Co., ASBCA No. 1601 (20 Apr 1954), motion for reconsideration denied 12 January 1955) and the Government-furnished property clause provides that the equitable adjustment shall be made in accordance with the procedures provided for in the changes clause. The Board also finds the figure for overhead to be reasonable. In addition, the contractor is entitled to a profit allowance for the increased work. 

He is so entitled irrespective of whether a AGO 9111A 61

CHANGES-Continued profit would have been made if suitable Government material had been furnished. Such profit allowance is in accordance with the method of computing equitable adjustments under the changes clause (see G. M. Co. Mfg., Inc., ASBCA No. 2883 (7 Nov 1957), 57-2 

BCA 1505) and that method is equally applicable to computing equitable adjustments under the Government-furnished property clause.

Chicago Garment Co., Inc., ASBCA No. 

4657, 13 April 1960, 60-1 BCA 2581. 

7. A Contractor Is Not Required To Assert a 

Claim for Adjustment in Price Due to a Change

Order Until the Effectiveness of the Change Order Is Fully Developed and the 30-Day Period for Filing the Claim Begins To Run. The con tractor entered into a contract for the manufacture and installation of cockpit procedure trainers based on Model F3H-2N aircraft, serial number 133554. Model F3H-2N aircraft were being manufactured by McDonald Aircraft Corporation and an aircraft with serial number 133554 was in existence. The Government by change order changed the specification from Model F3H-2N to Model F3H-2 and from serial number 133554 to serial number 

143412, that of an aircraft not yet in existence.

The change order contained the usual "notice" to the effect that if the change caused an increase in estimated cost or time required for performance, the contractor was required to advise the contracting officer within 30 days, and that claims for adjustment under the changes clause would not be considered unless submitted within the 30-day period. At the time the change order was issued, adequate data was not available to the contractor to determine the additional costs of performance, if any, caused by the change order. Such data became available to the contractor only gradually during its performance. Obtaining technical data sufficient to show the real differences between serial number 143412 of Model F3H-2 aircraft and serial number 133554 of Model 

F3H-2N aircraft continued to be a problem throughout performance. When it became clear to the contractor that additional costs were involved, the contracting officer was notified and a claim filed, it then being one year from the date of the change order. The contracting officer denied the claim on the ground that it was not asserted within the time limit stated in the Changes clause of the contract. 

The contractor appealed to the ASBCA. 

Held, for the contractor. The claim was timely filed. The issuance of an effective change order is a condition precedent to the contractor's obligation to file its claim within. the time stipulated in the changes clause. Todd 

Shipyards Corporation, ASBCA Nos. 2911 and 

2912 (25 Jan 1957), 57-1 BCA 1185; Pacific

Car and Foundry Co., ASBCA No. 4849 (15 

Jan 1960), 60-1 BCA 2505. The change order issued to the contractor in this case was not effective by its own terms. It embraced every new development, every change ordered, and every modification authorized subsequently by the Government in its contract with McDonald for the manufacture of aircraft serial number 

143412 of Model F3H-2. Further, even after the particular aircraft came into existence the changes and modifications made to this aircraft during its construction were not effective in the contractor's performance until knowledge of them became reasonably available. The contractor filed its claim for price adjustment before the effectiveness of the change order was fully developed, and such claim was timely. 

Burton-Rodgers, Inc., ASBCA No. 5438, 7 March 1960, 60-1 BCA 2558. 

[Note: The Board in the instant opinion also included a preliminary decision as to its jurisdiction. The Board noted that the changes article of the contract required that the claim for additional compensation for the change be asserted within 30 days, "provided, however, that the Contracting Officer, if he decides that the facts justify such action, may receive and act upon any such claim asserted at any time prior to final payment under [the] contract.

Thus, the contracting officer is given discretion as to whether or not a late claim should be considered. However, the question of whether a late claim should be received and acted upon was a matter about which the parties could, and did, dispute. The contracting officer rendered a decision in the matter by refusing to consider the late claim. In the absence of language in the changes clause giv- 99 62 AGO 9111A

CHANGES-Continued ing finality to such a decision, it is governed by the disputes clause, and the contractor may appeal an adverse decision under the disputes procedure. Thus, the Board finds that it has jurisdiction to consider the appeal. The Board considers this finding of jurisdiction to be a holding. (". . . we hold that the . . . decision . . . is appealable . . . under the . . disputes clause .") However, since the Board ultimately held that the claim was not late, but rather was timely filed, this preliminary "holding" is not necessary to its ultimate decision and therefore must be treated as dictum.] 

8. Increased Costs Caused by Government's Delay in Issuing Change Order and Temporary Suspension of Inspector's Power To Accept Delivered Supplies Not Compensable Under Changes Clause. In February 1955, the con tractor agreed to deliver 33,227 submachine guns to the Army. The total contract price was $662,546.38 and deliveries were to be completed by October 1956. The contract contained a Changes Clause which provided in part: 

The Contracting Officer may at any time, by a written order, and without notice to the sureties, make changes, within the general scope of this contract, in any one or more of the following: (i) drawings, designs, or specifications, where the supplies to be furnished are to be specially manufactured for the Government in accordance therewith; . . . If any such change causes an increase or decrease in the cost of, or the time required for, performance of this contract, an equitable adjustment shall be made in the contract price or delivery schedule, or both, and the contract shall be modified in writing accordingly. 

The contract also contained an Inspection 

Clause which provided in part: 

.. Final acceptance or rejection of the supplies shall be made as promptly as practicable after delivery, except as otherwise provided in this contract; but failure to inspect and accept or reject supplies shall neither relieve the Contractor from responsibility for such supplies as are not in accordance with the contract requirements nor impose liability on the Government therefor. 

The contractor awarded a subcontract for the stocks and receivers. After the subcontractor made dies for the work and produced initial quantities it was discovered that the stock and receiver, while meeting specifications, would not assemble. The contractor ordered the subcontractor to stop work and, in June 1955, requested the contracting officer to change the specifications. After a series of conferences, an engineering change was made in November 1955 and the subcontractor remade its dies and resumed work. Because of this delay, the contractor alleged its total production time was increased by eight months and its indirect costs increased by some $50,000. 

In October 1956, Government inspectors discovered what appeared to be rust in the barrel assembly. Pending the resolution of this problem, inspectors were told to stop accepting the machine guns but to continue the inspection process. There was no order, however, for the contractor to stop production. Within 9 days it was determined that the substance was not rust and the inspectors resumed accepting the delivered product. While no gun was rejected because of the foreign substance, the contractor alleged that the instruction to suspend acceptance disrupted production since the assembly line could not keep running if the product could not be accepted and shipped. The contractor, inter alia, claimed an equitable adjustment of $1,008 for costs incurred during the suspension of acceptance and some $50,000 for the specification defect. These claims were denied by the contracting officer and the contractor appealed.

Held, the appeal is denied. The Government argues that the Board has no jurisdiction to grant an equitable adjustment under the 

Changes Clause because the cause of the con tractor's increased costs was the issuance of defective specifications and the delay in correcting them, not the change order itself. This argument is sound for the change order, when finally issued, removed the obstacle to performance and ended the period of delay. Since there is no contract provision which expressly or impliedly authorizes a price adjustment for delay in issuing a change order, this Board is without jurisdiction. See Philips Electronics,

Inc., ASBCA No. 4443 (17 Jun 1958), 58-1 

BCA 1819.

The same reasoning applies to the contractor's increased costs due to the Government's suspension of acceptances. Even though the contract delivery schedule might have been af- AGO 9111A 63

CHANGES-Continued fected by this action, it should be noted that changes in the delivery schedule are not listed as authorized changes in the contract. Further, the Inspection Clause does not provide for an equitable adjustment if the method of inspection causes increased costs and in fact negatives Government liability for failure to reject or inspect supplies. This language, while specifically concerned with liability for supplies, precludes any intention that the Government shall be liable for delay by way of an equitable adjustment. Thus, even though the order to stop acceptance unreasonably disrupted the contractor's production and increased costs, neither the contract Changes nor

Inspection Clauses afford a basis for relief. 

Terry Industries, Inc., ASBCA No. 3718 (13 

Jan 1959), 59-1 BCA 2072.

Ithica Gun Company, Inc., ASBCA No. 5476, 

31 May 1960, 60-1 BCA 2643. 

9. Measure of Equitable Adjustment for Change Order Is Difference Between Market Value of Unchanged Work and Market Value of Changed Work at Time of Issuance of Change Order. The Corps of Engineers entered into a contract with the contractor for the construction of buildings at an air base. The contract specifications included a provision for concrete masonry blocks suitable for painting. 

A subcontractor supplied the contractor with the masonry blocks, but these were rejected by the area engineer as not being suitable for painting. The subcontractor then developed a new type of masonry block (referred to as "the sand block") which was acceptable to the area engineer. The subcontractor supplied the sand block at the same price as the block formerly supplied and credited the contractor with the full value of the rejected block which was returned to the subcontractor. The contracting officer then determined that the block originally submitted met the contract requirements and that an effective change order had been issued, entitling the contractor to an equitable adjustment. In its request for an equitable adjustment, the contractor claimed, among other items, the "increase in value" of the sand block over that of the block specified in the contract. 

In support of its contention that the sand block had a higher value than the original block, the contractor pointed to the fact that in a finding of fact on a subsequent contract, the contracting officer found that this sand block used on the subsequent contract had been billed to the prime contractor at a higher price, and that it was more costly to produce than the original block. This increase in price had resulted from an experienced rejection rate higher than anticipated. 

In his adjustment under this, the earlier contract, however, the contracting officer denied any recovery to the contractor for this item since the latter was neither billed nor did it pay any more for the sand block than for the original block. On appeal, the Corps of Engineers

BCA held that the measure of the equitable adjustment should be the difference between the market values of the two blocks. The Board then found that the subcontractor charged the contractor significantly higher prices for the new block in later contracts and that there was a disparity in prices quoted to the public for the two blocks. The Board also found that the contracting officer admitted that the new block "was more costly to produce," indicating that the market value of the new block was higher than that of the old. The Board accordingly awarded an equitable adjustment to the contractor for that item. Bruce Constr. Corp. et al.,

Eng. BCA No. 1359 (30 Jun 1959). The con tractor appealed to the ASBCA the denial of other items of its claim and the Government contended that the ASBCA should disallow the appeal in its entirety, including the portion awarded by the Corps of Engineers BCA. 

Held, for the Government. The ASBCA does not take issue with the Engineers BCA that the measure of an equitable adjustment is the difference between the fair market values of the two blocks. S. N. Nielsen Co. v. U.S., 141 Ct.

Cl. 793 (1958). But the Engineers BCA erred in its determination of fair market value. The measure of the market value of the sand block should be the prevailing fair market value at the time of the issuance of the change order and not the market value on a subsequent date.

See Lonergan Mfg. Co., ASBCA No. 1601 (20 

Apr 1964). Since the subcontractor agreed to and did supply the sand block to the contractor at the same price as the old, the market values 64 AGO 9111A

CHANGES-Continued of the two blocks at this time were the same, even though subsequent experience with the sand block indicated that it was more costly to produce and to handle and resulted in a higher price to the contractor on a later contract. 

Furthermore, no sale of the sand block was made to the public, and the evidence is insufficient to show that prices were ever quoted on the sand block to the public. Thus, the market values being the same, the contractor is not entitled to an equitable adjustment for this item of its claim. 

Bruce Constr. Corp. et al., ASBCA No. 5932, 30 August 1960, 60-2 BCA 2797. 

[Note: The instant opinion recognizes the authority of S. N. Nielsen Co. v. U.S. 141 Ct. 

Cl. 793 (1958), which has been cited for the proposition that an "objective" approach should be taken to the pricing of a change order, i.e., taking the difference between the fair market value (or other "reasonable" value) of the item prior to and subsequent to the issuance of the change order. The instant opinion, however, reaches a result which would be consistent with the "subjective," or "actual cost," approach to the pricing of change orders, an approach which was rejected in the Nielsen case, but which was apparently adopted in Lofstrand 

Company, ASBCA No. 4336 (10 Oct 1958), 58-2 BCA 1962.] 

10. Contractor Not Entitled to Remedy From 

ASBCA for Increased Costs of Unchanged

Work Caused Solely by Government Delay in Issuing Change Order. (ASBCA) See DISPUTES (par. 22) 11. Equitable Adjustment Should Be Based on Costs Reasonably Incurred by Contractor Even Though Based on Forward Pricing Later Proved Erroneous. In June 1958 the Ordnance 

Corps awarded appellant and IMF Company contracts identical in price and requirements. Both contracts contained the standard Changes Clause 

(ASPR 7-103.2). After award the contracts were transferred for administration, the appellant's to the Boston Ordnance District, that of 

IMF Company to the New York Ordnance Dis trict. Neither district knew of the other's contract. Before and after receiving its contract, the appellant obtained quotations from component suppliers, and late in June accepted the IMF Company's offer of certain items at a sum far below the next higher quotation. In 

July the Government secured from the appellant an estimate of $42,000 for a proposed acceleration in deliveries. Appellant based its figure in part on informal discussions with IMF Company. Although the record does not show whether IMF Company was asked to estimate acceleration costs, the New York District ordered that firm to accelerate with the proviso that acceleration costs would not exceed $42,- 500. Appellant was ordered in September to make the same acceleration and changes and accepted IMF Company's offer of $30,905 as the increase in the subcontract price for the new requirements. The increase was not made redeterminable and was paid to IMF Company shortly after deliveries were completed by both contractors in December. Meanwhile appellant claimed from the Government an equitable adjustment which included $30,905 for the increase in cost of the subcontracted components. 

While the Boston District considered this claim, the New York District received information of appellant's contract and an Army Audit Agency report of the IMF Company's change and ac celeration costs. The New York District, how ever, did not contact the Boston District. In 

April an employee of the Boston District phoned appellant to outline a proposed settlement which allowed less profit than appellant had sought, but included the $30,905 for the subcontracted parts. Appellant by letter shortly afterwards advised the Boston District that the telephone proposal was equitable and that the Government should prepare a contract modification so the appellant could submit a final billing. Three days after this letter was written, the Boston District was told by the New York District of the parallel contracts and the subcontract between appellant and IMF Company. 

The New York District suggested withholding settlement with appellant because the audit indicated the IMF Company had overcharged the appellant for the changes and acceleration. Appellant's subsequent invoice for the amount proposed in the telephone call was rejected by a letter which stated that the Changes clause provision for an equitable adjustment required appellant to protect its position vis-a-vis its AGO 9111A 65

CHANGES-Continued subcontractors. The letter proposed a settlement of $16,500 for increased subcontract costs. 

The figure was the amount for which the IMF Company settled its claim with the Government for the acceleration and changes. The appellant rejected the Government's offer, but promised to adjust its claim if the Government persuaded IMF Company to return part of the $30,905 received from appellant. From a decision against it by the contracting officer, the appellant timely appealed to the ASBCA. The focus of the dispute was whether $16,500 or $30,905 was the proper sum for the subcontract costs. 

The appellant contended the April telephone conversation and letter created a contract for the higher figure. The Government responded that the agent had no authority to make a binding agreement and had made no offer the appellant could accept. 

Held, appeal sustained. It is unnecessary to rule on the contention that the April communications created a contract, for on other grounds the $30,905 figure is proper. Equitable adjustments should be based on the reasonable costs of the contractor, not of another. Dibs Production and Engineering Company, ASBCA

No. 1438 (26 Mar 1954), as quoted in Modern Foods, Inc., ASBCA No. 2090 (26 Mar 1957), 

57-1 BCA 1229. The appellant's cost figure is reasonable. It differs from that of the IMF 

Company because appellant used prospective pricing and the IMF Company used retrospective pricing. In settling with suppliers, contractors should have the same choice between those two methods of pricing that the Board has given contractors and the Government for computing equitable adjustments. Bruce Constr. Corp.,

ASBCA No. 5932 (30 Aug 1960). The appellant does not appear to have been unreasonable in either selecting forward pricing or not making redeterminable the adjustment with its subcontractor. Moreover, the amount appellant paid was reasonable, viewed as it must befrom the time of prospective pricing. Appellant's July estimate of $42,000 did not shock the Government, and the change order the Government issued IMF Company in August contained a proviso that costs would not exceed $42,500. Appellant was reasonable in taking the new requirements to the old subcontractor, for alternate sources probably could not have been used at such a late phase of the contract. 

Reasonably prudent contractors would not have thought the adjusted price asked by IMF Company was excessive. The Government itself did not think $42,000 exorbitant until the audit report was received. Therefore, since appellant actually incurred a cost of $30,905 and did so reasonably, an adjustment to be equitable must be based on that amount. 

The Ensign-Bickford Co., ASBCA No. 6214, 

31 October 1960, 60-2 BCA 2817. 

12. Contractor Is Entitled to Equitable Adjustment Under Changes Clause for Revision of Drawing To Include Utilities of Which Contractor Had No Notice When He Bid. The appel lant's construction contract with the Air Force contained the standard Changes Clause (SF 

23A, par. 3) and a provision for utilities protection. The latter allowed the appellant extra compensation for repairing damages he caused to existing utilities not shown on the drawings or known to the appellant before excavation. 

After receiving the contract, the appellant learned there were more underground utilities than those shown on the original drawings furnished bidders. In response to the appellant's request for information about the utilities, the Government provided a revision to one of the drawings. The revision added twenty-two utilities. The appellant claimed additional compensation for delay and additional work allegedly caused by the extra utilities. From a denial of this claim by the contracting officer, the appellant appealed to the ASBCA. The 

Government argued on the appeal that the appellant should have been put on notice of the additional utilities by: 1) warnings in the original drawings and specifications that interference with utilities would have to be avoided; 

2) a site inspection which disclosed nearby buildings and manholes; 3) the detailed data on utilities available to the appellant at all times at the office of the Directorate of Civil Engineering.

Held, the revision was in effect a change for which the appellant is entitled to an equitable adjustment. The Government should reasonably have been expected to "specify the utilities best known to it." Identifying the utilities was 66 AGO 9111A

CHANGES-Continued a duty if the Government expected bidders to prepare realistic bids. Notice of the possible existence of some utilities may have been given by the warnings in the drawings and specifications, but those warnings were "inadequate to support the presence of the twenty-two additional encumbrances." This conclusion is strengthened by the protection of utilities clause, which allows compensation for the repair of damage to utilities not on the drawings or known to the appellant.

B. J. Lucarelli & Co., Inc., ASBCA No. 5628, 9 September 1960, 60-2 BCA 2764. 

13. Limitation of Costs Clause in CPFF Contract Not Applicable to Change Orders in Circumstances of This Case. (ASBCA) See CONTRACT CLAUSES (Limitation of Costs) (par. 1) 14. Approximate Doubling of Amount of Earthwork Required Held To Be Outside Scope of Contract and Therefore a Breach. In April 

1951 the plaintiff received a $12,575 Government contract for constructing a levee embankment. The contract, which contained the standard Changes Clause, was a unit price agreement calling for an estimated 5,500 cubic yards of embankment. In May, after part of the work was completed, a flood inundated the worksite and forced abandonment of the work until July. The severity of the flood indicated the levee originally required was inadequate, so a Government engineer prepared revised specifications calling for an embankment of 

7,950 cubic yards. The plaintiff's bid proposal on the new specification provided for the same unit prices as did the original contract. Later a change order was issued to require 13,264 cubic yards of embankment. The completion date was extended to 12 September, by which date the work was finished. On 1 September the plaintiff notified the. Government he was proceeding under protest and had been so operating for three weeks. The Government offered to pay the plaintiff the unit prices established by the contract, but the plaintiff contended that the change order constituted a breach of contract entitling him to damages. He filed suit in the 

Court of Claims. Insisting that the change order not only did not alter the quality, character, nature, or type of work contemplated by the contract but also was actually designed to achieve the contract's purpose, the Government defended the suit on the ground that the change was within the scope of the contract and was, therefore, authorized by the Changes 

Clause. 

Held, for the plaintiff. A determination whether a change is within the scope of the contract can be made only by considering the totality of the change, and to do that requires recourse to its magnitude as well as its quality. 

The number of changes is not by itself the test for determining whether alterations are beyond a contract's scope. On the one hand, in Magoba

Construction Co. v. United States, 99 Ct. Cl. 

662 (1943), the Government was held not to have breached its contract by making sixty-two changes. On the other hand, a single change may be beyond the scope of a contract. In Gen eral Contracting & Construction Co. v. United 

States, 84 Ct. Cl. 570 (1937), the Government issued a change order eliminating a building from a hospital complex. The court held the elimination "amounted to a cardinal alteration of the contract" and was a breach of contract.

In the instant case the change doubling the amount of earth to be placed was a cardinal change. The differences between contract situa tions will of course permit no mathematical definition of what changes are beyond a contract's scope. However, in the instant case several facts are significant with respect to the seriousness of the change. The contract was for small amount and was undertaken so the plaintiff could keep his men and equipment operating during the weeks preceding the opening of the summer construction season. Regardless of the delay caused by the flood, the contract period was extended by the addition of the new work. Moreover, the change required the plaintiff to recail to the jobsite equipment he had thought was no longer needed.

The plaintiff's proposal to provide an embankment of 7,950 yards at the unit price established by the contract did not waive his right to claim that the eventual change breached the contract. His proposal was made on an amount of earthwork only slightly larger than the original estimate and was not applicable to the amount eventually required.

AGO 9111A 67

CHANGES-Continued Saddler v. United States, 287 F.2d 411 (Ct.
