Change Was Timely Because It Was Filed 

Within 30 Days After the Fact That the 

Change Would Substantially Decrease the Volume of Work Became Clear. (Ct. Cl.) See TYPES OF CONTRACTS (Time and Materials) (par. 1) 17. Requirement of Site Investigation and Statement in Specifications That Ledge Might Be Encountered Do Not Prevail Over Changed Conditions Clause if Changed Condition Within Meaning of That Clause Was Encountered- Encountering Subsurface Ledge Was Changed 

Condition Even Though Specifications Warned Ledge Possibly Might Be Encountered. The appellant had constructed a runway and taxiway under a fixed-price contract. That contract was on a "classified" basis; that is, the excavation of boulder and ledge encountered in excess of the quantities estimated in the invitation for bids was to be paid for at an agreed rate per cubic yard. The area was one of glacial deposit and a very large sum had to be paid the appellant for unanticipated ledge and boulders. 

When a decision was made to extend the runway and taxiway, the Government determined that the contract would be awarded on an “unclassified" basis; that is, there would be no estimate of boulders and ledge and the contractor would be entitled to no relief for encountering boulders and ledge unless he could establish there was a changed condition within the meaning of the Changed Conditions Clause. 

At a pre-bid conference the appellant and other prospective bidders tried to persuade the Government to change the contract from an "unclassified" to a "classified" basis, but the

Government refused. During the conference, a Government representative stated he believed that subsurface boulders rather than ledge would be encountered in the excavation area. 

The boring logs attached to the invitation for bids showed "refusal points" (places where the sampling pipe met resistance preventing further penetration) well below the required excavation depth at all but a few of the 75 places where borings were made in the area to be excavated. After receiving the contract, which was awarded on an "unclassified" basis and contained the standard Changed Conditions Clause, the appellant encountered subsurface ledge and boulders. He filed a claim with the contracting officer for an equitable adjustment under the Changed Conditions Clause. He argued that he had not anticipated finding any ledge and that the boulders were five times more numerous than he had anticipated and some were so large that blasting was needed to remove them. He appealed to the ASBCA from the contracting officer's denial of his claim. He argued that he had reasonably relied on the boring logs, which he interpreted as indicating that within the excavation area there was neither a ledge nor a sizable number of boulders. The Government disputed the reasonableness of appellant's expectations, on the grounds that (1) the specifications stated that a site examination disclosed that subsurface boulder "will" be encountered and that there was a "possibility" that ledge "may" be encountered; (2) appellant was concerned about bidding on an "unclassified" basis; (3) appellant had encountered ledge and boulders in excavating for the original runway.

Held, appeal sustained as to the ledge and denied as to the boulders. The ledge constituted a changed condition. The requirement of a site investigation and the statement in the specifications of the possibility that ledge might be encountered do not prevail over the Changed Conditions Clause if a changed condition within the meaning of that clause was encountered. 

See, e.g., Fehlhaber Corp. v. United States, 138 

Ct. Cl. 571, 584 (1957); Calvada, Inc., ASBCA

No. 2062 (8 Aug. 1956), 56–2 BCA 1033. The appellant encountered a changed condition of the first type mentioned in the clause, namely a subsurface or latent physical condition at the site differing materially from those indicated in 68 AGO 9111A

CHANGES-Continued the contract. The fact that the Government incurred the expense of making 75 borings in the excavation area and then attached the boring logs to the invitation for bids supports the conclusion that the Government intended that the boring logs should be relied on as a representation of subsurface conditions, at least to the extent not contradicted by other relevant circumstances. The appellant encountered substantial subsurface ledge in the areas where the boring logs do not show a refusal point within the excavation depth. 

The statement in the specifications that "it is possible that ledge rock may be encountered" did not notify the appellant to anticipate a ledge. The words "possible" and "may" indicated something less than a probability. The specifications could properly be construed to mean that, at the worst, some but no substantial quantity of subsurface ledge might be encountered. The instant case is analogous to R. C. 

Huffman Constr. Co. v. United States, 100 Ct.

Cl. 80 (1943). In that case the contract's specifications stated that "some hardpan" would be encountered. The Court of Claims stated that the contractor could reasonably infer that the amount to be encountered "would not be great" and that, if the contractor encountered substantial quantities, the court "would conclude that the conditions did materially differ from that indicated by the specifications." Id. at 115.

The Government contends that a visual examination of the site, together with the appellant's experience under the contract for the original runway, should have alerted appellant to the presence of ledge. The simple answer is that the same information was available to the Government, but at the pre-bid conference a Government representative stated that he believed no ledge would be encountered. Moreover, the specifications stated that a site examination indicated merely the possibility that ledge would be encountered. The evidence presented at the hearing did not establish that a site examination revealed the presence of substantial subsurface ledge. Finally, because of the nature of a glacial deposit, the existence of subsurface ledge where the original runway was placed did not indicate there was ledge within the surrounding areas. 

Second, there was no changed condition as to the boulders. Neither the specifications nor the boring logs made any representation as to the quantity and size of boulders to be encountered. In fact, the boring logs specifically listed the presence of boulders within the excavation depths. 

Gil Wyner Co., ASBCA No. 6114, 31 March 1961, 61-1 BCA 2994. 

18. Readvertising Must Be Undertaken

When Substantial Changes Are Made in Specifications After Bid Opening and Before Award. (C.G.) See BIDS & AWARDS (par. 40) 19. Equitable Adjustment of Difference Between Cost of Domestic and Foreign Copper May Be Made Where Contract Inadvertently Added Copper to the Invitation for Bid's List of Items Exempt From Buy American Act Provisions and a Change Order Deleted Copper 

From the List After the Contractor Had Pur chased Foreign Copper. The Corps of Engi neers issued at invitation for bids for the con struction of Capehart Housing at Fort Lee, Virginia. The invitation included a "specimen housing contract" which provided in part: The eligible builder agrees that in the performance of the work under this Housing Contract the eligible builder shall use only such unmanufactured articles, materials and supplies (which term 'articles materials and supplies' is hereinafter referred to in this clause as 'supplies') as have been mined or produced in the United States, and only such manufactured supplies as have been manufactured in the United States substantially all from supplies mined, produced, or manufactured, as the case may be, in the United States. Pursuant to the Buy American Act (41 U.S.C. 10a-d), the foregoing provisions shall not apply with respect to supplies to be used in the performance of work under this Housing Contract which are of a class. . . determined by the head of the Department or his duly authorized representative not to be mined, produced, or manufactured, as the case may be, in the United States in sufficient and reasonably available commercial quantities and of a satisfactory quality.

The "specimen housing contract" listed materials that could be used in the work advertised without regard to the country of origin because they, or the materials used for their manufacture, are not "mined, produced or manufactured in the United States in AGO 9111A 69

CHANGES-Continued sufficient and reasonably available commercial quantities and of a satisfactory quality." 

Copper was not listed. The low, responsible bidder was sent a letter of acceptability dated 

20 April 1959, obligating the bidder to perform certain acts, including the execution of a written contract incorporating the provisions of the "specimen housing contract." A lengthy delay then occurred, apparently because of difficulties in arranging financing. On 11 

January 1960 another letter of acceptability, similar to the first, was sent the low bidder. 

A week later the parties signed a written contract in which, through the Government's inadvertence, the list of items exempt from the Buy American provisions differed from the list in the "specimen housing contract." Copper and aluminum were added and some items deleted. The contractor obtained foreign copper, but after a determination was made that copper could not properly be exempted, he was directed to substitute domestic copper. The contracting officer issued a change order deleting copper from the exempt list and providing an "equitable adjustment" of $60,700, which represented (1) the difference between the cost of foreign and domestic copper, (2) handling and shipping charges for disposal of the foreign copper, and (3) the costs of the contractor in revising his sequence of operations. The propriety of the change order was questioned, and the Comptroller General was asked for an opinion. 

Held, the contractor is entitled to a price adjustment. The housing project was authorized by 42 U.S.C. § 1594, which provides in part that "Before the Secretary shall enter into any contract for the construction of housing, he shall invite the submission of competitive bids after advertising in the manner presscribed in ... [10 U.S.C. § 2305]." This language indicates that Congress intended contracts to be awarded by competitive bid. A contract so awarded must be the same contract offered to all bidders by the invitation. Diamond v. City of Mankato, 89 Minn. 48, 93 N.W. 911 (1903).

The provisions of the bid form indicate that the parties intended that all material conditions of the contract be established by the bid documents. Since no material condition remain unsettled, acceptance of the bid by issuing the letter of acceptability created a binding contract, even though the parties contemplated later execution of a more formal document. 

Conti v. United States, 158 F. 2d 581 (1st Cir. 

1946); Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144012, 25 Jan 1961.

According to the invitation, the contractor was then obligated to execute a formal contract that would preclude the use of foreign copper.

Nevertheless, the formal document signed by the parties permitted the use of foreign copper but not of other foreign items that the invitation permitted. That formal document must be regarded as fixing the obligations of the parties unless the changes in the "Buy American" exemptions exceeded the power of the contracting officer and did not, therefore, bind the Government. 

Under the Buy American Act, the applicable regulations, and the formal contract between the parties, a proper determination could be made at any time to change the items on the exempt list. Any change after award that could reasonably be regarded as affecting bid prices should have been made through a change order, with an appropriate equitable adjustment in price. In the instant case the contractor could reasonably assume, and apparently did, that a proper determination had been made, that the change in contract language was adopted in lieu of a change order, and that no equitable adjustment was in order because the addition of some items to the exempt list was balanced by the deletion of other items. 

That assumption was particularly reasonable in view of the unusually long period between bid opening and the execution of the formal document. In reliance upon that assumption, which resulted solely from the contracting agency's negligence, the contractor committed himself to use foreign copper. Therefore, the contractor may be paid the difference between the cost of the foreign and domestic copper. 

As to the other costs in the "equitable adjustment" made by the contracting officer they were as the administrative report indicatedin the nature of consequential damages, which were outside the scope of the contract and not for inclusion in the adjustment. 70 AGO 9111A

Alleged Final Payment. (ASBCA) See ARMED SERVICES BOARD OF CONTRACT APPEALS (par. 12) 21. Where Facts Indicate That the Contracting Officer Had Notice, Either Actual or Con structive, of the Issuance of a Change by "Gov ernment Technical Personnel" the Government Had Duty Promptly To Issue a Modification; 

The Government Cannot Sit Passively Back and 

Then Refuse To Ratify. A contract for $12,780 was entered into in April 1959, calling for the installation of a double circuit lighting system along a taxiway at an Air Force base. It was contemplated that the wire laying would require the digging of a number of conduits under the taxiway. In May "responsible Government technical people 'discussed' " with the contractor a change from the double circuit required by the contract drawings to a single circuit. As a consequence of this discussion, the contractor proceeded with the installation of a single circuit system. In August, after the contractor had so proceeded without incident and without the issuance of any formal revisions of the contract drawings another conference was held with "Base engineering personnel" for the purpose of briefing the contractor's newly hired electrician. The discussions were with respect to a single circuit system, the type that was actually being installed by the contractor. At this time the contractor had completed all the trenching and conduits required for all the wiring except for one conduit necessary to close the circuit near one end of the taxiway. As a matter of fact all of the deviations from the original specifications that resulted from the installation of a single circuit system with the exception of this one conduit were depicted on revised drawings that were incorporated into the contract in November.

The appeal is from the contracting officer's refusal to compensate the contractor for the costs incurred in preparing this one conduit. 

The contractor understood Mr. S (Chief of the Base Electrical Maintenance Section) to say at the August meeting that the conduit should be run under the taxiway on a line between the last light on each side of the taxiway. 

Mr. S denied giving any such instruction, but admitted that he "could have drawn" a line on the contractor's drawing between those lights and across the taxiway. However, this would have been merely to show that the two electrical lines had to be closed, not necessarily that they had to be closed at that exact place. The contractor proceeded in accordance with his understanding and worked for over three weeks pushing a 2 inch conduit under the 150 foot taxiway. He encountered unusual difficulty becase of the more than average compaction of the underlying ground (this part of the taxiway had formerly been a runway) with the result that several holes had to be dug and much pipe was used up before a pipe was pushed all the way through. His alleged costs for this operation were in excess of $8,600. 

Immediately upon finishing this work and in the course of complying with orders received in conjunction with a hurricane alert, contractor's electrician walked some 300 feet beyond the last lights and toward the end of the taxiway and observed a manhole that was found to lead to an existing conduit under the taxiway. The next day at a meeting attended by the contractor, the contracting officer and "Base technical personnel" it was decided that this conduit should be used and the other one abandoned. It was at this meeting, held at the end of September, that the contracting officer was for the first time advised of the need for revised drawings in connection with the project. 

Compensation for the work done on the abandoned conduit was denied by the contracting officer on the grounds that (1) the work was not called for under the contract or any changes thereto, (2) the work had not been ordered by the contracting officer, (3) no au- AGO 9111A 71

CHANGES-Continued thority existed for the work to have been performed and (4) the conduit had not been and probably never would be tied into the electrical system.

Additional relevant facts were that the contract contained a "non-boiler plate" clause to the effect that only the contracting officer had authority to alter the contract; the "Base technical people" denied giving "directions" to the contractor, but assumed that he would approach the contracting officer about the issuance of formal contract amendments; the original contract drawings did not show the belatedly discovered existing conduit, and no representative of the Government recalled advising the contractor of its existence; and this was the contractor's first Government contract. 

Held, the contractor is entitled to recover, but the case is remanded to the contracting officer for a determination as to quantum. 

Here was a case where "the contractor, the contracting officer and the concerned Government technical personnel are all operating on the same military base. Performance proceeded almost from the outset under the eyes of assigned supervisory personnel in a manner patently at variance with the contract drawings. According to the testimony, the Base technical inspector visited the project at least once a week. The digging of the conduit in question continued in plain view along the taxiway at the Base every day for almost a month. 

Base technical personnel clearly knew what was going on and as clearly intended that the original drawings should not be followed. They may not have instructed the contractor to finish the job of making the final crossing as attempted but they were aware of the attempt and could readily have halted the work in favor of the alternative ultimately adopted had they wanted to. Presumably the Base engineer and contracting officer met not infrequently about projects at their Base of mutual concern, as this one surely must have been. Conceding therefore that the contracting officer was the only one empowered to authorize changes in the contract, and that a special clause was included to emphasize the limitations in the authority of the technical personnel, we must hold under the peculiar circumstances of this case that he had timely notice of the changes, if not actually then certainly constructively. Having such notice, it was the Government's duty promptly to issue new contract drawings which would correctly reflect what was in fact wanted and would show with reasonable precision the desired course of the single loop circuit; particularly so if it was not satisfied with the method the contractor was in fact employing. Not having done this, but instead sitting passively back and doing nothing, it can only be assumed now that appellant's methods were approved and we so find. 

Under these circumstances the Government is in a poor position after the event to ratify all the drawing revisions theretofore informally made except the one that alone turned out to be avoidable."

W. Southard Jones, Inc., ASBCA No. 6321, 20 October 1961, 61-2 BCA 3182.

25. Contractor Held Entitled to Costs of Acceleration Ordered by Contracting Officer Who Erroneously Failed To Give Contractor Credit for Time Extensions Due for Delays Caused by Operation of Priority System-Since Word

On 5 April 1954 the Corps of Engineers invited bids on the construction of fifteen buildings and related structures. In preparing a bid, the appellant requested and obtained quotations on steel. Neither the request for quotations nor the quotation from the R Co.-the steel fabricator the appellant later chose-mentioned when delivery was desired or would be made. The appellant thought delivery was assured by the fabricator's experience and by the priority assigned to the contract. For that priority, steel mills were required to reserve space upon their books for the acceptance of priority orders. 

The mills were required to allocate portions of their monthly rollings for the fulfillment of orders placed at least forty-five days before the first day of the month in which shipment was requested. 

The appellant was awarded the contract, which contained, besides the standard Changes

It was understood, however, that the chart's dates for delivery of steel conformed to the dates in the subcontract with the R Co. and that the chart would be revised when firm steel delivery dates were known. On

The appellant pointed out that only some types of steel needed could be obtained from warehouses and that substitutes for the other types could be obtained from warehouses but would be uneconomical and might not save time because they would involve extra engineering and fabrication. Government personnel agreed that warehouse purchases were not feasible and decided to try to expedite mill deliveries. The R Co. received steel from the mill during August and early September. A small quantity of fabricated steel, for which the R Co. used steel on hand, was delivered to the appellant in August. The remainder of the fabricated steel was delivered to the appellant in September and early October. On 8 September the contracting officer wrote appellant about the work being behind schedule. The contracting officer's letter ordered the appellant to "take such steps as may be necessary, including but not necessarily limited to, increased manpower, increased number of shifts, additional overtime operations, additional days of work and/or amount of construction plant to bring your operations up to schedule and to assure completion of your contract in accordance with your progress schedule." The appellant replied that construction was proceeding as rapidly as possible in view of the delayed deliveries of steel.

On a visit to the job site on 13 October the contracting officer stated that no time extension had been granted and that the appellant was not meeting the schedule furnished to the 

Government on 9 July. The contracting officer threatened to terminate the contract for default if the work was not completed in accordance with the 9 July schedule. On 20 October the contracting officer directed that overtime operations be increased. The appellant hired additional workers and had the crews work overtime. The appellant claimed a right, under the Changes Clause, to costs incurred in accelerating work. He appealed to the ASBCA from the contracting officer's denial of the claim. 

Held, appeal sustained. The contract gave the Government the privilege to demand acceleration only if the appellant fell behind a current progress schedule, one reflecting credit for extensions given to, and for excusable delays encountered by, the appellant. The contracting officer's comparison of progress with the 9 July schedule was improper, for the appellant was entitled to a time extension. The contract provided. for such an extension for delay due to the operation of the priorities and allocations system and not caused by the appellant. The record establishes that the appellant was in fact delayed for such a reason. 

Steel ordered from the mill shortly after appellant received the notice to proceed was not rolled until August. Under the priority the appellant could not have demanded earlier rolling. Contrary to the Government's contention, the appellant was not negligent in relying solely on mills for the steel. The evidence indicates that steel of the kind and quantity involved is not normally purchased from warehouses and would not have been available for immediate delivery from warehouses. 

The appellant realized that relying on the mills would delay construction. However, the appellant also knew that the contract provided for compensating time extensions. The contract provided for extensions even for delays that could have been anticipated at the time of bidding. Compensable 26. Board Holds Under Changes Clause a Shift in Method of Operations Caused by the Government's Imposition of a Requirement Inconsistent With What the Con tract Contemplated. The Raritan Arsenal issued an invitation for bids on a construction contract for the replacement of ties under railroad switches. When the invitation was received, the D Co., which later received the contract, found nothing restricting the method of performing the work. There was nothing about the volume of rail traffic or of making the facilities under repair available for traffic during the day or night. Before submitting a bid the D Co. had two agents tour the work site with an Arsenal official. After the tour and conversations with an Arsenal official, the D Co.'s agents concluded that the work could be performed throughout rather large areas at once. The bid price was therefore calculated on the assumption that the work could be handled by specialized crews, with each crew handling only one task, such as spike removal. 

After beginning performance, the D Co. was warned that the tracks would have to be ready for traffic at all times upon demand by the Government during the working day, and would have to be "buttoned up" at the end of each day to be ready for night traffic. The D Co. was forced to stop using specialized crews. The firm began using several crews, each of which could complete the entire replacement operation on a tie. The change in method of operation greatly decreased the efficiency of the work and increased the firm's costs. The firm filed a claim for an equitable adjustment under the contract's standard Changes Clause (cl. 3, SF 

23A, Mar. 1953 ed.). A timely appeal was taken from the contracting officer's denial of the claim. The D Co. presented evidence that in several other instances both the Raritan 

Arsenal and other Government installations had given specific warning before the bidding that the work would have to be opened for traffic on demand.

Among the documents made part of the Board's file was the "Information for Construc tion Bidders, Contractors, Subcontractors and their Employees." That document had been sent to bidders with the invitation and provided in part:

Foreman of contractor will advise the Chief, Sur veillance Division or Ammunition Division when reporting each morning of the location of work, the type of work and the number of employees. 

The information is essential in the event of an emergency or where, because of ammunition loading, unloading or movement, work by the contractor may be suspended for a period of time.

If work is suspended for any reason, Surveillance Division should be advised, prior to commencement of work by the contractor, the date the contractor intends to return. 

Held, appeal sustained. If, as the Government claims, the contract contemplated that all tracks would be kept in a condition to permit traffic on demand, there would have been no need for the provision quoted above about suspending work during emergencies or at other times. The contract contemplated the contractor might well tie up portions of the track, and the Arsenal was to be informed in advance so operations could be arranged accordingly or suspension orders could be issued. The quoted provision indicates the Government's solution for the problem of the D Co.'s interference with track usage. The solution did not by any means match the impact on performance caused by the change in operations the firm was required to make. That change, therefore, was compensable within the terms of the Changes 

Clause. 

George E. Detzel Co., ASBCA No. 5852, 31 

August 1961, 61-2 BCA 3142. 

27. Compensation Denied for Government's Revocation of Permission To Deviate From 

Specifications. A Navy contractor was granted permission to use Type 2 cable instead of the 

Type 1 cable required by the specifications.

The permission was given on the condition that all other contract requirements would be met.

Six months later the subcontractor who was to install the cable claimed that Type 2 cable would not be suitable and requested, through the contractor, that Type 3 cable be permitted. 

At the time of the request Type 2 cable had been ordered by the subcontractor but not delivered. The Navy Officer in Charge denied

AGO 9111A 75

CHANGES-Continued the request and, moreover, stated that the approval of substitution of Type 2 cable had been in error. Use of Type 1 cable was directed.

The subcontractor then submitted, through the contractor, a claim for extra expenses allegedly resulting from the Government's withdrawal of its approval of the substitution of Type 2 

for Type 1 cable. The claim was based on an allegation that the subcontractor had a less favorable bargaining position with respect to the Type 1 cable and that costs had been incurred because of the delay caused when the order for Type 2 cable was cancelled and a new order was placed for Type 1 cable. An appeal was taken to the ASBCA from the denial of the claim.

Held, appeal denied. Withdrawal of the permission to use Type 2 cable was not detrimental to the contractor or subcontractor. It was the latter who first alleged that Type 2 cable was unsuitable. In fact, when the allegation was made, the subcontractor had apparently abandoned his desire to use that type cable. Thus the Navy's response was little more than an expression of agreement with the subcontractor that both the request for and the granting of permission to use Type 2 cable had been in error. The evidence would not support a finding that the Government reneged its agreement to the substitution in a manner that would make the Government liable. After the agreement for the substitution of Type 2 cable had been renounced by mutual assent of the parties in recognition of error (or mutual mistake), Type 

1 cable remained as the only type permitted by the contract for installation. The Navy had no duty to approve a second proposal for substitution. 

Griffith Co., ASBCA No. 7277, 18 January 1962, 1962 BCA 3279. 

28. Comptroller General Holds That Contrac tor Is Not Entitled Under Changes Clause of Supply Contract to Equitable Adjustment for Costs Incurred Incident to Suspension of Work -"Excusable Causes" Provision of Default Clause Does Not Authorize Compensation for Delays-Federal Procurement Regulations Do Not Authorize Inclusion of Suspension of Work Clause in Supply Contract-Suspension of Work Clause May Not Be Added by Amend ment Unless Consideration Is Given to Government-Even in Absence of Suspension of Work 

Clause, Government Not Liable for Breach of Contract for Reasonable Suspension-Administrative Agency Lacks Authority To Settle Breach of Contract Claim. The I Co. received from the Post Office Department a formally advertised contract, dated 30 June 1959, for furnishing and installing a "Mail-Flo system" on the eighth and ninth floors of a post office.

The contract incorporated Standard Form 32 

(Oct. 1957 ed.), the Changes Clause of which provided in part:

The Contracting Officer may at any time make changes within the general scope of this contract, in any one or more of the following: (i) Drawings, designs, or specifications, where the supplies to be furnished are to be specially manufactured for the Government in accordance therewith; (ii) method of shipment or packing; and (iii) place of delivery. If any such change causes an increase or decrease in the cost of, or the time required for, the performance of any part of the work under this contract, whether changed or not changed by any such order, an equitable adjustment shall be made in the contract price or delivery schedule, or both, and the contract shall be modified in writing accordingly. . . 

Preparation of the system was apparently to begin immediately. Installation on the ninth floor was to begin between 4 and 11 January 

1960 and to be completed by June 1960; installation on the eighth floor was to begin when work on the ninth floor had been completed and to be completed by 1 October 1960. The per formance dates were determined primarily by (1) the fact that the post office could not permit postal operations on the eighth floor to be totally interrupted at any one time, and (2) during the 

Christmas mailing season from 1 November through 31 December, no installation on either floor could be permitted. The I Co. was aware of these factors. The Resident Engineer was given authority by the contract to "stop the work whenever such stoppage may be necessary to insure the proper execution of the contract. . . ." On 7 July 1959 a steel strike began. The contracting officer, apparently acting under para. c. of the contract's Default 

Clause (cl. 11, SF 32, Oct. 1957 ed.) allowed the I Co. a time extension of 132 days on account of the strike. Negotiations were con- 76 AGO 9111A

CHANGES-Continued ducted on a new work schedule, and about 13 May 1960 the I Co. was authorized to proceed with work on the eighth and ninth floors concurrently. Both floors were to be completed by 1 November 1960. After proceeding one month on the revised schedule, the I Co. was ordered by the Resident Engineer to stop work on the eighth floor. The suspension continued until 9 January 1961; at that time the date for completion of the work was extended by mutual agreement to 2 June 1961. 

In February 1961 the I Co. submitted a claim based on alleged additional costs resulting from the delay occasioned by the suspension of work on the eighth floor. The Postmaster General asked the Comptroller General: (1) whether the claim could be considered under the contract's Changes Clause; (2) if not, whether, on the assumption the I Co. had a valid claim for breach of contract, the contract could be amended to include a suspension of work clause as a contractual vehicle for administrative settlement of the claim; (3) if question 2 were answered in the negative, whether the Post Office Department could consider the claim and settle it on principles applicable to breach of contract cases. 

Held, all three questions are answered in the negative. For the answer to the first question,

United States v. Rice, 317 U.S. 61 (1942), is relevant. There a contractor sued to recover expenses incurred as a result of the Government's suspension of work under a construction contract. The suspension resulted from the fact that the construction site had to be changednecessitating other changes in the specifications-because the soil at the original site was found to be unsuitable. The contract contained the Changes Clause of Standard Form 23A (cl. 

3, Mar. 1953 ed.), which read in part: 

The contracting officer may at any time. . . make changes in the drawings and (or) specifications of this contract and within the general scope thereof. 

If such changes cause an increase or decrease in the amount due under this contract, or in the time required for its performance, an equitable adjustment shall be made..

In concluding that the contractor was not entitled to recover, the Court stated:

It seems wholly reasonable that an "increase or decrease in the amount due" should be met with an alteration of price, and that "an increase or decrease .. in the time required" should be met with an alteration of the time allowed; for "increase or decrease of costs" plainly applies to the changes in cost due to the structural changes required by the altered specification and not to consequential damages which might flow from delay taken care of in the "difference in time" provision.

To the same effect are General Contr. and 

Constr. Co. v. United States, 84 Ct. Cl. 570 

(1937), and Mount Vernon Contr. Corp. v. 

United States, 139 Ct. Cl. 688 (1957). In Ameri can Pipe & Steel Corp. v. Firestone Tire 

& Rubber Co., 186 F. Supp. 904 (S.D. Cal. 

1960), the court held that the costs occasioned by a delay while a change order was being prepared could not be recovered. The clause under which recovery was denied was identical with that in the I Co.'s contract except that the former lacked the phrase "whether changed or not changed by any such order." That addition in the I Co.'s contract is not an argument in favor of upholding that firm's claim. The phrase does not change the provision that an equitable adjustment may be given only for a change like that specified-that is, in the drawings, designs, specifications, method of shipment or delivery, and place of delivery. 

It is open to serious doubt whether the changes effected by the alterations in the I Co.'s installation schedules may be regarded as changes in specifications for which an equitable adjustment may be given. The clear holding of the Supreme Court and Court of Claims decisions cited above was that the changes in specifications covered by the clause are limited to structural changes and do not embrace changes in time of performance. The subcommittee of the ASPR Committee that drafted the revised form of the Changes Clause incorporated into the 1957 Standard Form 32 rejected a proposal to subtitute "schedule or place of delivery" for "place of delivery" in the last phrase of the first sentence. On the other hand, an administrative board has said that a stop order may itself be a change entitling the contractor to an equitable adjustment. Gutherie Electrical 

Constr., Interior BCA No. 22 (22 Jul 1955), citing Charles H. Schaefer, ASBCA No. 917 

(31 Jan 1952).

The matter was debated in a AGO 9111A 77

CHANGES—Continued construction Contracts Conference summarized in 3 Government Contractor par. 560 (1961). 

The arguments for regarding changes of time of performance as changes calling for an equitable adjustment are more readily applicable to construction contracts than to supply contracts, because of the differences between the changes articles in the standard forms for the two types and because time factors generally have a more far-reaching effect on other elements of a construction project than is true in production of a manufactured item. Although the instal lation requirements of the I Co.'s contract could readily have been incorporated in a 

Standard Form 23A construction contract, the contract actually was made on a standard form for supply contracts. Thus the provisions of 

Standard Form 23A should not be used to resolve problems under the I Co.'s contract.

Even if the conclusion should be reached, in spite of Rice and similar cases, that a change of delivery time might warrant an equitable adjustment under the Changes Clause of 

Standard Form 32, the circumstances of this case would not justify any substantial adjustment in the contract price. Even if the steel strike were an excusable cause of delay within the terms of the contract's default clause, the strike is no justification for increasing the contract price. The "excusable cause" provision of that clause does not entitle the contractor to compensation for delays. 

The contractor apparently argues that relief should be given because the original schedule was, in view of the delay caused by the strike, modified in May 1960 by mutual consent to permit work on both floors simultaneously, and that the work could have been completed by 1 November 1960 but for the Government's action in stopping work on the eighth floor. 

However, the Government's action does not appear to have been unauthorized by the contract or unreasonable. The schedule on which the work was done was approximately what would have been expected had there been no modifying agreements. The permission to work on the two floors simultaneously was not a waiver of the requirement that postal work should not be unduly interfered with or of the right of the Resident Engineer to stop the work when necessary to insure proper performance. 

As to the second question, the Suspension of

Work Clause in FPR 1-7.602-1 is authorized only for construction contracts. Thus the clause should not be added to the I Co.'s supply contract. In any event, incorporating the clause by an amendment would be improper without consideration. The clause could not be added by way of reformation unless there is proof that there was an intention to include the clause when the contract was executed.

As to the third question, the Government would not be liable for breach of contract for the suspension of work unless the stop order was unreasonable. Mount Vernon Contr. Corp. 

v. United States, 139 Ct. Cl. 688 (1957). The record does not establish that the Government acted unreasonably. Even if it did, however, there is no known authority that would permit the Post Office Department to settle the claim. 

32 Comp. Gen. 333,336 (1953). 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-140040, 8 January 1962, 41 Comp. Gen. 436.

30. Equitable Adjustment Based on Representations by Contractor of Material Facts That Were False May Be Corrected by Govern ment. The M Co.'s construction contract with the Veterans Administration contained the standard Changes Clause (cl. 3, SF 23A, Mar. 

1953 ed.). In the course of performance the firm submitted a proposal for certain alterations in the specifications. According to the proposal, the alterations would increase certain items of work and reduce others. The M Co. offered the Government a credit of $240 for one of the work reductions and said nothing about an equitable adjustment for the rest. The firm was given a notice to proceed with the proposed changes. Shortly thereafter the Government issued Change Order B, which incorporated some, but not all, of the alterations suggested in the M Co.'s proposal. The change order reduced the con- 78 AGO 9111A

CHOICE OF LAW 

tract price by $240. After the work was finished, the M Co. requested a price change for the alterations. The request was for an increase of $1,241.85, the difference between $2,301.60 for additional expense and $1,059.75, a credit to the Government. After extended negotiations the contracting officer notified the firm that Change Order B was being superseded by Change Order T, which provided for a credit to the Government of $1,594.20. The supercession was said to be necessary because of substantial errors in the proposal that the firm has made and that was used as a basis for 

Change Order B. As an example, the contract ing officer stated that, while the M Co.'s proposal had stated that more concrete would be required, the change order had resulted in much less concrete being used. The M Co. took the position that a change order could not be unilaterally reopened once it had been consummated and entered into as a formal contract modification. The firm stated that if the new change order were a decision of the contracting officer, an appeal was being taken to the contract appeals board. The VA treated that statement as an appeal. The VA Administrator submitted the matter to the General Accounting Office on the ground that the pending appeal would require consideration of GAO decisions relating to the Government's right to recover funds erroneously paid under mistake of law or fact. The Administrator asked the GAO whether the contractor's acceptance of Change

Order B created a final and binding modification in the nature of an accord and satisfaction. 

Held, the question is answered in the negative. There is no evidence establishing that 

Change Order B was ever accepted. However, the Change Order was a counteroffer, and under certain circumstances acceptance of a counteroffer may be inferred where the recipient performs his part of the counteroffer. 

Nevertheless, the modification would be invalid and could be rescinded if it were made upon an assumed state of material facts as to which there was a mutual mistake. See e.g.,

Road Improvement District No. 4 v. Wilkerson, 

5 F. 2d 416, 417 (8th Cir. 1925). As the Supreme Court has stated, it would be a mischievous doctrine if actions by public officials based only on guesses and without regard to the true facts could preclude recovery by the 

Government. United States ". Barlow, 132

U.S. 271 (1889). The Court enunciated the principle that contracts may be rescinded for misrepresentations of material facts. The 

Court's premise was that it would be unjust to allow one who has made false representations, even innocently, to retain the fruits of a bargain induced by those representations. In the instant case the contracting officer has found that the M Co.'s proposal did not include all elements of work and erroneously stated that the requested change would increase the amount of concrete required. 

Change Order B neither explicitly nor implicitly evidenced an intention to preclude adjustment of items that were omitted and might otherwise be considered according to the procedure prescribed in the contract. That consideration of the actual facts and all the material elements involved in the changes was mutually intended seems clear from the detailed specifications and the expressed provisions of the contract. Under the principles of fair dealing stated above, correction of the material mistakes in the determination of the equitable adjustment was justified and required under the circumstances. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145815, 5 February 1962.

CHOICE OF LAW 1. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals Holds in Suit Between Subcontractor and Government Prime Contractor That Federal Law Should Be Applied in Construing Subcontract. A Govern ment prime contractor, the P Co., required its subcontractor, the S Co., to make changes necessitated by the error of the P Co. in providing the S Co. with plans that deviated from the requirements of the prime contract. The 

P Co. compensated the S Co. for the cost of the changes, pursuant to a clause of the subcontract requiring an "equitable adjustment" for increased costs caused by change orders. The S 

Co. sued the P Co. for additional compensation for overhead losses caused by the partial work stoppage during a delay connected with the change. A federal district court, exercising jurisdiction because of the diversity of the AGO 9111A 79

CLAIMS AGAINST UNITED STATES 

parties' citizenship, held that an "equitable adjustment" had been made, so that no additional amount was due. The court relied upon federal law because the contract was characterized as a "government contract." The S Co. appealed to the Court of Appeals, arguing, among other things, that state rather than federal law was applicable.

Held, judgment affirmed. Since this is a diversity case, under Erie R.R. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64 (1938), state law would ordinarily be applicable. The district court held that federal law should be applied because the contract should be characterized as a "government contract." However, it is difficult to characterize a contract between two private parties as a "government contract." It has been held that the government-though a party to the prime contract has no contract with the subcontractor and is not liable to him nor suable by him. 

Severin v. United States, 99 Ct. Cl. 435 (1943), cert. denied, 322 U.S. 733 (1944). Further, if the contract were correctly characterized as a "government contract," the issue would still remain open in the trial court. In this circuit state law has previously been applied to a government contract in an action brought by the 

United States. Alameda County v. United States, 124 F. 2d 611 (9th Cir. 1941). The P 

Co. contends that the Erie case is inapplicable because the instant suit involves an area "in which the policy of the law is so dominated by the sweep of federal statutes" that legal relations within that area must be regulated by federal law. Citing, inter alia, Clearfield Trust 

Co. v. United States, 318 U.S. 363 (1943), the 

P Co. argues that the Erie doctrine does not apply to matters affecting the operation of the federal government, where the rules must be uniform throughout the country. This seems to be a better basis than that selected by the trial court for choosing the applicable law. The development of the law in this area, however, is still uncertain and unclear; the question is a close one. See Federal Jurisdiction: Law Applicable to Government Instruments, 45 Calif. L. 

Rev. 212 (1957). In general, the P Co. is correct that the construction of subcontracts, let under prime contracts connected with the national security, should be regulated by a uniform federal law. In the instant suit, for example, the prime contract apparently provides that an "equitable adjustment" in the contract price would be made in the event of a stop order. If this adjustment must reflect adjustments made under the subcontract, the cost of national security will be increased in the process. Congress' intention to decrease the high cost of defense by eliminating excessive profits from defense contracts may be seen in the Renegotiation Act, 50 U.S.C. §§ 1211–1233. 

The district court's conclusion that an "equitable adjustment" had been made will not be disturbed. What constitutes an "equitable adjustment" is a question of fact, United States v. Callahan Walker Co., 317 U.S. 56, 59 (1942), and the trial court's determination on such a question will not be upset in the absence of proof that the determination was clearly erroneous. Fed. R. Civ. P. 51.

American Pipe & Steel Corp. v. Firestone 

Tire & Rubber Co., 292 F. 2d 640 (9th Cir. 1961).

Claim by Inventor Against United States for Unauthorized Use of Patented Invention De veloped on Own Time While a Government Em ployee Denied Where Invention Related to Official Research and Development Responsibil ities. From December 1941 to June 1944, the plaintiff was employed by the Navy Bureau of 

Aeronautics as an aeronautical engineer and assigned to the preliminary aircraft design section. The section's function was to develop or consider possible methods of adapting existing aircraft to new uses and required a certain amount of preliminary research, ingenuity and 80 AGO 9111A

CLAIMS AGAINST UNITED STATES-Continued inventive ability. During his employment, the plaintiff developed and reduced to practice a mechanism for opening and closing external aircraft gunports. The invention was apparently perfected on the plaintiff's own time and with his own facilities. A patent application was filed in February 1944 and the patent was issued in 1948, after the Government employment had terminated. While the section supervisors exhibited no interest in the invention at first, an unauthorized use was subsequently made by the Government. The plaintiff brought action under 28 U.S.C. § 1498 (1952) to recover compensation for this use and the Government filed a motion to dismiss.

Held, the motion is granted. 28 U.S.C. § 1498 

(1952) provides in part:

Patent cases. 

A Government employee shall have the right to bring suit against the Government under this section except where he was in a position to order, influence, or induce use of the invention by the Government. This section shall not confer a right of action on any patentee or any assignee of such patentee with respect to any invention discovered or invented by a person while in the employment or service of the United States, where the invention was related to the official functions of the employee, in cases in which such functions included research and development, or in the making of which Government time, materials or facilities were used.

Assuming that the invention is the product of the plaintiff's own time and materials, this action is still barred if the invention is related to the official research and development responsibilities of a Government employee. The plaintiff was employed by a section which engaged in preliminary research and development when the invention was developed and reduced to practice. A mechanism for opening and closing aircraft gunports is generally related to the adaptation of aircraft to new uses, even though the section supervisors were not immediately interested. Consequently, the invention falls within the prohibitions of 28 U.S.C. § 1498. 

Myers v. United States, 177 F. Supp. 952 

(Ct. Cl. 1959). 

4. Where the Government Requires Cargo Operations at Ports During Unsafe Weather Conditions It Has Breached Its Safe Berth Warranty and Is Liable For Resultant Damage ---No Government Liability for Breach of Safe Berth Warranty in Areas Other Than Port or Place of Loading or Unloading. This is an ap peal from the contracting officer's denial of appellant's claim for loss and damage to the vessel's anchor and anchor cable allegedly caused prior to and during cargo loading operations under a time charter for the Government. During operation under the charter, the MSTS diverted the vessel to Villa do Porto, Santa 

Maria, Azores, to load cargo at anchorage there. When the vessel arrived at the port, the Portuguese Port Captain refused it permission to enter because of a heavy swell created by strong winds. 

He suggested that the vessel anchor at Sao Lourenco

Bay, 13 miles away, until weather conditions sufficiently improved to permit loading operations at Villa do Porto. The vessel proceeded to Sao Lourenco Bay and dropped starboard anchor. The following morning the port anchor was dropped to help steady the vessel. When the wind shifted, the Master ordered both anchors weighed in order to ride out the wind in the open sea. The port anchor was safely brought aboard but the starboard anchor chain parted with the loss of the anchor and 3½ shots (52½ fathoms) of chain. When the wind subsided sufficiently the ship obtained clearance to enter the anchorage area at Villa do Porto and dropped its port anchor there. When the MSTS representative insisted on the undertaking of cargo loading operations, the Master of the vessel orally protested the hazardous nature thereof. The protest was followed by written notice of an intention to hold the Government liable for any damage to the vessel resulting from loading cargo. Upon heaving in the port anchor incident to removing the vessel from the harbor as a safety precaution until weather conditions abated, it was disclosed that about one half the studs of the port anchor chain were missing and that many additional studs were loose and ready to fall out. After further protest by the Master due to the hazards of conducting cargo operations, MSTS directed the vessel to Praia, Terceira Island, Azores, to discharge the cargo previously loaded at Villa do 

Porto and to load other cargo for New York.

Both anchors (including a spare anchor on the AGO 9111A 81

CLAIMS AGAINST UNITED STATES-Continued starboard chain) were dropped, as weather conditions were similar to those prevailing at Villa do Porto, and cargo operations were likewise interrupted on occasion due to the rolling and pitching of the vessel. Appellant claims that further studs to both anchor chains were lost at this port. The contracting officer denied in its entirety appellant's claim for one lost starboard anchor, 4 lost shots of starboard chain, 6 damaged shots of starboard chain, and 10 damaged shots of port chain.

Held, appeal sustained in part and denied in part. There is no doubt that the Government's insistence on cargo operations at Villa do Porto and at Praia under the weather conditions then prevailing resulted in damage to the vessel's anchor chains and constituted a breach of the safe berth warranty (Article 8-Loading and 

Discharging). That article provides that cargo: shall be laden and discharged in any dock or at any wharf, place or open roadstead that Charterer may direct, provided the vessel can lie always safely afloat at any time of the tide. 

However, the safe berth warranty does not extend to areas related to other than the port or place of loading or discharging; it does not extend to areas to which the vessel may have to proceed as a matter of safety. Sao Lourenco is not a part of nor an approach to Villa do Porto, and therefore whatever hazards the vessel may have been exposed to there, as well as those hazards to which it would have been exposed if it had instead skirted the island until weather conditions abated, are "dangers and accidents of the seas," the risk of which the vessel owner has assumed under the exceptions clause of the charter. The Port Captain's suggestion that the vessel proceed to Sao Lourenco Bay coupled with the concurrence of MSTS therein do not constitute a direction to the Master to that effect. The Master could have instead skirted the island or taken to the open sea if he felt that would have been more prudent. Accordingly, to the extent the damage complained of was suffered at Sao Lourenco, the subject appeal is denied.

American President Lines, Ltd., ASBCA No. 

5368, 25 February 1960, 60-1 BCA 2565. 

5. United States Took Property Without Just Compensation When, Pursuant to Contract, It Destroyed the Value of Subcontract Liens by Requiring a Defaulting Prime Contractor to Transfer Title to All Contract Property to the United States. The contractor agreed to build 

11 personnel boats for the Navy. If a default occurred, the Navy reserved the right to terminate the contract and require the contractor to transfer title and deliver all completed and uncompleted work together with all manufacturing materials acquired for performance to the Government. The petitioners (subcontractors) furnished materials to the contractor for use in performance and, under Maine statutes, thereby acquired a lien on the materials which was enforceable by attachment. The contractor, however, defaulted and pursuant to the contract was required to transfer title and deliver all property on hand to the Government who removed it from the state. The petitioners, who had not been paid, brought an action against the Government and alleged that since the Government had destroyed the liens by making them unenforceable, their property had been taken without just compensation under the 

Fifth Amendment. The Court of Claims, rely ing on United States v. Ansonia Brass & Copper 

Co., 218 U.S. 452 (1910), held that there was no "taking" of property since the petitioners could not acquire enforceable liens on Government property. 169 F. Supp. 259. The Supreme 

Court granted certiorari.

Held, reversed and remanded to the Court of Claims to determine the value of the property taken. Sovereign immunity from the liens of laborers and materialmen extends only to property actually owned by the United States. 

United States v. Ansonia Brass & Copper Co., 218 U.S. 452, 471 (1910). Cf. United States v. 

Munsey Trust Co., 332 U.S. 234, 241 (1947).

Under the terms of this contract, the contractor had title to the vessels and work in progress until accepted by the Government upon final delivery or until title was transferred to the Government in the event of a default. While the Government made progress payments based upon a percentage of work completed, the payments were to be secured by a paramount lien on the property not the transfer of title. 

Finally, the contractor was required to immediately discharge any lien or right in rem 82 AGO 9111A

CLAIMS AGAINST UNITED STATES-Continued asserted against the property. The total effect of these contractual provisions is to vest title in the contractor during performance. Private liens, therefore, could validly attach to the property prior to the time that title was transferred to the Government.

A valid lien which is enforceable through an in rem proceeding constitutes a property right which the Government, under the Fifth Amendment, may not take without just compensation.

Louisville Bank v. Radford, 295 U.S. 555 

(1935). Even though the Government had a paramount lien to secure the progress payments, there is no evidence that the sale of the contractor's property would not produce receipts which exceed the Government's progress payment claim. The petitioners, therefore, have compensable property interests within the meaning of the Fifth Amendment. 

Prior to the contractor's transfer of title to the Government, the petitioners had valid liens which could be enforced by attachment under state law. After the title transfer, the liens were still valid, United States v. Alabama, 313 

U.S. 274 (1941), but could not be enforced because of the immunity of Government property from attachment. See United States v. 

Ansonia Brass & Copper Co., supra. The petitioners argue that the title transfer, by destroying valuable property rights, constituted a "taking" under the Fifth Amendment. The

Government argues that any action which deprives the petitioner of a remedy because of sovereign immunity cannot constitute a taking. 

This is true to the extent that property rights are destroyed as the consequential incidence of a valid regulatory measure. See United

States v. Central Eureka Mining Co., 357 U.S. 

155 (1958); Omnia Commercial Co. v. United States, 261 U.S. 502 (1923). The total destruc tion by the Government of all value of these liens, however, has every possible element of a 

Fifth Amendment "taking" and is not a mere "consequential incidence" of a valid regulatory measure. Before the liens were destroyed, the lienholders admittedly had compensable property. Immediately afterwards, they had none.

This was because the Government for its own advantage destroyed the value of the liens, something that the Government could do because its property was not subject to suit, but which no private purchaser could have done. 

Since this acquisition was for a public use, however accomplished, whether with an intent and purpose of extinguishing the liens or not, the Government's action did destroy them and in the circumstances of this case did thereby take the property value of those liens within the meaning of the Fifth Amendment. 

Armstrong v. United States, 364 U.S. 40 

[Note: Mr. Justice Harlan, with whom Mr.

Justice Frankfurter and Mr. Justice Clark joined, dissented and distinguished the instant case from those where the Government, in exercising its powers of eminent domain, extinguished all private claims which had previously attached to realty. In the eminent domain. cases, the lienholders were entitled to compensation for the value of their interests. 

Thibodo v. United States, 187 F. 2d 249 (9th

Cir. 1951). In this case, however, all the Government did was exercise its undoubted power to contract and to acquire title to the property, the consequent effect of which was to render the liens unenforceable because of the independent principle of sovereign immunity. The dissent concluded by stating that the "very nature of the doctrine of sovereign immunity precludes regarding its interposition as a Fifth 

Amendment 'taking'." "It seems to me that a

Court which, having established this immunity, then declares that the Government must pay for exercising it, is effectively negativing it."] 

6. Action For Breach Of Contract Where 

Damages Exceed $10,000 Brought Against Contracting Officer as Individual In Federal District 

Court Is Actually Claim Aganist United States Which Must Be Brought In Court Of Claims. 

In January 1959, the General Services Admin istration terminated for default the plaintiff's contract for the construction of dehumidified storage hutments and repurchased similar services from another source. The plaintiff, under the contract disputes clause, appealed to the Administrator of the GSA. While this appeal was still pending, the plaintiff sought a declaratory judgment that the contract was unlawfully terminated and damages exceeding $10,000 for breach of contract in a federal AGO 9111A 83

CLAIMS AGAINST UNITED STATES-Continued district court. The GSA Administrator and the contracting officer, who signed the contract, were named individually as defendants. The court dismissed the suit for the reason that venue as to the Administrator was improper and that there was no diversity of citizenship between the plaintiff and the defendant contracting officer. The plaintiff appealed. 

Held, affirmed on other grounds. Even though the GSA Administrator and the contracting officer were named as individual defendants, the action is in reality against the United States. It seeks a declaration of contract rights against the United States, see Mc- 

Kay v. Central Electric Power Co-op, 223 F. 2d 

623 (D.C. Cir. 1955), and claims damages for breach of contract which would be paid out of public funds. Cf. Mine Safety Appliances Co. v. Forrestal, 326 U.S. 371, 375 (1945). Since the contracting officer signed the contract as the Government's authorized representative he would not be personally liable for any breach of that contract.

Since this action is a contractual claim against the United States, the requirements of the Tucker Act, 28 U.S.C. Sec. 1491 (1958), must be met. This act gives the Court of Claims jurisdiction to render judgments upon any claim against the United States founded upon any express or implied contract with the United States. The federal district courts, however, have concurrent jurisdiction of contractual claims against the United States "not exceeding $10,000 in amount." 28 U.S.C. Sec. 1346(a) (2) (1958). The district court, therefore, had no jurisdiction of this action even though the United States had been made a party and properly served.

The plaintiff argues that this action seeks to review a legal wrong suffered because of agency action as permitted by Section 10 of the Ad ministrative Procedures Act, 5 U.S.C. Sec. 1009 

(1958). But this section defines procedures and the manner of judicial review and does not extend the jurisdiction of the federal courts to cases not otherwise within their competence.

Kansas City Power & Light Co. v. McKay, 225 

F. 2d 924. 932-933 (D.C. Cir. 1955), cert. denied, 350 U.S. 884 (1955). Further, since the plaintiff had an adequate remedy in the Court of Claims, judicial review would be precluded under section 10 (c). Finally, since the appeal under the Disputes clause is still pending, the plaintiff has failed to exhaust its administrative remedies and is not entitled to pursue legal remedies in a court of competent jurisdiction. 

United States v. Holpuch, 328 U.S. 234 (1946). 

Ove Gustavsson Contracting Co. v. Floete, 

278 F.2d 912 (2d Cir. 1960). 

[Note: For an opinion that the Administra tive Procedures Act is not applicable to the adjudication of disputes arising under Government contracts, see JAGT 1960/5842, 4 Feb ruary 1960, digested under DISPUTES, par. 

7. Tucker Act Does Not Give Consent to Declaratory Judgment Suits-Lessee of AEC Limited to Administrative Remedies. (9th Cir.) See SOVEREIGN IMMUNITY (par. 1) 8. United States in Contractual Capacity Not Liable in Damages for Breach of Contract Caused by Acts of United States in Sovereign 

Capacity. In December 1940, the plaintiff leased for two years part of a pier owned by the City of New York. A plant for processing and refining tungsten was established in the leased space. In August 1941, the plaintiff entered into a three year contract with a Reconstruction Finance Corporation subsidiary to process critical tungsten for the war. The plaintiff obtained additional pier space from the lessor and started performance.

In February 1942 the Secretary of War con demned approximately 55 acres of land on Staten Island, including the plaintiff's leasehold interest. The purpose of this condemnation was to facilitate and guard the secrecy of wartime troop movements. When the plaintiff was ordered to move, the RFC subsidiary agreed to a plan by which the Defense Plant Corporation, another RFC subsidiary, would buy a site on Long Island, build a plant there, and rent it to the plaintiff. The Government did not promise to pay the costs incurred by the plaintiff in moving. The removal was effected prior to 1 

October 1942 and the plaintiff successfully completed the contract at the new site. 

Pursuant to Private Law No. 997, 68 Stat.

A288 (1954), the plaintiff claimed damages in the amount of $130,877.16 resulting from the 84 AGO 9111A

CLAIMS AGAINST UNITED STATES-Continued 

War Department's obstruction of the tungsten contract with the RFC subsidiary. The defense 

Iwas that the United States acted in its sovereign rather than its contractual capacity.

Held, judgment for the plaintiff in the amount of $3,743.66. The action of the War 

Department clearly increased the cost of performing the tungsten contract with the RFC subsidiary. While the Government may be liable for breach of contract damages when acting in its contractual capacity, the United States as a contractor cannot be held liable directly or indirectly for the public acts of the United States as a sovereign. Jones v. United 

States, 1 Ct. Cl. 383, 385 (1865); Horowitz v. 

United States, 267 U.S. 458 (1925). As stated in Jones v. United States, 1 Ct. Cl. at 385:

The two characters which the government possesses as a contractor and as a sovereign cannot be thus fused; nor can the United States while sued in the one character be made liable in damages for their acts done in the other. Whatever acts the government may do, be they legislative or executive, so long as they be public and general, cannot be deemed specially to alter, modify, obstruct or violate the particular contracts into which it enters with private persons. 

In this court the United States appear simply as contractors; and they are to be held liable only within the same limits that any other defendant would be in any other court. Though their sovereign acts performed for the general good may work injury to some private contractors, such parties gain nothing by having the United States as their defendants. The plaintiff should derive no benefit or advantage from having the United States as a defendant. Thus, as stated in the Jones case, the plaintiff can recover damages only if a private person, substituted for the RFC subsidiary, would be liable for damages caused by the War Department's Act. This is not the case here. The plaintiff argues, however, that the condemnation was an isolated and nongeneral act of sovereignty and not, therefore, public and general. The guidelines here, however, are not susceptible to mechanical application. The condemnation purpose was to protect and facilitate the wartime movement of troops. It was not so arbitrary and unreasonable "as to remove it from the category of sovereign acts." Ottinger v. United States, 123 Ct. Cl. 23, 48 (1952). Consequently, the conclusion is that the condemnation was a public and general act of sovereignty performed for the public good regardless of its limited scope. 

While the Government is not liable for the cost of relocation, it is liable as a condemnor for the agreed value of the plaintiff's leasehold interest from the date of removal until the end of the lease. United States v. General Motors 

Corp., 323 U.S. 373 (1945). 

Wah Chang Corporation v. United States, 282 F.2d 728 (Ct. Cl. 1960). 

[Note: In Derecktor v. United States, 128 F. 

Supp. 136 (Ct. Cl. 1954), the court held that the State Department acted in its sovereign capacity when directing the Maritime Commission to breach a contract of sale with the plaintiff. The court reasoned that the State 

Department had probable cause to believe that the plaintiff would use the vessel being sold to jeopardize the foreign relations of the United

13. Payment of Interest on Court of Claims

Judgments Is Not Authorized by 28 U.S.C. 

§ 2517. In an action against the United States in the Court of Claims the plaintiff obtained a judgment for which funds were provided by AGO 9111A 85

CLAIMS AGAINST UNITED STATES-Continued the Second Supplemental Appropriation Act, 

1961, 74 Stat. 821 (1960). That statute appropriated funds for judgments, including "such amounts as may be necessary to pay interest (as and when specified in such judgments or provided by law)." The judgment did not provide for the payment of interest, but the plaintiff claimed he was entitled to interest as a matter of law. He contended that 28 U.S.C. § 2517 provides for paying interest on Court of Claims judgments against the United States. 

That statute says: (a) Every final judgment rendered by the Court of Claims against the United States shall be paid out of any general appropriation therefor, on pre sentation to the General Accounting Office of a certification of the judgment.... (b) Payment of any such judgment and of interest thereon shall be a full discharge to the United States of all claims and demands arising out of the matters involved in the case or controversy. 

Held, the claim is denied. The appropriation for payment of the plaintiff's judgment covers interest only when "provided by law." According to 28 U.S.C. § 2516 (a), interest on a claim against the United States may be allowed in a Court of Claims judgment "only under a contract or Act of Congress expressly providing for payment thereof." The rule in that statute is "a complete one covering all types of claims, including those arising out of preexisting judgments." United States v. N.Y. Rayon Importing 

Co., 329 U.S. 654, 661 (1947). It applies to

Court of Claims judgments. United States v. 

Eastport Steamship Corp., 255 F. 2d 795, 804 

(2d Cir. 1958). Congress has authorized the payment of interest on Court of Claims judgments (1) if they are affirmed by the Supreme Court after the Government requested review 

[28 U.S.C. § 2516(b)] and (2) when it is de termined that a claim used by the Government as a basis for withholding payment of a judg ment is without merit [31 U.S.C. § 227]. To view 28 U.S.C. § 2517 as blanket authority for paying interest on Court of Claims judgments would do violence to 28 U.S.C. § 2516(a) and would assign little significance to 28 U.S.C. 

§ 2516 (b) and 31 U.S.C. § 227. One should read 

28 U.S.C. § 2517, especially paragraph b, as merely stating what effect payment of a judgment, including interest where authorized, shall have. Compare Carpenter v. United States, 123 

Ct. Cl. 517, 520 (1952). That this interpretation is proper is clear from a reading of the source of 28 U.S.C. § 2517(b). That section is derived from 28 U.S.C. § 285 (1940), which 

The payment of the amount due by any judgment of the Court of Claims, and of any interest thereon allowed by law, as provided by law, shall be a full discharge to the United States of all claim and demand touching any of matters involved in the controversy. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-132815, 16 November 

1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 286.

Revenue Code of 1954. The contract was modi fied to make interim provision for the tax credit, which was yet undetermined. After the 

District Director of Internal Revenue calcu lated the tax credit, the contractor requested from the Army payment of the difference between the tax credit due and the total overpayment received from the Army. The contracting officer conceded the contractor was entitled to a credit, but decided it could cover only the overpayments, representing the difference between progress payments made and the redetermined contract price. He held that the difference between the amount he allowed and the tax credit should be recovered from the Internal Revenue Service as a tax overpayment. The ASBCA sustained the contractor's appeal from the contracting officer's decision. General Motors Corp., Allison 

Division, ASBCA Nos. 5206, 5207, and 5208 (25 Apr. 1960), 60-1 BCA 2614 [digested under

DISPUTES, par. 18], motion for reconsidera tion dismissed, 13 Dec. 1960, 61-1 BCA 2880 

[digested under DISPUTES, par. 29]. The contracting officer altered his determination to conform to the Board's decision. An Army finance officer asked the Comptroller General about the propriety of paying the contractor an amount in excess of that originally allowed by the contracting officer.

Held, the payment is authorized. The Direc tor, Tax Rulings Division, Internal Revenue 

Service, has stated that his office holds that Section 1481 is mandatory and confers upon taxpayers the right to have the amount of taxes paid on excess profits applied in settlement of accounts with a contracting agency. He indicated that the Internal Revenue Service will, only as a matter of policy, consider a tax credit due a contractor to be a tax overpayment if doing so will prevent the contractor from being shunted among government agencies. Section 

1481 makes no specific provision for tax credits in excess of contract overpayments. However, that section was designed to mitigate the effect of price decreases by renegotiation or redetermination. Where, as here, a contracting agency has funds available for making an appropri ate adjustment, the Internal Revenue Service's position is consistent with the statute. It is reasonable to assume that a refusal to make full allowance for tax credits is not justified merely because there is an unfavorable balance between the revised contract price and the total of the progress payments made under the contract.
