See INTEREST (par. 1) 23. Government Liable for Purchase Price But Not Fair Value of Property Sold to Individ ual and Later Repossessed Because Individual's Possession Violated Espionage Act. In July 

1950 the plaintiff bought radar units at a government property disposal sale. At the same sale, power units were sold to another bidder, who in turn sold the power units to the plaintiff. 

The plaintiff also bought from a private firm a "Dynamotor-Power Unit," that apparently was complementary to the radar and power units. [It is not clear whether the Government ever owned the "Dynamotor-Power Unit."] The plaintiff advertised all the equipment for sale. 

A few weeks later the Navy demanded the equipment on the grounds that it was "classified" and the plaintiff's possession of it violated the Espionage Act. That Act provided in pertinent part that: 

Whoever, lawfully or unlawfully having possession of, access to, control over, or being intrusted with any . . . instrument, appliance, or note relating to the national defense, willfully communicates or transmits or attempts to communicate or transmit the same to any person not entitled to receive it, or willfully retains the same and fails to deliver it on demand to the officer or employee of the 

United States entitled to receive it . . . Shall be fined . . . or imprisoned . . . or both. 62 Stat. 736, 737, 18 U.S.C. (1946 ed., Supp. III) § 793. 

The Korean police action had just begun, and plaintiff allowed the Navy to take the equip- AGO 9111A 87

CLAIMS AGAINST UNITED STATES-Continued ment because he was alarmed at the suggestion of espionage. The Navy gave him receipts stating that the taking was without prejudice to any of his rights including the "full right to compensation . . . ..." The plaintiff presented to various government officials a claim for what he alleged was the fair market value of the property. The Government offered only the purchase price of the radar units. The plaintiff rejected that offer and sued the Government in the Court of Claims. He argued (1) that there was a contract implied in fact that the Government would pay for the property or (2) that the property was taken for public use and he should receive just compensation under the 

Fifth Amendment. The Government and the plaintiff both moved for summary judgment. 

Held, both motions denied, with leave to renew if the parties can stipulate as to the relation of the property to the national defense. 

The property seems to be "instruments" or "appliances" "relating to the national defense," but the plaintiff points out that there is no proof of this at the present stage of the proceedings. If the parties cannot reach agreement, the case will have to go to trial. The trial will be limited to the issue of whether the property was "related to the national defense," within the meaning of the Espionage Act. 

The plaintiff is incorrect in arguing that even if the property were related to the national defense, his title to the property and his right to compensation for the Government's taking would not be impaired. The Espionage Act prohibits one having lawful or unlawful possession from willfully retaining the property and refusing to deliver it on demand to an authorized official. If the property related to the national defense, the plaintiff had no right to retain possession, even though his possession was lawful and the result of a mistake by government employees. His retaining possession, after surrender of the property was demanded, would have been a serious crime. Thus his title and possession were completely vulnerable.

The plaintiff's title is not safeguarded by 40 

U.S.C. § 484 (d), which provides that: 

A deed, bill of sale, lease or other instrument executed by or on behalf of any executive agency purporting to transfer title or any other interest in surplus property under this title shall be conclusive evidence of compliance with the provisions of this title insofar as concerns title or other interest of any bona fide grantee or transferee for value and without notice of lack of such com pliance. 

This section protects purchasers when government officials fail to take all the steps required by law as prerequisites to making property available for public sale. The section could not have been intended to legalize, in the face of the Espionage Act, the holding of national defense devices erroneously sold by the Government.

The plaintiff's position is not supported by 

Turney v. United States, 126 Ct. Cl. 202, 115 

F. Supp. 457 (1953). That case was completely unrelated to the Espionage Act provision involved here.

If the property seized from the plaintiff was related to the national defense, he is not entitled to the fair value of the property but may recover his out-of-pocket expenses in the abortive purchase. If a statute makes illegal the possession of narcotics, or spirituous liquors, or firearms, and they are seized by lawful authority, the possessor is not entitled to any compensation not specifically provided for by statute. The same is true of national defense devices that it is unlawful to keep. However, the plaintiff has an urgent equity in obtaining a refund of the out-of-pocket costs for the radar units he bought from the Government and for the power units he bought from a bidder who obtained those items at the sale where the plaintiff purchased the radar units. By its brief, the Government apparently indicates a willingness to make that refund.

Dubin v. United States, 289 F. 2d 651 (Ct. Cl.

27. United States Did Not Warrant That

Construction Contractors Would Be Able To Approach Work Site by City Streets They Had Planned To Use. The plaintiffs had a contract with the Corps of Engineers to reconstruct a retaining wall that had collapsed into an adjoining city street at an ordnance plant. Shortly after performance began, a flood brought about by a hurricane destroyed parts of streets adjacent to, as well as in the vicinity of, the construction site. The destruction rendered unavailable some city streets the plaintiffs had intended to use for access to the construction site. Consequently, the plaintiffs were compelled to change their intended method of operation, which was not part of the contract, to an unspecified extent. As a result of the hurricane and flood, an extension of time for performance was granted. The plaintiffs claimed compensation for additional costs of performance due to the change in the method of operation. The claim was denied. Lenry, Inc., ASBCA No. 

4674 (26 Jun 1958) [digested in DA Pam 71550-2, p. 103, par. 27]. The plaintiffs then filed suit in the Court of Claims. The United States moved for summary judgment. 

Held, the United States' motion is granted.

The sole issue to be determined is whether the plaintiffs are correct that the Government guaranteed in all events the continued existence and availability of certain city streets the plaintiffs intended to use as access roads. The plaintiffs relied upon the standard Changed Conditions

Clause (Cl. 4, SF 23A, Mar. 1953 ed.) and the following General Conditions: 

Site Investigation. The contractor acknowledges that he satisfied himself as to the nature and location of the work, the general and local conditions, including . those bearing upon transportation, disposal, handling and storage of materials, availability of . . . roads . . . Representations which are not expressly stated in the contract and for which liability is not expressly assumed by the Government in the contract shall be deemed only for the information of the contractor.

Operations and Storage Areas. . . . The Contractor shall, under regulations prescribed by the Contracting Office, use only established roadways or construct and use such temporary roadways as may be authorized by the Contracting Officer.

In addition the plaintiffs relied upon the fact that certain city streets at the construction site were in existence at the time of contracting, and a map incorporated into the contract showed those streets. The plaintiffs argued that these provisions establish that: (1) plaintiffs were obligated to visit the construction site to determine the availability of roads; (2) certain roads were in existence at the time the contract was made; (3) the plaintiffs were required to use established roads; (4) parts of the established roads were shown on the contract drawing; (5) the United States agreed to compensate plaintiffs for losses sustained by reason of unusual conditions. Thus, the plaintiffs' argument ran, the Government warranted, for the duration of the contract, the continued availability of the streets the plaintiffs intended to use as access roads. The plaintiffs appear to have done nothing more than juxtapose isolated provisions of the contract in an attempt to change the instrument's general tenor. The provisions cannot be taken from context and placed side by side to justify such extraordinary liability as the plaintiffs seek. Even if plaintiffs' method of establishing a cause of action were valid, their conclusion does not follow from their premises. There is no indication that the Government knew, or should have known, of the particular method of operation originally selected by the plaintiffs. 

Moreover, the hurricane and flood were acts of God, and the general rule is that neither party is responsible to the other for losses occasioned by such acts. Finally, the streets involved were under the control of municipal authorities, not the Government.

The plaintiffs have not attempted to define the scope of the warranty they find implicit in the contract. Had the Government ever intended to make such a unique and all-encompassing guarantee, and had plaintiffs expected it, the guarantee would have been made in clear and unmistakable language. 

Lenry, Inc., v. United States, 297 F. 2d 550 (Ct. Cl. 1962). AGO 9111A 89

4. Because Prompt Notice To Stop Work Under Invalid Letter of Intent Not Given, Government May Not Recover Amount Paid Pursuant to That Letter. (Ct. Cl.) See INVALID CONTRACTS (par. 6) 5. Comptroller General Reforms Contract To 

Delete Portion of Price for Royalties That,

When Fixed-Price Contract Was Negotiated, Both Contractor and Government Mistakenly 

Believed Contractor Was Obligated To Pay. In negotiating a firm fixed-price supply contract, the contractor included in his price 1.75 percent of the selling price for sales royalties payable to two other firms in connection with the equipment sold. A month before the contractor received the award, a federal district court had entered a decree in a suit brought by the United States against the firms to whom the contractor expected to pay royalties. The decree, of which neither the contractor nor the contracting officer was aware, had the effect of relieving the contractor of any obligation to pay the royalties included as an item of cost in the contract. After learning of the decree, the contracting officer withheld from payments due under the contract a sum approximately equal to the 1.75 percent for royalties. The contractor filed a claim with the Comptroller General for the withheld sum.

Held, claim denied. It is true that the contract was for a firm fixed price and that there was no deliberate misrepresentation about liability for royalties. However, the cost of equipment was overstated to the extent of the royalties the contractor was not required to, and did not, pay. The overstatement occurred because the contract was negotiated by the parties under the mistaken belief that royalties were payable. Had either the Government or the contractor been aware of the court decree, nothing for royalties would have been included in the contract price. The circumstances here justify reforming the contract. See Leathem Smith 

Putnam Nav. Co. v. National U. F. Ins. Co., 96 F. 2d 923 (7th Cir. 1938); 76 C.J.S. Reform ation of Instruments, § 29 (1952). The applicable legal principle is that mistake on one side and misrepresentation on the other, whether willful or accidental, constitute a ground for reformation when the party deceived has relied on the misrepresentation. Since it would be unjust to allow the party who makes a misrepresentation to retain the fruits of a bargain induced by the misrepresentation, restitution may be in order. See, e.g., Grand Trunk Western R. 

Co., v. H. W. Nelson Co., 116 F. 2d 823, 832 

(6th Cir. 1941); Restatement, Contracts, § 476, comment b (1932). In United States v. Barlow, 132 U.S. 271 (1889), the Supreme Court pointed out the mischief that would be produced if the Court held that actions by public officials operating on guesses only and without regard to the true facts could preclude the Government from recovering money paid for items not required or employed in performing a contract. The 90 AGO 9111A

COMPTROLLER GENERAL 

Court also referred to the rule of law that where money is paid to another under the influence of a mistake (that is, upon the supposition that a specific fact is true), and the money would not have been paid if the payer had known of the mistake, the money may be recovered. Compare Kostelac v. United States, 247 F. 2d 723 

(9th Cir. 1957) [digested in DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 61, par. 43].

The remedy of contract reformation to correct mutual mistakes has been applied con sistently by the General Accounting Office and the courts without regard to whether a contract is for a fixed price. See, e.g., United States v. 

Hurwitz, 174 F. Supp. 925 (S.D.N.Y. 1959);

Pacific Maritime Association v. United States, 

125 Ct. Cl. 216 (1953); 30 Comp. Gen. 220 (1950); 20 Comp. Gen. 782 (1941).

CONSIDERATION 1. Retroactive Contract Modification Allowing General Research Costs Must Be Supported by a New and Adequate Consideration. The contractor undertook a general research program for the Government. The contract, however, did not specifically authorize payment for general research costs incurred. After performance had started, Defense Supply Service asked whether the research costs were allowable AGO 9111A 91

CONSIDERATION-Continued under the contract and, if not, what consideration was required to support the addition, by modification, of an appropriate clause with retroactive effect.

Opinion: The general research expenses are not allowable unless the contract is modified to specifically provide for their payment. ASPR 

(2 Nov 1959)] Cf. JAGT 1959/6557, 17 Sep tember 1959. The modification, however, must be in the Government's best interest and supported by an adequate consideration furnished by the contractor to the Government. 15 Comp. 

Gen. 25 (1935). This means that the value received must be adequate when compared to the Government's expected cost. Normally, the contractor's promise to perform general research work for national defense would be adequate consideration. See DOD Directive 3210-1.

But where this promise or performance has already been given it cannot support a subsequent modification with retroactive effect. New consideration is required. 1 Williston, Contracts

Sec. 142. See JAGT 1959/1822, 12 February 

1959. This might take the form of reports, patent rights, or technical data which the contractor was not previously obligated to furnish. 

If, however, the modification expands the scope of work or includes additional property, full and free competition must be obtained, see 

ASPR 2-202 (1 Oct 1959) and ASPR 3-10 (20 

Apr 1959), unless the additional work or property was not contemplated by and is an inseparable part of the original contract.

JAGT 1959/6572, 8 October 1959. 

2. Contractor's Intention To Show Good Faith Is Inadequate Consideration To Support Contract Amendment Increasing Government's Termination Rights. On 1 May 1959, the con tractor entered into a contract with a legally constituted non-appropriated fund to supply custodial services to the Pirmasens family hous ing area in Germany. The original contract provided in part:

This contract extends to a period of 12 .. months, beginning on 1st of May 1959 and ending on 30th April 1960, and may be terminated at any time by either party by delivering a written notice to the other with the intention to terminate not later than 30 . . . days preceding the date of intended termination. 

On 8 May, after the contractor had worked 4 days, the contracting officer determined that the work was defective and recommended a termination. This recommendation was disapproved by the Post Commander. Immediately thereafter the contract was amended to provide: 

(a) The Fund may terminate this contract at any time and for any cause by a notice in writing from the Contracting Officer to the Firm. The 

Firm shall, unless the notice directs otherwise, immediately discontinue all work and services . . . (c) If the contract is terminated because of the failure on the part of the Firm to fulfill his undertakings under this contract, the Fund may take over the work and services and prosecute the same to completion by contract or otherwise, and the Firm shall be liable to the Fund for any excess occasioned to the Fund thereby. 

The contractor agreed to the amendment when informed that "it would show good faith." On 

15 May the contract was terminated under the amended clause for the contractor's failure to fulfill the agreement. The contractor appealed to the Commander-in-Chief, United States 

Army, Europe. 

Held, the appeal is sustained. The amendment was intended to eliminate the 30-day termination notice required by the original contract. Since no consideration moved from the 

Government to the party adversely affected, the amendment is unenforceable. Vulcanite 

Portland Cement Co. v. United States, 74 Ct. Cl. 

692 (1932). While the Government's termination did not comply with the reinstated clause in the original contract, the intention of the parties can best be effected by invoking that clause rather than requiring the contractor to pursue breach of contract remedies against the

Government. Accordingly, the contractor is entitled to payment at the contract price for 30 days after the date of termination in addition to reimbursement for work properly performed before the termination.

Firm Reinigungsdienst Kaiserslautern, USA- REUR BCA No. 134, 23 February 1960. 

3. Comptroller General Defines Consideration As Either Benefit to the Promisor or Detriment to the Promisee. To provide commercial facilities at a townsite near a reclamation project, the Interior Department sold lots to purchasers who agreed that within 120 days they 92 AGO 9111A

CONSIDERATION-Continued 

1 1 would pay any balance on the purchase price and obtain financing for permanent buildings. 

If these conditions were not met, the contracts of sale were to be terminated, the down payment was to be considered as rent and liquidated damages paid to the United States. Many purchasers found it impossible to secure financing, even after the period for doing so was doubled. The Interior Department then determined that it was in the Government's best interest to adopt a five-year time-payment plan for some of the purchasers. However, five purchase agreements expired before they could be altered to include time-payment provisions. Believing it was best to reinstate the agreements, the Interior Department asked the Comptroller General whether the vested right to forfeiture could be ignored.

Held, reinstatement of the contracts is proper. Vested rights may be released only for adequate legal consideration. Bausch & Lomb Optical Company v. United States, 78 Ct. Cl. 

584, 607 (1934), cert. denied, 292 U.S. 645 (1934). "A 'consideration' in the legal sense of the word is some right, interest, benefit, or advantage conferred on the promisor to which he is otherwise not lawfully entitled, or any detriment, prejudice, loss, or disadvantage suffered or undertaken by the promisee other than such as he is at the time of consent lawfully bound to suffer." Cuneo Press, Inc. v. Clayburn Corp., 90 F. 2d 233 (7th Cir. 1937). Since neither party had any legal duty after a forfeiture, there was consideration for the Government's waiver of the forfeiture in the purchaser's agreement to make time payments on the remaining price. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144329, 21 November 

1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 309.

5. There Was Consideration Flowing to Gov ernment When Fixed-Price Formal Contract Without Price-Redetermination Provision Was Made After Ninety Per Cent of Work Had Been 

Performed-Even if Lack of Price Redetermi nation Provision Made Contract a Cost-Plus-Percentage-of-Cost Arrangement, Contractor Was 

Entitled to Reimbursement on Quantum Meruit 

Basis-Whether Contract Should Be Reformed Is Question for Court To Answer on Evidence Adduced Before It and Not on Record Made Before Administrative Board of Review. After negotiating with a firm for the renovation of part of a building, the GSA on 28 December 

1950 sent the firm a letter of understanding.

The letter stated that the firm was to perform the work in accordance with specifications to be drawn by the GSA. The letter stated that the contractor would be entitled to a lump sum figure to be determined on the basis of 5% for profit and that a contemplated formal contract would include a clause providing for price redetermination after the work was completed. Another letter sent the firm the same day by the GSA stated the proposal and incorporated provisions of standard government forms that (1) the price would be subject to redetermination and (2) determinations on disputes of fact would be subject to departmental administrative review. The firm accepted these terms, apparently by a letter, and began work. Five months later, after approximately ninety percent of the work was completed, a formal contract was signed. That document stated a fixed price, but failed to include a price-redetermination provision. After completion of the work the Government proposed an audit of the firm's accounts for price-redetermination purposes. 

Although maintaining there was no contractual provision for redetermination, the firm allowed the audit in the belief that the contract might be subject to the Renegotiation Act of 1951. 65 

Stat. 7 (1951), 50 U.S.C. App. §§ 1211-24 

(1958). The contracting officer later ruled the firm had been overpaid $57,281.10. The firm contested the ruling before the GSA Board of Review on the ground that the contract did not provide for redetermination. The Board concluded that the redetermination provision had inadvertently been omitted from the formal contract and that both parties assumed the contract price was subject to redetermination. The 

Board said, alternatively, that if the omission of a redetermination article had been inten- AGO 9111A 93

CONSIDERATION-Continued tional, the modification of the original contract in favor of the firm was not supported by consideration. The Government sued the firm for the overpayment. The Government's motion for summary judgment was granted, and the firm appealed.

Held, reversed and remanded for further proceedings. The question whether the parties' exchange of letters created a valid contract need not be reached. If the letters were not sufficiently definite to form a contract, then the formal contract was sufficiently definite and supported by consideration. On the other hand, if there was a valid letter contract, it was superseded by the formal contract. The first issue that must be decided is whether, on the assumption that the omission of the redetermination provision from the formal contract was intentional, the Government received consideration for relinquishing the right to redetermination. Before the formal contract was executed, no fixed price had been set. Afterwards the firm obtained the opportunity of increasing its profit margin by economies in operation. 

This opportunity, however, was accompanied by the possibility of some risk, however, unlikely that risk might be. The Government acquired the benefit of a fixed maximum for the cost of the project. Thus, regardless of the legal effect of the prior negotiations, the formal contract was supported by consideration. The Government's view of the nature of consideration required to support a contract is incorrect. It is not unknown for profits to become dissipated or even to turn into losses because of factors encountered at the latest stages of performance. The mere possibility of such an occurrence is enough to constitute legal consideration.

The second question for decision is whether the formal contract, if it was supported by consideration, was void as a cost-plus-a-percentageof-cost contract barred by 63 Stat. 395 (1949), 41 U.S.C. § 254 (b) (1958). The Government's argument is that omission of a redetermination provision brought the formal contract within the prohibition of that statute, so the execution of the document was unauthorized. It is true that in dealing with the Government a firm is charged with the knowledge of the extent of the actual authority of the Government's contracting agent. However difficult the process may be, the agent's actual authority can be ascertained. National Electronic Labs, Inc. v. 

United States, 180 F.Supp. 337, 341-42 (Ct. Cl. 

1960). Nonetheless, the Government's argument fails to recognize that the formal contract established a fixed price. After the contract was executed, the contractor bore the risk that rising costs would dilute his profit margin. The 

Government has contended that at the late stage when the formal contract was made, risks were so calculable that the price merely disguised a cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost arrangement. Even if that contention be accepted, the 

Government's position on the appeal would not be aided. If the contract was made without authority, then perhaps no contract exists, but the firm is still entitled to the reasonable value of the benefits conferred on the Government. 

38 Comp. Gen. 38 (1958). The record does not reveal that computing the benefits conferred would produce the same sum that was fixed by the contracting officer as due under the redetermination provision he believed to be a part of the contract. Hence the judgment could not be affirmed even if the formal contract were invalid.

The third issue to be decided is the extent to which the GSA Board of Review's decision is final. The Government concedes that reforming the contract to express correctly the parties' intent is a function of the district court rather than of the GSA Board. Nevertheless, the Government argues, the Board had jurisdiction to determine whether the facts justify reformation, and the Board's findings on those facts can be disturbed only if "fradulent or capricious or arbitrary or so grossly erroneous as necessarily to imply bad faith, or not supported by substantial evidence." 68 Stat. 81 (1954), 41

U.S.C. § 321 (1958). Thus, the argument runs, the finding that the parties intended to include the renegotiation provision in the formal contract connot now be disturbed and provides a justification for the summary judgment in the Government's favor. The Government relies on 

Lowell O. West Lumber Sales v. United States, 270 F. 2d 12 (9th Cir. 1959), [digested in DA 

Pam 715-50-2, p. 259, par. 2], which held that 94 AGO 9111A

CONTINGENT FEES 

T. དྲ whether an arrangement was a "requirements" contract or merely a "call" agreement not binding on the Government was a question to be decided on the basis of the record before the administrative review board. The problem here is familiar to other areas of the law in which the allocation of functions between two authorities is in question. The problem is usually framed as whether the question involved is one of law or one of fact. A practical approach to the allocation of functions is to be followed. See 

Dobson v. Commissioner, 320 U.S. 489 (1943);

Davis, Administrative Law § 245 (1951). 

Whether grounds for reforming a contract exist is a question for a court to answer on evidence adduced before it and not on the record made before the board of review in the executive branch. Neither agency expertise in evaluation nor the need for an immediate decision calls for determination by the administrative board of the reformation issue. The judge of the district court was surely as well equipped, if indeed not better equipped than the GSA Board because of his experience in questions of general contract law, to resolve the reformation issue. Therefore, a summary judgment for the Government based on the administrative record alone was not appropriate. 

The district court did not reach the question whether the contract should be reformed. The answer must await the de novo evaluation of evidence adduced after the case is remanded.

The case is remanded to the district court for further proceedings consistent with this opinion. 

Blake Constr. Co. v. United States, 296 F. 2d 

393 (D.C. Cir. 1961).

CONTINGENT FEES 1. Where Prior To Entering Into a Contract With the Government the Contractor Made a 

Full Disclosure of a Contingent Fee Arrange ment With Its Sales Representatives, Govern ment Officials "Must Have" Determined That

Arrangement Did Not Violate Contingent Fee 

Warranty. Government Cannot, in the Absence of a Showing That the Evils Sought To Be Pre vented by the Warranty Are Present in the

Case, Rely on an Alleged Violation of the War ranty as Justification for an Earlier Cancellation Based on a Now Indefensible Ground. In 

September 1952, after 15 months of negotiating, the plaintiff entered into a contract to sell tungsten to the Government with deliveries to extend over a period of 34 months. Plaintiff corporation was formed for the purpose of encouraging the mining and marketing of tungsten in Portugal. Theretofore, tungsten mining had been a relatively unprofitable undertaking engaged in mainly by individuals working independently with picks and shovels and selling their product through dealers. 

Entrepreneurs of the plaintiff corporation felt that if a long term contract for the supply of a substantial quantity of the ore could be obtained, it would be possible to organize the industry along profitable lines. For reasons of economic mobilization, one stipulation in the contract was that plaintiff would supply only ore produced in Portugal. 

On October 27, 1952 the contracting officer in Washington received a wire from a United

States representative in London in which it was stated that another company, Pennsalt, had reported an attempt by plaintiff to purchase from it 100 tons of tungsten for resale to the United States. The contracting officer, considering this wire as concrete evidence of the allegations made therein, cancelled the con- AGO 9111A 95

CONTRACT CLAUSES 

tract citing as justification the plaintiff's attempt to make open market purchase for delivery under the contract.

Plaintiff after making attempts over a twomonth period to have its contract reinstated initiated this action for breach of contract. 

The Government urged in defense that plaintiff had breached the contract warranty against contingent fees and, in the alternative, that plaintiff suffered no damage since it would not have been able to perform the contract had it not been cancelled. The Government made no effort to show that plaintiff had breached the contract by attempting to obtain tungsten from an unauthorized source.

The evidence established that two Americans, P and W, had in fact been employed by plaintiff on a contingent fee basis for a fiveyear period as exclusive sales agents for the sale in the United States and other specified countries of various metals including tungsten. 

The employment agreement additionally called for P and W to work as industrial consultants without additional compensation. Early in the negotiation stage, W filed a copy of this agreement with the Government officials with whom he was dealing. The plaintiff represented by the warranty provision that it had retained no one to assist in obtaining the contract on a contingent fee basis except a bona fide employee or bona fide established commercial or selling agency maintained by the contractor for the purpose of securing business. In the event of a violation of this warranty, the Government could annul the contract without liability or it could deduct from the contract the amount of the fee involved. P had had extensive experience in mine management. His primary contribution to the venture was assisting and advising as to corporate structure and financing in the formation of plaintiff corporation. W concentrated his efforts on personally representing plaintiff's interests before and presenting its interests to various Government officials concerned in the negotiations. 

Held, the Government has breached its contract with the plaintiff and the latter is entitled to its anticipatory profits. 

The heart of plaintiff's venture was obtaining a long range contract which it did not have the sales force to do. It was this void which 

P and W were employed to fill, to which they applied their unusual qualifications and experience over the period of a year in presenting plaintiff's offer on its merits to the numerous Government officials concerned in the negotiations. This and the assistance rendered as industrial consultants lead to the conclusion that P and W were bona fide employees within the execption contemplated in the warranty provision.

The Government's system of requiring disclosure of the facts concerning any contingent fee selling arrangement with other than a full time employee was designed to allow the contracting officer to determine whether or not an exception to the policy existed. An affirmative determination was presumably made in the matter. The Government may not at this late date challenge that determination at least in the absence of a showing that the evils sought to be eliminated by the policy were in fact present.

Companhia Atlantica de Desen., etc. v. 

United States, 180 F. Supp. 342 (Ct. Cl. 1960); for Findings of Fact see 148 Ct. Cl. 71, 80

CONTRACT CLAUSES (Changed Conditions) 

(Changed Conditions) 1. Conditions Which Arose Long After Contract Execution Are Not Contemplated by the Changed Conditions Clause. (ASBCA) See CHANGES (par. 5) 2. Increase In Direct Costs Due To Government Delay In Removing Obstructions Authorized Under Changed Conditions Clause or Suspension of Work Clause. In January 1956, the 

Corps of Engineers, acting for the Air Force, entered into a fixed price contract with the contractor for the construction of two hangars.

The contract included, inter alia, the standard 

Changed Conditions Clause, SF23A, and the standard Suspension of Work Clause, AFPI 

7-3106.2. Shortly before beginning work in 

March 1956, the contractor discovered two water valves and one water hydrant so close to the proposed foundation lines that the foundations could not be completed until the valves and hydrant were relocated. These obstructions were neither disclosed by the drawings nor apparent from a reasonable site investigation and the Government recognized that their removal was its responsibility. While the appellant began installing foundations, it repeatedly made oral requests to the Project 

Engineer for removal of the obstructions. The

Project Engineer did not believe the valves and hydrant were delaying performance or that there was any hurry about their relocation. He relied in large measure on appellant's letter of 

14 June that foundation work had been halted because a strike had made structural steel unavailable. By the end of July the appellant had received enough steel to resume work, yet the valves and the hydrant were not removed until 

18 September and 18 October, respectively.

Meanwhile the appellant built all the foundations except for small gaps a few feet long near the obstructions. The foundations were finished on 30 November, 183 days after the anticipated date. Completion of the hangars was delayed by the dilatory construction of the foundations. For the 183 day delay in completing the foundations the company sought additional compensation of $34,820.82, including supervisory and overhead costs, profit, legal expenses, and direct labor costs due to piecemeal operation. The contracting officer and the Corps of Engineers

BCA successively ruled against the claim, and a timely appeal to the ASBCA was taken. The 

Government's principal contention was that the lack of structural steel was the sole cause of the delay in constructing the foundations. 

Held, the appeal is sustained in the amount of $2,480.31. That it was necessary to leave gaps in the foundations near the three obstructions proves that the dilatory removal of the obstructions not merely the steel shortage, interfered with performance. The obstructions were within the Changed Conditions Clause of the contract in that they were both "(1) subsurface or latent physical conditions at the site differing materially from those indicated in this contract," and "(2) unknown physical conditions at the site, of an unusual nature, differing materially from those ordinarily encountered and generally recognized as inhering in work of the character provided for in this contract." If it be argued that the interference with performance arose, not from the existence of the obstructions, but from the Government's unreasonable delay in removing those obstacles, the answer is that the Government's delay constituted a partial suspension of work within the Suspension of Work Clause. Thus, there may be an increase in the contract price for the increased costs of performance. 

However, the appellant is not entitled to all the compensation claimed. Of the 183 days delay, thirty must be deducted because filling in the small gaps should have been completed by the end of October, at the latest. About 

60 days are attributable to delay in receipt of steel and must be deducted. A substantial part of the remaining 93 days delay was due to appellant's failure to assign enough men to the job and to prosecute the work diligently on other phases which did not depend upon completion of the foundations. Therefore appellant is entitled to compensation only for the increase in direct costs caused by the disruptive effect of the obstructions. Appellant submitted evidence that these direct costs amounted to $2,049.86. Although this evidence leaves much to be desired, the amount stated is reasonable. 

Likewise, the claimed 10% for overhead and 10% for profit is reasonable. The appellant is entitled to a price increase of $2,480.31. AGO 9111A 97

INSPECTION & ACCEPTANCE CONTRACT CLAUSES (Limitation of Costs) (Limitation of Costs) 1. Limitation of Costs Clause in CPFF Contract Not Applicable to Change Orders in Circumstances of This Case-Letter Accompanying Supplemental Agreement Effective To Reserve Right of Contractor To Make Additional Claim. The Contractor's CPFF contract contained the standard Changes (ASPR 7203.2) and Limitation of Cost (ASPR 7-203.3) 

Clauses. By change orders issued on 18 May 

1955 and 19 July 1955, the Government increased the number of technicians the contractor was to furnish. On 26 July 1955 the contractor told the Government that the effect of the first change order had been to exhaust funds about 1 June 1955 and that a cost estimate for the second change order was being prepared.

The cost estimate was submitted in August 

1955. In November 1955 the Government sent the contractor a proposed supplemental agreement adding $12,000 to the fixed-fee and estimated costs of the contract in order to compensate for the work added by the second change order. The supplemental agreement stated that it was a final adjustment for the second change order. Because he had spent more than $12,000 under the authority of the second change order, the contractor was reluctant to accept an agreement that would prevent recovery of costs already incurred. On 23 December 1955 the contractor executed the agreement and sent it to the Government with a letter stating:

The increase in funds allotted by subject agreement in the amount of $12,000.00 is insufficient to cover services performed and to be performed under [the second change order] . . . . Contractor is still supplying such services . . . and will be required by the procuring agency to continue to furnish such services. In accepting subject agreement, Contractor understands that contract funds will be further increased beyond the amount allotted in subject agreement so as to compensate Contractor for services authorized by the [second change order] . . . . and that further authorization will be issued to permit continuance [sic] of the contemplated services.

The supplemental agreement was thereafter executed by the Government. Through June 

1956 the Government issued, and the contractor honored, calls for services under the contract. 

Until October 1959 both the contractor and the

Government's representatives attempted to secure additional funds for the contract. No additional funds were obtained, and the contractor was not reimbursed for more than $36,000 in costs. The contractor presented a claim for an additional fixed fee and for his unreimbursed costs. From the contracting officer's denial of the claim, an appeal was taken to the ASBCA. The Government contended that recovery was barred by the supplemental agreement as well as by the Limitation of Costs Clause.

Held, (by the three panel chairmen), the contractor may recover his unreimbursed costs plus an additional fixed fee. First, the supplemental agreement does not bar the contractor's claim. That agreement must be read together 98 AGO 9111A

CONTRACT CLAUSES (Limitation of Costs)-Continued with the contractor's letter. If the Government was dissatisfied with the conditions the contractor attached to his execution of the agreement, the Government need not have signed the agreement. The letter spoke of services to be performed in the future under the second change order, and the Government ordered such services until June 1956. To hold that the contractual authority in the second change order ended with the execution of the supplemental agreement would be to hold that responsible officials in the Government ordered services from the contractor without contractual authority. Such a holding is not called for. Moreover, the language of the contractor's letter made it quite clear that the contractor was not releasing his claim for unreimbursed costs by executing the supplemental agreement. 

Second, under the circumstances of this case, the Limitation of Costs Clause does not, as the

Government contends, prevent recovery. The contractor points to the final sentence of the 

Changes Clause, "However, nothing in this clause shall excuse the Contractor from proceeding with the contract as changed," and argues that the Limitation of Costs Clause does not apply to costs incurred in carrying out a change. 

Both the Government's and the contractor's interpretations of the contract clauses are arguably correct. In the instant case the ambiguity has been resolved by the parties. The Government exacted, and the contractor gave, services long after the estimated costs set forth in the schedule to the contract were exceeded. In fact, the second change order was issued after the contract funds had been used up, and performance was demanded under that change order for nearly a year after the contractor told the Government the contract funds had been exhausted.

Ryan Aeronautical Company, ASBCA No. 

6244, 23 January 1961, 61-1 BCA 2911. 

[Note: The Board added: 

This holding, even without the conduct of the parties, is in harmony with what we believe to be the consistent ruling of the Board that a fixed ceiling in a contract containing a price revision article has no application to a change which increases the costs under the contract.

In this connection, it should be noted that the limitation on costs in CPFF contracts does not serve the same function as price ceilings in price revision (fixed-price redeterminable or fixed-price incentive) contracts. In a price revision contract, the ceiling represents the limit on what the Government will pay for the service or finished item. The contractor must complete performance even if his actual costs exceed the ceiling. Accordingly, where a change order increases the contractor's costs, equity dictates that his ceiling be increased. In a CPFF contract the limit or ceiling represents the maximum amount that the Government is required to reimburse the contractor for costs incurred in performance. The contractor is not required to complete performance within the maximum reimbursable amount. Therefore, in a CPFF contract, the contractor may be allocated additional amounts after the ceiling is reached. This ceiling, then, constitutes merely a control on spending for a project, and it would appear that the ceiling should constitute the limit on spending for the project (unless additional funds are allocated), whether or not the project work is altered by change orders.] 

2. Limitation of Costs Clause Bars Contractor From Recovering Costs in Excess of Cost Ceiling Established by CPFF Contract. Appel lant's cost-plus-fixed-fee contract contained a 

Limitation of Cost Clause (Feb 1959 ed., ASPR 

7-402.2). That clause provided that (1) the appellant was to notify the Government when he had reason to believe either that the total cost to the Government (excluding fixed fee) would exceed the estimated cost set forth in the contract or that costs expected within the next 60 days would make the costs already incurred exceed 75% of that estimated cost; (2) the estimated cost set forth in the contract (or a modification) was the limit of the Government's obligation to reimburse the appellant and of the appellant's obligation to incur costs in perform ing. The Monthly Fund Report Clause required the appellant to submit monthly reports of the amount of funds committed and the uncommitted balance. The contract was received on 

25 June 1959 and completed on 10 February 

1960. Apparently monthly fund reports were submitted only in September and October 1959.

In mid-October the appellant notified the contracting officer that the estimated cost had al- AGO 9111A 99

CONTRACT CLAUSES (Suspension of Work) 

ready been exceeded by about $5,000 and a total overrun of $12,000 would be incurred in completing performance. The Government and appellant entered into a contract modification increasing by $11,320 the original estimated cost of $21,139. Two weeks after completing the contract, the appellant submitted a statement of costs incurred in performance. That statement showed costs of $18,682.92 greater than the limitation of costs prescribed by the contract as modified. The Government had received no earlier notice of the overrun, which apparently had begun in November 1959. The appellant claimed reimbursement for the overrun. 

He appealed to the ASBCA from the denial of his claim by the contracting officer. 

Held, appeal denied. The appeal involves much more than appellant's noncompliance with the requirements of monthly fund reports and notice of the likelihood of an overrun. On the one hand, the Government could waive the noncompliance; on the other hand, the Government could refuse to increase the estimated cost even had there been strict compliance. The appellant's claim is barred not by his noncompliance with the advance notification provisions but by the contractual provision that the Government had no obligation to reimburse him for costs greater than the estimated cost set forth in the contract as modified. See American Hydromath

Corp., ASBCA No. 4505, 3 Dec 1959, 59-2, 

BCA 2465. The Government may not make expenditures except to the extent appropriated funds are available. 31 U.S.C. § 665; 41 U.S.C. 

§ 11. The Limitation of Cost Clause is designed to give the Government an effective tool to prevent the over-expenditure of appropriated funds. Navy Contract Law § 8.36 (2d Ed. 

1959). The clause provides the Government an opportunity to determine-before funds are exhausted-whether additional funds can and should be committed. If the determination is affirmative, more funds may be provided in time to avoid suspending work under the contract. The clause provides safeguards to protect the contractor from incurring costs that will not be reimbursed. The appellant was responsible for knowing and informing the Government when the allotment of funds neared exhaustion. There was no obligation to continue performing after the cost limitation was reached. The appelant could not create an obligation against public funds by neglecting to inform the Government that the cost limitation was reached and by continuing to incur costs above the contractural ceiling. The appellant's allegations about the shortcomings of its personnel and accounting system are no excuse for his failure to comply with the contract's requirements.

A different case would be presented if a Government official acting within the scope of his authority had asked the appellant to continue performing after that official knew the appellant had reached the cost ceiling set in the contract. Thiokol Chemical Corp., ASBCA No. 

5726, 16 Nov 1960, 60–2 BCA 2852 [digested under INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS, par. 10]; Ryan Aeronautical Co., ASBCA No. 

6244, 23 Jan 1961, 61-1 BCA 2911 [digested under CONTRACT CLAUSES (Limitation of 

Costs), par. 1]. There is no evidence the appellant was asked to continue performance by any government representative who knew or had reason to know the cost ceiling had been reached.

Acme Precision Products, Inc., ASBCA No. 

6824, 22 May 1961, 61-1 BCA 3051. 

CONTRACT CLAUSES (Suspension of Work) (Suspension of Work) 1. Contractor Entitled to Equitable Adjustment Under Suspension of Work Clause Where Reason for Suspension Bears No Relation to Successful Contract Performance. In March 

1957, the contractor undertook the grading and construction of a dam and reservoir and the relocation of a road at Camp Schwab, Okinawa. 

The contract contained a Suspension of Work 

Clause, which provided:

The contracting officer may order the contractor to suspend all or part of the work for such period of time as may be determined by him to be necessary or desirable for the convenience of the 

Government. Unless such suspension unreasonably delays the progress of work and causes additional expense or loss to the contractor, no increase in contract price will be allowed. In the case of suspension of all or any part of the work for an unreasonable length of time causing additional expense or loss, not due to the fault or negligence of 100 AGO 9111A

CONTRACT CLAUSES (Suspension of Work)-Continued the contractor, the contracting officer shall make an equitable adjustment in the contract price and modify the contract accordingly. 

In November 1957, the contracting officer suspended work for three days, apparently to avoid the over-obligation of funds. The contracting officer granted a five-day time extension, but denied the contractor's claim for an equitable adjustment in contract price on the ground that the order suspending work was not unreasonable. The contractor appealed. 

Held, the appeal is sustained. Regardless of the factors causing the suspension order, the contractor is entitled to an equitable adjustment if work was unreasonably delayed for any length of time and additional expenses were incurred. Chris Berg and Associates, ASBCA 

No. 3466 (29 Aug 1958), DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 341 par. 12; E. V. Lane Corp., USARJ BCA 

Nos. 65 & 66. The delay was unreasonable here because the Government's reason for suspending work bore no relation to successful contract performance. Since the claim is not compensable under other contract clauses, the contractor is entitled to relief.

E. V. Lane Corporation, USARJ BCA No. 64, 24 November 1959. 

2. Use by Government of Civil Service Employees Is Not a Violation of Normal and Customary Labor Practices in Construction Indus try, Hence Strike Against Such Use Not a

Suspension of Work Under the Contract-The Taking of Possession Prior to Completion by · Government Not Basis for Compensation Because Not the Cause of the Work Stoppage- 

Neither Conceding to Union Demands Nor

Granting Contractor an Extension of Time Estops Government From Denying Contractor Contractual Recovery. The contractor appeals from the decision of the Corps of Engineers 

Claims and Appeals Board (C&A No. 1353 (5 

Dec 1958), DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 139, par. 7 (wherein appears a more detailed digest of the facts)) denying compensation for increased costs resulting from a 38-day work stoppage allegedly caused by the Government. Briefly, the Government chose to exercise its rights to take possession of two of four boilers under a beneficial occupancy clause in its construction contract with the contractor, thereby replacing maintenance personnel, all union members, with civil service employees. The Government knew that the union would probably force a stoppage of work on the other two boilers. The union did so and in fact set up picket lines effecting stoppage of work on all construction contracts on the air base on which the boilers were being constructed. After 38 days, the Government acceded to the union demands and took action to replace the civil service employees with union members through the medium of a maintenance contract with the contractor. The contractor claims compensation for increased costs resulting from the work stoppage on the alternative grounds of a suspension of work under the suspension of work clause in the contract, possession prior to completion under the possession prior to completion clause of the contract, or estoppel on the part of the Government to deny the claim. 

Held, the appeal is denied. The "Suspension of Work" clause provides the contractor an administrative remedy without creating any new or additional substantive rights. No right of recovery is created by the "Suspension of

Work" clause that would not otherwise exist in an action at law for damages. In order for the 

Government to be liable in damages, it must be found that the Government breached either an express or implied provision of the contract.

Thus, in order for the contractor to be entitled to compensation under the clause, the work stoppage must be shown to have been the result of a breach of a duty owed by the Government to the contractor. The Government was under a duty to the contractor not to cause a work stoppage by taking action inconsistent with the usual and recognized labor practices of the industry. However, there is no evidence that the takeover of the heating plant by the Government was contrary to the normal and customary labor practices of the construction industry, nor is there any evidence that unions customarily object to the operation of a heating plant by nonunion operating personnel under the circumstances prevailing at the air base. 

Nor does the record show that the Government's refusal to yield to the damands of the unions was in derogation of or interfered with the labor practices that were within the contempla- AGO 9111A 101

CONTRACT CLAUSES (Warranty) 

tion of the parties when the contracts were made, or that it placed the contractor or its subcontractor in violation of the applicable labor agreement, or that it was otherwise unreasonable. Thus, there was not a "suspension of work" by the Government. 

The taking of possession by the Government prior to completion of the heating plant was not the cause of the work stoppage. The unions did not object to the Government taking over from the contractor possession, use and occupancy of the heating plant prior to its completion; their objection was to the way in which the Government operated the heating plant after the takeover. Thus, there is a break in the chain of causation between possession prior to completion and the work stoppage, and the expenses claimed are not payable under the "Possession 

Prior to Completion" clause.

The contractor argues that the Government's returning the occupation of the heating plant to the contractor upon the same terms and conditions as existed during its operations prior to the strike works an estoppel against the Government's placing responsibility for the strike on the contractor. But even if the Board finds that the strike was not caused or contributed to by the contractor, it does not follow that the Government is liable to the contractor for the loss and additional expense suffered by the contractor as a result of the strike. Nor does the granting of a time extension for a delay due to a strike constitute an admission that the Government was responsible for the strike.

T. C. Bateson Constr. Co., ASBCA No. 5492, 

16 March 1960, 60-1 BCA 2552. [Note: In another decision involving three other contractors and five prime contracts affected by the same strike, recovery was also denied, the Board finding no suspension of work by the Government. Consolidated Constructors, Inc., Frederick Raff Company, Inc.,

Paul M. Sterling Company, Inc., ASBCA No. 

5463 (16 Mar 1960), 60-1 BCA 2561.]

CONTRACT CLAUSES (Warranty) (Warranty) 

1.

After Invoking the Second Option of the 

Warranty Clause and Later Changing to the First Option, the Government May Obtain 

Reimbursement for the Costs of 100% Screening Pursuant to the Second Option-Under the

First Option the Government May Adjust the Contract Price for Defective Goods Without Establishing the Exact Cost of Repairs or the Fact That Repairs Were Actually Made-Gov ernment Is Entitled to Full Cost of Irreparable 

Garments Made of Government-furnished Ma terial-Contractor Entitled to Credit for Allowable Defects and to Allowance for Garments

Sent to Salvage. The Warranty Clause of the contractor's Army contract for the supply of 

100,000 trousers provided in part that:

Notwithstanding any provisions of this contract with respect to inspection and acceptance, the Government shall have the remedies set forth in this clause, if, at the time of delivery, the supplies delivered hereunder do not conform to contract requirements. For the purpose of this clause, conformance with contract requirements will be determined under all applicable provisions of this 102 AGO 9111A

CONTRACT CLAUSES (Warranty)-Continued contract including those relating to specification tolerances, acceptable quality levels and sampling procedures except that, for sampling purposes, the

Government may choose such identifiable groups of supplies as are appropriate and the original inspection lots need not be reconstituted. Upon discovery by the Government of nonconforming supplies and after notice to the contractor of such discovery within one year of the last delivery under this contract the Government may either (1) require an equitable adjustment in the contract price, including an adjustment in the contract price of any groups of supplies determined through sampling to be nonconforming or (2) screen the supplies and return all nonconforming articles to the contractor for repair or replacement . . . . The 

Government shall be reimbursed by the contractor for all costs incurred by it incident to such screening, repair and replacement . . . 

Ten partial shipments, containing a total of 

73,231 trousers were rejected. The contractor was notified that the number of defects exceeded the Acceptable Quality Level, a contractual standard specifying the maximum permissible number of defects per hundred trousers.

Under option 2 of the Warranty Clause the contracting officer ordered a 100% screening. 

He later stopped the 100% screening after 

46,157 of the 73,231 units had been screened.

As a result of screening and a series of reinspections, a final figure of 28.5% reparable and 

2.7% irreparable was determined to be accurate. The Government's loss was determined to be $10,970.55 on the merchandise and $9,385.58 for the costs of screening, or a total of $20,- 

356.13. The contracting officer later decided to proceed under option 1 of the Warranty 

Clause, with the Government reserving the right to reimbursement for inspection costs incurred under the original election of option 2.

After efforts to reach a settlement under option 

1 proved fruitless, the contracting officer issued a finding of fact that the defects had exceeded the Acceptable Quality Level and that the contractor owed the Government $20,356.13. The contractor appealed to the ASBCA, arguing: (1) the Government was not entitled to reimbursement for the costs of 100% screening; (2) the Government had no right to insist that all trousers comply with specifications, without credit for allowable defects; (3) the contractor was not liable to the Government for the full cost of the irreparable garments; (4) the contractor was entitled to an allowance for garments sent to salvage; (5) the Government was obligated to prove repairs were actually made or to demonstrate how much repairs would have cost.

Held, only the second and fourth of the appellant's contentions, as listed above, are sustained. First, the contracting officer was vested with discretion about which option should be exercised. Not only may the Board not review his action, but there is no indication in the record that he abused his discretion. Therefore, once option 2 was invoked, the contractor was bound by that option's provision that "the Government shall be reimbursed by the contractor for all costs incurred by it incident to such screening, repair and replacement. . . ."

Second, although the contractor was obligated to produce trousers meeting the contract's specifications, he was not bound to produce every pair of trousers without a flaw. He was required only to produce trousers meeting the standard-set by the Acceptable Quality Level 

-that for the 73,231 trousers rejected there be not more than 2,929 major defects and a total of 18,301 major and minor defects. The contractor is entitled to a credit for the number of defects permitted by the contract's standard. 

Third, the Government-Furnished Property 

Clause of the contract provided in part that: [T]he contractor will be charged for all property of that type furnished by the Government in excess of the applicable unit allowances. . . . In determining whether the contractor exceeded the unit allowances for each type of property credit will be given for all property of that type returned undamaged, in the form of full pieces, short pieces and ends, but no credit will be given for property returned in the form of . . . irreparable items. . . .

Unless otherwise directed by the Contracting officer or otherwise provided in the contract, the contractor shall return to the point at which the property was originally furnished to the contractor hereunder all surplus property, scrap and all other property not returned in the form of ac ceptable articles. 

Under this clause the contractor is liable for the excess usage of Government-furnished property occasioned by the production of irreparable garments. He is also liable for the cost of manufacturing those garments. AGO 9111A 103

CONTRACTING OFFICER 

Fourth, no provision is made in the contract for a credit to the contractor for the salvage value of the material contained in the irreparable items. However, those items contain 

Government-furnished material for which the contractor must pay and which would have value as scrap or as irregular clothing. A reasonable construction of the contract is that the contractor is entitled to a credit for the salvage value of the irreparable trousers.

Fifth, option 1 of the Warranty Clause pro vides that a sampling procedure may be used to determine which supplies do not meet specifications. That option does not contemplate that repairs must be made. Unlike Sidran

Sportswear, Inc., ASBCA No. 5775 (1 Sep 

1960), 60-2 BCA 2766, the instant case is one where there is ample evidence from the screening and inspection-about the nature and extent of the defects. Consequently, the Government, having established the approximate extent and costs of repairs, is entitled to a price adjustment without establishing the exact costs of repairs or the fact that repairs were actually made.

Penn State Coat and Apron Mfg. Co., ASBCA No. 6151, 30 December 1960, 61-1

B-142971 (6 Jul 1960) that although reproduced signatures of contracting officers on reproduced copies of DD Form 1155 used as purchase orders for supplies or services costing $2,500 or less are facsimile signatures, a copy marked "duplicate original" with the reproduced signature will be acceptable to the GAO where the entire form including the signature is reproduced. Earlier decisions had indicated that where a signature for the Government was required, a facsimile signature would be acceptable only if accompanied by the handwritten initials of the individual whose 104 AGO 9111A

GAO. AR 600-6, par. 3b, and APP 30-2026 

should be amended to reflect the Comptroller General's approval of facsimile signatures on reproduced copies of DD Form 1155. Subse quent revisions of APP may be made to reflect approval obtained as to other forms. It should be noted that even though the Comptroller General may approve facsimile signatures on other forms, restrictions on the use of such signatures may be dictated by administrative and policy considerations. In this regard, attention should be paid the fact that changes that are virtually undetectable on a reproduced copy can be made on a reproducible mat after the contracting officer has affixed his signature.

There is no assurance that the contracting officer will have an opportunity to review the reproduced copy for correctness, as he may do when he must handwrite his signature.

10. Contracting Officers Are Personally Immune From Tort Suits for Acts Based on Decisions That the Officers Should Be Free To 

Make Without Fear of Suit. After making an investigation regarding the plaintiff's delay in completing a GSA construction contract, the assistant contracting officer recommended that the contract be terminated for default. 

The contracting officer agreed. A report was AGO 9111A 105

CONTRACTING OFFICER-Continued sent to the Washington office of the GSA. The report was approved and termination was authorized by the Washington office. The contract was terminated for default. The plaintiff appealed to the GSA Administrator from the termination. The appeal is still pending. The plaintiff sued the GSA Administrator, the contracting officer, and the assistant contracting officer, in their official capacities, for an injunction against award of a repurchase contract, for a review of the termination action, and for damages. The suit was dismissed for want of jurisdiction. Ove Gustavsson Contr. Co. v. 

Floete, 176 F. Supp. 544 (S.D.N.Y. 1959), aff'd 

278 F. 2d 912 (2d Cir. 1960) [digested under

CLAIMS AGAINST UNITED STATES, par. 6], cert. denied 364 U.S. 894 (1960).

The plaintiff, while the first suit was pending, sued the contracting officer and his assistant, in their individual capacities, for damages. The complaint alleged that the defendants, with intent to harm the plaintiff, had wilfully and maliciously made untruthful reports of the plaintiff's performance of the contract and, by such reports, had caused the termination. The defendants' motion for summary judgment was granted. 187 F. Supp. 839 (E.D.N.Y. 1960). The plaintiff appealed.

Held, affirmed. The rule is that federal officials are not personally liable for alleged torts based upon acts, done within the scope of the officials' duties, that necessarily involve the exercise of a judgment or discretion that public policy requires be made without fear of personal liability. See, e.g., Barr v. Matteo, 360 

U.S. 564 (1959); Howard v. Lyons, 360 U.S. 

593 (1959); Gregoire v. Biddle, 177 F. 2d 579 (2d Cir. 1949). The rule is designed to allow officials to make decisions free of the dread of the burden and hazard of a trial. The rule is obviously applicable here. An official charged with inspecting the performance of Government contracts would find it difficult honestly and independently to pass upon the work if he knew that an unfavorable report, coupled with an allegation of falsity and malice, could subject him to the risk, the inconvenience, and the embarrassment of a public trial and to possible personal liability. Moreover, the allegedly injured party is not without a remedy.

An appeal to the administrative agency is far from perfunctory. If the termination is sustained by the agency, the Administrative Procedure Act offers relief through limited court review. The Government may be sued in the 

Court of Claims. In addition, it should not be assumed that the executive branch will condone or overlook dishonest or malicious performance of duties such as those exercised by the defendants.

There is no reason to doubt that the reasons underlying the rule extend protection to officials of less than high rank. It is not improbable that lesser officials might feel the pressure of lawsuits as much as would officials of high rank. Comparisons of rank are odious and unprofitable. Sound policy seems to place on the same ground all official duties involving the exercise of judgment and discretion.

There is no merit in any of the plaintiff's arguments for holding that the general rule is inapplicable here. First, the plaintiff argued that the reports on his performance were not within the scope of official duty because the Government had not and could not authorize tortious behavior. If the plaintiff's distinction were adopted, the immunity doctrine would be defeated; officials would be immune only when tortious conduct was not alleged. According to Gregoire v. Biddle, what is meant by saying that the officer must be acting within his power cannot be more than that the occasion must be such as would have justified the act, if he had been using his power for any of the purposes on whose account it was vested in him. 177 F. 2d 579, 581.

Second, the plaintiff argued that the general rule applies only to Government officials who exercise discretion as contrasted with those, like the defendants, whose functions are ministerial. There is no litmus paper test to distinguish acts of discretion. To require a finding of "discretion" would simply postpone, for one step in the reasoning, the determination of the real question: is the act complained of the result of a judgment or decision that an official must be free to make without fear of vexatious or fictitious suits and alleged personal liability?

The plaintiff argued that, since the Government cannot invoke its governmental privileges 106 AGO 9111A

CONTRACTING OFFICER-Continued when it steps down into the market place, the 

Government's employees in the market place are not entitled to immunity. Both the premise and the reasoning must fail. As to the premise, see Hart & Wechsler, The Federal Courts and the Federal System 109, n. 1 (1953); compare 

2 Harper & James, Torts § 29.6 (1956). Even if a line could be drawn between the Government's "governmental" and "commercial" activities, the policy of the immunity doctrine is applicable to both. In any event, the contracting with the plaintiff was a governmental function.

Consideration must be given to those exceptional cases where Government officials were said to be subject to suit for their torts. E.g., Philadelphia Co. v. Stimson, 223 U.S. 605, 61920 (1912); Scranton v. Wheeler, 179 U.S. 141, 152 (1900); United States v. Lee, 106 U.S. 

196, 200-21 (1882). The exception seems to have been made only when the officials authority had been exceeded or had not been validly conferred. Yearsley v. W. A. Ross 

Constr. Co., 309 U.S. 18, 21 (1940); Banco De 

Espana v. Federal Reserve Bank, 114 F. 2d 438 (2d Cir. 1940). Thus the plaintiff's claim is not within the exception. Even if the exception required merely "a specific res held in the guise of public authority, but claimed by the plaintiff on the basis of a title superior to that of the sovereign... [and] a plaintiff may obtain his own property, real or personal, even from the agents of the sovereign itself." Banco De Espana v. Federal Reserve Bank, supra, at 447, the exception is consistent with the policy behind the immunity doctrine, since the official does not risk personal liability. Even if the assumption is made, arguendo, that the plaintiff's contract right was a "property right," the plaintiff's claim is not within the exception because no tangible property is involved and personal liability is the sole aim of the suit. 

Ove Gustavsson Contr. Co. v. Floete, 299 F. 

2d 655 (2d Cir. 1962). 

[Note: Judge Waterman concurred in the result on the ground that: the alleged tortious acts not only occurred in the necessary course of [the defendants'] obviously important official duties as contracting officers . . ., but were acts required of them if they were conscientiously to perform those duties.

He declined fully to join the majority because he questioned the soundness of what he viewed as a holding that the law grants immunity from personal tort liability to all governmental employees performing official duties that can be represented by the actors to be duties involving the exercise of judgment and discretion.

He argued that even the most routine jobs require the exercise of some degree of judgment and discretion. He objected to extending to all 

Government employees a doctrine originally created to protect high-ranking policy-making officers.] 

11. Agency Held Subject to Suit for Declara tory and Injunctive Relief for Activities for 

Which Government Agents Would Be Personally Immune From Damage Suits-Firm Whose Business Was Allegedly Directly Harmed by Government Agency's Press Release Has Stand ing To Sue.

Many banks insured by the Federal 

Deposit Insurance Act, 64 Stat. 873 (1950), 

12 U.S.C. § 1811 (1958), require borrowers to maintain on deposit a "compensating balance" representing a specified percentage of their loans. For a fee the B Corp. had been making deposits in insured banks to provide the necessary balances. For its deposits the 

B Corp. received certificates of deposit, which were then sold to investors upon the representation that the deposits were insured. The 

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation issued a press release stating that deposits of the type described would not be regarded as qualifying for insurance. The B Corp. sued the FDIC for a declaratory judgment that the deposits were insured and for an injunction restraining the FDIC from stating otherwise. The complaint as amended alleged that the officers of the agency knowingly acted in excess of their authority for the specific purpose of destroying the B Corp.'s business and that, as a result, the firm was and would be prevented from carrying on a lawful business. The defense's motion to dismiss was granted on the grounds that (1) no claim upon which relief could be granted had been stated because the defendant, as a federal agency, had an absolute privilege to make a statement within the scope of its AGO 9111A 107

COST CONTRACTS 

official function even though the business relations of a firm were interfered with or damaged; (2) the B Corp. lacked standing to sue.

The B Corp. appealed to the Court of Appeals. 

Held, reversed and remanded. In holding that the complaint failed to state a claim upon which relief could be granted, the district court relied on Howard v. Lyons, 360 U.S. 593 (1959), and Barr v. Mattco, 360 U.S. 564 (1959). Those cases, however, held only that individual Government agents who issue public statements in the discharge of their official duties have an absolute privilege from personal liability in actions for money damages. The 

Supreme Court stated that the privilege was recognized because— officials of government should be free to exercise their duties unembarrassed by the fear of damage suits in respect of acts done in the course of those duties suits which would consume time and energies which would otherwise be devoted to governmental service and the threat of which might appreciably inhibit the fearless, vigorous and effective administration of policies of government. 

There is no basis in reason or authority for extending the immunity against civil damage suits afforded to individual public officials by the Barr and Howard cases to actions for declaratory and injunctive relief against a government agency. That no such extension should be made is indicated by Joint Anti- 

Fascist Refugee Committee v. McGrath, 341

U.S. 123 (1951), which seems to control the case here. There the Court stated:

These complaints do not raise the question of the personal liability of public officials for money damages caused by their ultra vires acts. See Spalding v. Vilas, 161 U.S. 483 (1896) [a leading case on the privilege of public officials]. They ask only for declaratory and injunctive relief striking the names of the designated organizations from the Attorney General's published list and, as far as practicable, correcting the public records. as SO The respondents are not immune from such a proceeding. Only recently, this Court recognized that "the action of an officer of the sovereign (be it holding, taking or otherwise legally affecting the plaintiff's property) can be regarded 'illegal' as to permit a suit for specific relief against the officer as an individual * **if it is not within the officer's statutory powers or, if within those powers * ** if the powers, or their exercise in the particular case are constitutionally void." Larson v. Domestic and Foreign Commerce 

Corp., 337 U.S. 682, 701-02. * * * The same is true here, where the acts complained of are beyond the officer's authority under the Executive Order. 341 

U.S. 123, at 139-40.

The district court's ruling that the B Corp. lacked standing to sue was apparently based on a belief that the firm had not alleged that the FDIC had addressed a statement to the firm or one of the firm's customers, or made specific reference to the firm, as distinguished from a general statement applicable to all in like lines of activity. However, the record discloses that the firm alleged adequately enough that it was singled out as a specific target. Under the Joint Anti-Fascist Committee case the test of standing is "the substantiality of the present or imminent harm which the administrative action inflicts on the plaintiff." 3 Davis, Ad ministrative Law § 21.07 (1958). That test is met here; the B Corp. has amply alleged past and impending serious damage caused by the FDIC's statement. The motion to dismiss admitted the uncontroverted allegations that the officers of the FDIC knowingly acted in excess of their authority for the specific purpose of destroying the B Corp's business and that as a result the firm has been and will be prevented from exercising its right to carrying on a lawful business activity. The FDIC has argued that the firm stated only a hypothetical case. There was, however, nothing hypothetical about the allegations of a misrepresentation that was deliberately designed to and did injure the B Corp. There is no merit in the contention that a private business has no protection against attack by a Government agency so long as the agency uses artful generality. 

B. C. Morton International Corp. v. Federal 

Deposit Insurance Corp., 305 F. 2d 692 (1st 

Cir. 1962).
