MENTS 1. Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee Contractor Under No Obligation To Complete Research and Development Contract When Estimated Costs are Inadequate and Failure of Government To Provide Additional Funds Is Excusable Cause of 

Default. In May 1955, the contractor entered into a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract with the Air Force for the development and delivery of an 108 AGO 9111A

COST-PLUS-PERCENTAGE-OF-COSTS 

antenna test support structure. Total estimated costs were $67,705.55 and the delivery date was 

15 March 1957. Under the contract, the contractor was to notify the contracting officer in writing if at any time there was reason to believe that total performance costs would exceed the estimate. In the event of a termination for convenience, the contractor was to be paid "a percentage of the fee equivalent to the percentage of work contemplated by the contract ." If the termination was for default, "the total fixed fee payable shall be such proportionate part of the fee . . . as the total number of articles delivered to and accepted by the Government bears to the total number of articles of a like kind called for by this contract." The contract provided for termination whenever "the contractor shall default in performance of this contract in accordance with its terms. and shall fail to cure such default within a period of ten days. . . ." Under the Excusable 

Delays provision, however, the contractor would not be in default if the failure to perform was caused by "acts of the Government." [ASPR 8-708 (5 Sep 1958).] 

On 25 February 1957, the contractor stopped work and, by written notice, advised the Government that, as of 31 January 1957, $73,733 had been spent on the project and estimated that an additional $33,736.17 would be required to complete performance. Apparently, the contractor had orally informed the contracting officer prior to the written notice that an overrun was expected. While the Government desired to complete performance and was satisfied with the contractor's work, it failed to provide the requested additional funds. On 12 September 

1957, the contract was terminated for default on the ground that the contractor failed to complete the contract in accordance with its terms, and the contracting officer refused to pay any part of the fixed-fee. The contractor appealed. 

Held, the appeal is sustained. The Govern ment argues that the default termination was proper since the contractor failed to give a timely written notice that the estimated costs of performance would be exceeded. The contractor, however, is a small company whose accounting records are several weeks behind actual expenditures. Further, the contracting officer had advance oral notice of a possible overrun. Under these circumstances the contractor did not materially breach the contract by failing to give an earlier written notice. 

It is clear that contractor did not fail to make satisfactory progress or even come close to defaulting. Work did not stop until the estimated costs were exceeded by the actual costs of performance. The cause of the default, therefore, was the Government's failure to allot more money to the contract rather than the quality or progress of the contractor's work. Unlike a fixed-price research and development contract where the Government may be entitled to work that costs more than the contract price, see

Sam Tour & Co., Inc., ASBCA No. 4332 (2 Oct 

1958), the contractor is not obligated under a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract to continue performance where the estimated costs of performance have been exceeded. Thus, the failure of the 

Government to allot additional funds was an "act of the Government" which excused the default under the "Excusable Delays" provision of the contract. Since the termination should have been for the convenience of the Government, the contractor is entitled to a fixed-fee based upon the percentage of performance completed at the time of termination.

Sterling Precision Corporation, ASBCA No. 

4646, 12 October 1959, 59-2 BCA 2371.

COST-PLUS-PERCENTAGE-OF-COSTS 1. Price Revision Clause Does Not Violate Prohibition Against Cost-Plus-Percentage-of- 

Costs Contracts.

In 1951, the contractor entered AGO 9111A 109

COURT OF CLAIMS 

into two negotiated fixed-price-with-redetermination type contracts with the Signal Corps for the supply of shutter assemblies. The contracts provided for price revision after deliveries were completed. A price ceiling was established for upward revision but not for downward revision. After the contracts were successfully completed the contracting officer revised their combined prices downward from $283,354.01 to $207,410.11. On appeal, the 

ASBCA further reduced the price to $178,- 

946.20. The contractor then brought suit in the Court of Claims to reform the contract on the theory that the price revision clause violated the prohibition against cost-plus-percent age-of-costs contracting. The Government de nied the allegation and filed a counterclaim for the amount of price revision due.

Held, for the Government. The Congressional prohibition against cost-plus-percentage-of-cost contracting, 10 U.S.C. §2306 (a), is intended to prevent a contractor from padding costs in order to obtain a greater profit. On the other hand, Congress has approved the cost-plusfixed-fee method of contracting where the fee or profit does not exceed specified percentages of estimated costs at the time of contracting. 

The contractor argues that the price revision clause is within the prohibition because it induces a contractor to increase costs in order to obtain more profit. This is true to the extent that contract administrators are unable to detect uneconomical performance in assessing the contractor's efficiency, economy and ingenuity or the price revision ceiling minus profit is not exceeded. Congress, however, has sanctioned the procurement of supplies and services on the basis of actual future costs in the cost-plusfixed-fee contract and it is inevitable that contractors will have a certain amount of indifference to performance costs. The conclusion is, therefore, that the price revision clause is closer to being an authorized cost-plus-fixed-fee arrangement than a prohibited cost-plus-percentage-of-costs contract and is not invalid.

National Electronic Laboratories, Inc. v. 

United States, 180 F. Supp. 337 (Ct. Cl. 1960).

2. Court of Claims Rejects Government's Claim for Damages for Contractor's Breach on Grounds That Government Did Not Make Re purchase and Could Not Prove Losses Had Been Incurred. In September 1950 there was created within the General Services Administration an Emergency Procurement Service (EPS) with authority to purchase certain materials pursuant to the Strategic and Critical Materials 110 AGO 9111A

DAMAGES-Continued Stockpiling Act of 1946, 60 Stat. 596 (1946), as amended, 50 U.S.C.

§ 98 (1958), and the 

Defense Production Act of 1950, 64 Stat. 801 

(1950), as amended, 50 U.S.C. § 2093 (1958). 

In August 1951 the EPS agreed to buy, and the plaintiff promised to supply, 2,400,000 pounds of an ore to be mined in British Guiana. The contract stated it was made pursuant to the Strategic and Critical Materials Stock piling Act of 1946. Deliveries were to begin within 6 months after signing of the contract and continue through June 1957. In August 

1951 the President, by Executive Order 10281, 16 Fed. Reg. 8789 (1951), established the De fense Materials Procurement Agency (DMPA) 

and gave it authority, pursuant to the Defense Production Act of 1950, to purchase, and to encourage the development of, strategic minerals. Four months later the plaintiff asked 

DMPA for a loan to be used for the exploration of land in British Guiana to locate the type of ore covered by the contract with the EPS. 

DMPA officials apparently objected to the EPS contract and even demanded its cancellation by the plaintiff before a loan would be granted. 

DMPA not only believed that the plaintiff would be unable to perform the EPS contract profitably but also wished to procure the same ore. 

The plaintiff was reluctant to cancel the EPS contract. Negotiations for the loan collapsed in April 1952, in part because of the conflict over the EPS contract. Lacking capital, the plaintiff was unable to deliver any ore to EPS.

The contract was terminated on 17 February 1953 pursuant to a contract clause giving the Government the option to terminate if no deliveries were made before 15 February 1953. 

The EPS did not repurchase the 2,400,000 pounds of ore the plaintiff had failed to deliver. 

On 28 May 1952 the DMPA had issued a regulation providing for the purchase, over a period of several years, of 15,000,000 pounds of the type of ore involved in plaintiff's EPS contract. The regulation was issued pursuant to the authority given by the Defense Production Act of 1950 and Executive Order 10281. By the end of 1956 the DMPA purchased the 15,- 000,000 pounds specified in the regulation at the published price. In the meantime the plaintiff was asked to pay the Government $976,000 as damages for breach of the EPS contract.

That figure was based on the "replacement cost" of the ore and was calculated in terms of the price DMPA was paying for ore purchased under its regulation. The plaintiff refused to pay the alleged damages. When he sued in the 

Court of Claims alleging, among other things, that the Government had breached a promise to make a loan to him, the Government filed a counterclaim for the $976,000. After finding the Government was not liable to the plaintiff, the court turned to the counterclaim.

Held, the Government may not recover anything. Plaintiff's failure to deliver the ore promised the EPS was a breach of contract. 

Therefore, the Government is entitled to damages equal to the losses incurred as the natural and proximate consequences of the plaintiff's breach. The Government argues that the "weight of authority" has "well established" that a buyer aggrieved by a seller's breach of contract need not repurchase the undelivered goods to recover damages measured by the difference between the market and contract prices.

The only authority cited by the Government is 

United States v. U.S. Foreign Corp., 151 F. 

Supp. 658 (S.D. N.Y. 1957); there a moderated statement of the proposition is only unsupported obiter dicta of the district judge. In the classic case of a vendor's breach of contract, the vendee is often said to be entitled to damages of the difference between the contract and market prices. However, general propositions concerning the measure of damages are relevant to a particular suit only if they reasonably represent the nature of the loss the claimant can prove actually and proximately resulted from the vendor's nonperformance. Stated another way, the measure of damages to be applied in the particular case is irrelevant until the claimant has established the fact of losses that were the natural and proximate result of the breach of contract. Otherwise the doctrine of mitigation of damages would lose much of its significance. The claimant bears the burden of proving the fact of loss with certainty, as well as the burden of proving the amount of the loss with sufficient certainty so that the determination of the amount of damages will be more certain than mere speculation. Winn- AGO 9111A 111

DAVIS-BACON ACT Senter Construction Co. v. United States, 110 

Ct. Cl. 34, 63 (1948).

The Government has not discharged either burden. The Government has not attempted to show that the EPS tried to replace the ore the plaintiff failed to deliver, or even that a loss was suffered in any respect as a result of the plaintiff's breach. The Government has argued that, if the plaintiff had made deliveries to the EPS, the DMPA could have reduced its requirements. No reason is offered to support the argument. In fact the EPS and DMPA undertook procurements pursuant to different delegations of statutory authority. Moreover, the 

DMPA directive was issued at a time when the EPS could reasonably have expected to receive delivery from the plaintiff. It seems reasonable to conclude that the DMPA purchases would have been made even if plaintiff had fulfilled his contract. The DMPA regulation states that it is designed to encourage expansion of ore production rather than to draw upon the normal market of the ore. Important in this regard is testimony that after the DMPA program the ore price fell drastically to levels below that in the plaintiff's contract with the EPS.

2. Contract Must Be Readvertised if Davis- Bacon Wage Determination Incorporated in Specifications Expires Before Award Is Made. 

A Public Health Service invitation for bids on a construction contract included in the specifications minimum hourly wages to be paid by the contractor. The wage rates had been determined by the Secretary of Labor pursuant to the 

Davis-Bacon Act, 46 Stat. 1494 (1931), as amended, 40 U.S.C. § 276a (Supp. II, 1961). 

The L Co. submitted the low bid for both the entire job and alternates that were parts of the entire job. Award was delayed by the L Co.'s allegation of error in its bid on one of the alternates. Then a determination was made that an award would be made for the entire job, which would not be affected by the allegation of error. However, the wage determination had expired. [Such determinations become obsolete ninety days after issuance if no contract has been awarded. 29 C.F.R. § 5.4(a) (Supp. 1962).] It was informally learned that the new determination would decrease the hourly rate for one class of workers and increase it for another class. The Comptroller 

General's approval was sought for a proposal that a new wage determination be sought from the Secretary of Labor and an award made to the L Co. either at the bid price or at a figure to be negotiated on the basis of the new determination. The procuring activity argued that the proposed action would benefit the Government because readvertising, the only alternative, would harm the principle of competitive bidding and would probably result in increasing the cost of the project. The procuring activity noted that the L Co.'s bid was nearly $7,000 less than the next bid, a difference apparently materially greater than any change that would result from the new wage determination. 

Held, the procurement must be readvertised. 

Award of a formally advertised contract must be on the same terms offered to all bidders. See, e.g., 37 Comp. Gen. 524, 527 (1958). In situations involving a change in wage rates, the Government may not require or permit an otherwise successful bidder to perform at his original price or a different price in the absence of a provision in the invitation for bids specifically providing for that procedure. It may well be that in this case the changes in wage rates would not change the relative standing of the low bidder. However, the formal advertising statutes neither contemplate nor sanction selection of winning bidders on the basis of an estimate of what those bidders would have quoted on terms that were not advertised. The actual contract to be executed must be advertised. See, e.g., 17 Comp. Gen. 427 (1937). 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-148284, 13 March 1962. 

3. Davis-Bacon Act Does Not Apply to Construction, Alterations, or Repair, in Accord ance With Government Specifications, of Build ings To Be Leased to Government. The Secre- 

112 AGO 9111A

DEBARMENT OF BIDDERS 

tary of Labor asked the Comptroller General for a decision whether the Davis-Bacon Act applies to the construction, alteration, or repair, in accordance with Government specifications, of buildings to be occupied by the Government under term leases. The Solicitor of Labor had prepared a memorandum concluding that the act did apply.

Held, the act is inapplicable. The Solicitor's conclusion was largely based on the fact that the act requires inclusion of appropriate minimum wage provisions in the advertised specifications for "every" contract covering work of the character described by the act and states that "every" contract based on those specifications shall contain related implementing stipulations. The argument is apparently that the inclusive nature of "every" is intended to subject to coverage all contracts involving work referred to in the act regardless whether title or ownership of the premises being constructed will ever vest in the Government. However, the act applies to entire contracts, not to individual items, and the test for determining applicability is not whether incidental construction work may be performed but whether the contract as a whole substantially or essentially contemplates the performance of "construction, alteration, and/or repair, including painting and decorating." See 40 Comp. Gen. 565 (1961) [digested under LABOR, par. 6] and cases cited there. In view of that, and of the basic distinction between the procurement of a right to use improvements, even though constructed for that particular usage, and the actual procurement of such improvements, the fact that construction work is prerequisite to supplying a public need does not give the work a Davis- Bacon character. No case has been found where the act has been applied to agreements for use or occupancy of construction, as distinguished from acquisition. Special legislative provisions have been deemed necessary to establish minimum wage programs where improvements were not acquired directly by the Government and a public interest arose indirectly out of contributions, loans, or insurance. 

The decision at 34 Comp. Gen. 697 (1955) holding that the act applied to lease-purchase agreements by the Post Office Department was not intended to suggest that the acquisition of ownership is unimportant. Due to a binding agreement to acquire the improvements with public funds, the construction involved there was being purchased by the Government even though a private builder was completing the construction with private funds. Moreover, in that case the legislation authorizing lease-purchase agreements made it clear that the agreements were not to be exempt from the application of the Davis-Bacon Act. These factors are not present with respect to lease and leaseoption agreements. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-122382, 18 July 1962. 

DEBARMENT OF BIDDERS 1. Government Invitations and Contracts May Contain a Provision That All Subcontracts Are Subject to the Approval of the Contracting Officer on the Basis of the Proposed Subcontractor's Qualifications To Perform in a Capable and Responsible Manner. (JAGT) See SUBCONTRACTS (par. 6) 2. Firm Has Standing To Contest Being In cluded on List of Debarred Bidders-Debarment is Authorized Sanction for Violation of Eight Hour Law. After being held to have vio lated an Eight Hour Law (40 U.S.C. § 324) by intentionally underpaying employees for overtime work, the plaintiff paid the United States the statutory penalties and reimbursed the underpaid employees for their overtime. On the recommendation of the Army, the Department of Labor requested the Comptroller General to place the plaintiff's name on the list of those barred from doing business with the Government, and the Comptroller General complied. 

The plaintiff brought suit in a Federal district court against the Comptroller General, the 

Secretary of Labor, and the Secretary of the

Army. Among the relief sought was a judgment declaring unlawful the regulation (29 

C.F.R. § 5.6 (b) (Supp. 1961)) under which the debarment was made. The district court dismissed the complaint, holding that the plaintiff lacked standing and that the debarment was authorized. The plaintiff appealed to the court of appeals.

Held, the plaintiff has standing, but the debarment was authorized. The debarment was AGO 9111A 113

DEBARMENT OF BIDDERS-Continued specifically directed against the plaintiff. It limited for three years the plaintiff's opportunity to work on government projects, which at the time of the listing constituted' approximately 70% of the plaintiff's business. The debarment was a sanction in addition to the fines that the law imposed and the plaintiff paid. The plaintiff hardly could be said to lack standing to contest the fines. There is no significant difference, for purposes of standing, between the fines and the debarment. This case is unlike Perkins v. Lukens 

Steel Co., 310 U.S. 113 (1940), where the plaintiffs sought to contest the validity of conditions of general application for government procurement. The conditions applied not only to the plaintiffs but also to all other manufacturers in an entire nation-wide industry. The plaintiff is prohibited from competing on an equal basis with others in the same industry, whereas in the Lukens Steel case the plaintiffs failed to show "an injury or threat to a particular right of their own, as distinguished from the public's interest in the administration of the law." 310 U.S., at 125. While he has no right to contract with the United States on his own terms, the plaintiff has a right not invalidly to be denied equal opportunity under applicable law to seek contracts on government projects. 

If deprived of that right, the plaintiff suffers a "legal wrong" giving him access to the courts under Section 10 of the Administrative Procedures Act, 5 U.S.C. § 1009. Compare George v. Mitchell, 282 F. 2d 486 (D.C. Cir. 1960).

As to the merits, the central issue is the authority to debar the plaintiff. The Government relies upon the Reorganization Act of 1949 (5) 

U.S.C. §§ 133z to 133z-15), the Reorganization Plan No. 14 of 1950 (15 Fed. Reg. 3176 

(1950)), adopted thereunder, and departmental regulations (cited above). The Plan provided that: 

In order to assure coordination of administration and consistency of enforcement of the labor standards provisions of each of the following Acts by the Federal agencies responsible for the administration thereof, the Secretary of Labor shall prescribe appropriate standards, regulations, and procedures, which shall be observed by these agencies, and cause to be made by the Department of Labor such investigations, with respect to compliance with and enforcement of such labor standards, as he deems desirable, namely: . . (d) the 

Act of 19 June 1912 (37 Stat. 137, ch. 174), as amended [the statute plaintiff violated]. 

This provision was implemented by the regulation under which the plaintiff was debarred. 

Reasonable deference must be given the Secretary's interpretation of his authority in administering the labor acts. Commissioner v. 

South Texas Lbr. Co., 333 U.S. 496 (1948). The requirement that penal provisions be strictly construed is inapplicable here. If a provision is designed to implement congressional purposes it does not become a penalty merely because it adversely affects some parties. According to 

Steuart & Bro., Inc. v. Bowles, 322 U.S. 398 

(1944), the test to be applied to the debarment provision to determine whether it is penal is whether it is relevant to the maintenance of responsible bidding under, and compliance with, the labor acts. Under that test, the debarment provision is not penal. Congress and contracting agencies have used temporary debarments to implement some labor acts. See, e.g., the

Davis-Bacon Act, 40 U.S.C. § 276a-2 (a). The provision in the Eight Hour Laws for civil and criminal penalties does not negative the authority of an enforcement agency to use debarment as an additional means of accomplishing the congressional purpose. Steuart & Bro., Inc. v. Bowles, supra. Moreover, in the instant case the debarment was not absolute. The plaintiff petitioned the Secretary for removal from the Comptroller General's list, and upon a proper showing relief would have been granted. 

It was denied because the Department of Labor, after a hearing, could not conclude that the plaintiff could "be relied upon by the United States and Federal Agencies as responsible persons who will comply with" the required standards.

Even though not a penalty, the debarment is required to have been properly authorized. Authority is found in the fact that, in order to secure compliance with the wage and hour standards and to obtain responsible bidding, the Army could have included a debarment provision when asking for bids and awarding contracts. Compare Schlesinger v. Gates, 249 

F. 2d 111 (D.C. Cir. 1957). It would seem then that the Secretary of Labor clearly could establish a debarment regulation. 114 AGO 9111A

DEFAULT The regulation meets the requirement that it be reasonable. Congress has itself authorized debarment in several instances. See, e.g., the

Davis-Bacon Act, supra, and the Walsh-Healey Act, 41 U.S.C. § 37. Inclusion of a provision for debarment in some statutes does not, contrary to the plaintiff's argument, preclude its use to implement statutes that omit it. Because debarment is an enforcement measure utilized in kindred statutes, Congress' authorization in 

Plan No. 14 that the Secretary assure "coordination of administration and consistency of enforcement of the labor standards provisions" of the acts specified in the Plan, and to that end to "prescribe appropriate standards, regulations, and procedures," would seem to permit the Secretary to prescribe a rule that the contracting agency could prescribe, especially one of the character Congress has approved for similar statutes.

Finally, no decisive effect should be given to the views expressed by the Comptroller General and relief on by the plaintiff. The Comptroller General followed the recommendation of the Secretary in listing the plaintiff, but by letter expressed the opinion that the debarment regulation offended Section 5 (a) (4) of the Reorganization Act (5 U.S.C. § 133z-3 (a) (4)). 

He reasoned that since this section of the Act precludes any plan that authorizes "any agency to exercise any function which is not expressly authorized by law at the time the plan is transmitted to the Congress," the debarment condition, which had not been adopted by the contracting agency, was unauthorized. However, the debarment regulation does not enlarge functions theretofore residing in the agencies. 

Those functions included the power to enter into contracts in accordance with relevant statutes. That power authorized the establishment of sanctions, including disbarment, for the enforcement of labor standards. The transfer to the Secretary of Labor was a transfer and coordination of authority already reposing within the several agencies.

Copper Plumbing & Heating Co. v. Campbell, 290 F. 2d 368 (D.C. Cir. 1961). 

[Note: In George v. Mitchell, 282 F. 2d 486 (D.C. Cir. 1960), digested under LABOR, par. 

3, cited in the instant opinion, the court held that Government contractors had standing to seek a declaratory judgment when they were threatened with debarment for violation of the 

Walsh-Healey Act (41 U.S.C. §§35-45). The court noted that standing to enjoin the Secretary of Labor from establishing a minimum wage pursuant to the Walsh-Healey Act had been denied in the Lukens Steel Co. case, also cited in the instant opinion, because "no legal rights of respondents were shown to have been invaded or threatened." 310 U.S. at 185. The court held that the Lukens Steel Co. case, as it related to the Walsh-Healey Act, was overruled by the Fullbright Amendment (41 U.S.C. § 43a (c)) to that Act. The Amendment provided: 

Notwithstanding the inclusion of any stipulations required by any provision of sections 35-45 of this title in any contract subject to said sections, any interested person shall have the right of judicial review of any legal question which might otherwise be raised, including, but not limited to, wage determinations and the interpretation of the terms 'locality', 'regular dealer', 'manufacturer', and 'open market.'

The court reasoned that under the Amendment the standard of "any interested person" replaces the "legal wrong" criterion of Lukens 

Steel Co., and "the right of judicial review of any legal question" is established once a dispute arises under a Government contract covered or alleged to be covered by the Walsh-Healey Act. 

The instant opinion goes farther by arguing that the Lukens Steel Co. doctrine is inapplicable to any suit to prevent debarment.] DEFAULT 

See also CLAIMS BY U.S., DISPUTES, TERMINATION 1. Where Contracting Officer Elects To Permit Defaulting Contractor To Continue Performance, May Wait a Reasonable Time and Terminate the Contract for Default if Substantial Deliveries Are Not Made. In July 1957, the contractor was awarded a contract to manufacture 325,000 pairs of fatigue trousers for a total price of $263,250. Under the contract, 54,040 pairs of trousers were to be delivered by 29 

October 1957 and a like amount each month thereafter until the contract was completed. 

The contract contained an Inspection clause, see ASPR 7-103.5, and the standard Default article, ASPR 8-707 (5 Sep 1958). The Gov ernment agreed to furnish the material out of AGO 9111A 115

DEFAULT-Continued which the trousers would be cut. To establish a production line to sew the trousers the contractor placed orders for necessary parts and attachments with subcontractors. The contractor planned to have seven production lines in operation by 15 September and to average 1,205 trousers per line per week until the first delivery date.

The Government furnished material was delivered on time and the cutting began in early September. The sewing, however, could not begin on schedule for the parts and attachments necessary to establish a production line were not ready for delivery. By 2 October, only two lines were ready for production and the seventh line was not completed until 15 November. During the early months cutting was delayed by defective Government furnished material. How ever, at no time during the entire period did the capacity of the production line to sew exceed the quantity of cut trousers on hand. A further difficulty was caused when the subcontractor's shipper went on strike in September.

This did not affect performance, however, because the delivery of necessary parts and attachments by the subcontractor was delayed until the strike was nearly over. In fact, the final deliveries were made after the strike was settled on 22 October. 

In early October, only two production lines were in operation and the contractor was one month behind schedule. By 29 October, the first delivery date, the contractor had cut 23,745 pairs of trousers but had sewn only 4,000 pairs. 

Further, no lot had been delivered to the Government for inspection. While the contractor was clearly in default, the contracting officer took no action until 5 November. At that time a termination for default was threatened unless certain conditions were met by 15 November.

These conditions were not agreed to, although the contractor continued to cut and sew. Accordingly, on 27 November the contracting officer gave notice that unless substantial progress was made within 10 days the contract would be terminated for default. See ASPR 8-707 a (ii) 

(5 Sep 1958). Upon receipt of this notice, the contractor discharged 250 employees, discontinued further cutting operations and requested an extension in the delivery schedule, which was denied. On 10 December, an original lot of 1,400 trousers was inspected and accepted by the Government. On 19 December, the contract was partially terminated for failure to deliver goods on time, see ASPR 8-707 a(i), but the contractor was ordered to complete work on the 65,453 pairs of trousers already cut. In a subsequent repurchase the Government realized a saving. The contractor filed an appeal from the termination and argued that the default was excusable and should be recharacterized as a termination for convenience. In the alternative, the contractor urged that the contracting officer had elected to continue performance after the 29 October default and had not permitted a reasonable time for further deliveries.

Held, the appeal is denied. A substantial part of the contractor's 29 October default was caused by the subcontractor's delay in delivering necessary parts and attachments for the production line, not by the strike. Further, a flood and the defective Government materials did not affect performance since at the time they occurred the production line was either not in operation or not keeping up with the supply of cut trousers on hand. The subcontractor delay is excusable since the contractor used reasonable business judgment in placing the order and expediting its delivery. Since two production lines were in operation from 10 October, however, the contract could have delivered some acceptable trousers. Yet only 4,000 pairs had been manufactured and they had not been inspected by the Government. At least twosevenths of the default, therefore, was due to the contractor's lack of know-how. 

The contracting officer, however, did not terminate the contract and when, by 15 November, the contractor had not agreed to the conditions prescribed in the letter of 5 November, an election to continue performance was made. At this point the contracting officer had three choices. First, a new, reasonable delivery schedule could have been negotiated with the contractor which would have mooted the question of excusability. Second, a reasonable delivery schedule could have been unilaterally prescribed. If this procedure were followed the issue of excusability would survive and the rea- 116 AGO 9111A

DEFAULT-Continued sonableness of the new schedule would be open to question. Third, the contracting officer, as was done here, could wait for a reasonable time and terminate the contract for default. This is probably the least satisfactory since the contractor is not informed of his delivery obligation and both reasonableness and excusability are unresolved. 

The contracting officer in the instant case waited 12 days before issuing the ten day notice and actually terminated the contract 22 days later. Considering the contractor's position on 

15 November, it is concluded that the additional time for performance was reasonable. Since the contractor had sufficient cut parts and a production line capable of producing over 7,000 trousers a week, the failure to make any deliveries during the 12 days justified the ten day notice. And after this notice there is no satisfactory evidence that the contractor could have produced specification trousers in accord with any reasonable delivery schedule. The contractor should have been able to produce between 

16,000 and 25,000 acceptable trousers in 10 days. Instead, the contractor reduced its work force, discontinued cutting, sought a time extension and delivered but 1,400 acceptable items. This latter delivery amounted to one week's work for one production line and its acceptance cannot be regarded as a waiver of the right to terminate or an election to continue performance. The contractor was given reasonable time to demonstrate its ability to produce a sufficient quantity of acceptable trousers. 

In view of the facts, the contractor was in default on 19 December and the contract was properly terminated for default.

(ASBCA) See COST CONTRACTS (par. 1) 4. Contractor, in Appeal From Assessment of Excess Costs, Permitted To Attack Timeliness of Government's Termination for Default. 

On 25 May 1955, the contractor was awarded a contract to repair and overhaul 500 Lycoming

Engines for the Air Force. The contract con tained a standard Default clause, ASPR 8-707 

(5 Sep 1958), and a Government Furnished Property clause, see ASPR 13-502 (14 May 

1958), under which the Government agreed to furnish "all parts and materials required for the performance of the work." The contractor was to furnish "(A)ll parts and materials which are the responsibility of the Government to furnish but which will not be available from USAF stock in sufficient time to prevent productions delay." The first deliveries of reconditioned engines to the Government were to be made 45 days after the contractor had received a 30-day supply of parts. Prior to 30 June 

1955, the Government delivered 530 engines to the contractor for repair and overhaul, and prepared requisitions so the contractor could obtain a 30-day stock level. The requisitions were unrealistic, however, and provided sufficient parts for only 3.75 days. While the Air Force had sufficient parts in stock, it concluded that the approved requisition was adequate to establish a 30-day stock supply and refused the contractor's request for a change. Consequently, the contractor unsuccessfully tried to obtain the required parts through local purchases. During this period no effort was made to employ a labor force to complete operations on any engine. 

On 6 January 1956 the Government an nounced that final action had been taken on the requisitions and that the 45-day delivery period had started. Meanwhile, the contractor submitted for Air Force approval local purchase orders which were both inadequate in the number of parts obtained and the number of subcontractors solicited. On 10 February 1956, the contracting officer notified the contractor that performance was endangered because of the failure to obtain adequate personnel and facilities and that the contract would be terminated for default if these defects were not corrected within ten days. ASPR 8-707(a) (ii) (5 Sep 

1958). The contractor argued that it had not been provided a sufficient number of parts to AGO 9111A 117

DEFAULT-Continued permit continuous operations. No further progress was made, however, and the contract was terminated for default on 1 May 1956. The contractor did not appeal.

The Government repurchased the repair and overhauling services from another contractor and incurred excess costs of $177,225.41. The contract was let after negotiations with only one producer, whose unit price bid was higher than that of five bidders on the original contract. The contractor appealed from the assessment of excess costs.

Held, the appeal is sustained and the termination deemed for the convenience of the 

Government. The contractor challenges the propriety of both the termination and the assessment of excess costs and asks that the termination be recharacterized for the convenience of the Government. These issues are all before the Board. Fulford Manufacturing Company, ASBCA Nos. 2143 & 2144 (20 May 1955), DA Pam 715-50-1, p. 252, par. 70. While the circumstances raise the question of whether the contractor's alleged failure to perform was excusable, a more basic issue is presented: was the contractor ever under an obligation to deliver or make progress under the terms of the contract? While some confusion exists over the precise effect of the delivery schedule and the obligations of the Government to furnish property, it is clear that the Government's determination of a 30-day stock pile was erroneous.

Government-furnished property comprised all parts required to perform the work and it has not been shown that the Government furnished all that was available from stock. Thus, since the Government failed to furnish a full 30-day stock level the 45-day delivery schedule never became effective. As such, the contractor's failure to prepare for continuous production prior to the start of the delivery period could not endanger performance of the contract and the termination for default was premature. While unnecessary to this decision, the repurchase procedure in this case constitutes a flagrant disregard of the Government's duty to mitigate damages. See Bar-Ray Products, Inc., ASBCA 

No. 3065 (4 Nov 1957), [See also, Office Equipment Co., ASBCA No. 5040 (27 July 1957), as digested and noted in DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 211, par. 1].

5. Time Extension Denied Under Construction Contract but Granted Under Supply Contract Where Cause of Delay Was Foreseeable but Beyond Control and Without Fault or Negligence of Contractor. (C.G.) See EXCUSABLE CAUSE (par. 3) 6. Contract Properly Defaulted for Breach of Davis-Bacon Act Wage Requirements Where Contractor Fails To Prove That Restitution Was Made Before Termination Date. In April 

1958, the contractor was awarded three contracts [hereafter identified as A, B, and C] to paint facilities at Dobbins Air Force Base, Georgia. Each contract authorized a termination for default "(I)f the contractor refuses or fails to prosecute the work... with such diligence as will insure its completion within the time specified in the contract. . . ." In addition, contract A contained a schedule of job classifications and corresponding wage rates as de termined by the Secretary of Labor pursuant to the Davis-Bacon Act, 40 U.S.C. 276(a). Con tract A also provided: 

(b) In the event it is found by the Contracting Officer that any laborer or mechanic employed by the Contractor . . . directly on the site of the work covered by this contract has been or is being paid at a rate of wages less than the rate of wages required . . the Contracting Officer may (1) terminate his right to proceed with the work and (2) prosecute the work to completion whereupon such Contractor and his sureties shall be liable to the Government for any excess costs occasioned the Government thereby. Work under all contracts started in May 1958 and was to be completed before August 1958. 

From the beginning, however, considerable friction developed between the contractor and the Air Force job inspector. This friction had two interrelated causes. First, the inspector continually supervised and directed the work done by employees on all three contracts without clearing through the contractor. The second cause arose from an admitted violation by the contractor of the Davis-Bacon Act. The inspec tor discovered, through interviews with employees, that during the first two weeks of work the contractor had paid wages below the mini- 118 AGO 9111A

DEFAULT-Continued mum scale and without regard to job classification. The inspector informed employees of this situation and denounced the violation as criminal conduct. The contractor asserted that the inspector's overall conduct constituted malicious harassment which caused dissension among the employees and hindered contract performance. 

On 2 June the contractor demanded that the base commander appoint a new inspector and arrange a conference with Air Force officials to iron out difficulties. A new inspector was appointed the next day but the conference was postponed pending further investigation. Apparently, the new inspector continued his predecessor's practice of supervising and directing the painting without consulting the contractor. 

On 7 June, the contractor informed the base commander that continued harassment necessitated a suspension of work until a conference could be arranged which would resolve and eliminate the friction. By 9 June, all of the contractor's men and equipment had been removed from the work site. In the next 3 days the 

Government issued a stop work order for each contract and informed the contractor that all contracts would be terminated for default unless facts were presented within ten days which justified continuance. The contractor reiterated the reasons for suspending work but made no effort to return. In August 1958, all contracts were terminated for default for the contractor's failure to diligently prosecute the work. The 

Davis-Bacon Act violation was cited as an additional ground for terminating contract A. The contractor appealed from the terminations and from a subsequent assessment of excess profits. 

Held, the appeals are denied. With regard to contract A, the Air Force was responsible for insuring compliance with the Davis-Bacon Act. 

The inspector was fulfilling this responsibility when his interviews with employees disclosed the contractor's admitted violation. AFPI 12404.7 (12 Dec 1958). While his subsequent comments to the employees may have been too "enthusiastic" they were motivated by the contractor's wrongful conduct and did not harm the work being performed. There is no convincing or compelling evidence that the contractor paid the wage deficiency between the date work was suspended and the date of termination. 

The burden is on the contractor to prove that restitution was made, not on the Government to prove that it was not. Consequently, the default termination of contract A for violations of the Davis-Bacon Act was proper and there is no need to decide whether or not the contractor failed to diligently prosecute the work. 

With regard to contracts B and C, the contractor was not in default when work was suspended in June. The contractor's claim that the work suspension was justified by the inspector's harassment and malicious interference is without merit. The inspector was conscientiously and justifiably performing his duty to assure quality performance in accord with specifications. While his conduct was perhaps "overzealous" and caused friction, the work performed was not harmed. The conclusion is, therefore, that the contractor's work suspension was unjustified and that the failure to resume work constituted a default. This obligation to continue work could not be avoided merely by shifting to the base commander the burden of arranging a conference which would remove the friction, especially since a new inspector had been appointed. 

The sum of $7,951.30 was properly assessed by the contracting officer as excess costs incurred under all three contracts.

L. L. Cheek Contracting Co., ASBCA Nos. 

5261 and 5448, 30 October 1959, 59-2 BCA 

2409. par. 2409. 

7. Contractor Must Appeal Within Thirty Days of Notice of Excess Cost Assessment Even Though No Express Determination of Nonexcusability Has Been Made. In June 1954, the contractor was awarded a $15,287 contract to install pipe fittings and other equipment at Valley Forge Army Hospital. Due to a disagreement with the Government over a matter not within the disputes procedure, the contractor never started work and the contract was terminated for default ten months after award. The termination notice warned that the services would be repurchased and excess costs assessed, but the contractor did not appeal. In 

April 1956, the contractor was notified that excess costs of $4,577 had been assessed but not that the default was determined to be non- AGO 9111A 119

DEFAULT-Continued excusable. Again, the contractor did not appeal. In April 1959, the contractor attacked both the termination and assessment notices for failing to comply with APP 7-103.11 and 

7-103.12. [Now rescinded, see ASPR 8-602.3 

(5 May 1958)]. The contracting officer refused to take action on the ground that the objections were untimely and the contractor appealed. 

Held, the appeal is denied. The contractor argues that the question of excusability is before the Board since neither the notice of termination nor assessment contained an express finding that the default was not excusable. Clearly, this issue could be raised by an appeal within 30 days after receiving the notice of termination or the notice of assessment. Fulford Manu facturing Co., ASBCA Nos. 2143 and 2144 (20 

May 1955). The required determination of nonexcusability inheres in both the termination and assessment notices, even though not expressly made. Virginia Dare Extract Co.,

Inc., ASBCA No. 4916 (24 Apr 1959), 59-1 

BCA 2188. Since the contractor did not appeal within 30 days after receiving the assessment notice the appeal is untimely and should be dismissed.

Oxygen Equipment Service Co., ASBCA No. 

5690, 20 January 1960, 60-1 BCA 2495. [Note: A notice that excess costs have been assessed permits the contractor, by a timely appeal, to argue either that the assessment was defective, Office Equipment Co., ASBCA No. 

5040 (27 Jul 1959), 59-2 BCA 2303, DA Pam 

715-50-2, p. 211, par. 1, or that the default was excusable. Fulford Mfg. Co., supra. Each is an independent ground for avoiding excess costs. 

See ASPR 8-707 (b) and (c) (5 Sep 1958). 

Virginia Dare, supra, held that a contractor may argue excusability in a timely appeal from an assessment even though the notice did not contain an express finding of nonexcusability. 

See the analysis of Virginia Dare in DA Pam 

715-50-2, p. 240, par. 14. The instant case extends Virginia Dare by holding, under similar facts, that the inherent finding of nonexcusability in an assessment must be appealed within 30 days of the notice. This seems squarely to overrule Hofmann Industries, Inc., ASBCA No. 

2367 (23 May 1955), DA Pam 715-50-1, p. 

253, par. 71, and implies that the contractor assumes the risk of misinterpreting the assessment notice. Confusion in this area is avoidable if the contracting officer makes an express determination of excusability, either before the assessment as required by ASPR 8–602.3(g) (5 Sep 1958) or in the notice of assessment itself.] 

8. Excess Costs Incurred in Establishing a 

New Source as Opposed to Replacing a De faulted Source Not Assessable. (ASBCA) See EXCESS COSTS (par. 2) 9. Claim for Payment for Work Done Pre maturely Asserted in Appeal From a Termina tion for Default. (ASBCA) See DISPUTES (par. 14) 10. In Case of Resale for Account of Defaulting Purchaser, Storage and Other Charges Assessed Against Defaulter Are To Be De frayed From Proceeds of Resale Rather Than

From Original Purchase Price Where Contract 

So Provides. In September 1958 appellant was the successful bidder on a Government surplus aircraft. In February 1959, five months after he had paid the purchase price of $1,500, appellant, not having removed the aircraft, received a letter from the contracting officer warning that unless the aircraft was removed within 12 days the terms of Clause 7 of the contract would be enforced and the aircraft would be resold. Clause 7 provided (1) that the purchaser could be charged a reasonable storage charge if he failed to remove the aircraft by a specified date and (2) that the Government could upon 10 days written notice given twenty or more days after the date specified for removal resell the aircraft "applying the proceeds therefrom against the storage and any other costs incurred for purchaser's account."

The aircraft was resold for $1,750. The contracting officer assessed storage charges and administrative costs in the amount of $210 which sum he withheld from the $1,500 paid by appellant. This appeal is brought to recover the $210, appellant claiming that the excess of the resale price over his purchase price being greater than the damages chargeable to him, he is entitled to refund of his full purchase price. 120 AGO 9111A

DEFAULT-Continued 20 Held, the appeal is sustained. Under the provisions of Clause 7 which is determinative of the matter of the appellant's obligation, storage and other costs should be defrayed from the proceeds of the resale; it was error for the contracting officer to charge appellant for them separately.

James E. Laugel, ASBCA No. 6013, 23 Feb ruary 1960, 60-1 BCA 2522. 

11. In Repurchasing Upon Termination For 

Default, a Contracting Officer May Properly

Limit the Area of Solicitation to That Capable of Supplying the Need Promptly-Excess Costs 

Were Properly Assessed. The contractor contracted to supply 42,000 board feet of lumber f.o.b. Raritan Arsenal, Metuchen, New Jersey, by contract dated 12 November 1958, naming the B&O Lumber Company as its supplier. The supplier then "renigged on their contract" and on 18 November 1958 the contractor designated a new supplier, an Oregon firm, to supply the lumber under the contract. Delivery date under the contract was 22 December 1958. Normal freight transit time from Oregon to New Jersey is from twenty-five to thirty days, with some shipments running to 50 days. The new supplier delayed shipment. As the lumber was needed promptly by the Raritan Arsenal and it had not been shipped, the contract was terminated for default by letter dated 23 December 1958. The contracting officer meanwhile requested proposals for the lumber from lumber dealers in Georgia, Mississippi, North Carolina, Virginia, and New Jersey. A proposal from a

North Carolina dealer was accepted on 24 December. Delivery was called for and effected by 23 January 1959. Excess costs were assessed against the defaulted contractor. The latter appealed from the assessment, alleging that its 

Oregon supplier was willing and able to supply the lumber at a price lower than the repurchase price and that a proposal should have been solicited from him.

Held, appeal denied. The assessment of excess costs is proper. Even if the contracting officer had known at the time he solicited proposals that the Oregon source would be willing to furnish the lumber, repurchase from a West Coast source would have involved an undue risk of disruption of planned activities for which the lumber is currently needed. Where, as here, it appears that the original contractor cannot or will not deliver supplies at the time specified in the contract and that the supplies are required to fill an immediate need of the Government, a contracting officer on repurchase may properly limit the area of solicitation to that capable of supplying the need promptly. In this situation, time as well as price must be considered.

Pacific Western Lumber Co., ASBCA No. 

5518, 15 March 1960, 60-1 BCA 2603. 

[Note: The principal case should be compared with Office Equipment Co., ASBCA No. 

5040 (27 Jul 1959), 59-2 BCA 2302, DA Pam 

715-50-2, p. 211, par. 1. In the latter, the failure of the Government on repurchase to solicit bids from two bidders who had submitted bids in response to the original invitation which were substantially below the repurchase price was considered sufficient to show failure on the part of the Government to mitigate damages, as it is contractually required to do. However, in that case, the Government failed to sustain its claim that an insufficient time existed in which to repurchase properly. 

In the instant decision it is not disputed that the lumber in question was needed promptly upon termination of the original contract, thus excusing the Government's failure to solicit from more distant sources. An extensive review of the cases involving appropriateness of repurchase procedure and burden of proof is set forth in the note following the digest of 

Office Equipment Co., DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 

211, par. 1.]

(ASBCA) 

See DISPUTES (par. 19) 13. Where Contractor Not Incapacitated, Failure To Deliver Acceptable Sample of Standard Item Is Not a Failure To Make Progress so as To Endanger Performance of Contract. In 

December 1957, the contractor agreed to deliver various quantities of wall mounted soap holders to the Navy on or before 19 March 

1958. The contract contained the standard De fault clause, ASPR 8-707, paragraph (a) (ii) AGO 9111A 121

DEFAULT-Continued of which provided that the Government, by written notice of default to the contractor, might terminate the whole or any part of the contract: 

If the Contractor fails to perform any of the other provisions of this contract, or so fails to make progress as to endanger performance of this contract in accordance with its terms, and in either of these two circumstances does not cure such failure within a period of 10 days . . . after receipt of notice from the Contracting Officer specifying such failure.

After the award the contractor discovered an error in the bid price but was advised by the Government that the recision was not warranted. In addition, a sample soap holder was rejected by the Government. The contractor then submitted a second sample made by a different supplier and suggested that the Government either accept the holder or cancel the order without prejudice to either party. The second sample was also rejected, and on 3 

February 1958, the contracting officer gave the contractor until 13 February 1958 to advise whether or not the contract would be performed in accordance with its terms. In response, the contractor advised that while performance would be at a tremendous financial loss, a new supplier had been contacted and performance would be completed. On 14 February 1958, however, the contracting officer terminated the contract under paragraph (a) (ii) of the Default Clause for failure to make progress as to endanger performance of the contract in accordance with its terms. The contractor appealed. 

Held, the appeal is sustained. At the time of termination the contractor had not failed to deliver soap holders within the time specified in the contract. ASPR 8-707 (a) (i). The only progress defect was the inability to submit an acceptable sample by 3 February 1958, the date of the ten day notice. This failure cannot be equated to a failure to make acceptable deliveries on 19 March 1958. The contractor, therefore, did not fail to perform any other provision of this contract. Further, the 3 February notice does not mention progress and no specific standard of progress short of final delivery is apparent from the contract. In the procurement of a simple and readily obtainable item, progress does not have the same connotation as in a contract for capital goods or technically complicated articles. There is no evidence that the contractor, despite the defective samples, would be unable to deliver specification soap holders on 19 March 1958. See

Bolinders Co., ASBCA No. 2457 (3 Nov 1955). 

At no time prior to 14 February did the contractor repudiate the contract or, by conduct, obviously and positively incapacitate itself from performing. While the contractor indicated that further performance would be at a financial loss, an intention to complete the contract was evinced. This does not authorize the Government to terminate the contract for default. 

But cf. David R. Levin, Trustee, ASBCA No. 

5077 (21 Jan 1959), 59-1 BCA 2061 [DA Pam 

715-50-2, p. 182, par. 60, and note following].

Manhattan Lighting Equip. Co., Inc., ASBCA 

No. 5113, 18 May 1960, 60-1 BCA 2646. 

14. Default Termination Based on Contractor's Failure To Correct Discrepancies Improper Where Contractor Has Substantially 

Performed. The contractor agreed to furnish and install certain designated terminal strips by means of which Government installed main feeder cables were to be connected to Government furnished intercommunication desk sets. 

The contractor was also to make these connections by soldering wires from the desk sets and wires from the cables to appropriate metal lugs on the terminal strips. He was to be guided in making the connections by color charts which identified the particular wires from the feeder cables which were to be connected to each intercom set, but because of the security classification of the project he was denied access to the master plan for the installation of the sets. 

Within the time allowed for performance (as extended) the contractor notified the Government that the job was complete and ready for inspection. Three inspections conducted in the next twenty days disclosed discrepancies listed as (1) too much solder, (2) improper lacing and fanning of wires and (3) split pairs. The parties agreed that the system would not operate when these inspections were made. The contractor was given a 10 day notice to correct these deficiencies; he took no action and on 5 

July 1957, upon the expiration of such period, 122 AGO 9111A

DEFAULT-Continued the contract was terminated pursuant to the Default clause. The work was completed by enlisted men on the station. The contractor appealed the termination. 

As to the excess solder discrepancies the Board found that only a small portion of them affected the operation of the system; the rest affected appearance only and were attributable to the Government's having designated too small a terminal strip for the number of wires required in some instances to be attached to a single lug. The Board found that the lacing and fanning discrepancies did not affect the operation of the system. Some were explained by the contractor as due to the fact that so many wires were put on one strip that there was no room for fanning; others by the fact that the Government installed cables had been cut off too short to permit fanning. Finally, the Board found that responsibility for the split pairs and the resulting operational failures could not be established because some changes in the system which affected connections already made by the contractor were accomplished by the Government, thus the faulty work could have been the product of either.

Held, appeal sustained. While the job was neither a perfect one nor even a creditable one, it represented substantial compliance with the contract. 

The classified nature of the work which required the contractor to connect designated pieces of Government installed equipment without his being able to test the correctness of the installation and the fact that the Government as a result of changes reworked some connections previously made by the contractor, resulted in conditions which made some errors in the performance of work almost inevitable. In addition it did not appear that the Government technical representative, who was constantly available to supervise and correct the work as it was done, made any complaint or suggestion until after the work was finished. 

Under the circumstances the contractor substantially performed the contract before it was terminated. The number of operational errors attributable to the contractor seems neither material nor unreasonable. The errors affecting the appearance of the work were due in part, at least, to the Government's design of the in stallation. 

Conway Electric Co., ASBCA No. 4570, 30 August 1960, 60-2 BCA 2782. 

15. Determination of Excess Costs Prior to the Completion of Reprocurement Would Be Premature. (JAGT) See EXCESS COSTS (par. 4) 16. Default Clause Retains for Government the Right to Common-law Damages for Breach of Contract. Pursuant to the standard Default clause (ASPR 8-707) in the contractor's two Army supply contracts, the Government terminated the contracts for non-performance. The 

Government purchased replacements and charged the excess costs to the contractor. The 

ASBCA held the contractor was in default, but exonerated him from liability for excess costs because the repurchase was delayed too long to have been authorized by the Default clause. 

George S. Rumley, ASBCA Nos. 799 and 1009 

(12 Sep 1952). When the contractor sued in the Court of Claims for the purchase price of another contract, the Government counterclaimed for common-law damages for the breach of the two defaulted contracts. The 

Government based its counterclaim on paragraph (f) of the Default clause, which saves to the Government "any other rights and remedies provided by law." As the measure of its damages, the Government claimed the difference between the contract price and the reasonable replacement cost of the contract items. 

Held, the Government may recover the amount by which its cost of obtaining performance was increased by the contractor's default. 

The provision in the Default clause for assessing excess costs (ASPR 8-707 (c)) has only one function. It takes the common-law rule for determining damages for breach of contract (reasonable cost of obtaining performance after the breach minus the contract price) and provides that if the Government makes a timely repurchase, the repurchase cost will be accepted without further proof as the reasonable cost of obtaining performance. Although this right was lost by tardiness in repurchasing, paragraph (f) allows the Government to recover as common-law damages the amount by which AGO 9111A 123

DEFAULT-Continued it can prove the breach increased the cost of obtaining performance. [The court then computed damages by estimating how much replacement items would have cost immediately after the breach.]

Rumley v. United States, 285 F.2d 773 (Ct. 

Cl. 1961). 

17. It Is a Breach of Contract To Terminate for Default When Contractor Did Not Fail To Perform but Only Failed To Meet Delivery Date 

Waived by Government. (Ct. Cl.) 

See TERMINATION (par. 7) 18. Failure To Perform Not Excusable if It Was Caused by a Reluctance To Buy Materials 

Procurable Only at a Cost Higher Than Originally Anticipated-Where Substantial Reduc tion of Quantity Repurchased Caused Unit 

Price To Increase by Amount That May Be

Calculated With Reasonable Accuracy, Excess Costs May Not Include That Amount. On a procurement of 467 test bench cable kits, the

A Co. and the C Co. bid $585 and $362 per kit, respectively. The contract was awarded to the 

C Co., but was later terminated, pursuant to the 

Default Clause (Cl. 11, SF 32, Oct. 1957 ed.), for a failure to deliver the required preproduction sample. When the Government decided to make a repurchase, only 267 kits were needed, so a contract for that number at $697.47 per kit was negotiated with the A Co. The contracting officer assessed against the C Co. excess costs of 267 times the difference between $697.47 and $362. The C Co. timely appealed to the ASBCA from the decisions terminating the contract and assessing excess costs. Admitting it had defaulted the contract, the C Co. contended that its failure to perform was due to causes beyond its control and without its fault or negligence because subsequent to award of the Government contract the C Co.'s major subcontractor had unexpectedly increased his quotation by an amount that if paid would have caused the C Co. to become bankrupt. The prices quoted by alternate suppliers would also, according to the C Co., have caused bankruptcy. 

The firm resisted the assessment of excess costs on the grounds that the repurchase was not for supplies "similar to those . . . terminated" because the repurchase contract was for a quantity far smaller than the original contract.

The difference in quantity, the firm contended, caused the increase in unit price.

Held, the appeal is sustained only to the extent that the excess costs will be calculated in terms of a repurchase price of $585. First, the failure to perform did not arise out of causes beyond the control of the firm and without its fault or negligence. There is no convincing evidence that the firm lacked working capital for performing the contract. The firm was unwilling to perform because it would have sustained a substantial loss. The firm relies on 

Paromel Electronics Corporation, ASBCA No. 

4025 (28 Oct. 1957), 57-2 BCA 1503 [digested in DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 171, par. 32], but has not shown that "supervening financial reverses, so severe as to render performance impossible" arose without fault or negligence of the firm, as Paromel requires. The instant case is like those where the Board and the courts have held that financial difficulties do not render the failure to perform excusable if needed supplies are procurable at an increased cost. See, e.g., Whitlock Corp. v. United States, 141 Ct. Cl. 758 

(1958); Central Canning Co., ASBCA No. 6011 

(30 Sept. 1960), 60-2 BCA 2820. 

Second, the excess costs assessed must be reduced. The firm contends that the change from 467 to 267 units constitutes so substantial a change in the terms and conditions of the original contract that no excess costs may be assessed. However, the Government exercised proper discretion in procuring only 267 units when no more were needed. Absent a showing of abuse of discretion in placing the repurchase contract, the Government is entitled under the 

Default Clause to excess costs. The question to be resolved in this case is whether the amount of excess costs was affected by the decrease in the number of units repurchased and, if so, how the excess costs should then be treated. 

The Government has conceded that the increase in unit price was "primarily due" to the decrease in quantity. However, the decreased quantity and increased price are not alone enough to invalidate the entire claim for excess costs. If the amount of price increase caused by a decrease in quantity may be tabulated, excess costs should not be extended by that 124 AGO 9111A

DEFAULT-Continued amount. In the instant case the record fails to show the exact price increase attributable to the quantity reduction. It would be highly inequitable, though, to hold that the C Co.'s entire liability is expunged. The record gives sufficient facts upon which the amount of excess costs properly assessable may be determined with reasonable accuracy. The A Co. bid $585 for the 467 kits in the original contract and $697.47 for the 267 kits in the repurchase contract. Since the Government admits that the increase in unit price was "primarily due" to the decrease in quantity, the difference of $112.47 reasonably represents the increase in the unit repurchase price attributable to the quantity reduction. The C Co. therefore is liable for excess costs of 267 times the difference between $585 and $362. 

Consolidated Airborne Systems, Inc., ASB- 

CA No. 5498, 31 January, 1961, 61-1 BCA 2933. 

19. Delivery Dates Were Automatically Extended by Government's Failure To Act Prompt ly on Preproduction Drawings Submitted for 

Approval Termination for Default When Contractor Was Not in Default Should Be 

Transmuted to Termination for Convenience. 

The appellant's two Navy supply contracts called for the delivery of 171 fans on 26 June and 100 fans on 8 July. The contracts contained the Default and Termination for Con venience Clauses of Standard Form 32 (Oct. 

1957 ed.). The start of manufacturing was conditioned upon submission and approval of preproduction drawings. On 26 and 29 May the contractor submitted drawings to the Government. These were rejected as not being sufficiently detailed on 2 June. On 10 June the appellant again submitted a set of drawings. 

On several occasions in June and July the appellant attempted to obtain information from the Government about the acceptability of drawings, but he was unsuccessful. Around 

1 July the Government sent a speed letter promising information. On 27 July the appellant wrote the Government about his unsuccessful efforts to procure information and requested an early reply so that he could proceed with the contract. On 11 August the Government noti fied the appellant that the drawings submitted were unacceptable. On the same day the Government terminated the contract for default for failure to make deliveries as scheduled and to submit acceptable preproduction plans. A timely appeal was taken from the termination. 

Held, appeal sustained. Although the contracts' delivery dates had passed, the appellant Iwas not in default. The Government was obligated to do nothing to hinder appellant's performance. See, e.g., Corbin, Contracts § 1264 (1951). The drawings were timely submitted, and the Government was obligated to act on them within a reasonable time. Not until forty-six days after the delivery date in one contract and thirty-four days afterward in the other did the Government advise the appellant that the drawings were unacceptable. On the same day, without giving the appellant a reasonable time to submit corrected drawings, the Government terminated the contracts. Thus by its own action the Government prevented the appellant from performing its obligations under the contracts. The Government's action was not authorized by any contractual provision.

A more reasonable conclusion is that the delivery time was necessarily extended by the same period that it took the Government to act on the drawings. Since the delivery time as so extended had not expired, the appellant was not in default when the terminations were made. 

See, e.g., The Cowan Co., ASBCA Nos. 2373 and 

2374 (28 Feb. 1955) [digested in DA Pam 71550-1, p. 223, par. 11]. The termination should be deemed to be one for the convenience of the Government.

Remsel Industries, Inc., ASBCA No. 5899, 21 

December 1960, 61-1 BCA 2909. [Note: The instant case was decided before the opinion in Klein v. United States, 285 F. 2d 778 (Ct. Cl. 1961), digested under TERMINA- 

TION, par. 7, was handed down. Under the doctrine of the Klein case, the improper termination for default in the instant case would be a breach of contract by the Government. The contractor could sue for damages and need not accept a convenience settlement.] 

20. If Government Assesses Excess Costs While Appeal From Termination Is Pending, the Issuance of Excess Costs May Be Consid ered Together With the Propriety of the Termi- AGO 9111A 125

DEFAULT-Continued nation Even Though No Separate Appeal From the Assessment Is Filed. (ASBCA) See DISPUTES (par. 32) 21. Court of Claims Rejects Government's Claim for Damages for Contractor's Breach on Grounds That Government Did Not Make Re purchase and Could Not Prove Losses Had Been 

Incurred. (Ct. Cl.) See DAMAGES (par. 2) 22. Comptroller General Declines To Upset Contracting Officer's Decision Not To Terminate 

Contract for Default. Three months after a contract for the supply of 323 ambulances to the Army was awarded through formal advertising, a disappointed bidder protested to the Comptroller General against the acceptance of any of the more than 300 vehicles yet undelivered. The protest alleged that deliveries were behind schedule and that none of the units already delivered met the advertised specifications. The protest also complained that the contractor's facilities were inadequate to produce the vehicles. The Army's report to the Comptroller General indicated that the contracting officer held the delays in deliveries were justified by a shift made by the contractor in the location of his plant and facilities. The report stated the contractor was making deliveries in accordance with a contract modification that changed the production rate to compensate for the earlier slippage. As to the failure to meet specifications, the report advised that problems encountered in connection with the first twenty units had been solved, so that the vehicles being accepted complied with the advertised specifications, as modified by authorized deviations. The deviations were stated by the report to be minor since they had no adverse effect on function, interchangeability, or safety.

Held, protest denied. ASPR 8-602.3 provides that, in determining whether to terminate a contract for default, the contracting officer should consider a variety of factors, such as the specific failure of the contractor, the urgency of the Government's need, and the possibility that the defaulting contractor will be able to make deliveries before a repurchase contractor could. ASPR 8-602.4 provides that the contracting officer may permit the contractor to continue performance of the contract under a revised delivery schedule in lieu of termination for default. Thus the contracting officer has some discretion in determining whether to terminate a contract. In any event, the administrative report indicates there is at present no basis for termination for default. On the basis of the present record, the GAO would not be justified in questioning the contracting officer's action in revising the delivery schedule and permitting continued performance. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-146245, 12 October 1961.
