24. Failure To Provide Preproduction Sample 

Meeting "Or Equal" Requirement Was Ground for Default Termination. The Army formally advertised a contract for 5,340 female and 10,- 480 male couplings. No drawings or specifications were given. The invitation requested H 

Co. couplings "or equal." The contract was awarded to the S Co., which offered its own couplings. The contract contained, besides the provisions of Standard Form 32 (Oct 1957 ed.), the following: 

b. The term 'or equal' means: 

An item that is produced or manufactured by or for other than the manufacturer or user whose symbol appears in the item description, but which item is equal to the specified item(s) in materials and finishes, performance potential, and adaptability for use; and which is interchangeable functionally and dimensionally with the specified item(s); and whose component parts, but only those component parts that are set forth on the schedule page, after the item description, are functionally and dimensionally interchangeable with their counterparts in the specified item(s). This interchangeability of component parts is required because the Government services and carries the parts in stock. 

c. Bidders who propose to deliver an 'or equal,' and who specify and/or identify the item that they propose to deliver by a particular part number or name and/or by drawing and specification, or sample, will be deemed to have offered to deliver the item strictly as set forth in the item description and [the clause quoted above], unless it is manifest that the bidder is offering an item other than the specified item or an 'or equal' thereof, in which case the bid will be 126 AGO 9111A

DEFAULT-Continued disregarded as nonresponsive. Acceptance of such a bid fixes the responsibility on the contractor bidder to insure that the item he has offered and will deliver is, in fact, an 'or equal,' as defined [in the clause quoted above]. Prior to acceptance of a bid the Government will make no evaluation of an item or sample offered as an or equal' to determine if, in fact, it is an 'or equal'; and the Government does not admit or concede, by acceptance of such a bid, that the item is an 'or equal,' or is acceptable to the 

Government. 

After receiving the contract, the S Co. requested and obtained from the Government some drawings of the H Co.'s units. Those drawings showed envelope dimensions and exterior configurations. However, the dimensions of those configurations and the existence of component parts were shown by neither the Government's drawings nor the H Co.'s catalog. 

The contract required submission of a "preproduction sample" within 30 days after receipt of the contract. If the sample were rejected, another was to be submitted within 30 days after notice that the first had been rejected. Failure timely to provide an acceptable sample was stated to be a cause for termination for default. Despite the language about preproduction samples, both parties knew they were dealing with "shelf" items; there would be no production unless an item was out of stock.

The appellant timely furnished a preproduction sample of its own couplings. The sample was rejected as not equal, on the ground that the S Co.'s couplings were not interchangeable with the H Co.'s couplings. The S Co.'s male coupling would fit the S Co.'s female coupling, but the C Co.'s male coupling would not fit the 

H Co.'s female coupling and the H Co.'s male coupling would not fit the S Co.'s female coupling. The Government asked the S Co. for a second sample consisting of either the H Co.'s coupling or of a coupling meeting the Government's interpretation of equality. The S Co. contended that its own coupling was equal. No second sample was submitted, and the contract was terminated for default. A repurchase was made, and excess costs were assessed against the S Co. The firm timely appealed from the termination and the assessment.

Held, appeal denied. Because the S Co. items will not couple with the H Co. items, the Government argues that the former are not interchangeable functionally with the latter, as the contractual definition of "or equal" required.

The S Co. argues that the ability of the male unit to couple with a female unit is not a "function" but a "design dimensioned characteristic."

The firm stresses, and the Government does not dispute, that as a coupled unit (with male and female couplings taken together), the S Co.'s units are functionally and dimensionally inter changeable with the H Co.'s unit. The S Co. 

contends that the contract is not ambiguous as to the meaning of equality, but that if there is any ambiguity, it should be resolved in the firm's favor. The firm's arguments are not persuasive. If the Government had been buying coupler units (with each unit having a male and a female part), the S Co.'s arguments would appear to be sound. However, the Government was buying 5,340 female couplings as one item and 10, 480 male couplings as another item. A person selling female couplings would understand they were being purchased for use with male couplings. A similar proposition holds for the sale of male couplings. The primary purpose of a coupling is to couple.

From the record, the judgment may be drawn that normally one buys S Co. female couplings for use with S Co. male couplings, not with the male couplings of another manufacturer. Normally the buyer and seller of S Co. couplings would have that understanding. This understanding, however, yields to the contractual definition of "or equal," which requires that a unit be functionally interchangeable. The only reasonable interpretation is that an equal male and female coupling would couple with an H Co. female and male coupling, respectively. 

Contrary to the S Co.'s argument, the Board's interpretation would not restrict competition to the H Co.'s product. The record shows that other manufacturers produce couplings that couple with the H Co.'s units.

The S Co.'s failure timely to deliver a sample meeting the "or equal" requirement was a proper ground for the default termination. [The Board also holds that (1) there was no AGO 9111A 127

DEFAULT-Continued excusable cause for the default, and (2) the S Co. is liable for the excess costs.] 

Snap-Tite, Inc., ASBCA Nos. 7106 and 7498, 8 November 1961, 61–2 BCA 3209. [Note: Mr. Spector concurred in the result, with the following explanation: It is not necessary to reach the issue of whether the S Co.'s sample complied with the contract specifications. The firm's failure timely to deliver was within the firm's control and not without fault or negligence by the firm. This was certainly true when no second sample was furnished. The firm, if it wanted to avoid termination, should have furnished a preproduction sample acceptable to the Government, reserving a claim for any additional costs thereby occasioned.]

27. After Delivery Schedule Is "Waived,"

Contracting Officer Must Either Reach Agreement With Contractor on New Schedule or Give Contractor Explicit Notice of a New Schedule Allowing a Reasonable Time for Delivery. The appellant failed to deliver a "first article" by the date his Air Force contract set. The contract's delivery schedule, however, had been "waived." No explicit schedule was ever substituted. The article was not delivered within the first two months after the original due date, so at the end of that period the contracting officer notified the appellant by letter that the Air Force was considering termination of the contract because of the delinquency in delivery of the article. The letter, which apparently was the first indication to the appellant that prompt delivery was important, gave him ten days to submit a statement of any circumstances excusing the failure to perform. The appellant provided a statement listing what he thought were excuses. Two weeks later the Air 

Force terminated the contract, pursuant to the default clause, for failure to submit the "first article."

In an appeal to the ASBCA from the termination, the appellant argued that, after the delivery schedule was "waived," the Air Force was obligated to provide notice of a new delivery schedule that allowed a reasonable time for performance. He relied on 3 Williston, Contracts § 856 (rev. ed.) and Restatement, Contracts § 311 (1932). Citing cases such as Clad International Corp., ASBCA No. 4813 

(13 Oct 1959), 59-2 BCA 2385, the Government argued that by law a new delivery date was established as a reasonble time after the "waiver," so no notice was required. 

Held, appeal sustained. The principle supported by the appellant's citations has been adopted in ASBCA opinions. For example, it is stated in Midwest Engineering Development 

Co., ASBCA Nos. 982, 983 (11 Mar 1953), that: 

In Pierson & Co. v. American Steel Export Co., 

185 N.Y.S., 527, 194 App. Div. 555 it was held: "The rule is well settled that, where time of performance is waived, 'neither party can thereafter rescind the contract on account of such delay without notice to the other, requiring performance within a reasonable time, to be specified in the notice or the contract would be abrogated. 

This Board adopts that rule. . . . 

Once there is a "waiver," the Government should (if there is no supervening factor such as impossibility of performance or abandonment of the contract) do either of the following: (1) reach an agreement with the contractor on a new delivery schedule; (2) give the contractor notice of a new delivery schedule giving a reasonable time for performance after receipt of the notice. What is a reasonable time will depend in part on the contractor's situation at the time of the notice. 

In this case [from facts not detailed in this digest] the contracting officer knew or should have known that the "first article" could not have been delivered in less than five weeks from the time the show cause letter was written. However he gave the appellant only ten days to show cause before a threatened termination and thus in effect gave only ten days to make delivery. Ten days was not a reasonable time in view of the appellant's 128 AGO 9111A

DESCRIPTION OF WORK 

situation. Not even the period between the show cause notice and the termination was a reasonable period for performance. Consequently, the termination for default was premature and must be considered to have been for the convenience of the Government. 

Lumen, Inc., ASBCA No. 6431, 2 November 

1961, 61-2 BCA 3210. 

[Note: The Board's opinion contained two caveats about what it did not hold. First, the opinion was said not to disturb the law on "forbearance," the interval after passage of the delivery date within which the contracting officer may, without waiving the delivery schedule, decide whether to terminate. Second, the opinion declined to reach the issue of the effect of a termination for default a reasonable period after a notice is given making time again of the essence but not setting a specific date or period for performance.]

DISPUTES See also ARMED SERVICES BOARD OF CONTRACT APPEALS 1. Where Decision Is Final Under Disputes Article and Rules of ASBCA, It May Not Be 

Reopened by Government in Later Appeal by 

Contractor Under Same Contract. In December 

1954, the ASBCA sustained three appeals arising under a single contract for the reason that the contractor's alleged default was excusable. 

Atlas Can Corporation, ASBCA Nos. 1957, 1958 

& 2121 (24 Dec 1954). A Government motion for reconsideration was denied on 11 April 1955. When the parties were unable to agree upon a termination for convenience settlement, the contractor filed a new appeal from the contracting officer's unilateral settlement. The 

Government then filed a motion to reopen the question of excusability on the ground that the earlier decision was erroneous and that new evidence had been discovered. The contractor objected.

Held, the motion is denied. The relief requested by the contractor in this appeal is different from that sought in the previous appeals. Yet the Government seeks to reopen a question of fact which the Board has already decided, i.e., that the default was excusable. According to the Disputes article in the contract, ASPR 7-103.12, this decision was final unless determined by a court of competent jurisdiction to be fradulent, arbitrary, capricious, or so grossly erroneous as necessarily to imply bad faith. No authority to reopen a final decision is contained in the contract. The Rules of the 

ASBCA grant an aggrieved party 30 days in which to file a motion for reconsideration. [Rule 

29. See ASPR A12 (27 Feb 1959)]. While this rule postpones finality until a motion for reconsideration is either decided by the Board or not filed within 30 days, it does not authorize a subsequent reopening of the controversy. The 

Government's motion, therefore, improperly seeks to reopen a final determination by the Board of a question of fact. AGO 9111A 129

DISPUTES-Continued Atlas Can Corporation, ASBCA No. 3381, 25 September 1959, 59-2 BCA 2361. 

2. ASBCA Has Jurisdiction To Determine Liability of Bailee for Pilferage of Government- Owned Goods. In November 1952, the S.S. Co lumbia Trader was hired by the Government to transport consumable goods from the United 

States to Germany. The Government was to load and unload the vessel and to prepare a manifest of the goods shipped. While the owner was not responsible for the tally of goods loaded or unloaded, the time charter party provided a measure of value in the event of loss or damage during shipment and incorporated, for the owner's benefit, specific exemptions from lia bility contained in the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act. The contract also contained a Disputes 

Clause, see ASPR 7-103.12.

After the vessel was unloaded in Germany, the Government alleged that $214.77 worth of goods had been pilfered and determined that the owner, as bailee, was liable under the contract. The owner appealed and argued that the shipping manifest and tally sheets of the Government failed to state a prima facie claim. 

Since the charter party did not provide for pilferage claims, the Board requested briefs on the question of jurisdiction.

Held, the appeal is sustained. The owner is a bailee of Government property under a contract which sets forth a measure of valuation in the event of loss or damage to shipped goods and provides specific defenses to liability. The contract, therefore, by necessary implication, places liability on the owner for any loss or damage from pilferage and confers jurisdiction upon the Board to hear the dispute. 

To state a prima facie claim, the Government must show that the pilfered goods were loaded aboard the vessel in good condition and that the loss occurred while they were bailed to the owner. If this burden is sustained, the owner, to escape liability, must prove that the loss was within one of the exemptions of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act. The Government, how ever, has failed to state a prima facie claim. 

The shipping manifest does not show by whom it was prepared and some of the goods which the Government claims were pilfered do not appear on the manfest. Further, the claim is based on reports received from inland depots, far removed from the unloading point. The pilferage, therefore, could have occurred while the goods were bailed to another carrier. Since the Government assumed full responsibility for loading and unloading the goods and for compiling a tally, it cannot complain if the method employed limited the available evidence when a dispute arose.

West Coast Steamship Co., ASBCA No. 4379, 

18 September 1959, 59-2 BCA 2366. [Note: In dissent, Member Culp argued that since the contract did not mention pilferage claims, a dispute over liability for pilferage was not a question of fact within the meaning of the 

Disputes clause. Further, the contract as a whole did not authorize an administrative appeal from a determination of any liability claim. 

Consequently, unless a collateral directive by the Secretary enlarging the Board's jurisdiction can be found, the mere fact that a bailment of Government property is involved does not support jurisdiction. While such a collateral directive previously existed, see Secretarial Memorandum of 4 July 1944, discussed in Columbia

Constructors, Inc., WD BCA No. 579 (7 Jul 

1944), 2 CCF 942, its repeal in December 1958 deprived the Board of jurisdiction to hear this appeal.] 

3. ASBCA Has No Jurisdiction Where Written Contract Containing Disputes Clause Not 

Executed. In June 1952, the contractor, pursuant to a combined letter of intent and notice to proceed, performed architect-engineering serv ices for Army Ordnance in France. A definitive contract containing a Disputes clause was to be executed at a later date. The Disputes clause authorized an appeal to the Board of Contract 

Appeals, Headquarters, U.S. Army, Europe 

(USAREUR) and from that decision, if the amount claimed was more than $50,000, to the 

ASBCA. The contracting officer, however, determined that the contractor's work was defective. Accordingly, he withdrew the proposed definitive contract and denied a claim by the contractor in the amount of $87,100. The contractor filed a direct appeal with both the

ASBCA and the USAREUR Board. The form er was dismissed on the ground that the Disputes clause which was a part of the proposed 130 AGO 9111A

DISPUTES-Continued contract did not authorize an original appeal to the ASBCA. The latter was dismissed for the reason that there was neither an executed contract containing a Disputes clause nor a directive from the Commander-in-Chief, USAREUR, conferring jurisdiction on the 

USAREUR Board. The contractor appealed this decision to the ASBCA and the Government filed a motion to dismiss. 

Held, the motion is granted. Regardless of whether the contractor's performance in reliance upon the letter of intent supports a claim under the proposed contract, it is clear that a written contract containing a Disputes clause was not executed. Further, there is no evidence that the appeal was authorized by either a directive of the Commander-in-Chief, USAREUR, or other agreement between the parties. This 

Board, therefore, has no jurisdiction to hear the appeal. F & C Realty Co., ASBCA No. 3224 

(29 Nov 1957), 57–2 BCA 1544; Christian J.

Engineer Board resolved one issue in favor of the contractor and the other in favor of the 

Government. Under the contract Disputes clause, these decisions were final unless vacated by an appeal, within 30 days, to the ASBCA.

The contractor appealed to the ASBCA. 

When the Government failed to appeal, the contractor argued that the ASBCA had jurisdiction to hear only that portion of the Engineer Board decision from which the contractor appealed. The ASBCA took jurisdiction of the entire appeal on the theory that the dispute involved two related issues arising out of a single set of facts. Morrison-Knudsen Com pany, Inc., and Ford J. 5318 (27 Jul 1959), 59-2 BCA 2286, DA Pam 

715-50-2, p. 208, par. 46. This Board is authorized to hear only appeals on disputed questions which have been decided by contracting officers or other authorities pursuant to contract provisions. There is no existing dispute here since the contractor has withdrawn its appeal and the Government has offered no objection. The possibility that a dispute may arise in the future is immaterial, Morrison-Knudsen Company, Inc., and Ford

J. Twaits Company, ASBCA No. 5318, 9 No vember 1959, 59-2 BCA 2402.

AGO 9111A 131

DISPUTES-Continued Arising Under Government Contracts. The Special Investigations Subcommittee of the House Armed Services Committee inquired if the Administrative Procedures Act of 1946, 60 

Stat. 238, 5 U.S.C. 1001, was applicable to the adjudication of disputes arising under Government contracts.

Opinion: The Administrative Procedures Act is only applicable in cases where adjudication is "required by statute to be determined on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing." The adjudication of disputes by the contracting officer or the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals, however, is required by the contract rather than by a statute. [See ASPR 

7-103.12 (18 Sep 1958).] Consequently, the

Administrative Procedures Act is not for application. See Clifton Engineering Company, BCA Nos. 1201 and 1202, 28 July 1947; 4

Davis, Administrative Law 28.14 (1958); Sen ate Doc. No. 248, 79th Cong., 2d Sess. 359 (1946). See Also, Volentine & Littleton v. 

United States, 136 Ct. Cl. 638, 645-651 (1956) (Act applies only to agencies who are not parties to dispute involved).

11. Where Contractor Alleges That Admin istrative Decision Is Erroneous and Not Supported by Substantial Evidence, District Court 

Review Under Wunderlich Act Limited to Record of Proceedings. (D. Ore.) See JUDICIAL & ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW (par. 4) 12. Contractor Not Required To Appeal Within 30 Days From Government Change Order Unless Identified by Written Notice or Surrounding Circumstances as Final, Appealable Decision Under the Disputes Clause. In 

1956, the contractor was awarded two contracts by the Philadelphia Quartermaster Depot for the supply of khaki shorts.

Both contained the standard Disputes Clause, ASPR 7-103.12 

(15 Mar 1960). After award, the Government eliminated a specification requirement and, on 

21 March 1957, notified the contractor that $1,979, for savings realized was being charged to its account. On 6 May 1957, the contracting officer unilaterally reduced the contract price to reflect the savings. A minor correction in price was made by another change order dated 15 August 1957. Both actions were taken under the Changes clause, ASPR 7-103.2 (17 Mar 

1958). The contractor, by a letter dated 26

November 1958, objected to the amount claimed and requested a reconsideration. On 7 May 

1959, after an exchange of correspondence, the contracting officer refused to consider the claim since it was submitted more than 30 days after the contractor received notice of the price adjustment. The contractor appealed and the 

Government filed a motion to dismiss. 

Held, the motion is denied. The Government argues that the contractor's failure to submit its claim within 30 days after receiving notice of the price change requires a dismissal of this appeal. This would be true if a claim by the contractor for a price increase due to a change order were involved. But this appeal involves a dispute over the amount of a price reduction sought by the Government. Even though the dispute arose because of a change order, the time limitations of the Disputes Clause rather than the Changes Clause govern this appeal.

Specialty Assembling & Packing Co., ASBCA No. 4523 et seq. (29 Sep 1959), 59-2 BCA 2370; A. DuBois & Son, Inc. ASBCA No. 4063 

(30 Jul 1958), 58-2 BCA 1879. 

The issue for decision is whether the contracting officer ever made a final determination of a disputed question of fact from which the contractor, under the Disputes Clause, was required to appeal within 30 days. If the letter of 21 March 1957 or either of the two price reductions amount to a final determination by the contracting officer, the appeal must be denied. In trying to reach a mutual agreement with the contractor on disputed issues of fact, a contracting officer makes many decisions which are not intended to be final. Consequently, a final decision must be clearly identified to avoid confusion and premature appeals. In

Army contracts, this identification is achieved by a written notice, sent by registered or certified mail to the contractor, APP 7-103.12, containing a concluding paragraph which in- 132 AGO 9111A

DISPUTES-Continued forms the contractor that the decision is final and that a right to appeal exists. APP 7103.12b (2) (b). In neither the letter of 21 March nor the two price reductions were these identifications made. Further, neither their contents nor the surrounding circumstances indicated an intention to make a final, appealable decision. The customary procedure at the Philadelphia Quartermaster Depot is to clearly identify final decisions. The omission in this case and the contracting officer's correction of the first price reduction support the conclusion that a final decision was not intended, Standard Coil 

Products Co., Inc., ASBCA No. 5274 (18 May 

1959), 59-1 BCA 2217; J. D. Barter Construc tion Co., ASBCA No. 2774 (13 Feb 1956), even though an appeal may be taken from a written change order modifying a contract. Parkside

Clothes, Inc., ASBCA No. 1860 (13 Aug 1954). 

The contracting officer's decision of 7 May 1959, therefore, was the first final decision within the meaning of the Disputes Clause and the contractor's appeal from that decision was timely. 

Wood of Texas Industries, ASBCA No. 5697, 23 December 1959, 59-2 BCA 2464. 

13. Official Designated by Contract or Secretarial Directive Must Personally Decide Disputed Questions of Fact. Between 1946 and 

1953 the contractor performed a series of costplus-fixed-fee contracts for the Navy. A large percentage of these contracts authorized the contracting officer to determine all disputed questions of fact. The remaining contracts authorized the Chief, Bureau of Supplies and

Accounts (Bu SANDA) to decide all disputes involving the allowability of costs. The decisions under all contracts were final unless appealed to the Secretary of the Navy or his authorized representative within 30 days. In addition to the contract disputes clauses, two 

1945 Navy Directives provided noncontractual disputes procedures. The first, a Secretarial 

Directive, required that all cost disputes arising under cost-reimbursement contracts be re ferred to the Chief, Bu SANDA for a deter mination of allowability. "Decisions with respect to such disputes shall be final and conclusive, subject to appeal by the contractor within thirty days to the Secretary of the Navy or his duly authorized representative." The second directive, issued by Bu SANDA, required that all cost disputes be referred by the contracting officer to a Bureau Cost Inspector for determination. If the cost was disallowed, the Inspector was directed to formalize the decision by "written communications to the contractors setting forth the item, period, amount, and reason for disallowance." The

Directive further provided: 

Each disallowance heretofore made in writing by a Cost Inspector is hereby administratively approved as the decision of the Chief of the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts, unless the contractor files an appeal and review brief with the 

Cost Inspector within 60 days from the date of receipt of this directive by the contractor. 

While the Bureau Directive authorized the Chief, Bu SANDA and the Cost Inspector to resolve cost disputes, they were not designated as contracting officers. 

During contract performance, all overhead cost disputes were submitted by the contracting officer to the Cost Inspector for determination. In many cases the Inspector neither finally resolved the dispute nor complied with the formal notice requirements of the Bureau directive. In fact, the Inspector's conduct evidenced a continued and consistent indifference to the question of finality. In March 

1957, more than 90 days after the last negotiations between the contractor and the Inspector, the Navy Controller [successor in interest to the Chief, Bu SANDA] denied the con tractor's appeal from the Inspector's purported decisions disallowing disputed costs. The basis of this decision was the 1945 Bureau Directive. 

In a timely appeal to the ASBCA, the contractor argued that the Inspector had never made a final decision under the directive and that even so, the decision was made by an official not empowered to do so by the contract. 

The Government, in a special defense, argued that both the Contractor's contractual and noncontractual rights to appeal were lost by failing to appeal from the Cost Inspector's decisions. 

Held, the Government's defense is denied.

The Government has failed to prove that the Cost Inspector ever made a final determination or complied with the noncontractual directives in considering cost disputes which were AGO 9111A 133

DISPUTES-Continued submitted for decision. But even if proper decisions were made, it concluded that the contractor has neither lost its contractual nor noncontractual appeal rights. In a minor percentage of the contracts involved, the contractor was contractually obligated to appeal from the determination of all cost disputes by the 

Chief, Bu SANDA. The Bureau Directive, however, authorized a Cost Inspector to make these determinations in the Chief's name. This determination was to be final unless appealed to the Chief within 60 days and from then to the Secretary within 30 days. A final decision rendered under a contract disputes clause must be personally made by the official designated by the contract. John McShain v. United 

States, 65 F. Supp. 589 (Ct. Cl. 1946); Climatic 

Rainwear Co., Inc. v. United States, 88 F.

Supp. 415 (Ct. Cl. 1950). This requirement is not satisfied when the purported decision is actually made by another official in the name of the designated official. Since the contractor was not contractually bound by the Bureau directive and since the purported decisions were made by a Cost Inspector rather than the 

Chief, Bu SANDA, the contractor had no contractual obligation to appeal until the decision of March 1957 was made.

In the major number of contracts, all disputes including those involving cost allowability were to be decided by the contracting officer.

Clearly, the contracting officer never resolved any of these disputes and the contractor had no contractual obligation to appeal. Yet while the contractor was not contractually bound by the Navy Directives, they afforded noncontractual remedies to the contractor if certain conditions were met. Here the contractor argues that the decision of March 1957 by the successor to the Chief, Bu SANDA was a final decision within the meaning of the Secretarial Directive which entitled it to a noncontractual appeal. The Government argues that the decisions from which an appeal should have been taken were those of the Cost Inspector, since they automatically became the decisions of the 

Chief. But the Secretarial Directive is a substantial paraphrase of the Bureau Directive in that it requires a decision by the Chief, Bu 

SANDA. Consequently, a decision by the Cost 

Inspector rather than the Chief would not require an appeal to preserve the noncontractual remedies. Whether the contractor seeks to appeal under the contract disputes clause or the noncontractual Secretarial Directive, the first decision from which an appeal was required was made in March 1957. The decisions of the Cost Inspector, if proper decisions at all, were made by an official other than that named in the contract or the Directive.

The Martin Company, ASBCA No. 4381, 29 

January 1960, 60-1 BCA 2509. 

14. Claim for Payment for Work Done Pre maturely Asserted in Appeal From a Termination for Default. The Contractor agreed to paint certain water tanks and towers at the 

Naval Supply Depot in Bayonne, New Jersey, by 26 November 1958. In addition to a stand ard Default Clause, ASPR 8-707, the contract contained a Gratuities Clause which provided in part: (a) The Government may, by written notice to the Contractor, terminate the right of the Contractor to proceed under this contract if it is found, after notice and hearing, by the Secretary or his duly authorized representative, that gratuities (in the form of entertainment, gifts, or otherwise) were offered or given by the Contractor, or any agent or representative of the Contractor, to any officer or employee of the Government with a view toward securing a contract or securing favorable treatment with respect to the awarding or amending, or the making of any determinations with respect to the performing, of such contract; 

Provided, that the existence of the facts upon which the Secretary or his duly authorized representative makes such findings shall be in issue and may be reviewed in any competent court. 

On 5 November 1958 the contractor's president was arrested for attempting to bribe an inspector at the Depot to overlook unsatisfactory work. The next day the Depot Commander, as a security measure, barred the president and his employees from the work site. On 28 November 1958, the contract was terminated for the contractor's failure to prosecute the work to completion within the time specified. The termination remedy in the Gratuities Clause, however, was not utilized. The contractor, whose president was indicted under 18 U.S.C. 

201 for the attempted bribe, appealed the termination and argued that its default was 134 AGO 9111A

DISPUTES-Continued excused because the Government prevented performance without just cause. Appeal proceedings were suspended until the contractor's president, after a plea of not guilty, was convicted in a Federal district court of attempted bribery. At this point the Government filed a motion for summary judgment on the theory that the criminal conviction was conclusive on the factual questions of whether the default was excusable and whether the Gratuities had been violated. The contractor, in a reply memorandum, argued that a criminal conviction was not conclusive evidence in a civil proceeding but did not assert that a factual issue of excusability still existed. Rather, the principal argument seemed to be that the work performed prior to the termination was satisfactory and that the contractor was entitled to partial payments. The case was submitted for decision on the record.

Held, both the contractor's appeal and the Government's motion for summary judgment are denied. Before its president was actually convicted of attempted bribery, the contractor, in an appeal from the termination, argued that the default was excusable. In view of the subsequent conviction, if excusability were the only issue involved it might be concluded that the record does not evidence a reasonable prospect that a rehearing of those facts would result in a decision contrary to that sought by the summary judgment. See P. L. S. Coat & Suit Co. 

v. United States, 180 F. Supp. 400 (Ct. Cl. 

1960), digested under JUDICIAL and ADMIN- ISTRATIVE REVIEW, par. 2. This would fol low even though the authorities disagree as to whether a criminal judgment is conclusive evidence in a civil proceeding. Further, while the 

Government did not rely upon the Gratuities 

Clause for termination authority, it is difficult to see how the contractor could have avoided the conclusive effect of the criminal judgment as to the cause of default in a plenary appeal proceeding under the Disputes Clause. 

The contractor's response to the Govern ment's motion for summary judgment, however, does not allude to the existence of a factual dispute over the cause of the default. The basic argument appears to be that the contractor is entitled to payment for work performed prior to the termination. It is concluded, therefore, that payment rather than excusability is the real issue in this appeal. Since this issue has not been submitted to the contracting officer for determination the appeal is premature and should be dismissed.

General Ship Contracting Corp., ASBCA No. 

5419, 2 February 1960, 60-1 BCA 2557. [Note: In view of the procedural requirements in the Gratuities Clause, i.e., notice and hearing by the Secretary or his representative before the contractor is defaulted for offering gratuities, note the Board's dictum that if the Government had used that remedy the criminal conviction might be conclusive as to the cause of default in appeals under the Dispute Clause.] 15. ASBCA Has Jurisdiction To Determine if Supplemental Agreement Subsequent to Downward Price Redetermination Authorized Contracting Agency To Pay Federal Income Tax Credit Due the Contractor Under IRC Section 1481. Between September 1953 and 

May 1954, the contractor entered into three fixed-price-with-redetermination type contracts with the Army to design and develop tank transmissions. The target price for all work was $1,026,080. Pursuant to APP 3-403.50a (3) (d), the contracting officer determined that a downward price revision would be required when the contracts were completed. Accordingly, he withheld payments due the contractor to cover the estimated downward revision and subsequently entered into modifications with the contractor which adjusted the contract prices pending final redetermination. The contractor, however, had paid income tax on contract payments received prior to the modifications and notified the contracting officer that it was entitled to a tax credit under section 1481, Internal Revenue Code of 1954. [Section 1481, while using the word renegotiation, has been interpreted to include a price redetermination. 

See Int. Rev. Bull. 1953-1, 479.] The Army 

Procurement Procedure had anticipated this situation and directed the contracting officer to "execute a contract supplement to reduce the contract price, prior to the date on which the contractor files his completed income tax return." APP 3-403.50c. APP 3-403.50a (3) (g) further provided: 

(g) Section 1481 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 . . . provides for certain tax credits in connection with contract price refunds

The con- 

tract clauses prescribed in Section VII, APP do not alter the effect of those statutory provisions. 

Contracts shall be administered in such manner as to allow this statutory tax credit whenever applicable under the circumstances. 

The contractor was informed by the contracting officer that tax credits would be "taken care of" at the final contract price review. The final tax credit had not been determined at that time, but the contractor was led to believe that it would be paid the redetermined price for work performed plus the amount of tax credit allowed. Subsequently, each of the contracts was modified to make interim provision for the undetermined tax credits. The modifications set forth the redetermined contract prices, the total overpayments made to the contractor and directed the contractor to secure a determination of the tax credit due. The modifications further provided:

At the time of submission of such determination the contract shall be further amended to set forth the amounts of said tax credits and to provide for the necessary adjustments in the contract price Pending determination of the foregoing tax credits, the total contract price will be neither increased nor decreased at this time. 

The Michigan District Director of Internal 

Revenue determined that the total tax credit to which the contractor was entitled was $49,- 655. The contractor then requested payment of the difference between the tax credit due and the total sum of overpayments received from the Army, some $39,526. The contracting officer determined that the contractor could offset the overpayments from the tax credit but that the contract did not authorize payment of the difference. Further, the Internal Revenue Serv ice refused to pay the difference for the reason 136 AGO 9111A

DISPUTES-Continued that it "should be paid to the contractor by the Army in settlement of the account." The contractor appealed, whereupon the ASBCA issued an order to show cause why the appeals should not be dismissed. Upon the concurrence of both parties, however, the appeals were heard on the merits along with the order to show cause. 

Held, the order to show cause is dismissed and the appeal is sustained. The facts of this appeal show a present and continuing failure of the contracting officer and the contractor to agree upon the amounts payable under the contract terms and the effect of the interim agreement following the final price determination.

This Board has jurisdiction to hear appeals by contractors from decisions on disputed questions of fact by contracting officers and may decide all questions of law necessary for the com plete adjudication of the issue presented. The decision must be in accordance with applicable contract provisions and in accordance with the pertinent law. The issues framed between the contracting officer's findings and the contractor's understanding are typical of those regularly brought before this Board for decision. 

See, e.g., Wm. E. Goetz & Sons, ASBCA No. 

4837 (22 Jan. 1959), 59-1 BCA 2068; Birn baum, Questions of Law & Fact and the Jurisdiction of the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals, 19 Fed. B.J. 120 (1959). The 

Board, therefore, has jurisdiction and the order to show cause is dismissed.

On the merits, the interim agreements appear to be meaningless and surplusage unless the contractor's interpretation of their meaning is adopted. The Government's contention that they authorized only an offset of tax credits to the extent of overpayments is inconsistent with the interim nature of the modification and the references to "full tax credit" and "further amendments." From the logic of the Government's argument, if the contractor had been overpaid the full amount of tax credit it would appear that no objection would be raised to a full offset of that credit. It is difficult to believe that the parties were agreeing to settle their final accounts on the basis of anything as imprecise as the estimated amounts being withheld in anticipation of a probable price reduction. 

This decision does not interpret the effect of 

Section 1481. The interim agreements, while motivated by section 1481, did not depend upon nor were they prohibited by that section. It is concluded, therefore, that the contract and its supplemental agreements intended to reimburse the contractor for tax credits through the contracting agency rather than the Internal Reve nue Service. 

General Motors Corporation, Allison Divi sion, ASBCA Nos. 5206, 5207 & 5208, 25 April 1960, 60-1 BCA 2614. 

[Note: The Board observed that the real diffi culty appeared to be the nonavailability of Army funds to pay the remaining tax credit. 

The contractor argued that this fact plus the unwillingness of the Internal Revenue Service to pay the refund placed it in a "box." While noting that the problem should be resolved without further delay, the Board held that it had no jurisdiction to consider the availability of Army funds and the propriety of expending particular funds for particular purposes.

19. ASBCA Reviews Propriety of Default Termination of DD Form 1155 Purchase Order Which Did Not Contain Default Clause. In 

January 1959, the Navy, in a negotiated procurement, requested the contractor to quote prices on Scotchlite decals and to submit a proposed delivery schedule. The contractor responded by letter: "We are happy to quote on the basis of three or four weeks delivery, samples in approximately ten days, on approximately 3,000... Scotchlite reflective decals at $0.28 each, net and prepaid." On 23 January 

1959, the contracting officer issued a purchase order on DD Form 1155 which requested the contractor to "furnish" 3,000 decals at $0.28 per unit, "including delivery as indicated." The order requested samples and included several general provisions, including a Disputes clause. 

A Default clause, however, was not included. 

Despite efforts by the contracting officer to expedite performance, the contractor failed to deliver the promised samples within ten days. 

After extended correspondence the Navy, on 

26 February 1959, cancelled the purchase order and notified the contractor by telegraph. The AGO 9111A 137

DISPUTES-Continued contractor appealed the termination and asserted a claim for $761.60 incurred in endeavoring to perform. In two affirmative defenses, the Government urged that the purchase order "was a unilateral offer which never ripened into a contract" and that since DD Form 1155 did not contain a Default clause the contractor's claim is for breach of contract damages and beyond the jurisdiction of the Board. 

Held, the appeal is denied. A series of negotiations between parties does not "ripen into a contract" until the parties close their negotiation and express assent to all terms of the transaction together. At that time the terms of the contract are determined by an examination of the written correspondence. 1. Corbin, Contracts 

31. Here, in response to a Navy request, the contractor quoted prices and indicated delivery dates. Thereafter, the contracting officer issued a purchase order which was consistent in all significant respects with the quotation and in fact incorporated that quotation by reference. 

Between the date of the purchase order and this appeal both parties conducted themselves as if they understood that a contract existed. 

Therefore, it is concluded that a valid contract existed. 99 The next question is whether the use of DD Form 1155, which did not contain a Default clause, precludes this Board from entertaining an appeal by the contractor from the Government's cancellation. ASPR 16-303.2(c) suggests that DD Form 1155s, which contains a Default clause, should be used when the parties intend to "consummate a binding contract . . . before the contractor undertakes performance.' 

Further, ASPR 8-000 (b), in considering the inclusion of Default clauses, states: "Contracts which do not contain the applicable clauses may, where it is in the best interest of the Government, be amended by agreement prior to or after the termination of the contract, to include or substitute such a clause." Since the contractor failed to deliver the promised samples within 10 days and in view of the standard Default clauses, including that set out in DD Form 1155s, it is concluded that the contracting officer "would have" the right to terminate the whole purchase order without prior notice due to the contractor's default. Finally, from the record before us there is no evidence that the failure to perform was beyond the contractor's control or not due to its fault or negligence. 

Universal Transistor Products Corp., ASBCA 

No. 5317 (18 May 1959).

Southwestern Stamp Works, ASBCA No. 

5656, 17 May 1960, 60-1, BCA 2653. 

[Note: The contractor's response to the Navy request for price quotes was by letter rather than on Standard Form 18. This form, which supersedes DD Form 747, is prescribed for use by potential suppliers in providing price and delivery information to the Government in negotiated-fixed-price contracts. See ASPR 16201.2 (1 Jul 1960). Price quotes on SF 18, however, are for information only and do not constitute an offer which the Government may accept. JAGT 1960/5827, 10 February 1960, digested under BIDS AND AWARDS, par. 8. 

Thus, the Navy's issuance of DD Form 1155 in response to the contractor's letter undoubtedly created a binding contract since it requested the contractor to furnish the stipulated number of decals at the quoted price in accordance with the suggested delivery schedule. On the other hand, if the contractor had used SF 18, the purchase order, whether issued on DD Form 1155 or 1155s, would have been an offer rather than an acceptance. Further, the Judge Advocate

General has advised that a DD Form 1155 purchase order issued in response to information provided on SF 18 requests exact performance by the contractor rather than a promise to perform, i.e., a unilateral contract. JAGT 1960/ 

6146, 14 April 1960, digested under TYPES OF CONTRACTS (PURCHASE ORDER), par. 2. 

The importance, therefore, of ascertaining whether or not SF 18 was used is clear. Where a letter rather than the form is used, a DD Form 1155 purchase order may constitute an acceptance and create a contract which can be terminated or cancelled in the event of a performance failure. Where SF 18 is used, a DD

Form 1155 purchase order is merely an offer looking forward to a unilateral contract. Thus, if the contractor fails to perform the exact act requested, no contract exists which can be terminated.

If the Navy desired to solicit an offer from the contractor, DD Form 746 should have been 138 AGO 9111A

DISPUTES-Continued used. See ASPR 16-203 (1 Jul 1960). See also,

ASPR 16-303 (c) (1 Jul 1960). The acceptance of this offer on DD Form 1155s would have insured a binding contract prior to performance which contained a Default clause. Conversely, if the Navy desired to make an offer on the basis of information supplied by the contractor, SF 18 and DD Forms 1155 or 1155s should have been used. The result of the improper use of forms in this case was a binding contract prior to performance which did not contain a Default clause. This was recognized by the contracting officer who labelled his action a "cancellation" and made no effort to assess excess costs. Cf. Industrial Precision Products

Co., ASBCA No. 3171 (30 Mar 1956). Yet the 

ASBCA took jurisdiction of the contractor's appeal and evaluated the termination propriety under the Default clause. While the basis of this jurisdiction is not entirely clear, the decision is impressed with a recognition that the contract could be amended by agreement to include the missing Default clause. ASPR 8-000 (b) (1 Jul 1960). In view of this possibility, the Board apparently reasoned that a useful purpose would be served by advising the parties what the decision would be if the contract were amended. The only other jurisdictional explanation is that the Board unilaterally inserted the Default clause in "the best interest of the Government" even though the parties had not so agreed. But regardless of the merits of these alternate possibilities, the decision should serve the practical purpose of resolving the contract dispute.]

22. Contractor Not Entitled to Remedy From ASBCA for Increased Costs of Unchanged Work Caused Solely by Government Delay in Issuing Change Order. The Government suspended work on a Navy construction project pending the pricing of a change order. The contractor resumed work when the Government rescinded the change order and granted authority to proceed. The contractor then sought an equitable adjustment under the contract's Changes 

Clause (cl. 3, SF 23A, Mar. 1953 ed.) for standby costs and the increase in material and labor costs caused by delay of contract completion. 

The contracting officer ruled that such increased costs of unchanged work were not compensable under the Changes Clause or any other contract provision. (The contract did not con tain a Suspension of Work Clause [APP 

7-1501].) Accordingly, he denied the claim because it sought damages for breach of contract. 

On this same ground, the Government moved that the contractor's appeal to the ASBCA should be dismissed for want of jurisdiction. 

Held, appeal denied in part and dismissed in part. The contractor failed to distinguish Laburnum Constr. Corp., ASBCA No. 5525 (10 

Aug 1959), 59-2 BCA 2309, and Blount Bros. 

Constr. Co., ASBCA No. 5842 (29 Apr 1960), 60-1 BCA 2634. Those cases held that the 

Changes Clause allows the Government to delay performance a reasonable time while issuing change orders, and that if the Government abuses its right, claims for the extra cost of unchanged work seek damages for breach of contract. Such claims, those cases held, are beyond the Board's jurisdiction unless specifically made compensable by a contract provision.

The contractor here can rely on no clause other than that for changes. Therefore, to the extent the Government reasonably exercised its right under the Changes Clause, the appeal is denied. To the extent the Government acted unreasonably, the appeal is dismissed for want of jurisdiction. 

Allen M. Campbell Co., ASBCA No. 6085, 23 

September 1960, 60-2 BCA 2804. [Note: Another recent case reaching the same result, on the authority of the Laburnum decision, was Roscoe Engineering Corporation and Charles Rose, ASBCA No. 6193 (29 Jul 1960), 60-2 BCA 2721.] 

23.

Board Has Discretion on Motion for Re consideration To Admit Evidence Considered at Original Hearing. The Government submitted affidavits to support its timely motion for reconsideration of a decision by the ASBCA. The contractor objected to reception of the affidavits on the ground they contained only information considered at the original hearing. 

Held, the affidavits will be received. Though the affidavits merely confirm evidence received before, the Board has no rule limiting evidence on reconsideration to that discovered after the original hearing. The Board has in individual cases refused evidence not shown to be unavailable at the earlier proceeding, but the reception of evidence is within the Board's discretion. 

After disclosure of what it will be, evidence considered at the original hearing may be received if it is thought essential for a proper reconsideration of the original decision. 

G. M. Co. Mfg., Inc., ASBCA No. 5345, 21 

September 1960, 60-2 BCA 2759.

June 1952, was dismissed in 1958 on the ground that the Government had procured the adjustment agreement by fraud. Apparently, the suspended ASBCA appeal was never decided.

July 1959, the contracting officer unilaterally determined a downward price adjustment for the entire contract period. Held, "[I]n view of the confusion and delay which has occurred in the carrying out of the administrative steps prescribed in the contract, the plaintiff should, at its option, be permitted to get its rights and those of the Government determined in the instant suit, without further resort to the administrative procedure stipulated in the contract."

In paying the plaintiff in

The contracting officer later discovered an error in computing the deduction, and on 3 May 1955 he demanded $76.71 from the plaintiff. In reply, the plaintiff on 10 June 1955 denied using extra Government property and requested payment of the amount deducted. By a letter on 23 June 1955 the contracting officer affirmed that the deduction was proper and repeated the demand for $76.71. 

The letter neither stated that it was a final decision nor reminded the plaintiff of his right to appeal under the standard Disputes Clause in the contract. (ASPR 7-103.12). No further action was taken by either party until December 1957, when the plaintiff requested a determination of his rights. The contracting officer AGO 9111A 141

DISPUTES-Continued replied that the 23 June 1955 decision had become final when no timely appeal was filed. An appeal to the ASBCA from the contracting officer's letter of December 1957 was dismissed on the ground that the ruling of 23 June 1955 had been a final decision which was not timely ap pealed. Bostwick-Batterson Co., ASBCA No. 

4787 (22 May 1958), 58-2 BCA 1837. The plaintiff then sued in the Court of Claims to recover the $683.27 deduction. The Government's only defense was that the plaintiff had failed to appeal the 23 June 1955 decision.

Held, the plaintiff may recover. An Army regulation (now APP 7-103.12b (2) (b)), promulgated 9 September 1954, requires a contracting officer to furnish the contractor with findings of fact and to include in his decision. a paragraph advising the contractor of his right to appeal. The letter of 23 June 1955 did not comply with this regulation and, therefore, cannot be treated as a final decision. Poloron 

Productions, Inc. v. United States, 126 Ct. Cl. 

816, 116 F. Supp. 588 (1953) was decided before the Army regulation referred to was promulgated.

Bostwick-Batterson Co. v. United States, 283 

F.2d 956 (Ct. Cl. 1960). 

[Note: The rule in the instant decision ap pears to apply now to all three services, in view of the 3 October 1960 revision to ASPR. 

(ASPR 1-314). That revision requires every final decision of a contracting officer to state that it is final and to advise the contractor of his right to appeal. The instant decision should be compared with a recent ASBCA opinion, Wood of Texas Industries, ASBCA No. 5697 

(23 Dec 1959), 59-2 BCA 2464, digested under

DISPUTES, par. 12. In holding several de terminations were not final, the Board relied in part on the failure to comply with APP 7103.12b (2) (b). However, the Board indicated that the circumstances surrounding a decision could make it final even though it did not comply with the regulation. 

28. An Appeal Cannot Be Denied on the Merits Without a Hearing if the Contractor's Complaint Alleges Grounds Upon Which Relief May Be Granted-Final Payment and Accord and Satisfaction Cannot Be Raised in a Motion 

To Dismiss. The contractor submitted a claim for an equitable adjustment under the Changes 

Clause of his contract. The contracting offi cer decided that the claim was barred by a supplemental agreement and that the contract was closed. Appealing this decision to the 

ASBCA, the contractor filed a complaint alleging that he was entitled to an equitable adjustment, that the supplemental agreement did not bar his claim, and that there had been no final payment under the contract. The Government filed a Motion To Dismiss or Deny, contending that the appellant's claim was barred by final payment and by an accord and satis faction. The Government asked the ASBCA 

to reject the appellant's allegations solely on the basis of documents filed as exhibits pursuant to Rule 6 of the Board.

Held, the Government's motion is denied. The 

Board's rules do not provide for a motion to deny an appeal on the merits without a hearing. Permitting such a motion would violate the rights the Disputes Clause gives the con tractor to have a hearing and to present evidence. The only Board rule permitting dismissal of appeals, Rule 11, applies only when an appellant would not be entitled to relief even if he proved all the allegations in his complaint. 

Here the appellant's complaint states a case upon which the Board could grant relief. 

The grounds on which the Government relies, final payment and accord and satisfaction, are affirmative defenses and cannot be raised in a motion to dismiss. Robert L. Guyler, ASBCA

No. 4822 (3 Nov 1958), 58-2 BCA 1999. 

F. J. Stokes Corporation, ASBCA No. 6532, 30 November 1960, 61-1 BCA 2866. 

29. ASBCA Will Neither Reconsider Nor Vacate Decision After Contracting Officer Issues Contract Modifications in Accord With That Decision. Immediately after the ASBCA de cided an appeal in favor of the contractor, the contracting officer prepared contract modifications which conformed to the Board's decision. 

The modifications were transmitted to the contractor six months later, a week before the

Board's hearing on the Government's motion for reconsideration of the original decision. The contractor asked that the motion for reconsideration be denied on the ground that the modifications had removed "any need for 142 AGO 9111A

DISPUTES-Continued further action by the Board." The Government contended that: (1) the Board had jurisdiction to reconsider the original decision, but (2) if the Board decided it lacked jurisdiction, the original decision should be vacated and the appeal dismissed.

Held, the motion for reconsideration is dismissed, without prejudice to its reinstatement if the mootness of the appeal is removed. In view of the contract modifications it is difficult to understand why a motion for reconsideration of the original decision was filed. The Government relies on Pace Corporation, ASBCA No. 

5954 (30 Jun 1960), 60-2 BCA 2698, and Park side Clothes, Inc., ASBCA No. 4184 (1 Jul 

1960), 60-2 BCA 2760. However, those cases held only that an adverse decision by a contracting officer is appealable, and that the contracting officer may not oust the Board of jurisdiction by attempting to withdraw a decision from which an appeal has been filed. 

Here the contracting officer's modified decision is in complete accord with the Board's original opinion. It would be an idle exercise to reconsider that opinion.

The Government may not have the original opinion vacated and the appeal dismissed. The

Government cites in support of its argument 

Brownlow v. Schwartz, 261 U.S. 216 (1922), in which the Supreme Court held that it must "dispose of the case, not merely of the appellate proceeding which brought it here." However, there does not exist the same relationship between the contracting officer and the ASBCA as existed between the Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court in the Brownlow case or in the other cases cited by the Government. In one of those cases, the Court's purpose was "to prevent a judgment, unreviewable because of mootness, from spawning any legal consequences." United States v. Munsingwear, 340

U.S. 36 (1950). There is no such problem here, for the Board's decision resolved the dispute and the contracting officer apparently is in accord with that decision. The Government's motion for reconsideration should, therefore, be dismissed, without prejudice to its reinstatement if the present mootness of the appeal is eliminated by, for example, an attack on the contract modifications. 

General Motors Corporation, Allison Division, 

ASBCA Nos. 5206, 5207, and 5208, 13 December 1960, 61-1 BCA 2880. 

30. ASBCA Lacks Jurisdiction Because Ap pellant's Formally Advertised Contract Was 

Awarded on Basis of Unresponsive Bid-Government Not Estopped To Deny Validity of Contract Made Invalid by Violation of Statute and Regulations. The appellant submitted the low bid in response to an invitation for bids on 25,000 yards of cotton duck for West Point cadets' uniforms. When asked by the West 

Point contracting officer why the bid was markedly higher than the price on earlier procurements, the appellant stated that experience had shown that weaving cloth to meet the rigorous standards was very difficult. The contracting officer decided all bids were too high, so he rejected the bids and readvertised the procurement. Appellant again submitted the low bid, one substantially lower than his earlier offer, but not based on the invitation's specifications. Although the invitation did not provide for alternate bids, the appellant offered, instead of specification cloth, a substitute he thought would meet the Government's needs but would be easier to weave. The bid included a sample of the offered material, which any expert could easily have determined varied in several respects from the cloth required by the specifications. However, the cloth sample was approved by men at West Point and the appellant's bid was declared responsive. The contract awarded the appellant contained the invitation's specifications, with the proviso "per sample submitted .. [by appellant]." The contract contained the standard Disputes Clause. (ASPR 7-103.2). 

While the cloth was being woven, the Government obtained and tested a sample from a production run. The cloth failed to meet the invitation's specifications and was useless for cadets' uniforms. When the appellant was informed that the cloth was deficient, he replied that the material conformed to the bid sample, that no higher standard was set by the contract, and that the entire order had been produced and was ready for delivery. The contracting officer then issued a determination that there had never been a valid contract because the parties had failed to agree on the cloth to be produced. This determination was appealed to the ASBCA. 

AGO 9111A 143

DISPUTES-Continued Held, appeal dismissed. The Board lacks jurisdiction because the appellant's contract is invalid. The defect is not that the parties never agreed what cloth was to be supplied. The appellant's bid was a clear and unambiguous offer to provide cloth conforming to a particular sample, and the award of the contract was an unqualified acceptance of the appellant's offer. 

If only general principles of contract law were applicable, a binding agreement would have been made for the cloth appellant offered. However, the award was made to the appellant in violation of applicable statutes and regulations. 

Save when any of seventeen exceptions permit the use of negotiation, procurements must be made by formal advertising. 10 U.S.C. § 2304 

(a). For the procurement from appellant the only exception possibly applicable was the one in 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (15) permitting negotiation after formal advertising has produced unreasonable prices. Use of that exception requires that certain determinations first be made at the secretarial level. 10 U.S.C. §§ 2304 (a) 

(15), 2311. Since this requirement was not met in the instant case, formal advertising was required. In formally advertised procurement, only responsive bids may legally be accepted. 

10 U.S.C. § 2305; ASPR 2–403, 2-406. Because the appellant's bid offered an unauthorized alternate, it was unresponsive. See, e.g., 9 

Comp. Gen. 24 (1929). The deviation was not minor, so it could not have been waived by the contracting officer. See, e.g., 39 Comp. Gen. 

832 (1960). The violation of the statute and the regulations rendered the appellant's contract invalid.

The Government is not estopped to assert the invalidity of the contract, even though the appellant was induced to enter into the agreement and to produce the entire quantity of goods in reliance on the conduct of Government officials. None of the cases cited by the appellant hold that the Government is estopped to deny the validity of a contract entered into in violation of statutory requirements. Robbins v. 

United States, 86 Ct. Cl. 39 (1937), and 

Mahoning Investment Co. v. United States, 78 

Ct. Cl. 231 (1933), involved estoppels running against taxpayers suing the Government. The doctrines of no estoppel against the Government and no apparent authority of Government agents are grounded on the principle that the authority of a Federal agent must be found in a public statute or a proper delegation pursuant thereto. Since persons dealing with a Federal agent are presumed to have knowledge of the law, they may not be justified in relying on any appearance or representation of authority that is contrary to law. See McIntire, Authority of

Government Contracting Officers: Estoppel and 

Apparent Authority, 25 Geo. Wash. L. Rev. 162 (1957). There have been a few cases where the doctrines of apparent authority and estoppel have been applied against the Government. 

Whike Constr. Co. v. United States, 135 Ct. Cl 

126 (1956); Knight v. United States, 35 Ct. Cl. 

129 (1900); Duval v. United States, 25 Ct. Cl. 

46 (1889). The suggestion has been made that those decisions are limited to instances where the contracting officer acts within general area of his authority and where the illegality or lack of authority results from circumstances not known to the public. See McIntire, op. cit. supra. In this case, the rules violated appear in an act of Congress and in implementing regulations published in the Federal Register, of which the appellant had constructive notice. 

Perhaps the appellant may secure relief elsewhere. He acted reasonably and in good faith both in submitting the bid and in producing the cloth. Bidders frequently submit unresponsive bids, and contracting officers have the responsibility of detecting such bids. The appellant tried to save the Government money by offering substitute cloth, and he frequently notified the Government that he was not providing material called for by the specifications. 

The Comptroller General and the Court of Claims have in some instances allowed compensation to contractors who proceeded in good faith with performance pursuant to contracts that were invalid because applicable statutes and regulations were violated. See, e.g., 39

Comp. Gen. 832 (1960); 30 Comp. Gen. 179 

(1950); Ms. Comp. Gen. B-116109, 23 Novem ber 1953. New York Mail & Newspaper Trans. 

Co. v. United States, 139 Ct. Cl. 751 (1957).

Prestex, Inc., ASBCA No. 6572, 30 January 

1961, 61-1 BCA 2937.

If Government Assesses Excess Costs While Appeal From Termination Is Pending, the Issuance of Excess Costs May Be Consid ered Together With the Propriety of the Ter mination Even Though No Separate Appeal From the Assessment Is Filed. On 10 December 

1958, by a letter that made no specific reference to excess costs, the contracting officer terminated the appellant's contract pursuant to the standard Default Clause (Cl. 11, SF 32, Nov 

1949 ed.). On 9 January 1959 the appellant filed a timely appeal to the ASBCA from "the decision of the Contracting Officer terminating the... contract for default." On 14 March 

1959 the appellant received a notice of assessment of excess costs. The notice stated that it was a final and appealable decision. The appellant did nothing about the notice until he filed a complaint on 27 July 1960 and stated therein a challenge to the necessity and propriety of the 

Government's repurchase. The Government moved to dismiss the portion of the appeal relating to excess costs on the ground that no timely appeal had been taken from the March assessment notice.

Held, motion denied. The Default Clause must be construed as a whole. Subparagraphs (b) through (e) of the clause set forth the rights of the Government and the contractor if the contract is terminated pursuant to subparagraph (a). Thus, in view of the specific language of the various subparagraphs, a notice of termination for default is also a notice that the Government may exercise the rights given it by the clause in the event of termination. 

The same reasoning indicates that an appeal from the default termination is broad enough to cover any exercise by the Government of its rights under the Default Clause. If the Government exercises any of those rights while a dispute over the termination is pending, disputes over those rights and their exercise may properly be heard with the dispute over the termination. See Glyco Products Co., ASBCA 

No. 934 (30 Apr. 1952), motion for rehearing, 31 July 1953. There the Board reopened the hearing to consider the question of excess costs. 

The assessment had been made while the termination was pending, but did not come to the attention of the Board before a decision on the termination was issued.

There are three advantages to proceeding in the manner suggested: (1) The entire dispute triggered by the default termination will be disposed of expeditiously. (2) Consonant with the maxim, "the law abhors a useless act," the contracting officer will not need to render piecemeal decisions, and the contractor will be saved the time, money, and effort involved in appealing from separate decisions. (3) There will be no multiplicity of proceedings. These three reasons have been applied by the Board before. 

The Board has accepted jurisdiction of the issue of excess costs where during an appeal from a default termination an assessment of excess costs was challenged, even though (a) no final decision of the contracting officer had issued but the question of excess costs had been placed before the Board by the parties, Emco 

Metal Manufacturing Corp., ASBCA No. 4983 

(15 Jan. 1960), 60-1 BCA 2502; and (b) a notice of assessment of excess costs had issued but the Board considered the notice not a formal decision but merely the commencement of a dispute between the parties, and an appeal from the notice would have been premature,

Bar-Ray Products, Inc., ASBCA No. 3065 (4 

Nov. 1957), 57-2 BCA 1502.

El-Tronics, Inc., ASBCA No. 5457, 28 Febru ary 1961, 61-1 BCA 2961.
