35. Disputes Clause Not Applicable to Con troversy Arising After Contract Expired- After Government Made, and Contractor Joined, Motion to Dismiss Contractor's Appeal to ASBCA on Ground Board Lacked Jurisdiction, Government May Not Succeed in Claim That Contractor Failed To Exhaust Administrative 

Remedies. The defendants' lease of land from the Army ran from 1 July 1952 until 31 December 1956. The lease contained a standard disputes clause providing that the contracting officer should decide "all disputes concerning questions of fact which may arise under" the lease. The clause made the contracting officer's decision subject to an appeal to the ASBCA.

After the lease expired a controversy arose over whether the defendants had complied with several of the lease's provisions. In December 

1957 the contracting officer issued written determinations that the defendants had breached the lease provisions and owed the Government $113,366.12. The defendants timely appealed to the ASBCA. The Government moved to dismiss the appeal. The motion claimed (1) that the appeal was for damages for breach of contract and, hence beyond the Board's jurisdiction, and (2) that even if the Board decided to make findings of fact, those findings would not be binding on the courts. 

The defendants joined in the Government's motion. The ASBCA dismissed the appeal.

Heaton & Pitman, ASBCA No. 4928 (30 Sep 1958), 58-2 BCA 1945. The Government sued the defendants in a federal district court, praying for judgment of $113,366.12 for the defendants' failure to comply with the lease. The

Government moved for summary judgment, contending that the contracting officer's findings of fact were binding in the suit. 

Held, motion denied. The disputes clause was not applicable to the controversy. First, the clause did not apply to disputes arising after the lease terminated. United States v. Duggan, 210 F. 2d 926 (8th Cir. 1954); see also E. I.

DuPont De Nemours & Co. v. Lyles & Lang 

Constr. Co., 219 F. 2d 328 (4th Cir. 1955).

Second, the disputes clause is not applicable to controversies over damages for breach of con tract. Silberblatt & Lasker Inc. v. United 

States, 101 Ct. Cl. 54, 81 (1944); Boomer v. 

Abbett, 121 Cal. App. 2d 449, 263 P. 2d 479 (1953). On both grounds the disputes clause was inapplicable.

A comment is warranted regarding the 

Government's contention that the contracting officer's findings are binding because the defendants failed to exhaust administrative remedies. This contention would be unacceptable even if those findings were authorized by the disputes clause. Having moved to dismiss the appeal to the ASBCA, the Government is in a weak position in urging that the defendants failed to exhaust administrative relief. The main argument of the Government is that the motion to dismiss was based on faulty grounds, that the defendants had the burden of perceiving the defect in the motion, and that for their failure to do so the defendants are foreclosed from challenging the administrative findings of fact. It is true that "those dealing with the 

Government must no doubt turn square corners." United States v. Blair, 321 U.S. 730, 738 (1944) (Frankfurter, J., dissenting). However, there appears to be a corresponding doctrine that the Government must not lead its contractors down the path and then argue there was no right to follow.

In Idaho Falls Bonded Produce & Supply Co. 

v. United States, 123 Ct. Cl. 842, 107 F. Supp. 

952 (1952), the plaintiff withdrew his appeal before the ASBCA after the Government filed a motion to dismiss. The Court of Claims rejected the Government's argument that the plaintiff's suit could not succeed because administrative remedies had not been exhausted. 

The court said, "[T]he Government may not rely upon a failure to pursue administrative remedies when it, itself, has taken the position that there was no . . . remedy available and its adversary has acceded to that contention." 

While in the instant case the Government did not argue there was no remedy, it did argue the futility of pursuing the remedy. No valid distinction can be drawn between the two arguments.

In United States v. Harvey, 131 F. Supp. 493 

(N.D. Tex. 1954), the defendant had been sent a notice indicating he would be given a cotton acreage allotment for 1950. The defendant never was sent an allotment notice, which was 146 AGO 9111A

DISPUTES-Continued required by statute and regulations, and he grew cotton on several acres. After he harvested and sold that cotton, he was sent a penalty notice informing him that he had not been given an acreage allotment for 1950. In suing to enforce a penalty, the Government contended that the defendant had no defense since he had failed to exhaust his administrative recourse against the denial of an allotment. The court held the Government could not, in the face of the "muddle, manifesting faulty administration of the law," rely on a failure to exhaust administrative remedies. The Harvey case is not factually in point, but the "muddle" there is akin to the Government's action in this case. 

The steps taken by the Government to dismiss the defendants' appeal to the ASBCA were based upon an assessment of the law as it then existed. If hindsight now reveals the assessment was faulty, the Government's mistake should not be a basis for profiting at the defendants' expense. 

In Moen v. United States, 128 Ct. Cl. 579, 121 

F. Supp. 677 (1954), the court held that an agreement between the plaintiff and the Government that an appeal to the tax court was unnecessary, rendered unsound the Government's contention that the plaintiff's suit had to fail because administrative remedies had not been exhausted. In the instant case, the defendants agreed with the Government that an appeal would have been fruitless. That agreement, according to the Moen case, made the appeal unnecessary. 

In Fireman's Fund Ins. Co. v. United States Army LST 34, 132 F. Supp. 414 (S.D.N.Y. 

1955), the court said:

It would be improper to read a claimant out of court under a disputes clause if the claimant can show that any recourse to administrative procedure would have been vain, unavailable or inadequate. 

In the instant case, the arguments made by the Government in moving to dismiss the appeal indicate that the appeal proceedings were vain and inadequate.

The Government has argued that a failure to exhaust administrative remedies is fatal to a private party's position unless the failure is caused by the Government itself, as was true in 

Lennox Metal Mfg. Co., 131 F. Supp. 717 (E.D.N.Y. 1954). In that case the contractor was unable to appeal because the contracting officer's refusal to make a record prevented the contractor from preparing a memorandum asserting the issues to be considered. However, there need not be an actual "prevention." As the cases discussed above disclose, certain conduct of the Government falling short of "prevention" is sufficient to excuse further pursuit of administrative remedies.

It has been held that the fact that the Government discourages the taking of an appeal does not excuse a failure to exhaust administrative remedies. Burnham Chemical Co. v. Krug, 81 F. Supp. 911 (D.D.C. 1949). The Govern ment's action in the instant case went far beyond the mere discouragement in the Burnham case. Here there was positive action taken to defeat the appeal. That action liberated the defendants from the obligation to exhaust ad ministrative remedies. 

United States v. Heaton, 195 F. Supp. 742 

(D. Neb. 1961). 

36. Whether Contract Should Be Reformed Is Question for Court To Answer on Evidence 

Adduced Before It and Not on Record Made

Before Administrative Board of Review. (D.C. 

Cir.)

See CONSIDERATION (par. 5) 37. When Milk Powder Infestation Occurred, 

When It Was Discoverable, and Whether Notice of Rejection Was Timely Given Are Questions of Fact-Court Defines Substantial Evidence- Warranties of Description, Fitness for a Special 

Purpose, and Merchantability Were Breached

By Delivery of Milk Powder With Latent Infes tation. The defendant entered into contracts with the Commodity Credit Corporation for the supply of powdered milk fit for human consumption. The contracts contained the follow ing Disputes Clause: 

Any dispute concerning questions of fact which may arise under the contract... shall be decided by the officer executing the contract in behalf of the Agency ... [C]ontractor may appeal to the head of Agency, whose decision or that of his designated representative shall be final and conclusive upon the parties. . . 

Between 20 May 1950 and 12 June 1950 the defendant delivered to two Government ware- AGO 9111A 147

DISPUTES-Continued houses powder that the Government had inspected and accepted. In July 1950 state and federal inspectors discovered maggots in the defendant's plant. Just prior to that discovery the defendant had shipped four cars of powder to the Government. Although that powder had originally passed Government inspection, a reinspection after maggots were found in the defendant's plant disclosed that the powder was infested. Upon the request of the contracting officer, the defendant agreed to accept the return of that powder. In September 1950 the 

Government reinspected the May and June shipments and found them infested. When requested to accept a return of the powder, the defendant refused, in part because of the length of the delay between delivery and rejection.

The CCC sold the powder as animal feed at a loss to the United States. The defendant appealed from a decision of the contracting officer that the powder was infested at the time of delivery and that the defendant was liable for the losses sustained. The Contract Disputes 

Board found that the Government warehouses where the powder was stored were free from infestation, that powder received from other manufacturers stored in those warehouses was similarly free from infestation, that defendant's milk was infested at time of delivery, that this infestation was a latent defect which did not preclude subsequent rejection of the powder, and that therefore defendant was liable for the Government's losses. The defendant refused to pay the Government's losses, so the Government filed suit. The federal district court granted the 

Government's motion for summary judgment. 

United States v. Hamden Cooperative Creamery Co., 185 F. Supp. 541 (E.D.N.Y. 1960). The defendant appealed.

Held, judgment affirmed. When the infestation occurred and when it was discoverable were questions of fact especially appropriate for administrative determination under the 

Disputes Clause. Court review is limited to determining whether the Board's decision is supported by substantial evidence and whether it is free from fraud, caprice, arbitrary conduct, and bad faith. 68 Stat. 81 (1954), 41 U.S.C. 

§ 321 (1958). "Substantial evidence. . . means such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclu sion." Consolidated Edison v. NLRB, 305 U.S. 

197, 229 (1938). Substantial evidence supports the Board's decision that the powder was infested when delivered but that the infestation was not discoverable until later. 

Answers to interrogatories posed to the Government's witnesses for use in the trial before the district court disclosed that in 1950, during the times herein pertinent, two lots of powder produced by other manufacturers and stored in one of the warehouses where defendant's powder was stored were infested, although eighty-eight other lots and the warehouse itself were free from infestation. Had this evidence been more significant, there would have been presented the difficult question whether the district court should have considered the evidence. However, the evidence was too insignificant to shake the determination that the Board's findings were supported by substantial evidence and were free from fraud or other infirmities.

Because its powder was not fit for human consumption, the defendant breached implied warranties of description, fitness for a special purpose and merchantability. N.Y. Personal

Property Law ch. 41, §§ 95, 96(1), (2); Uniform Sales Act §§ 14, 15(1), (2). Since in festation such as that involved here can be latent at delivery, a buyer is forced to rely upon a seller's care in keeping a sanitary plant. The 

Government's failure to discover the infestation upon inspection did not relieve the defendant of liability under its warranties. See N.Y. Per sonal Property Law § 96 (3); Uniform Sales 

Act 15 (3); J. Aron & Co. v. Sills, 240 N.Y. 

588, 148 N.E. 717 (1925).

New York law provides: 

[I]f, after acceptance of the goods, the buyer fails to give notice to the seller of the breach of any promise or warranty within a reasonable time after the buyer knows, or ought to know, of such breach, the seller shall not be liable therefor. New York 

Personal Property Law ch. 41, § 130. 

Neither party knew of any infestation until July. In that month the defendant's plant and another supply of powder was discovered to be infested. The powder involved here was discovered in September to be infested, and the 148 AGO 9111A

DISPUTES-Continued appellant was given formal notice in October of the breach. Whether notice is given within a reasonable time is a question for the trier of fact. See, e.g., Lembo v. Andola, 100 N.Y.S. 

2d 561 (App. Div. 1950); 9 Wigmore, Evidence § 2553 (3d ed. 1940). That the notice given the defendant was timely and adequate was a factual question for the Board to decide. In view of the extraordinary powers given the Board by 41 U.S.C. § 321, the court below could not try the issue anew unless the evidence were so insubstantial as to make the question one of law. This court on the record cannot disturb the Board's conclusion. 

United States v. Hamden Cooperative Cream ery Co., 297 F. 2d 130 (2d Cir. 1961). [Note: The court in the instant case pointed out that the parties had not raised the issue whether the New York sales law applied to the contracts of its own force or as incorporated by federal law.] 38. Board Lacks Jurisdiction Over Dispute Created by Government's Attempt To Obtain From Architect-Engineer Compensation for Damages Suffered on Construction Sites Allegedly Because of Faulty Design Work. In several decisions the contracting officer found that the Government had suffered damage, in specified sums, for "errors, deficiencies and omissions" in the appellant's design services under an architect-engineering contract. He stated the damages would be set off against retained percentages under the contract. The appellant recognized that the alleged damages arose out of incidents occurring in the performance of the subsequent construction contracts that embodied the plans and specifications furnished by the appellant but protested the contemplated withholding as unauthorized by the architect-engineering contract. When the appellant took timely appeals to the ASBCA, the Government moved to dismiss. 

The Government conceded that the deduction was not based on the contract but upon the common law governing professional liability of architects. The appellant resisted dismissal on the ground that one of the basic issues was the existence of errors, deficiencies or omissions, an issue presenting a question of fact. Moreover, argued the appellant, the appeal involved the validity of the proposed reduction of the contract price.

Held, appeal dismissed for want of jurisdiction. The Government is not seeking to reduce the contract price commensurate with the reasonable value of the allegedly faulty design work, but rather to obtain compensation for damages sustained on various construction sites caused by the allegedly negligent conduct of the architect-engineer in designing. The architect-engineer contract had no warranty clause or other provision for indemnification for such damages. The cause of action sounds essentially in tort. See Benedict, Beckler & As sociates, ASBCA No. 7172 (31 Aug. 1962) [digested under ARMED SERVICES BOARD OF CONTRACT APPEALS, par. 14] and cases cited there. In the Benedict case the Board decided it lacked jurisdiction over tort cases and over claims for damages for breach of contract.

43. ASBCA Holds Appeal May Be Taken From Contracting Officer's Refusal To Issue a 

Decision That Refers to Disputes Clause and the Contractor's Right To Appeal. On 3 May and 11 May 1960 the appellant offered to place, free of charge, ceramic tile in the tub recesses of certain living quarters being constructed AGO 9111A 149

ESTOPPEL 

by the appellant if the contracting officer would permit the use of mastic instead of concrete mortar for setting all tile. On 26 May 1960 the contracting officer wrote that the specifications required tile in the tub recesses and that the request to use mastic would have to be submitted with with detailed information. Apparently there was no further correspondence between the parties on the matter until 13 April 1961, when the appellant asked for a price increase for installing the tile in the tub recesses. On 28 April 1961 the contracting officer stated that the proposed change in the tile was being reviewed and that a decision would be provided in the near future. On 5 

May 1961 he wrote that his position remained as stated on 26 May 1960. The appellant replied on 17 July 1961 that the contracting officer's letter of 26 May 1960 was not a final decision under the disputes article and that such a decision was requested. On 4 August 

1961 the contracting officer wrote that he considered his 26 May 1960 letter a decision that had become final in the absence of an appeal. 

The appellant took an appeal from what was alleged to be a refusal by the contracting officer to make a decision. The Government moved to dismiss, contending that the 26 May 1960 letter was a final decision, or, if it was not, the letter of 5 May 1961 was. 

Held, motion denied. The letters of 26 May 

1960 and 5 May 1961 failed to mention either the contract's disputes clause or the contractor's right to appeal. Since the applicable procurement regulations [AFPI] then in effect advised reference to that clause and the right of appeal, the failure to mention them in a letter vitiates its finality as a decision under that clause. Frank Gust Decorating Service,

3200 and cases cited there. The Board has held that a contracting officer's refusal to make a decision on a contractor's claim is itself ap pealable. Leader Manufacturing Co., ASBCA No. 4416 (31 July 1958), 58-2 BCA 1877. This principle is also applicable to his refusal to issue a final decision complying with the requirements of the procurement instructions. 

The correspondence makes clear the contracting officer's position on the appellant's claim. 

No useful purpose would be served by returning the file to him for further action.

1. Government Not Estopped by Agent's Unauthorized Conduct Where Contractor, Although Relying to Detriment, Misinterpreted Scope of Statute Under Which Agent Purported to Act. 

Section 1446 (c) of the Agriculture Act of 1949, 7 U.S.C.A. § 1421, authorized the Secretary of 

Agriculture to make price supports available to the producers of milk and milk products "through loans on, or purchases of, the products of milk and butterfat." Prior to March 

1954, Department of Agriculture Regulations established a procedure whereby handlers could sell and ship butter to the Commodity Credit

Corporation at specified prices and then repurchase the same or similar butter at a lower price. The gain realized by the handlers was to be reflected in the price paid their suppliers.

After 9 March 1954, new regulations authorized butter handlers to "sell and repurchase" their produce without actually shipping it to the CCC. The defendant, relying upon representations of the Department of Agriculture, utilized the new procedure and received from the Government the difference between the purchase and repurchase price. Subsequently, the Comptroller General ruled that the new procedure was a paper transaction which did not constitute a "purchase" within the meaning of 7 U.S.C.A. § 1446 (c). In May 1956, after a demand for repayment had been refused, the 

United States brought suit to recover unauthorized payments made to the defendant.

The defendant filed a motion for summary judgment and argued that it had relied upon the good faith representations of Government agents. Further, the procedure followed was not so palpably unauthorized that the defendant could be charged without actual knowledge. 

Held, the defendant must return the unauthorized payments with interest from the date of this judgment. It is clear that the paper transaction exceeded the authority granted to the Department of Agriculture by 7 U.S.C.A. 

§ 1446 (c), since an actual purchase was not 150 AGO 9111A

EXCESS COSTS 

involved. Kraft Foods Co. of Wisconsin v. 

CCC., 164 F. Supp. 168 (W.D. Wis. 1958), aff'd, 266 F. 2d 254 (7th Cir. 1959); United

States v. Swift & Co., 152 F. Supp. 738 (D. Md. 

1957), aff'd, 257 F. 2d 787 (4th Cir. 1958), cert. denied, 358 U.S. 837. The defendant, therefore, relied to its detriment on unauthorized departmental procedures and representations. 

Regardless of the presence of a detrimental reliance, the United States is not contractually bound by the apparent authority of its agents. 

Persons dealing with the Government are bound to ascertain the agent's actual authority from Acts of Congress and implementing regu lations. Federal Crop Insurance Corp. v. Mer rill, 332 U.S. 380 (1947). A necessary extension of this rule is that the Government will not be estopped by the conduct or representations of an agent not within the scope of his actual authority, even though a detrimental reliance has occurred. Sanders v. Comm'r of 

Internal Revenue, 225 F. 2d 629 (10th Cir. 

1955). This case may be distinguished from 

Merrill because the defendant's reliance precluded him from obtaining the price difference by actually shipping the butter under alternate departmental procedures. In Merrill, there was no alternate source from which the crop insurance could be obtained. But Merrill does not turn on the lack of detrimental reliance. The basic proposition is that he who deals with the Government bears the burden of ascertaining not only the actual authority of its agents but also the scope of statutes and regulations under which those agents purport to act. Consequently, the defendant bore the risk of misinterpreting section 1446 (c) and must return the unauthorized payments received. While the defendant is bound by constructive knowledge of the statute's true scope, there is no legal duty to repay until it knew or should have known that the payment was unauthorized. Consequently, interest will be computed from the date of this judgment rather than the date of the actual payment or the demand for repayment.

United States v. Zenith-Godley Co., 180 F. 

Supp. 611 (S.D.N.Y. 1960), aff'd 259 F. 2d 634 

(2d Cir. 1961).

2. Excess Costs Incurred In Establishing a 

New Source as Opposed to Replacing a Default ed Source Not Assessable. The Contractor promised to deliver 15,000 asbestos fire fighting suits to the Government for a fixed price of $911,022. The contracting officer had an option to increase the required quantity but, when the contractor appeared close to default, decided to obtain 5,000 additional suits from another source. Accordingly, a new contract was awarded by formal advertising at a higher unit price. The contractor was then properly terminated for default and, in repurchasing the 15,000 suits, the Government incurred excess costs of $77,461.32. The excess costs incurred under both contracts were assessed against the contractor, who appealed.

Held, the appeal is sustained in part and denied in part. The contractor first asserts that excess costs incurred in purchasing the 5,000 suits should not be included in the assessment. 

This is correct, since the contracting officer was establishing a new and independent source rather than replacing suits ordered under a defaulted contract. The contractor next argues that excess costs incurred in the actual repurchase were caused by different requirements AGO 9111A 151

than contained in the original procurement, i.e, a pre-bid sample, identification of suppliers and a shorter time between invitation and bid opening. The contracting officer, however, had to satisfy the Government's need and overcome the delay caused by the contractor's default. The differences in the method and manner of repurchase, therefore, were justified under the circumstances and did not constitute an abuse of the contracting officer's discretion.

4. Determination of Excess Costs Prior to the Completion of Reprocurement Would Be Premature. The opinion of The Judge Advo cate General of the Army was requested as to the propriety of a contracting officer's plan to assess excess costs against a defaulting contractor and, if unsuccessful in effecting collection to forward the matter to the Comptroller of the Army so the latter might recover by setoff from amounts otherwise due the contractor under the contract. The proposed determination of excess costs was based on the repurchase contract, performance thereof not having been completed. 

Held, a finding of excess costs would be premature because the extent of the contractor's liability therefor cannot be known until the actual cost of the reprocurement is determined and such a determination cannot be made until reprocurement is complete.

The responsibility of the Comptroller of the Army under the debt collection program does not include the adjudication of claims, but rather is confined to assisting in the collection of established indebtednesses when efforts of field installations to that end have failed. Thus, compliance with existing regulations, in partic ular AR 35-3290 with Changes No. 1, dated 

5 June 1957, requires that reprocurement be complete and the amount of excess costs known before any resulting indebtedness is processed to the Comptroller of the Army for action. 

JAGT 1960/7655, 7 December 1960.

1. Threat on Life of Contractor is Excusable Cause for Default. The contractor, a manu facturer of coat fronts, employed workers which the Amalgamated Clothing Workers Union would not accept as members. Consequently, the coat fronts were nonunion and unacceptable to the trade. The Government, however, did not require union-made clothing and awarded a $7,670 contract for the manufacture of uniform coat fronts to the contractor. Shortly thereafter, the contractor received an anonymous threat which promised bodily harm unless 152 AGO 9111A

EXCUSABLE CAUSE-Continued he got out of the coat front business. Relying upon this threat, the contractor discontinued performance and forced the Government to terminate the contract for default. Excess costs of $584.69 were assessed and the contractor appealed, arguing that the default was excusable. 

Held, the appeal is sustained. The only evidence of the threat was the testimony of the contractor. This is substantiated by his earnest and veracious demeanor and the fact that no other apparent benefit was to be derived from discontinuing performance. The default was beyond the control and without the fault or negligence of the contractor. The fact that the nonunion goods were unacceptable to the commercial trade does not make the contractor negligent in entering a contract with the Government or failing to foresee the threat on his life.

American Coat Front Co., Inc.. ASBCA No. 

5626, 16 September 1959, 59-2 BCA 2341.

9. Impossibility of Meeting Performance Specifications Held Not To Excuse Failure To Perform When the Contractor Originated the Design and the Performance Specifications. The 

Navy requested proposals on a contract to produce a digital data recording system meeting certain requirements of precision. The Navy suggested in general terms a design that was thought to be adequate, but several prospective AGO 9111A 153

EXCUSABLE CAUSE-Continued contractors, including the appellant, convinced the Navy that the design was inadequate. The appellant negotiated with the Navy on the basis of an alternate design, which scientific estimates indicated would be adequate. During the negotiations, the appellant stated that a contract based on the alternate design could be fulfilled, that the precision of the equipment would be higher than the Navy's original specifications had demanded, and that the appellant would promise to provide the higher precision. The appellant accepted a fixed-price contract which provided that the specifications, incorporating the appellant's design, were primarily performance-type specifications and that "complete compliance with the performance requirements [would] be required." The contract contained the standard Default Clause. (Cl. 11, SF 32, Nov. 1949 ed.). The performance requirements obligated the appellant to produce well beyond the state of the art in data recording. From the outset the appellant was unable to obtain the precision required. The time for performance was frequently extended, but after more than two years the Navy became anxious for delivery. The contracting officer pressed the appellant for a promise about completion, and the appellant set a date five months away for delivery of equipment the appellant thought would meet the Government's needs even though it would be less precise than the contract required. The contracting officer terminated the contract for default when the appellant refused to guarantee delivery of specification equipment in five weeks. The appellant timely appealed the termination to the ASBCA, claiming that the termination should be converted to one for convenience, pursuant to paragraph (e) of the Default Clause, because the failure to perform had been due to causes beyond the control and without the fault or negligence of the appellant. Using legal definitions of "control," "fault," and "negligence," the appellant argued that it was not in default if its practices during performance accorded with generally accepted and recognized practices used by careful, prudent, and competent engineers.

Held, appeal denied. The appellant's argument incorrectly assumes that under paragraph (e) of the Default Clause, impossibility of performance is always an excusable cause for nonperformance if the contractor has acted with diligence. There are, however, many kinds of impossibility, and the rights of a contractor vary with circumstances. See Corbin, Contracts ch. 74. The kind involved here is that in which parties execute a fixed-price contract for the production of an article meeting impossibly difficult specifications. When the contract is terminated for default, a determination must be made about which party agreed to bear the risk of impossibility of performance. On the one hand, in cases where the Government assumed that risk, impossibility is an excuse for non-performance, and the appellant's interpretation of the extent of the contractor's duty is correct for such cases. See, for example, E. L.

Cournand & Co.. ASBCA No. 2995 (29 Sept. 

1960), 60-2 BCA 2840, where the contractor neither knew nor had reason to know that a design provided by the Government was inadequate for producing an item meeting the contract's requirements. On the other hand, impossibility is not an excusable cause for failure to perform a contract that places on the contractor the risk of achieving a new or difficult objective. Under such a contract, the contractor's obligation is not limited to the exercise of the skill and competence of prudent and skillful craftsmen engaged in a similar enterprise. He is required to perform or, if performance is impossible, to bear the cost of his failure. See, for example, Aerosonic Instrument Corp., ASBCA No. 4129 (12 Mar. 1959), 59-1 BCA 2115, where the contractor knew or should have known at the time of contracting that it was obligating itself to produce beyond the state of the art. When the contract there was terminated for default, the Board refused to find that the failure to perform the requirements that were impossible to meet was due to causes beyond the control and without the fault or negligence of the contractor.

The facts of the instant case indicate it should be governed by the principles applied in Aerosonic. Although the negotiations originated with a request for proposals based on the Government's design, the appellant and other contractors recognized that a different design 154 AGO 9111A

EXCUSABLE CAUSE-Continued would be required to produce the desired precision. The appellant produced an alternate design which the appellant claimed would provide higher precision than the Government originally had required. The design and the higher precision requirements that originated with the appellant were incorporated into the contract. 

With full knowledge of the hazards involved, the appellant agreed for a fixed price to produce equipment with a precision never before attained. It thus appears that the appellant agreed to bear the risk that performance might be impossible. The failure to perform is not excused by the Default Clause. As stated in

Aerosonic, "The real test under the Default Article is whether impossibility of performance came about through circumstances which were beyond the control and without the fault or negligence of the contractor." The impossibility in the instant case had its origin in matters over which the appellant had control. 

The Austin Company. ASBCA No. 4255, 12 

January 1961, 61-1 BCA 2927.

If Government Assesses Excess Costs While Appeal From Termination Is Pending, the Issuance of Excess Costs May be Consid ered Together With the Propriety of the Ter mination Even Though No Separate Appeal From the Assessment Is Filed. (ASBCA) See DISPUTES (par. 32) 11. Inability To Obtain Steel Because of Strike Was Not Excusable Cause Since Another Metal, Meeting Specifications but More Expen sive, Was Available. On 20 June 1959 the appellant received a supply contract for 106 aircraft-missile engine trailers with technical data and spare parts. The appellant was to deliver a first article for testing by 17 November 1959; a draft of a testing program was to be submitted by the appellant forty-five days earlier. When work began late in June 1959, the appellant had commitments from its suppliers for almost all materials-except for the metal for the frame and two rails that were major components-needed for the first article. 

The imminence of a steel strike had depleted the supply of steel so much that mills were quoting September delivery for orders placed early in June. Moreover, the appellant had not decided whether to use high tensile steel or "mild steel" for the frame and rails. The appellant did not select and order high tensile steel until 12 August 1959. The steel mills were closed by a strike from 15 July to 9 November 1959, and the appellant's order was not accepted by the supplier. At no time did the appellant order aluminum for the frame and rails, even thought that metal was readily available, would have met the specifications, and the Government suggested its use. Aluminum was substantially more expensive than high tensile steel, and the appellant believed that if aluminum were used in the first article, that metal would have to be used in the other trailers. Because of that belief and the additional one that the steel strike excused failure to adhere to the contract schedule for submitting a proposed test program and delivering a first article, the appellant failed to be diligent in fulfilling his obligations. After giving the appellant a ten-day notice, the Government terminated the contract on 12 Novem ber 1959, pursuant to the Default Clause (Cl. 

11, SF 32, Oct. 1957 ed.) because of (1) delays that made timely delivery of a first article impossible, and (2) failure timely to submit the proposed test program. The appellant appealed to the ASBCA. Relying on the fact that high tensile steel was unobtainable while steel workers were on strike, the appellant argued that the termination was improper because the Default Clause excused non-performance caused by a strike at a supplier's plant. 

Held, appeal denied. The overriding consideration is the last sentence of paragraph 11 (c) 

of the Default Clause: 

If the failure to perform is caused by the default of a subcontractor, and if such default arises out of causes beyond the control of both the Contractor and subcontractor, and without the fault or negligence of either of them, the Contractor shall not be liable for any excess costs for failure to perform, unless the supplies or services to be furnished by the subcontractor were obtainable from other sources in sufficient time to permit the Contractor to meet the required delivery schedule. 

The specifications did not require steel for the frame and rails. Aluminum, which was equally sanctioned by the specifications, was available on the open market during the steel strike. The 

Government left the selection of the metal entirely to appellant. The complaint is made by AGO 9111A 155

EXCUSABLE CAUSE-Continued the appellant that aluminum was so expensive that its use would have caused production costs to exceed the contract price. The Default 

Clause, however, does not relieve a contractor of the duty to perform if, as here, the "supplies ... to be furnished by the subcontractor were obtainable in sufficient time to permit the contractor to meet the required delivery schedule."

Alabama Bridge & Iron Co., ASBCA No. 

6124, 15 March 1961, 61-1 BCA 2970. 

12. Failure of Government Timely To Deliver Government-Furnished Property Held To Be Excusable Cause of Contractor's Failure To Perform. (ASBCA) See GOVERNMENT-FURNISHED PROP- ERTY (par. 3) 13. ASBCA Reaffirms Andresen Doctrine. 

(ASBCA) 

See LIQUIDATED DAMAGES (par. 2) 14. Contractor's Inability To Find Subcontractor Willing To Agree To Inclusion of Davis- Bacon Act Clause in Subcontract Was, Under Circumstances of This Case, an Excusable Cause of Failure To Perform-Excusability Test Applied to Failure To Show Progress-Two Items in Single Contract Held To Be Severable for Purposes of Default Clause. The appellant was low bidder on item 1 (inspecting, testing, and repairing several electrical substations) and item 2 (repairing certain equipment and replacing an existing wood structure with a steel structure housed in aluminum) of a formally advertised Army contract. The appellant's bid on item 1 was so much lower than the other bids that the Government suspected an error had been made and, accordingly, a request was made that the price be verified. 

When the request was received, the appellant knew that an error had made the price too low.

The price, however, was confirmed in order, according to the appellant, to avoid creating a reputation for irresponsibility that would prejudice attempts to obtain future Government contracts. The appellant was awarded a single contract for items 1 and 2. The contract contained the Termination for Default 

Damages for Delay-Time Extensions Clause in ASPR 8-709 and clauses imposing Davis- Bacon Act wage schedules and procedures on the appellant and requiring that identical Davis-Bacon Act provisions be included in subcontracts. 

Item 1 required work that could be performed by only a few large concerns, and the appellant intended to subcontract that work. However, no prospective subcontractor was willing to take a subcontract containing the Davis-Bacon Act provisions. After trying without success to help the appellant place the subcontract, the 

Government suggested the following procedure: a subcontract would be awarded with Davis- Bacon Act provisions to the G Co., the firm that had quoted the lowest prices to the appellant and with whom the appellant had done the most negotiating. The G Co. would then advise the Government through the appellant that only supervisors or technicians, not laborers or mechanics, would be used. The Government would then advise that compliance with the Davis-Bacon Act was not required for their work. The appellant and the G Co. both opposed the suggestion. Negotiations by the appellant with another prospective subcontractor were fruitless. After giving two weeks notice (mentioned below in relation to item 2), the Government terminated the contract as to item 

1 for failure to show satisfactory progress. A repurchase contract was made with the same labor clauses but different minimum wages. A subcontract was made with the G Co. In response to a question from the repurchase contractor, the contracting officer stated that

Davis-Bacon Act provisions had to be in the subcontract, but that if the G Co. utilized supervisory engineers and technicians, the Davis- 

Bacon Act would not apply. Apparently the 

G Co. furnished only supervisory personnel and technicians. 

With respect to item 2, the appellant before bidding had reached what was apparently an informal understanding with a supplier about the steel structure with an aluminum housing. 

Sometime after award of the contract in June, the appellant sent the supplier an order for the structure. On 3 August the supplier gave notice that delivery would take six weeks from the time complete information about dimensions was obtained, a period that could be reduced if steel was substituted for aluminum in the 156 AGO 9111A

EXCUSABLE CAUSE-Continued housing. On 1 September the appellant furnished the Government with shop drawings that the supplier had just prepared. The appellant pointed out that the drawings showed a steel housing. The appellant stated that use of steel would cut in half the twelve weeks that would be required for delivery of an aluminum housing. Twelve weeks from 1 September extended well past the contract completion date of 14

October. The Government insisted on an aluminum housing. The appellant submitted corrected shop drawings, which were approved by the Government on 29 September. On 14

October the supplier notified the appellant that delivery could not be made by that date, but an attempt would be made to deliver before 23 

November. Thus on 14 October, when item 2 

Iwas to have been completed, no work had been done. On 16 October the appellant forwarded to the Government the supplier's 14 October letter and requested a sixty day time extension. By letter of 16 November the contracting officer replied, stating that there appeared to be no excusable reason for the failure to perform. 

He warned that the contract would be terminated unless satisfactory progress were shown by 30 November. (The warning also applied to item 1, on which appellant was having the difficulties mentioned above.) On 24 November the supplier asked for an extension until 23

December for delivery of the steel structure. 

The same day the appellant asked the Government for an unspecified time extension. On 25 

November the request was denied, and the warning of the 16 November letter was repeated. The contract was terminated on 1 

December (as to both items 1 and 2). A day or two later the supplier delivered the structure to the appellant.

An appeal was taken from the termination, the appellant contending that any delays were the result of excusable causes. Excess costs of about $4,000 were assessed on the repurchase of item 1, and an appeal was taken from the assessment. That assessment took into account a $717 saving realized by the Government on the repurchase of item 2. In connection with item 2, the appellant appealed from a denial of a claim for $2,554 for materials purchased in anticipation of performance. 

Held, the appeal is sustained as to item 1 and denied as to item 2. As to the former, the 

Government knew or should have known that the work required the use of expensive equipment that only a few large companies possess. 

The appellant knew the work would have to be subcontracted, and knew that the willingness of a firm to take a subcontract would depend in part on the subcontract clauses. Yet in prebid negotiations with potential subcontractors, the appellant did not advise them about the labor provisions or determine that the potential subcontractor knew of those provisions. Thus, at the time of bidding the appellant had no reasonable basis for believing that a subcontractor willing to accept the labor provisions could be found. There are, however, facts that make appellant's pre-bid negligence of no importance. Because of the bid mistake, the appellant could have avoided receiving the contract. When the appellant became irrevocably committed to the contract, a written quotation had been received from the G Co., which stated an intention to comply with all applicable federal laws. The only reasonable construction the appellant could have placed on that statement is that the labor provisions were acceptable. Thus, it was unforeseeable, when the appellant took the prime contract, that no subcontractor willing to abide by the labor provisions could be found. The unavailability of subcontractors was beyond the appellant's control and without that firm's fault or negligence.

As to item 2, the Board finds that during the period covered by the notice to show satisfactory progress (16 through 30 November), the appellant made no showing of progress. It now appears that some progress was made during that time because the steel structure was delivered to the appellant on or shortly after 2 December. The Board can only speculate about what action the contracting officer would have taken on 1 December if, on the preceding day, the appellant had showed that the structure would be delivered in a few days. On the basis of the record the Board cannot find that the appellant's failure to show progress by 30 

November was the result of some unforeseeable cause beyond the appellant's control and without that firm's fault or negligence.

AGO 9111A 157

EXHAUSTION OF ADMINISTRATIVE REMEDIES 

The appellant's failure to perform the work required by item 2 (as distinguished from the failure to show progress) was caused by the subcontractor's failure to deliver the steel structure in time for completion of the work before the termination. The record does not warrant holding that cause to have been unforeseeable and beyond the control and without the fault or negligence of the appellant. First, the evidence is unpersuasive that the appellant before bidding made a reliable arrangement with the prospective supplier. Second, there is no evidence that the appellant placed an order with the supplier promptly after receiving the prime contract. Third, there is no evidence that the order to the supplier required performance that was timely in relation to the performance required by the appellant's contract with the 

Government. Fourth, the appellant's proposal that the Government change the housing material to steel served only to delay fabrication of the structure at a critical time; that delay could have been avoided by the appellant.

Thus there was an excusable cause only for the failure to perform one of the two items. 

The two items may be treated separately in this appeal. The contract was clearly a divisible one. 

The Government had reserved the right to award a separate contract on each item. The two items were put in a single contract only because the appellant was the lowest bidder on each of those items. Separate contracts could have been written, but a single one was used for convenience. The parties seem to have treated the two items as distinct. Seldom did either party discuss both items in one conmmunication. The contracting officer apparently terminated each item because of a delay related solely to that item. On occassion a termination may be upheld if it is supported by a valid reason, even though the termination was originally based on an invalid reason. This is not such a case.

R. E. Lee Electric Co., ASBCA Nos. 6195, 

6447, 31 March 1961, 61-1 BCA 3002.

1962), the Board treated items in a hardware contract as severable. A default termination was upheld as to twelve items and found improper as to three items. The Board stated, "The various items under this contract were individually priced and, as to those delivered prior to termination, were individually paid for.

Experts and Consultants Is $56.50. 5 U.S.C. § 55a authorizes the head of any department, when authorized in an appropriation or other act, to employ the temporary or intermittent services of experts or consultants by contract.

For agencies subject to the Classification Act of 

1949 the rates payable will not be in excess of the per diem equivalent of the highest rate payable under the Classification Act unless other rates are specifically provided in the appropriation or other law. As no specific rate is provided in the Department of Defense Appro priation Act, 1961, although acts prior to the Fiscal Year 1960 have contained a $50.00 per day limitation, the Classification Act limitation controls. 

The Comptroller General has interpreted the provisions of 5 U.S.C. § 55a as limiting the daily compensation of experts and consultants under contract with the United States to the highest amount payable to personnel who may 158 AGO 9111A

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-94309, 17 May 1950, and

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-13645, 17 January 1958). 

The highest rate payable to a person in grade 

GS-15 is $14,690 per annum, and the number of days worked annually by personnel under the 

Classification Act is 260. Accordingly, the per diem equivalent and the highest daily rate payable to consultants is $56.50.

2. Rules on Application of Conflict-of-Interest Statutes to Intermittent Consultants and Advisers. The President asked the Attorney Gen eral for an opinion as to the application of the conflict-of-interest laws to persons utilized by Government departments and agencies as occasional consultants or advisers or as members of part-time advisory boards. The Attorney

General provided the following opinion: 

There are four conflict-of-interest statutes governing persons when employed by the Gov ernment. By 18 U.S.C. § 281 an officer or em ployee of the United States is prohibited from receiving compensation for any services rendered by himself or another in relation to a proceeding, contract, claim, or other matter before a department, agency, or office where the Government is a party or is directly or indi rectly interested. By 18 U.S.C. § 283 an officer or employee of the United States is prohibited from acting as an agent or attorney for prosecuting any claim against the United States, or assisting the prosecution of such a claim (except in the discharge of his official duties), or receiving any gratuity or any share or interest in such a claim in consideration of assistance in prosecuting it. By 18 U.S.C. § 434 an officer or agent of the Government who is interested in the profits or contracts of any business entity is prohibited from acting for the Government in the transaction of business with that entity. By 

18 U.S.C. § 1914 a Government official is prohibited from receiving any salary in connection with his services for the Government except from the Government or a state, county, or municipality. 

There are two conflict-of-interest statutes affecting former employees. By 18 U.S.C. § 284 

a former employee or commissioned officer of the United States is prohibited, for two years after his Government employment or service has ceased, from prosecuting in a representative capacity any claim against the United States involving any subject matter with which he was directly connected as a Government official. By 5 U.S.C. § 99 a former officer or em ployee of an executive department is prohibited (but without a criminal penalty), for a period of two years after his employment with the department has ceased, from prosecuting in a representative capacity, or aiding in the prosecution of, any claim pending in any department during his incumbency.

These statutes were designed in general to cover full-time employees of the Government. 

However, preceding Attorneys General have consistently held that these statutes also apply to temporary expert consultants, and even to persons who serve the Government in that capacity without compensation. E.g., 40 Ops. 

Att'y Gen. 289 (1943). The same approach has been taken by the Supreme Court in con nection with the applicability of 18 U.S.C. § 434 

to a temporary and part-time consultant.

United States v. Mississippi Valley Generating 

Co., 364 U.S. 520, 552 (1961) digested under

INVALID CONTRACTS, par. 1. Congress has enacted statutes exempting particular consultants or boards from some or all of the conflict-of-interest statutes. E.g., 68 Stat. 951 

(1954), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2203 (Supp. 

II, 1961). Thus Congress seems to take the view that, absent exemptions, consultants and board members are subject to the conflict-ofinterest statutes.

There thus appears to be no doubt that a temporary consultant or adviser is an "officer or employee" within the meaning of the conflict-of-interest statutes. There is no judicial or administrative exploration of whether an occasional or intermittent consultant or adviser is an "officer or employee" when he is not actually serving the Government. However, the application of the conflict-of-interest statutes at a given time does not appear to depend on whether a consultant or adviser is actually performing service at that time. AGO 9111A 159

EXPERTS AND CONSULTANTS-Continued 

The prohibition against the prosecution of claims in a representative capacity applies in the two post-employment statutes, 18 U.S.C. 

§ 284 and 5 U.S.C. § 99, as well as in the present employment statutes, 18 U.S.C. §§ 281 

and 283. It is extremely unlikely, as a result of the overlap among those statutes, that any case involving a claim will turn on whether a consultant was an "officer or employee" on the days he was away from Government service.

It is safe to conclude that consultants may not prosecute claims against the United States on those days in any event, or for two years following the last employment. Although the pro hibitions of 18 U.S.C. §§ 281 and 283 and 5 

U.S.C. § 99 are too broad when applied to intermittent personnel, and the prohibition of 18 U.S.C. § 284 is more appropriate, new legislation is required to resolve such matters. 

A "Government official or employee" is prohibited by 18 U.S.C. § 1914 from receiving compensation from a non-public source "in connection with" his Government service. That statute applies only to those days when a consultant actually is employed by the Government. Moreover, where a consultant serves an occasional period of a few days at most, there would seem to be no violation of the statute if he continues to receive his usual compensation from an outside employer, particularly when he is paid by the latter on a monthly or annual basis. Where the length or frequency of Government service may raise a question whether Section 1914 applies, a determination must be made whether the consultant's continued outside compensation is fairly related to past or future service for the outside employer rather than to the service for the Government. 

In the Mississippi Valley Generating Co. 

case, cited above, the Supreme Court determined that 18 U.S.C. § 434 applied to an intermittent adviser, but found it unnecessary to inquire whether the adviser was paid on the days when he transacted business as a Government representative. It must, therefore, be concluded that Section 434 by its own terms prohibits any consultant or adviser from acting for the Government in the transaction of business with a private entity in which he has a financial interest. However, the limitation of the statute to the transaction of business may not be adequate in all cases to insure proper conduct by intermittent consultants. For example, a consultant should not advise the Government with respect to contracts with a corporation in which he has a financial interest, and certainly not without informing the Government of his interest.

It is possible that a court would hold that 18 U.S.C. § 281 never applies to an intermittent consultant on days when he is not actually employed by the Government. However, in view of the salutary purposes of the section, including the discouragement of influence peddling, the following is a reasonable interpretation of how the section would be applied to an intermittent consultant: He is subject to the full impact of the section on all days when the Government is actually making use of his services. The section applies, on days when his services are not actually being used, to an intermittent consultant whose Government employment during the period of his availability occupies a substantial portion of that period or affords his principal means of livelihood. 

The section applies at all times a person is carried as a consultant if he receives compensation for his services to a private party before a Government department other than as an incidental part of his normal salary arrangement.

Present statutes are inadequate to protect the Government in all respects from the possibility of bias, corruption, or other improper activities. This is an appropriate area for presidential action designed to close loopholes which presently exist and to create more uniformity of practice by Government departments and agencies with respect to intermittent consultants. There should be issued detailed regulations that will emphasize the responsibility of consultants and advisers to disclose all outside interests and to refrain from conduct that is, or that might be thought to be, contrary to the public interest. In some instances the 

Government may be required to seek advice from particularly well-qualified scientists and technical experts in situations where there is a potential conflict of interest but where none of the existing statutes is violated. In such 160 AGO 9111A

EXPERTS AND CONSULTANTS-Continued instances the advice can and should be sought only where the responsible Government officials are fully aware of the potential conflict of interest. 

42 Ops. Att'y Gen. No. 6 (1962). 

[Note: On 9 February 1962 the President issued to the heads of executive departments and agencies a memorandum entitled "Prevent ing Conflicts of Interest on the Part of Advisers and Consultants to the Government." 27

Fed. Reg. 1341 (1962). The memorandum was designed to achieve as much uniformity as possible throughout the Government with respect to regulations applicable to intermittent consultants and advisers. The memorandum was incorporated in Department of Defense 

Directive 5500.8, 12 March 1962. The follow ing are some of the rules established by the memorandum and directive: 

It would be most advisable for a department or agency, in order to minimize the occurrence of conflicts of interest, to avoid appointing to advisory positions individuals who are employed or consulted by contractors or others having a substantial amount of business with that department or agency. However, the Government of necessity has become increasingly concerned with highly technical areas of specialization, and the number of individuals expert in those areas is frequently very small. Therefore, in many instances a department or agency will not be able to obtain a competent adviser or consultant who is not employed or consulted by firms doing business with the department or agency. An advisory group may of necessity be composed largely or wholly of persons of a common class or group whose employers may benefit from the advice given. In such circumstances particular care should be exercised to exclude from the consultant's or adviser's duties his employer's or client's contracts or other transactions with the Government. 

The following rules should be employed with respect to 18 U.S.C. § 281. 

"(a) No appointment should extend beyond the end of the current fiscal year. "(b) The period of appointment to be made for a part, or all, of the fiscal year, or of the remaining part of the fiscal year, should reflect the agency's best estimate of its employment of the individual. "(c) Whether the estimate is that the consultant or adviser will be employed intermittently throughout the entire fiscal year or that part of the year which remains at the time of appointment, or throughout a shorter interval, the appointment should be made as follows: "(1) If the agency estimates that the consultant or adviser will be employed 

40 percent or more of the time. within the period designated, the individual should be carried on the rolls as a Government employee for the entire period and should be informed that he is administratively regarded as subject to Section 281 for the entire period. "(2) If the agency estimates the consultant or adviser will be employed less than 40 percent of the period designated, the individual may be carried on the rolls as an intermittent consultant or adviser pursuant to an arrangement by which he would receive implementing appointments from time to time within the period, rather than an appointment for the entire period, and the individual should be informed that he will be treated as a Government employee for purposes of Section 281 only on the day or days within the pertinent period covered by implementing appointments. "(3) If the consultant or adviser is serving more than one department or agency, he shall inform each of his arrangements with the others so that appropriate administrative measures may be effected by the departments or agencies involved. "(4) For consultative or advisory boards, individual appointments should be made for the entire fiscal year, or such other period as may be prescribed by law, and the appointee informed that insofar as his board AGO 9111A 161

EXPERTS AND CONSULTANTS-Continued membership is concerned, he will be regarded as a Government officer or employee only on the days when the board meets." 

A consultant or adviser who is subject to Section 281 only on the days he serves the Government should make every effort to avoid any personal contact with respect to negotiations for contracts or grants with the department or agency he is advising if the subject matter is related to the subject matter of his consultancy. 

Where the circumstances make achieving that goal impossible, the consultant or adviser should participate in the negotiations only with the knowledge and approval of a responsible Government official, who should note his approval in appropriate form.

A consultant or adviser who, under the foregoing rules, is subject to Section 281 only on the days he serves the Government should be barred at all times during the designated period of his availability for service from activities before a Government department or agency in relation to a matter in which the Government is interested if he is to receive compensation for such activities from a non-Governmental source in addition to or in lieu of a normal salary or fee arrangement.

It should be noted that the prohibition of Section 281 against certain compensated activities "before" a department or agency may go beyond a personal appearance at the department or agency. When he is subject to Section 

281, a consultant or adviser should not prepare or assist in preparing proposals for contracts or grants to be presented to a department or agency by or on behalf of a private firm or organization from which he receives compensation.

Because of the overlap among 18 U.S.C. §§ 283 and 284 and 5 U.S.C. § 99 a consultant or adviser is subject to 18 U.S.C.

§ 283 or one or both of 18 U.S.C. § 284 and 5 U.S.C. § 99 at all times until the end of his last period of service to the Government. For two years thereafter he would be bound by 18 U.S.C. § 284 and 5

U.S.C. § 99. 

By its terms, 18 U.S.C. § 434 prohibits a consultant or adviser during the span of his service from acting for the Government in the transaction of business with any business entity in the profits of which he has an interest. It is in the best interest of the Government to extend the policy of this section beyond the literal statutory language. "Accordingly, an adviser or consultant should be disqualified from the performance of duties involving the transaction of business with, or the rendering of advice which will have a direct and predictable effect upon the interests of, a business entity by which he is employed, or to which he renders consultant service, or in which he has a financial interest." [Emphasis that of the President.]

However, he need not be precluded from rendering general advice from which no preference or advantage might be gained by any particular business entity. A non-profit organization or educational institution shall be a "business entity" for the purposes of this paragraph. 

Regardless whether he receives payment from the Government, a consultant or adviser is subject to the prohibition in 18 U.S.C. § 1914 against receiving compensation "in connection with" his Government service from a source other than the Federal Government or a State, county, or municipality. Where a consultant or adviser serves occasionally and for short periods, he may continue to receive his usual compensation from an outside private employer. Continuation of outside private compensation during a period of as much as 30 days a year of Government service would ordinarily be permissible on the assumption that the compensation is not "in connection with" his Government services but a part of his normal salary arrangements with the private employer. 

However, if the length of service exceeds those limits, a determination must be made whether the compensation is related to the consultant's or adviser's service to the Government and thus improper. The chief legal officer of the department or agency should be asked to examine the facts and make a recommendation.

If a consultant or adviser is appointed pursuant to a statute exempting him from one or more of the conflict-of-interest laws, he must secure permission of the head of the department or the agency concerned before taking any action that, but for the exemption, would be within any of those statutes. That permission may not be given unless there is a finding that 162 AGO 9111A

FACILITIES CONTRACTS 

the consultant's or adviser's proposed action is consistent with the Government's interests. 

Intermittent consultants and advisers are of course subject to the elementary rules that exist for the conduct of public business. The first principle of ethical behavior for the intermittent consultant or adviser is that he must refrain from any use of his public office that is motivated by, or gives the appearance of being motivated by, the desire for private gain for himself or persons with whom he has family, business, or financial ties. It matters not whether the desired gain is to be at the Government's expense. Thus a consultant or adviser may not use inside information as the basis for speculation and must be careful in his personal financial activities to avoid any appearance of acting on the basis of information obtained in the course of Government duties. A consultant or adviser may utilize in his non-Government employment information pertinent to his Government services that is generally available to any affected industry. However, information not generally available to persons outside the Government may not be used by a consultant or adviser for the special benefit of an entity that employs or retains him or in which he has a financial interest.

Occasionally, after a man is designated a Government consultant or adviser he is requested by a private enterprise to act in a similar capacity for the enterprise. Where the consultant or adviser has reason to believe that the request for his services is motivated by a desire of the private employer to secure inside information, a choice must be made between the private and the Government position. Whether or not he accepts the private position, the consultant or adviser should discuss the matter with the chief legal officer of his Government department or agency.

The departments and agencies should discourage the practice by private enterprises or organizations of urging the appointment of particular individuals to Government consultancies. 

Any initiative in connection with the appointment of consultants, or in securing the names of qualified persons, should come from the Government.

An adviser or consultant may not use his position in any way to coerce, or give the appearance of coercing, another person to provide any financial benefit to him or to persons with whom he has family, business, or financial connections. Nor may he receive or solicit anything of value as a gift, gratuity, or favor for himself or for persons with whom he has family, business, or financial ties if (1) he has reason to believe the gift would not be made but for his position with the Government, or (2) the acceptance of the gift would result in, or give the appearance of resulting in, his loss of complete independence and impartiality in serving the Government.

In connection with the appointment of an adviser or consultant each military department or defense agency shall (1) require him to file before appointment a statement setting forth his Government employment and, as prescribed by the rules summarized above, his private employment and financial interests; (2) determine whether the number of days he will be expected to work for any Government agency during the period covered by the appointment will be forty percent or more of the normal Government working days during the period; (3) bring to his attention DOD Directive 5500.8, 12 March 

1962, and the accompanying memorandum of the President; and (4) provide him with advice whether, for the purpose of the President's memorandum, the consultant or adviser will be considered a Government employee during the entire period covered by his appointment, or only on the days on which he performs Government service.

The DOD Directive, which was effective immediately, does not cover (1) physicians, dentists, and allied medical specialists performing care and service to patients; (2) veterinarians providing veterinary service to animals; and (3) lecturers participating in educational ac tivities.]

Executed Upon the Approval of the Facilities 

Contract. The Army Signal Corps has a par tially constructed micrometeorological wind tunnel at Colorado State University, completion of which is deemed essential to a Signal Corps research and development program. 

Completion of the tunnel requires the acquisition or construction by, or furnishing to, the University of certain additional facilities at a cost of $275,195, a substantial part of which represents the cost of nondisposable, nonseverable facilities. At the present time, there is no research and development contract in effect which requires the use of the tunnel, but an R&D contract requiring the use of the tunnel is in final form and will be executed upon the approval of the facilities contract by the 

Assistant Secretary of the Army (Logistics). 

Although the facilities contract requires the approval of the Secretary prior to becoming effective, the R&D contract does not. The question presented is whether the facilities contract may be approved by the Secretary pursuant to 

10 U.S.C. § 2353 without an existing contract for research and development for the performance of which the facilities are necessary. The legislative history of 10 U.S.C. § 2353 supports the position that the facilities contract may be approved prior to execution of the R&D contract on the strength of the existing research and development program requiring use of the facilities, but the matter is not free from doubt. 

On the understanding that an R&D contract requiring the use of the facilities is in final form and will be executed when the facilities contract has been approved by the Secretary, the latter may be approved by the Secretary under the authority of 10 U.S.C. § 2353.

Section 4241 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 

imposes a tax of twenty percent of dues and membership fees paid to any social, athletic, or sporting club or organization. In June 1961 

an Internal Revenue Service agent raised the question whether the Pentagon Officers'

Athletic Center (POAC) was subject to Section 

4241. See JAGT 1961/6688, 16 Jun 1961. The

Deputy Secretary of Defense requested the Commissioner of Internal Revenue to issue a ruling that the POAC was not subject to Section 4241. See JAGT 1961/7298, 25 Sep 1961.

The Judge Advocate General notified DCSPER 

and the Commanding General, MDW, of the following reply, dated 30 October 1961, from the Commissioner of Internal Revenue. 

Held, the POAC is not a social, athletic, or sporting club or organization within the pur view of Section 4241. Generally the IRS has held that Section 4241 does not apply to officers' and noncommissioned officers' clubs, open messes, and the like that are operated at military or naval establishments, occupy facilities constructed or acquired out of funds appropriated for military or naval purposes, and are supervised and controlled by military or naval authorities. Those clubs and similar organizations in most instances have social, athletic, or sporting features. They are supported by receipts from dues or membership fees, or the sale of refreshments, food, and services, together with funds from other nonappropriated fund activities. However, these features and the source of revenue of the organizations are incidental to the predominantly military or naval purpose. 

The POAC, although having membership classifications and limitations, is under the direct command jurisdiction of the Command ing General of the MDW. The POAC's activities are conducted in facilities acquired through funds appropriated for military purposes. The 

POAC offers facilities to implement programs of the Armed Forces to maintain physical fitness and morale. An annual audit of the 

POAC's funds is required to be made by Headquarters, MDW. Supervisory and command personnel are assigned by the Commanding 

General.
