Prohibition of Unauthorized Advanced Payments Not Violated by Payment Under Total Costs Clause Even Though Unliquidated Progress Payments Already Exceed Fair Value of Work Accomplished on Undelivered Portion of Contract. (JAGT) See ADVANCE PAYMENTS (par. 1) 4. Under Partial Payments Clause in Prime Contract, Government Obtained Title to Material Prime Contractor Ordered Shipped Direct ly to Subcontractor. After receiving a formallyadvertised contract for the supply of napalm bombs, the D Co. entered into a subcontract with the defendant for some aluminum parts. 

The subcontract bound the defendant to the terms and agreements of the prime contract. 

The prime contract was subsequently amended to provide for the making of partial payments to the D Co. The amendment stated in part: 

Upon the making of any partial payment under this contract, title to all parts, materials, inventories, work in process and nondurable tools *** shall forthwith vest in the government; and title to all like property thereafter acquired or produced *** shall vest in the government forthwith upon said acquisition or production * *

The D Co. ordered aluminum that was shipped directly to the defendant, and the Government made a partial payment to the D Co. for the cost of the aluminum. After the D Co. was adjudicated to be bankrupt, the Government sued the defendant (1) to replevy some aluminum possessed by the defendant, and (2) to recover the proceeds of some aluminum sold by the defendant. The defendant argued, first, that the "Partial Payments" amendment was not binding on the defendant; second, that the aluminum items involved were not "materials ***required or produced by the contractor for the performance of [the] Contract, and properly chargeable thereto under sound accounting practices." The federal district court where suit was brought granted the Government's motion for summary judgment, and the defendant appealed. 

Held, judgment affirmed. First, under the express terms of the "Partial Payments" provision, the Government and the D Co. agreed that when a payment was made to the D Co., title to the material involved would vest in the Government immediately. There is no am- biguity in the words that title would "forthwith vest in the Government," and there is no reason why that provision should not be enforced. The defendant claims that it was an "innocent purchaser of the aluminum for value and without notice" and that the title to the aluminum never vested in the Government. The defendant stresses that its proposal to the D Co. for a subcontract stated, "We agree to purchase the material * * * from the [D Co.] * 

The defendant argues that the subsequent transactions by which the aluminum was delivered to the defendant and placed in warehouses in the defendant's name constituted a sale and transfer of the aluminum to the defendant. However, there is no contention that the defendant had any title to the aluminum except what was obtained from the D Co. By the express terms of the "Partial Payments" 

provision, the Government, not the D Co. had title to the aluminum. Second, there is no dispute that the aluminum involved was "required for the performance of the prime contract."

The defendant contends, however, that the aluminum was not "properly chargeable" to the prime contract "under, sound accounting practices." It is true that if the material had become incorporated into the finished product, the cost of the material would not have been separately charged but would have been a part of the charge for the product. Nevertheless, upon the bankruptcy of the D Co., all work under the contract and the subcontract ceased and thereafter the aluminum involved here had to be separately dealt with upon any accounting. 

Shepard Engineering Co. v. United States, 287 F. 2d 737 (8th Cir. 1961). 

[Note: The defendant's petition for rehearing was denied, 289 F. 2d 681 (8th Cir. 1961). The only new argument presented by the petition was that the Government, even if it had received title, was estopped to claim title after investing the D Co. with such evidence of ownership as to mislead the defendant, a good faith purchaser for value. The court relied on the doctrine that the United States will not be estopped by acts of its agents even where there are grounds for estoppel. See, e.g., Utah Power & Light Co. v. United States, 243 U.S. 389, 408, 409 (1917); Stone v. United States, 286 F. 2d 

56, 59 (8th Cir. 1961). The court also indicated 

166 AGO 9111A

GENERAL SERVICES ADMINISTRATION 

that the grounds for an estoppel were not present because there was nothing in the record to indicate that the Government, directly or indirectly, took any action calculated to show that the aluminum belonged to the D Co. or otherwise to mislead Shepard.] 

5. Comptroller General Approves SBA's Standby Loan Program Providing 100% Deferred Participation by SBA in Private Loans to Small Business Investment Corporations. 

Section 303 of the Small Business Investment Act of 1958, 72 Stat. 692 (1958), 15 U. S. C. § 

683 (1958), as amended in 1961, 75 Stat. 752 

(b) To encourage the formation and growth of small business investment companies, the [Small Business] Administration is authorized (but only to the extent that the necessary funds are not available to the company involved from private sources on reasonable terms) to lend funds to such companies through the purchase of their obligations which shall bear interest at such rate, and contain such other terms, as the Administration may fix. 

The total amount of obligations of any one company which may be purchased and outstanding at any one time by the Administration under this subsection (including commitments to purchase such obligations) shall not exceed 50 percent of the paid-in capital and surplus of such company or $4,000,000, whichever is less. All loans made by the Administration under this subsection shall be of such sound value as reasonably to assure repayment. [Emphasis added to the 1961 amend ments.] 

As part of the implementation of that section, the SBA developed a standby program to encourage private financing of small business investment corporations. Under the program the 

SBA assigned a corporation's note to a bank, which assumed an obligation to disburse funds to the corporation when directed by the SBA to do so. The agreement between the SBA and the bank provided that the bank could reassign the note to SBA at any time and SBA would thereupon pay the bank the outstanding principal under the note. The SBA could also require a reassignment of the note. Some banks doubted the SBA's authority to create the standby program, so the SBA Administrator asked the Comptroller General whether the program was legally proper. 

Held, the program is proper. In other small business programs Congress has given specific authority for loans by the SBA in participation or deferred participation with private lenders. 

72 Stat. 387 (1958), as amended, 15 U.S.C. 

§ 636 (a) and (b); 72 Stat. 697 (1958), as amended, 15 U.S.C. § 696. There is a general statement of policy that the small business investment program should "be carried out in such manner as to insure the maximum participation of private financing sources." 72 Stat. 

689 (1958), 15 U.S.C. § 661 (1958). However, there is no other indication in the 1958 act or its amendments that Congress intended to authorize such deferred participation with private lenders for Section 303 (b) loans as is provided for by the standby program. Moreover, where 

Congress has given authority for participation loans for small business programs, the permissible amount of deferred participation has been limited to ninety per cent of the loan balance outstanding at the time of disbursement. It would ordinarily be difficult to argue that the general statement of policy in 15 U.S.C. § 661 

is authority for making 100 per cent deferred participation loans when a portion of the same act (15 U.S.C. § 696) specifically gives authority to participation loans limited to ninety per cent of the outstanding balance.

However, the legislative history of the 1961 

amendments to Section 303 (b) clearly shows that Congress intended the standby program should be continued. The legislative record makes manifest that the omission of specific authority to follow the standby procedure was not due to lack of congressional intent to provide the authority but rather to the fact that both the SBA and Congress did not believe an explicit provision was required. If Congress had disapproved the standby program, the disapproval would have been expressed either in the statute or in the record. Failure to express disapproval, together with the positive statements of approval in the record, requires the conclusion that the program is not inconsistent with the intent of the statute. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-149685, 4 September 1962.

Consistent With Execution of Functions and 

Responsibilities. In accord with the invitation for bids, the Tennessee Valley Authority refused to consider a bid which was physically received after the time set for bid opening. The rejected bidder protested on the ground that the delay was due solely to the mails and, under

Services Act of 1949, as amended, 68 Stat.

1126 

(1954), 40 U.S.C. §§ 471-486 (1958), and the implementing Federal Procurement Regula tions. These regulations are applicable to all federal agencies to the extent specified in the 

Act. FPR § 1-1.004. While the basic policy is to establish uniform procedures for all Government agencies and wholly owned Government corporations, exemptions are provided to the extent that literal compliance will impair the performance of particular functions and responsibilities. With regard to the TVA, section 

602 (d) (12) of the Act provides:

Nothing in this Act shall impair or affect any authority of . . . the Tennessee Valley Authority with respect to nonpersonal services . . . and with respect to any property acquired or to be acquired for or in connection with any program of processing, manufacture, production, or force account construction; Provided, That the Tennessee Valley

Authority shall to the maximum extent that it may deem practicable, consistent with the fulfillment of the purpose of its program and the effective and efficient conduct of its business, coordinate its operations with the requirements of this Act and the policies and regulations prescribed pursuant thereto. 

The intent is that consistent and uniform procedures shall be followed except to the limited extent that agency programs are impaired or affected. The Act does not authorize a deviation based upon a unilateral determination that a particular regulation is impractical or incorrect. The TVA should give further consideration to the reasons justifying a variance from the Federal Procurement Regulations and should avail itself of the procedure for obtaining deviations in matters which are peculiar to 

TVA operations. See FPR § 1-1.009.

See INVALID CONTRACTS (par. 2) 4. Except in Special Circumstances the Government Should Not Contract With a Corporation Controlled by Government Employees. Air 

Force employees own 897 of 1104 shares of stock in the S Corp. and constitute all of the officers and a majority of the corporation's directors. The Air Force employees perform substantially the same services for the corporation that they perform for the Government. The S 

Corp. wished to do business with an Army installation, mostly through small purchase pro cedures (ASPR Section III, Part 6), but perhaps through an occasional small value, formally advertised contract. The Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army (I&L) (Log- 168 AGO 9111A

GOVERNMENT-FURNISHED PROPERTY 

istics) requested a decision about the propriety of contracting with the S Corp. 

Held, the contracting would be improper.

Contracts between the Government and its employees have long been criticized on the grounds of possible favoritism or preferential treatment. Such contracts should not be made except for the most cogent reasons. See, e.g., 27 Comp. Gen. 735 (1948). The same policy has been applied to municipal corporations who wish to contract with their employees. See, e.g., 63 C.J.S. Municipal Corporations (1950). 

That policy has resulted in the invalidation of a municipal contract where a municipal officer or employee is a member, stockholder or employee of the contracting company. See, e.g., 63

C.J.S. Municipal Corporations (1950). 

This case does not require a determination whether the holding of a small amount of stock by Government employees is sufficient to bring a corporation within the rule that the Government should not contract with its employees.

The ownership of eighty per cent of the stock of S Corp., and the holding of so many positions as officers and directors, by Government employees places the corporation in the same relationship that the individual employees have with the Government with respect to the making of contracts. A contract between the 

Government and a corporation owned and controlled like the S Corp. would afford the same grounds for complaint as to alleged favoritism and possible fraud that would be afforded by a contract between the Government and its individual employees. Such a contract should be authorized only in those exceptional cases where the needs of the Government cannot reasonably be otherwise supplied. Since there is no indication in this case that the S Corp.'s products are unique, contracting with that firm would be improper. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-148092, 28 February 1962.

(ASBCA) See CHANGES (par. 6) 2. Severin Doctrine Does Not Apply to Government Delays Under Government-Furnished Property Clause, ASPR 13-502. (ASBCA) See SUBCONTRACTS (par. 4) 3. Failure of Government Timely To Deliver Government-Furnished Property Held To Be Excusable Cause of Contractor's Failure To 

Perform. An Army invitation for bids on a fixed-price contract for the supply of 206,000 drifle sight assemblies contained the standard 

Government-Furnished Property Clause 

(ASPR 13-502), which stated in part: 

The Government shall deliver to the Contractor, for use in connection with and under the terms of this contract, the property described in the 

Schedule or specifications. . . . The delivery or performance dates for the supplies or services to be funished by the Contractor under this contract are based upon the expectation that Governmentfurnished property suitable for use will be delivered to the Contractor at the times stated in the Schedule or, if not so stated, in sufficient time to enable the Contractor to meet such delivery or performance dates.

However, the invitation also stated that fifteen items of special tooling, weighing about 300 pounds, were available for use by the successful bidder on a "no charge loan basis" and "where is and as is." The invitation stated that no representation was made by the Government that the tools would produce the sight assemblies in accordance with the contract drawings. 

Bidders were invited to inspect the tooling and to indicate in their bids whether they desired to use it. The low bidder stated in his bid that he desired to use the tooling. After receiving the contract, the low bidder requested that the

Government ship him the tooling. It was delivered thirty days after it was orally requested and about twenty-five days after the Government had received a formal written request. 

About forty days after the tooling was delivered, the first deliveries under the contract were due but were not made. The Government shortly afterwards terminated the contract for default. An appeal was timely taken to the 

ASBCA. 

AGO 9111A 169

GOVERNMENT-FURNISHED PROPERTY-Continued 

Held, appeal sustained. The principal purpose of the contract, to the extent it pertained to Government-owned tooling, was to make available to the successful bidder, without charge and without warranty as to suitability, any or all of the fifteen items of special tooling if the contractor requested them. There is no requirement that a formal request for the tooling be made; even if there had been such a requirement, the Government's delay of twenty-five days is clearly excessive by at least ten days. The low bidder has offered evidence that his failure to perform in accordance with the contract was caused by the Government's failure timely to deliver the tooling. By his evidence he has sustained the burden of proving that his failure to make deliveries as promised in the contract was the result of a cause beyond his control and without his fault or negligence. Accordingly, the termination will be deemed to have been for the convenience of the Government.

4. Government Required, by Clause Promis ing Cloth "Suitable for Use," To Reimburse

The plaintiff's Army contracts for the supply of one million field jackets required the Government to furnish cloth pursuant to a clause providing in part:

Government-Furnished Property (a) The Gov ernment shall deliver to the Contractor, for use in connection with and under the terms of this contract, the property which the schedule or the specifications state the Government will furnish (hereinafter referred to as "Government-Furnished property"). The delivery or performance dates for the supplies or services to be furnished by the Contractor under this contract are based upon the expectation that Government-Furnished property of a type suitable for use will be delivered to the Contractor at the times stated in the schedule or if not so stated in sufficient time to enable the Contractor to meet such delivery or performance dates. . . . The Government shall not be liable to the Contractor for damages or loss of profit by reason of any delay in delivery of or failure to deliver any or all of the Government-Furnished property, except that in case of such delay or failure upon the written request of the Contractor, an equitable adjustment shall be made in the delivery or performance dates, or price, or both, and in any other contractual provision affected thereby, in accordance with the procedures provided for in the clause of this contract entitled "Changes." [Emphasis in original.] 

The only description of the cloth by the contracts was "Cloth, Cotton, Sateen, 8.5 oz. OD- 

7"; the Department of Defense did, however, have a military specification controlling the manufacture of cloth of that description. The cloth delivered to the plaintiff met that specification, but most was so hard and "boardy" that the plaintiff experienced considerable difficulty in folding and sewing the cloth. The

Government recognized that problems were caused by the hard cloth and promised that softer cloth would be provided. The promise was fulfilled as to only a small amount of cloth. 

The plaintiff filed a claim with the contracting officer for additional compensation for extra costs caused by the hardness of the cloth. The claim was denied. The ASBCA affirmed, holding that there had been no showing that the cloth furnished was unsuitable. Topkis Broth ers Co., ASBCA No. 2382 (23 Aug 1955). The plaintiff sued in the Court of Claims.

Held, the plaintiff may recover. The Govern ment interprets the "suitable for use" phrase in the Government-Furnished Property Clause as requiring only that the cloth furnished be specification fabric from which the jackets contracted for could be manufactured. Under that interpretation, the phrase "suitable for use" in the second sentence of the clause is meaningless, for the first sentence makes clear that the Government was to furnish specification cloth that was to be used, and could be used, to manufacture the jackets. A preferable interpretation, one that will give meaning to all the provisions of the clause, is that the Government undertook to furnish cloth that not only met the specifications established for that type of cloth but was also "suitable for use." Suitability taken in context, refers to the appropriateness of the Government-furnished property for use in the manufacture of the jackets. This interpretation finds support in Gillsam Mfg. Co., ASBCA No. 

4461 (16 Sep 1958), 58-2 BCA 1924, and Globe

Crayon Co., ASBCA No. 1496 (11 Jun 1954). 

Whether property is actually "suitable for use" is a question of fact to be decided in light 170 AGO 9111A

GOVERNMENT PROPERTY 

of the circumstances of each case. The ASBCA found there had been no satisfactory showing that the cloth furnished the plaintiff was not "suitable for use." However, the plaintiff has discharged the burden of showing that the Board's conclusion was "fraudulent or capricious or arbitrary or so grossly erroneous as necessarily to imply bad faith, or . . . not supported by substantial evidence." 68 Stat. 81 

(1954), 41 U.S.C. § 321 (1958). Suitability of cloth for the manufacture of garments on a mass production basis is not necessarily established by a showing that the cloth met the Government's specification for the particular fabric. 

The record is clear that the plaintiff had considerable difficulties with the cloth, and the remedial measures the plaintiff was able to take were not too successful. There is no indication that the hardness of the cloth was not the cause of the difficulties or that the plaintiff was lax in trying to cope with them. Although aware of the difficulties, the Government apparently could do nothing except promise softer cloth.

Topkis Brothers Co. v. United States, 297 F. 

2d 536 (Ct. Cl. 1961). 

[Note: The Government's motion for recon sideration and clarification in the instant case was denied. 299 F. 2d 952 (Ct. Cl. 1962). The motion had expressed the fear that the opinion tended to create a new cause of action. The 

Court of Claims said that the fear was unfounded because the basis for the plaintiff's recovery was an affirmative obligation clearly expressed in the contract. The court indicated that its interpretation of the phrase "suitable for use" was not new, as the Government contended, but rather was in harmony with the interpretation adopted by the ASBCA in earlier cases.]

INDEMNITY 

1. Review Made of the Position of the Office of the Judge Advocate General on Problems

Relating to Indemnification of Contractors Against Ultrahazardous Risks. The following summarizes the position of the Office of the Judge Advocate General on various issues in volving product liability: 

a. The problem. Defense items like nuclear materials, missiles, and special fuels involve the risk of enormous loss of life, limb, and property. A Government contractor may be subject to absolute liability for any harm resulting from ultrahazardous activities. Restatement, Torts 519 (1938). A contractor's negligence may be the basis of liability, under the so-called "product liability" rule, for harm resulting from property on which title has passed to the 

Government. MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co., 

217 N.Y. 382, 111 N.E. 1050 (1916). Perhaps a manufacturer of all or some integral part of a hazardous item might be held absolutely liable on a combination of the absolute liability and product liability rules. Government contractors have a legitimate concern with protecting themselves against financial ruin by catastrophes. 

The Army also has significant interests. Obligating the Government to pay potentially enormous sums is hardly very desirable, even if legally permissible. On the other hand, when adequate insurance is not available at reason- AGO 9111A 171

INDEMNITY-Continued able rates, prospective contractors may refuse to perform unless the Government provides indemnity.

The basic legal problem is created by the following statutes: 

No contract or purchase on behalf of the United 

States shall be made, unless the same is authorized by law or is under an appropriation adequate to its fulfillment. . . . Rev. Stat. 3732 (1875), as amended, 41 U.S.C. § 11 (1958). 

No officer or employee of the United States shall make or authorize an expenditure from or create or authorize an obligation under any appropriation or fund in excess of the amount available therein; nor shall any such officer or employee involve the Government in any contract or other obligation, for the payment of money for any purpose, in advance of appropriations made for such purpose, unless such contract or obligation is authorized by law. Rev. Stat. 3679 (1875), as amended, 31

U.S.C. § 665 (a) (1958). 

Since a contractor's losses from ultrahazardous activities might exceed available appropriations, the quoted statutes would be violated if the Government provides indemnity without authorization by law. 

b. Authorization by 10 U.S.C. § 2306. The Office of the Judge Advocate General has held that, in connection with cost contracts permitted by 10 U.S.C. § 2306, there may legally be an agreement by the Government to indemnify the contractor for any losses suffered, whether for liability to third persons or for damages to contractor-owned property. JAGT 1952/5074 

(13 Jun 1952). The rationale of the cited opinion is that 10 U.S.C. § 2306 is a contract authorization act within the meaning of 41

U.S.C. § 11 and 31 U.S.C. § 665 (a). 

The Insurance-Liability to Third Persons 

Clause (ASPR 7-203.22) in cost contracts appears sufficiently broad to cover product liability. It has been held that the Government's liability under that clause is not limited by the total amount obligated under the contract or by the availability of appropriated funds when the liability is incurred. JAGT 1955/2767 (15 

Jun 1955). This holding applies regardless of the presence of the Limitation of Cost Clause (ASPR 7-203.3). JAGT 1957/7982 (25 Oct 

1957) [digested in DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 15, par. 11]. This view of the effect of the Limi tation of Cost Clause has been criticized. See, for example, Ms. Comp. Gen. B-141387 (29 

Mar 1960), where the Comptroller General indicated in passing that the clause "in effect imposes a contractual ceiling on the obligation of the Government to reimburse the contractor for incurred costs." See also inclosures to 

JAGT 1957/751 (24 Dec 1957); memorandum of Assistant General Counsel, Fiscal Matters, OSD (Comp), inclosed with JAGT 1958/7778 

(10 Nov 1958). 

It appears permissible, though there is no case specifically in point, to include an indemnity clause in a fixed-price contract, provided the determination required by 10 U.S.C. § 2306 for a cost contract can be made with respect to that clause. The same view is expressed in 

Navy Contract Law § 8.51 (2d ed. 1959), though under the Navy's approach available appropriations set a ceiling on Government liability. 

c. Authorization by 10 U.S.C. § 2354. The military departments are authorized to indemnify research or development contractors against claims and losses arising out of direct performance of a Government contract and from a risk the contract defines as unusually hazardous. 70A Stat. 134 (1956), 10 U.S.C. 

§ 2354 (1958). The approval of the Secretary or the Assistant Secretary of the Army (R&D) is required for including the clause. There is no known implementation of the statutory power to redelegate approving authority to "the chief, and one assistant to the chief, of any technical service, bureau, or office."

The contract must be for "research or development, or both." The Office of the Judge 

Advocate General has concurred in interpreting these words to include a contract using RDT&E, A, funds for the procurement of specialized spare parts for use with a nuclear power plant being designed and constructed by the spare parts supplier under a separate research and development contract. JAGT 

1961/7230 (6 Sep 1961). The concurrence was based on the theory that 10 U.S.C. § 2354 should be read in the light of 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (11), relating to negotiation of contracts for "property . . . that [the Secretary] determines to be for experimental, developmental, or research work, or for making or furnishing 172 AGO 9111A

INDEMNITY-Continued property for experiment, test, development or research." 

Section 2354 (a) states that a contract "may provide that the United States will indemnify the contractor against ."; it is clear that these words authorize the Government to obligate itself to indemnify a contractor against the type of losses listed to the full extent even though the required payments may exceed available appropriations. This is confirmed by 

Section 2354 (d), which provides that payments under Section 2354 (a) may be made from: (1) funds obligated for the performance of the contract concerned; (2) funds available for research or development, or both, and not otherwise obligated; or (3) funds appropriated for those payments. 

See, e.g., JAGT 1961/7230 (6 Sep 1961);

JAGT 1960/6719 (17 Jun 1960). The Comp troller General, however, has suggested that the statute does not clearly indicate that available appropriations do not establish a limit. 

See, e.g., Ms. Comp. Gen. B-141387 (29 Mar 

1960). Nevertheless, in the cited opinion the 

Comptroller General recognized that at least two of the military departments presently were interpreting 10 U.S.C. § 2354 as authority for indemnity agreements without limit as to amount or availability of appropriations and that Congress intended the statute to be a contract authorization act to the full extent of statutorily recognized losses. The General 

Counsel for both the Navy and the Air Force view the statute as a contract authorization act up to the full amount of recognized losses incurred by a contractor.

The Office of the Judge Advocate General has taken the position that the statute's indemnity benefits may be extended to subcontractors. 

See, e.g., par. c of DEFINITIONS-FURTHER

PROVISIONS, inclosed with JAGT 1961/7230 (6 Sep 1961). The General Counsel of the 

Air Force has agreed. Lyons, Government

Indemnification against Unusually Hazardous Risks for Military Research and Development 

Contractors, 17 Fed. B.J. 314, 326, n. 38. Since the reason for indemnifying prime contractors, reluctance of prospective contractors to undertake ultrahazardous work, applies as well to subcontractors, 10 U.S.C. § 2354 should be interpreted liberally as applicable to subcon tractors. The Comptroller General has sug gested that the matter be clarified in connection with indemnification legislation proposed for 

NASA. See Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143241 (26 Jul 

1960); Ms. Comp. Gen. B-141387 (29 Mar 1960).

The limitation of indemnity under 10 U.S.C. $ 2354 to losses that "arise out of the direct performance of the contract" (emphasis added) raises the question whether product liability may be indemnified. The Office of the Judge 

Advocate General, the Air Force General Coun sel, and the Navy General Counsel have held that indemnity may be extended to include product liability. See inclosure to JAGT 1960/ 

6719 (17 Jun 1960); inclosure to JAGT 1958/ 

3142 (9 Apr 1958); Navy Contract Law § 8.53 (2d ed. 1959). Product liability falls within the general purpose of the statute and would be a proper interpretation of the term "performance." 

Section 2354 has been held to authorize indemnity against losses to a contractor's property even though caused by his employee's negligence, but not against "claims by third persons or for loss of or damage to the property of the Contractor which results from willful misconduct or lack of good faith on the part of any of the Contractor's directors or officers. ." Par. (a) of Indemnification Clause attached to JAGT 1961/7390 (9 Oct 

1961). Under Section 2354 indemnity is proper only for "unusually hazardous" risks. The Comptroller General has criticized the lack of further definition of this phrase. It is recommended that implementing regulations should not define what specific risks are unusually hazardous, but should give a definition in general terms that will obviate the need for future. amendments covering risks not previously known. One solution would be to define the term as "ultrahazardous activity" as defined in Re statement, Torts § 835j (1938). 

Apparently the only implementation of 10

U.S.C. § 2354 is by the Navy in NPD 10-351. 

The Comptroller General has criticized the lack AGO 9111A 173

INSPECTION & ACCEPTANCE 

of implementation. The ASPR Committee ap parently at one time informally approved a clause. It is now proposed to resubmit the whole problem of indemnification to that Committee. 

d. Authorization by P.L. 85-804. Public 

Law 85-804 provides statutory authority to indemnify all Army contractors when the Secretary makes a determination that indemnity would facilitate the national defense. 72 Stat. 

972 (1958), 50 U.S.C. § 1431 (1958). The congressional hearings are replete with statements that the statute is authority to indemnify. 

The hearings indicate that the authority is sufficiently broad to provide indemnification for product liability. Hearings before Subcommit tee No. 4 of the House Committee on the Judici ary on H.R. 12894, 85th Cong. 2d Sess., ser. 

20, at 10 (1958). It has been held that indemnity for product liability is so authorized. 

JAGT 1961/7305 (25 Sep 1961). No discussion of other problems, such as indemnification of subcontractors, has been found. However, the language of Public Law 85-804 is at least equally broad as 10 U.S.C. § 2354. 

The implementation of Public Law 85-804 by 

Executive Order No. 10789, 23 Fed. Reg. 8897 (1958), presents a serious question about the extent to which the clear statutory authority to indemnify may be used by the Army. The 

Executive order reads in part: 

• .. ." 

1. The Department of Defense is authorized, with in the limits of the amounts appropriated and the contract authorization provided therefore [sic], to enter into contracts and to make advance payments thereon. [Emphasis added].

Executive orders implementing Title II of the First War Powers Act, the precursor of Public 

Law 85-804, contained different language, which was interpreted as providing unlimited authority to indemnify, though recognizing that payments could be made only from available appropriations. JAGT 1958/2851 (29 Apr 

1958); SPJGC 1944/10016 (5 Sep 1944).

Moreover, reference to authority to make payments other than advance payments was contained in the same section of the earlier executive orders as the language interpreted as justification for indemnification. However, only advance payments are authorized by Section 1 of the current executive order. Thus, an interpretation of the words italicized above as limiting only payments appears strained. The 

Navy General Counsel holds that the executive orders do not permit indemnification greater than the available appropriation. Navy Con tract Law § 8.51 (2d ed. 1959). It has been held that there is no authority under Public 

Law 85-804 and implementing regulations to enter into or amend a contract unless the increased funding requirements under the contract can be absorbed within the total amount of construction authorized in the mentioned current and future Military Construction Acts, plus the cost variations permitted by certain of those acts, and within the appropriations, if any, remaining available for that purpose under the mentioned current and future Ap propriation Acts. 

JAGT 1961/5783 (19 Jan 1961). 

JAGT 1961/7603 (19 Dec 1961). 

INSPECTION & ACCEPTANCE 1. Latent Defects Are Those Existing at Time of Acceptance Which Are Not Known to the Inspector and Cannot Be Discovered by a 

Reasonable Inspection. In March 1953, the con tractor agreed to manufacture 2,600 torque drive assemblies for incorporation into the M45 multiple machine gun mount. The assemblies were to be inspected and accepted at the contractor's plant in Detroit, Michigan. The contract provided that: (d) The inspection and test by the Government of any supplies. . . does not relieve the Contractor from any responsibility regarding defects... which may be discovered prior to final acceptance. Except as otherwise provided in this contract, final acceptance shall be conclusive except as regards latent defects, fraud, or such gross mistakes as amount to fraud. [See ASPR 7-103.5 (d) (14 May 

1958)] 

During the assembly process, dimensional defects were discovered in some of the units. 

To compensate for these errors the contractor filled space with washers and shims and performed other nonspecification tooling operations. No effort was made to conceal the defects however, and the Government inspector was apparently aware that compensating devices were being used. While all but one of 174 AGO 9111A

INSPECTION & ACCEPTANCE-Continued the defects could have been discovered by measurement, the inspector's examination was essentially visual. All assemblies were accepted prior to 20 February 1954. Four years later the contracting officer rejected 516 assemblies on the ground that they contained latent defects. and that the inspector's acceptance had been obtained by fraud. The contractor appealed.

Held, the appeal is sustained. The earlier acceptance is conclusive unless the Government can prove that latent defects existed or that fraud occurred. Cf. Neuhoff Brothers Packers,

ASBCA No. 4817, 23 March 1959, 59-1 BCA 

2138. Latent defects are those existing at the time of acceptance which cannot be discovered by a reasonable inspection. If defects could be discovered by a reasonable inspection they do not become latent because an inadequate inspection failed to reveal them. C. A. Dunham Com pany, ASBCA No. 2008, 21 October 1954. All but one defect could have been discovered if the completed units had been measured. Since the dimensional defects were serious enough to warrant rejection by the contracting officer it is reasonable to expect that measurements should have been taken before final acceptance. 

Otherwise the contract inspection provisions would be unduly restricted. While one defect could not be discovered without disassembling the unit, the inspector was aware of its existence. Clearly, a known defect cannot be a latent defect. Finally, there is no fraud here since the defects were not concealed and the contractor exerted no undue influence to induce acceptance by the inspector. 

Hercules Engineering & Mfg. Company,

ACBCA No. 4979, 9 December 1959, 59-2 BCA 

2426. [Note: For a definition of "inherent" defects which relieve a contractor from responsibility under an Air Force construction contract 

Guaranty clause, see J. S. Brown-E. F. Olds

Plumbing and Heating Corp., ASBCA No. 

4974, 30 April 1959, 59-1 BCA 2209, DA Pam 

715-50-2, p. 234, par. 5.]

3. If Contracting Officer Accepts Goods Know ing They Do Not Conform to Specifications and 

Without Requiring Price Reduction Under Inspection Clause, He May Not Later Take a

Credit for the Government Pursuant to the 

Changes Clause. The appellant's Army contract for producing overcoats contained the standard 

Changes (ASPR 7-103.2) and Inspection 

(ASPR 7-103.5) Clauses. During contract performance the Government inspector reported that the appellant's subcontractor was not fulfilling the contract's requirement that linings be pressed smooth with a heated iron. A formal 

Report of Deviation stated that the pressing operation had been omitted on 4,000 overcoats, but that the omission did not affect the appearance or serviceability of the end item or cause the completed overcoats to fail to meet the end-product specifications. The contracting officer issued a decision accepting the 4,000 overcoats at no price reduction. "providing the lining is smooth when finished; further providing that the appearance of the end item is not affected and meets requirements specified in applicable S.I.P."

The contracting officer apparently later claimed a price reduction under the Changes Clause for alleged savings resulting from omission of the pressing. The contractor timely appealed to the 

ASBCA. 

Held, appeal sustained. This case is controlled by the decision in Style Craft Manufacturing

Co., ASBCA No. 4465 (27 Feb 1958), 58-1 

BCA 1637. In that case the Government accepted clothing not conforming to specifications, and the contracting officer exercised neither of his rights, pursuant to subparagraph (b) of the Inspection Clause, to require correction of deficiencies or to require delivery at an equitable price reduction. The Board quoted subpara graph (d) of the Inspection Clause: 

... Except as otherwise provided in this contract, final acceptance shall be conclusive except as regards latent defects, fraud, or such gross mistakes as amount to fraud.

The Board held that the rights given the Government in subparagraph (b) must be exer- AGO 9111A 175

INTERDEPARTMENTAL PROCUREMENT 

cised before or at the time of final acceptance; otherwise, subparagraph (d) would be meaningless. In the Style Craft case, as in this, the deviations were known to the appellant and the contracting officer and, hence, could not be considered latent. In neither case was fraud alleged.

American Fashion Clothes, Inc., ASBCA 

Nos. 4159 and 4162, 14 February 1961, 61-1

BCA 2944. 

4. Warranties of Description, Fitness for a Special Purpose, and Merchantability Were Breached by Delivery of Milk Powder With Latent Infestation. (2d Cir.) See DISPUTES (par. 37) INTERDEPARTMENTAL PROCUREMENT 1. Voucher for Transfer Between Appropri ations May Not Be Certified for Payment Unless Supported by Evidence That Billed Agency 

Received and Accepted Supplies and Services From Billing Agency. The National Science 

Foundation made $25,000 available to the Army Ballistic Missile Agency for specified research during the Geophysical Year. Because the work performed was intangible, officials of NSF were unable to certify that the supplies and services had been received and rendered in accordance with the inter-agency arrangement. The NSF 

Certifying Officer requested an opinion as to whether he was authorized to certify a $25,000 voucher for payment to the Army Ordnance 

Missile Command. 

Opinion: On these facts the voucher should not be certified for payment. When reimbursements between Government agencies are involved, the authorized certifying officer of the agency billed must certify that the supplies or services furnished by the billing agency were actually received and accepted. 7 GAO Policy and Procedures Manual 4040.20. The certifying officer must insure that the facts stated are correct and that the proposed payment is lawful under the appropriation charged. 31 U.S.C. § 82c (1958); 33 Comp. Gen 650 (1954). Since the voucher in question here is unsupported by evidence that the services and materials were furnished and accepted, its certification for payment is not authorized. 23 Comp. Gen. 181 (1943). 

Where vouchers for transfers between appropriations of funds are involved, a sound receiving system to verify the receipt of supplies, materials, and services should be estab lished. 7 GAO Policy and Procedures Manual 

4070. While NSF has authority to "prescribe, with the approval of the Comptroller General of the United States, the extent to which vouchers for funds expended under contracts for scientific research shall be subject to itemization or substantiation prior to payment, without regard to the limitations of other laws relating to the expenditure of public funds and accounting therefor. . . .", 2 U.S.C. § 1870 (1958), no procedures have been filed with the General Accounting Office. In order to make a proper determination here, the certifying officer of NSF should obtain ABMA progress reports from the Department of the Army. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-141167, 29 January 1960, 39 Comp. Gen. 548.

INTEREST See also DISPUTES 1. Interest May Be Charged Contractor From Date of Contracting Officer's Unilateral Determination of Amount of Overpayment Made to Contractor, Even Though ASBCA Later Held Lower Amount Had Been Overpaid. 

The plaintiff's contract provided for a redetermination of the price after work was completed and permitted the contracting officer unilaterally to make the redetermination if he could not reach agreement with the plaintiff. On 21 

July 1955 the contracting officer unilaterally determined that the plaintiff had been overpaid $60,929.16. The plaintiff was notified to repay that sum. While the plaintiff's appeal from this determination was pending before the ASBCA, the Government withheld, as a setoff against the overpayment, $46,607.50 from amounts due the plaintiff on other contracts. On 29 July 

1957 the ASBCA issued a decision that the plaintiff had been overpaid only $45,547.46. The 

Government applied the $46,607.50 already withheld, plus $2,455.60 from another contract, to the $45,547.46 debt and to interest on that debt, computed at 5% yearly from 21 July 

1955, the date the decision appealed from was made. The plaintiff sued in a federal district 176 AGO 9111A

INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS 

court to recover the interest withheld. The 

United States' motion for summary judgment was granted, and the contractor appealed. 

Held, judgment affirmed. The crucial question, is whether, as on 21 July 1955, the plaintiff owed the United States any amount upon which interest could be charged. The plaintiff asserts that until he has exhausted his administrative remedies and a final determination was made by the ASBCA, he owed nothing or at least he was not liable for interest because the amount of the debt was unliquidated. However, on 21 

July 1955, the contracting officer, acting pursuant to the contract, unilaterally determined the amount due the Government. The government's right to interest on the overpayment is not defeated by the fact that neither the contract nor any statute at that time provided that interest could be charged on the overpayment. 

See, e.g., Billings v. United States, 232 U.S. 261, 286 (1914). The United States may recover interest on money due even though the liability was unilaterally determined. United States v. 

Philmac Mfg. Co., 192 F.2d 517 (3d Cir. 1951).

There would be no question that the plaintiff would owe interest if, without appealing to the ASBCA, the plaintiff had failed to pay the $60,929.16 assessed against him. That the plaintiff appealed makes no difference. Charging the plaintiff interest offends no equitable principle. He had the use of the government's money during the period for which he was required to pay interest. Moreover, in two analogous situations interest is charged. First, the fact that a judgment or decree is reduced on appeal does not prevent the exaction of interest upon the reduced amount from the date of the original judgment or decree. See, e.g., Bates v. Dresser, 251 U.S. 524, 531, 532 (1920). Sec ond, in the renegotiation of war contracts, interest has been held payable on excess profits from the time the Secretary of War determined unilaterally what sum was due, even though the Tax Court later reduced that sum. Ring 

Constr. Corp. v. United States, 209 F.2d 668 (8th Cir. 1954). 

Swartzbaugh Manufacturing Co. v. United 

States, 289 F.2d 81 (6th Cir. 1961). [Note: The court also held that the district court had discretion in setting the rate of interest, Royal Indemnity Co. v. United States, 313 U.S. 289, 296 (1941), and that the Government had acted properly in offsetting amounts due the plaintiff on other contracts, United 

States v. Munsey Trust Co., 332 U.S. 234, 239 (1947).] 

INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS See also CONTRACT CLAUSES, SPECI- FICATIONS & DRAWINGS 1. Where Reasonable Time Has Elapsed Since Award of Construction Contract, Contracting Officer Must Issue Notice To Proceed Even Though Work Site Is Not Ready. 

(ASBCA) See SITE CONDITIONS (par. 1) 2. ASBCA Has Jurisdiction To Determine Liability of Bailee for Pilferage of Government- Owned Goods. (ASBCA) See DISPUTES (par. 2) 3. Subcontract Terms Used To Give Prime Contract Meaning Where Not Inconsistent and Previously Approved by Contracting Officer. 

The Army awarded the contractor a fixed-pricewith-redetermination contract to provide services in the development of range facilities and range instrumentation capabilities at White 

Sands Proving Ground, New Mexico (ARIS).

The initial ceiling price of $110,000 limited costs to $100,000 and allowed a profit of $10,000. Because of insufficient funds, the fixed-price contract was intended to cover only a portion of the total services required and had a cutoff date of 25 June 1957. A cost-plus-fixed fee type contract was awarded to the contractor to continue the services from 26 June 1957 until completion. Article I of the second contract provided, in part, that the contractor shall, for the consideration of the fixed fee "together with reimbursement for expenses incurred in accordance with the provisions of this contract..., commencing on the date of execution hereof, utilize its facilities for the continuation of" the ARIS program, and that "(T)he work herein provided for shall be a continuation of the studies initiated under" the earlier fixed-price contract.

During the performance of the first contract the contractor engaged the services of a sub- AGO 9111A 177

INTERPRETATION-Continued contractor which were to be continued under the second contract. This necessitated the drafting of a new subcontract which would be submitted to the contracting officer for approval. 

The difficulty was that neither prime contract provided a method of allocating subcontractor or any other work to a specific contract. The 

Government adopted the practical rule that work performed before the cutoff date would be allocated to the first contract. Because of the cost limitation in the first contract, however, the contractor inserted a clause in the new subcontract which provided that work performed between 31 March 1957 and the cutoff date would be allocated to the second prime contract. This subcontract and the allocation note was approved by the contracting officer prior to the execution of the cost-plus-fixedfee contract. In July 1957, the contractor sought reimbursement for the ceiling price under the first contract. The costs submitted barely exceeded the $100,000 cost limitation and did not include subcontractor costs of $15,- 

625.49 which were incurred between 31 March 

1957 and the cutoff date. These latter costs were submitted for payment under the second contract and denied by the contracting officer.

On appeal, the Government argued that the subcontractor costs were not reimbursable under either contract since they were excluded by the cost limitation in the first and were incurred prior to the execution date of the second. The ASBCA, however, interpreted the second contract to permit, by implication, reimbursement for anticipatory costs. Dunlap and Associates, Inc., ASBCA No. 4903, 25 June 

1959, 59-2 BCA 2277. The Government filed a motion for reconsideration and argued that the ASBCA had reformed rather than interpreted the second contract and had thus exceeded its jurisdiction.

Held, the motion is denied. The Government argues that the contractor was to perform specific services during two specific time periods with the cutoff date of the first period determining work allocability. Accordingly, the second contract is characterized as an integrated and unambiguous writing which limits reimbursable costs to those "commencing on the date of execution" and precludes consideration of other evidence of intention. From this it is argued that payment under the second contract of subcontractor costs incurred prior to the date of execution varies the terms of the contract and amounts to a reformation. This approach, however, ignores the fact that the second contract was intended to continue work started under the first contract and does not purport to represent the entire agreement of the parties. Further, since neither contract provides a method of allocating work which overlapped the cutoff date, their terms are not varied or modified by the allocation method proposed by the contractor. In other words, the allocation to the second contract of subcontract costs incurred before the date of execution is not inconsistent with its terms. Since there is no conflict between the subcontract and the second prime contract and since the contracting officer approved the subcontract, it affords the only definite basis for allocation and should be interpreted along with the second contract to give it full effect. See 3 Williston,

Contracts § 628 (1936). 

Regardless of whether ambiguity exists, the facts and circumstances surrounding the execution of a contract are always admissible to determine its true meaning. Restatement, Con tracts 230; 3 Williston, Contracts §§ 617, 629 

(1936). Considering that the second contract was intended to continue services started under the first contract, a more logical interpretation of "commencing at the date of execution" is that it establishes an affirmative date to start performance rather than a method of allocating costs between the two contracts. 

Dunlap and Associates, Inc., ASBCA No. 

4903, 25 November 1959, 59-2 BCA 2416. 

4. Prior Contracts Between Parties Exam ined and Significance Attached to the Deletion 

From Current Contract of Clause Previously Used To Establish Contractor's Liability for Articles Stored in Building Being Repaired. 

Appellant held a contract to repair the roof of an Army warehouse. On the day following the contractor's removal of a portion of the roof, and in anticipation of a heavy rain, Government representatives requested contractor to cover the exposed portion of the roof with roofing paper. This he did not do. Government 178 AGO 9111A

INTERPRETATION-Continued personnel did move some stored materials out from under the open portions of the roof and covered some of the remaining materials. A heavy rain caused damage to that stored property which had been neither covered nor moved. 

The contracting officer asserted a claim in excess of $17,000 from which this appeal was made.

The contract provided that the contractor was responsible for preserving and protecting "all materials, supplies, and equipment (including property which may be Governmentfurnished or owned) and all work performed." (GC-8) It was further the contractor's responsibility "to protect all existing structures, utilities, and work of any kind against damage 99 

(SC-9) Three previous contracts be tween the two parties for similar work had, besides provisions identical to those just mentioned, an additional one under which the contractor was to ". . . be responsible for the protection against rain and water for any damage of stored materials and perishable goods in the warehouse under this contract."

Held, appeal sustained. In interpreting this contract it is necessary to consider prior dealings between the parties. It is significant that the parties have omitted from this contract the separate provision which under the previous contracts made contractor responsible for protecting stored materials. To avoid an interpretation that would render that provision redundant it is necessary to conclude that the "stored materials" referred to therein are other than the "materials, supplies and equipment" mentioned in GC-8 and are not included in the "existing structures, utilities and work" covered in SC-9. Such a conclusion is reasonable. 

A provision similar to GC-8 is commonly used in construction contracts and is construed to relate to responsibility for the materials, supplies, etc. which are intended to be used in the performance of the contract. Responsibility for any materials stored in the building which is the subject of the contract would be covered by a separate provision. Clearly "stored materials" are not within the intendment of the "existing structures and work" referred to in 

SC-9. 

Insofar as interpreting the present contract is concerned, the deletion of the provision relating to "stored materials" does not require placing a different meaning on GC-8 and SC-9 than was placed on them in construing the previous contracts. Furthermore, in view of the means available to the Government to protect stored materials by covering or removing, without having to give appellant's workmen access to the building, it is not unreasonable for the appellant to have assumed that the Government had decided to bear the burden of protecting such material. The conclusion is that the contract placed no burden on appellant to protect stored materials. 

Sacramento Roofing & Insulation Co., Inc. 

and C. E. Swift Roofing Co., ASBCA No. 5365, 23 February 1960, 60-1 BCA 2528.

10. If the Contractor Would Not Have Been Permitted To Cease Performance, the Govern ment May Not Avoid Overrun Costs on the 

Ground That Is Was Denied the Right Given by the Limitation of Cost Clause To Choose Whether Performance Should Be Allowed at an Increased Cost. The contractor's Air Force contract called for the production and delivery of 48 rocket engines from 30 June 1958 through 

1 September 1958. The contract, a cost-plus fixed-fee research and development type, con tained a Limitation of Cost Clause substantially like that in ASPR 7-402.2. The contract had the highest priority because it was part of the Argus program, which was being carried out on a "crash" basis. Forced by the accelerated production to forego the usual time consuming step-by-step analysis process prior to commencing actual manufacture, the contractor experienced an abnormally high rejection rate. During the early part of August 1958, the contractor became aware of a cost overrun and notified the Government. Two weeks later the contractor gave notice that the costs already exceeded the contract estimate by $12,648, and that the total overrun involved in completing the contract would be $25,275. The contracting officer misunderstood the notice and postponed reviewing the contractor's overrun request pending clarification. A few months later the contractor recalculated the overrun in accordance with later cost data and advised the contracting officer that the overrun was $33,878. The contracting officer allowed $25,275, but denied the contractor's claim for the remainder on the ground that the contractor had failed to allow the Government to exercise its right under the 

Limitation of Cost Clause to decide whether the contract should be continued at an increased cost. From this partial denial, the contractor appealed to the ASBCA. 

Held, appeal allowed. Although the Limitation of Cost Clause allows the Government to decide whether a contract may be continued despite a cost overrun, the language conferring that privilege must be deemed a mere shadow of a formality in this situation. The contract, though in a form for research and development, had as its real purpose the production of engines. It is uncontroverted that the 

Government never would have permitted the contractor to discontinue performance. The 

Government took all possible steps to ensure that the delivery of engines would not be delayed. The Government now claims the contractor should have given more timely notice of an overrun. But even if the contractor had done so, there is no evidence that the Government would have allowed the contract to expire for lack of additional funds to complete it. The record shows the contrary. Moreover, since the unusually high rejection rate was known to the Government, it must have been aware how that rate would affect costs. The Government also knew that the contractor's accounting system required some time for tabulating costs. The 

Government did not ask that a more current record of costs be kept for the obvious reason that the contractor was not free to discontinue performance in any circumstances. 

When told of a cost overrun in August 1958, the Government neither abated its insistence that all forty-eight engines be delivered nor did it tell the contractor to manufacture engines only to the extent of the coverage afforded by an additional $25,275. Moreover, in paying the original overrun estimate, the Government brushed aside the technicality it now urges. 

The Limitation of Cost Clause has been con strued as containing reciprocal ceilings so far as the two parties' obligations are concerned. 

Navy Contract Law § 8.36 (2d ed. 1959). Hav ing insisted that the contractor achieve sustained performance until delivery was made, the Government must pay the overrun costs incurred by reason of that insistence. 

Thiokol Chemical Corporation, ASBCA No. 

5726, 16 November 1960, 60-2 BCA 2852.

2. Supreme Court Invalidates Dixon-Yates Power Contract Because of Government Negotiator's Indirect Financial Interest in Con- 

180 AGO 9111A

INVALID CONTRACTS-Continued 

3 tractor. In 1953, the Government decided to transfer from the Tennessee Valley Authority to private industry the responsibility for furnishing electric power to the Atomic Energy Commission. The Director of the Bureau of the 

Budget obtained Mr. Adolphe Wenzell, a public utility financing expert, as a part-time consultant on a per diem basis, to prepare a study on the extent to which the Government was subsidizing the T.V.A. Wenzell was an officer of First Boston Corporation, a leading investment bank, and retained both his First Boston position and salary during the four months that the report was being prepared. The final report concluded that the Government was to a considerable extent subsidizing T.V.A. It also established, through a number of unsolicited and gratuitous opinions, that Wenzell was an advocate of private power for governmental use.

By January 1954, the Government, had initiated through the A.E.C., contract negotiations with the contractor [respondent in this case] to build and operate a generator plant near 

Memphis, Tennessee and to sell the electrical power generated to the A.E.C. Wenzell's services were again obtained by the Budget Bureau on a per diem basis and without requiring the severing of his First Boston connections. His primary duty was to advise on the cost of money which would be needed to finance the contract. In addition, Wenzell's influence was used to expedite the bargaining process and to obtain from the contractor a firm proposal which was based upon reasonable cost estimates. The contractor's final proposal relied upon the rate of interest that First Boston would charge on money borrowed to finance the contract. At the request of the contractor, Wenzell furnished these figures as an officer of First Boston and with that Corporation's approval. While the contractor actually discussed these rates at 

First Boston in New York, no binding financial commitment was made until Wenzell had completed his service for the Government. 

In February 1954, the contractor, on the advice of counsel, suggested to Wenzell that, because of the public-private power issue and the fact that First Boston would be a logical choice as the financing institution when the contract was awarded, his position presented a possible conflict of interest. While officials of the Budget 

Bureau thought that the problem was "exaggerated" Wenzell was advised to consult First

Boston's attorneys. Upon consultation, Wenzell was advised to resign immediately and in writing. Despite this advice, Wenzell did not resign and the Budget Bureau merely requested that he "finish his work with the Bureau as quickly as possible." On 3 April 1954, Wenzell performed his last service for the Government. 

Final negotiations with the contractor began in July 1954 and the contract was awarded on 

11 November 1954. Sometime after 3 April 

1954, First Boston agreed to arrange for the major part of the financing of the project, although it subsequently decided not to accept a fee.

In August 1955, the contract was terminated for convenience when the Government's need for electrical power in the Memphis area ceased. Subsequently, the contractor was informed that no termination costs would be allowed because the entire contract was invalidated by Wenzell's conflict of interest. The contractor, asserting that no conflict of interest existed, brought suit in the Court of Claims and was awarded a judgment in the amount of $1,867,545.56. Mississippi Valley Generating 

Co. v. United States, 175 F. Supp. 505 (Ct. Cl. 

1959), [digested in DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 257, par. 12]. The Supreme Court granted certio rari.

Held, reversed. The activities of Wenzell constitute a violation of 18 U.S.C. § 434 (1958) and render the contract unenforceable. Section 434 reads as follows: 

Whoever, being an officer, agent or member of, or directly or indirectly interested in the pecuniary profits or contracts of any corporation, joint-stock company, or association, or of any firm or partnership or other business entity, is employed or acts as an officer or agent of the United States for the transaction of business with such business entity, shall be fined not more than $2,000 or imprisoned not more than two years, or both.

This comprehensive enactment is designed to insure honesty in the Government's business dealings by preventing federal agents who have interests adverse to those of the Government from advancing their own interests at the ex- AGO 9111A 181

INVALID CONTRACTS—Continued pense of the public welfare. U. S. v.

Chemical Foundation, 272 U.S. 1, 18 (1926). The statute establishes an objective standard of conduct the breach of which does not depend upon the presence of actual corruption or loss to the Government. It attempts to prevent honest government agents from succumbing to temptation by making it illegal for them to enter into relationships which are fraught with temptation. Rankin v. U.S., 98 Ct. Cl. 357 (1943). The question is, therefore, did Wenzell violate this rigid rule established by Congress?

Wenzell acted as "an officer or agent of the 

United States for the transaction of business."

He was the Government's major representative in the formative negotiations: the real architect of the final contract. Despite the fact that Wenzell took no oath of office, had no tenure and received no salary, he was a key representative who was just as likely to subordinate the Government's interest to his own as was a regular, full-time, compensated civil servant. Respondent also argues that since Wenzell had no authority to sign a binding contract and did not participate in the final negotiations his activities did not constitute "the transaction of business." Yet Wenzell was responsible for the ultimate agreement between contractor and the Government on the important cost of financing involved, a cost which the Government was to bear. While the final contract may contain nothing of Wenzell's work, that it was made at all may have been a result of his work. Thus, it is unrealistic to limit the statute's application to agents who participate in the final stages of negotiation and award. 

Wenzell was also "directly or indirectly interested in the pecuniary profits or contracts" of the contractors. At the very least Wenzell had an indirect interest in the contract that the respondent was trying to obtain. That interest may be described as follows: Wenzell was an officer and executive of First Boston; he not only shared in the profits which First Boston made during the year, but he also received a bonus for any business which he brought to the firm; if a contract between the Government and the contractors was ultimately agreed upon, there was a substantial probability that, because of its prior experience in the area of private power financing, First Boston would be hired to secure the financing for the proposed 

Memphis project. If First Boston received the contract it would directly profit, both in monetary return and future business, and Wenzell would benefit from this. While Wenzell's ambivalent position may be ascribed to the logic of circumstances, the prospective contractors were in a position to benefit him and he was, to say the least, subconsciously tempted to ingratiate himself with the contractors and to accede to their demands, even though such concessions might be adverse to the best interests of the Government. [The Court then listed several situations where Wenzell could have been tempted.]

The absence of a formal contract or understanding between First Boston and the contractors during the period of Wenzell's service is not determinative. The key factor is that 

Wenzell would probably benefit from an award to the contractors and was thus subject to the temptations which the statute seeks to avoid.

In an objective standard such as this, Wenzell's alleged ignorance of his compromising position has no bearing. Finally, the knowledge and apparent acquiescence in Wenzell's position by the Budget Bureau does not operate to exempt him from the statute. This decision holds, therefore, that 18 U.S.C. § 434 forbids a government agent from engaging in business transactions on behalf of the Government if, by virtue of his private interests he may benefit financially from the outcome of those transactions. 

Upon careful consideration it is concluded that the sanction of nonenforcement of the contract in question is consistent with and essential to effectuating the policy of Section 434, even though that remedy is not specifically prescribed by the statute. If the Government's only remedy in this case is a criminal prosecution, then the public will be forced to bear the burden of complying with the sort of contract which the statute sought to prevent. This case is to be distinguished from Muschany v. United 

States, 324 U.S. 49 (1945), where the contract was specifically authorized by statute and could therefore be enforced, even though certain aspects of it were against public policy. Although nonenforcement may appear to be a harsh rem- 182 AGO 9111A

INVALID CONTRACTS-Continued edy in a case where the contractors could not have controlled Wenzell and were guilty of no wrongdoing, the purpose of Section 434 is to protect the integrity of the federal contracting process: the policy is clearly expressed and leaves no room for equitable considerations. 

The question before us is whether the Government may disaffirm a contract which is infected by an illegal conflict of interest, not whether the Government can avoid a contract merely because it turned out to be a bad bargain. It is clear that nonenforcement is required in order to extend to the public the full protection which 

Congress decreed by enacting Section 434. 

United States v. Mississippi Valley Generat ing Co., 364 U.S. 520 (1961). [Note: Mr. Justice Harlan, with whom Mr. 

Justice Whittaker and Mr. Justice Stewart joined, dissented. His basic point was that 

Wenzell was not "interested" within the meaning of Section 434: the probability that First 

Boston would finance the contractor is not sufficient to constitute an indirect interest on the part of Wenzell in the contractor. Since there was no "commitment, arrangement, or understanding" in existence between First

Boston and the contractor during the term of Wenzell's Government service, there was no conflict of interest. To support this proposition, Mr. Justice Harlan made four points: (1) Section 434 does not speak of expectations or of probabilities but of a present status or precuniary interest arising from an existing relationship, (2) Section 434 seems to cover a case where a Government agent is knowingly tempted to exploit an existing adverse interest, not where, as here, the contractor could readily obtain his financing from another source after the agent's services had terminated, despite any undue advantage conferred, (3) the decision introduces uncertainty into an area that demands clear standards: such illusive factors as "substantial probability" and "logic of circumstances" should not be imported into a statute governing the conduct primarily of laymen serving the Government, and (4) the broad implications of this decision will in practical effect prevent a prudent man from later acquiring an interest in a contract which he helped to negotiate during a previous term of government employment. This absolute disqualification is inconsistent with other statutes which impose a two year restriction upon former government agents' aiding or participating in a claim in their private capacity which was pending at the time of their Government 

U.S.C. § 284 (1958).] 3. Comptroller General Permits No Compensation for Costs Incurred With Respect to Items Not Paid for or Delivered Before Con tract Was Determined To Be Invalid. In response to a disappointed bidder's protest against the award of a contract for seventyeight radial overarm saws, the Comptroller 

General ruled that the winning bid had not been responsive. He directed the procuring agency to disavow the contract and to advise the contractor that no further deliveries would be accepted. 39 Comp. Gen. 832 (1960). When the contract was canceled, eighteen saws had been accepted and paid for at the contract price. The firm that had received the contract submitted to the Comptroller General a claim for the costs incurred in obtaining supplies and otherwise preparing to manufacture the remaining sixty saws. The claim was subject to reduction by the amount obtained from disposition of salvable supplies.

Held, no part of the claim may be allowed, irrespective of the outcome of the effort to salvage supplies. The procurement was required to be formally advertised, and only a responsive bid could legally have been accepted. 10 

U.S.C. §§ 2304 (a) and 2305 (c). Because it was based on an unresponsive bid, the contract for the saws was void ab initio. See, e.g., Hudson

City Contract Co. v. Jersey City Incinerator 

Authority, 17 N.J. 297, 111 A. 2d 385 (1955).

Such a contract confers no rights on the purported contractor. See, e.g., United States v.

Ellicott, 223 U.S. 524 (1912). Compensation for the eighteen saws accepted is governed by the rule-followed by the General Accounting Office and the Federal courts-that payment on a quantum meruit or quantum valebat basis is authorized for benefits received before the determination of the invalidity of a contract. 

See, e.g., South Boston Iron Co. v. United 

States, 118, U.S. 37 (1886); Clark v. United AGO 9111A 183

INVALID CONTRACTS-Continued States, 95 U.S. 539 (1877); Salomon v. United 

States, 86 U.S. 17; 38 Comp. Gen. 368 (1958);

Annot., 154 A.L.R. 356 (1945). Quantum meruit or quantum valebat payment is authorized on the basis of the value received by the Government. The justification is that it would be unfair for one party to have the benefit of the labor of another without recompense. Recovery is limited "to such sum as will reasonably compensate the party whose services or property have been devoted to the advantage of the other." Gee v. City of Sutton, 149 Neb. 

603, 31 N.W. 2d 747 (1948).

Different principles apply to the costs incurred with respect to the sixty undelivered saws. First, there is strong precedent for holding that a contract made invalid by a failure to follow required procedures creates no right to compensation except that received before the determination of invalidity is made. See, e.g.,

Layne-Western Co. v. Buchanan County, 85 F. 

2d 343 (8th Cir. 1936); Federal Paving Corp. 

v. City of Wauwatosa, 231 Wis. 655, 286 N.W. 

546 (1939); 10 McQuillin, Municipal Corporations §§ 29.02, 29.26, and 29.41. The same authorities indicate that the good faith of the parties is irrelevant. Second, the weight of judicial authority holds there may be no compensation for any contractor's costs that did not result in a benefit to, or in receipt of valuable goods or services by, the Government. It is true that in New York Mail & Newspaper

Trans. Co. v. United States, 139 Ct. Cl. 751 

(1957), the majority stated that no strict quantum meruit basis would be adhered to, but that an amount would be given that would place the parties in substantially the same position they would have been in had there been no attempted contract. Perhaps the judgment in that case exceeded what would have been allowed on a quantum meruit basis. Yet even if the rule in that case is accepted, and the strong dissent and the contrary precedent are ignored, the record in the instant case does not show that the pre-award position of the parties could be restored any more by paying the claim than by leaving the parties in status quo. In any event, however, the Supreme Court has settled the matter by its recent holding that there may be no recovery on a quantum valebat basis unless the Government has received tangible benefits from the purported contractor. United

States v. Mississippi Valley Generating Co., 364 

U.S. 520, 566, n. 22 (1961). Therefore, no compensation may be given for the expenses incurred with respect to the sixty undelivered saws.

It may seem harsh to require firm that acted in good faith to absorb the cost of producing undelivered items. In this connection, it should be noted that the firm claimed $832 per saw, while the contract price was only $728 per saw. However, to make the Government liable for anything other than benefits received would in effect permit Government agents to obligate the United States in violation of rules prescribed by statutes, regulations, and administrative and judicial determinations. Such a result is not in the public interest. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-142716, 6 February 1961, 40 Comp. Gen. 447.
