5. Government Not Estopped To Deny Validity of Contract Made Invalid by Violation of Statute and Regulations. (ASBCA) See DISPUTES (par. 30) 6. Court of Claims Denies Recovery of Reasonable Value of Services Rendered Under Letters of Intent Signed by Government Agent Without Authority-Because Prompt Notice To Stop Work Under Invalid Letter of Intent Not Given, Government May Not Recover Amount Paid Pursuant to That Letter. During 1949 the National Capital Sesquicentennial 

Commission, a Federal agency, considered holding a fair. The plaintiffs voluntarily gave the Commission help in planning the fair. One plaintiff was a firm of architects, engineers, and builders; the other was in the business of displays and exhibits. Both hoped to be awarded contracts if the Commission definitely decided to hold the fair. The plaintiffs had liaison with the Commission through its executive vice chairman, Mr. Barron. A lawyer registered as a lobbyist for the plaintiffs 184 AGO 9111A

INVALID CONTRACTS-Continued worked closely with Barron. In mid-October 

1949, Congress appropriated the funds requested by the Commission, including an amount to be used in connection with the fair. 

Immediately thereafter, the lobbyist for the plaintiffs prepared letters of intent addressed to his clients and delivered the letters to Barron for his signature. The Commission's Director advised Barron that the letters of intent were out of order and that Barron had no authority to sign them. In November 1949, without the knowledge of the Director or any members of the Commission, Barron signed the letters of intent and sent them to the plaintiffs. Barron never had been given any authority to execute the letters. The plaintiffs incurred expenses in carrying out work under the letters. On 2 

December 1949 Barron told the Commission about the letters of intent he had executed. 

That group discussed those letters as well as proposed contracts with the plaintiffs. Neither then nor later did the Commission approve or ratify the letters of intent. Although the proposed contracts were put into writing, they were never signed by the Government. After the Commission's executive committee decided on 30 December 1949 that the fair should be postponed, the Commission's Director sent letters to the plaintiffs directing them to discontinue all work undertaken as a result of the letters of intent. Thereafter, the plaintiffs submitted claims to the Commission, which recommended to the General Accounting Office that the plaintiffs be allowed profit and reasonable out-of-pocket expenses for work done pursuant to the letters of intent. The GAO offered settlements, but they were rejected. The plaintiffs then sued in the Court of Claims seeking either the reasonable value of the services rendered under the letters of intent or damages for breach of the written contracts. The Government denied all liability, contending that the contracts were never executed and that Barron lacked authority to sign the letters of intent. 

The Government counterclaimed for $35,119 paid by the Commission to one of the plaintiffs between 30 December 1949 and 21 April 1950.

The Government argued the payments were made under the mistaken belief that the plaintiff's letter of intent had been validly executed. 

Held, the claims and the counterclaim are denied. First, there may be no recovery on the contracts. The Government never executed them. Nor did the parties ever bind themselves to the promises incorporated in the unexecuted, written documents. As a general rule, the mere fact that parties intend a subsequent contract to be made is evidence that they do not intend their earlier negotiations to be binding. This case comes within that rule because the Government never acceded to the terms of the written documents and, therefore, further negotiations were required. Ship Constr. & Trading Co. v. United States, 91 Ct. Cl. 419, 456 (1940). 

Second, the plaintiffs may not recover the reasonable value of the services rendered under the letters of intent. The plaintiffs began as volunteers with the hope of obtaining highly lucrative contracts. When that hope was not fulfilled, the plaintiffs sought by this action to reduce the expenses incurred in trying to obtain the contracts. However, the plaintiffs may not recover because their status as volunteers never changed. Although the Commission had authority to enter into contracts, it does not follow that the Commission would be bound by an agreement signed by one of its officers. 

Unless it appears that he acted within the scope of his authority, a Government agent's acts may not bind the Government. Whiteside v. 

United States, 93 U.S. 247, 257 (1876). Such a restriction conforms to the basic principle of agency that one must look to the authority of an agent. Persons dealing with a Government agent must take notice of the authority given him. Hawkins v. United States, 96 U.S. 689 (1877); Gay Street Corp. v. United States, 130 Ct. Cl. 341, 348 (1955). To hold the contrary would permit two people to effect a drain on the public treasury. Barron had no authority to issue the letters of intent. The plaintiffs were not inexperienced persons to whom knowledge of the limitations on the authority of Government agents should not be imputed. 

Gay Street Corp. v. United States, supra. The plaintiffs were highly experienced contractors and relied on the advice of a lawyer who long had dealt with Government contracts. 

There was no ratification of the letters of intent. The plaintiffs were aware of all pro- AGO 9111A 185

INVALID CONTRACTS-Continued ceedings by the Commission and knew that Barron's issuance of the letters was not endorsed. The absence of endorsement served as notice to the plaintiffs that the letters were not ratified.

The Government is not estopped to deny the validity of the letters of intent. Estoppel cannot be established against the Government on the basis of an act performed by an agent without authority. Ship Constr. & Trading Co. v. 

United States, supra. 

Finally, the defendant's counterclaim must fail. The money paid the plaintiff was expended pursuant to a plan intended to benefit the Government. Although the plan was dropped, expenses were incurred in determining the feasibility of executing it. The expenses were incurred voluntarily or under unauthorized letters of intent until 2 December 1949, but a full month passed before the Commission formally notified the plaintiffs of the decision to halt the work in progress. During that month the Commission knew the plaintiffs were spending money. Even though the delay did not amount to a ratification of the letters of intent, the parties should-in fairness to the plaintiffs-be placed substantially in the same position they would have occupied without the attempted contract. Denying the counterclaim will accomplish this. Moreover, since the counterclaim is substantially less than the plaintiff's expenses and the Government received the benefit of the plaintiffs' services, the ends of justice would best be served by leaving the parties in the position in which their actions placed them. 

Byrne Organization, Inc. v. United States,

Gardner Displays of New York, Inc. v. United 

States, 287 F. 2d 582 (Ct. Cl. 1961). 

7. No Binding Contract Formed Because Parties Failed To Agree on Subject Matter. 

A Signal Depot telephoned the contractor to obtain a quotation on a conduit with attached coupling. The Depot thought the quote of $1.15 given by the contractor was for each ten-foot length. The contractor thought his quote was $1.15 per foot. The Depot issued a purchase order for 208 ten-foot lengths for $239.20. After delivering 208 ten-foot lengths, the contractor submitted an invoice for $2,392, or $1.15 per foot. The contractor and the Depot disputed each other's interpretation of the bargain. The contractor requested that the contract price be increased from $239.20 to $2,392 and submitted evidence that the reasonable value of the conduit was $1.15 per foot, de livered to the Depot. The Comptroller General was asked for a ruling. 

Held, for the contractor. The contractor's quotation was oral, and there is nothing to establish definitely that the price quoted was for a ten-foot length of conduit. Moreover, we concur with the administrative report's statement that the Depot purchasing agent should have realized that 21/2" conduit, with coupling attached, could not have been profitably furnished at $1.15 per ten-foot length, notwithstanding the Government's estimate of 50¢ each. We think it may reasonably be concluded that there was no meeting of the minds on the subject matter and that no binding contract was formed. The company has delivered the required conduit and has not been paid for it. 

Accordingly, $1.15 per foot may be paid, as recommended by the contracting officer. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144834, 2 February 1961.

ASBCA Lacks Jurisdiction To Consider Claim Under Termination for Convenience Clause for Costs Incurred Before and as a Result of Contract Cancellation Ordered by Comptroller General. Subsequent Review, Reaches a Contrary Conclusion. Between December 1953 and May 1954 

the contractor entered into three contracts with the Government for the supply of wood prod ucts. Contract No. 1 was successfully completed but the other two were terminated for default when the contractor became insolvent. In both cases the contracting officer determined that the cause of default was not excusable and, after repurchase contracts were awarded, notified the contractor that excess costs of $5,795.87 and $2,758.52 respectively had been assessed.

The contractor failed to appeal from the de terminations under contract No. 2. An appeal from the termination of contract No. 3 was denied for the reason that the insolvency was not excusable. Herman Adams, d/b/a Adams 

Manufacturing Co., ASBCA No. 2555 (31 May 

1954).

In 1958, the Government filed suit in a Federal district court to recover unpaid excess costs which had been assessed under contract No. 2.

The suit was dismissed on the ground that the contractor's default was excusable. The court found that the Government had improperly rejected goods delivered under contract No. 1 thereby causing the contractor's insolvency and the default under contract No. 2. United States v. Adams, 160 F. Supp. 143 (W.D. Ark. 1958). 

The question of whether the termination for default should be converted to a termination for convenience, however, was not raised. In light of the court's judgment, the contractor requested the contracting officer to convert the terminations of both contract No. 2 and con tract No.

3 into terminations for the convenience of the Government. [See ASPR 8-707 (e) (5 Sep 1958).] The requests were denied and the contractor appealed. The Government filed a motion to dismiss.

Held, the motion to dismiss is granted. The contractor failed to appeal from the termination of contract No. 2 for default or the subsequent assessment of excess costs. Normally, this failure to exhaust administrative remedies would preclude judicial review of the contracting officer's decision. United States v. Joseph Holpuch 

Co., 328 U.S. 234 (1946). But even though the

Government's suit to recover excess costs enabled the court to review the question of ex- AGO 9111A 187

7-102.12 (18 Sep 1958), and is not subject to an administrative re-examination Atlas Can 

Corporation, ASBCA Nos. 1957, 1958 & 2121 (10 Sep 1959), 59-2 BCA 2354. In the absence of an express mandate, therefore, the court's determination that the Government was not entitled to excess costs because the default was excusable does not require this Board to convert the termination for default into a termination for convenience.

The appeal under contract No. 3 is dismissed because the decision from which the appeal was taken was not made by the contracting officer. 

Even so, the Board's prior decision in this matter was not challenged in the judicial proceedings and is final and conclusive under the 

Wunderlich Act, 41 U.S.C.A. 321. 

Herman Adams, d/b/a Adams Manufacturing Company, ASBCA Nos. 5321 & 5507, 18

2. Government Motion for Summary Judgment Granted by Court of Claims Where Contractor's Proposed Evidence Offers No Reasonable Prospect That Trial De Novo Would Find ASBCA Decision Defective Under Wunderlich 

Act. Two contractors were each awarded two contracts for the manufacture of raincoats with Government-furnished material. If the material was defective the contractors could make a written request for an equitable adjustment in contract price [ASPR 13-502 (a) (14 May 1958)]. The adjustment was to be made under the Changes Clause and before final payment.

The contracts also contained the standard Disputes Clause. In all cases, the materials furnished had some imperfections which caused the contractors to incur excess costs. Apparently a timely request for an equitable adjustment was made under all but one contract. In that case the claim was made 7 months after final payment. The contracting officer denied all requests and the contractors appealed. Despite the Government's argument that the claim under one contract was untimely, the ASBCA found that the Government-furnished materials were not defective and denied all claims on the merits. The contractors, consolidating their claims, filed suit in the Court of Claims to recover the excess costs incurred. 

The Government filed a motion for summary judgment.

Held, the motion is granted and the case is dismissed. With regard to the first contract, the Government asserts that the claim was not timely because the contractor did not request an equitable adjustment until 7 months after final payment. Even though the ASBCA decided the merits of the appeal, the timeliness issue is a question of law which the Court of Claims may decide. Poloran Products, Inc. v. 

United States, 126 Ct. Cl. 816, 824 (1953).

Consequently, this claim is dismissed because the contractor did not adhere to provisions of the contract which afforded a method of settling disputes on the administrative level. United 

States v. Holpuch Co., 328 U.S. 234 (1945). 

With regard to the remaining contracts, the ASBCA decision on the merits is final unless the contractor proves that the ruling was "fraudulent or capricious or arbitrary or so grossly erroneous as necessarily to imply bad faith, or is not supported by substantial evidence." Wunderlich Act, 41 U.S.C. 321. A mere reiteration of the derogatory language of the statute is insufficient. The contractor's pleading and affidavits must raise a genuine issue of material fact within the meaning of the Wunderlich Act before a trial in the Court of Claims will be granted. Volentine & Littleton v. United States, 136 Ct. Cl. 638 (1956). Here the contractor's proposed evidence does not meet this standard. In fact, the allegations of fact by both parties indicate that the furnished materials were not defective and did not constitute a change. There is, therefore, no reasonable prospect that a trial would result in a decision favorable to the contractors. The motion for summary judgment is granted.

P.L.S. Coat & Suit Corp. v. United States, 

180 F. Supp. 400 (Ct. Cl. 1960).

Review Under Wunderlich Act Limited to Record of Proceedings. In December 1950, the con tractor entered into a construction contract with the Corps of Engineers. During perform ance, the Engineer Claims and Appeals Board denied an $11,705.85 claim for extra work on the ground that neither reasonable precautions were taken nor sound construction practices employed. The plaintiff, as the contractor's executor, brought action in a federal district court under the Tucker Act, 28 U.S.C.A. 1346- (a) (2) and alleged that the Board's decision. was erroneous and not supported by substantial evidence. At the trial the plaintiff introduced evidence in addition to the record of the Board's proceeding. The United States objected and argued that the Court was limited to a review of the record and that the plaintiff was not entitled to a trial de novo. 

Held, for the United States. Under the

Wunderlich Act, 41 U.S.C. 321, the determination by a duly authorized administrative board of a factual dispute arising under a Government contract shall bind a federal district court unless "fraudulent or capricious or arbitrary or so grossly erroneous as necessarily to imply bad faith, or is not supported by substantial evidence." See Lowell O. West Lumber Sales v. 

United States, 270 F. 2d 12 (9th Cir. 1959), [digested in DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 259, par. 2].

If the determination is alleged to be fraudulent under the Wunderlich Act, this court may consider evidence in addition to the Board's record. 

In this case, however, the plaintiff only asserts that the decision was erroneous and not supported by substantial evidence. As such, this court is limited in review to the administrative record and may not consider additional evi dence. Mann Chemical Laboratories v. United States, 174 F. Supp. 563 (D. Mass. 1958). A 

review of the record demonstrates that the Board's decision was not erroneous and is supported by substantial evidence. 

United States National Bank v. United 

States, 178 F. Supp. 910 (D. Ore. 1959).

Purposes of Determining Applicability of the Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act. The Atomic 

Energy Commission issued an invitation for bids for 50,000 tons of coal in one or more lots, the minimum bid to be 1,800 tons. In response to this bid, the contractor submitted six bids on separate forms, each for 1,800 tons, and each naming a different mine as the source of the coal to be supplied thereunder. Five of the six bids when computed were in amounts less than $10,000 and the sixth was in an amount in excess of $10,000. The six bids totaled $57,- 

312.00. The Walsh-Healey Act is applicable to contracts for supplies or services only where the contract amount is in excess of $10,000. 

41 U.S.C. § 35. The Secretary of Labor deter mined that the six contracts were all subject to the Walsh-Healey Act since they should be treated as a single contract. The contractor filed suit in the District Court for the District of Columbia, seeking a declaratory judgment that the contracts were not subject to the Act AGO 9111A 189

LABOR-Continued and an injunction restraining the Secretary of

Labor and Comptroller General from placing him and one of his suppliers on the debarred bidders list. The contractor and the Government both moved for summary judgment and the Government's motion was granted. The contractor appealed to the Circuit Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia.

Held, judgment affirmed. The contractor should not be permitted to evade the restrictions and covenants of the Walsh-Healey Act merely because of the number of sheets of paper on which he elects to submit his bids. Congress, in setting the $10,000 minimum amount for coverage under the Act, did not intend to encourage the development of a group of shielding middlemen who earn a significant portion of their livelihood by facilitating avoidance of a fundamental public policy-fair wages and safe working conditions.

George v. Mitchell, 282 F. 2d 486 (D.C. Cir. 

1960). 

4. Lawful Picketing Not Unfair Labor Practice Simply Because Employees of Neutral Employers Honor Picket Line-"Moore Dry Dock Tests" Are Evidentiary Only and Not Conclusive on Issue of Primary or Secondary Picketing-Picketing To Compel Execution of Hiring- Hall Agreement Is An Unfair Labor Practice. 

G was the prime and S was one of eight subcontractors on a construction site. All of the men working on the site were members of the labor union, U. Then S hired several non-union day laborers through the state employment bureau. U's business agent visited the site on the same day and told one of G's employees to stop work. The latter did so. When asked by G's foreman what would have to be done to avoid picketing by U, U's business agent replied that S would have to pay the non-union men union scale and to sign a contract with U. 

On the same afternoon, U picketed the site with a sign carrying the legend: [S] Co. 

Refuses to Pay

Union Wages 

& Conditions 

Laborers Local 1140

This Dispute With Above 

Employer Only

On the following day, U's business agent informed G and S that the project would be picketed again if S did not pay union scale and sign a contract with U. S agreed to comply with the wage demand but refused to sign a contract. U picketed the site again and all union employees of G, S and the other subcontractors refused to cross the picket line. 

On that day, S discharged his non-union employees, but the picketing continued. U informed G that S would have to be blacklisted by the Associated General Contractors of 

Nebraska, a group of which G's secretary was president. Pickets remained on the job site daily for two weeks until they were removed pursuant to a temporary restraining order by a federal district court. 

The National Labor Relations Board found 

U guilty of an unfair labor practice in that: (1) U had "induced and coerced" secondary employees to cease work; (2) there was "coercion and restraint" of a secondary employer; (3) U's picketing had the unlawful "secondary boycott" objective of forcing G to cease doing business with S; and (4) because U was not certified as the bargaining representative of S's employees, the picketing had an unlawful "recognition" objective. The NLRB accordingly issued a "cease and desist" order against the union and petitioned the Circuit Court of 

Appeals to enforce the order.

Held, the cease and desist order is sustained [with minor modifications not pertinent here]. 

Broadly stated, the question is whether the challenged activities of U fall within the practices proscribed by § 8(b) (4) (i) and (ii) (B) 

of the Labor Management Relations Act, 1947, as amended by the Labor-Management Report ing and Disclosure Act of 1959, 29 U.S.C. 

[hereinafter referred to as "the Act"]. Insofar as pertinent here, that section provides: (b) It shall be an unfair labor pratice for a labor organization or its agents-... (4) (i) to engage in, or to induce or encourage any individual employed by any person engaged in commerce to engage in, a strike or a refusal... to perform any service; or 190 AGO 9111A

LABOR-Continued 

(ii) to threaten, coerce, or restrain any person engaged in commerce. where in either case an object thereof is- (B) forcing or requiring any person to cease doing business with any other person, or forcing or requiring any other employer to recognize or bargain with a labor organization as the representative of such employee under the provisions of § 9. Provided, That nothing contained in this clause (B) shall be construed to make unlawful, where not otherwise unlawful, any primary strike or primary picketing.

While it has long been recognized that picketing, otherwise lawful, will not run afoul of the statute simply because employees of neutral employers do honor the picket line and that this is one of the lawful benefits which may be expected to accrue from such union activities, nevertheless § 8(b) (4) (i), (ii) (B) of the Act sets out the legal limits of such picketing: the union may not "induce, coerce, or restrain" neutral employees or employers with the unlawful object of effecting secondary boycotts. 

Whether or not a union has exceeded the legal limits presents a difficult question when, as here, a "common situs" is involved, i.e., a neutral employer is engaged along with the primary employer in different activities on the same premises. To resolve the numerous problems which stem from common-situs activities, and to protect a union's right to carry on its lawful activities against the primary employer, as well as adequately to protect the neutral employers and employees, strangers to the dispute, certain evidentiary standards were evolved for distinguishing between primary and secondary picketing at a common situs. These are known as the "Moore Dry Dock tests" and were first set forth in Sailors' Union of the Pacific, AFL 

and Moore Dry Dck Company, 92 NLRB 547, 

549 (1950). Under the situation presented in that case, the Board ruled that picketing the premises of a secondary employer was primary if it meets the following conditions: a) The picketing is strictly limited to times when the situs of dispute is located on the secondary employer's premises; b) at the time of the picketing the primary employer is engaged in its normal business at the situs; c) the picketing is limited to places reasonably close to the location of the situs and d) the picketing discloses clearly that the dispute is with the primary employer U argues that all of these tests were met in this instance and, therefore, the picketing was lawful. U assumes too much by proceeding upon the theory that the "Moore Dry Dock tests" are the single guide for decision. Those tests were created for determining the character of the picketing. They are evidentiary in nature and are to be employed in the absence of more direct evidence of the intent and purposes of the labor organization. In the instant case, there was ample direct and uncontradicted evidence pointing to the intent of U. The NLRB could have arrived at no other conclusion than that the activities here were intended to "induce and encourage" secondary employees to cease work, to "coerce and restrain" G, to force G to cease doing business with S, and to bring about the unlawful "recognition" objective prescribed by 

§ 8(b) (4) (ii) (B) of the Act. U attempts to demonstrate the legality of its objectives by citing § 8(f) of the 1959 amendments, which in summary provides that it shall not be an unfair labor practice under subsections (a) and (b) of § 8 for a labor organization and an employer engaged primarily in the building and construction industry to enter into a hiring-hall agreement. Although Congress has given validity to such an agreement, voluntarily entered into by the parties, Congress did not approve the use of strikes or picketing to compel execution of such an agreement. Indeed, the legislative history indicates the contrary to be true.

N.L.R.B. v. International Hod Carriers, Etc., 285 F. 2d 397 (8th Cir. 1960). 

5. Where the Secretary of Labor Issues a Letter of Inadvertence as to a Davis-Bacon Minimum Wage Schedule, a Contract Incorporating the Schedule Need Not Be Amended if the Mistake Was One of Judgment Rather 

Than a Clerical Error. On 29 August 1960 the

Army awarded a construction contract for the clearing of a reservoir area. The contract in corporated specifications containing a minimum wage schedule, as required by the Davis-Bacon 

Act, to reflect the 19 July 1960 determinations of the Secretary of Labor as to the prevailing minimum wages in the area for "heavy and highway construction." On 25 October 1960 the Secretary of Labor issued a "letter of inadvertence" calling for higher minimum wages AGO 9111A 191

LABOR-Continued on the basis that the contract work should have been considered "dam construction," to which higher rates were applicable. The Army asked the Comptroller General whether the corrected wage rates prescribed in the letter of inadvertence had to be incorporated into the contract by a modification and, if so, whether the Government had to pay the contractor any increased costs resulting from the modification. 

Held, the corrected wage rates prescribed in the letter of inadvertence need not be incorporated into the contract by a modification, Thus, the question of whether the Government need pay the contractor's increased costs does not arise. Inadvertent errors of a clerical nature can and should be corrected by ordinary change orders and amendments. 37 Comp. Gen. 326 

(1957). However, so-called "inadvertences" that represent a change in judgment as to what types of classification of work are applicable to the contract should not be so corrected. Since in the instant case the original certifications of the prevailing wage rates for the particular contract appear to have correctly stated the determinations actually made at that time, modification of the contract is not required.

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145009, 3 April 1961, 40 Comp. Gen. 557. 1961. 

[Note: Where a clerical error in a wage schedule is corrected by a modification of the contract, a change in the contract price is not automatically authorized. 37 Comp. Gen. 326 (1957). In the first place, an equitable adjustment must be authorized by a contractual provision such as the Changes Clause. In the second place, the contractor must have incurred a change in his costs as a result of the modification correcting the wage schedule. For example, where the contract set forth a minimum wage rate of $1.85 per hour and the contractor paid that sum to his employees, a subsequent correction of the wage rate to $2.05 per hour entitled the contractor to an equitable adjustment. 36 Comp. Gen. 341 (1956). However, where the contract set forth a minimum wage rate of $2.85 per hour but the contractor paid only $2.75 per hour, a subsequent correction of the minimum wage rate to $2.75 per hour did not entitle the Government to an adjustment in the contract price. Ms. Comp. Gen. B-119373, 27 July 1954.] 

6. Davis-Bacon Act Does Not Apply to Subcontracts Under a Prime Contract That Does 

Not Essentially or Substantially Contemplate 

Construction, Alteration, or Repair of Public Buildings or Public Works-Contracting Officer's Decision That Davis-Bacon Act Does Not Apply Cannot Be Reversed by Department of Labor-Davis-Bacon Act Representations Not Included in Contract Are Not Binding on Contractor and May Not Be Added by Modification. 

By a contract made in 1951 and annually renewed thereafter, the contractor agreed to operate an ordnance plant for the Government. 

The contractor was made responsible for the maintenance of the plant. The contract provided for payment to the contractor of several million dollars annually. In 1960 the contractor proposed to award a subcontract of approximately $160,000 for tie replacement and the surfacing and lining of railroad tracks essential to the plant's operation. The work involved resulted from the deferral for several years of the track maintenance. That deferral had sacrificed certain safety factors but had not prevented full and continuous use of the tracks. 

Before it was advertised, the subcontract was examined by the contracting officer, who determined that the work was within the maintenance responsibility of the prime contract.

The subcontract was advertised and awarded without Davis-Bacon Act clauses. The sub contract provided that it was considered part of the prime contract and was not for the construction, alteration or repair of public buildings or public works. After the work under the subcontract had been substantially completed, the Department of Labor ruled that the work involved in the subcontract was subject to the Davis-Bacon Act and that the subcontract should have included the appropriate provisions for implementing the Act. The Department of 

Labor directed the contracting agency to amend the contract to include appropriate Davis-Bacon clauses and wage determinations. The contracting agency posed two questions to the Comp troller General: (1) Can the judgment of a contracting officer with respect to the applicability of the Davis-Bacon Act be reversed by 192 AGO 9111A

LABOR-Continued 

(a a ruling of the Department of Labor if the contracting officer acted in good faith and in accord with the prescribed regulations of his department? (2) If the first question is answered in the affirmative, may the Department of Labor's ruling be applied retroactively to contracts or subcontracts already awarded or completed? 

Held, the contracting officer's decision that the subcontract work is not subject to the Davis-Bacon Act will not be disturbed. The 

Davis-Bacon Act directs that "The advertised specifications for every contract . . . for construction, alteration, and/or repair, including painting and decorating . . . shall contain" certain minimum wage provisions. This language indicates that it is not necessarily the nature of specific work but the content of the overall contract that governs applicability of the Act. 

A proper test to determine applicability would be whether the contract essentially or substantially contemplates the performance of work described in the Davis-Bacon Act. The prime contract was not, when considered as a whole, essentially or substantially a "contract . . . for .. repair." The Department of Labor has been applying a test concerned exclusively with the nature of the work rather than the nature of the contract. Nevertheless, the work is not subject to the Act even under the Department of Labor's standard. Certain maintenance and repair work, even if a predominant element of a contract, is not necessarily within the scope of the Act. The average expenditure per mile for maintaining the track under the subcontract was $1,800 and can hardly be considered as evidence of reconstruction or major repair, in view of the estimated replacement cost of $134,800 per mile. Further, the subcontract amount is not disproportionate to the amount of the prime contract. Nor does the fact that it was necessary to have the work performed by subcontract, rather than by permanent employees, alter the work's status as a proper and incidental item under the prime contract.

With respect to the first question submitted, it should be noted that, although the Depart ment of Labor, under Reorganization Plan No. 

14 of 1950, 5 U.S.C. § 133z-15, is given authority to "prescribe standards, regulations and procedures" to ensure coordination of administration and enforcement, the actual enforcement and administration of labor standards remain vested in the individual agencies and departments of the Government. S. Rep. 

No. 1546, 81st Cong. Thus, the ruling of the

Department of Labor in the instant case, transmitting wage rates for retroactive inclusion in the contract, has advisory force only. Of course, this does not mean that there is not an area of decision within which the application and interpretation of the regulations and labor laws by the Department of Labor under Reorganization Plan No. 14 of 1950 would be authoritative. 

With respect to the second question submitted, the omission of minimum wage representations and stipulations, even if they should have been included, cannot be cured retroactively. The conditions established by the Act are effective only when, as expressly directed, they are included in "advertised specifications." 

40 U.S.C. § 276a. Unless the Act's conditions are in the contract, the Act is not binding on the contractor. The only method of correcting an omission of the Act's conditions from a contract is through cancellation and readvertisement, and such corrective action should not be taken where the work is substantially completed or other practical considerations render the action unreasonable. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144901, 10 April 1961, 40

Comp. Gen. 565.

9. In Strike Against Primary Employer,

Picketing at Gate Used Only by Neutral Contractors Is Legal Where Contractors Performed Conventional Maintenance Work and Illegal Where Contractors Performed Work Uncon nected With the Normal Operations of the 

Primary Employer. The G Company operated a plant employing 10,500 employees. Several independent contractors performed work on the premises, such as construction work, retooling work, and "general maintenance." A separate gate was set aside by the G Co. for use exclu- AGO 9111A 193

LABOR-Continued sively by the independent contractors. The reason for the G Co.'s action was the desire to insulate the G Co. employees from the frequent labor disputes in which the independent contractors were involved. A strike against the G 

Co. was called by a union representing 7,600 

G Co. employees over 24 unsettled grievances.

All the gates including the one set aside for independent contractors, were picketed. The 

G Co. filed a complaint with the National Labor 

Relations Board, alleging that picketing before the gate used exclusively by independent contractors was conduct proscribed by § 8(b) (4) 

(A) of the Labor-Management Relations Act of 1947 (29 U.S.C. § 141 et seq.). That section provides that it shall be an unfair labor practice for a labor organization: 

to engage in, or to induce or encourage the employees of any empolyer to engage in, a strike or a concerted refusal in the course of their employment to use, manufacture, process, transport, or otherwise handle or work on any goods, articles, materials, or commodities or to perform any service, where an objective thereof is: (A) forcing or requiring any employer or other person to cease doing business with any other person. 

Despite the Trial Examiner's recommendation that the complaint be dismissed, the NLRB 

found a violation of § 8(b) (4) (A). The Board ordered the union to cease and desist picketing the gate. On request of the Board, the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia granted enforcement of the order. 278 F. 2d 282 (D.C.

Cir. 1960). The Supreme Court granted cer tiorari, 364 U.S. 869 (1960). 

Held, judgment reversed; the case must be remanded by the Court of Appeals to the NLRB 

for determination of the nature of the work performed by the independent contractors. If the instances of the independent contractors performing maintenance work necessary to the normal operations of the plant are de minimis, then the order may be enforced. Otherwise, enforcement must be denied.

Almost all picketing, even at the situs of the primary employer, is intended to achieve the forbidden objective of inducing neutral persons to honor the strike. But picketing that induces secondary employees to respect a picket line is not the equivalent of picketing that has an object of inducing those employees to engage in concerted conduct against their employer in order to force him to refuse to deal with the struck employer. Labor Board v. International Rice Milling Co., 341 U.S. 665 (1951). It is very difficult to draw the line between legal and illegal picketing. One principle that has evolved is that a union must minimize the effect of its picketing on the operations of neutral employers. Whether the independent contractors in the instant case are "neutral employers" depends on the type of work that is being performed by those who use the separate gate. In a case similar to the instant one, the Court of 

Appeals for the Second Circuit sustained the NLRB in its application of § 8(b) (4) (A) to a separate-gate situation. "There must be a separate gate, marked and set apart from other gates; the work done by the men who use the gate must be unrelated to the normal operations of the employer, and the work must be of a kind that would not, if done when the plant were engaged in its regular operations, necessitate curtailing those operations." United

Steelworkers v. NLRB, 289 F. 2d 591 (2d Cir. 

1961). These seem to us to be the controlling considerations. The indicated limitations on picketing activity respect the balance of competing interests that Congress has required the NLRB to enforce. 

Local 761, Union of Electrical, Radio and

Machine Workers, AFL-CIO v. NLRB, 366 

10. Architect of the Capitol Is Not Bound by Executive Order 10925 on Nondiscrimination in Employment-Nondiscrimination in Employment Clause Does Not So Restrict Competitive Base as To Violate Advertising Statutes. The Architect of the Capitol asked the General Ac counting Office whether in letting contracts for construction and other work he was required to observe the provisions of Executive Order 10925, 6 March 1961, on nondiscrimination in employment. If the answer was negative, the

Architect wanted to know whether he could include in contracts a nondiscrimination provision like that required by E.O. 10925. 

Held, the Architect may, but need not, in clude nondiscrimination provisions. An Execu tive Order must be authorized by either the 

Constitution or an Act of Congress. Youngs- 

194 AGO 9111A

LEASES 

town Co. v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579, 585 (1952).

Since it is not based on a statute, E.O. 10925 must be based on the general executive power conferred by Article II of the Constitution. 

The Architect of the Capitol is a member of the legislative branch. 22 Comp. Gen. 1132 

(1943). Without a statement of congressional intent, executive authority over a part of the legislative branch should not be implied. 34 

Comp. Gen. 485 (1955). Therefore, the Architect is not bound by E.O. 10925.

There is no reason to object to including nondiscrimination provisions in the Architect's contracts. It is true that 41 U.S.C. § 5 requires that a broad competitive base be obtained. However, the similar restrictions imposed on execu tive agencies by 41 U.S.C. § 252 (c) and 10 

U.S.C. § 2304 (a) have never been held violated by the nondiscrimination clauses included in contracts of the executive branch since 1941.

Congress has not proscribed use of those clauses. Moreover, the restriction of competition is too speculative to violate the advertising statutes. The nondiscrimination clause is no more restrictive restrictive of competition than the covenant against contingent fees or the provision forbidding the employment of state prisoners. See Executive Orders 9001, 27 December 

1941; 9519, 7 February 1945; and 235A, 18

May 1905. Those executive orders have been regarded as valid even though they were not based on explicit congressional authorization. 

See J. D. Streett & Co. v. United States, 256 

F.2d 557 (8th Cir. 1958), affirming as modified

See DAVIS-BACON ACT (par. 2) LEASES 1. Plan Where Proposed Lessees of Government-Owned Facilities Are Required, as Part of Consideration, To Maintain Specified Common Facilities in a State of Preparedness Is Authorized by 10 U.S.C. §2667. The Army pro posed to lease a substantial portion of the St. 

Louis Ordnance plant for commercial purposes in order to create a "stand-by reserve" of industrial facilities. The lease would transfer the responsibility of maintaining the premises and certain common facilities to the lessee. This duty, coupled with the plant's size, made it improbable that a single lessee could be obtained. Accordingly, a plan was evolved which divided responsibility among several lessees and required each, as part of the consideration, to maintain a specified portion of the common facilities. The Chief of Engineers submitted a single lease for approval to the Assistant Secre tary of the Army (Logistics). 

Opinion: The plan is concurred in. The plan is practical and easy to administer since each lessee will repair common facilities which are reasonably related to the leased the leased portion.

Further, the lease is authorized by 10 U.S.C. 

§ 2667 (1958). Subsection (b) (5) provides: 

(5) may (b) A lease under subsection (a) provide, notwithstanding section 303b of title 40 or any other provision of law, for the maintenance, protection, repair, or restoration, by the lessee, of the property leased, or of the entire unit or installation where a substantial part of it is leased, as part or all of the consideration for the lease. 

This act was intended to authorize the leasing of Government-owned industrial facilities for commercial use to create a "stand-by reserve" in the event of national emergencies. In return for the use of facilities, the Government may require the lessee to maintain the premises in a state of preparedness. The act requires that a "substantial part" of the premises be leased. 

There is no indication, however, that a single lessee of that part is required or that a lease of something less than the "entire unit or installation" is prohibited. If this were so, the "stand-by reserve" program would be seriously impaired if a single lessee could not be induced to assume the entire maintenance responsibility. Since the lease in question is part of an overall plan to lease a substantial part of the ordnance plant to several lessees and it is improbable that a single lessee can be obtained to maintain all of the common facilities, the lease is authorized by 10 U.S.C. § 2667.

1. Reasonable Storage Charges Are Not Penalty Even Though in Excess of Purchase Price. The Comptroller General May Remit Liquidated Damages in Sales Contracts. The 

Government sold surplus property on two spot bid sales to two contractors. Each contract provided for the assessment of storage charges for property not removed from the Government premises within 20 days after notice of award, the storage charges to be computed at the rate of $.0334 per day per hundred pounds for the first 5 days and $.072 per day per hundred pounds for the succeeding days. The storage charges were derived from the motor freight tariffs which are applicable when a carrier is required to store freight. One contractor was assessed storage charges for 95 days' delay in removal and the other was assessed for 36 days' delay. The assessments were as follows:

Contractor A Contractor B Contract amount Storage charge 

$1,377.88 $22,337.59 

2,684.00 6,565.43

The Comptroller General was asked to decide (1) whether these charges amounted to a penalty; and (2) whether the equitable powers given the Comptroller General by 10 U.S.C. 

2312 or 41 U.S.C. 256a extend to the remission of liquidated storage charges under contracts for the sale of surplus Government property. 

Held, question 1 is answered in the negative and question 2 in the affirmative. There is no showing that the storage rates were unreasonable and the fact that the property was not removed until the charges for storage were in excess of the purchase price does not establish that the agreed storage rate was unreasonable and, therefore, a penalty. 

With regard to the remission of liquidated damages, the Comptroller General is given the power to remit, on the recommendation of the head of an agency, all or part of liquidated damages assessed for delay, as in his discretion is just and equitable under the provisions of 

10 U.S.C. 2312 and 41 U.S.C. 256a. However, 10 U.S.C. 2312 is part of a chapter pertaining to procurement and, therefore, does not apply to sales contracts. On the other hand, 41 U.S.C. 

256a, although located in a chapter dealing with procurement, was not enacted as part of any other act. It thus must be considered apart from any other provisions of law. Since Section 

256a is not by its terms limited to procurement contracts it may be regarded as applicable to all types of contracts, including sales contracts. 

Accordingly, consideration may be given under the provisions of 41 U.S.C. 256a to the requests of the purchasers here involved for the remission of the liquidated storage charges as may be just and equitable. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143542, 30 August 1960, 40 Comp. Gen. 143. 

2. ASBCA reaffirms Andresen Doctrine. The appellant's contract with the Corps of Engineers for the replacement of chapel furniture required the use of small businesses as subcontractors to the maximum extent consistent with the efficient performance of the contract. 

On 13 March 1959, as soon as the appellant knew he would receive the contract, a subcontract for plywood was made with the only small business manufacturing the item. The Subcon tractor promised delivery within six or seven weeks. The appellant had done business twice previously with the subcontractor (and once subsequently) and had received deliveries as promised. The subcontractor, however, had difficulty obtaining veneer suitable for the chapel furniture and did not ship the plywood until 14 May 1959. Shortly thereafter the appellant requested, but the Government did not grant, a time extension for the delay in receipt of the plywood. The contract was eventually terminated after the furniture tendered by the appellant was repeatedly rejected for failure to comply with specifications. The appellant was assessed with liquidated damages for 205 days under contract clauses providing for such damages. One of the clauses provided in part: 

5. TERMINATION FOR DEFAULT-DAM- AGES FOR DELAY-TIME EXTENSIONS 

(c) The right of the Contractor to proceed shall not be terminated, as provided in paragraph (a) hereof, nor the Contractor charged with liquidated or actual damages, as provided in paragraph (b) hereof because of any delays in the completion of the work due to causes other than normal weather beyond the control and without the fault or negli- 196 AGO 9111A

gence of the Contractor, including, but not restricted to, acts of God, or of the public enemy, acts of the Government in either its sovereign or contractual capacity, acts of another contractor in the performance of a contract with the Government, fires, floods, epidemics, quarantine restrictions, strikes, freight embargoes, and unusually severe weather, or delays of subcontractors or suppliers due to such causes.

An appeal was taken to the Corps of Engineers 

Board of Contract Appeals arguing, among other things, that difficulties with the plywood subcontractor justified a reduction in the liquidated damages. That Board refused the reduc tion. Relying on 39 Comp. Gen. 343 (1959) and

The evidence shows that fifteen days of the delay by the appellant were excusable. The appellant's actions in subcontracting for plywood were contemplated by the prime contract, and the delay occasioned it by the subcontractor was undoubtedly excusable. The appellant had no reason to anticipate difficulty with the plywood subcontractor with whom dealings had previously been satisfactory. The rule in John 

Andresen & Co., ASBCA No. 633 (13 Dec. 

1960), 5 CCF 61182, applies to the contract provision and the facts of this case.

MEDICAL SERVICE CONTRACTS 1. Full Time Contract Surgeon Under AR 40-11 Contractually Obligated To Provide Free Emergency Treatment to Military Personnel at Any Time. An enlisted man, injured while on pass, received emergency treatment from a full-time Army contract surgeon. The treat ment was initially given at a time other than normal duty hours and in a private hospital. 

The Army Staff Judge Advocate, Headquarters, Sixth U.S. Army, rendered an opinion that neither the United States nor the enlisted man were legally obligated to pay the surgeon's bill in the amount of $847.

Opinion: The opinion is concurred in. Since contract surgeons employed under AR 40-11 no longer may be considered to be serving in the Army in a status equivalent to that of an officer, JAGA 1950/2692, their duties are determined solely by the terms of the contract. In the instant case the contract surgeon agreed: 

to perform for and on behalf of the Government, the professional and administrative duties of an officer of the Medical Corps, United States Army, in accordance with laws and regulations in effect upon the execution of this contract and as they may be amended or changed from time to time. 

It is clear that a Medical Corps officer could not refuse to render the emergency treatment involved here simply because he was not on duty at the time. Even though the contract does not expressly prohibit private practice, a full-time contract surgeon must order that practice to make his services available at any time, free of charge to military personnel. 

JAGT 1960/6758, 2 August 1960.

MILLER ACT 1. Assignor of Proceeds of Subcontract Is a Proper Use Plaintiff in Action Under Miller Act Where Debt Secured Is Less Than Proceeds Due Under Contract and Assignee Consents To 

Bringing of Action.

This action was brought under the Miller Act (40 U.S.C. §§ 270a-270d) 

to recover from a Government prime contractor and the latter's sureties in behalf of Allen Construction Company, a subcontractor, for material and labor furnished to and used by the prime contractor in connection with the performance of a Government contract. The defendants moved for summary judgment on the ground that the use plaintiff, Allen, was not the real party in interest and hence was not a proper plaintiff under Rule 17 (a) of the Fed eral Rules of Civil Procedure. In support of this contention it was alleged that Allen assigned all amounts due or to become due under its contract to a bank as collateral for a loan and thus that it had no interest left in any amounts which may be due under the contract. 

The bank brought a separate action against the defendants seeking the balance (about $33,000) of the amounts owed to it by Allen. By agreement the two actions were consolidated for trial.

Opinion: Defendant's motion for summary judgment on the complaint is denied. Rule 

17(a) of the FRCP requires that an action in Federal court "be prosecuted in the name of the party who, by the substantive law, has the right sought to be enforced." 3 Moore, Federal

Practice § 17.07 (2d ed. 1948). In deciding what party possesses such right this Court should apply the law of the State in which it sits since the issue does not involve the interpretation of a Federal statute nor does any supervening Federal interest indicate a need for Federal uniformity. Under State law the assignor of a chose in action for collateral security has an enforceable right against the debtor where the chose in action is substantially greater than the debt secured and where the assignee assents, expressly or impliedly, to a suit by the assignor in his own name.

The facts disclose that the Bank's interest in the assignment is limited to the extent of the unpaid balance of its loan; that such balance is only about one-fifth of the assigned proceeds claimed to be owing by the defendants; and, finally, the Bank has consented to the maintenance of this suit by Allen in its own name. 

The application of these facts to the foregoing principle of law leads to the conclusions that Allen has an enforceable right, that it is thus a real party in interest within the meaning of the FRCP, and that the defendant's motion for summary judgment is without merit. 

U.S. v. Verrier, 179 F. Supp. 336 (D. Me. 

1959). 

2. In Order To Recover Under the Miller Act, a Materialman Is Not Required To Prove That 

His Materials Were Actually Used in the Prose cution of Work of the Prime Contract, But Only 

That He Reasonably Believed That Materials 

Were Intended for Such Use. The United

States instituted suit under the Miller Act in the name of a materialman for the purchase price of materials supplied to a subcontractor on a Government construction project. Under the Miller Act, a sub-subcontractor or materialman of a subcontractor is required to give written notice of its claim to the prime contractor "within ninety (90) days from the date on which such person . . . furnished or supplied the last of the material for which such claim is made

The bulk of the materials were supplied by 16 October 1957 for which $3,962.51 has not been paid. In addition, the subcontractor on the project obtained another $2.11 worth of materials on 31 December 1957 from the materialman. The purchase order of the subcontractor and the sales ticket made out by the materialman's employee for the latter materials showed the job number to be that of the Government project. In fact, the materials were used on a different project not covered by the Miller Act. There was no evidence of anything to put the materialman on notice that the materials were not intended for use on the Government project whose number appeared on the purchase order. The materialman sent a notice to the prime contractor claiming $3,962.51 which was received by the prime contractor on 16 January 1958 or 91 days after the bulk of the materials had been delivered. However, plaintiff sent another notice on 18 February 1958 claiming $3,964.62, an increase of 198 AGO 9111A

MILLER ACT-Continued 

$2.11 over the amount as stated in the original notice. This notice was sent within 90 days of the purchase of the $2.11 item on 31 December 

1957. Thus, if the $2.11 item may be included as part of the materials furnished for use in the prosecution of work on the project, then the notice required by the Miller Act was timely given. 

Held, for the materialman. The materials furnished on 31 December 1957 were part of the materials furnished for use on the contract and notice of the claim was given within the statutory 90-day period. In order to recover under the Miller Act, it is not required of the materialman that he prove that his materials were actually used in the prosecution of the work of the prime contract, but only that in good faith he reasonably believed that the materials were so intended. 

United States v. Endebrock-White Co., 275 

F.2d 57 (4th Cir. 1960).

5. Third Tier Materialman Who Supplies a Second Tier Subcontractor Is Not Protected by Miller Act Payment Bond. In an Air Force construction contract the contractor, pursuant to the Miller Act, 40 U.S.C. § 270a (1958), furnished a payment bond which guaranteed prompt payment "to all persons supplying labor and material in the prosecution of the work provided for in the contract." [See S.F. 

25A.] The contractor let part of the work required by the prime contract to a first-tier subcontractor who then let a portion of that work to a second-tier subcontractor. The plaintiff, a materialman on the third tier, furnished supplies to the second-tier subcontractor and was not paid. After giving the required written notice to the contractor, the plaintiff brought this action against the contractor, its surety and the second-tier subcontractor to recover on the payment bond. A motion to dismiss was made on the theory that the plaintiff was not entitled to protection under the Miller Act.

Held, the motion is granted. The Miller Act extends payment bond protection to two classes of persons: 1) materialmen, laborers and subcontractors who deal directly with the contractor, and 2) materialmen, laborers and subcontractors who have a "direct contractual relationship with a subcontractor" but not with. 

the contractor. 40 U.S.C. § 270b (1958). In 

MacEvoy Co. v. United States, 322 U.S. 102 (1944), the Court held that a second-tier materialman who supplied a first-tier materialman was not protected by the Act. This result was based upon the conclusion that Congress intended to adopt the technical definition of "subcontractor" used in the building trade: "A subcontractor is one who performs for and takes from the prime contractor a specific part of the labor or material requirements of the original contract, thus excluding ordinary laborers and materialmen." 322 U.S. at 109.

The plaintiff seeks to distinguish MacEvoy from the instant case and argues that the Miller Act payment bond protects a third-tier materialman who supplies a second-tier subcontractor, or sub-subcontractor. It is concluded, however, that the "subcontractor" supplied AGO 9111A 199

MILLER ACT-Continued must be in a direct contractual relationship with the contractor. See Elmer v. United States 

Fid. & Guar. Co., 275 F. 2d 89 (5th Cir. 1960).

Contra: McGregor A. Iron Co. v. Merritt-Chapman & Scott Corp., 150 F. Supp. 323 (M.D. Pa. 

1957). 

United States v. Deschenes Constr. Co., 188

F. Supp. 270 (D. Mass. 1960). 

[Note: Even though an unpaid materialman, supplier or subcontractor has furnished labor and material in the prosecution of work under the prime contract and has complied with the notice requirement and the one year statute of limitations, his right to recover under the payment bond is not assured. He must be in a direct contractual relationship with the contractor or in a direct contractual relationship with a first-tier subcontractor as defined by 

MacEvoy. No person on the third tier may recover for labor or materials furnished to any person on the second tier, even though the party on the second tier is a "subcontractor" to the extent that he performs work under the prime contract. This conclusion is based primarily upon the persuasive dictum of Mac-

Act." 322 U.S. at 107-08. See H.R. Rep. No.

This notice must evidence an intent to make a claim and state "with substantial accuracy" the amount claimed and the person for whom the work was done. See

United States v. Thompson Constr. Corp., 273 

F. 2d 873 (2d Cir. 1959).

1959), a second-tier materialman supplied a subcontractor under a series of purchase orders.

All materials furnished were used by the subcontractor to perform a single prime contract.

The court held that the materialman was protected under all of the purchase orders: the requirement of a direct contractual relationship between the plaintiff and a subcontractor was satisfied by a series of single orders under a continuous contractual arrangement if the materials were used for a single prime contract and a written notice was given within 90 days of the last delivery.

6. Subcontractor's Suit Will Not Be Stayed Pending Administrative Determination of Corresponding Claim by Prime Contractor Against 

Government. A firm that received a Government construction contract entered into a painting subcontract which provided that the subcontractor would furnish material and perform labor in accordance with the general conditions and the drawings and specifications of the prime contract. The standard Disputes 

Clause was included in the prime contract. 

(Cl. 6, SF 23A, Mar 1953 ed.) During the per formance of the contract, considerable repainting was required for several reasons, and the subcontractor made a claim upon the prime contractor for the extra work and materials. The prime contractor submitted a corresponding claim to the contracting officer, and then appealed to the ASBCA the contracting officer's denial of the claim. While the appeal was pending, the subcontractor filed suit in a federal district court pursuant to the Miller Act (40 

U.S.C. § 270a et seq.) to recover from the prime contractor and its bondsman for the extra work and materials. The defendants contended that the prime contract's Disputes Clause was in corporated into the subcontract and that no suit under the Miller Act could be maintained until the claim submitted under the Disputes Clause was finally determined. The district court granted judgment for the subcontractor, and an appeal was taken.

Held, judgment affirmed. The parties to the subcontract did not intend that compliance by the subcontractor with the provisions of the 

Disputes Clause in the prime contract should be a prerequisite to the maintenance of a suit under the Miller Act. The Disputes Clause is only for the prime contractor's benefit. The subcontractor has no standing before the contracting officer or the ASBCA, and no provision is made for the hearing of disputes between the prime contractor and the subcontractor. The remedy for a subcontractor seeking recovery for labor and materials furnished for a Government contract is under the Miller 

Act. Ordinarily the fact that a prime contractor has a claim for the same amounts pending under the Disputes Clause of the prime contract does not affect Miller Act cases. John A. Johnson & Sons v. United States, 153 F. 2d 534 (4th

Cir. 1946), cert. denied, 328 U.S. 868 (1946). 

It appears that, as in the instant case, when a subcontractor's claim is being litigated, the administrative proceeding pertaining to the corresponding claim of the prime contractor will often be delayed until there is a determination of the prime contractor's liability. If the subcontractor fails to sustain his claim in a Miller Act suit, there would be no basis for the prime contractor's claim then pending administrative decision. In addition, if the subcontractor is limited to presenting his claims as provided in the Disputes Clause of the prime contract, his right to the benefits of the Miller

Act would be annulled. The findings of the administrative authorities as to the amount he is entitled to recover would be conclusive, unless a court found them to be "fraudulent, arbitrary, capricious, or so grossly erroneous as necessarily to imply bad faith." See 41 U.S.C. § 321.

Such a result should be reached only to implement plain language of the subcontract and is not required here. In the instant case the subcontract references are to the "general conditions" of the prime contract, not to the "general provisions." Moreover, the subcontract references relate generally to performance of the contract according to specifications, not to the settlement of disputes or to the subcontractor's right of suit under the Miller Act.

Fanderlik-Locke Co. v. United States, 285 

F. 2d 939 (10th Cir. 1960), cert. denied, 365

[Note: The same result was reached in 

Wymard and Stark v. McCloskey & Co., 190 F.

Supp. 420 (E.D. Penn. 1960). There a sub subcontract under a Government prime contract for construction provided that disputes between the sub-subcontractor and the subcontractor would be submitted to the contracting officer for determination in accordance with AGO 9111A 201

In the meantime, the sub-subcontractor sued the subcontractor on the subcontract and an oral modification of it providing for payment to the sub-subcontractor for the extra work. 

The subcontractor moved to stay the suit on the ground that the sub-subcontractor was bound to await the outcome of the prime con tractor's appeal to the ASBCA. The court re fused to grant the stay. The court argued that the prime contractor's submission of his appeal to the ASBCA was not a presentation for arbitration of the dispute between the subcontractor and the sub-subcontractor. The court's argument placed heavy reliance on the fact that the prime contractor had agreed with the Government to perform for a fixed price the extra work undertaken by the sub-subcontractor, while the subcontractor had promised to pay the sub-subcontractor on a cost-plus basis. The court concluded that the sub-subcontractor became free to sue after it tried in vain to obtain a decision by the contracting officer.
