7. Personal Service on Third-Party Defendant in Miller Act Suit May Be Made Outside State Where Suit Is Brought. A subcontractor on a Government contract to be performed solely in Colorado failed to pay for materials furnished. In a Miller Act suit in the federal district court for Colorado to recover for those materials, the defendants-the prime contractors and the surety on its bond-filed a thirdparty complaint against L and others. That complaint alleged (1) that the third-party defendants had agreed to indemnify the prime for any failure of the subcontractor to perform, and (2) that the main action was based on the non-performance of the subcontractor. L was personally served with summons in Arkansas. 

He moved to quash the service and to dismiss the complaint. The motions were denied. Judgment was entered against L and in favor of the prime and its surety. L appealed.

Held, judgment affirmed. Miller Act suits are governed by the Federal Rules of Civil 

Procedure. According to Rule 4(f), only when a statute of the United States so provides may service in a suit in a federal district court be made beyond the territorial limits of the state where the court is held. Authority for serving process on L in Arkansas may be derived from the statute providing that every suit under the 

Miller Act must be brought "in the United

States District Court for any district in which the contract was to be performed and executed. 

40 U.S.C. § 270b. 

The Miller Act's predecessor, the Heard Act, also provided that suits could be brought only in the district in which the contract was to be performed. 33 Stat. 812 (1905). This restric tion in the Heard Act was held to permit service, under a statute substantially the same as Rule 4b of the current federal rules, in any district where the defendant could be found. 

United States v. Congress Constr. Co., 222 U.S. 

199 (1911).

The principle of that case applies to the Miller Act and Rule 4b. The Supreme 

Court has stated that the Miller Act, like the Heard Act, is "highly remedial in nature" and must be liberally construed "to effectuate the Congressional intent to protect those whose labor and materials go into public projects." 

United States v. Carter, 353 U.S. 210, 216 

(1957). Congress cannot have intended to render the Miller Act ineffective by permitting suit only against defendants who could be served within a State where the contract was to be performed. The practical operation of the 

Act requires that service run beyond the boundaries of the State where suit is commenced. 202 AGO 9111A

MILLER ACT-Continued 

2 1 L's contention is that this principle may not be extended to permit extra-territorial service on a third-party defendant. The argument is that the third-party practice permitted by Rule 14 is limited by Rule 82, which forbids the construction of the rules "to extend or limit the jurisdiction of the United States district courts of the venue of actions therein." However, in 

Mississippi Publishing Corp. v. Murphree, 326

U.S. 438 (1946), the Court held that Rule 82 refers to venue and jurisdiction over the subject matter, not over the person. Under the Mississippi Publishing case, serving L in Arkansas did not infringe upon his rights. The procedure followed is sensible. The purpose of Rule 14 is to avoid hearing separately two actions that should be tried together. Determining the liability of the prime contractor and of his indemnitor in one action accords with the liberal spirit of the Miller Act and of the Federal Rules of 

Civil Procedure. 

Limerick v. T. F. Scholes, Inc., 292 F. 2d 195 (10th Cir. 1961). 

8. Court Rejects Defense of Lack of Compli ance With the Miller Act's Requirement of 

Notice to the Prime That the Materialman Has 

Not Been Paid. The plaintiff furnished material to the T Co., a subcontractor performing masonry work for a prime contractor on a Government construction project. The T Co. failed to pay the plaintiff adequately and promptly. The plaintiff brought the state of the account to the attention of the prime contractor and its surety on a Miller Act payment bond and received assurances that some money would be forthcoming. Finally the prime-who was also having difficulty with the T Co.-took over the masonry work, urged the plaintiff to continue to furnish materials, and promised to pay the T Co.'s account with the plaintiff. The plaintiff continued to supply materials, the price of which was charged to the T Co.'s account. 

Early in July, with the work nearing completion, the prime paid the plaintiff all the prime claimed was due on the T Co.'s account. The plaintiff thought the payment was inadequate. 

On 27 July, the plaintiff furnished $15.80 worth of materials, including six bags of "slik lime." 

On 29 July three bags of "slik lime" were supplied. No other materials were furnished until 

3 October, when one of the prime's employees picked up one bag of "slik lime," valued at $1.55, from the plaintiff. Between 29 July and 

3 October there were no written communications between the plaintiff and the prime. On 

29 October, the plaintiff wrote the prime demanding payment. After the prime repeatedly promised but failed to make payment, the plaintiff notified the prime's surety on the Miller Act bond. Finally the prime admitted that more than $11,000 was due on the T Co.'s account, but denied liability on the ground that the notice required by 40 U.S.C. § 270b (a) had not been timely provided. According to Section 270b (a): [A]ny person having direct contractual relationship with a subcontractor but no contractual relationship express or implied with the contractor furnishing said payment bond shall have a right of action upon the said payment bond upon giving written notice to said contractor within ninety days from the date on which such person did or performed the last of the labor or furnished or supplied the last of the material for which such claim is made....

The plaintiff then filed suit, under the Miller Act, against the prime and its surety. The sole defense was the lack of timely notice. 

Held, judgment for the plaintiff. The notice provision was inserted in the Miller Act to protect the prime contractor who may with impunity pay his subcontractors after the ninety day period if no claims by laborers or materialmen against the subcontractors have been brought to his attention by written notice. 

Bowden v. United States, 239 F. 2d 572 (9th 

Cir. 1956). However, the primary purpose of the act is to protect persons whose labor and materials go into Government projects, and the act's provisions are liberally construed to achieve that purpose. United States v. Carter, 353 U.S. 210 (1957).

The plaintiff's conduct afforded the prime more notice of the claim than would have been provided had the plaintiff merely complied with the statutory notice requirement. If the plaintiff in fact did not comply with the technicalities of the notice requirement, the defendants were not prejudiced. On the contrary, the prime AGO 9111A 203

MISTAKES IN BIDS 

may have harmed the plaintiff by lulling him into a false sense of security during the statutory ninety day notice period by the repeated assurances of payment. Under these circumstances some courts might hold the defendants estopped from relying on any lack of notice. 

See, e.g., United States v. Peerless Casualty Co., 255 F. 2d 137 (8th Cir. 1958). However, it is questionable whether the defendants may be estopped from asserting the defense. United

States v. Fraser Constr. Co., 87 F. Supp. 1 

(W.D. Ark. 1949).

In assuming that notice was required, the defense overlooks the fact that no notice is needed where the materialman has a direct contractual relationship, express or implied, with the prime. Here there was an implied contract between the plaintiff and the prime.

The prime took over the masonry subcontract for which the plaintiff was furnishing materials. The prime both urged the plaintiff to continue furnishing the materials and promised to take care of the T Co.'s account. The prime made a payment on that account, and the plaintiff provided the materials needed by the prime to finish the masonry work. 

If timely notice had been needed, it was provided. The ninety day period began on 3 October when the plaintiff furnished one bag of "slik lime" to the plaintiff. The plaintiff's written notice of 29 October, therefore, was timely. The defendants' contention is that the ninety day period began on 29 July, when three bags of "slik lime" were furnished. The argument is that since the 3 October purchase was delivered to the prime and not to the T Co., the purchase is not relevant. However, on both 29

July and 3 October the materials were ordered and charged to the same account. On both occasions the prime was performing the masonry work. The 3 October purchase was made by the prime's employee. 

United States v. James Stewart Co., 195 F. 

Supp. 715 (D. Idaho 1961).

MISTAKES IN BIDS 1. Contracting Officer Not on Notice of Prob able Error Where Bid Is Low in Relation to

Current Prices and Performance Costs. The low bid for an electronics contract contained two cost errors. The contracting officer was informed of one error before the notice of award was received but the low bidder subsequently agreed to absorb the cost of this error. 

After the notice of award was received, the low bidder alleged the existence of a second error which, if taken into account, would make his bid second low. The General Accounting

Office denied relief for the reason that the error was first alleged after a valid contract had been formed. Ms. Comp. Gen. B-139757, 15

July 1959. The low bidder requested a reconsideration and argued that the gross divergence between bids and other economic factors should have put the contracting officer on notice of probable error.

Held, the decision is affirmed. By agreeing to absorb additional costs, the low bidder is estopped from protesting the award because of the first error. This estoppel may also apply to the second error since the low bidder had a duty to verify all cost elements when the first error was discovered and failed to do so. In any event, since the second error was alleged after the notice of award was received, there is a binding contract unless the contracting officer was on actual or constructive notice of probable error.

There was nothing on the face of the bid to put the contracting officer on notice. While the second low bid exceeded the low bid by 11.6%, a similar variance existed between several of the other bids submitted. For example, bid number three exceeded bid number two by 13% and bid number five exceeded bid number four by 23%. These differences are insufficient to indicate probable error, particularly in view of the strong competition in the electronics industry. In Monroe Manufacturing Co. v. United 

States, 143 F. Supp. 449 (E.D. Mich. 1956), the contracting officer had actual notice of error when the average of the three low bids was six times higher than the low bid. Here the average of the three low bids is 1.74 times higher than the low bid and does not amount to an obvious gross mistake on the face of the bid which would require the contracting officer to verify before making the award. Cf. 37 Comp.

Gen. 786 (1959). 

204 AGO 9111A

MISTAKES IN BIDS-Continued 

The low bidder argues that the contracting officer, in the light of inflation and increased performance costs, should have known that an error existed since the low bidder had submitted a bid for the same item at the same price four years ago. One of the purposes of competitive bidding, however, is to obtain the lowest responsive bid under procedures which permit free and full competition. This procedure would be adversely affected if the contracting officer were under a duty to assure himself that a low bid was computed in accord with current economic conditions and prices, especially where there is no error apparent on the bid's face. While the Government must, in good faith, protect bidders against gross, apparent errors [See Ms. Comp. Gen. B-139435, 14 May 

1959, DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 278, par. 5], this duty does not arise merely because a particular bid is low in relation to the existing economic climate.

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-139757, 1 December 1959, 39 Comp. Gen. 405. 

2. Contracting Officer on Notice of Error 

When Price of Only Bid Submitted Is Less

Than One-Half of the Government's Estimate of Actual Costs. The only bid received in response to a Quartermaster invitation quoted a unit price of $2.35 for caterpillar parts. Even though the Army's estimated unit cost was $4.85, the contract was awarded without requesting a bid verification. In preparing the voucher, the contractor discovered that a typographical error had been made in submitting the bid and that the unit price should have been $6.35. The contractor requested an increase in the unit price.

Held, the unit price should be increased to $6.35. The facts show that a bona fide error occurred since no bidder would intentionally quote a price which was less than one-half of actual costs. This error is apparent from the fact that the Army's estimated unit cost more than doubled the contractor's bid. The contracting officer, therefore, should have required a verification even though only one bid was submitted. Under these circumstances, it would be unconscionable to require performance at the erroneous unit price. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-141568, 11 January 1960. 

[Note: The contracting officer is required to request a verification if a gross error is apparent on the face of the bid, Ms. Comp. Gen. 

B-139435, 14 May 1959, DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 278, par. 5, i.e., apparent after the low bid is compared with other competitive bids on the same procurement. See Monroe Manufacturing

Co. v. United States, 143 F. Supp. 449 (E.D. 

Mich. 1956) (contracting officer on notice of error where average of three low bids is six times higher than lowest bid). Ms. Comp. Gen.

B-139757, 1 December 1959, digested under MISTAKES IN BIDS, par. 1, held that if a comparison of bids does not reveal error, the contracting officer is not on notice of error because the low bid is out of line with current prices and performance costs, particularly in a highly competitive industry. The instant case modifies that decision to this extent. If a comparison of competitive bids is impossible, the contracting officer will be on notice of error if the low bid is unreasonably low in relation to an estimate of performance costs prepared by the procuring authority.] 

3. Award May Be Cancelled and Purchase 

Price Refunded Where Mistake Alleged Before

Award Is Corroborated by Bidder's Work Sheets and by Fact That Award Would Result in a Rate of Return Double the Normal Rate Experienced in Sale of Surplus Property. The high bid submitted on item 46 of a group of items of Government property offered for sale was in the amount of 1,435,000 French Francs.

Other bids for the same item ranged from FF 

351,000 to FF 288,880. A few minutes after the bid opening a representative of the high bidder claimed that a mistake of FF 1,000,000 had been made in the bid on this item. This bidder's total bid on 69 items was FF 

11,330,903. Accompanying the bid was a deposit consisting of five checks totaling FF 

2,500,000. On one page of the bidder's work sheets opposite item number 46 appeared the notations "Value Dollar 43.582,80" and "FF 

435.000". On another page appeared the figure "FF 11.330.903" as the total bid price and "FF 

2.500.000" as the bid deposit. The total of the prices bid on all 69 items would be FF 

11,330,903 only if the bid on item 46 were con- AGO 9111A 205

MISTAKES IN BIDS-Continued sidered as FF 435,000. If the figure FF 1,435,- 

000 were used then the total bid would amount to FF 12,330,903. The bidder explained the excess of its deposit over the required 20 percent of the total bid by saying that it was impossible to get certified checks for "fractional amounts" and so it preferred to deposit the greater amount. Sales of surplus automotive parts normally result in a return of 2 to 4 percent of the original purchase price, rarely in excess of 5 percent. The bid in question would result in a return of 7.8 percent.

The contractor seeks cancellation of the award to it of item 46, the award having been made after the disclosure of the foregoing facts to the property disposal officer.

Held, there is substantial basis for concluding that a unilateral error resulted from the bidder's carelessness in preparing its bid. The disposal officer having had actual notice of this error prior to his acceptance of the bid and award of the contract, no valid and binding contract resulted from the purported award. 

The award may be cancelled as to item 46 and since the property is still in the hands of the 

Government, the bidder's purchase price may be refunded. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-141569, 29 January 1960. 

4. Bidder Must Be Given Notice of Suspected 

Error by Contracting Officer. Although the contractor's bid on hose assembly units ($4.49 each) was markedly lower than the other bids (from $7.65 to $19.70 each), the contracting officer's representative did not warn the contractor about the difference, but merely asked for a confirmation of bid price and delivery schedule and for data about small business status and use of Government-owned equipment. The contractor was awarded the contract after supplying the requested confirmation and data. He quickly alleged error when he discovered two weeks later that his bid was based on an erroneously low quote from a supplier.

After the contract was later terminated for default, the successor contracting officer recommended rescission of the contract and cancellation of the termination because the contractor had not been put on notice of the suspected error. The Comptroller General was asked for an opinion. 

Held, the contract should be canceled without liability to the contractor. Because he was not told of the reason for the price confirmation request, the contractor could easily have construed the request as an attempt to perfect the parties' understanding rather than as a notice of possible error. Therefore he had insufficient opportunity to check his quotation. In such circumstances a purported acceptance does not create a binding agreement, and a contract may be canceled even after default, without liability to the contractor for excess costs. 35 

Comp. Gen. 136 (1955). 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144252-20 October 1960. 

[Note: The Comptroller General earlier held that contracting officers must protect bidders from the consequences of obvious errors in bids, and that this duty is not fulfilled simply by requesting a verification that no error was made. Ms. Comp. Gen. B-134428, 16 January 

1958, DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 277, par. 4. The contracting officer must identify the suspected error and ask the contractor to recheck work sheets and recompute the bid. Ms. Comp. Gen. 

B-139435, 14 May 1959, DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 278, par. 5. However, it seems that a request for verification based on re-examination of cost data fulfills the contracting officer's duty, even though the bidder was unable to find his error during the re-examination. Ms. Comp. Gen. 

B-139519, 11 June 1959, noted after DA Pam 

715-50-2, p. 278, par. 5.] 

5. Officials and Officers Listed in ASPR 17203(b) Have Authority To Rescind Contracts 

To Provide Relief for Mistakes Alleged After 

Award. ASPR 2-406.4 (g) requires certain bid mistake cases to be processed under ASPR

Section XVII. Several procuring activities informally expressed disapproval of that requirement because Section XVII does not specifically authorize contract rescission, a remedy needed in some cases. The Judge Advocate General was asked by DCSLOG for an opinion whether officers and officials listed in ASPR 17-203 (b) are authorized to rescind contracts to provide relief for mistakes alleged after award.

Held, the officers and officials have the necessary authority. By ASPR 17-203 (a) (ii) the officers and officials listed in ASPR 17-203 (b) have authority 206 AGO 9111A

MISTAKES IN BIDS-Continued to approve, authorize and direct appropriate action ... in the examples of mistake and informal commitment described in 17-204.3 and 17-204.4, including, where necessary thereto, authority to modify or release unaccrued obligations of any sort. . . 

[Emphasis added by the opinion.] 

Under ASPR 17-204.3, a contract may be amended or modified to correct "or mitigate the effect" of a mistake. Rescission is in some circumstances an appropriate remedy in cases of mistakes in Government contracts. See, e.g., C. N. Monroe Manufacturing Co. v. United 

States, 143 F. Supp. 449 (E.D. Mich. 1956) [digested in DA Pam 715-50-1, p. 363, par. 

15]; Ms. Comp. Gen. B-139435, 14 May 1959 [digested in DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 278, par 

5]. Therefore, the authority to correct or modify contracts in order to correct "or mitigate the effect" of mistakes should be taken to include the authority to rescind contracts unless that authority is specifically withheld else where in Section XVII. 

The authority limitations in ASPR 17-205 do not prohibit rescission. ASPR 17-205.2 (iii) provides that the action taken should not release à contractor from performance of an obligation "(A) priced in excess of $50,000; or (B) where reprocurement is contemplated, unless the approving authority finds that the estimated actual or potential increase in cost to the Government will not exceed $50,000." 

This provision clearly suggests that, within the restrictions of (A) and (B), a contract may be rescinded. 

Rescission is not precluded by the limitation of authority to the release of unaccrued obligations. In view of both the purpose of Section 

XVII and the considerations discussed in this opinion, the proper construction of the phrase "unaccrued obligations," as used in ASPR 17-203 (a) (ii), is that the obligations are uncertain, contested, or not absolute. See, e.g.,

United States v. Safety Car Heating & Light ing Co., 297 U.S. 88, 93-94 (1936); United 

States v. Munro-Van Helms Co., 243 F. 2d 10, 12-13 (5th Cir. 1957). A contractors obligation to perform under a contract entered into on the basis of a mistake within the examples of ASPR 17-204.3 is unaccrued within the meaning of ASPR 17-203 (a) (ii). Those examples are situations in which the contractor could ordinarily obtain relief such as reformation or rescission in a court of equity. Restate ment, Contracts §§ 502-04 (1932). The con tractor's obligation to perform, therefore, is not absolute or certain.

Two considerations indicate that rescission may in meritorious cases be particularly appropriate in the exercise of the extraordinary authority conferred by Public Law 85-804.

First, the officers and officials listed in ASPR 17-203 (b), all of whom are below the secretarial level, are limited in their authority to correct mistakes by ASPR 17-205.2 (vi), which provides: the correction of a contract because of a mistake in its making shall not result in increasing the original contract price above the next lowest responsive bid of a responsible bidder in the case of a formally advertised procurement, or the amount of the next lowest responsible proposal of a responsible offeror considered in the case of a negotiated procurement.

Although this limitation is not made by the regulations to apply to the Army Contract Adjustment Board, an opinion of the Office of The Judge Advocate General as stated there are policy considerations indicating that the Board should observe the limitation except in unusual circumstances. JAGT 1960/7307, 28 Sep 1960, digested under PUBLIC LAW 85-804, par. 1. 

The purpose of the limitation appears to be to assure that any extraordinary relief approved by officers and officials below the secretarial level follows the Comptroller General's rule of limiting relief in cases of mistakes in bids to the amount of the next lowest correct bid. See 

37 Comp. Gen. 685 (1958). Applications for relief under Public Law 85-804 based on mistake could be presented in which, because of the mistake's nature or extent, correction to the amount of the next lowest bid might be inequitable or work undue hardship upon the contractor. In such circumstances the only appropriate remedy may be rescission. If officers and officials below the secretarial level lack authority to permit rescission, they might be unable to give contractors "proper assurance that... mistakes will be corrected. . . fairly," pursuant to ASPR 17-204.3. Second, ASPR 

17-204.3 provides: AGO 9111A 207

NEGLIGENCE 

Amending contracts to correct mistakes with the least possible delay normally will facilitate the national defense by expediting the procurement program and by giving contractors proper assurance that such mistakes will be corrected expeditiously and fairly.

Kemp v. United States, 38 F. Supp. 568 (D. 

Md. 1941) is apropos of that provision. In that case the Government had refused, on the ground of lack of authority, to rescind a contract after a contractor had alleged an error in his bid after receiving the award. The court took the Government to task for the "arbitrary attitude by Government departments and their officials" that would "destroy confidence on the part of our citizens and taxpayers in the conduct of our Government." This language and the statement in ASPR 17-204.3 illustrate how rescission of a contract may facilitate the national defense.

Therefore, the authority of officers and officials listed in ASPR 17-203 (b) appears to include the authority to authorize and direct the rescission of a contract entered into on the basis of a mistake within the examples of mistakes contained in ASPR 17-204.3, provided that the limitations of ASPR 17-205, particularly ASPR 17-205.2 (iii), are observed.

Rescission can be accomplished by cancellation of the award if a formal agreement has not been executed for by an amendment to the contract in the form of a supplemental agreement. Both cancellation and a supplemental agreement must contain the information required by ASPR 17-206 (i)-(iii) and be authorized by a Memorandum of Decision as required by ASPR 17-208.2.

JAGT 1961/7280, 27 September 1961.

1. Contractor's Negligence May Be Inferred From Nature of Damage and Its Occurrence While Contractor Was Probably in Sole Control. 

Under his stevedoring contract with the Government the appellant removed servicemen's private cars from aboard ship and pushed or towed them to a nearby Army storage area. 

The contract obligated the appellant to abide by all appropriate safety rules and to report any damage suffered by the cars during his handling. The Army post rules similarly required all Government employees to report all accidents to vehicles. The cars had been inspected before loading and immediately before the appellant unloaded them. A Government employee checked the cars again some time after the appellant delivered them to the stor age area. Each inspector prepared detailed forms describing the cars' condition, and damage noted on the form for the storage area inspection but not on the forms for earlier checks was rechecked by another Government employee. He checked the vehicles, verified the earlier inspectors' findings, and sent the appellant a notice of estimated repair costs for damage thought to have occurred during appellant's handling. The notice called on the appellant to admit or deny liability under the contract's "Liability and Insurance Clause," 

which provided:

The Contractor 

(1) shall be liable to the Government for any and all loss of or damage to cargo, vessels, piers, or any other property of every kind and description, and (2) shall be responsible for and shall hold the 

Government harmless from any and all loss, damage, liability and expense for cargo, vessels, piers, or any other property of every kind and description, whether or not owned by the Government, occasioned either in whole or in part by the negligence or fault of the Contractor, his officers, agents, or employees in the performance of work under this contract.

The Contractor shall not be responsible to the Government for and does not agree to hold the 

Government harmless from loss or damage to property... if the damage resulted solely from an act or omission of the Government or its employees. 

Four test cases were selected from 2,500 where the appellant denied liability. Inspection at the storage area had been made three days after delivery there in two cases and the next day in two. All four cars had chipped and dented sides or fenders, and some had other damage.

In none of the four cases was there a report 208 AGO 9111A

NEGLIGENCE-Continued 

1 by appellant of harm to the cars or any other direct evidence of the cause of damage. The contracting officer, nevertheless, found appellant's negligence to be the cause and charged appellant with the estimated repair costs, without specifying whether section (1) or (2) of the "Liability and Insurance Clause" was the basis.

The appellant timely appealed to the 

ASBCA pursuant to the standard Disputes 

Clause in the contract. See ASPR 7-103.12 (Jan 1958). At the time of the appeal only one of the four car owners had availed himself of 

10 U.S.C. § 2732 and AR 25-100 which au thorize the Government to pay servicemen for damage not otherwise compensable by carriers or insurers. The Government, however, conceded the appellant could not be charged except to the extent the Government eventually had to pay the car owners pursuant to law. In the appeal the appellant denied responsibility for the damage and asserted there was no evidence of the cause, documents alone being insufficient. 

He also argued that the contracting officer lacked authority to adjudge liability under sec tion (2) of the "Liability and Insurance Clause" 

when the "Army had or would have no liability." The Government answered that the appellant's responsibility could reasonably be inferred from the reports of damage existing after and not before appellant's handling and from the nature of the damage. The Government also argued that before the car owners filed claims the appellant could be charged in indefinite terms with whatever amount the Government eventually had to pay the owners. 

At the Board hearing the appellant moved for "summary judgment," contending: (a) there was no dispute within the contract terms until the car owners filed claims; (b) the error of the contracting officer in charging appellant with the estimated repair costs vitiates the entire action and cannot be corrected by the Government's concession that appellant is liable only for whatever sum the Government pays the owners; (c) the difference between the phrasing of appellant's obligations in sections 

(1) and (2) of the "Liability and Insurance 

Clause" indicates that the latter binds appellant only to reimburse the Government after claims are paid the owners. 

Held, the motion for summary judgment is denied; the appeal is denied in part and sustained in part as modified by the Government's concession as to the extent of appellant's liability. The grounds urged for summary judgment are unsound: (a) the Disputes Clause refers to disputes of fact and the existence of damage and appellant's responsibility are such disputes and should be decided while memories are still fresh without a delay for inchoate legal rights to vest: (b) the contracting officer's error in charging estimated repair costs does not destroy his whole decision, and the Board may correct any errors by substituting its own decision for the erroneous parts of the contracting officer's decision; (c) even if appellant is correct that his obligation, if any, arose under section (2), his request for summary judgment is blocked by the long-settled rule that an agreement to indemnify against liability operates when facts occur giving rise to liability, regardless whether a claim is filed to liquidate the liability. American Stevedores, Inc., ASBCA No. 2132 (25 Jan 1955). 

On the merits of the appeal, it is unnecessary to decide, because of the reasons given below and the Government's concession on the extent of liability, whether appellant's liability rests on section (1) or (2). Appellant misses the mark by objecting to the basing of liability solely on documents. The critical question is the sufficiency, not the source, of evidence, and documents alone may be enough. Negligence must be proved by the Government and will not be presumed. Imparato Stevedoring Corporation, ASBCA No. 3181 (29 Aug 1957), 57-2 BCA 1427. The Government must also prove the negligence was the appellant's and caused the damage. American Stevedores, Inc.,

ASBCA No. 5286 (29 Jun 1960), 60-2 BCA 

2686. However, the appellant's negligence may be inferred from circumstantial evidence, and the appellant has the burden of coming forward to refute such evidence. American Stevedores,

Inc., ASBCA Nos. 5288 and 5380 (7 Jul 1960), 

60-2 BCA 2734. The type of damage is one basis for an inference of negligence. Chrysler 

Corporation Export Division v. Munson Steamship Line, The Southern Cross, 1940 A.M.C. 

59. The injury must be traced to a specific

AGO 9111A 209

NEGOTIATED CONTRACTS 

cause for which appellant was responsible or it must be shown that appellant was responsible for all reasonably probable causes. Prosser, Torts, 2d Ed. (1955), p. 205. These principles justify the Government's approach of inferring appellant negligently caused the damage noted after but not before his handling, provided it is not likely that the damage was caused solely by someone other than the appellant. The appellant was solely responsible for unloading the cars and moving them to the storage area. 

The forms reporting the results of the inspections before and after appellant's handling are required by regulation, and there is a wellestablished presumption that a Government official properly carried out a duty required by regulation and ascertained the truth. United 

States v. Pugh, 99 U.S. 262 (1878); Johnson v. United States, 225 U.S. 405 (1911). Appellant attacked the accuracy of the investigation immediately before the unloading on the ground that the light and time were inadequate, particularly since the cars were dirty. However, the damage charged was so serious it would have been noted under the most adverse conditions described. The appellant did not attack the inspections at the storage area and the evidence indicates they were conscientiously performed. However, the first such inspection in two of the cases was made three days after appellant delivered the cars. In that interval 

Government employees or others may have caused the damage and failed to abide by the rules requiring a report of accidents. It appears equally likely that the appellant or others caused the damage and in such circumstances the party with the burden of proof, here the Government, must lose. Pennsylvania R.R. v. 

Chamberlain, 283 U.S. 333, 339 (1932). In the other two cases the first storage area inspection took place the day after delivery and there is little likelihood the damage was caused by anyone other than the appellant. Moreover, the nature of the damage supports an inference of negligence. Those two appeals will be denied as corrected by the Government's concession on the extent of liability. 

American Stevedores, Inc., ASBCA Nos. 

5607, 5608, 5609, and 5613, 26 September 1960, 60-2 BCA 2796.

BUSINESS 1. Circumstances Under Which Army Con tracts May Be Negotiated Without Determinations and Findings on the Secretarial Level. 

The Under Secretary of the Army requested an opinion as to the circumstances under which Army contracts could be negotiated without determinations and findings on the secretarial level. 

Opinion: Determinations and findings by the 

Secretary, the Under Secretary or an Assistant 

Secretary are required in only six cases: 1) experimental, developmental, or research work or property for experiment, test, development or research, 2) classified purchases, 3) technical equipment requiring standardization and interchangeability of parts, 4) technical or specialized supplies requiring a substantial initial investment or extended period of preparation for manufacture, 5) purchases where advertising has proved unsatisfactory, and 6) purchases in the interest of national defense or industrial mobilization. 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (11)-(16) (1958); 10 U.S.C. § 2311 (1958). 

Authority to negotiate experimental or research and development contracts without secretarial determinations and findings may be delegated where the dollar amount does not exceed $25,000, 10 U.S.C. § 2311 (1958) or, as in the present situation, a state of national emergency exists and the dollar amount does not exceed $100,000. 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (1) (1958); ASPR 3-201 (b) (iii) (30 Jun 1959). 210 AGO 9111A

If the contract is with an educational institution, however, the monetary limitations are inapplicable and secretarial findings and determinations are not required. 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a)

Prices on Cheaper Components That Might Become Available After Technical Proposals Are Accepted. (C.G.) See BIDS & AWARDS (par. 35) 5. Propriety of Negotiating Contract Pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 2304(a) (10) Upheld. The Air 

Force negotiated a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract for the furnishing of maintenance, modification, and repair services on complex equipment such as cranes, demineralizers, and hydraulic aircraft assembly jacks. The contracting officer determined that the exact nature, amount, and cost of the work to be performed was not known. He cited as authority for negotiating the contract 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (10), which covers contracts for property or services for which "it is impractical to obtain competition." 

The fifteen proposals received were evaluated on a weighted point basis, with points given for such factors as key personnel, prior comparable experience, estimated cost, and fee. 

The contract was negotiated with the firm receiving the highest number of points. A disappointed offeror protested to the Comptroller General, urging that the contract should have been formally advertised. 

Held, protest denied. The protesting concern has based one of its arguments on the fact that it was a successful bidder on a similar contract that was formally advertised. However, that contract involved the repair and overhaul of various types of general purpose vehicles for which there was adequate and reliable labor-cost data to permit interested bidders to compete on the basis of price and for the procuring agency properly to evaluate bids. In the instant procurement there was no such data available and, moreover, there was no existing information that would have made it possible to draft specifications in such a way that competitive bids could have been realistically compared. There is no factual basis in the present record to question the administrative determinations regarding negotiation, especially since adequate competition was obtained. In addition, it is evident that the award was not made on the basis of price alone, but also on the basis of other factors relating to the contractor's capabilities, both technical and financial. 

The protesting concern suggested that the instant procurement was similar to that considered in 37 Comp. Gen. 72 (1957). There it was held that negotiation under 10 U.S.C. § 

2304 (a) (10) was improper after proposals for the preparation of technical manuscripts were received from sixteen responsible firms and evaluated on the basis of price alone. In the present case, however, the evaluation was not based solely on price. Moreover, the fact that fifteen proposals were received did not of itself render the procurement susceptible to formal advertising. ASPR 3-210.2 (ix) expressly provides that negotiation is proper in the type of procurement involved here. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144082, 15 March 1961, 40 Comp. Gen. 508. 

6. Comptroller General Disapproves of Handling Substantial Rehabilitation of Building by Issuance of a Change Order to Contractor Already Adding New Wings to Building. The 

Navy decided to rehabilitate the six existing wings of a hall at the Naval Academy. An architect-engineer contract was awarded for the preparation of such plans and specifications as might be required to arrange for the rehabilitation by "a competitive bidding type of construction contract." The specifications were included in an invitation for bids, and the architect-engineer expressed the opinion that the work could suitably be let through competi- AGO 9111A 211

NEGOTIATED CONTRACTS-Continued tive bidding. However, before formal advertising could be completely carried out, a decision was made to accomplish the work by change orders to a contract then being performed by the B Co. for the construction of additional wings on the hall. Two change orders for the first increment of the work were issued, involving a cost to the Government of $5,950,- 000. The change orders were negotiated under the provisions of 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (10). The 

Comptroller General requested a statement of the justification for failure to obtain competi tion. The Navy provided these arguments: (1) 

although the plans and specifications were fairly complete, a complete description that eliminated all uncertainties was impossible; (2) formal advertising would not produce a satisfactory bid, because a responsible contractor without special knowledge of the site might include in his bid contingency factors to protect himself against hidden or buried conditions; (3) through lack of special knowledge of the site, the low bidder might fail to include contingency factors protecting against hidden conditions and thus cause delays or produce inferior work because of pressure to economize when hidden conditions produce unexpected costs; (4) because of availability at the site and familiarity with the hall and the academic schedules to which work had to be adjusted, the B Co. offered the greatest assurance that the technical and scheduling requirements of the project would be met. 

Held, none of the arguments advanced to justify the failure to use formal advertising are persuasive. As to the first one, there is no requirement that specifications eliminate all possibility that the contractor may encounter hidden conditions or be forced to do work not described. The specifications prepared by the architect-engineer appear to have been accepted by the Navy as definitive and complete to the extent practicable under the circumstances. 

That hidden conditions might make those specifications incomplete does not justify a failure to obtain full and free competition by submitting the specifications to competitive bidding.

As to the second and third arguments, there can be little or no problem about inflated or inadequate bids when appropriate provisions are in the invitation for bids. The contracting agency may either warrant the completeness and accuracy of the plans and specifications or provide for adjustment of the contract price for work not specified in or contemplated by the plans and specifications. It should be noted, in this connection, that the specifications in the change order under which the B Co. was ordered to perform the rehabilitation provide for adjusting the contract price if the earthwork proves to be substantially different from that shown in the specifications. Moreover, the provisons of Standard Form 23A and NAV- 

DOCKS 113 relating to changed conditions and omissions and misdescriptions in the specifications and drawings were made applicable to the rehabilitation.

When there is no warranty as to the accuracy and completeness of the specifications and no express provision for adjusting the contract price for changed or unknown conditions, there is, of course, the possibility of inflated and inadequate bids. However, there appears to be no sound basis for contending that the possibility of receiving such bids justifies the failure to submit a procurement to competitive bidding. If all bids are excessive, they may be rejected and the procurement negotiated under 

10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (15). If a contracting offi cer believes a bid is improvidently low he should have the price verified, and, if there is no error justifying rejection, he should accept the bid and protect the Government's interests by vigilant inspection and supervision of the work to assure that the quality accords with the contract requirements.

To support the fourth argument listed above, the Navy gave the following bases for believing that the B Co. offered the best assurance of adequate and timely performance: the firm is a large, experienced concern, is financially capable and well qualified to perform the work; the firm is mobilized at the site and able to commence work immediately; the firm has manifested a performance meeting the high standards involved; the firm has been cooperative and demonstrated extensive ability to meet schedules on the same general type of work; 212 AGO 9111A

OFFSHORE PROCUREMENT 

only firms with experience in the type of work and with proved know-how and an organization familiar with the hall could meet the Government's needs; there was no reason to believe that formal advertising would produce a bidder with the required qualifications. None of these factors standing alone justifies the failure to obtain competition or the determination to ne gotiate under 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (10). Col lectively, they indicate that the Navy considered the B Co. the most highly qualified firm, that the nature of the work justified an award to the most highly qualified firm, and that negotiation with the B Co. was therefore proper. 

Whether the B Co. was in fact the most highly qualified is conjectural. Both the invitation for bids that was originally prepared and the change order finally issued incorporated a statement that the concern was required to submit proof of recent experience with work similar to the rehabilitation of the hall. There is no evidence that the Navy determined that the B Co. met, or failed to meet, the experience requirement. It is not beyond question that the 

B Co.'s experience in constructing new wings would provide special knowledge of the old wings. Other contractors working at the Academy in the past few years share the familiarity the B Co. has of the general work conditions and requirements at the Academy.

Even if the assumption is made that the B Co. was the most highly qualified firm, the question remains whether other firms may be denied an opportunity to compete. In passing the act from which 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) is derived, Congress rejected a proposal to permit negotiation for supplies or services as to which the agency head determines that advertising and competitive bidding would not secure supplies or services of a quality shown to be necessary in the interest of the 

Government. 

The Senate Armed Services Committee rejected the proposal because it would be open to administrative abuse and would be difficult to control. The rejection must be taken as a prohibition of negotiation based on the circumstances stated in the quotation. The circumstances relied upon by the Navy for negotiating with the B Co. place the procurement within that prohibition. 

Legislative history indicates that Congress intended that the Comptroller General should not reverse bona fide determinations of im practicability under 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (10) 

where any reasonable ground exists for the determinations. No reasonable ground has been presented in this case. However, the extent of performance renders any corrective action impracticable at this late date. It is recommended, however, that full consideration be given to awarding on a competitive basis contracts for the remaining increments of the rehabilitation. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145598, 31 January 1962, 41 Comp. Gen. 484.

OFFSHORE PROCUREMENT 1. Court of Claims Has No Jurisdiction Over Claim Arising Under "Requisition Order-Demand" Issued by United States Army as Agent of Allied High Commission in Germany. In 

1949 the United States, Great Britain, and

France established the Allied High Commission as the supreme Allied agency of control of Germany. The Commission was empowered to secure the "Protection, prestige, and security of Allied forces, dependents, employees, and representatives, their immunities and satisfaction of occupation costs and their other require ments." By Executive Order of the President of the United States, the U.S. member of the 

High Commission was made "the supreme 

United States authority in Germany" and "the

United States Military Governor under all international agreements." In 1953, as part of a program of the Western Allies to improve the defense facilities in western Germany, the United States Army solicited bids for con struction of an ammunition storage area. The 

AGO 9111A 213

PATENTS & COPYRIGHTS 

Army served upon the plaintiff, the successful bidder, a "Requisition Order-Demand," which apparently described the work to be performed and gave the bid price. The plaintiff was to be paid through orders directed to the appropriate 

West German finance agency for payment out of funds supplied by Germany to the High

Commission. Because he completed the project late, the plaintiff was charged with liquidated damages. The plaintiff also incurred substantial extra costs, allegedly because (1) he had been required to do work others were supposed to have done, and (2) the rainfall had been abnormally heavy. After going bankrupt, the plaintiff through its receiver asserted a claim for the extra costs and for remission of the liquidated damages. Failing to obtain satisfaction through administrative proceedings of the United States Army in Europe or from the Comptroller General, the plaintiff brought suit in the Court of Claims. The United States moved for summary judgment on the ground that the Army had not made a contract with the plaintiff but was only exercising the authority of an occupying power to requisition needed supplies and services from the population of an occupied territory. The invitation for bids had provided that the serving of the "Requisition Order-Demand" "will not constitute a contract under U.S., International, or 

German law." Apparently the "Requisition

Order-Demand" served on plaintiff had provided that it would "in no way be construed as a contract but... [was] a Requisition Demand under provisions of U.S. and International Law." Procurement instructions issued by Headquarters, U.S. Army, Europe made the same statement about the "Requisition Order- Demand." 

Held, the defendant's motion for summary judgment is granted, and the complaints are dismissed. Any German contractor should have been familiar with the occupying forces' practice of requisitioning goods to be paid for by an order on German officials. Even though by 

1953 a substantial measure of law and order had been established in Germany, any intelligent person knew that Germany was still paying occupation costs to the victorious allies. 

Although the United States Army established a procedure, including inviting bids and making an award to the lowest bidder, like that used for contracting in the United States, the Army neither intended to make a contract that would obligate the United States nor would have had authority to make such a contract. 

The United States Army in Germany, in the relation involved in this case, was an agency of the High Commission, an international body with no capacity to be sued. The Army repeatedly warned the plaintiff that no contract was being made, and the plaintiff could not reasonably have expected that he was obtaining contractual rights.

Contrary to the plaintiff's argument, the court has no jurisdiction over the claim as one founded upon the Constitution for the taking of property without just compensation. 

There probably was no taking, but even if there had been, the taking was not by the United States but by the High Commission. 

Best v. United States, 292 F. 2d 274 (Ct. Cl. 1961).

1. ASBC Award Not Final Where Contractor Intends To Contest in Court of Claims and Government Should Not Pay Amount Due Until Release of All Claims Arising Under Con tract Is Obtained. Acme Coppersmithing and 

Machine Company appealed to the ASBCA from the formula settlement of a termination for convenience claim. The Board denied the appeal in part [Acme Coppersmithing & Ma chine Co., ASBCA Nos. 4473 & 5016, 16 March 

1959, reconsidered, 17 August 1959, DA Pam 

715-50-2, p. 368, par. 28], whereupon Acme announced that, pursuant to the Disputes 214 AGO 9111A

PERSONAL SERVICE 

clause, ASPR 7-103.12 (4 Jan 1960), further relief would be sought in the Court of Claims. 

Pending this decision, Acme requested payment of the amount determined by the ASBCA to be due. This request was based upon the Termination for Convenience article, ASPR 8-701 (g), which provided that where the contracting officer has made a formula determination, 66 . . the Government shall pay to the Contractor the following: ... (ii) if an appeal has been taken, the amount finally determined on such appeal." ASA (log) requested an opinion as to whether payment could be legally made to Acme without obtaining a full release of all claims arising under the contract. 

Opinion. While no legal objection exists, payment of the amount due without obtaining a full release would not be in the best interest of the Government. The Government is not required to pay a termination claim until the amount due is finally determined on appeal. 

When the Termination clause is read in conjunction with the Disputes clause, a permissible interpretation is that "finally determined on such appeal" includes an appeal to the Court of Claims. On the other hand, there is no legal objection to paying an amount determined by either the contracting officer or the ASBCA to be due while a further appeal is pending. 

The question is whether making payment without obtaining a full release would be in the best interest of the United States. In the instant case, if no release were obtained and payment were made, the Government might be prejudiced if the Court should find that Acme was entitled to less than that awarded by the 

ASBCA. Payment without a release is not in the best interest of the Government. While a partial release specifically excluding matters to be argued in the Court of Claims is not legally objectionable, Acme should receive no payments for the excluded items. Further, the partial release should not prevent the Government from using a counterclaim to reopen other matters and obtain a more favorable judgment. In view of these difficulties, it is recommended that payment should be made only if a full release of all claims arising under the contract is obtained.

JAGT 1959/7630, 13 November 1959. 

2. Reservation of Government's Right To Recover Any Refund Should Accompany Final Payment on Contract Having Tax Refund Litigation Pending. The Judge Advocate General has expressed the opinion that final payment is no bar to reimbursement of a contractor under the standard Tax clause for a tax which was not contemplated when payment was accepted (JAGT 1954/6812, 12 November 1954, digested in DA Pam 715-50-1, p. 433, par. 13), and is no bar to recoupment by the Government of taxes refunded to the contractor where final payment was not intended as a complete settlement of all tax matters. However, where litigation involving possible tax refunds is known to be pending, a specific provision preserving the Government's right to any tax refund should be inserted in the agreement accompanying the final payment. The matter should be referred to the Office of the Judge Advocate General in the event exceptional circumstances (e.g., impending insolvency of the contractor) exist at the time of final payment. 

JAGT 1960/5941, 16 February 1960.

On 15 May 1956, the contractor was awarded a contract to supply two electric circuit breakers and specified spare AGO 9111A 215

PRICE ADJUSTMENT-Continued parts. The contract price of $22,170 included $3,303 which was, as required by the invitation for bids, identified as import duties on materials and equipment of foreign manufacture. 

The contract also provided: 

If, after the contract date, the Contractor is relieved in whole or in part from the payment or the burden of any direct tax. . . included in the contract price the Contractor agrees promptly to notify the Contracting Officer of such relief, and the contract price shall be correspondingly decreased or the amount of such relief paid over to the Government. ...

The contract was to be completed by April 1957 and liquidated damages of $20 per day were to be assessed in the event of delay. The contractor was unable to meet the delivery date and, early in 1958, notified the contracting officer that the foreign equipment did not meet contract specifications and requested permission to obtain domestic equipment. This change was granted at the contractor's expense but nothing was done to alter the Government's contract right to recover any savings in import duties. 

The contract was finally completed in May 1958. In preparing the original voucher, $3,303 was deducted from the contract price as savings in import duties. The contractor protested that the savings condition did not apply since the source of equipment had been changed. Upon reconsideration, the contracting officer submitted for advance consideration a new voucher which did not adjust the contract price for import duty savings.

Opinion: The voucher may not be paid. The only change made in the contract was the source of equipment to be used by the contractor. The 

Government's contract right to recapture import savings remained and there was no indication that it would not be enforced. In fact, the contracting officer admitted that he "did not think of the question" of import savings. This omission was not a mistake which would support a contract reformation. Further, even though the contractor thought that the savings condition would not apply after the change, the contract expresses the "true agreement" of the parties and cannot be reformed because one or both were mistaken as to its legal effect. See

Tokio Marine & Fire Ins. Co. v. National Union 

Fire Ins. Co., 91 F. 2d 964 (2d Cir. 1937);

Godwin v. Orgain, 160 F. Supp. 757 (S.D. Ala. 

1958). It is immaterial that the parties might have reached a different agreement if aware of all the facts. See 26 Comp. Gen. 654, 657 (1947), and cases cited. Consequently, there is no basis for reforming the contract and the contract price should be reduced in the amount of import duties saved.

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-140667, 17 November 1959, 39 Comp. Gen. 380. 

[Note: Compare this opinion with the digest of JAGT 1959/7810, 25 November 1959, and accompanying note which appear in DA Pam 

715-50-2, p. 295, par. 8.] 

3. Contractor Denied Price Adjustment Where No Convincing Proof That Incurring Unauthorized Costs Was Imperative in View of Unforeseen Conditions. In March 1956, the contractor, for a fixed price of $938,000, started the construction of a sanitary sewerage system at the Navy Industrial Reserve Shipyard. A 

trench 24' deep and 2200' long was required for the installation of sewer pipe. The contract specifications required that:

Excavations shall be shored and braced by members of suitable sizes and arrangement where necessary to prevent danger to persons or structures, injurious caving, or erosion. Except as otherwise indicated, shoring, bracing, and sheeting shall be removed as the excavations are backfilled, in a manner such as to prevent injurious caving. 

As excavations progressed, the contractor encountered soil which appeared to differ from the Government's test borings. The contractor concluded that a serious cave-in would occur if the shoring materials were removed as the trench was filled in. The contracting officer, however, insisted that the shoring be removed. 

In effect, the contractor was ordered to comply with the specifications regardless of the consequences. Convinced that a cave-in would occur, the contractor left the shoring materials in the trench and submitted a $47,627.36 claim for their cost under the Changed Conditions Clause (Cl. 4, SF23A, Mar 1953 ed). When this was denied, the contractor appealed and submitted an independent laboratory report which concluded that subsurface soil conditions justified the course of action taken. The Government offered evidence that no changed soil condition 216 AGO 9111A

PRICE REDETERMINATION 

existed and argued that since neither the contract nor the contracting officer authorized the additional costs the appeal should be denied. 

Held, the appeal is denied. The Government could refuse to relieve the contractor of its contractual responsibility to remove the shorings. 

Yet this right to refuse does not mean that the contractor cannot recover the additional costs of expedient but unauthorized action taken where materially different conditions are encountered. Where unforeseen conditions exist which make a course of action imperative, the Government cannot avoid liability to the contractor by adhering to its original judgment come what may. Carlos Bianchi & Co. v. United

States, 169 F. Supp. 514 (Ct. Cl. 1959). Yet the contractor must prove that the unauthorized action was imperative in light of the unforeseen condition. The proof must be so convincing that the natural resistance to the adoption of one party's judgment over that of another where either could be correct is overcome. Here the contractor's primary evidence consists of a laboratory report which concludes that a cavein would have occurred if the shorings were removed. This report is not persuasive since the person preparing it was not present and subject to cross examination. Further, there is no evidence that the contractor actually removed shorings to observe if a cave-in resulted. 

Consequently, the burden of proof has not been sustained and the appeal is denied. 

Shoreland Construction Co., ASBCA No. 

4845, 30 December 1959, 60-1 BCA 2548.

Several contracts with firms in Louisiana in- 

Icluded the Standard Tax Article (ASPR 11401.1), which provides in part: (b) Except as may be otherwise provided in this contract, the contract price includes all . . . State taxes and duties in effect and applicable to this 

contract on the tax inclusive date. (c) (1) If the contractor is required to pay or bear the burden (i) of any tax or duty, which was not to be included in the contract price pursuant to the requirements of paragraph (b);... or (ii) of an increase in rate of any tax or duty, whether or not such tax or duty was excluded from the contract price the contract price shall be correspondingly increased; (4) Nothing in this paragraph (c) shall be applicable to . . . any State . . . taxes, except those levied on or measured by the contract or sales price of the services or completed supplies furnished under this contract.... · • A Louisiana occupational license tax was in effect on the tax inclusive date of the contracts, and the rate, application, and effect of the levy have not changed since that date. (47 La. Rev. 

Stats. § 377 (1950).) There was no agreement to exclude that tax from the contract price. The

See DISPUTES (par. 18) 3. Prospective Price Redetermination Not Converted Into Retroactive Price Adjustment Under Cost Contract Principles Where Contrac- 

AGO 9111A 217

PRICE REDETERMINATION-Continued 

tor Obtained No Advantage by Failing To Submit Cost Data Until the Actual Costs of Performance Were Known. On 16 July 1951, the contractor, who was fabricating G-2 compass systems for the Navy at its West Lynn plant, was notified that it would be awarded a second contract for the production of the compass system at its Somersworth plant. The contractor was authorized to proceed with production by a letter of intent dated 5 October 1951, but the contract was not formally executed until 21 August 1952. By that time, preproduction costs of $150,000 had been incurred. 

In addition, costs of $170,000 were incurred between the contract date and actual production in 1953. 

The preproduction costs at the Somersworth plant were consolidated with those at the West Lynn plant and written off by the contractor as operating expenses for the year in which they were incurred.

The contractor was awarded a fixed-pricewith-redetermination type contract whose stated amended price of $4,170,927.24 included a 

12% profit allowance. The price redetermination clause provided, in part: 

(a) Promptly after delivery by the Contractor of forty per cent (40%) of the total number of equipments set forth in this contract. . . the Contractor shall submit to the Contracting Officer a breakdown of costs incurred and an estimate of the costs expected to be incurred in the performance of this contract. . . . On the basis of such information. . . the contract prices set forth in this contract shall be redetermined by agreement of the 

Contracting Officer and the Contractor in such manner as may be equitable under all the circumstances.

After the contractor had performed 15% of the contract the Navy determined that the Somersworth plant was no longer needed as a second source of the G-2 compass system. By a con tract amendment in December 1953, performance was transferred to the West Lynn plant. 

Performance at that plant was 40% completed in April 1954 and final deliveries were made in 

March 1955. In September 1955, 17 months after the 40% completion point had been attained, the contractor submitted initial cost data for the price redetermination. The parties, however, could not agree upon an equitable price adjustment and, in May 1957, the contracting officer unilaterally redetermined the contract price to be $3,762,162.69. In so doing he denied the $320,000 claimed for preproduction costs and reduced the profit allowance from 

12 to 7%. The contractor appealed.

Held, the appeal is sustained. Since the contractor and the contracting officer could not agree upon a price redetermination, this Board must determine the ultimate price of the contractor's performance upon the record made in a de novo hearing. See Weber Dental Manufacturing Co., ASBCA Nos. 3808 and 3830 (10 

Jun 1959), 59-1 BCA 2262. In justifying the contracting officer's denial of preproduction expenses the Government argues that the contractor, by consolidating the Somersworth preproduction expenses with those of West Lynn and charging both to operating expenses, liquidated them prior to the redetermination. Further, it is asserted that $150,000 of the expenses cannot be paid because they were incurred prior to the contract. This latter argument may have substance in a cost-reimbursement contract in which a specific clause prohibited the payment of costs incurred in anticipation of award. 

Further, while the contractor's treatment of these costs may have liquidated them for purposes of internal accounting there is no evidence that payment was ever received from the Government. Neither the contractor's accounting system nor the technical failure to formalize a contract at an early date will prevent the reimbursement through a price redetermination of preproduction costs necessary to the performance of a contract subsequently executed. See 

Aeronca Manufacturing Corp., ASBCA Nos. 

3844, 4015 (18 Apr 1958), 58-1 BCA 1724. 

The Government's sole reason for reducing the profit allowance from 12 to 7% was the contractor's failure to submit price redetermination cost data when the contract was 40% completed. By this, it is argued, the risk of estimating the cost of the remaining performance was avoided since actual costs were known at the final price redetermination. Accordingly, the contracting officer determined that it was fair and equitable to reduce the profit allowance to that customarily paid in a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract. There is no doubt that the profit of a contractor performing a negotiated fixed-price contract should vary with the amount of risk 218 AGO 9111A

PROGRESS PAYMENTS 

assumed, see ASPR 3-808, and that a delay in submitting price redetermination cost data should be considered in computing profit. See 

NAVEXOS-P 1001 (Oct 1953). It is an over simplification, however, to state that mere delay in submitting cost data converts a prospective price redetermination into a retroactive price adjustment along cost-reimbursement lines. In the instant case there is no evidence that the contractor benefited by the delay. In fact, the dispute over preproduction costs would have delayed the final redetermination beyond the date of contract completion even if the cost data had been submitted on time. Further, since the real dispute involved costs incurred prior to the time that cost data should have been submitted the contractor gained no advantage by having actual rather than estimated performance costs when the final redetermination was made. 

General Electric Company, ASBCA No. 4865, 1 July 1960, 60-2 BCA 2705, 2743.

1. Prohibition of Unauthorized Payments Not Violated by Payment Under Total Costs Clause Even Though Unliquidated Progress Payments Already Exceed Fair Value of Work Accomplished on Undelivered Portion of Contract. (JAGT) See ADVANCE PAYMENTS (par. 1) 2. Under Partial Payments Clause in Prime Contract, Government Obtained Title to Material Prime Contractor Ordered Shipped Di rectly to Subcontractor. (8th Cir.)

See FINANCING (par. 4) PROPERTY DISPOSAL See also GOVERNMENT PROPERTY 1. Where Material Variation Between De scription of Goods Offered for Sale and Those

Actually Delivered, Contract May Be Rescinded. 

The Government offered for sale in Japan one lot of unused clothing "as is, where is" and with no warranty of description. The major item of clothing was represented to be 13,000 yards of cotton duck which comprised over 50% of the entire cost of the lot. It is not clear whether the high bidder was afforded an opportunity to make a complete inspection prior to award. After award, however, the contractor, K. K. Tokyo 

Sangyo, discovered that 80% of the material represented as cotton duck was in fact a relatively inexpensive cheesecloth. The contractor now requests, through the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Logistics, either a rescission or an adjustment in the contract price.

Opinion: The contract should be rescinded. 

In a sale such as this, there is normally no implied warranty that goods will answer the description given. Consequently, unless the Government has acted in bad faith the successful bidder can neither rescind the contract nor recover money paid for property which does not answer the description. Mottram v. United 

States, 271 U.S. 15 (1925); Triad Corporation v. United States, 63 Ct. Cl. 442 (1927). An exception to this rule occurs where the discrepancy between goods described and goods delivered is so great as to constitute a "case of ordering apples and getting oranges." Standard Magnesium Corp. v. United States, 241 F. 

2d 677, 679 (10th Cir. 1957). The exception is for application here and since no goods have been accepted by the contractor the contract may be rescinded. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-141337, 18 December 1959.

2. Where Miscellaneous Items Intermingled With Specific Property Offered for Sale, Buyer 

Only Entitled to Those Items Which Are Nor mal Complements of Specified Property. In 

July 1958, the Government offered an estimated 200,000 pounds of scrap canvas for sale "as is, where is" at Anniston Ordnance Depot, Bynum, Alabama. The invitation for bids stated that the Government's liability to the purchaser in any case shall not exceed a "refund of the purchase price" but provided for a price adjustment in the event the quantity or weight of the items listed for sale varied from that actually delivered. After inspecting the goods, the high bidder offered $0.0011 per pound and was awarded the contract. After paying the contract price of $220, the contractor, under Government supervision, started to load the scrap canvas for removal. Intermingled with the canvas was a 5-gallon can of antifreeze, a large number of axe heads and ball-bearing pillow blocks, and 1,500 pounds of No. 1 steel scrap.

The Government refused to permit the contractor to load these items on the ground that they were not covered by the terms of sale. When the contracting officer denied a claim for $125 the contractor appealed.

Held, the appeal is dismissed in part and denied in part. To the extent that the contractor seeks unliquidated damages for an alleged breach of contract by the Government, the appeal is dismissed. This Board has no jurisdiction to make a price adjustment unless authorized by the contract itself. Dadourian Export 

Corp., ASBCA No. 4222 (15 Jan 1958). To the extent that the contractor seeks a price adjustment under the contract, the appeal is denied. 

The Government advertised for sale a lot of scrap canvas, not a miscellaneous lot of surplus property. Since the items of scrap metal were not a normal complement of scrap canvas, such as grommets and hangers, the contractor was not entitled to them. The removal of the scrap metal from the canvas, therefore, did not constitute a variation in quantity or weight under the contract.

Salvage, Inc., ASBCA No. 5774, 9 December 

1959, 59-2 BCA 2424.
