6. Removal of Salvage From Accountability Records and Failure To Promptly Recover Does Not Constitute An Abandonment of Foreign Excess Property Under AR 755-10. In 1955 an 

Army helicopter crashed in the Guatemalan jungle. All salvable parts were removed and the remains were left in the jungle and dropped from Army property accountability records. 

After extended negotiations with the Disposal 

Officer, U.S. Army Caribbean, the appellant

AGO 9111A 221

PROPERTY DISPOSAL-Continued purchased the helicopter remains for $50. Negotiations started in March 1957 and were completed with the execution of a bill of sale in May 1957. The sale was conducted in accordance with AR 755-10, entitled "Disposition of

Foreign Excess Personal Property." On 1 April 

1957, however, an agent of the appellee discovered the helicopter and removed it to Camp Sohio, Guatemala. Subsequently, the appellant, under authority of the bill of sale, removed the remains from the camp and shipped them to the United States. The appellee then brought suit against the appellant to recover the value of the helicopter. The district court entered a $7,000 judgment on the theory that the Army had abandoned the helicopter and the appellee therefor acquired title by taking possession. Appellant appealed.

Held, reversed and remanded with instructions to enter judgment for the appellant. The legal rights of the parties to this appeal are governed by AR 755-10, which in turn is based upon the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949, 40 U.S.C. Sec. 511 (1958). 

This regulation defines excess personal property as that under the control of any federal agency and not required for its needs or responsibilities, including scrap, salvage and property which cannot be economically repaired. Foreign excess property is defined as that which is located outside the United States, Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the Virgin Islands. 

Since the helicopter was not lost and the Army retained administrative control, it is clearly foreign excess personal property within the meaning of AR 755-10. Paragraph 22 of AR 

755-10 provides that: "Foreign excess property will be disposed of by property disposal officers in accordance with these regulations by . . sale; or . . . abandonment." But if abandonment is intended, paragraph 29 (a) requires a responsible officer to find, subject to approval by a board of one or more officers, that the abandonment was required by military necessity or economic impracticality. Also relevant is 40

U.S.C. Sec. 483 (b) (1958) which directs exec tive agencies to dispose of excess property "as promptly as possible in accordance with authority delegated and regulations prescribed...." 

Despite the absence of an abandonment finding under AR 755-10, the appellee argues that an abandonment had in fact occurred since the helicopter was dropped from Army property accountability records. Accountability, how ever, relates to the internal administration of Army property and the responsibility of particular persons for its care. There is no necessary relationship between this internal procedure and the abandonment or other disposition of the property. The fact that an officer other than the Disposal Officer informed the appellee that the helicopter had been abandoned "as is, where is" is of no significance since he was without authority to relinquish title. Further, the Army's mere inactivity or neglect with regard to the remains does not constitute an abandonment. United States, ex rel. Tennessee Valley Authority v. Caylor, 159 F. Supp. 410, 413 (E.D. Tenn 1958). The ap pellee argues, however, that the Army had a duty to act promptly to either recover the remains or to abandon them. Since they were not recovered it must be presumed that the responsible officers performed their duties and abandoned the property. Presumptions, like swords, sometimes cut two ways. If appellee can claim presumptive abandonment, appellant can claim presumptive validity of the bill of sale. United States v. Jones, 176 F. 2d 278, 282 (9th Cir. 1949). If the Army had a duty to abandon the property it also had a duty not to subsequently sell it. As the Army did sell the wreck, it cannot be presumed that it was abandoned. The conclusion is. therefore, that the 

Army did not abandon the wreck and the appellee did not become the owner by taking possession. 

Kern Copters, Inc v. Allied Helicopters Serv ice, Inc., 277 F. 2d 308 (9th Cir. 1960). 

7. Where Description of Goods Offered for Sale Differs as to Identity From Those Actually Delivered, Contract May Be Rescinded Even if Contractor Failed To Inspect the Property Before Bidding-Where Contract Clause Limits Government's Liability to Refund of the Purchase Price Contractor May Not Recover Freight Costs in Addition to Purchase Price. 

The Government offered for sale a lot of surplus goods, described as: "CUSHION, Leatherette... UNUSED.. The contractor submitted a bid without inspecting the goods.

The 

222 AGO 9111A

PROPERTY DISPOSAL Continued bid was accepted and the goods were shipped freight collect to the contractor. The contractor upon receipt of the goods found that they were not cushions, but seats with a plywood bottom containing threaded holes for screwing into pedestals or legs to make a chair. 

The contracting officer, on being notified of the error in description of the goods, determined that the contractor could not be afforded relief because of the "as is, where is" clause of the contract (which stated that the description of of the goods did not constitute a warranty, express or implied, "as to quantity, kind, character, quality, weight, size, or description of any of the property, or its fitness for any use or purpose"). The contracting officer acknowledged the responsibility of the Government to furnish the contractor with the "best available information" as to the description of the goods, but determined that the description in the invitation for bids was based on the best available evidence. He also found that the contractor's difficulties resulted from his failure to inspect, although urged to do so by the invitation. The contractor appealed to the 

ASBCA requesting refund of the purchase price and the freight costs incurred.

Held, the contractor may obtain refund of the purchase price. The Government may not rely on its invitation to inspect to avoid accepting responsibility for accuracy as to the identity of the thing offered for sale. While the bidder must accept the risk as to "quantity, kind, character, quality, weight, size, or description," he is not required to accept the risk as to identity. "He is not required to accept oranges when he bid on apples."

He is entitled under the contract to an adjustment for a variation in quantity of the described item from the quantity delivered to the contractor. Since no cushions were delivered, there was here a 100% variation between the quantity of cushions specified in the contract and the quantity delivered, and the contractor is entitled to an adjustment of the full amount of the purchase price paid. However, recovery of the freight costs is precluded by the contract clause limiting the Government's liability to refund of the purchase price.

Tulsa Army and Navy Store, ASBCA No. 

6449, 7 September 1960, 60-2 BCA 2785, decision on motion for reconsideration digested under PROPERTY DISPOSAL, par. 12.

December 1959, digested under PROPERTY DISPOSAL, par. 1.

10. A Statement of the Number of Garages in an Apartment Project Offered for Sale Is a Warranty-Disclaimer Clauses Will Be Con strued Against the Government if It Drafted 

Them. A Federal Housing Administration pro spectus advertising an apartment project for AGO 9111A 223

PROPERTY DISPOSAL Continued sale stated that the project contained 100 garages, renting at $4 each. The prospectus provided: 

The purchaser will be expected to accept the property in its present condition without warranty by FHA as to physical condition. . . . Information provided herein is all to be made available by FHA and is furnished without responsibility on the part of FHA. Those interested are expected to acquaint themselves with the property and to develop their own expectations as to rental income, operating expenses, etc.

The plaintiffs, high bidders, signed a purchase contract which incorporated the prospectus. 

They shortly thereafter discovered that the project contained only fifty rental garages because what appeared to be a two-car garage had space for only one car. The plaintiffs then sued the FHA in a federal district court for breach of warranty. The district court granted summary judgment for the defendant, and the plaintiffs appealed 

Held, judgment reversed. The statement that there were 100 garages was, standing alone, a representation in the nature of a warranty, not a mere estimate. The Government contends that descriptions of quantity, particularly in Government "surplus sales," are understood as only the latter. While it is doubtful that the sale of a single piece of real estate by the FHA is in the category of a surplus sale, the nature of the sale is not the sole test. While the nature of the sale is no doubt included among the relevant factors, so also are the definiteness of the language used and the apparent ability, or inability, of the seller to ascertain the actual facts. There is a wide, obvious difference, for example, between the Government's statement of the "approximate" total weight of surplus junk metal located at a number of forts, and the flat statement that a certain structure has rentable garage space for 100 cars. latter cannot be regarded on its face as anything but a positive statement of a known fact.

In addition, an invitation to inspect may be relevant in interpreting a statement that is evenly balanced between an estimate and an affirmation of fact. However, here the nature of the statement is clear, and the invitation to inspect cannot relieve the defendant. United States v. 

Utah, etc., Stage Co., 199 U.S. 414 (1905). See

The also Hollerbach v. United States, 233 U.S. 165 

The disclaimer provisions of the prospectus and the contract do not exonerate the defendant. They are to be construed against their draftsman. Reconstruction Finance Corp. v. 

Sullivan Mining Co., 230 F. 2d 247, 250 (9th 

Cir. 1956). They are to be limited, if possible, to avoid conflict with other provisions. Fair banks, Morse & Co. v. Consolidated Fisheries 

Co,. 190 F. 2d 817, 821-22 (3d Cir. 1951). The district court was incorrect in believing that disclaimer provisions in Government contracts should be more favorably construed because they were "imposed to protect the public treasury." The Government may protect itself by statutes or regulations, but when it relies on contractual provisions it has no more protection than private contractors have. The excluded warranty as to physical condition in its more natural sense means a warranty as to the condition at the moment. Complete non-existence is a difference in kind, not in degree, and is beyond the disclaimer's language. The rest of the disclaiming language seems addressed to additional information useful in predicting revenue prospects. Stronger language or circumstances would be required to annul the fundamental, basic description of the property. 

Krupp v. Federal Housing Administration, 

285 F. 2d 833 (1st Cir. 1961).

224 AGO 9111A

Quantity or Weight." The Board found a 100

13. Comptroller General Deems Unauthorized an Army Regulation Not Requiring Approval by 

Reviewing Authority of Sales of Property With 

Acquisition Cost Between $10,000 and $100,000. 

An Army general depot advertised for sale tank tracks with an acquisition cost of $2.6 million. 

After the bid opening the contracting officer twice told the U Co., one of the high bidders, that the sale of a substantial number of tank tracks to the firm was final. No reviewing authority ever approved the sale to the U Co. In fact, the commanding general of the depot ordered a readvertisement on the ground that the U Co.'s offer did not represent a reasonable monetary return to the Government. When the 

U Co. protested to the Comptroller General about the Army's denial that a contract had come into existence, the Army relied on Army and GSA regulations providing that approval by a reviewing authority was required for sales of property with an acquisition cost as high as AGO 9111A 225

PROPERTY DISPOSAL-Continued that of the tank tracks. In the course of deciding that there was no binding contract absent approval by a reviewing authority, the Comptroller General noted an inconsistency between the Army and the GSA regulations. The 

GSA regulation required approval by a reviewing authority for sales of items with an acquisition cost greater than $10,000. 44 C.F.R. § 

55.50 (1960). The Army regulation's figure was $100,000. AR 755-8, par. 31 (10 June 1960). 

Held, the Army provision that approval by reviewing authority is not needed for items costing between $10,000 and $100,000 is unauthorized and without legal effect. Exceptions from the GSA regulations are permitted only with the approval of the General Services 

Administrator. 44 C.F.R. § 55.73 (1960). 

Nothing in the records indicates, and the Army and GSA informally have stated they have no knowledge, that an exception has been obtained from the Administrator. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-147367, 31 January 1962. 

14. Navy May Transfer Excess Real Property in Guam to Other Federal Agencies Without 

Reimbursement. By Section 202, Title II of the Federal Property and Administrative Services 

Act of 1949, 63 Stat.

384 (1949), as amended, 40 U.S.C. § 483 (1958), the Administrator of 

General Services is expressly authorized, with the approval of the Director of the Bureau of the Budget, to prescribe the extent of reimbursement for transfers of excess property among federal agencies. The regulation issued pursuant to that authority is limited to transfers of excess real property among the states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and the 

Virgin Islands. GSA Reg. 2-IV-202.07. In view of that limitation, the Assistant Secretary of the Navy (Installations and Logistics) asked the Comptroller General whether the Navy Department is authorized under the Federal 

Property and Administrative Services Act of 

1949 to transfer real property in Guam to other federal agencies without reimbursement. The 

Assistant Secretary pointed out that, although 

Title IV of the Act. specifically 63 Stat. 391 

(1949), 40 U.S.C. § 511 (1958), makes each executive agency responsible for disposing of its foreign excess property, there is no express provision with respect to property utilization or reimbursement for transfers of property among agencies. 

Held, under 40 U.S.C. §§ 511 and 512 (1958), the Navy is authorized to transfer control of excess real property in Guam to other federal agencies needing the property; there need be no reimbursement. Section 202 (a) of the Fed eral Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949 deals with property located in the 

United States. In Title IV of the Act, 40 U.S.C. 

§ 511 relates to foreign excess property. The two sections are complementary in purpose-to provide for effective handling of excess property-but are independent of each other in scope and operation. Under 40 U.S.C. § 512, the head of the executive agency concerned may dispose of foreign excess property by sale, exchange, lease, or transfer, upon such terms as he deems proper. Although there is no express provision for the transfer of foreign excess property between federal agencies, the matter was considered by Congress H.R. 670, 81st 

Cong., 1st Sess. 6 (1949); 95 Cong. Rec. 7443 (1949). The absence of express authority to transfer foreign excess property from one federal agency to another stemmed from a recognition by the Congress of the limited general use of such property by agencies operating abroad. 

Therefore, in view of the very broad powers given to agencies to dispose of foreign excess property, and in consideration of the fact that one of the primary objectives of the Federal 

Property and Administrative Services Act of 

1949 is to enable the Government to utilize its property to the fullest, there is no legal basis for viewing 40 U.S.C. § 512 as precluding the 

Navy from transferring excess real property in Guam to other federal agencies needing the property. Since there is nothing in Title IV regarding the extent of reimbursement for transfers of excess property among agencies, the agency controlling the property may prescribe terms and conditions within the broad author ity of 40 U.S.C. § 512. 

Ms Comp. Gen. B-138264, 10 July 1962.

PUBLIC LAW 85-804 

1. Army Contract Adjustment Board Has Authority Under P.L. 85-804 To Grant Relief in Excess of Next Lowest Bid or Proposal. The 

Judge Advocate General was asked whether the

Army Contract Adjustment Board has author ity to grant extraordinary contractual relief, under the authority of Public Law 85-804, 50

U.S.C. §§ 1431-35 (1958), in an amount which would increase the original contract price above the next lowest bid in the case of a formally advertised procurement, or the amount of the next lowest proposal of a negotiated procurement.

Opinion: Except for the statutory prohibition against increasing the contract price to an amount higher than the lowest rejected bid of any responsible bidder where a contract has been negotiated under the authority of 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (15), the Board does have such authority. However, the legislative his tory of the Act and the provisions of ASPR 17102 suggest policy considerations that indicate that this authority should be exercised only in unusual and exceptional circumstances. It is clear, of course, from ASPR 17-205.2 (vi) that the officers and officials listed in ASPR 17-203 (b) do not have this authority in correcting mistakes under ASPR 17-203 (a) (ii). 

JAGT 1960/7307, 28 September 1960. 

2. Government Procurement Personnel May Properly Furnish Guidance to Persons Asserting Claims Under Public Law 85-804. Section 

283 of 18 U.S.C. provides that:

Whoever, being an officer or employee of the United 

States or any department or agency thereof... acts as an agent or attorney for prosecuting any claim against the United States, or aids or assists in the prosecution or support of any such claim otherwise than in the proper discharge of his official duties . . . shall be fined not more than $10,000 or imprisoned not more than one year, or both.

DCSLOG asked the Judge Advocate General for an opinion whether that statute would be violated by a contracting officer who furnished guidance to contractors asserting a right to re quest relief under Public Law 85-804, 50 U.S.C. 

SS 1431-1435. 

Held, Government procurement personnel may, without violating 18 U.S.C. § 283, furnish guidance to contractors concerning the submission of requests for relief under P.L. 85-804.

The so-called Contract Authorization Act, P.L. 

85-804, was not passed for the benefit of contractors, and action can be taken under the authority of the act only when the national defense would be facilitated. The act confers no rights on contractors, and the denial of relief gives rise to no legal or equitable claim. The fact that an individual contractor will benefit from action taken under the authority of the act is merely incidental. See, e.g., Bolinders 

Co. v. United States, 139 Ct. Cl. 677, 153 F. 

Supp. 381 (1957), cert. denied, 355 U.S. 953 

(1958); Cooper Tire and Rubber Co. v. United 

States, 138 Ct. Cl. 539, 150 F. Supp. 840 (1957).

S. Rept. No. 2281, 85th Cong., 2d Sess. 3 (1958). 

Therefore, it is not clear that a contractor's request for relief under P.L. 85-804 is a claim against the United States within the meaning of 18 U.S.C. § 283 (1958). It is, however, not necessary to express an opinion on this issue.

Aiding or assisting the prosecution or support of a claim against the United States is prohibited by 18 U.S.C. § 283 only when the aid or assistance is given by an officer or employee "otherwise than in the proper discharge of his official duties." Since relief under P.L. 85-804 

can be granted to a contractor only when the relief will "facilitate the national defense," an assumption may be made that the Government is benefited by the Facilitation of the national defense in all cases where the contractor's request for relief under the act is granted. If granting relief to a contractor under P.L. 85-804 will facilitate the national defense, then, a fortiori, the national defense also is facilitated by providing appropriate assistance to contractors in their attempts to point out instances in which the national defense can or will be facilitated by the Government's taking appropriate action (such as granting relief to the contractor). 

Consequently, procurement personnel furnishing guidance to contractors about the submission of requests for relief under P.L. 85-804 are acting in the best interests of the United States and in the proper discharge of their official duties. Such action would not be prohibited by 

18 U.S.C. $283.

The extent to which assistance or guidance AGO 9111A 227

QUANTUM MERUIT 

properly may be furnished to a contractor necessarily will vary with the circumstances of the individual case. However, it is not improper in a given case to furnish any available information or suggestions to a contractor about the manner in which requests under this act should be submitted, including references to P.L. 85804 and an explanation of the substantive pro visions and procedural requirements of Section XVII of ASPR. 

JAGT 1961/6130, 19 June 1961.

1. Release Not Avoidable for Economic Du ress if Hardship Neither Irremediable nor 

Caused by Governmental Coercion. In August 

1952, the Government entered into a fixed-price contract for the construction of several Navy gunboats. Under the contract, which included the standard Changes Clause (ASPR 7-103.2), the Government agreed to furnish plans and several components. In April 1954, the Government issued a change order which authorized additional work to correct defects caused by delays in furnishing plans and materials. 

Resulting price increases were to be adjusted later. The contractor then submitted a claim of $303,508.02 for increased costs. Upon request of the Supervisor of Shipbuilding, the contractor agreed to exclude two items, totaling $133,- 693, with the understanding that they could be claimed at a later date. These two items were for increased costs resulting from delays in delivery of Government furnished property. 

A supplemental agreement which did not include these two items was then executed. Subsequently, the contractor submitted a second claim for $354,416, which included the two omitted items. At negotiations on this claim in 

Jacksonville, Florida, the contractor revealed that its shipyard had been closed for lack of funds. Arguing that the change order was completely liquidated in the first supplemental agreement, the Government offered $150,000 in settlement of all claims except the two omitted items. The contractor rejected this offer and three days later renewed negotiations with the contracting officer in Washington, D.C. When told of the shipyard's financial straits, the contracting officer stated that while he did not wish 228 AGO 9111A

REQUIREMENTS CONTRACTS 

to take advantage of the contractor's distress, he had neither authority nor reason to reopen the change order. Initially the offer made in 

Jacksonville was repeated, with $22,000 added for items not included in the second claim. At a later stage in the negotiations, however, the contracting officer decided that the Jacksonville offer was a reasonable settlement for all the contractor's claims, including the two omitted items. The contracting officer's alternative of fer, which was rejected, was to split the $172,000 in half and let the contractor pursue separately its claim for the items omitted from the first supplemental agreement. The contractor and the Government then executed a second supplemental agreement which, for $172,000, discharged all liability of the Government for delays up to the time of the amendment. After unsuccessfully seeking relief under Title II of the First War Powers Act for a mutual mistake in the coverage of the amendment, the contractor demanded a third supplemental agreement to increase the contract price $133,693 for the two items omitted from the earlier supplemental agreements. From the denial of this demand the contractor appealed to the ASBCA, arguing that the second agreement was executed under duress.

Held, the appeal is denied. The elements of economic duress are (1) involuntary acceptance of terms; (2) circumstances permitting no alternative; and (3) causation of those circumstances by the dominant party. See Fruhauf 

Southwest Garment Co. v. United States, 126 

Ct. Cl. 51, 62 (1953). The contractor, not the

Government, was pressing for a settlement. At both the Jacksonville and Washington negotiations the contractor could have accepted $150,000 without releasing its claim for the two excluded items. Thus, the contractor's acceptance of the second agreement was voluntary and not the product of governmental coercion. 

Georgia Shipbuilding Corp., ASBCA No. 

3079, 19 July 1960, 60-2 BCA 2677. 

[Note: See Kelley Boat Works, ASBCA No. 

6119 (31 May 1960), 60-2 BCA 2670, where the 

ASBCA also concluded that a general release was not induced by "mistake, duress or overreaching on the part of the Government."] 

REQUIREMENTS CONTRACTS See also TYPES OF CONTRACTS 1. Contract Which Lists Estimated Quantities and Obligates Contracting Officer To Order Services Which He Determines Are Needed Is for Requirements Rather Than Fixed Quantity. 

The contractor agreed to perform all work in connection with the collection and disposal of garbage and the unloading and hauling of coal at Camp Hale, Colorado during fiscal year 1956, unless sooner terminated for the convenience of the Government. The contract established a firm price per ton of material handled. The annual quantity of material to be collected or handled was estimated at 4,000 tons for garbage and 11,000 tons for coal. In addition, the contract contained the following special provisions: 

5. ESTIMATED QUANTITIES: Quantities of the various items listed herein are based upon the best information obtainable and represent the estimated and not the actual amounts for which supplies and/or services may be required during the contract period. The fact that specific quantities cannot be determined and given in this instrument shall not relieve the Government of its obligation to order from the Contractor all the supplies and/or services, which, in the judgment of the Contracting 

Officer, may be needed, and shall not in any case relieve the Contractor of his obligation to fill all orders for supplies and/or services which he may be required to furnish during the contract period. 

QUANTITIES OF WORK TO BE DONE: The qualities of work to be performed are outlined in the Invitation to Bid. The quantity is estimated only and will be used in formulating and comparing bids. The quantity may vary from 75% to 125% of the figure. The contractor will be required to complete the work specified herein at the contract unit price regardless of the quantity of the work.

During fiscal year 1956, the Government's actual collection and hauling requirements were only 55% of the estimated 4,000 tons of garbage and 63% of the estimated 11,000 tons of coal. 

The contractor was fully paid for the work done but subsequently filed a termination claim for that portion of the estimated services which had not been ordered by the Government. The contracting officer's denial was appealed to the ASBCA which affirmed, holding that a requirements contract had been entered into by the parties and that the Government had acted in good faith. The sole issue in this suit is wheth AGO 9111A 229

RESCISSION 

er the quantity of the contract services to be performed by the contractor were fixed and definite or to be measured by the Government's requirements. 

Held, the petition is dismissed. In a requirements contract, one party promises to supply all the specific goods or services which the other party may need during a certain period at an agreed price. Commercial necessity dictates their enforceability even though definable signposts of quantity are lacking. Walker Mfg. Co. v. Swift & Co., 200 Fed. 529 (5th Cir. 1912).

Since the requirements contract often establishes a firm unit price, there is a temptation for one party to take advantage of the other in the quantity ordered in periods of price fluctuation. Thus, where the quantity ordered is considerably more or less than that estimated by the contract, a test of good faith will be applied. Standard Magnesium Corp. v. United 

States, 241 F. 2d 677 (10th Cir. 1957).

In the instant case, the contract provided that listed quantities were estimates only. The dominant measure of quantity was the amount of disposal and hauling which the contracting officer, in good faith, judged to be needed at

Camp Hale during fiscal year 1956. Thus, the contract was for requirements and the inclusion of estimated quantities was merely to assist the parties to reach an agreement. See Brawley v.

United States, 96 U.S. 168 (1877). This con clusion is not affected by the contract language permitting a variation between 75% and 125% of the estimated quantities. Rather than establishing maximum and minimum requirements, Johnstown Coal & Coke Co. v. United States, 66 Ct. Cl. 616 (1929), this provision simply further qualifies the qualified estimate of need and does not alter the contract's clear meaning. 

See Marx v. American Malting Co., 169 Fed. 

582 (6th Cir. 1909). This is not a case of bad faith, Gemsco, Inc. v. United States, 115 Ct. Cl. 

209 (1950), or where the contract gave the Government an unconscionable advantage. See

Sylvan Crest Sand & Gravel Co. v. United States, 150 F. 2d 642 (2d Cir. 1945). The Gov ernment fully performed the contract by purchasing, in good faith, all of its requirements from the contractor. 

Shader Contractors, Inc. v. United States, 276 F. 2d 1 (Ct. Cl. 1960). 

[Note: The Court observed: "It would have been impossible, as the plaintiff well knew, for the defendant to guarantee or warranty that any amount of refuse would be generated or that any specific amount of coal would be consumed during the contract period. The exigencies of national security in today's world make the number of troops situated at any given installation subject to sudden, unexpected upward and downward fluctuations." This, of course, is an extremely important factor in determining the intention of the parties. The instant decision should be distinguished from those where the issue was whether the Government had actually promised to order when requirements arose. See Lowell O. West Lumber 

Sales Corp. v. United States, 270 F. 2d 12 (9th 

Cir. 1959), DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 259, par. 2 (call type contract compared with requirements contract). See also, Pennsylvania Exchange 

Bank v. United States, 170 F. Supp. 629 (Ct. Cl. 

1959), DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 86, par. 2 (industrial preparedness contract).]

RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT 1. Teaching Expenses Are Allowable Indirect Cost of Research Contract With Educational 

Institution Although Not Actually Affected by 

Research Project. From July 1951 until Decem ber 1958, George Washington University, under two cost-reimbursable type contracts, engaged in psychological research for the Government. 

This project was entitled "The Human Resources Research Office" (HumRRO). From 

November 1955 until June 1957, the University, under another cost-reimbursable type contract, engaged in a logistical research project entitled the "Modern Army Supply System" (MASS). 

Both project sites were physically isolated from regular university activity and had little or no contact with the traditional university functions of teaching and basic departmental research. 

Prior to 30 September 1955, indirect costs under the HumRRO contracts were reimbursed on the basis of a predetermined percentage of direct salaries and wages; 38% for on-campus activities and 10% for off-campus activities.

After 30 September 1955, however, indirect costs for the HumRRO project and the new MASS project were to be reimbursed on the basis of post-determined percentages. This necessitated the negotiation of final percentages after the current accounting period had passed. 

The contracts for both projects provided that the negotiation was to be governed by ASPR 

Section XV, Part 3, and a Government pamphlet entitled "Explanation of Principles for Determination of Costs Under Government Research and Development Contracts With Education Institutions." (Blue Book) The Blue Book is more detailed than ASPR Section XV and governs this appeal.

The Blue Book's purpose is to create an "equitable accounting understanding between the Government and education institutions as the latter have been generally accustomed to conducting their business affairs." It provides, inter alia, that an educational institution shall be reimbursed for indirect costs allocable to the contract. General and administrative and gen eral expenses, as indirect costs, are given extensive treatment. G&A expenses include "all expense of the general executive and administrative offices of institutions, also all expenses which are of a general character and which do not relate to any specific division of the institution," except the cost of equipment, library expense and operation and maintenance overhead. 

General expenses include those "affecting the institution as a whole" and, more specifically, certain expenses which are directly related to the institution's teaching function. With regard to this, the Blue Book comments: 

It is recognized that certain of these items [general expenses] are primarily related to instruction. 

However, certain other items, such as salaries and expenses of offices and college deans and instructional department heads which relate at least in part to research, have been excluded and not recognized as indirect expense. ... The two groups of items are considered as reasonably offsetting each other in most instances.

In the first accounting period for which postdetermined percentages were to be negotiated, the University claimed the following: 

HumRRO, 32.53% on-campus, 14.27% off-campus; MASS, 35.27% on-campus, 17.02% offcampus. The Army Audit Agency, however, found that the University's G&A pool contained expenses which could be directly related to the instruction function. Accordingly, these expenses were separated from the audited research for the purpose of determining the reimbursable amount of indirect costs. Further, the Audit Agency determined that the 

Operation and Maintenance pool should have been apportioned on the basis of square footage occupied rather than wages and salaries. As a result of these findings, the Audit Agency approved percentages of 13.14 and 3.89 for the

HumRRO project and 21.34 and 4.94 for the 

MASS project, thus reducing the total amount claimed by $197,646. The University appealed.

Held, the appeal is sustained in part and denied in part. The Government points out that both research projects were physically isolated from and unsupported by regular university activities. Further, the audited research in no way contributed to the expense of instruction which was included by the University in the G&A pool. From this it is concluded that the instruction expense can be directly charged to a "specific function" and cannot be reimbursed as an indirect expense. The difficulty with this AGO 9111A 231

RESPONSIBLE BIDDERS 

argument is that the Blue Book specifically allocates a proper proportion of instruction expense to audited research even though the research does not contribute to the expense. 

The fact that the instruction expense specifically included in the G&A pool is not offset by other exclusions in this case is immaterial, for the Blue Book contemplates that over a long period of contract administration an equitable offset will occur. Thus, the audit result rewrites the terms of the contract and cannot be accepted. Further, it eliminates from consideration the teaching element which is essential to qualify an organization as an educational in stitution under the Blue Book. 

[The Board then approved the apportionment of the Operation and Maintenance pool on the basis of square footage rather than salaries and wages and allowed final percentages of 22.87 and 15.28 for HumRRO and 25.62 and 18.03 for

MASS.] George Washington University, ASBCA Nos. 

4725, 4726 and 4727, 22 October 1959, 59-2

BCA 2376. 

[Note: For an indication that the doctrine of the instant case does not apply to expenses generated by every activity which benefits an educational institution, i.e., "auxiliary enterprises and noneducational activities," see Georgetown 

University, ASBCA Nos. 3516, 3517, 29 October 1959, 59-2 BCA 2377.] 

2. Review Made of the Position of the Office of the Judge Advocate General on Problems Relating to Indemnification of Contractors Against Ultrahazardous Risks. (JAGT) See INDEMNITY (par. 1) RESPONSIBLE BIDDERS See also BIDS & AWARDS, DEBAR- MENT OF BIDDERS 1. Failure To Maintain Equipment in Proper Condition for Performance of Contract Is Aspect of Responsibility Not Covered by SBA Certificate of Competency. (C.G.) See SMALL BUSINESS (par. 9) SET-ASIDES 

See also SMALL BUSINESS 1. In Set Aside for Small Business Concerns in Labor Surplus Area, Government Required To Negotiate With Bidder Who Had Highest Unit Price Awarded in Regular Course of Contracting on Unrestricted Portion. The Military 

Clothing Agency requested bids for furnishing 3,000 paulins and set aside an additional 3,000 units for possible award to concerns in labor surplus areas. Bid prices were to include all applicable Federal, State, and local taxes, except those from which the supplies were exempt. Bidder A submitted a unit price bid of $55 on the unrestricted portion plus a $4.38 

Federal excise tax if applicable. Bidder B, who had obtained an Internal Revenue ruling that the excise tax was not applicable, submitted a unit price bid of $58.68. At the time of bid opening, the contracting officer thought that the excise tax was applicable and that B had submitted a tax inclusive bid. Accordingly, he added $4.38 to A's bid and awarded the unrestricted portion of the contract to B as low bidder. When the mistake was discovered it was determined that A was actually the low bidder. The Office of the Quartermaster Gen eral recommended that B's contract be cancelled and awarded to A, but that negotiations on the set aside portion be made with B. The Deputy 

Chief of Staff for Logistics requested an opinion.

Held, the award to B is valid but the set aside should be negotiated with A. B's bid conformed to the invitation in all respects since it did not include taxes which were known to be inapplicable. The contracting officer awarded the contract in good faith to B on the mistaken assumption that B's bid included an applicable excise tax. It is likely, therefore, that a court would find that a binding contract was created by the contracting officer's acceptance. Further, the Government's best interest would not be served by cancellation since the contractor has incurred preproduction expenses of $14,500 which may be claimed.

The regulations, however, do not require that negotiations be made with B on the set aside portion. While B's price was the "highest unit price" awarded on the unrestricted portion, see 

ASPR 1-804 (30 Jun 1959), it was arrived at through error. If the set aside portion were awarded to B instead of A the Government would lose approximately $8,800. This justifies 232 AGO 9111A

SET-ASIDES-Continued the conclusion that "highest unit price" means the price arrived at in the regular course of contracting rather than that arrived at through error, and in no case should be construed to require an award at a price higher than bid by the party entitled to the award. Accordingly, the set aside should be negotiated with A. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-141577, 8 January 1960, 39 Comp. Gen. 503. 

2. Comptroller General Rules That The Defense Department Is Prohibited From Using Total Set-Asides for Labor-Surplus-Area Con cerns. The President asked the Department of

Defense and several other agencies for recommendations as to improved means for channeling contracts to labor-surplus areas. The concensus was that to increase measurably the volume of awards to labor-surplus areas, total set-asides for award only to firms in such areas should be made. The Assistant Secretary of

Defense (I&L) asked the Comptroller General whether such set-asides would violate the pro hibition in Section 523 of the Defense Appro priation Act against paying price differentials on contracts made to relieve economic dislocations. The Assistant Secretary suggested that no question of a price differential would arise if total set-asides were made only where there was a reasonable expectation that bids or proposals would be obtained from enough responsible labor-surplus-area concerns to insure fair and reasonable prices.

Held, the proposed use of total set-asides is disapproved. Both the small-business and laborsurplus-area preferences in Government pro curement originated in the Defense Production 

Act of 1950, 64 Stat. 798, and amendments and supplementary directives thereto. It was held that the preferences thus established could not be implemented by awarding contracts solely on the basis of small-business or labor-surplusarea considerations in procurements required by law to be formally advertised. It was stated, however, that there would be no objection to negotiation of contracts with small-business or labor-surplus-area concerns pursuant to the authority (now in 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a) (1)) to negotiate contracts during a national emergency proclaimed by the President. The smallbusiness preference was later given more express legislative sanction by the Small Business 

Act of 1953, 67 Stat. 232. However, by a proviso like that in Section 523 of the Defense Appropriation Act of 1961, the Congress in 1954 began prohibiting the expenditure of appropriated funds to pay price differentials on contracts made to relieve economic dislocations. 

The legislative history indicates that the limitation precludes awarding contracts to laborsurplus-area concerns for a price greater than the lowest obtainable in an unrestricted solicitation of bids or proposals. The limitation cannot be avoided by obtaining offers from enough labor-surplus-area concerns to insure fair and reasonable prices. In the absence of free and unrestricted competition, no showing of a fair and reasonable price would be taken as establishing that the price was the lowest obtainable. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145136, 3 March 1961, 40

Comp. Gen. 489. 

3. Unresponsive Bidder on Non-Set-Aside 

Portion Is Ineligible for Negotiations on Portion 

Set Aside for Labor-Surplus-Area Concerns. An 

Army invitation for bids stated that a contract for 500 boats would be awarded to the low responsive responsible bidder, and that an equal quantity would be procured through negotiation under a labor-surplus set aside. The R Co. would have been eligible for first consideration on the set-aside portion, except that the firm failed to acknowledge an amendment making the specifications more stringent. After bid opening the R Co. claimed it had not received the amendment but would meet the more stringent specifications at the bid price. The Comptroller General was asked whether negotiation with the R Co. on the set-aside portion would be proper. 

Held, the R Co. is ineligible for participation in the set-aside portion. Failure to acknowledge receipt of an amendment making material changes in specifications clearly precludes award on advertised procurement. 40

Comp. Gen. 126 (1960). The invitation pro vided: area concerns Negotiations for award of the set-aside portion will be conducted only with responsible labor surplus who have submitted responsive bids or proposals on the non-set-aside portion at a unit price within 120 percent of the highest award made on the non-set-aside portion. AGO 9111A 233

SET-ASIDES-Continued 

The purpose of this requirement is to limit participation in negotiations on the set-aside portion to firms who seriously competed for the non-set-aside portion. The requirement would be nullified if nonresponsive bidders are considered for award on the set-aside portion. 

Even though award on the set-aside portion is not subject to the strict rules on formal advertising, limitations on eligibility for negotiation that are stated in an invitation should be followed. See 41 Comp. Gen. 160 (1961); 39

Comp. Gen. 17 (1959).

4. When Non-Set-Aside Portion Has Several Different Destinations, Each Destination May Be Treated Separately for the Purpose of Deter mining Both the Lowest Responsible Bidder and the Unit Price To Be Awarded on the Set-Aside 

Portion. The Army invited bids for the supply of shorts, f.o.b. destination, to four different cities. The invitation called for varying size ranges and quantities for the different destinations. Plaintiff was the low bidder for two destinations, with prices of $2.61 and $2.63; the X

Co. was the low bidder for the other two, with prices of $2.70 and $2.74. Each firm was awarded a single contract for the two destinations on which it was low bidder. The invitation also provided for a partial small business set-aside for each of the four destinations. The appropriate ASPR provision then in effect provided that: 

Negotiation shall be conducted with such small business concerns in the order of their bids or proposals on the non-set-aside portion beginning with the lowest responsive bid or initial proposal. Multiple awards shall be made where appropriate. . . .

Contracts for the set-aside portion shall be at prices determined as follows: (i) when the procurement of the non-set-aside portion has resulted in one contract only, or in multiple awards all at the same price, any awards for the set-aside portion shall be made at the unit price of the non-set-aside portion; (ii) when the procurement of the non-set-aside portion has resulted in multiple awards at different unit prices, any awards for the set-aside portion shall be made at the highest unit price of the non-set-aside portion. ASPR 1-706.6 (d). 

The plaintiff was asked to negotiate only for the set-aside portion applicable to the two destinations for which the plaintiff had received an award on the non-set-aside portion. The same procedure was followed for the X Co. The plaintiff contended that, as the lowest bidder (with the $2.61 price), he was entitled to be solicited for the entire set-aside portion at the $2.74 price. The Army rejected the contention.

The Comptroller General approved the Army's action. 38 Comp. Gen. 596 (1959) [digested in 

DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 328, par. 1 under Set 

Asides]. The plaintiff was awarded a contract for the set-aside portion for the two destinations for which he had been the lowest bidder on the non-set-aside portion; the contract price was the same as he had bid for the non-set-aside portion for each destination. He sued in the Court of 

Claims for "the difference between the unit price awarded" for the "set-aside of... [the] procurement and the highest unit price awarded for the advertised portion of the same procurement." [The opinion does not state whether the unit price was to be multiplied by the number of units involved in the entire set aside or only the portion of the set aside awarded to the plaintiff.]

Held, the claim for relief is denied, and the plaintiff's petition is dismissed. Although the cited ASPR provision, if read literally, supports the plaintiff's position, the provision has never been so applied; established administrative practice cannot be overruled without sound reason. Plaintiff would require that the entire advertised portion of the procurement be treated as a unit. However, that portion involved deliveries of varying quantities f.o.b. to widely separated cities. Varying size ranges as well as varying monthly delivery schedules were required with respect to the different destinations. 

These are variables that obviously would affect bid prices, but to what extent is not readily ascertainable in any given case. Freight costs, for example, would vary from bidder to bidder. 

Because of the variables, separate destinations may properly be treated as separate matters for determining both the lowest bidder on the advertised portion and the unit prices on the setaside portion. To do otherwise would remove the only basis on which the Army could evaluate bids by a common criterion and would, in effect, result in unwarranted premiums to some contractors. 234 AGO 9111A

SET-ASIDES-Continued 

Greenberg v. United States, 300 F.2d 443 (Ct. Cl. 1962). 

[Note: The court apparently dismissed the plaintiff's petition on the merits. There is, however, some question about the basis for jurisdiction and the plaintiff's standing to sue. The plaintiff sought to recover what he would have received under a contract that was never made. 

Jurisdiction apparently was not based on the ground that the plaintiff sought reformation of the contract that was made. There was no suggestion that the contract did not accurately express the bargain the parties intended to make. 

Indeed, the contract clearly was the one that the Army, with the Comptroller General's approval, intended to make. Perhaps the court viewed the plaintiff's claim as founded upon a "regulation of an executive department." See 28

U.S.C. § 1491 (1958). If so, a statement by the court about what suits may be brought for breach of executive regulations would be helpful. The scope of judicial review would be substantially broadened if the court would take jurisdiction of any suit asking damages for violation of an executive regulation. 

The instant case silently found standing to sue in circumstances where no case before has explicitly done so. In Perkins v. Lukens Steel 

Co., 310 U.S. 113 (1940), the Supreme Court held that an offeror has no standing to challenge an agency's actions under the formal advertising statutes. One of the theories underlying that doctrine that the statutes were merely internal directives controlling agents of the Government-seems equally applicable to the regulation the court interpreted in the instant case. 

That regulation arguably was only for the Government's benefit and conferred no enforceable right on any offeror. At least two exceptions have been made to the Perkins doc trine. Copper Plumbing & Heating Co. v. 

Campbell, 290 F. 2d 368 (D.C. Cir. 1961) [digested under DEBARMENT OF BIDDERS, par. 2] (firm had standing to resist placement on list of debarred bidders); Heyer Products 

Co. v. United States, 140 F. Supp. 409 (Ct. Cl. 

1956) [digested in DA Pam 715-50-1, p. 78, par. 12] (bidder had standing to seek the expenses of bid preparation as damages for breach of a promise fairly to consider all bids submitted), petition dismissed, 177 F. Supp. 251 (Ct.

Cl. 1959) [digested under BIDS AND 

AWARDS, par. 2]. The instant case apparently creates another exception, one of unknown scope.] 

5. Propriety of Options for Additional Quantities in Set-Aside Procurements Discussed. In 

JAGT 1955/6778 (22 Aug. 1955) a suggested option clause in the non-set-aside portion of a small business set-aside procurement was held improper. The clause was designed to discourage a bid below cost on the non-set-aside portion because such a bid would defeat the small business program if it were so low as to preclude bidders from being within the 120% range for negotiation on the set-aside portion. The opinion held the clause, which presumably might be used to require a below-cost bidder to take the set-aside portion, might itself defeat the small business program. An Army procuring activity considering using option clauses in small business and labor surplus set-aside procurements apparently was uncertain about the scope of JAGT 1955/6778 and submitted to OTJAG the following questions: a. Is an option clause on the non-set-aside portion of a small business partial set-aside procurement objectionable in all instances? b. Is an option clause on the set-aside portion of a small business total or partial set-aside procurement objectionable in all instances? c. Will the objection be removed if language such as the following is used to give bidders a choice about accepting the option clause: 

Set forth immediately below is an option clause. 

Bidders are not required to accept this clause. 

Acceptance or nonacceptance of the clause will not be a factor in the evaluation of bids. Bidders accepting the option clause shall check the following block 

Failure to check the block will mean that the option. clause will not be included in an award based on this bid. 

d. Will the objection be removed by restricting the option quantity to less than 100 per cent of the base quantity? e. Will the objection be removed by prohibiting the option in the non-set-aside portion from being exercised with respect to the set-aside portion?

AGO 9111A 235

SET-OFF f. To what extent, if any, do the answers to the foregoing apply to labor surplus set-asides? 

Held, the questions are answered as follows, subject to compliance with the policies concerning options as set forth in Section I, Part 15 of ASPR: a and b. An option clause in the set-aside or non-set-aside portions of a small business setaside is not legally objectionable in all instances. c. Use of the quoted clause is not recommended. When an option clause is used, ASPR 1-1504 permits a provision stating either that the optional quantity will not be considered in bid evaluation or that it will be considered. However, that ASPR section apparently does not indicate that bids may be evaluated against each other where some provide for the option and others do not. Such evaluation could not be fair. 

Cf. Ms. Comp. Gen. B-149186, 11 July 1960. d. Option quantities should normally be less than 100% of the known requirements. 19

Comp. Gen. 980 (1940) and Ms. Comp. Gen. B- 

148019, 20 April 1962. Quantities used in small business set-aside procurements should be of a size that complies with the requirement that set-aside portions be in quantities that one or more small businesses may reasonably be expected to have the productive capacity to furnish at a reasonable price. ASPR 1-702(b) (iii); ASPR 1-706.6 (a) (iii); APP 1-701.51d.

In applying that criterion any optional quantities must be taken into account. Consequently, where the known requirement is such that, without any option, most small businesses could not furnish the entire quantity, and bids on partial amounts may be considered under the invitation for bids, an option clause would not be appropriate. Likewise, if partial bidding is not permitted, and if the required quantity represents the approximate limit of small business capacity, an option for an additional quantity would be inappropriate. There are other situations where, in view of the nature of the setaside procedure, particularly partial set-asides where two or more contracts may result, options may have unintended results. See, for example, Ms. Comp. Gen. B-148255 (25 May 

1962), which involved the use of a partial setaside in which the invitation called for special tooling items. The making of separate contracts resulted in the Government obtaining two sets of special tooling instead of the one set originally contemplated. e. The question is difficult to answer because it is not stated in terms corresponding to the facts of set-aside procurements. In a total setaside permitting bidding on partial quantities, an option would be improper. In a total setaside in which bids must be on an all or none basis, where the quantity, including the optional amount, is reasonable for small business production, there are no separate non-set-aside and set-aside portions. In a partial set-aside one or more contracts may be made, and as stated above, where bidding on partial quantities is permitted or necessary for small business participation, an option is inappropriate. Where the partial set-aside results in separate contracts with different contractors, the option in one of the contracts cannot be applied against quantities in the other. f. Because total labor surplus set-asides are not permitted, and in view of other differences between labor surplus and small business setasides, no answer to the question is necessary beyond the statement that an option clause for increased quantities is not considered to be legally objectionable in all instances involving labor surplus set-asides. 

Since JAGT 1955/6778 (22 Aug. 1955) did not address itself generally to the use of options for increased quantities in set-aside procurements, it is not in conflict with this opinion. 

JAGT 1962/6489, 31 July 1962. SET-OFF

1. Where Reasonable Time Has Elapsed Since Award of Construction Contract, Contracting Officer Must Issue Notice To Proceed Even Though Work Site Is Not Ready. On 23 April 

1957, the contractor was awarded a fixed-price contract for the construction of two radar tow ers at Watertown Air Force Station, N.Y. The contract price of $61,772 was computed on the assumption that the project could be completed durng the summer months. This was possible under the terms of the contract, for after the issuance of a notice to proceed by the contracting officer the contractor had 10 days in which to start work and 120 days to complete the project. The invitation for bids stated that a "Notice to proceed will normally be given within thirty (30) days after the date set for the bid opening." The contractor knew, however, that another contractor was in the process of pouring concrete foundations for the towers and that the work site would not be ready for at least 90 days. The contract also contained a

Suspension of Work Clause, AFPI 7-3106.12 

(15 Nov 1957), which provided:

The Contracting Officer may order the Contractor to suspend all or any part of the work for such period of time as may be determined by him to be necessary or desirable for the convenience of the 

Government. Unless such suspension unreasonably delays the progress of the work and causes additional expense or loss to the Contractor, no increase in contract price will be allowed. In the case of suspension of all or any part of the work for an unreasonable length of time, causing additional expense or loss, not due to the fault or negli gence of the Contractor, the Contracting Officer shall make an equitable adjustment in the contract price and modify the contract accordingly. 

Because of delays by the foundation contractor, the work site was not ready within 90 days. 

On 24 July 1957, the contractor requested that a notice to proceed be issued and warned that further delays in pouring the foundation would require work in the winter months. On 24 September, 5 months after the contract was awarded, a notice to proceed was finally issued by the contracting officer. Even so, the site was not completely ready when the contractor started work. After the work was completed the contractor claimed $12,024.60 in additional costs incurred because of the Government's unreasonable delay in issuing the notice to proceed. The claim was denied by the contracting officer and the contractor appealed. 

Held, the appeal is sustained. The question for decision is whether the Government, by failing to issue a notice to proceed until the construction site was almost ready for work, unreasonably delayed performance and caused the contractor additional costs within the meaning of the Suspension of Work Clause. While no time was specified in the contract, the Government was under an implied duty to issue the notice within a reasonable time. Ross Engineering Company v. United States, 92 Ct. Cl. 

253, 258 (1940). Where, as here, the contract called for completion of the work within 120 days after notice to proceed, which would "normally" be given within 30 days after bid opening on 17 April, and the contractor believed the site would be ready for him within 90 days, a five month delay is unreasonable on its face.

The fact that the site was not ready for work does not justify the delay. The Government unreasonably substituted its own judgment for that of the contractor with respect to work preparation requirements and the extent to which work would be hampered by the foundation contractor's presence on the site. More reasonably, the Government should have responded to the contractor's letter of 24 July by

AGO 9111A 237

SMALL BUSINESS 

issuing a notice to proceed, conditioned upon completion of the foundations. This notice would enable the contractor to exercise its own judgment as to when and to what extent workmen, equipment and subcontractors should be mobilized. In addition, the responsibility for delay in completing the site would have been shifted from the Government to the foundation contractor. 

The notice to proceed should have been issued on 24 July 1957. By delaying until 24

September, the Government in fact both suspended and unreasonably delayed the contractor's work and afforded a basis for relief under the Suspension of Work Clause. John A. Johnson & Sons, Inc., ASBCA No. 4403 (11 Feb 

1959), 59-1 BCA 2088. The case is remanded to the contracting officer to determine the amount of damage suffered by the contractor and whether the Government caused the delay by the foundation contractor on the work site. 

Kraft Construction Co., Inc. ASBCA No. 

4976, 15 September 1959, 59-2 BCA 2347.
