4. Small Business Administration Does Not 

Lose Priority of United States in Bankruptcy by Participating With Private Bank in Loan to Small Business Concern. The Small Business Administration (S.B.A.), pursuant to the Small 

Business Act of 1953, participated with a private bank in making a $20,000 loan to a small business concern. $15,000 of this loan came from federal funds. Nine months later an involuntary petition in bankruptcy was filed against the small business concern by other creditors. The S.B.A. filed a claim with the trustee for the entire unpaid balance of the loan, some $16,355.69, and argued that it was a debt due the United States, 31 U.S.C. § 191, which gave the S.B.A. status as a preferred creditor. 

See 11 U.S.C. § 104 (a) (5) (debts owing to any person, including the United States, who by the laws of the United States is entitled to priority, are preferred). The lower federal courts denied the priority because the S.B.A. had agreed to share 25% of the money collected with the private bank: A private party cannot be permitted to benefit from a priority which belongs to the United States alone. In Re Byquist. 168 F. Supp. 483 (1958), aff'd. S.B.A. v. 

McClellan, 272 F. 2d 143 (10th Cir. 1959). The 

Supreme Court granted certiorari. 

Held, reversed. The denial of a bankruptcy priority handicaps the S.B.A. in the effective performance of duties imposed upon it by Congress.

The S.B.A. is an integral part of the governmental mechanism created by Congress to obligate federal funds for the benefit of small business concerns. It is not a separate legal entity or Government corporation in which private persons may own stock, Sloan Shipyards Corp. v. U.S. Fleet Corp., 285 U.S. (1922), or which has independent capacity to sue or be sued. 

R.F.C. v. Menihan Corp.. 312 U.S. 81 (1941). 

Consequently, the S.B.A. is entitled to all priorities that are accorded to the United States when its seeks to collect federal funds loaned to private persons or concerns. See United States

Dept. of Agriculture, E.C. & F. Loans v. Remund, 330 U.S. 539 (1947) (Farm Credit Ad ministration get priority in bankruptcy). 

The United States loses its priority when acting as a collection agent for private persons. 

Nathanson v. N.L.R.B., 344 U.S. 25 (1952) (N.L.R.B. attempts to collect wages for employees). Here, however, the S.B.A. has a financial interest in the claim and the debt is owed to the United States. The priority assures that the United States will be able to collect the 238 AGO 9111A

SMALL BUSINESS-Continued 

1 debt and satisfy its financial interest. Once the debt is collected it is immaterial that the S.B.A. is required by contract to disburse a portion of that amount to a private bank who has no priority. 

Appellee's argument finds no support in the purpose and method of S.B.A. financial assistance. The S.B.A. must use the participation device as a method of stimulating private financing of small business concerns. If the use of this required device deprives the United States of priority, it will become more difficult for the S.B.A. to perform its duties. Any preference obtained by the private bank comes from its contract with the S.B.A., not from an unequal distribution by the bankruptcy court. 

S.B.A. v. McClellan, 364 U.S. 446 (1960). [Note: $575 million of the $975 million revolving fund established for use by the S.B.A. is earmarked for loans to small business concerns. See 72 Stat. 384-387 (1958), 15 U.S.C. 

§ 631-636 (1958). Loans are available for the expansion of productive facilities, working capital for both commercial and defense production and to insure a well balanced economy, but shall be of such sound value or so secured as reasonably to assure repayment.

The basic policy of the Act is to stimulate private financing of small business concerns with a minimum involvement of appropriated funds. Accordingly, if a small business concern cannot obtain adequate financing from private sources at reasonable rates, the S.B.A. may reduce the risk to the private lending institution by offering a "deferred" participation. Under this arrangement, a private bank initially satisfies the financial needs of the small business applicant. Upon call by the bank, however, the 

S.B.A. agrees to assume up to 90% of the loan.

If the "deferred" participation is not satisfactory, the S.B.A. may provide a percentage of the loan from the outset. This is an "immediate" participation and was apparently the arrangement involved in S.B.A. v. McClellan. If neither form of participation is available, the S.B.A. is authorized to make a direct loan of appropriated funds at no more than 512%. See

Hellerstein & Speidel, Government Assistance and Private Economic Organization For De fense, 9 Military L. Rev. 99, 106 (July 1960).

From the inception of the Small Business loan program in 1953 through 30 June 1959, $582,- 394,919 was disbursed on 12,914 loans to small business concerns. The S.B.A.'s share of the funds disbursed was $490,583,060, or 85% of the total. H.R. Rep. No. 1252, 86th Cong., 2d Sess. 37 (1960). These statistics support the 

Court's conclusion that a denial of priority in bankruptcy would handicap the S.B.A. in the effective performance of duties imposed upon it by Congress. The existence of a priority is clearly an added inducement to private lending on a participation basis. But of more importance, since appropriated funds comprise 85% of the total amount loaned to small business, and 75% in the instant case, the United States has a substantial financial investment which should be protected in the event of the borrower's bankruptcy.] 

5. No Binding Contract Was Made by Award to Firm Subsequently Found by SBA Not To 

Have Been Small Business at Time of Award- In Procurement Set Aside for Award to Small Business, Improper To Hasten Award in Order To Preclude Protest That Low Bidder Is Not 

Small Business. The low bidder on a formally advertised contract that was set aside for award to small businesses claimed, by checking the appropriate box on the bid form, to be a small business. On the day after the bid opening, an award was made to the low bidder and the second low bidder protested to the SBA that the low bidder was not a small business. 

The SBA undertook to look into the matter, but determined-after learning that an award had already been made to check the low bidder's status only for purposes of future procurements. However, the contracting agency later ordered work halted pending action on the protest, and the SBA consequently decided to handle the protest expeditiously for application to the instant procurement. The SBA determined that the low bidder was not a small business when the award was made. The second low bidder asked the Comptroller General for 

Held, the award to the low bidder should be cancelled. The determination by the SBA is conclusive as to the small business status of a concern. See 37 Comp. Gen. 679 (1958). In view of the SBA determination in the instant case, the provisions of the Small Business Act, AGO 9111A 239

SMALL BUSINESS-Continued and the restriction of the instant procurement to small businesses, no binding contract could have been made with a firm found by the SBA not to have been a small business at the time of award. 34 Comp. Gen. 115, 117 (1954). See also Ms. Comp. Gen. B-138415, 24 September 

1959. In the instant case the protesting bidder alleged facts tending to establish that the unusual speed in making award was designed to prevent the second low bidder from questioning the small business status of the low bidder. 

The award was technically proper since under ASPR 1-703 (a) the contracting officer may accept at face value self-certification as to size and any other party must, under ASPR 1-703 (b) (1), question a certification prior to award by filing a written protest. However, the circumstances lend support to the protesting bidder's allegations. It is contrary to the intent of the Small Business Act to accelerate the award process to circumvent a bidder's right to question a size certification. This viewpoint should be called to the attention of contracting officers. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145644, 26 May 1961. 

[Note: By letter of the Adjutant General, 24 

July 1961, Army procurement officials were advised of the Comptroller General's criticism of the hasty award in this case and were instructed to take appropriate action to ensure there is no criticism of this nature in the future.] 

6. Where Cancellation Would Cause Unacceptable Delay in Construction Needed for National Defense, Contract Should Not Be Can celled Even Though It Was Awarded on Basis of Erroneous Determination That Bidder Was a Small Business. (C.G.) See BIDS & AWARDS (par. 38) 7. Comptroller General Considers Cases Involving Self-Certification Procedure. (a) In Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145236, 29 March 1961, 40 

Comp. Gen. 550, the invitation restricted bidding to small business firms and provided that bids from firms that were not small businesses would be considered nonresponsive. One of the bidders, the C Co., indicated in its bid that it was not a small business. After the bid opening the city where the C Co. performed its operations was added to the Department of

Labor's list of substantial unemployment areas. 

A week later the SBA amended its rules to increase by 25 percent the size a firm located in an area of substantial labor surplus could be before being too large to qualify as a small business for procurement purposes. The amendment provided that the determination of whether a place was within a substantial labor surplus area should be made as of the time of contract award. Two days later, before award of a contract, the procuring agency was notified that the SBA had ruled, as of that date, that the C Co. was a small business. The procuring agency asked whether the C Co.'s bid could be considered.

Held, the bid was nonresponsive. In Ms. 

Comp. Gen. B-143630, 13 October 1960, the P 

Co. had represented in its bids on two advertised procurements restricted to small businesses that it was a small business. On 20 May, after the bid openings, another bidder protested that the P Co. was not a small business. Five days later the SBA Regional Office notified the procuring agency that the P Co., the low bidder, was not a small business. Meanwhile the P Co. had applied to the SBA for a small business certificate, and on 31 May the P Co. was certified as a small business, effective that date.

The contracts were then awarded to the P Co. 

That action was upheld on the ground that generally the final determination whether a firm qualifies as a small business is made as of the date of award. That decision, however, is not applicable where, as here, a bidder does not, and cannot in good faith. represent himself before or at the bid opening as qualifying for small business status. The self-certification procedure was designed to simplify and expedite procurements and size determinations. The hope was that 95 to 99 percent of the cases would be handled by self-certifications. A congressional subcommittee was concerned about whether bidders would be required in every instance to certify size status at the time of submitting bids. The subcommittee was assured there would be such a requirement. Hearings before Subcommittee No. 2 of the House Select Committee on Small Business, 84th Cong. 2d sess. 25-27 (1956). The subcommittee's concern is significant. Unless bidding on a total set-aside for small business can be restricted to firms who in good faith can certify in their bids 240 AGO 9111A

SMALL BUSINESS-Continued that they are small businesses, no useful purpose would be served by requiring self-certification of size status in every instance. The effectiveness of the small-business set-aside procedure would be seriously impaired if bidders who cannot in their bids certify themselves as small businesses may be permitted to delay contract awards in order to apply to the

SBA for a small business certificate on the ground that their status changed after opening. Usually a bidder is in a very good position to know his size. If he cannot honestly represent he is a small business, his bid should be considered nonresponsive. 

There is an additional reason for holding the bid nonresponsive. It is reasonable to assume that other large businesses honored the restriction limiting bids to small businesses and did not submit bids. To the extent that such concerns could also have qualified as small businesses after the size standards were changed, those concerns would be prejudiced by an award to a bidder who did not honor the restriction. (b) In Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144621, 1 August 

1961, 41 Comp. Gen. 47, the St. Louis Air Pro curement District had asked the Kansas City 

SBA Office on 9 June for a determination whether the S Co. was a small business for government procurement purposes. The question was referred to the SBA's Washington, D.C. office. On 7 July the S Co. submitted a form describing its affiliation with other concerns. 

The Director of the Office of Small Business 

Size Standards determined that the S Co. was not a small business because of affiliation, through ownership of its stock, with other concerns. According to the records of the Kansas 

City SBA Office, the president of the S Co. was notified on 12 August of the determination that the firm was not a small business. He denied having received notice of the determination. 

Meanwhile, on 18 July, the Corps of Engineers had issued an invitation for bids on a procurement restricted to small business. When the bids were opened on 17 August, it was discovered that the S Co. was the low bidder. The S 

Co. had stated in its bid that it was a small business. In response to a protest that the S 

Co. was not a small business the contracting officer asked the Kansas City SBA Office to evaluate the firm's size status. Two weeks later the Acting Deputy Administrator of the SBA 

issued a determination that the S Co. was not a small business because of its affiliation with other concerns. After learning of this determination the S Co. arranged for changes in the ownership of its stock. In view of the changes, the SBA Deputy Administrator determined that the firm was a small business. It was awarded the Corps of Engineers' contract. A disap pointed bidder protested to the Comptroller 

General and appealed to the SBA Size Appeals 

Board from the determination by the SBA Deputy Administrator. The Board held that the changes in stock ownership had not eliminated the affiliation with other concerns and, therefore, the firm was not a small business. The 

Comptroller General was thus required to determine whether the award to the S Co. could stand. At the time of the Comptroller General's decision, two prototypes under the contract had been approved, and delivery of one-fifth of the contract's requirements was anticipated within 

40 days. 

Held, the contract should be canceled. The first question is what effect should be given to the fact that before submitting its bid the S Co. knew that its size status was subject to question. The underlying idea in Ms. Comp. 

Gen. B-145236, 29 March 1961, was that bidders must use the self-certification procedure prudently if it is to work efficiently. Here, as early as 7 July the S Co. knew there was a question about its size status. On that date the firm, in submitting a form describing its affiliations, stated, "You have consistently raised the question of affiliation . . . " Moreover, the S Co. has not presented proof adequate to overcome the presumption in favor of the correctness of the statement in the administrative report that the firm was notified on 12 August of the SBA's determination that it was not a small business. 

Under the circumstances it is difficult to understand how a reasonably prudent bidder could certify itself as a small business without first making a formal application for a small business certificate. Sufficient time was available for applying, particularly if, as appears to be true, the S Co. was aware as early as 7 July of the question about its size status. On the facts of this case, the S Co.'s bid should not have been considered for award.

AGO 9111A 241

SMALL BUSINESS-Continued 

The second question is, in view of the fact the S Co. has proceeded with performance, what effect should be given the determination by the SBA Size Appeals Board that the S Co. is not a small business. That determination apparently was based on the same facts used for the contrary determination made just before the contract was awarded and thus in effect indicated that the S Co. was not a small business when the contract was awarded. Ordinarily the date of award is the time when a firm's qualification as a small business is to be determined. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-143630, 13 October 1960. 

This general rule, however, should not be applied to permit a large business to certify itself as a small business and then to take affirmative action between bid opening and award of the contract in order to qualify as a small business. 

Cf. Ms. Comp. Gen. B-145236, 29 March 1961. 

Any other view would (1) give a low bidder otherwise responsive to the invitation a second chance at an award; (2) circumvent the small business set-aside program, one of the statutory purposes of which is to place with small businesses a fair proportion of Government contracts. In this case the change in stock ownership was made solely to qualify the S Co.'s bid for consideration. 

The foregoing indicates the award should be canceled. Since the S Co. has proceeded with work on the contract, however, the first installment of one-fifth of the contract's requirements, as well as the two prototypes already delivered, may be accepted and paid for on a quantum valebant basis. The contract price for the units may be regarded as the amount to be paid. (c) In Ms. Comp. Gen. B-146438, 16 October 

1961, 41 Comp. Gen. 252, the D Co. in November 1960 had requested a size determination, and the SBA Deputy Administrator for Procurement and Technical Assistance had determined that the firm was not a small business because of its affiliation with another firm. After a reorganization of the D Co.'s connections, the SBA Acting Deputy Administrator determined, on 13 February 1961, that the D Co. could self-certify it was a small business. 

May 1961 a competitor claimed the D Co. was ineligible, because of its size, to receive a Navy In contract reserved for small business.

In re- 

sponse, the Director of the SBA Office of Small Business Size Standards determined on 6 June 

1961 that the D Co. was a small business. This determination was appealed to the SBA Size 

Appeals Board on 14 June 1961. Meanwhile, on 8 June 1961, the Army issued an invitation for bids on a procurement reserved for small business. Bids were opened on 27 June 1961.

The D Co.'s bid, which certified the firm was a small business, was low, and the firm was awarded the contract on 30 June 1961. The SBA Size Appeals Board on 8 August 1961, decided that the D Co. was not a small business.

After the award to the D Co. a protest was filed with Comptroller General. 

Held, the award may stand. Under ASPR 1703 a contracting officer must accept at face value a small-business self-certification unless there is a timely written protest by other bidders. In this case three size determinations for the D Co. were made before bids on the 

Army contract were solicited. The second two of those determinations were that the firm was a small business. A fourth, and the final, determination, that the firm was not a small business, was made more than a month after the 

D Co. received the contract. Thus the selfcertification was in full force on the date of award. There is no evidence that the D Co. was imprudent or lacking in good faith when it certified itself as a small business, since the two most recent determinations were that the firm was a small business. Thus the award was in accord with the applicable regulations. 

Furthermore, in the absence of a protest prior to award a contract awarded in good faith on the basis of a bidder's statement that he is a small business is not void ab initio but is only voidable at the option of the Government. Ms.

Comp. Gen. B-137689, 21 January 1959. In the present case cancellation of the contract would be inequitable and would serve no useful purpose. 

8. Allowing SBA Fewer Than Ten Days To Issue Certificate of Competency Was Justified by Desirability of Obligating Funds Before Expiration of Fiscal Year and Avoiding Possible Delay in Obtaining Funds During Next Fiscal 

Year.

The Army requested submission of pro- 242 AGO 9111A

SMALL BUSINESS-Continued posals by 13 June 1961 for furnishing radar interference trainers. After 13 June negotiations were undertaken with the three firms that had submitted the lowest prices. On 20 June a preaward survey was made of the T Co., which had submitted the lowest price. The Contractor

Evaluation Board, with the contracting officer's concurrence, determined that the T Co. lacked the technical ability to perform the contract. 

ASPR 1-705.6 (b) provided at the time that:

If a small business concern has submitted an otherwise acceptable bid or proposal but has been found by the contracting officer to be nonresponsible as to capacity or credit, and if the bid or proposal is to be rejected for this reason alone, (i) SBA shall be notified of the circumstances so as to permit it to issue a certificate of competency and (ii) award shall be withheld pending either SBA issuance of a certificate of competency or the expiration of ten working days after SBA is so notified, whichever is earlier, subject to the following: (A) This procedure is not mandatory where the contracting officer certifies in writing that award must be made without delay and includes in the contract file a statement signed by him which justifies the certificate.

Pursuant to this regulation the contracting officer on 24 June referred the matter to the SBA, with the request that action be expedited since award had to be made by 30 June. When the SBA was unable to process the case by 30 

June, the contracting officer determined that award should be made without further delay.

He awarded the contract to the firm that had submitted the second low proposal. The T Co. protested to the Comptroller General against the award. The protest alleged that the award was made on 30 June 1961 to prevent the lapse of fiscal year 1961 funds and that the SBA should have been given more time to issue a certificate of competency.

Held, protest denied. The equipment was urgently needed. Procurement of the equipment was a firm requirement of the fiscal year 1961 program and had been funded with oneyear money. If the award had not been made before 1 July 1961, the funds would not have been available for obligation, and a significant period might have elapsed before other funds became available. The lapse of funds alone would not be a valid reason for hastening an award. However, where, as here, the lapse would result in additional delay because funds were not available and the requirement would have to be reprogrammed for the next fiscal year, the hastening appears justifiable.

There appears to have been no undue delay in referring the matter to the SBA. Moreover, since there were fewer than ten working days between the date of the contracting officer's determination of nonresponsibility and 30 June, an immediate award without referral to the 

SBA would have been justified under ASPR 1705.6. See 38 Comp. Gen. 248 (1958).

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-146316, 16 October 1961. 

9. Failure To Maintain Equipment in Proper Condition for Performance of Contract Is Aspect of Responsibility Not Covered by SBA Certificate of Competency. The low bid on a total small business set-aside procurement was rejected because an affirmative determination that the bidder was responsible was prevented by the bidder's poor record of performance under prior contracts for similar work. The question of the bidder's responsibility was not re ferred to the Small Business Administration. 

The bidder protested to the Comptroller General. 

Held, protest rejected. Determination of a prospective contractor's ability to perform is primarily the function of the administrative office concerned and will not be overruled by the General Accounting Office in the absence of a showing of bad faith or lack of a reasonable basis for the determination. 37 Comp. Gen. 

430, 435 (1957). Here there is no sufficient reason to overturn the administrative finding. 

It was not necessary to refer the question of responsibility to the SBA for issuance or denial of a certificate of competency. Referral is necessary only where a prospective contractor is not found responsible because of a lack of capacity or credit. ASPR 1-705.6. See 37

Comp. Gen. 798 (1958). Here the contracting officer's decision was that the unsatisfactory record of performance was not attributable to inadequate capacity or credit but rather to the failure to follow good business practices by not maintaining the equipment in proper condition for performance of the contract. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-148189, 16 April 1962.

3. Imprest Funds May Be Used To Pay Local Cartage but Not Intercity Transportation 

Charges. An imprest fund cashier claimed reimbursement for transportation charges on c.o.d. shipments carried between cities. In view of the prohibition in AR 37-103, par. 16-2 

C-2, and 38 Comp. Gen. 462 (1959) against using imprest funds for transportation charges, the Comptroller General was asked if reimbursement was proper. The Comptroller General's attention was directed to an apparent inconsistency between the prohibition in AR 

37-103 and the statement in ASPR 3–604.4 allowing use of imprest funds for "the cost of c.o.d., parcel post, or other delivery charges" for cash purchases on a delivered basis. 

Held, the use of imprest funds for intercity transportation charges is improper, but reimbursement in this case will not be objected to. 

There is difference between between "delivery charges," which are payments for local cartage, and "transportation charges," which are payments for line-haul or intercity carriage. This distinction reconciles AR 37-103 and ASPR 3604.4. The ASPR provisions, when read in context, refer only to local cartage payments. 

The conditions for use specified in ASPR 3604.1, taken collectively, restrict the use of imprest funds to purchases made in the local area where the supplies or services are to be used or rendered. The documentation requirements in 

ASPR 3-604.2 indicate imprest funds may be used only when the vendor is obligated to deliver. Thus, the imprest fund cashier violated the regulations and, ordinarily, could not be reimbursed. An exception will be made in this case because the charges are very small and the cashier acted in good faith and secured adequate receipts. However, prompt action should be taken to prevent the unauthorized use of imprest funds in the future. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-144026, 6 October 1960, 40

Comp. Gen. 199.

7! 86 diction already exists. 3. Japanese Companies May Sue the United

States for Breach of Contracts Even Though They Cannot Prove the Japanese Government Is Subject to the Same Type of Suit by Americans. Section 2502 of 28 U.S.C. provides that: 

Citizens or subjects of any foreign government which accords to citizens of the United States the right to prosecute claims against their government in its courts may sue the United States in the Court of Claims if the subject matter is otherwise within such court's jurisdiction.

Relying on this statute, two Japanese corporations sued the United States for breach of contract. The corporations submitted statements by a Japanese lawyer and Japanese Government officials that citizens of the United States are given equal rights with Japanese citizens to sue the Japanese Government for breach of contract. The United States asked that the suits be dismissed for want of jurisdiction because 

Section 2502 permits suit only if an American could maintain against the Japanese Government the precise type of suit pressed by the corporations. The United States pointed out that the corporations had failed to submit provisions from the Japanese constitution and code permitting breach of contract suits against the Government or any translations of cases in which such suits had been maintained. 

Held, the court has jurisdiction. The term 

'claims' in Section 2502 should not be read narrowly to mean only claims of the precise nature filed in the Court of Claims. Section 

2502 requires that American citizens enjoy equal standing with foreigners in actions against the foreign state, not that the scope of actions possible in the two countries be exactly identical. Brodie v. United States, 62 Ct. Cl. 29 (1926); Marcos v. United States, 122 Ct. Cl. 

641 (1952). Perhaps there is a minimum amount of sovereign liability that must be proved by an alien wishing to sue the United 

States in the Court of Claims. The scope of the Court's jurisdiction would be carefully measured where the practice of a foreign nation belied a rule that formally permitted Americans to sue the government. This is not such a case, for the corporations have adequately proved that the Japanese open their courts to Americans in many suits, including-according to most authorities-suits for breach of contract. 

The difference between the legal system of the United States and that of Japan minimizes the effect of the corporations' failure to submit cases in which the Japanese Government was sued on contract claims. The Japanese utilize forms of dispute-resolution other than law, and those disputes involving public law that do arise are usually settled in tribunals other than courts Moreover, only in recent years have the few available published court decisions included a full statement of facts. The difference in legal systems also accounts for the failure of the Japanese constitution and code to provide specifically for contract actions against the Government. Less than a century ago, the Japanese took their law bodily from the systems of AGO 9111A 245

SOVEREIGN IMMUNITY-Continued continental Europe, where the doctrine of sovereign immunity was rejected. The Japanese transferred broad teachings, but not specific rules of governmental responsibility. Thus state liability in Japan is a commonly accepted fact, but its proof by statutes and cases is difficult. 

Nippon Hodo Company v. United States, Fuiji Sangyo Kabushiki Kaisha v. United 

States,, 285 F.2d 766 (Ct. Cl. 1961). [Note: Judge Laramore dissented, relying in part on a Japan-United States treaty, the applicability of which the majority of the Court declined to reach. The treaty language found important by Judge Laramore states: 

Nationals. . . of either party shall be accorded national treatment. . . with respect to access to the courts. . . . The term 'national treatment' means treatment accorded within the territories of a party upon terms no less favorable than the treatment accorded therein, in like situations to nationals . . . of such party. Treaty of Friendship, Com merce and Navigation with Japan, 30 October 1953, T.I.A.S. No. 2863, Art. 1, para. 1, Art. XXII, para. 1. 

Judge Laramore construed this treaty and Section 2502 to require each government to give 'equal treatment' to the nationals of the other with respect to access to courts. He contended the corporations had the burden of proving that an American citizen could sue the Japanese Government for breach of contract. He found the corporations had failed to meet this burden because they had not put in evidence any constitutional or statutory provision from which the court could conclusively find that the Japanese Government could be sued on contract claims. 

In fact, he argued, the Japanese constitutions show that only suits in tort are cognizable by the courts of Japan. He would overrule the 

Brodie and Marcos cases, relied on by the majority, to the extent those decisions are in conflict with his views.] 

4. Court of Appeals Decides Sovereign Immunity Does Not Shield Government Agent Sued in Ejectment Action To Obtain Possession of Land He Held in Government's Behalf. The plaintiffs brought an ejectment action in a State court against both the United States and a Forest Service official who held land in the Government's behalf. The plaintiffs sought damages as well as a writ of possession. After the case was removed to a Federal district court, the action as to the United States was dismissed because process had not been properly served. The Forest Service official moved to have the action as to him dismissed on the grounds that it was in effect against the United States and sovereign immunity to the suit had not been waived. The court granted the motion, and the plaintiffs appealed to the Court of Appeals. 

Held, judgment reversed. It is conceded that the United States will not be bound by the judgment in this case. The sole question is whether the Forest Service official may have the action dismissed because he is shielded by the Government's sovereign immunity. At the outset, it should be noted that the court below, in claiming agreement with Jones v. United 

States, 127 F. Supp. 31 (E.D.N.C. 1954), could have relied only on the language of Jones, not the holding. That case involved not only ejectment, but also partition of lands in which the plaintiff claimed to own an interest taken by the United States without the payment of just compensation. In Jones, moreover, the agent in charge of the land did not move for dismissal of the action as to him.

Distinguishing Jones, however, does not dispose of this case, for the Forest Service official has put in issue the vitality of United States v. 

Lee, 106 U.S. 196 (1882). The facts in Lee and in this case are identical in their legal effect. 

Lee involved an ejectment action against Government agents possessing land purchased in a tax sale which the plaintiff claimed was invalid. 

The Supreme Court decided the Government agents were not protected by the Government's sovereign immunity. Although some language in Lee referred to a taking of property without just compensation, the real basis of the decision was that the Government agents were ordinary tort feasors and were not immunized against the consequences of their wrongful trespass by their claim that they acted for the Government. 

The Court stated in part: 

[W]hile acceding to the general proposition that in no court can the United States be sued directly. by original process as a defendant, there is abundant evidence in the decisions of this court that the 246 AGO 9111A

SOVEREIGN IMMUNITY-Continued doctrine, if not absolutely limited to cases in which the United States are made defendants by name, is not permitted to interfere with judicial enforcement of the established rights of plaintiffs when the United States is not a defendant or a necessary party to the suit. . . . [T]he proposition that when an individual is sued in regard to property which he holds as officer or agent of the United States, his possession cannot be disturbed when that fact is brought to the attention of the court, has been overruled and denied in every case where it has been necessary to decide it. . It cannot be that when, in a suit between two citizens for the ownership of real estate, one of them has established his right to the possession of the property according to all the forms of judicial procedure, . . . the wrongful possessor can say successfully to the court, Stop here, I hold by order of the President, and the progress of justice must be stayed. That, though the nature of the controversy is one peculiarly appropriate to the judicial function, though the United States is no party to the suit, . . . the unsuccessful party can interpose an absolute veto upon that judgment by the production of an order of the Secretary of War, which that officer had no more authority to make than the humblest private citizen . . [T]he government is always at liberty, notwithstanding any [judgment against the agent] to avail itself of all the remedies which the law allows to every person for the vindication and assertion of its rights. Hence, taking the present case as an illustration, the United States may proceed by a bill in chancery to quiet its title, in aid of which, if a proper case is made, a writ of injunction may be obtained. Or it may bring an action of ejectment, in which .. the title of the 

United States could be judicially determined. 106 

U.S. at 207-08, 215-16, 221, 222. [Emphasis added by Court of Appeals.] 

These excerpts suffice to show that if Lee has any vitality at all, the judgment below must be reversed.

Neither the court below nor the Forest Service official has argued that Lee has been overruled. Quoting from Jones, the court below said, "with the possibility of the landowner recovering just compensation for the wrongful taking, there may be no cases at all in which 

United States v. Lee will permit suit today."

This statement was entirely without foundation. 

Examination of Shepard's United States Cita tions reveals that Lee has been cited 396 times. 

The Supreme Court has cited it in fifty-eight cases, in seven of which it was "distinguished" and in four "explained." This indicates that the editors of Shepard's consider that, in the remaining forty-seven cases, no fault has been found with Lee. Nobody has suggested that there is any authoritative holding that Lee does not cover ejectment actions just as fully as it did the day of its rendition. The argument that its application has been severely limited has arisen when a litigant has sought to apply the principles of the case to other and often quite different situations that were controlled by entirely different rules. Those cases also indicate that there have been no clear-cut distinctions between the facts to which Lee's principles apply and those to which they do not apply. 

As recently as 1947, in Land v. Dollar, 330 

U.S. 731 (1947), the Supreme Court applied the principles of Lee as they are reinforced by other Supreme Court decisions. In Dollar, the members of the U.S. Maritime Commission were sued on the ground they wrongfully withheld the plaintiff's property. All eight members of the Court hearing the case agreed that the trial court had authority to determine whether the withholding was tortious and thus a ground on which the defendants would be liable. The 

Court stated in part: 

Where the right to possession or enjoyment of property under general law is at issue, and the defendants claim as officers or agents of the sovereign, the rule of United States v. Lee ... has been repeatedly approved. [Eight Supreme Court cases, cited] . . . In . . . Lec . . . [t]he force of the decree 

was to grant possession to the private claimant. 

Though the judgment was not res judicata against the United States. . . it settled as between the parties the controversy over possession . . . Public officials became tort-feasors by exceeding the limits of their authority. And where they unlawfully seize or hold a citizen's realty or chattels, recoverable by appropriate action at law or in equity, he is not relegated to the Court of Claims to recover a money judgment. The dominant interest of the sovereign is then on the side of the victim who may bring his possessory action to reclaim that which is wrongfully withheld. 330 U.S. at 737-39. 

[Emphasis added by Court of Appeals.] 

The main reliance of the court below and the Forest Service official was on Larson v. Domes tic and Foreign Commerce Corp., 337 U.S. 682 

(1949). That case involved a suit against the

War Assets Administrator to prevent the trans- AGO 9111A 247

SOVEREIGN IMMUNITY-Continued fer of certain property to anyone but the plaintiff. The Court held the Administrator was shielded by the Government's sovereign immunity. The majority opinion may be construed as questioning some of the fundamental bases of Lee and similar decisions. There are several reasons, however, why less than full force need be given that opinion's language.

First, the opinion had the unconditional concurrence of only four members of the Court, three of whom had concurred in Dollar. Mr. Justice 

Douglas, the author of Dollar, joined the Larson opinion on the ground that application of less rigid principles to the sale of Government property would clog the sale of Government property with intolerable burdens by making the right to sue the agent turn on whether title had passed to the buyer. Second, the majority opinion did not overrule Lee or Dollar, but merely tried to distinguish those cases. Mr. 

Justice Douglas' opinion helps to clarify the scope and content of the distinction made. The fact that three Justices who had concurred two years earlier in Dollar also concurred in Larson carries a strong implication that they were not subscribing in the latter case to a doctrine that would seriously undermine Dollar and Lee. 

Third, whatever language in Larson seems to conflict with Lee and Dollar is explainable by this passage in Mr. Justice Frankfurter's dissent:

There is an appearance of inconsistency in some of the cases only because opinions also are prey to the frailties of composition. Familiar phrases are not always used with critical precision or with due relevance to the circumstances of a particular case. 

337 U.S. at 713. 

Fourth, since Larson, neither Lee nor Dollar has been questioned by the Court. Lee has been cited with approval in a concurring opinion of Mr. Justice Frankfurter and by him in an opinion for a unanimous Court. Dollar has been cited in a concurring opinion of Mr. Justice 

Douglas. 

Moreover, Larson does not support the claim of the Forest Service official to be protected by sovereign immunity. That case stressed that there was no contention that the War Assets 

Administrator had any personal interest in the property or that he had taken any wrongful action. The crucial portion of Larson, and the part that differentiates that case from this and supports jurisdiction over the Forest Service official, states: 

There is not involved any question of the immunization of Government officers against responsibility for their wrongful actions. If those actions are such as to create a personal liability, whether sounding in tort or contract, the fact that the officer is an instrumentality of the sovereign does not, of course, forbid a court from taking jurisdiction over a suit against him. 337 U.S. at 686. [Empha sis added by Court of Appeals.] 

Finally, the court below cited, besides Larson and Jones, a decision of this court, Rambo v. 

United States, 145 F. 2d 670, 671 (5th Cir. 

1945), cert. denied, 324 U.S. 848 (1945). However, that suit tried a title to land. Although the plaintiffs here must show title in themselves as a basis for their action, the judgment sought involves merely possession, not title. 

In summary, however broad the apparent sweep of the limitations some courts have placed on Lee, it is clear that the Supreme Court has never questioned its controlling validity in possessory actions like ejectment that seek to oust Government agents from wrongful possession growing out of their tortious or illegal acts. 

That is all this case involves. The unanimity with which the principles approved here have been upheld springs from both the conviction that the implied immunity of the Government should be extended to its agents only with great caution and the realization that the Government in a suit like this has the simple option of testing its title by a counterclaim or independent 

Bowdoin v. Malone, 284 F. 2d 95 (5th Cir. 

1960), [rev'd 369 U.S. 643 (1962), digested un der SOVEREIGN IMMUNITY, par. 6]. 

He 

[Note: Chief Judge Rives dissented. 

contended that the Forest Service official might not be immunized from personal liability in damages, but a writ to oust him from the possession of land held solely on behalf of the 

United States would interfere with governmental functions. He thought that the full discussion in Larson indicated that the instant case was one in which the Government agent was entitled to the protection of sovereign immunity.] 248 AGO 9111A

Contractor to Compensation Under Suspension of Work Clause. (ASBCA) See SUSPENSION OF WORK (par. 4) 6. Supreme Court Holds Sovereign Immunity Bars Ejectment Action Against Agent Holding 

Land on Government's Behalf. The respondents filed a common-law action of ejectment against the petitioner, a forest service official who held certain land in connection with his official duties. The suit asked for damages as well as a writ of possession. The petitioner moved to dismiss on the ground that the suit was in substance and effect one against the federal government, which had not waived its sovereign immunity to the suit. The federal district court granted the motion, relying on 

Larson v. Domestic & Foreign Corp., 337 U.S. 

682 (1949). Doe v. Roe, 186 F. Supp. 407 

(M.D. Ga. 1959). The Court of Appeals re versed. Bowdoin v. Malone, 284 F. 2d 95 (5th

Cir. 1960) [digested under SOVEREIGN IM- MUNITY, par. 4]. The Supreme Court granted certiorari. 368 U.S. 811 (1961).

Held, reversed. The Court of Appeals principally relied on United States v. Lee, 106 U.S. 

196 (1882). In Lee an ejectment action was filed against the custodians of lands on which a federal military installation and cemetery had been established. The trial court held that title was in the plaintiff and that the defendants' possession was illegal. The Supreme Court held that in such circumstances a suit against the defendants was not a suit against the sovereign. 

After Lee the Court was frequently faced with the issue whether the sovereign's immunity applied to Government agents. To reconcile completely all the Court's decisions on that issue prior to 1949 would be a Procrustean task. 

That task, however, is made unnecessary by the 

Court's 1949 Larson decision where the Court thoroughly reviewed the prior decisions and made an informed and carefully considered choice between the seemingly conflicting precedents. Larson was a suit against the War 

Assets Administrator to enjoin him from selling surplus coal that the Administrator had allegedly already sold the plaintiff. Cutting through the tangle of previous decisions, the Court postulated the rule that the action of a federal officer affecting property claimed by a plaintiff can be made the basis of a suit for specific relief against the officer as an individual only if the officer's action is "not within the officer's statutory powers or, if within those powers, only if the powers, or their exercise in the particular case, are constitutionally void.” 

337 U.S. 682, 692 (1949). While not expressly overruling United States v. Lee, the Court in 

Larson limited Lee in such a way that it is inapplicable here. The Court pointed out that at the time of Lee the plaintiff had no remedy for recovering compensation for the taking of his land. The respondents, however, could have sued in the Court of Claims for just compensation for the taking of their land. United States v. Causby, 328 U.S. 256, 267 (1946). The Lee case has continuing vitality only "where there is a claim that the holding constitutes an unconstitutional taking of property without just compensation." 337 U.S. 682, 697. There was no such claim in this case. Nor was it asserted that the petitioner was exceeding his delegated powers in occupying the land or that he possessed the land in anything other than his capacity as a United States officer. This suit, therefore, is not within the class of cases in which, under Larson, specific relief can be obtained against a Government officer. 

Malone v. Bowdoin, 369 U.S. 643 (1962). 

[Note: Justices Frankfurter and White took no part in deciding the case. Justice Douglas, with whom Justice Harlan joined, dissented in an opinion that argued as follows: The Lee case, which serves a useful function, should be followed in this case. In both cases the contest was over real estate held by a Government official against the plaintiff's claim. Here, as there, if the federal agent's possession is illegal, the suit is not against the sovereign. Lee was a five-to-four decision. However, as late as 1947 seven members of the Court agreed to the statement that "where the right to possession or enjoyment of property under general law is in issue, and the defendants claim as officers or agents of the sovereign, the rule of United AGO 9111A 249

SPECIFICATIONS & DRAWINGS 

States v. Lee... has been repeatedly approved.

" 

Land v. Dollar, 330 U.S. 731, 737 (1947). The holding in Lee has not before today been repudiated or necessarily restricted. In Larson the Lee case was distinguished in the manner indicated by the Court in the instant case. 

However, the Larson decision was six to three. 

Of the six, Justice Rutledge only concurred in the result. Justice Douglas concurred on the ground that the suit was for specific performance of a contract to sell Government property and the application of any other rule than the one adopted would clog the governmental function with intolerable burdens. Ejectment, on the other hand, is the classic form of actions to try title. The action takes place where the land is located; the local judges are best qualified to decide. Ejectment is a convenient and ready form of remedy for possession of land. Since it is not a party, the United States is not bound by the decision. If it is aggrieved by the ruling on title, the United States can take appropriate steps. Eminent domain, with the power immediately to take possession, is available. 

Under the majority's holding, the citizen is precluded from any relief except a suit for damages. The advantage is placed with an allpowerful government, not with the citizen. The citizen may not obtain his property, even though the Government is not the rightful claimant.

Sovereign immunity has become more and more out of date, as the powers of the Government and its vast bureaucracy have increased. 

Keifer & Keifer v. Reconstruction Finance 

Corp., 306 U.S. 381, 390 et seq. (1939). The balance between a citizen's convenience and the management of public affairs is a recurring consideration in suits by citizens against Government officials. See Williams v. Fanning, 332 

U.S. 490 (1947). The balance is on the citizen's side when he claims realty in the possession of a Government official and where there are ready means for adjudicating the title. If the citizen has legal title, and if the official's action in possessing the land under authority of the 

United States is ultra vires, what objectionable interference with governmental functions exists?] 

7. Contracting Officers Are Personally Immune From Tort Suits for Acts Based on Decisions That the Officers Should Be Free To Make Without Fear of Suit. (2d Cir.) See CONTRACTING OFFICER (par. 10) SPECIFICATIONS & DRAWINGS 

See also BIDS & AWARDS, CHANGES,

INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS 1. Contractor Is Entitled to Equitable Adjustment Under Changes Clause for Revision of Drawing To Include Utilities of Which Contractor Had No Notice When He Bid. (ASBCA) See CHANGES (par. 12) 2. Contractor Entitled to Administrative Re lief for Increase in Subcontractor's Price Caused by Defective Specifications-Since Original Specifications Were Faulty, Material That Allegedly Fails To Meet Specifications May Be Considered as Termination Inventory-Material That Can't Be Delivered to Government May Be Considered as Termination Inventory. On 13 

May 1955 the appellant received two Army contracts for the supply of ponchos. Deliveries were scheduled for July through September 

1955 under the first contract and for October 

1955 through February 1956 for the second contract. The appellant experienced considerable difficulty in complying with the cloth's specifications, which the Government later admitted could not feasibly have been met. 

Shortly after receiving the contracts, the appellant entered into a subcontract for the supply of enough cloth for both contracts at 76 cents per yard, with final delivery due in February 1956. The Government took for testing samples of each roll of cloth the subcontractor delivered.

During the early stages of performance, the appellant did not delay production of ponchos until he received the results of the cloth tests. as he was prohibited by the contract from so delaying performance. Every sample tested failed to meet the contracts' specifications, so the appellant and the Government negotiated a price reduction. After producing 21,000 ponchos out of cloth that testing reports later showed was inadequate, the appellant began 250 AGO 9111A

SPECIFICATIONS & DRAWINGS-Continued delaying manufacture until the test report of failure was received and a price reduction was negotiated. Beset with difficulties because of the failure of the cloth to meet the contracts' specifications, the appellant in February and 

March 1956 asked the subcontractor to "hold back" deliveries of the cloth and then to cease deliveries. In August 1956 the Government altered the specifications so that they could be met. The appellant contacted the subcontractor about resuming shipments and was told that the price per yard would be raised to 91 cents.

After ascertaining that he could not obtain a price lower than 91 cents, the appellant accepted the subcontractor's new price. The first contract was completed, although tardily; the second contract was terminated for convenience on 25 March 1957 as to the 64,987 units yet undelivered. At the time the termination was made, the appellant had 206,024 yards of cloth, which the Government conceded was termination inventory. The subcontractor had on hand 

28,304 yards that the Government claimed was not termination inventory because the cloth did not meet specifications. [Apparently the specifications referred to were the original, faulty ones.] The contracting officer denied claims 

(1) that the appellant should be reimbursed for the extra costs caused by the faulty specifications; (2) that the cloth regarded as termination inventory should be valued at 91 cents, not 

76 cents, per yard; (3) that the 28,304 yards of cloth in the subcontractor's possession was termination inventory. A timely appeal was taken to the ASBCA. 

Held, appeal sustained as to each claim. To the first claim, the Government raised two defenses. The first was that reimbursement could be made only in a suit for breach of contract. The Board has ruled before that administrative relief may and should be given for extra costs caused by defective specifications. 

Spencer Explosives, Inc., ASBCA No. 4800 (26 

Aug 1960), 60-2 BCA 2795. The second defense was that the normal consequences of defects in Government-drawn specifications should not follow in this case because the specifications of the cloth were adopted after a joint Government-industry effort. However, participation by industry does not alter the fact that the Government dictated what specifications would be included in the contracts. 

Since there is no evidence that the appellant participated in formulating the specifications, no opinion will be expressed as to the result that might be reached if the appellant had personal responsibility for the defective portions of the specifications. The Government also has cited two ASBCA cases, neither of which furnish it any support. In H & H Manufactur ing Co., Inc., ASBCA No. 4353 (30 Nov 1959), 

59-2 BCA 2425, the Board held that performance, while intricate, was reasonably possible. 

In Reliable Manufacturing Co., ASBCA No. 

5305 (30 Dec 1959), 59-2 BCA 2466, the

Board ruled that the Government had the right to insist on strict compliance with contract specifications even though that compliance required special machinery, extra training of personnel, and utilization of processes not customary in commercial manufacturing. Whether the supplies delivered to the Government were better than the less expensive commercial counterpart was held to be of no contractual significance. In the instant case, the original specifications were self-defeating in that compliance with one requirement prevented attainment of another.

The second claim, that the Government should pay the difference between 91 cents per yard and the original subcontract price of 76 cents, is well founded. Telling the subcontractor to "hold back" and then to cease shipment constituted a breach of the appellant's obligation to take delivery by February 1956. 

The breach was reasonably appropriate and the proximate consequence of the faulty specifications. The subcontractor acted within his rights in insisting on an increase in price to 91 cents per yard, and the appellant acted reasonably in agreeing to pay that increase. The subcontractor did not send any formal written notice to the appellant of an intention to hold the appellant for the breach. Such a notice. would obviously have been appropriate in view of the anticipatory breach aspects of the situation. However, the evidence indicates that the subcontractor sufficiently apprised the appellant that the fabric would not be available at the original price of 76 cents per yard. [The AGO 9111A 251

STATE & LOCAL REGULATIONS 

Board's opinion gives no hint about when the subcontractor first notified the appellant of the price change.] 

The third claim, regarding the 28,304 yards of cloth possessed by the subcontractor at the time of termination, must be sustained. The

Government refused to consider the cloth as termination inventory because of an alleged failure to meet specifications. In view of the faulty nature of the original specifications, the cloth may be considered as termination inventory. The 28,304 yards were sold by the appellant in view of the contracting officer's refusal to accept the cloth as termination inventory. The Government does not wish to allow the appellant anything for the cloth because it cannot be delivered to the Government. The pertinent regulations and contract articles are set forth in Bolinders Co., ASBCA No. 5740 (15 Sep 1960), 60-2 BCA 2746. The termination clause of the contract involved in the instant case provides for deduction from the amounts otherwise payable to the contractor of the "fair value" of missing termination inventory. The appellant made appropriate efforts to get the best price, and that sum, offered by the appellant as a credit, will be taken as the "fair value." The appellant is entitled, on the third claim, to 91 cents for each of the 28,304 yards, plus a profit, less the "fair value" credit.

Regent Manufacturing Co., Inc., ASBCA 

Nos. 5397, 6164, and 6165, 28 February 1961, 61-1 BCA 2956. 

STATE & LOCAL REGULATIONS 1. California Milk Stabilization Act Held Unconstitutional As Applied To Military Installations Within Exclusive Jurisdiction of United States. The California Milk Stabilization Act (Calif. Agric. Code §§ 4200-4420) provides for the establishment throughout the state of marketing areas within which minimum milk prices are set. The duty to observe the minimum prices, and civil and criminal penalties for failure to do so, are imposed not only upon milk producers and distributors, but also upon all retail stores, restaurants, or other places for consumption on or off the premises if milk is purchased from distributors or sold to consumers. The Act makes it illegal to handle within the marketing areas milk that is to be sold at less than established minimum prices "at any place . . . whether . . . part of the marketing area or not." California officials filed actions in various state courts to secure injunctive relief and civil penalties against sellers who entered into contracts to supply several Army and Air Force installations within California with milk for on-base commissary sales and mess-hall consumption. The officials also sued in a federal district court for a declaratory judgment of the state's right to enforce the Act as to milk sales made at an Air Force base in the state. Suit was filed by the United States in the federal district court to test the constitutionality of the Act as applied to three military installations in California. The United States contended that the state's attempts to enforce the Act interfered with the purchase of milk and milk products by the United States at military installations under exclusive federal jurisdiction and conflicted with federal competitive bidding policy and procedures, as expressed in

ASPR and APP. The United States alleged that additional operating costs, totalling more than $400,000 annually for the three installations, were incurred because milk could not be obtained for less than the minimum price prescribed by the state. The United States argued that the Act could not constitutionally be applied to lands under exclusive federal legislative jurisdiction, and that the Act's enforcement violated the prohibition of the Supremacy 

Clause of the Constitution (Art. VI, Cl. 2) 

against state interference with the exercise of a federal function. 

Held, the Act is unconstitutional and void to the extent that it prohibits or authorizes the prohibiting of milk sales to the military installations at rates lower than those established by the state. In Penn Dairies v. Milk Control 

Commission, 318 U.S. 261 (1943), the Supreme

Court held that the Pennsylvania Milk Control 

Commission should not be enjoined from enforcing an act similar to the one involved here or from refusing to license a milk distributor who had sold milk to the United States at a military installation at prices below the state's prescribed minimum. In that case, however, 252 AGO 9111A

STATE & LOCAL REGULATIONS-Continued the Court noted that the military installation was situated, not on land over which the United States had exclusive jurisdiction, but on land over which the State of Pennsylvania had retained its jurisdiction. On the same day, the

Court held in Pacific Coast Dairy, Inc. v. De partment of Agriculture, 318 U.S. 285 (1943), that the California Department of Agriculture could not enforce the California milk code by revoking the license of a milk distributor for selling milk below the state's prescribed minimum prices to a military installation. That installation, not one of those involved here, was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the United

States. Recognizing that the results reached in the two cases might seem contradictory, the Court noted that "in preserving the balance between national and state power, seemingly inconsequential differences often require diverse results." 318 U.S. at 295. In the instant case the state contends that the installations involved are not within the exclusive jurisdiction of the United States, but an examination of the details of the transfer of the property shows clearly that the state relinquished all jurisdiction to the United States.

Moreover, even if the installations were not within the exclusive jurisdiction of the United 

States, a conflict between the California Milk

Stabilization Act and federal procurement rules requires nullification of the Act as applied to the installations. It is true that in Penn Dairies the Supreme Court held that the Pennsylvania Milk Control Act, which is similar to the California Act, was not in conflict with any federal procurement statute, regulation or policy. However, in the later case, Public Utilities Commission of California v. United States, 355 U.S. 534 (1958) [DA Pam 715-50-2: p. 346, par. 1], the Court held that there was a clear conflict between a California statute and federal procurement regulations. The statute provided that a state commission could establish the conditions under which common carriers could transport goods at reduced rates for the United States. The federal procurement regulations entrusted to federal procurement officers the task of determining when existing freight rates would be accepted and when negotiation for lower rates would be undertaken. The Court · stated that "Congress has provided a comprehensive policy governing procurement." 355 

U.S. at 540. Federal procurement policy, whether in relation to the obtaining of milk or transportation or any other property or service, is set forth in the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947, now codified in 10 U.S.C. § 2301 et seq. That Act was described by a congressional report as “a comprehensive revision and restatement of the laws governing the procurement of supplies and services." H. R. Rep. 109, 80th Cong. 1st Sess. 6 (1946). Competitive bidding is the cornerstone of federal procurement policy. See 10 U.S.C. § 2304 (a); 32 

C.F.R. 1-301 (1960). In addition, milk and milk products are included within a general procurement scheme so comprehensive that it is designed, not only for economy and efficiency, but also for health and quality control. See 32

C.F.R. §§ 156.1, 156.2, 608.1, 608.3 (1960). 

Therefore, it is evident, as stated in the Public Utilities case, that Congress has provided a comprehensive policy governing procurement. 

This is as true in the case of milk purchases as it is in the case of transportation-rate contracts. 

Even if the Public Utilities case did not overrule Penn Dairies, the former should be applied here. In Public Utilities the Court distinguished Penn Dairies on the ground that in the latter the state regulation imposed no prohibition on the national government or its officers. 

In the instant case, as in Public Utilities, the United States and its officers are subjected by the broad statutory language to the same prohibitions and penalties as everyone else. Moreover, there is no substantial difference between the Public Utilities case and the instant one.

The federal procurement statutes, regulations, and policy involved in the two cases are substantially similar. Both statutes applied to the

United States as a consumer of goods or services and subjected the United States to the discretionary authority of a state agency for the terms on which services or goods could be obtained. The state in this case disclaims any intent to enforce the penal provisions of the Act against the United States or its porcurement officers, but a similar disclaimer proved of no avail in the Public Utilities case.

AGO 9111A 253

United States v. Warne, 190 F. Supp. 645 

(N.D. Calif, 1960), aff'd sub nom. Paul v.

United States, 371 U.S. 245 (1963). 

STATE & LOCAL TAXES 1. State Tax Unconstitutionally Discrimi nates Against United States and Its Lessee. In 

1948, the Government leased real property, located in Moore County, Texas, to the appellant for use in the commercial manufacture of ammonia. The duration of the lease was 15 years but the Government reserved the right to terminate if the property were to be sold. Apparently, the annual rent of more than $1,000,000 was not to be adjusted for state taxes which the appellant was required to pay. 

Article 7173 of the Texas Statutes provided: 

Propery hold under a lease for a term of three years or more . . . belonging to this State, or that is exempt by law from taxation in the hands of the owner thereof, shall be considered for all the purposes of taxation, as the property of the person so holding the same. 

Article 5248 of the Texas Statutes, as amended in 1950, dealt solely with Government realty and provided: 

any portion of said lands and improvements which is used and occupied by any person, firm, association of persons or corporation in its private capacity, or which is being used or occupied in the conduct of any private business or enterprise, shall be subject to taxation by this State and its political subdivisions. 

In comparing these two statutes and interpretive state court decisions, three differences in the treatment of state and federal property ap pear. First, Article 7173 exempts from taxation leases of state realty for a term less than three years while Article 5248 applies to all leases of Government property regardless of duration. 

Second, Texas courts have held that the tax measure under Article 7173 is the cash value of the leasehold interest while the measure under Article 5248 is the full value of the fee. Finally, Texas courts have held that a lease of state property which the lessor may terminate in the event of sale is not a "lease for a term of three years or more" under Article 7173. This holding does extend to lessees of Government realty.

In 1954, the appellee assessed, for the years 1949-54, a tax against the appellant's leasehold interest in the Government realty measured by the full value of the fee. The appellant alleged that the tax was an unconstitutional discrimination against the Government and brought an action in the state courts to enjoin its collection. The appellee did not deny that a difference in classification existed, or that the appellant, as a lessee of state instead of Government realty, would have been exempt from taxation. Rather, the apparent discrimination was justified as an incentive to lease state property and as necessary to counteract the serious impact of federal immunity from taxation on the financial operations of local Gov ernments. The Texas Supreme Court held for the appellee and the appellant appealed to the 

United States Supreme Court. 

Held, the tax is an unconstitutional discrimination against the United States and those with whom it deals. The power of the state to tax the appellant's use of Government realty is not contested. See United States v. City of De troit, 355 U.S. 466 (1958); United States v. 

Township of Muskegon, 355 U.S. 484 (1958) 

[DA Pam 715-50-2, pp. 351-352, pars. 8-9].

Rather, the constitutional power of Texas to impose substantially greater taxes on lessees of Government realty than lessees of state realty is questioned. The fact that the tax discriminates against the Government and its lessees, however, does not ipso facto invalidate it. Tax statutes do not operate in a vacuum and this

Court must examine the entire tax structure of the state to determine the effect on other taxpayers similarly situated. This examination reveals that the difference in classification between lessees of state realty and lessees of Government realty cannot be justified. While the state may legitimately encourage the leasing of state property, an incentive which discriminates against the Government is not proper. Further, no effort was made to impose the tax on the basis of local need. Article 5248 applies to all lessees of Government realty regardless of the burden of tax exemption on the finances of a particular locality. While the appellee's justification may be reasonable and adequate under the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment, Allied Stores v. Bowers, 254 AGO 9111A

STATE & LOCAL TAXES-Continued 

358 U.S. 522, 528 (1959), the standards differ when Governmental immunity is involved. 

Weighing the interest and prerogatives of the Government against the appellee's justifications, it is concluded that an unconstitutional discrimination has occurred. The Constitution requires Texas to treat those with whom the United States deals on the same basis as those with whom the state deals. 

Phillips Chemical Co. v. Dumas Independent

School District, 361 U.S. 367 (1960). 

2. Manager of AEC Facilities Is Agent of United States and Immune From State Sales and Use Tax. In June 1950, the du Pont Company, by a letter contract, undertook the construction of nine plants and supporting facilities for the Atomic Energy Commission in South Carolina. When construction was completed in 1953, the parties entered into a more definitive contract which was retroactive to 1950. Under this contract, du Pont agreed to operate and manage the Government owned facilities for cost plus a fixed fee of $1. Du 

Pont was given broad authority to purchase, in the name of the United States, materials, tools, machinery and equipment for use in contract performance. Title to this property was to vest in the Government at the time that title passed from the vendor to du Pont, subject to subsequent inspection and acceptance, and the purchase price was to be paid by du Pont from a deposit of public money made in a bank by the Government. The AEC exercised considerable control over withdrawals from this fund and the general operations of du Pont. 

Prior to 1953, section 9 (b) of the Atomic

Energy Act of 1946, 60 Stat. 759, 42 U.S.C.A. 

2061, specifically exempted the property and activities of the AEC from state taxation.

When this section was repealed, South Carolina assessed an excise tax on property purchased and used by du Pont to perform the contract. 

Under the state statute, the tax was applicable if the purchaser or user were an agent of the Government but not if the tax were prohibited by the Federal Constitution. The total amount claimed was $1,752,000. The Government and du Pont brought suit in a federal district court to enjoin the collection of the tax on the ground that du Pont was an agent of the Government and that the legal incidence of the tax, therefore, fell upon the United States. The defendant State Tax Commission filed a motion to dismiss for the reason that the federal district court had no jurisdiction and, in the alternative, that du Pont was not immune from state taxation. 

Held, in a 2-1 decision by a three judge court, the motion to dismiss is denied and the injunction is granted. Congress has declared that: "The district courts shall not enjoin, suspend or restrain the assessment, levy or collection of any tax under State law where a plain, speedy and efficient remedy may be had in the courts of such state." 28 U.S.C.A. 1341 (1950).

Congress did not intend, however, to deny the United States access to federal courts when the assessment of a state tax raises a constitutional question of governmental immunity. This is particularly true where the statute is clear and unambiguous and not fairly subject to a state interpretation which would avoid or narrow the constitutional issue. But cf. Harrison v. 

NAACP, 360 U.S. 167 (1959). Further, since

South Carolina does not award interest when a prepaid tax has been successfully contested, the state remedy is inadequate. The conclusion is, therefore, that the federal district court has jurisdiction to consider the merits.

Since Congress repealed the specific exemption from taxation contained in the original 

Atomic Energy Act, cf. Carson v. Roane- 

Anderson Co., 342 U.S. 232 (1952), this case depends upon a consideration of the Government's implied immunity from taxation. See 

McCulloch v. Maryland, 4 Wheat. 316 (1819). [For a lucid explanation of implied immunity, see Helvering v. Gerhardt, 304 U.S. 405 (1938).] The unquestioned rule is that the property and essential operations of the Government and its agents are not subject to state taxation. If, however, the legal incidence of state taxation falls upon Government contractors, the doctrine of immunity is not for application even though the Government, by the terms of the contract, bears the economic burden of the tax. James v. Dravo Contracting 

Co., 302 U.S. 134 (1937); Alabama v. King &

Boozer, 314 U.S. 1 (1941). In King & Boozer, the legal incidence of a state sales tax fell on a AGO 9111A 255

STATE & LOCAL TAXES-Continued cost-plus-fixed-fee contractor who purchased lumber for use in performing a Government contract. This tax was upheld even though the economic burden was borne by the Government since the lumber was purchased on the contractor's own credit and the Government had no obligation to reimburse costs until the lumber had been delivered and accepted. In 

Kern-Limerick v. Scurlock, 347 U.S. 110 

(1954), however, the contractor, under a costplus-fixed-fee contract, was designated a purchasing agent for the Government and authorized to purchase goods in the name of and on the credit of the United States. In addition, title vested directly in the Government when the contractor made a purchase. Consequently, the contractor was an agent of the Government and immune from state taxation. 

The instant case is more like Kern-Limerick than King & Boozer, even though du Pont was not specifically designated a purchasing agent.

Du Pont made purchases in the Government's name with public funds and title vested directly in the Government, subject to subsequent inspection. The purchasing activities were openly on behalf of the United States and under the supervision of the AEC. It is concluded, therefore that du Pont was in fact an agent of the United States and not subject to the South Carolina sales and use tax, and was operating under a valid delegation of authority from the 

AEC. 

The defendant urges that du Pont possessed a separate beneficial interest in the Government property used to perform the contract and that this interest was taxable. Detroit v. Murray 

Corp., 355 U.S. 489 (1958). Du Pont, however, received no profit from this contract. Even so, du Pont was an agent of the Government employed to operate and manage Governmentowned facilities. Its activities, therefore, were completely those of the Government and not those of a separate business enterprise deriving a profitable advantage from the use of Government property.

United States v. Livingston, 179 F. Supp. 9 (E.D.S.C. 1959), aff'd 364 U.S. 281 (1960). 

[Note: Pursuant to a Department of Defense decision in January 1955, the Department of the Army has advised that the "purchasing agent" theory will not be used to contest state taxes imposed on Government contractors. 

JAGT 1957/8158, 17 October 1957. For an opinion that a Florida Statute which appears to tax sales to agents of the United States is unconstitutional, see Ms. Comp. Gen.
