See PRICE ADJUSTMENT (par. 5) 5. Federal Court Uses Philips Chemical Co. 

Doctrine To Invalidate Illinois Tax That Discriminated Against United States. The Illinois Retailers' Occupation Tax Act [Smith-Hurd Stat. Ann. ch. 120 § 440 et seq. (Supp. 1960)] 

imposed a tax on the gross receipts from retail sales in Illinois of tangible personal property. 

Exempted from the tax were the proceeds of sales to "the State of Illinois, any county, political subdivision or municipality thereof, or to any instrumentality or institution of any of the governmental units aforesaid" and to "any corporation, society, association, foundation, or institution organized and operated exclusively for charitable, religious or educational purposes." The United States and one of its contractors sued to obtain a declaration that the Act was unconstitutional, void, and of no effect so far as it permitted taxation of receipts from sales of tangible personal property to the United States. The suit also asked for an injunction against the assessment of taxes on the receipts of such sales. The contractor had sold in Illinois nearly a million dollars worth of personal property to the United States, and the State claimed a tax of more than $27,000. More than 1440 other persons and firms in Illinois were also engaged in sales to agencies of the Defense Department, and the contracts for such sales totalled more than $623,000,000. The 

United States asserted that under existing contract provisions it was obligated to reimburse 256 AGO 9111A

STATE & LOCAL TAXES-Continued contractors for any taxes paid under the Act. 

The complaint alleged the Act was unconstitutional because (1) failure to treat the United States and its contractors like the State and its contractors were treated was discriminatory, and (2) the United States' immunity from state and local taxation was violated. 

Held, the tax is unconstitutional. The parties discussed Alabama v. King & Boozer, 314 U. S. 

1 (1941) and Kern-Limerick v. Scurlock, 347 

U.S. 110 (1953), which turned on whether the legal incidence of the challenged taxes fell on the United States. Those cases are not decisive here. Under the Illinois Act, the legal incidence of a tax falls upon the contractor. No statutory provision compels him to collect the tax from the purchaser, who in this case would be the United States. In view of the decisions of the 

Supreme Court since Panhandle Oil Co. v. Knox, 277 U.S. 218 (1927), the contractor here cannot be held to be such an agent or instrumentality of the federal government that the incidence of the tax falls upon that sovereign. The mere fact that a private corporation conducts its business under a contract with the United States does not make it an instrumentality of the Government. See, e.g., United States v.

Detroit, 355 U.S. 466 (1958) [DA Pam 71550-2: p. 352, par. 10]. Therefore, the principle of sovereign immunity from local taxation is not involved here.

The crucial question is whether the tax is discriminatory. There is a strong presumption favoring the validity of a legislative classification if any state of facts can reasonably be conceived to sustain it; the existence of such a state of facts is presumed. Tax statutes exempting a class necessarily impose a greater burden on the taxed class than would be imposed if no exemptions were made. However, a legislature may constitutionally grant an exemption according to its view of public policy so long as the classification is not unreasonable or arbitrary. Hart Refineries v. Harmon, 278

U.S. 499, 502 (1928). The exemption in the Illi nois Act for retailers dealing with the state and its subdivisions has the beneficent objective of reducing the costs of governmental administration. Therefore, the power of the legislature to create exemption is not questioned. However, a retailer dealing with the federal government falls within the same class as a retailer dealing with the State. The exemption is made for dealings with a governmental entity, and no reason has been offered to justify the distinction between state and federal contractors. It is difficult to find any such reason. If the exemption has the laudable public purpose of reducing governmental costs, the exemption is equally applicable to the federal government in order to benefit all citizens of the United States, including citizens of Illinois. Moreover, imposing a tax on federal contractors and not on state contractors means that the federal government must pay more to deal with the same persons with whom the state deals. The federal government is also discriminated against in contrast to charitable, religious, and educational groups. The discrimination against the federal government is condemned by Phillips 

Chemical Co. v. Dumas Independent School Dis trict, 361 U.S. 376 (1960). There the Court stated: "a State may not single out those who deal with the Government, in one capacity or another, for a tax burden not imposed on others similarly situated. . . . [I]t does not seem too much to require that the State treat those who Ideal with the Government as well as it treats those with whom it deals itself." Id. at 383, 385.

United States v. Department of Revenue of the State of Illinois, 191 F. Supp. 723 (N.D. Ill. 

1961), subsequent decision digested under 

STATE AND LOCAL TAXES, par. 8.

6. Arizona Transaction Privilege Tax and Education Excise Tax Are Not Applicable to Purchases of Typewriters From Manufacturers Outside Arizona-Army Activity Need Not Question Rate Billed for Federal Manufacturers Excise Tax So Long as Statutory Rate Not Exceeded-Where Arizona Transaction Privilege Tax and Education Excise Tax Apply, They Should Be Calculated on Amount That Includes Federal Manufacturers Excise Tax. Three tax questions raised by an Army activity in Arizona were referred to The Judge Advocate General. The first was whether the Arizona transaction privilege tax and the Arizona education excise tax were applicable to the Army activity's purchase of four typewriters from a firm that manufactured the typewriters outside

Arizona. The typewriters were purchased pursuant to ASPR and APP 5-101 and in accordance with a GSA Federal Supply Schedule that provided that "Orders should be forwarded to the contractor at the nearest branch office as listed in the price list." The nearest branch office for the typewriters was in Phoenix,

Arizona. The Arizona taxes were imposed "upon every person engaging . . . in the business of selling any tangible personal property whatever, at retail. . . ." Ariz. Rev. Stat. §§ 

42-1312A (1956), 42-1362 (Supp. 1961). A statutory exemption was made for sales "made directly... to the United States Government, its departments or agencies by a manufacturer, modifier, assembler or repairer." Ariz. Rev.

Stat. §§ 42-1321B (1956), 42-1362 (Supp. 

1961). The state tax commission's regulation stated that the exemption applied only to “persons or firms engaged in the business of manufacturing, modifying, assembling, or repairing in the State of Arizona."

The second question was whether a contractor selling to the Army activity could properly bill the federal manufacturers excise tax at a rate lower than that prescribed by the statute. 

Int. Rev. Code of 1954, § 4191. The third ques tion was whether the two Arizona taxes could properly be computed on an amount that included the federal manufacturers excise tax. 

Held, the first question is answered in the negative and the second in the affirmative; the answer to the first question renders the third moot. With respect to the first question, the 

Arizona law by its terms does not make the exemption turn on whether a manufacturer performs his manufacturing within Arizona.

The state tax commission cannot impose by regulation a qualification not authorized by the statutes. Furthermore, it is arguable that even if the Arizona statute denied the exemption to out-of-state manufacturers, the discrimination in favor of manufacturers in Arizona might be an unconstitutional attempt by a state to regulate interstate commerce. U.S. Const. art. I, 258 AGO 9111A

STATE & LOCAL TAXES-Continued § 8, cl. 3. Consult Bethlehem Motors Corp. v. 

Flynt, 256 U.S. 421, 426 (1921).

With respect to the second question, a purchasing federal agency is not required to challenge the rate billed for the federal manufacturers excise tax so long as the statutory rate is not exceeded. It is possible that special factors account for the rate billed being lower than what the statute apparently authorizes. 

In any case, the tax billed is subject to audit by the Internal Revenue Service. With respect to the third question, the federal manufacturers excise tax is part of a manufacturer's cost of an item sold and would generally be included in the gross receipts subject to the Arizona tax. 

However, as explained above, the Arizona tax is not properly applicable to the purchase of the typewriters. 

JAGT 1961/7028, 28 August 1961. 

7. The Judge Advocate General Construes Statutes and Regulations Governing Exemptions From West Virginia Gasoline Excise Tax. 

West Virginia imposes "upon every person who is a distributor, retail dealer . . . an excise tax based on the quantities of all gasoline produced, purchased, sold or used" in the state. W. Va.

Code ch. 11, art. 14, § 3 (1961). A statutory exemption is provided for persons buying “in quantities of twenty-five gallons or more, at any one time, gasoline" for any of seven specified purposes, including the operation of motor vehicles on other than public thoroughfares. 

W. Va. Code ch. 11, art. 14, § 20 (1961). A 

regulation of the West Virginia Tax Commission provides an exemption in favor of the United States for purchases of gasoline in quantities over 500 gallons; Standard Form 

1094 is to be used as a claim for a refund or in lieu of payment of the tax. CCH State Tax 

Rep. par. 43-209 (1961). The Judge Advocate 

General issued an opinion based on the cited regulation and statutes.

Held, first, the United States is entitled to an exemption from, or a refund of, the state tax on purchases of gasoline in quantities of 500 gallons or more. Standard Form 1094 should, in accordance with the state regulation, be used to support the exemption or refund. Second, the United States should pay the state tax when purchasing gasoline in quantities exceeding twenty-five gallons but less than 500 gallons. 

A refund should be applied for only if the gasoline is used for one of the seven purposes enumerated in W. Va. Code ch. 11, art. 14, § 20. 

Third, on purchases of gasoline in quantities less than 25 gallons, the United States should pay the state tax and make no application for a refund. Fourth, the exemption under the state regulation may be obtained only if there is a delivery of 500 gallons or more at one time to one agency. The fact that the same credit card is used on more than one occasion by the same party purchasing from the same vendor does not make the exemption apply. There can be no accumulation on one invoice to qualify for the exemption. 

JAGT 1961/7088, 28 August 1961. 

8. Tax Levied on Sales to United States But 

Not on Sales to Charitable, Religious, and Educational Bodies Is Not Unconstitutionally Discriminatory-Legal Incidence of Illinois Occupation Tax Is Not on United States. In United 

States v. Department of Revenue of the State of Illinois, 191 F. Supp. 723 (N.D. Ill. 1961) 

[digested under STATE AND LOCAL TAXES, par. 5], a three-judge federal district court held unconstitutional Section 441 of the Illinois. Retailers' Occupation Tax Act. That section imposed a tax on the gross receipts from retail sales of tangible personal property, but exempted the proceeds of sales to the State of Illinois, its subdivisions, and charitable, educational, or religious bodies. In a suit by the 

United States and one of its contractors, the court held that the tax unconstitutionally discriminated against the United States and in favor of state agencies as well as charitable, religious, and educational bodies. The court enjoined assessment of the tax on the receipts from sales to the United States. Subsequently, the Illinois Supreme Court in an unreported opinion, Holland Coal Co. v. Isaacs [noted after the digest under STATE AND LOCAL TAXES, par.

5] held unconstitutional and void the exemption portions of Section 441. Then the 

Illinois legislature exempted from the tax levied by Section 441 all proceeds of sales to bodies organized and operated exclusively for charitable, religious, or educational purposes AGO 9111A 259

STATE & LOCAL TAXES-Continued unless the creation of such an exemption will automatically, and contrary to the intent of this Act, exempt from the measure of the Retailers' Occupation Tax Act the proceeds of sales to the United States Government, its agencies and instrumenalities and contractors with that Government. 

Smith-Hurd Stat. Ann. ch. 120, § 441 (Supp. 1961). 

The Illinois Supreme Court upheld this exemp tion. Holland Coal Co. v. Isaacs, 22 Ill. 2d 477, 

176 N.E. 2d 889 (1961). When the United

States Supreme Court received an appeal from the decision of the three-judge district court, the case was remanded "for further consideration in the light of the developments which.. occurred since the injunction was issued." De partment of Revenue of Illinois v. United States, 368 U.S. 30 (1961). The United States and its contractor filed an amended complaint, which (1) objected to the discrimination against the United States as compared to charitable, religious, and educational institutions, and (2) claimed the tax was invalid because it is borne in law and fact by the United 

States. 

Held, the exemption does not unconstitutionally discriminate against the United States, and the tax is valid. The distinction betwen governmental units, on the one hand, and charitable, religious, and educational bodies, on the other, is reasonable and based on differences between the two classes. It is an old and well-established policy in Illinois to exempt from taxation nongovernmental units operated for charitable, religious, and educational purposes. Many states and the federal income tax have provided such an exemption. The exemption encourages the existence of charitable, religious, and educational institutions and relieves the state of the burden of providing many services. The Illinois constitution prohibits the use of public funds or property for church or sectarian purposes. Ill. 

Const. art. VIII, § 3. Religious institutions and governmental bodies are thus obviously dissimilar. Moreover, while the government can and does perform charitable and educational tasks, the revenue used is derived from the power and authority of the government to tax. 

No compulsory process exists to exact contributions to non-governmental organizations dedicated to the moral, spiritual, and physical well-being of mankind. Those organizations obtain their funds from voluntary gifts. Thus the exemption for charitable, religious, and educational institutions appears justifiable. Language to the contrary in the first opinion on this case was unnecessary and is hereby deleted from that opinion.

The amended complaint alleges that the retailers' occupation tax is in fact and law borne by the purchaser, in this case the United States. 

The allegation relies on the operation of that tax in relation to the Illinois use tax. The latter tax is imposed on purchasers of tangible personal property, but is collected and remitted by retailers that have a place of business in Illinois or are specially authorized as collection and remitting agents. Smith-Hurd Stat. Ann. ch. 120, § 439.3 (Supp. 1961). The tax is not collected from retailers that have paid the occupation tax. Smith-Hurd Stat. Ann. ch. 120 § 439.8 

(Supp. 1961). The state recognizes that the use tax cannot constitutionally be collected from the United States, but provides that retailers are liable for the occupation tax on receipts from sales to the United States. The plaintiffs here argue that a retailer who sells to the federal government must pay the occupation tax out of his own pocket because he cannot collect the use tax from the purchasing sovereign, while a retailer dealing with a purchaser that lacks immunity to the use tax need not pay the occupation tax when he collects the use tax from the purchaser. However, a "discrimination" resulting from the doctrine of sovereign immunity is not only reasonable but mandatory. Moreover, the contention of discrimination contradicts the plaintiff's theory. The crux of that theory is that by custom and usage the retailer has "passed" his occupation tax to the buyer including the federal government, even though the legal incidence of the tax falls on him alone. 

However, the practice of "passing" the tax to the buyer does not change that tax into the use tax and is unrelated to any action taken by the state. The legal incidence is the critical factor in judging the constitutionality of a tax. So far as a different view has prevailed, see Panhandle 

Oil v. Knox, 277 U.S. 218 (1927), the Supreme 

Court has rejected it "as no longer tenable." 

Alabama v. King & Boozer, 314 U.S. 1, 8-9 (1941). 260 AGO 9111A

STATE & LOCAL TAXES-Continued United States v. Department of Revenue, 202 

F. Supp. 757 (N.D. Ill. 1962), affd per curiam

[T]here is no legal justification for eleemosynary institutions being elevated to a position superior to that of the Federal Government, which has the primary responsibility of protecting our welfare and serving the public good. Assuming, as is pointed out in the cases, that technically there is a basis for differentiating between the two classifications because the Government has a means for self-support, whereas charities do not, it does not follow that the classifications exempted are entitled to receive or may receive any more favored treatment than the Government itself.... 11. GSA's Sale of Surplus Government Property Declared Exempt From Texas Sales Tax. 

An official of the GSA asked the Comptroller 

General whether certification for payment could be given to a voucher for $146.09, the amount of the Texas sales tax remitted to GSA by purchasers of surplus federal property. 

A memorandum prepared by the Dallas Regional Office of GSA stated that application of the Texas Limited Sales, Excise and Use Tax to an agency of the federal government would require the agency to apply to the State Comptroller for a permit to conduct business as a seller, to collect the tax, to maintain additional accountability records of receipts and deposits, and to remit quarterly to the State Comptroller. 

The memorandum pointed out that the Texas Act contains no provision for exempting sales by the federal government and that doubt about the exemption was created by Colorado National Bank of Denver v. Bedford, 310 U.S. 41 (1940).

Held, the state may not properly require the 

GSA to comply with the tax statute, but the voucher in question may be certified for payment. In the Bank of Denver case the Court held constitutional a state law requiring a national bank to collect and remit from its safe deposit box users a percentage tax. It is true that a national bank has been held to be a federal instrumentality for certain purposes. 

Guthrie v. Harkness, 199 U.S. 148 (1905).

Nevertheless, such a bank is not in the same category as an agency such as the GSA. National banks are private corporations organized under a federal law. The banks have their own capital, are run for private gain, and are managed by officers and employees chosen by the banks. The GSA is part of the executive branch of the Government, and the agency's employees are United States employees. Thus, the instant case is distinguishable from the Bank of Denver case.

The general principle to be applied in this case is that states have no power by taxation to retard, impede, burden, or in any manner control the operation of constitutional laws enacted by Congress to implement the powers vested in the federal government. 31 Comp. 

Gen. 81 (1951) and cases cited there. In disposing of federal surplus property, the GSA is conducting an activity under the Federal 

Property and Administrative Services Act of 

1949, as amended. The Texas statute, insofar as the exercise of the activities of the Federal government is concerned, infringe upon the right of the Government to conduct such activities free from state interference or control. 

The voucher here involved may be certified for payment, however, because disposing of the funds in such a fashion would be less burdensome for the Government. Payment will not signify acquiescence by the United 

States to the Texas statute. The State Comp troller should be so advised and furnished a copy of this decision. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-148226, 12 April 1962. 262 AGO 9111A

Subcontract Exculpatory Clause Which Covers Extra Costs Caused By Delay Does Not Preclude Appeal By Prime Contractor On Behalf of Subcontractor Where Extra Costs Caused By Government's Efforts To Expedite Performance. In October 1956, the prime con tractor entered into a $19,400,000 contract for the construction of the Air Force Academy academic complex. When performance was delayed by strikes, change orders and material shortages, the prime contractor was ordered to work overtime and to employ more personnel so that construction could be completed within the original time schedule. The contracting officer then denied the prime contractor's claim for the extra cost incurred. On appeal the 

ASBCA found that the delay was excusable under SF 23A, clause 5 (c) and held that the contracting officer improperly denied a time extension. Consequently, the costs incurred because of the order to expedite performance were reimbursable under the Changes Clause 

(Cl. 3, SF 23A, Mar. 1953 ed.). Farnsworth & Chambers Co., ASBCA Nos. 4945, 4978, and 5129 (24 Nov 1959) [digested under APPRO- PRIATIONS par. 2]. 

As the result of the Government's action, a series of claims for extra costs were made by subcontractors against the prime contractor. 

These were submitted by the prime contractor to the contracting officer and denied. The prime contractor then appealed in its own name to the ASBCA on behalf of the subcontractors. 

The Government filed a motion to dismiss on the ground that each subcontract contained an exculpatory clause which deprived the prime contract of a financial interest in the appeal. 

This clause provided: 

(c) Contractor shall not be liable to Subcontractor for any delay to Subcontractor's work resulting from the act, negligence or default of the Owner or the Architect, or by reason of fire or other casualty, or on account of riots, strikes or other combined action of the workmen or others, or on account of any acts of God or any other cause beyond Contractor's control; or on account of any circumstances caused or contributed to by Subcontractor. 

Held, the motion to dismiss is denied. A prime contractor may appeal to this Board on behalf of a subcontractor provided that the contracting officer's decision is addressed to and the notice of appeal is signed by the prime contractor, the prime contractor has not relinquished its pecuniary interest and the subcontract does not contain an exculpatory clause. 

See Farnsworth & Chambers Co., Inc., ASBCA 

No. 5488 (11 Feb 1960). Cf. Severin v. United

States, 99 Ct. Cl. 435 (1943). [But see General Installation Co., ASBCA No. 2061 (14 Dec 

1954), DA Pam 715-50-1, p. 131, par. 7, where a prime contractor with no pecuniary interest was permitted to appeal on behalf of a subcontractor.] While the subcontracts involved in this appeal contained exculpatory clauses, the exculpation applied to liability from delay not efforts to expedite performance. Since these two are opposites, it is concluded that the exculpatory clauses do not preclude the instant 

Farnsworth & Chambers Company, Inc., ASBCA Nos. 5768, 5869-5872, 5966, and 5967, 26 July 1960, 60-2 BCA 2717. 

[Note: In Morrison-Knudsen, Inc., ASBCA 

No. 4929 (15 Aug 1960), 60–2 BCA 2799, the

Army panel unequivocally stated that the Severin doctrine did not apply where a prime contractor appealed on behalf of a subcontractor to obtain a prime contract price adjustment under the Changed Conditions clause. 

Relief under this clause is conditioned upon proof that a changed condition has caused either the prime contractor or the subcontractor to incur additional costs. The fact that the prime contractor may have protected itself

4. Severin Doctrine Does Not Apply to Government Delays Under Government Furnished Property Clause, ASPR 13-502. In March 1951, the contractor agreed to manufacture 50,000 cotton overcoats for the Government. The 

Government promised to furnish cloth in sufficient time to permit the contractor to meet the delivery schedule. In the event of delay, the 

1958)] The contracting officer shall, if duly requested by the contractor, make a determination of the delay occasioned the contractor thereby and an equitable adjustment on account of such delay under the section of this contract entitled 'Changes'. . . . 

A subcontractor agreed to perform the manufacturing operations after the cloth had been cut. The subcontract provided that the prime contractor "shall not be liable for failure on its part to deliver goods to (the subcontractor) if such failure is due to delay by the Government,...." Further, it was stipulated that "any increases in costs. ... shall be borne by (the subcontractor)" but "in the event of any such increase, (the contractor) will make every effort to obtain from the Government an equal increase for (the subcontractor's) benefit." 

The Government delayed in furnishing cloth and caused increased costs to both the contractor and the subcontractor. A claim for all costs was denied by the contracting officer whereupon the contractor appealed to the 

ASBCA. The Government filed a motion to dismiss the appeal to the extent that increased costs were incurred by the subcontractor.

Held, the motion is denied. The Govern ment's motion is based upon the so-called Severin doctrine, which holds that a prime contractor may not bring an action in the Court of Claims on behalf of a subcontractor for damages caused by the Government's breach of contract where the subcontract contains a clause which exonerates the prime contractor from liability to the subcontractor for that breach. See Severin v. United States, 99 Ct. 

Cl. 435 (1943); Continental Illinois Nat'l Bank 

& Trust Co. v. United States, 126 Ct. Cl. 

631 (1953).

In this case, however, the Govern ment-Furnished Property Clause authorizes an equitable adjustment for delay which is not conditioned upon the prime contractor's pecuniary liability to the subcontractor. The extra costs are sought by a prime contractor in privity with the Government and are expressly and unequivocally authorized by the Government- 

Furnished Property Clause, regardless of whether they were incurred by the prime con tractor or the subcontractor. The remarks of the Court in Blair v. United States, 321 U.S. 

731, 737 (1944), lend support to this conclusion.

The Court below made no finding, and the subcontract as introduced into the record does not expressly indicate, that respondent was liable to the subcontractor for the acts of the Government upon which the claim was based. 

Clearly, the subcontractor could not recover this claim in a suit against the United States, for there was no express or implied contract between him and the Government. . . . But it does not follow that respondent [prime contractor] is barred from suing for this amount. Respondent was the only person legally bound to perform his contract with the Government and he had the undoubted right to recover from the Government the contract price for the tile, terrazzo, marble and soapstone work whether that work was performed personally or through another. This necessarily implied the right to recover extra costs and services wrongfully demanded of respondent under the contract, regardless of whether such costs were incurred or such services were performed personally or through a subcontractor. Respondent's contract with the

Government is thus sufficient to sustain an action for extra costs wrongfully demanded under that contract. . . . 

In view of the prime contract's clear language, the terms of the subcontract have no bearing on the contractor's right to claim all of the extra costs incurred. Even so, the terms of the subcontract protect the subcontractor if the contractor is able to obtain "an equal increase" of costs under the prime contract. 264 AGO 9111A

SUBCONTRACTS-Continued 

-1 Therefore, the subcontract exculpatory clause applies only to increased costs that exceed those which the contractor is able to recover from the 

Government. Cf. Donovan Constr. Co. v. United 

States, 138 Ct. Cl. 97 (1957). Since the Government is responsible under the contract for all costs caused by the delay, the contractor is liable to the subcontractor for an allocable portion of the amount recovered. [On the merits, the appeal was sustained in the amount of $54,325.08.]

5. Third Tier Materialman Who Supplies a Second Tier Subcontractor Is Not Protected by Miller Act Payment Bond. (D. Mass.) See MILLER ACT (par. 5) 6. Government Invitations and Contracts May Contain A Provision That All Subcontracts Are Subject To The Approval Of The Contracting Officer On The Basis Of The Proposed Subcontractor's Qualifications To Perform In A Capable And Responsible Manner. In 1951 The 

Judge Advocate General issued an opinion advising that in neither advertised nor negotiated procurement could the Government legally require inclusion of a contractual prohibition against using suspended contractors as subcontractors. JAGT 1951/3008, 7 March 1951.

The opinion accorded with statements of the Comptroller General that "as a general rule all bids should be received and given consideration on an equal basis" and that "prior unsatisfactory service or irregularity in performance was not a valid reason for subsequent refusal to consider bids." 14 Comp. Gen. 313 (1934). In recent years, however, more extensive and complicated procurements have resulted in more definite and specialized administrative needs. It has been generally recognized that establishing bidders' qualifications is primarily a function of the administrative office and that the exercise of administrative discretion should be questioned only upon a showing of bad faith or lack of a reasonable factual basis. 

36 Comp. Gen. 649 (1957); 35 Comp. Gen. 167 (1955). General recognition has also been given the fact that reasonable qualifications encompass areas not only of financial responsibility but of "judgment, skill, integrity, and fitness and ability to perform." See, e.g., 30

Comp. Gen. 235 (1950). The Comptroller Gen eral has stated that the proper use of controls to preclude performance by incompetent or irresponsible contractors or subcontractors is not inconsistent with the functioning or objectives of the competitive procurement system. 

He suggested that the least complicated form of control would be a contract provision-to which invitations should call special attentionthat no work be subcontracted except subject to approval by the contracting officer of the proposed subcontractors' qualifications to perform the work in a capable and responsible manner. 37 Comp. Gen. 544 (1958). The 1951 opinion of The Judge Advocate General should be modified to provide that, although a Government contract may not prohibit using suspended contractors as subcontractors, invitations and contracts may include a provision like that suggested by the Comptroller General. 

In ascertaining the fitness of subcontractors, the contracting officer may apply the same standards used in determining the fitness of the prime contractor.

JAGT 1961/5920, 21 February 1961.

See CONTRACT CLAUSES (Suspension of Work) (par. 2) 2. Where Contract Provides That Notice To Proceed Will Be Issued Not Later Than a Certain Date and the Work Site Is Not Ready by That Date the Government Has Suspended the Work. The Government awarded a contract to the contractor for construction of one of the buildings at the new Air Force Academy. The contract stated that a notice to proceed would be issued by the Government not later than 15 April 1957. Completion was required within 

470 days after receipt by the contractor of written notice to proceed. Thus, it was anticipated that the contract would be completed before the winter of 1958. The Government's grading contractor had not completed its work when the notice to proceed was issued on 15 April and the site was not ready for the contractor to begin work until 5 July. This delay in starting caused the contractor to schedule some of its work in the winter of 1958-59 and several time extensions were granted. The scheduling of work during the winter required that the contractor furnish temporary heat for the construction. It sought reimbursement for these costs. The contract contained the following 

SP 1-12 [Suspension of Work]. The Contracting 

Officer may order the Contractor to suspend all or any part of the work for such period of time as may be determined by him to be necessary or desirable for the convenience of the Government. 

Unless such suspension unreasonably delays the progress of the work and causes additional expense or loss to the Contractor, no increase in contract price will be allowed. In the case of suspension of all or any part of the work for an unreasonable length of time, causing additional expense or loss, not due to the fault or negligence of the Contractor, the Contracting Officer shall make an equitable adjustment in the contract price and modify the contract accordingly. 

SP 1-48 (d). Payment will be made for the cost of furnishing heat during any period for which such heat is required which extends beyond that stipulated in the contract, for the completion of construction, in cases in which such extended period of time results directly from changes made in the drawings or specifications pursuant to the provisions of [the Changes clause], and no payment will be made on account of any other items of cost of delay, whether occasioned by a change in the specifications or otherwise.

From an adverse decision of the Contracting 

Officer, the contractor appealed to the ASBCA.

The appeal was decided by the three panel chairmen. 

Held, the contractor is entitled to reimbursement for its heating costs. The Government covenanted to give and gave a notice to proceed but it was given at a time when the site was not ready for the contractor to begin its operations. This had the effect of suspending the work which the Government had a right to do under the suspension of work provision. Ab bett Electric Corp. v. United States, 162 F. 

Supp. 772 (Ct. Cl. 1958), digested in DA Pam 

715-50-2, p. 119, par. 32. The contractor is entitled to its material and labor costs and overhead but not to an allowance for profit since Special Provision 1-48 (d) does not provide for an equitable adjustment in price but only for the payment of costs. 

T. C. Bateson Construction Co., ASBCA No. 

5985, 31 August 1960, 60-2 BCA 2767. [Note: In a vigorous dissent, the chairman 266 AGO 9111A

SUSPENSION OF WORK-Continued of the Army panel argued that the majority opinion pushes the Suspension of Work clause "beyond any frontier to which it has heretofore been extended." This decision cannot be reconciled with its own companion case, see infra, in which relief was denied the contractor and no suspension of work found. The Abbett case relied on by the majority can be readily distinguished from this case. In Abbett the parties contracted without knowledge of the delaying factors which were later to prevent the contractor from proceeding on the site. The contrary is true in this case. Being fully aware of the existence of the grading contractor, the contractor had no right to assume that this preceding contractor would evaporate, and it therefore had no right to do work which necessarily had to follow grading work, until the latter was completed. Thus, it could have made provision in its bid for any increased costs which could result from its obligation to await completion of the preceding contract. 

Further, the temporary heat costs incurred were precisely of the type contemplated by 

Special Provision 1-48 (d). Paradoxically, the majority, after applying the Suspension of

Work clause to permit recovery, limits recovery to the type of expense contemplated by 

SP 1-48 (d), although SP 1-12, the "Suspension" clause, contains no such limitation. This claim for relief should have been evaluated under SP 1-48 (d). If the facts do not support relief under that provision relief should be denied.

The companion case referred to in the dissenting opinion was T. C. Bateson Construc tion Co., ASBCA No. 6128 (22 Aug 1960), 60-2 

BCA 2757. The contract was for construction of another building at the same site. As in the principal case, notice to proceed was issued on 15 April 1957 but the site was not ready for several months (until 4 July). The contract, however, did not state that notice to proceed would be issued by a specific date. The Board there held that the mere issuance of a notice to proceed did not cause a suspension of work, cit ing John A. Johnson & Sons, Incs., ASBCA No. 

4403 (11 Feb 1959), 59-1 BCA 2088, digested in 

DA Pam 715-50-2, p. 139, par. 7. The sole difference between the two Bateson cases appears to be that in one the Government was obligated by contract to issue a notice to proceed by a specified date, while in the other the Government was not so obligated.] 

3. ASBCA Allows Recovery of Cost of Keeping Equipment Idle During Year-long Suspention of Work-Claim Under Suspension of Work Clause Valid Even Though Filed Long After Stop Work Order Lifted and After Final Pay ment Made on Contract. The appellant had an 

Air Force contract requiring him to construct, among other things, an access road to a "Localizer Site." The contract contained the stand ard Changes Clause (Cl. 3, SF 23A, Mar. 1953 ed.) and a Suspension of Work Clause stating: 

(a) The Contracting Officer may order the Con tractor to suspend all or any part of the work for such period of time as may be determined by him to be necessary or desirable for the convenience of the Government. Unless such suspension unreasonably delays the progress of the work and causes additional expense or loss to the Contractor, no increase in contract price will be allowed. In the case of suspension of all or any part of the work for an unreasonble length of time, causing additional expense or loss, not due to the fault or negligence of the Contractor, the Contracting Offi cer shall make an equitable adjustment in the contract price and modify the contract accordingly. (b) An equitable extension of time for the completion of the work in the event of any such suspension will be allowed the Contractor, provided, however, that the suspension was not due to the fault or negligence of the Contractor. 

Work on the road began in October 1956 and was to be completed by 10 March 1957. The appellant's subcontractor who was to handle the excavating, grading, and road work moved several pieces of construction equipment onto the work site and began work. On 20 Novem ber 1956 the Air Force issued a Stop Work Or der to halt construction of the access road pending a determination whether the "Localizer Site" should be moved. While work was stopped by the order, the construction equipment of the subcontractor remained idle most of the time, though-according to the appellant -the equipment was used on other work whenever possible. Not until September 1957 did the Air Force begin discussions with the appellant about the plans for relocating the "Localizer Site." After more than a month of dis- AGO 9111A 267

SUSPENSION OF WORK-Continued cussions, the appellant submitted, and the Air Force accepted, a proposal regarding changes in the road necessitated by the relocation of the "Localizer Site." The proposal stated that the changes would not require "extra construction costs." Shortly afterwards the proposal was incorporated in a no-cost supplemental agreement executed pursuant to the Changes Clause. The road was completed and accepted by 21 June 1958, and final payment was accepted by the appellant on that date. On 12 October 

1958 the appellant advised the Air Force that he was preparing a claim for additional expenses incurred as a result of the Stop Work Order and that a formal claim would be filed as soon as the necessary information was collected and organized. On 16 December 1959 a formal claim was filed for the cost of maintaining the construction equipment at the work site while the Stop Work Order was in effect. The contracting officer declined to consider the claim because it was not filed in writing within thirty days and because final payment had been made before the claim was asserted. A timely appeal from the contracting officer's action was taken to the ASBCA. 

Held, appeal sustained. The claim is not barred by the fact that the appellant could have asserted his claim at the time the supplemental agreement was executed. The claim was not waived or abandoned by not being incorporated in the supplemental agreement. There was no requirement, contractual or otherwise, that the claim had to be in the supplemental agreement.

The delay in filing the claim did not prejudice the Government. Moreover, the appellant is seeking relief not under the Changes Clause, which was the authority for the supplemental agreement, but under the Suspension of Work provision. Unlike the Changes Clause, the Sus pension of Work provision contains no limit on when claims may be filed.

The Government relies on the appellant's proposal, which stated that the revision of the work would not require "extra construction costs." Suffice it to say that the appellant had in mind not the expenses caused by the Stop Work Order but only the construction costs directly related to the revised work. 

The claim is not barred by the fact that it was not formally filed until long after final payment. The acceptance of the final payment was not an accord and satisfaction of an unliquidated claim. The final check represented the liquidated balance due under the contract. The final voucher and payment were in no manner releases and certainly were not meant to encompass or bar a claim of the type involved here. Moreover, there is some evidence, although disputed by the Government, that the contracting officer who executed the contract and administered it for most of its duration knew about the appellant's idle equipment claim long before it was filed. The successor contracting officer confessed that a one-year suspension is "exceptional," that losses ensue from idle equipment, and that he knew there was the possibility of a claim arising out of the 

Stop Work Order. Under the circumstances, therefore, the appellant should not be precluded from asserting his claim. 

The finding, therefore, is that the Stop Work Order issued at the convenience of the Government for a partial cessation of the work for approximately one year unreasonably delayed the progress of the work and caused the appellant additional expenses or losses which should be reimbursed by an equitable adjustment in price. The unreasonable length of the suspension and the losses or expenses flowing therefrom were not due to the fault or negligence of the contractor. Since adequate extensions of time were granted, all that remains to be done is to decide the amount of loss or additional expense caused by the Stop Work Order. [The 

Board than examined the evidence and calculated the amount to be awarded.] 

Roten Constr. Co., ASBC ANo. 6268, 30 June 1961, 61-1 BCA 3093. [Note: Although it created a right to an equitable adjustment under certain circumstances, the Suspension of Work Clause in the contract involved in the instant case was silent as to whether or when a contractor was required to claim an adjustment. The current Air Force 

Suspension of Work Clause provides that an equitable adjustment will not be made unless the claim for it is "asserted in writing as soon as practicable after the termination of

4. Suspending Construction Work at Airbase During Lebanon Crisis Held To Have Been Not a Sovereign Act but a Contractual Act Entitling 

Contractor to Compensation Under Suspension of Work Clause-Definition Given of Term "Unreasonable" in Suspension of Work Clause. The 

Army Corps of Engineers awarded the appellant a fixed-price contract for the construction of aircraft fueling facilities at an Air Force SAC base. The contract contained the following clause:

SUSPENSION OF WORK.-The Contracting Offi cer may order the contractor to suspend all or any part of the work for such period of time as may be determined by him to be necessary or desirable for the convenience of the Government. Unless such suspension unreasonably delays the progress of the work and causes additional expense to the contractor, no increase in contract price will be allowed. In the case of suspension of all or any part of the work for an unreasonable length of time causing additional expense, not due to the fault or negligence of the contractor, the Contracting Officer shall make an adjustment in the contract price in the amount of the additional expense and modify the contract accordingly. An extension of time for the completion of the work in the event of any such suspension will be allowed the contractor; provided however, that the suspension was not due to the fault or negligence of the contractor.

Part of the contract work required the appellant to cut into the pavements of taxiways and parking areas at the base. The contract provided that the work was to be performed while military operations continued; the appellant was required to conduct work so as not to endanger contemplated military operations. On 

15 July 1958 the SAC placed the base on an alert status in connection with the dispatch of troops to Lebanon. The next day the Base 

Commander notified the contracting officer that any work involving the cutting of pavement of flight facilities was prohibited until further notice. The contracting officer notified the appellant of this order and confirmed the notice the next day in writing. The appellant promised compliance but pointed out that the delay would produce additional costs. The alert was lifted on 28 July. The next day the contracting officer wired the appellant, "Re suspension of work my letter 21 July, contract number DA-19-016-Eng-5804... you are hereby directed to resume full operation." The appellant was granted a sixteen-day time extension because of the alert. Holding that the suspension of work had been caused by sovereign acts of the Government, both the contracting officer and the Corps of Engineers 

Board of Contract Appeals denied the appel lant's claim for additional costs incurred be cause of the delay. Empire Gas Engineering Co., Eng. BCA No. 1854. An appeal was taken to the ASBCA. 

Held, appeal sustained. Both the appellant and the Government have assumed that the sovereign act doctrine is applicable to claims under the Suspension of Work Clause on the same basis as in court decisions in actions for breach of contract. The appeal will be considered on the basis that the sovereign act doctrine applies to claims under the Suspension of Work 

Clause. Citing Derecktor v. United States, 129 Ct. Cl. 103 (1954), and Stack, The Liability of the United States for Breach of Contract, 44 

Geo. L.J. 77 (1955), the Government contends that the purpose of the sovereign act doctrine is to prevent the United States from being hampered in performing sovereign functions by the apprehension of incurring liability to contractors for increased costs. The majority opinion in Derecktor does tend to support the Government's argument that the Government may with impunity violate the terms of its contracts whenever the national interest so requires. 

However, the case cannot be accepted as authority for that proposition because the Su AGO 9111A 269

SUSPENSION OF WORK-Continued preme Court granted certiorari (348 U.S. 926 (1955)) and the Government settled the case before the Court rendered any decision. [Certiorari was dismissed, 350 U.S. 802 (1956).] The

Derecktor case was virtually overruled by 

Miller v. United States, 135 Ct. Cl. 1, 140 

F. Supp. 789 (1956), where the opinion was written by a judge who dissented in Derecktor. 

He made this statement about the doctrine of Government privilege to violate its contracts with impunity when the national interest re quires: 

This is a privilege no sovereign enjoys except in a despotic society. It is abhorrent to the conscience of free men.

It cannot be tolerated under the laws or according to the morals of the American people. 

No rule of law immunizes the Government from liability for the consequences of an act solely on the ground that the act was necessary to protect the national interests or necessary to national security. Miller v. United States, supra.

Although the Government cannot contractually bind itself not to perform sovereign acts, it may by contract obligate itself to bear the consequences of its sovereign acts. Gerhardt F. 

Meyne Co. v. United States, 110 Ct. Cl. 527, 550 (1948); Sunswick Corp. v. United States, 109 

Ct. Cl. 772, 798 (1948). The Government may, by a suspension of work clause, contract to compensate a contractor for increased costs resulting from a suspension of work by a sovereign act. That this is true may be shown by another line of reasoning. The basic principle of the sovereign act doctrine is that the Government as a contractor should be treated, with respect to the effect of sovereign acts, like any private contractor. In determining what would have been the effect of the Government act if a private party were substituted for the Government in its contractual capacity, attention must be paid to the terms of the contract itself. 

The Suspension of Work Clause provides for price adjustment only where the suspension "unreasonably delays the progress of work... for an unreasonable length of time." The Government argues that the work suspension during the alert was reasonable in the sense that it was necessary for safety and did not remain in effect longer than the alert made necessary. 

However, the term "unreasonable" in the Sus pension of Work Clause does not relate to the necessity of suspending work or to the Government's purpose or motive. The proper test of unreasonableness is whether, in the absence of the clause, the work suspension violates a duty the Government owes the contractor. T. 

C. Bateson Constr. Co., ASBCA No. 5492 (16 

Mar 1960), 60-1 BCA 2552, on motion for reconsideration (30 Sep 1960), 60-2 BCA 2815.

The state of alert was not the normal military operation at the base. Therefore, in the absence of the Suspension of Work Clause, the Govern ment's suspending the work during the alert would have breached a duty not to interfere with the appellant's performance. 

The Government cannot escape contractual liability for the suspension on the ground that it was necessary to implement a military alert established to protect national security. The 

Government's argument that the suspension of work was caused by the SAC alert ordered on account of the Lebanon crisis confuses the reason for and purpose of the suspension with the act or order causing the suspension. See Baruch Corp. v. United States, 93 Ct. Cl. 107 (1947). In that case work was suspended to carry out a general program of reduction of expenditures. When he issued the suspension order, the contracting officer had no discretion in the matter but was merely carrying out instructions of higher authority. The court held the contractor was entitled to recover for the increased costs of performance incurred as a result of the contracting officer's order.

One of the tests most commonly applied by the Court of Claims for determining whether a Government act comes within the sovereign act doctrine is whether the act was that of the contracting agency. Compare Clemmer Constr. 

Co. v. United States, 108 Ct. Cl. 718 (1947), with Beuttas v. United States, 111 Ct. Cl. 

532 (1948). The circumstance that the act was by a Government agency insulated from the contracting agency is treated by the courts as a strong indication that the act was a sovereign act. That an act was by the contracting agency is regarded as evidence that it was not a soveriegn act. In no case has an order issued by a contracting officer directly to a contractor 270 AGO 9111A

TAXES 

been held to be a sovereign act. In the instant case the fact that the suspension of work order was in writing addressed to the contractor by name, referring to the contract by number, and signed by the contracting officer as contracting officer is almost conclusive proof that the order was (1) an act of the Government in its contractual capacity and (2) issued pursuant to the Government's right to suspend the work under the Suspension of Work Clause. 

Empire Gas Engineering Co., ASBCA No. 

7190, 15 March 1962, 62-1 BCA 3323.

4. Where the Government

Treats the Contract as Rescinded the Contractor Can Dispose of the Termination Inventory and Still Receive Termination Costs-Measure of Termination Costs is Difference Between Market Value of Lumber Prior To Being 

Processed Under the Contract and After Being 

So Processed Plus Processing and Settlement Costs. The Government contracted to purchase lumber from the contractor by contract award ed 4 June 1956. On 5 June 1956, the contractor proceeded to saw 21,420 board feet of relatively valuable select grade maple 6" thick and 6" wide or wider into pieces 3" thick and 4" thick, and to rip the same material into pieces exactly 6" wide. The resulting material was substantially less valuable because its possible uses had become more limited. On 6 June 1956, the 

Government notified the contractor that the material was no longer needed. By letter dated 

6 December 1956, the contracting officer took the position that the contract had been "rescinded" as of 6 June 1956. On 23 April 1958, the ASBCA held that the contract had been terminated, rather than rescinded, and that the contractor was entitled to be paid under the 

"Termination for Convenience of the Govern ment" clause of the contract. Prior to its successful appeal, the contractor, finding it financially impracticable to set the material aside and wait for the outcome of litigation, took the processed lumber out of storage and put it through its millwork plant in the normal course of its operations. The items thus manufactured AGO 9111A 271

TERMINATION-Continued from termination inventory were commingled with others and sold commercially. They are not indentified. The contractor essentially claims the difference between the dollar amount that the material would have brought on the market before processing under the contract and the market price of the material after having been sawed and ripped to smaller dimensions. The contracting officer denied this part of the claim on the ground that the contractor had disposed of the inventory contrary to the requirement of the Termination clause that title be transferred to the Government. 

Held, for the contractor. For approximately seventeen months the Government contended unequivocally that the contract had been rescinded. This unequivocal assertion of rescission destroyed all capacity of the Government, as the party disavowing its obligations, to assert rights under the contract afterward, because in this instance the contractor acted upon the disavowal during the interval that the Government adhered to it, and has credited the Government with the fair market price of the inventory disposed of. (See 12 Am. Jur., Contracts, § 382, p. 960.) Moreover, it is the policy of the Department of Defense that a termination settlement should compensate the contractor fairly for the work done and the preparations made for the terminated portions of the contract. (See ASPR 8-301 (a), Revised 

1 July 1960.) The contractor is entitled to the difference in market values of the lumber before and after processing for the contract, plus processing and settlement costs. The contractor is not entitled to litigation expenses for either appeal as they are costs of prosecuting claims against the United States. (See Reed 

& Prince Mfg. Co., ASBCA No. 3172 (17 Apr 

1959), 59-1 BCA 2172.)

The Maryland Lumber Co., ASBCA No. 5760, 28 March 1960, 60-1 BCA 2599. 

5. Recovery For Nonspecification Supplies As Termination Inventory Allowed. In March 1955, the Government entered into a fixed-price supply contract requiring the contractor's Georgia plant to manufacture 235,305 Air Force shirts from Government-furnished material. The contract contained the standard Termination for Convenience Clause, ASPR 8-701. De fective Government-furnished cloth for a trousers contract created difficulties at the Georgia plant, so the shirt contract was amended to allow production in another company's plant in Waco, Texas. A Waco bank provided financing secured by chattel mortgages on the shirts to be produced. The Government's failure to remedy the difficulties caused by the trousers contract so worsened the contractor's financial condition that the cooperation and management needed for the Waco production were not provided. More than 50,000 shirts were produced but rejected because samples inspected from each lot had more defects than allowed by the contract's Acceptable Quality Level. The inspection reports showed a continuous deficiency of poor workmanship and inadequate inspection by the contractor. They contained comments indicating that rejections were provisional and that the contractor was expected to rescreen or rework the shirts so they could be resubmitted.

After the bank learned of the rejections it stopped financing and took possession of the shirts. Having received information of this and the fact that the Waco plant had closed, the contracting officer sent the contractor a telegram on 28 October 1955 terminating the contract for default. Thereafter, the contracting officer conferred with the contractor to determine whether the contractor could rework the shirts at its Georgia plant. However, a survey of that plant disclosed that it did not have sufficient capacity, and the contract was formally terminated for default on 15 December 1955. 

The appeal from this decision was sustained and the termination was converted to one for the convenience of the Government on the grounds that the contractor's difficulties in performing the shirt contract arose from his weak financial condition caused by the Government's action of furnishing defective material for the trousers contract. The Douglas 

Corp., ASBCA Nos. 3349, 3741 (24 Apr 1958), 58-1 BCA 1727. On 2 December 1958 the con tractor submitted an Interim Settlement Proposal claiming the rejected shirts as termination inventory at the contract unit price.

The shirts were then in storage at a Govern- 272 AGO 9111A

TERMINATION-Continued 

1 ment installation pursuant to a court order. 

Subsequently, the court entered judgment that title to the shirts was in the Government. 

The contracting officer denied the claim for the reason that as the shirts did not conform to specifications and were irreparable, the costs incurred in their manufacture could not be considered allocable to the terminated portion of the contract. On appeal the position of the Government was that although the shirts would be retained because they were made of Government-furnished cloth, they would not be paid for since they failed to meet specifications. 

In support of its position the Government cited Chris Kaye Plastics Mfg. Co., ASBCA 

No. 3367 (26 Nov 1956), 56-2 BCA 1124, in which it was held that a termination for convenience created no right to recover for goods which would not have been paid for had the contract not been terminated. 

Held, the appeal is sustained. Chris Kaye

Plastics Mfg. Co. is not applicable to this appeal, for in that case it was not alleged either that failure of the supplies to comply with specifications was the Government's fault or that the supplies were serviceable or economically reparable. Moreover, no Government-furnished property was involved and the Government did not retain the nonspecification supplies. 

Appellant's entitlement to to compensation must be determined under the Termination for 

Convenience of the Government Clause. That clause gives the Government the right to require the contractor to transfer to the Government all completed and uncompleted supplies and work in process without reference to whether the supplies comply with specifications or are serviceable or are economically reparable, with payment for completed supplies to be at the contract price "appropriately adjusted.”

This language is broad enough to cover payment for acceptable nonspecification serviceable completed supplies at an equitable reduction in the contract unit price. All other work is to be paid for on the basis of costs incurred in its production. There is nothing in the language of the clause to distinguish between serviceable and unserviceable supplies or between reparable and irreparable supplies.

Similarly, the Statement of Principles for con sideration of costs set forth in Part 4 of Section 

VIII of ASPR, incorporated in this contract by reference (the current termination clause in corporates Section XV of ASPR) made no such distinction, and the only provision in such Statement of Principles that could be interpreted as making unallowable the costs of producing non-specification items is the general provision pertaining to reasonableness, generally accepted accounting principles and practices, and allowability. The board then notes that the problem of rejects as an allowable cost in a termination claim was dealt with by Termina tion Cost Memorandum No. 8 on Rejects issued by the Director of War Mobilization on 30 Sep tember 1944, as Appendix B of the joint Termination Regulations, page 2545. After examining that directive and noting that costs of producing defective work and costs of reworking rejects are normally reimbursable under a cost-reimbursement type contract unless it is established that the effective production resulted from the contractor's own fault or folly or careless conduct of the work or other disregard of his contractual duties, factors not proven against this contractor, the board concluded that there was no basis in fact, law, or accounting principles for disallowance of any of the costs incurred in the performance of the work terminated. In addition the board noted that pursuant to the definition contained in ASPR 8–101.25 and "Since the Government has taken possession of the shirts and is the legal owner therof, they must be included in the termination inventory." 

The board next considered whether the costs incurred should be reduced pursuant to the 

Termination Clause's provisions for "adjust ment for loss" [e (2)], property "undeliverable to the Government" [e (3)], and claims of the Government against the contractor [h]. Although it held a reduction should be made if an audit showed the contract would have produced a loss, the board held the other two provisions inapplicable because all the shirts were delivered and any obligation the contractor had to correct defective work ceased when the Government terminated the contract. Because of lack of evidence, the board was unable to determine whether the Government might have a AGO 9111A 273

TERMINATION-Continued claim for use of Government-furnished material in excess of allowances.

The Douglas Corporation, ASBCA No. 5550, 19 February 1960, 60-1 BCA 2531. [Note:

Corporation, ASBCA No. 3381 (6 Jun 1960), 60-1 BCA 2542, 2651, where the ASBCA allowed as termination inventory items which were non-specification because of the Government's fault and could not be reworked to meet specifications.]

7. It Is a Breach of Contract To Terminate for Default When Contractor Did Not Fail To Perform but Only Failed To Meet Delivery Date 

Waived by Government. In June 1951 the Corps of Engineers negotiated with the contractor a fixed-price contract requiring delivery of 1,000 lighting sets from 20 November through 22

April 1952. The contract contained the standard clauses for Termination for Convenience (now 

ASPR 8-701) and Default (now ASPR 8-707).

The contractor subcontracted the manufacture of a special cable required for the sets. By 20 

November 1951 none of the cable had been produced; two sample cables had been rejected by a Government testing laboratory. Between 

20 November 1951 and 9 February 1952, when a new sample cable was submitted for testing, the contracting officer took no steps to terminate the contract, and he issued several change orders and made plans for inspecting finished items. The cable sample submitted on February 9 failed to meet specifications, and another sample was submitted on February 26. On April 

1, more than a month before the laboratory report on the new sample was issued, the contracting officer terminated the contract under the Default clause for the contractor's failure to meet the delivery schedule. In the contractor's appeal from the default termination, the AS- BCA held: [I]t would seem reasonable to assume [in view of the contracting officer's activity in issuing change orders and making inspection plans after the delivery date passed] that having waived strict enforcement of the time elements of the contract, the contracting officer would at least have given appellant some reasonable indication. of an intent in the future to terminate the contract if the cable was not supplied from some other source. . . . Under the circumstances of this case we are of the opinion that the proper remedy was that of termination for the convenience of the Government, if termination, was desired. . . . Appellant's failure to live up to contract time of performance was quite obviously the result of the awaiting of tests, in which delay the Government was active in participating and which it accepted as an incident of performance. It was an excusable delay, and should not subject appellant to the liability of a default at least until the appellant had received a reasonable warning that the Government was not going to await the result of tests any longer. 

Beam Radionics Corp., ASBCA No. 1344 (1 Oct 

1953).

Pursuant to this decision, the contracting officer on 27 November 1953 notified the contractor that the Government deemed the termination had been one for the convenience of the Government. The contractor took the position that the termination had breached the contract, and he sued in the Court of Claims for his costs and lost profits.

Held, the plaintiff may recover. Not until after the ASBCA's decision did the contracting officer consider whether a termination for convenience was appropriate. If the contracting officer were put back in the situation he faced on 1 April 1952, with the benefit of the corrections made by the ASBCA, he would have difficulty deciding whether to terminate for convenience. He would have to consider additional facts, such as when the Government would be likely to obtain the needed sets if he cancelled the contract with the only firm subcontracting the cable development. It would require pure speculation to determine what the contracting officer would have done.

The Government cannot rely on paragraph (e) of the Default clause (now ASPR 8-707 (e)) to convert the termination for default to one for convenience. Paragraph (e), by its terms, applies only when there has been a failure to perform that is found to be excusable. 

Compare Telco Electronic Co., ASBCA No. 724 

(31 Jul 1951). In the instant case the ASBCA found that the contractor was not in default; that finding is well supported by the evidence. 

By its words and conduct, the Government ex- 274 AGO 9111A

TERMINATION-Continued tended the time for performance. Until the extra time elapsed, the contractor was not in default.

The cases the Government relies on are not persuasive. First, in College Point Boat Cor poration v. United States, 267 U.S. 12 (1925), it was held that the Act of 15 June 1917, 40 Stat. 

182, gave the President an absolute right to cancel shipbuilding contracts, providing just compensation was made. Here the Government has only the rights provided by the contract, not a right to cancel like that conferred by the 1917 statute. Second, this case does not resemble one where a valid reason for terminating a contract is discovered after the stated reason for the termination is held invalid. Here the Government has never presented any valid reason for the termination. Third, no weight can be given the ASBCA's statement that any termination desired should have been for convenience. The statement was dictum and obviously wrong. Fourth, The Commonwealth 

Engineering Company v. United States, 180 F. 

Supp. 396 (Ct. Cl. 1960) (cert. denied, 364 U.S. 

820 (1960)) is distinguishable. There the contracting officer had terminated for convenience, as he had the right to do in the circumstances of that case. The court's statement in that case that, even if the contractor were not in default, the Government could terminate for convenience under paragraph (e) (ASPR 8707 (e)), was dictum and erroneous. It would mean that the Government has an unqualified right to terminate every contract containing a provision like paragraph (e), a right which such contracts do not contemplate. 

Klein v. United States, 285 F. 2d 788 (Ct. Cl. 

1961). [Note: Chief Judge Jones dissented, giving two reasons for concluding that the contractor should recover no more than what he would receive in a settlement for a termination for convenience, including any damages for the delay in properly designating the termination. The first reason was that if the Government had the right to terminate for any reason, there was at most a mislabeling of the termination, not a breach of contract. He supported this contention by drawing analogies to: 1) cases where a party to a lawsuit proves more or less than he pleaded and then amends his pleadings to conform to the proof; 2) cases in the law of sales holding that stating an invalid reason for refusing a tendered performance does not preclude a later defense based on a valid reason. The 

Chief Judge argued that the Government could properly have terminated the contract for convenience in April 1952. He contended that the contractual rights of the Government in the instant case were scarcely less broad than the right to cancel given by the statute in the Col lege Point Boat case. The contract permitted termination in the "best interests of the Government," and, absent fraud or caprice, the contracting officer's determination of those interests should be conclusive. The Chief

Judge's review of the evidence convinced him that the contract could properly have been terminated for convenience. 

The second reason for the Chief Judge's dissent was that paragraph (e) of the Default clause could be applied to convert the termination to one for convenience. He conceded the majority's argument that paragraph (e) applies only to excusable failures, but he contended that the contractor had failed to deliver the lighting sets on time. He based his contention on the fact that the Government had never extended the delivery dates by contract modifications. Even though he decided that the 

Government's delay in testing the cable samples excused the contractor's failure, he concluded that the contractor's delay should not be equated to full performance by allowing recovery of all lost profits.]
