15. Partial Payments to Government Construction Contractor at Contract Unit Price for Completed Items Do Not Entitle Contractor to Compensation at Such Prices When Contract Is 

Subsequently Terminated for Government's 

Convenience; Compensation To Be Determined Under the Convenience Clause on the Basis of 

"Cost of Such Work." A quarter of a million dollar construction contract was terminated for the convenience of the Government after the contractor had completed items 1, 2 and 3 of the "contract payment items" (removal of old paving and performing certain excavation).

Before the termination the contractor had received progress payments on these items amounting to about $26,000. After termination. but before he had submitted his settlement proposal, he received about $8,700, which represented the balance due for these items, computed at the stated unit prices minus $100 that was withheld pending final settlement. After three years of unsuccessful negotiations on the termination settlement, the contracting officer unilaterally determined that the contractor was entitled to some $19,000, which-when subtracted from the amount already paid him-left him indebted to the Government for about $16,000. The contracting officer, in making his computations, relied on that portion of paragraph (e) of the Termination for Convenience Clause that provides that upon the failure of the parties to agree to a settlement, the contracting officer shall pay the contractor the amount unilaterally determined to be due the contractor as follows: 

(1) In respect of all contract work performed prior to the effective date of the Notice of 

Termination, the total . . . of- 

(i) the cost of such work; (ii) the cost of settling and paying claims .; and 

[Emphasis added.] The contractor appealed from this determination, arguing that his right to payment for completed items at the contract unit price was established by the Government's acceptance of those items, as evidenced by its payment of the full price therefor (less $100). He argued, further, that such right could not be abrogated by the application of the Termination for Convenience Clause.

Held, the contractor is not entitled to payment for completed items without regard to costs incurred. The application of the "cost of such work" limitation of the termination clause is not limited or precluded by any language in the contract nor by any actions of the Government. The contract is one for a completed project; it is not one for the performance of individual and separable items of work. This is the clear import of the clauses entitled "State ment of Work," "DESCRIPTION OF WORK" and "SCOPE OF WORK." Furthermore, paragraph (d) of General Provision 7 (SF 23A), entitled "PAYMENTS TO CONTRACTORS," 

contemplates final acceptance of the project as a completed unit rather than by individual units of work.

Next to be considered is the effect on the rights of the parties of the progress payments made pursuant to General Provision 7 (SF 23A, 

Mar. 1953 ed.), which provides in part: 276 AGO 9111A

TERMINATION-Continued 

(a) Unless otherwise provided in the specifications, partial payments will be made as the work progresses at the end of each calender month, . 

(b) In making such partial payments there shall be retained 10 percent of the estimated amount until final completion and acceptance of all work covered by the contract: . . . provided . . . That on completion and acceptance of each separate building, public work, or other division of the contract, on which the price is stated separately in the contract, payment may be made in full, including retained percentages thereon, less authorized deductions. (c) All material and work covered by partial payments made thereupon shall become the sole property of the Government, but this provision shall not be construed as relieving the Contractor from the sole responsibility for all materials and work upon which payments have been made or the restoration of any damaged work, or as a waiver of the right of the Government to require the ful fillment of the terms of the contract. [Emphasis added by the Board.] 

Nothing in the above paragraphs, or elsewhere in the contract, justifies a conclusion that the parties contemplated that the making of a 100% payment on any individual payment item would constitute a final acceptance of that item of work without regard to any rights reserved to the respective parties by other clauses of the contract. Paragraph (c) specifically negates any such result and saves for applicability the provisions of the Termination for Convenience Clause. 

The Termination for Convenience Clause in construction contracts limits the contractor to entitlement to compensation for all work done under the contract on the basis of costs incurred with an allowance for profit thereon. In this respect the clause differs from that common to fixed-price supply contracts, pursuant to which compensation for completed and accepted supplies is based on the contract unit price. This difference in method of computation is explained by the fact that bidders on construction contracts have an opportunity to charge proportionately more profit and overhead to items that will be paid for early in the contract. The construction contract termination clause removes any advantage that would otherwise accrue to the maker of an unbalanced bid in the event of termination.

George Chica Company, Eng. BCA No. 1914, 7 November 1961. 

16. Subcontractor's "Standby Costs" Compensable Under Termination for Convenience Settlement Procedures So Long As Government Payment Thereof Is Necessary Fairly To Compensate for Work Done and Preparation Made on Terminated Portion of Contract. Four Gov ernment contracts with the same company were terminated for convenience on 25 March 1957. 

On 11 July 1960 a final supplemental agreement was entered into which, besides providing for a lump sum payment by the Government, reserved the rights and liabilities of the parties with respect to two items. One of these items was the contractor's claim in behalf of a subcontractor for about $280,000 which represented expenses of operation during a standby period from 1 September 1955 to 31 March 1957. This item had been denied because the contracting officer considered it not to be "within the purview of the Termination for Convenience article of the contract." The contractor submitted to the Comptroller General a claim for $232,450 of the disputed item. The contracting officer stated in a report that, in his opinion, this amount was reasonable and should be paid.

Held, nothing in the contract or in the applicable provisions of ASPR indicates that "standby costs" are to be included in or excluded from determinations of the compensation due a contractor when the Government exercises its contractual right to terminate a contract for convenience. 

There is no reason why "standby costs" actually incurred and attributable to performance prior to termination for convenience may not be included in a settlement agreement. The test is whether payment of those costs by the Government is necessary fairly to compensate the contractor for work done and preparations made for the terminated portion of the contract (ASPR 8-301). Whether and to what extent the claimed costs meet that test are matters for determination in the first instance by the contracting officer. [The file was forwarded to the Department of the Army with a recommendation that it be AGO 9111A 277

TERMINATION—Continued returned to the contracting officer for his determination and his compliance with specified procedural requirements (ASPR 8-209.2 and 8-211).] 

Ms. Comp. Gen B-128375, 5 December 1961, 41 Comp. Gen. 379.

"standby costs" are properly compensable under the termination for convenience procedures in a case in which there was no indication that the contract contained a Suspension of Work 

Clause. L. P. Kooken Co., ASBCA No. 2091 (14

Comptroller General Rules That Contracting Agency Is Primarily Responsible for Deter mining Whether Negotiated Contract Should Be Terminated for Convenience and Reawarded to 

Firm That Would Have Received Contract if Erroneous Determination on Ability To Per form Had Not Been Made. A negotiated contract for overhauling engines was awarded to the C Co. after the contracting officer decided that the A Co., which had offered a lower price, could not perform the terms of its offer. The 

A Co. protested, and the C Co. was issued a stop work order. The protest was found to be justified. It was administratively estimated that the C Co. had incurred only nominal expenses. However, in view of the cost of shipping the engines from the C Co. to the A Co., the cost of termination and reaward would exceed by $5,855 the difference between the prices of the two firms. Nevertheless, the contracting officer and counsel for the procuring activity recommended that the C Co.'s contract be terminated for convenience and award made to the A Co. The Comptroller General was asked to rule on the propriety of the recommended action. 

Held, the recommended action may be taken.

Whether contracts may be terminated for the convenience of the Government depends upon whether such action is in the best interest of the 

Government. Determination of the public interest in cases like the present is primarily a meter for the administrative agency. 34

Comp. Gen. 74, 76 (1954); 18 Comp. Gen. 

826, 828 (1939). Therefore, and in view of the facts involved here, no objection will be made if the C Co.'s contract is terminated for convenience and award is made to the A Co. on the basis of a determination that such action is in the Government's best interests. 

Ms. Comp. Gen. B-147579, 27 November 

1961. 

19. Recovery Allowed for Costs of Producing Nonreworkable, Nonspecification Items That Government Rejected Contractor Permitted To Have Termination Claim Considered on Total Cost Rather Than Inventory Basis Even Though Contracting Officer Had Not Given Advance Approval-Contractor's Letter Termed 

Adequate as Notice of Appeal Even Though Inexpertly Worded and Not Addressed to Sec retary of Department or ASBCA. The C Co.'s fixed-price Army contract for the supply of 83,000 wrenches was terminated for default after 23,392 wrenches had been produced. Only 

1,600 wrenches had been accepted; the others had been rejected for failure to meet specifications. The ASBCA held that the termination 278 AGO 9111A

TERMINATION-Continued 

"│“! should be deemed to have been made for the convenience of the Government. Caskel Forge, Inc., ASBCA No. 6028 (22 Aug 1960), 60–2

BCA 2718. The C Co. filed a termination claim in letter form on a total cost basis. The Government then furnished forms for a settlement claim on an inventory basis. The C Co.'s claim as resubmitted on those forms was in the same amount as originally filed and was in practical effect on a total cost basis. The claim sought compensation for the 21,792 wrenches that had been rejected and that the contractor apparently conceded were nonspecification and not economically reworkable. Within thirty days. after receiving the contracting officer's final decision denying most of the claim, the C Co. sent a letter to "Department of the Army, Chicago 

Ordnance District . . .," stating that the contracting officer's decision was "completely un acceptable." Before the ASBCA the Govern ment argued that (1) the C Co.'s letter was insufficient to serve as a notice of appeal, (2) the firm's proposal should have been on an inventory rather than a total cost basis, and (3) no compensation should be given for the cost of the rejected wrenches.

Held, the letter was adequate to take an appeal, and the appeal is sustained. First, the officer of the firm who signed the letter was not familiar with the disputes procedure. There is no significance to the fact that the letter was addressed as it was instead of to the Secretary of the Army or the ASBCA. The contracting officer's decision stated that any notice of appeal "must be sent to the contracting officer," and the letter was timely sent to him. The letter indicated dissatisfaction with the decision and evinced an intent to "go over the head" of the contracting officer to obtain relief from his final decision. While not in correct legal phrasing, the letter was sufficient as a notice of appeal. 

Second, under ASPR 8-307.2 the inventory basis is "preferred," while the total cost basis may be used when "approved in advance by the contracting officer" and when the inventory basis is not practicable or will unduly delay settlement. That ASPR provision is not part of the contract and is not binding on the C Co. 

So far as this appeal is concerned, the only significant difference between settlements on the two bases is that the inventory basis involves the task of dividing the contractor's performance costs between the 1,600 accepted wrenches and the rest of the work. That task, which is avoided by the total cost basis, is made impossible by the condition of the C Co.'s records, which, while ordinarily adequate for such a small concern, are inadequate for preparing a termination claim on the inventory basis. Since the nature of the firm's records makes use of the inventory basis impracticable, the termination claim should be considered on a total cost basis. As pointed out in The Doug las Corporation, ASBCA No. 5550 (19 Feb. 

1960), 60-1 BCA 2531 [digested under TER- MINATION, par. 5] the inventory and total cost bases are only methods and should produce the same result. Moreover, whether the contractor may be reimbursed for the costs of producing the rejected wrenches depends in no way on which basis is used. 

Third, in the Douglas case cited above, the

Board concluded that the standard Termination for the Convenience of the Government Clause and applicable regulations provide no basis for disallowing reasonable costs of producing nonspecification, economically reworkable supplies. 

The Board indicated that the general effect of the Termination Clause is to convert the terminated portion of a contract into a cost reimbursement contract and to provide for allowance of all costs incurred in performance of the terminated portion. In Atlas Can Corp., ASBCA No. 3381 (6 June 1960), 60-1 BCA 

2651, the principle of Douglas was extended to nonreworkable rejects. The Government correctly argues that in Atlas Can, unlike the instant case, the failure of the nonreworkable rejects to meet the specifications was the Government's fault. However, the failure of the rejects in Douglas to meet specifications was not the Government's fault. There is no basis in the contract for distinguishing between reworkable rejects and nonreworkable ones or between cases where the Government is and cases where it is not the cause of the failure to meet specifications. 

The Government argues for application of the principle in Chris Kaye Plastics Manu- AGO 9111A 279

TRANSPORTATION 

facturing Co., ASBCA No. 3667 (26 Nov. 

1956), 56-2 BCA 1124, where costs of producing nonreworkable rejects were disallowed on the broad ground that "appellant should not be allowed costs for accomplishing a nonspecified result." In Douglas, Chris Kaye was distinguished on four grounds, one of them that the rejects in the latter case were nonreworkable. Atlas Can distinguished Chris Kaye on the grounds that in the latter case the failure to meet specifications was not shown to be the Government's fault and there was no proof that the costs of producing the rejects were reasonably incurred.

The broad principle of Chris Kaye Plastics is unsound and should be overruled. The result in that case appears to be based on the unproved assumption that, if the contract had not been terminated for convenience, the contractor would not have been permitted to recover for nonspecification items. Although a fixed-price contractor is not paid for nonspecification goods as such, ordinarily the contract price is adequate to enable him to recover all his costs of performance, including the costs for rejects generated in performing. Termination of the contract for the convenience of the Government deprives the contractor of the opportunity to recoup the expense of excessive rejects in the early stages of performance.

The costs of the C Co.'s production of the rejected wrenches are allowable only if they were reasonable. The number rejected was far greater than normal spoilage and what could be accounted for as legitimate starting load losses. Under the special circumstances of this case, the costs of producing the rejected wrenches were not the result of the C Co.'s fault or folly or careless conduct of the work or other disregard of its contractual duties. The 

Board found in the earlier appeal that the firm had erred in beginning production with oversized stock, but the concern felt compelled to proceed with that stock because of a belief, induced by the Government, that the wrenches were urgently needed and were wanted even though not meeting the specifications. Most of the rejected wrenches had been produced while the C Co. was awaiting a decision on its request for approval of a deviation from the specified tolerances. The Government had encouraged submission of that request. Neither the 1,600 accepted nor the 21,792 rejected wrenches met the specifications, although all the wrenches were usable for the intended purpose. 

Caskel Forge, Inc., ASBCA No. 7638, 14 March 1962, 1962 BCA 3318. 

[Note: In Power Generators, Inc., ASBCA 

No. 7607 (20 April 1962), 1962 BCA 3358, the

Board considered an appeal from a settlement proposed by the contracting officer after the Board had earlier held that the default termination of the fixed-price contract had been premature and thus should be deemed to have been for the convenience of the Government. The appeal involved $19,000 incurred by the contractor in attempting to repair a defective item. 

The Government had not directed the repair but apparently was willing to allow the sum in the termination settlement. The contractor wanted the sum allowed as a cost but left out of the calculations used in reducing the settlement to adjust for the indicated rate of loss by the contractor. In July 1960 the appellant was awarded a contract for the services, "As per schedule for the period beginning 1 August 1960 and ending 30

The total quantities specified herein are estimates only. The amounts which the Contractor may be required to furnish and the Government to accept hereunder shall be the amounts which shall from time to time be ordered hereunder by the Government during the ordering period of this contract. 

In any event, however, the Government shall order supplies (or services) hereunder having an aggregate value at the unit prices specified herein of not less than $100.00; and the Government shall be entitled to order and the Contractor shall be required to furnish supplies (or services) hereunder amounting to not more than the total estimated quantities set forth herein. If the Government orders and the Contractor furnishes more than the foregoing maximum amount, the total quantity ordered and furnished shall be treated for all purposes as having been ordered and furnished under the terms of this contract and payment therefor shall be made at the unit contract price or prices.

The appellant performed the contract until 21 October 1960, when he was orally advised by the Government that he would not print future issues. Subsequent issues were printed, but by someone other than the appellant. Apparently the Government ordered no services from the appellant after 21 October 1960. The appellant then claimed $5,713.59 on the grounds that the cancellation left him in possession of excess inventory and that he had incurred reasonable and necessary costs in connection with the contract. The contracting officer denied the claim for the reason that the Government's only obligation under the contract was to order at least $100 of services and materials. The contractor timely appealed to the ASBCA. 

Held, appeal sustained and case remanded to contracting officer. No reasonable or prudent person could have understood the contract to be for anything other than weekly delivery of the Shipworker from 1 August 1960 through 30

June 1961, provided the Government needed AGO 9111A 281

TYPES OF CONTRACTS (Indefinite Quantity, Indefinite Delivery) 

the newspaper printed during that period. If the need were eliminated before 30 June 1961, the Government's duties were to be discharged through the Indefinite Quantities Clause. There is nothing in the contract giving the Government the privilege arbitrarily to have the newspaper printed by someone other than the appellant during the contract period. Appellant had the right to expect its services would be required until the expiration date, unless just cause for placing the business elsewhere were shown. The Government advances no justification. When the Government without appropriate reasons ceased having the appellant publish the Shipworker, the contract was terminated for the Government's convenience. Under the circumstances, the parties' rights are gov erned by the Termination for Convenience 

Clause, and the contracting officer should take appropriate action.

Neil A. Goldwasser d/b/a Century Offset 

Company, ASBCA No. 7027, 11 August 1961, 61-2 BCA 3124. 

TYPES OF CONTRACTS (Indefinite Quantity, Indefinite Delivery) 1. Where Maintenance and Repair Contract Established Only Estimated Quantities and Provided That Delivery Orders Would Be Used To Request Specific Work, Delivery Order Held To Establish Contractural Rights That Could Be Altered Only Pursuant to Changes Clause. The appellant's Air Force contract to provide maintenance and repair at a base established a price of four cents per square foot for painting an estimated 1,862,000 square feet of housing. Delivery orders were to be issued when work was needed. 

The contracting officer issued an order for two coats of interior painting on 252,000 square feet at eight cents per square foot. Before any paint was applied, the contracting officer decided that only one coat was needed, so he modified the delivery order accordingly. The appellant timely claimed an equitable adjustment under the stand ard Changes Clause of the contract. The claims sought compensation for such items as materials, freight, handling, engineering, overhead, and extra travel while converting two coats to one. The contracting officer denied the claim, relying on a special provision that stated:

In the event that the requirements of the Government establishment issuing this contract for the supplies and services described herein do not materialize in the quantities specified as either 'estimated' or 'maximum' in the schedule, such failure shall not constitute grounds for equitable adjustment under this contract, except as may be specifically provided in the schedule. 

The appellant appealed to the ASBCA, maintaining that after the quantity was fixed in the delivery order the quantity was no longer an estimated requirement covered by the special provision. 

Held, appeal allowed. It makes little difference whether the initial delivery order irrevocably established the Government's objective requirements as two coats or whether those requirements were effectively changed by the amendment. The important fact is that contractual rights were established by the delivery order. Only under the 

Changes Clause did the contracting officer have authority to amend the order. The appellant has a valid claim under the Changes Clause to the extent he experienced increased costs because of the amendment of the delivery order. 

Marinell & Campbell, Inc., ASBCA No. 6550, 31 January 1961, 61-1 BCA 2935. 

TYPES OF CONTRACTS (Purchase Order) 1. SF 44 Purchase Order Not for Use as Delivery Order Against Indefinite Delivery Type Contract. DCSLOG requested an opinion as to whether SF 44 (purchase order-invoice-voucher) could be used as a delivery order under indefinite quantity contracts. The use of that form in utility service contracts had been questioned by the 

Finance Officer at Headquarters, Third U.S. 

Army, since there was no space on the form for the inclusion of information required by AR 420-41, par. 11 (30 Apr 1958). [This AR provided that, in utility contracts, "(T)he delivery order or invoice will show the various quantities and unit prices with any adjustments such as for fuel cost, power factor, credits, and discounts, making up the total billing."] Further, APP 3-605.50d (3) (1 Nov. 

1957), which authorizes the use of SF 44 to place delivery orders against indefinite delivery type contracts, appeared to deviate from the Armed 

Services Procurement Regulations. 

Opinion: SF 44 was neither designed for use as a delivery order under indefinite quantity contracts, nor is such use authorized by ASPR. DD 282 AGO 9111A

TYPES OF CONTRACTS (Purchase Order)-Continued 

Form 1155 is the only form which is specifically designated and authorized for use as a delivery order. ASPR 16-303.2(d) (14 May 1958). ASPR 

3-605 (27 Feb 1957) prescribes that SF 44 shall be used for small purchases only where four conditions are met: the transaction does not exceed $2,500, the supplies or services are immediately available from the local trade area, one delivery and one payment will be made, and its use is more economical and efficient than other small purchase methods. See also, ASPR 16-302 (14 May 1958) (SF 44 shall be used as prescribed by ASPR 

3-605). The Federal Procurement Regulations accord similar treatment to SF 44. See FPR 

1-3,605.1; FPR 1-16.301-2. The conclusion is, therefore, that the APP's authorization of SF 44 for use as a delivery order against an indefinite quantity contract conflicts with ASPR. Further, because of the requirements of AR 420-41, par. 11, the form is not designed or intended for use in indefinite delivery type contracts.

JAGT 1959/7733, 23 December 1959. 

2. DD Form 1155, Purchase Order, Is an Offer Looking Forward to Unilateral Contract, and No Binding Contract Exists Until Offeree Performs 

Exact Act Requested. In response to price quotations received from a supplier, Raritan Arsenal issued the following purchase order on DD Form 

1155: "In accordance with your (quotation) please furnish (paint) on the terms specified on both sides of this order and on the attached sheets, if any, including delivery as indicated." The supplier delivered paint which was rejected for not conforming to the specifications. Excess costs were incurred in a subsequent repurchase action and DCSLOG requested an opinion as to whether they could be legally assessed against the supplier. 

Opinion: The excess costs may not be charged to the supplier. The purchase order was an offer to the supplier rather than an acceptance of a price quotation. JAGT 1960/5827, 10 February 1960.

If the offer looked forward to a bilateral contract, i.e., a promise by the offeree to perform, the supplier's tendered but rejected performance was an acceptance which created a contract. If the offer looked forward to a unilateral contract, i.e., actual performance rather than a promise to perform, the supplier's tendered but rejected performance did not create a contract since it was not the exact act requested by the Government's offer. 

See 1 Williston, Contracts § 71 (3d ed. 1957);

Restatement, Contracts §§ 12, 59. This distinction is important because the Government's right to excess costs is predicated upon the supplier's failure to perform a binding contract. Where an offer looks forward to a unilateral contract, the offeree's partial or defective performance does not amount to an acceptance which creates an obligation to complete performance. Northampton Inst. for 

Savings v. Putnam, 331 Mass. 1, 45 N.E. 2d 936 (1943). I Williston, Contracts § 60 (3d ed. 1957);

Restatement, Contracts § 45, comment b. At best, the tendered performance makes the offer irrevo cable, 1 Corbin, Contracts § 52 (1950), or consti tutes a counteroffer which the Government must accept to create a contract. See JAGT 1959/5739, 14 September 1959. Thus, if the supplier has no obligation to perform, a breach of contract is impossible and the assessment of excess costs is not legally justified. 

Does DD Form 1155 look forward to a unilateral contract? The language clearly requests an act as performance. Even so, a bilateral contract is contemplated if the offeror expects a return promise and the offeree so understands. Corbin, Contracts 

§ 70 (1950). See Restatement, Contracts § 60 

(courts, whenever possible, will find bilateral contract to protect parties). Yet ASPR 16-303.1(a) (ii) authorizes the use of an alternate purchase order form, DD Form 1155s, where it is "deemed to be in the best interest of the Government to consumate a binding contract between the parties before the contractor undertakes performance." 

In view of the failure to use the alternate form and the wording of the form actually employed, it is concluded that the Government made an offer which looked forward to a unilateral contract. The supplier's defective performance, therefore, was not that act bargained for by the Government and amounted to a counteroffer which was rejected. 

Consequently, a contract was never created and the excess costs cannot be legally assessed against the supplier. 

JAGT 1960/6146, 14 April 1960. 

3. ASBCA Reviews Propriety of Default Termination of DD Form 1155 Purchase Order Which Did Not Contain Default Clause. (ASBCA) See DISPUTES (par. 19) 

AGO 9111A 283

TYPES OF CONTRACTS (Requirements) 

1. Plaintiff May Recover for Breach of Requirements Contract That Did Not Compel the Government To Assign Requirements to Him. 

The plaintiff and three other firms had similar 

GSA Federal Supply Schedule contracts for type writer servicing in the San Diego area. The contracts provided for listing the firms in a Federal 

Supply Schedule distributed to Government agencies in the area. Although certain agencies were required to assign their service requirements to listed firms, no particular order in choosing from the schedule was prescribed. Other agencies were given the option of using firms on the schedule. 

The contractors were obligated to accept work from the agencies that were required to use listed firms. After the plaintiff, the low bidder on the list, received business for several months under his contract, the contracting officer terminated the contract for default and had plaintiffs' name striken from the schedule. The contractors remaining on the schedule continued to receive business under their contracts. On plaintiff's appeal, the GSA Board of Review held the contract was terminated without proper cause, but denied compensation for lost profits, defamation of character, and loss of other business. The plaintiff then sued in the Court of Claims for damages for the improper termination. The Government's motion to dismiss the complaint for failure to state a cause of action was based on two contentions: 1) the contract was a requirements contract and neither guaranteed that any minimum requirement would exist nor compelled the Government to assign any requirements to the plaintiff; 2) any damages suffered were too speculative to permit of proof. 

Held, the plaintiff may recover, but the trial commissioner must determine certain facts on which the amount of recovery depends. It is well settled that requirements contracts are enforceable because there is a reasonable expectation by both parties that there will be requirements. See, e.g.,

Ready-Mix Concrete Co. v. United States, 131 Ct. 

Cl. 204, 130 F. Supp. 390 (1955). Since the plaintiff in the past received nearly all his business under Government contracts similar to the one involved in this suit, it is unbelievable that the wrongfully terminated contract gave the plaintiff only the right to have his name printed in the supply schedule. Being listed created a reasonable probability that business would be obtained, particularly since the plaintiff was the low bidder among the firms originally listed. Although the contract did not prevent the Government from enlarging its own repair facilities to meet its needs, the record shows the Government did have more service requirements than it could handle. Presumably these requirements were awarded to listed contractors. Plaintiff's chance to obtain some of these awards by being on the schedule and competing with other listed contractors had value in a business sense. The Government's breach deprived the plaintiff of this value, for which he paid valuable consideration. The case of Zephyr Aircraft Corp. 

v. United States, 122 Ct. Cl. 523, 104 F. Supp. 990 (1952), cert. denied, 344 U.S. 878 (1952), is distinguishable, for there the plaintiff never had any chance to obtain business. Here the plaintiff had the chance to obtain at least one-fourth of the business let by the Government. Several occurrences might have disappointed plaintiff's reasonable expectations, but the value of his chance for profit was not outweighed by a countervailing risk of loss.

The amount of damages may not be certain, but recovery should be allowed if a fair and reasonable approximation can be made. See e.g., Stern v.

Dunlap Co., 228 F. 2d 939 (10th Cir. 1955). The trial commissioner must determine: 1) the total amount of business for which plaintiff would have been eligible save for the breach; 2) whether any material facts would have tended to prevent the plaintiff from receiving his proportionate share of such business; 3) the average per unit cost normally incurred in the type of work involved; 4) the plaintiff's expenses, other than the cost of bidding, in preparing to fulfill his obligation. 

Locke v. United States, 283 F. 2d 521 (Ct. Cl. 

1960). 

2. Decrease in Quantity Ordered From Quantity Estimated in Requirements Contract Is Not a Compensable Change. The Air Force advertised for bids for operating mess halls and other food services at an air base. The contractor was to furnish only personnel and management. The major item in the invitation was an annual meal 284 AGO 9111A

TYPES OF CONTRACTS (Time and Materials) 

​胥 ​requirement of 1,060,000 meals. Bidders were required to bid on a per meal basis. There was no provision for renegotiating the contract price in case of a substantial reduction in the number of meals required. The following Estimated Quanti ties Clause was included:

The amount of supplies and services which will be required during the period covered by this contract will depend upon the needs of the Government establishment issuing this contract. Quantities of supplies and services specified herein are based on the best information available as to those requirements, but are not definitely purchased hereby. 

Notwithstanding the foregoing, the Contractor agrees to furnish at the prices herein specified all supplies and services of the kind herein described which the Contracting Officer may call for during the above-mentioned period and the Government will call on the Contractor for all such supplies and services which the Government establishment issuing this contract may require during such period. 

The appellant protested the method of pricing on the ground that the cost of operation would be relatively fixed and would not vary with the number of meals served. However, the appellant was finally awarded the contract at a fixed-price per meal. Before performance began a supplemental agreement reduced the contract period to eleven months and the estimated meal requirement to 971,666; the price per meal was not changed. Only about 761,000 meals were actually served during the contract period. The decrease was largely due to a drop in the number of personnel at the air base. The appellant contended that the decrease was caused by a reduction in the training program at the base, a reduction that the Air Force knew, long before executing the contract, would occur. The appellant claimed he was entitled to an equitable adjustment for a change. 

He appealed to the ASBCA from a denial of his claim. 

Held, appeal denied. It is clear from the Estimated Quantities Clause that the agreement was a requirements contract, so the Government's only obligation was to order services as required. 

Shader Contractors, Inc., ASBCA Nos. 3957 and 

4276, 8 Jan. 1958, 58-1 BCA 1579, [digested under 

REQUIREMENTS CONTRACTS, par. 1]. The appellant relies heavily on H. L. Yoh Co. v. 

United States, 288 F. 2d 493 (Ct. Cl. 1961) 

[digested under TYPES OF CONTRACTS (TIME AND MATERIALS), par. 1], which held the Government liable for increased overhead costs resulting from a substantial decrease in the volume of work. However, the contract involved in Yoh had no provision similar to the Estimated 

Quantities Clause in the appellant's contract. The purpose of the Estimated Quantities Clause is to relieve the Government of any obligation for increased unit costs resulting from a decrease in orders. Appellant recognized that fact by protesting that the pricing method was unrealistic. 

Even if it is assumed, arguendo, that the Government misstated a material fact to the appellant before the contract was executed, the Board is powerless to provide equitable relief. 

Beiser Aviation Corp., ASBCA No. 6215, 21 

September 1961, 61-2 BCA 3155. 

TYPES OF CONTRACTS (Time and Materials) 1. Contractor May Recover Increased Overhead Expenses Caused by Reduction in Volume of Work From Government Figure Relied on by Contractor in Forecasting His Overhead Rate- Claim Under Changes Clause Not Submitted Within 30 Days of Receipt of Notice of Change Was Timely Because It Was Filed Within 30 Days After the Fact That the Change Would Substantially Decrease the Volume of Work Became Clear-Court of Claims May Hear Case Based on Theory Different From That Advanced Before ASBCA. The Army negotiated a contract with the plaintiff for the conversion of automotive drawings and parts lists maintained at the Detroit Arsenal. 

The contract contained a Changes Clause identical to that in ASPR 7-103.2. A time and materials contract had been used because the number of drawings and parts lists was not known and obtaining an accurate estimate would have been prohibitively expensive. When the contract had been signed, the Government had contemplated that the project would include all automotive drawings and parts lists at the arsenal. It was later discovered that many drawings were obsolete and would not need conversion. The contracting officer, therefore, changed the program to one of only partial conversion. The contract had provided for a maximum of $5,000,000 to be spent on the project, but only $3,371,980 was spent. The plaintiff claimed his overhead expenses were proportionately increased as the expenditure on the AGO 9111A 285

TYPES OF CONTRACTS (Time and Materials)-Continued project was reduced. Before the contract had been awarded, his overhead rate for nonproduction personnel had been 32%. Relying on the Government's representation about the volume of work the contract entailed, he had calculated an overhead rate of 25.97% for the contract. He claimed that the 25.97% rate, which had been fixed in the contract, should be changed. The contracting officer and the ASBCA successively denied the claim. The plaintiff then sued in the Court of 

Claims. He introduced no evidence to show that he lost money in performing the contract or that the allowance of 25.97% for overhead failed to cover his actual overhead expenses. 

Held, the plaintiff may recover. While admitting that it benefitted by accepting a bid with an overhead rate under 32%, the Government contends the plaintiff is bound by the contract rate. The Government, of course, might not have accepted the plaintiff's bid had it contained a 32% rate, but that fact is not important. The only issue is whether the Government is liable when it unilaterally made a work reduction that resulted in increased costs to the contractor. The court has previously held the Government liable for the increased costs caused when there was a change from the estimated volume given a contractor as a basis for bid computation. Fehlhaber Corporation v. 

United States, 138 Ct. Cl. 571, 584 (1957), cert denied, 355 U.S. 877 (1957). A case with facts more similar to those in this case was Peter 

Kiewit Sons' Co. v. United States, 109 Ct. Cl. 517 (1947). There the plaintiffs were to obtain fill from three areas in different amounts: 700,000 cubic yards from area one, 1,600,000 cubic yards from area two, and 2,300,000 cubic yards from area three. The plaintiffs prepared their estimate on those volumes, with a different unit price for each area. The prices computed were 31.392, 52.23, and 29.77 cents per cubic yard for areas one, two, and three, respectively. The plaintiffs were then told to submit a composite bid for the three areas. They computed a weighted average and arrived at a price of 37.476 cents per cubic yard.

While the work was being performed, the Government notified the plaintiffs that the amount of fill from area three would be reduced by 750,000 cubic yards. The plaintiff complained that the reduction would increase their unit costs. The court allowed the plaintiffs an equitable adjustment. In the instant case the Changes Clause clearly authorized the Government to make the reduction in volume. 

However, payment must be made for the increased costs caused by the reduction. There is no merit to the Government's defense that the plaintiff cannot recover because he failed to prove he sustained a loss. A contractor may suffer damage by having his profit reduced as well as by sustaining a loss. There will be future proceedings to determine the amount of the plaintiff's recovery.

The Government contended that the plaintiff is barred from recovering because he failed to present his claim to the contracting officer within the 

30-day period established by the Changes Clause. 

However, even though the plaintiff did not file his claim within 30 days after receiving notice of the change, he satisfied the requirement of the Changes 

Clause by filing his claim within 30 days of the time when it became evident that less than $5,000,000 would be expended on the project. The 

Government has also argued that the plaintiff failed to exhaust his administrative remedy because the theory he relied on before the courtthat he was entitled to an adjustment for a change was not advanced before the ASBCA.

Consideration of the new theory is permitted by the line of Court of Claims cases holding that review of an administrative decision shall not be limited to the record before the agency, but may also be based on evidence presented in a trial de novo. Fehlhaber Corporation v. United States, Volentine and Littleton v. United States, 136 Ct. Cl. 368 (1956). 

supra.

H. L. Yoh Co. v. United States, 288 F. 2d 493

ASBCA No. 5663, 19 June 1961, 61-1 BCA 3083.

The Government later increased the work under the first part and reduced to 500 the number of item descriptions ordered under the second part.
